rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that the Income Tax Department had not complied with the mandatory requirements of section 245 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 before trying to set off Tata Communications Ltd.’s refund against alleged outstanding tax demands. Tata Communications had filed its AY 2019-20 return showing total income of Rs. 638.05 crore, tax liability of Rs. 220.62 crore, tax credits of Rs. 425.84 crore (TDS of Rs. 425.84 crore and TCS of Rs. 25,787), and a refund claim of Rs. 205.21 crore. In an earlier writ petition, the High Court had already directed on 11 January 2021 that the refund with interest be released within two weeks of receipt of the order, and Tata Communications forwarded that order to the Department on 14 January 2021 requesting compliance.

Instead of simply issuing the refund, the CPC issued an intimation under section 143(1) on 17 January 2021 determining a refund with interest of Rs. 227.27 crore, but stated that separate section 245 intimation would be issued to adjust the refund against alleged outstanding demands, including Rs. 153.91 crore for AY 2007-08 and Rs. 138.26 crore for AY 2008-09. Tata Communications challenged this because it had not actually received any valid section 245 notice and therefore had not been given the opportunity to respond before the proposed adjustment. The Court rejected the Department’s position and emphasized that section 245 procedure must be followed before any refund adjustment is made; the authorities could not rely on a technical argument that the earlier High Court order did not bind the ITAT-related matters because the Union of India was not a party there.

For compliance purposes, the ruling is a clear reminder that the tax department cannot unilaterally withhold or set off a refund against disputed or outstanding demands without first issuing proper section 245 notice and obtaining the taxpayer’s response, especially where a court has already directed release of the refund. The judgment also reinforces the expectation that the revenue authorities act as a “model litigant,” meaning they should comply promptly and fairly with judicial directions rather than prolonging refund processing through procedural shortcuts.

rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that a reassessment notice issued under section 148 and a consequential reassessment order under sections 147/144 are invalid if they are issued in the name of a company that had already ceased to exist because of amalgamation. In this case, Tecnovate Esolutions Pvt. Ltd. had amalgamated with Intelnet Global Services Pvt. Ltd. effective 1 April 2010, so by the time the Income Tax Department issued the notice on 30 March 2019 and passed the reassessment order on 31 December 2019, Tecnovate no longer existed as a legal entity. The Court treated this as a jurisdictional defect, not a mere procedural irregularity, and held that it could not be cured by section 292B; the fact that the successor company participated in the reassessment proceedings did not create estoppel or validate the proceedings.

The Court also affirmed that the Bombay High Court had territorial writ jurisdiction even though the challenged notice was issued by the Delhi tax authority, because the assessee was based in Mumbai and part of the cause of action arose there. For compliance purposes, the key practical rule is that any tax notice, reopening, or reassessment must be addressed to the correct surviving legal entity after an amalgamation, merger, or name change, and authorities cannot validly proceed against a non-existent predecessor company. The judgment is for assessment year 2012–13 and was pronounced on 9 April 2021, with publication on 24 April 2021.

However, shares issued to shareholders of an amalgamating company in terms of a scheme of amalgamation does not fall within the sweep of the deeming provisions of s. 56(2) (viib). The so-called excess value of assets vested on amalgamation cannot be notionally termed as premium over the face value for the purposes of the deeming provision (AS-14 issued by the ICAI & CBDT Circular No 3/2012 dated 12-6-2012 referred) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Income from other sources DCIT v. Ozone India Ltd.( IT.A. Nos. 2081/Ahd/2018 dated April 13, 2021 )(AY. 2013-14) 56(2)(viib) : Income from other Sources – Excess over Fair market Value of Shares – Deemed Income – Not applicable – shares issued under a scheme of amalgamation. Facts: The assessee company filed its return of income for AY 2013-14 in question which was subjected to scrutiny assessment. In the course of assessment proceedings, it was gathered by the AO that one M/s. Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. (KEPL) amalgamated with the assessee company under the scheme of amalgamation. The object of amalgamation was stated to achieve better utilization of resources, higher return on capital, economy of scale, optimum utilization of available resources and effective control for better profitability. The scheme of amalgamation of KEPL with assessee company was approved by the Hon’ble Gujarat High Court vide order dated 7-9-2012 effective from 1-4-2012 whereby all the assets and liabilities of M/s. KEPL were vested with the assessee company as per scheme placed before the Hon’ble Court. Hence, on coming into effect of the scheme on 1-4-2012, all the assets except land and all the liabilities of KEPL were taken in the books of assessee at book value and land parcels were taken at revalued price. As stated, the transaction of amalgamation has been accounted under the ‘pooling of interest’ method as prescribed by the Accounting Statndard-AS-14 issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) consequent upon which the difference between net assets of KEPL vested with assessee company and value of shares of assessee company correspondingly issued was accounted for as capital receipts and treated as capital reserve. The excess value of net assets vis-à-vis corresponding value of shares issued towards consideration for amalgamation was thus credited in the books of assessee company as ‘capital reserve’. The AO noted that on the date of amalgamation, the issued and paid up capital of assessee company stood at Rs. 21,00,000/- divided into 2,10,000 equity shares of Rs. 10/- each and that of KEPL stood at Rs. 5,00,000/- divided into 50,000 equity-shares of Rs. 10/- each. Pursuant to scheme of amalgamation, shareholders of KEPL got 300 equity shares of assessee company for each share of KEPL towards consideration for transfer of its assets and liabilities. The AO observed that the amalgamated company i.e. assessee received assets worth Rs.60,26,55,864/- and liabilities worth Rs. 6,05,39,708/- of the amalgamating company i.e. KEPL. Thus, assessee received net assets worth Rs. 54,21,16,156/- against corresponding issue of shares having face value of Rs. 15,00,00,000/- to the shareholders of KEPL. The AO thus observed that assessee has received excess net asset worth Rs. 39,21,16,156/- on account of amalgamation which was credited by it as capital reserve of the amalgamated company. In the opinion of the AO, the excess value of assets so received by assessee company was liable for taxation in the hands of the assessee being excess consideration for issue of its share. HELD: The issue of shares at ‘face value’ by the amalgamated company (assessee) to the shareholders of amalgamating company in pursuance of scheme of amalgamation legally recognized in the Court of Law neither falls with scope & ambit of clause (viib) to section 56(2) of the Act, when tested on the touchstone of objects and purpose of such insertion (Memorandum Explaining Finance Bill, 2012 and CBDT Circular No. 3 of 2012 dated June 12, 2012) i.e. to deem unjustifie
rows.summary:
The ITAT Ahmedabad held in **DCIT v. Ozone India Ltd.** that **section 56(2)(viib)** cannot be applied to tax the alleged “excess” arising when a company issues shares to the shareholders of an amalgamating company under a **court-approved scheme of amalgamation**. The case involved **AY 2013-14**, and the amalgamation of **M/s. Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. (KEPL)** into Ozone India Ltd. had been approved by the **Gujarat High Court on 7 September 2012**, with the scheme made effective from **1 April 2012**; under the scheme, KEPL’s assets and liabilities vested in the assessee company, and the shareholders of KEPL received **300 equity shares of Ozone India Ltd. for each KEPL share**.

The Assessing Officer had treated the transaction as if the company had received shares in excess of fair value, noting that Ozone India Ltd. received assets of **Rs. 60,26,55,864** and liabilities of **Rs. 6,05,39,708**, resulting in net assets of **Rs. 54,21,16,156**, while only **Rs. 15,00,00,000** of equity share face value was issued to KEPL shareholders; the AO therefore viewed the difference of **Rs. 39,21,16,156** as taxable income and argued that the amount credited to **capital reserve** represented excessive consideration for share issuance. The tribunal rejected that approach, emphasizing that the shares were issued at **face value** pursuant to a legally recognized amalgamation and that the difference arising on pooling of interest/accounting treatment under **AS-14** is not the kind of “excess share premium” targeted by section 56(2)(viib).

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that **section 56(2)(viib)** is aimed at taxing **unjustified premium received by private companies on issue of shares without corresponding underlying value**, but it does **not** extend to share issuance under a bona fide **scheme of amalgamation** approved by a court. The tribunal relied on the legislative intent reflected in the **Memorandum explaining the Finance Bill, 2012** and **CBDT Circular No. 3/2012 dated 12 June 2012**, and held that the notional excess of net assets over the face value of shares issued in amalgamation cannot be treated as deemed income under this provision. In practical terms, companies implementing court-approved amalgamations should document the scheme, the court approval, the effective date, the share exchange ratio, and the accounting treatment carefully, because the ruling supports non-taxability of the resulting capital reserve under section 56(2)(viib) where the transaction is genuinely an amalgamation rather than a share-premium raising exercise.

This appeal, filed by the assessee, calls into question the correctness of the order dated th 28 May 2019 passed by the learned CIT(A) in the matter of assessment under section 143(3) read with section 147 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, or the assessment year 2011-12. 2. When this appeal was called out for hearing, it was noticed that the variation in the sale consideration as disclosed by the assessee vis-à-vis the valuation adopted by the Stamp Duty Valuation authority is only 6.55%, and it was put to the learned Departmental Representative as to why the assessee not be allowed the benefit of the third proviso to Section 50C(1) as the variation is much less than the prescribed permissible variation of up to 10%. Learned Departmental Representative pointed out to us that the third proviso to Section ITA No. 4850/Mum/2019 Assessment year: 2011-12 50 C (1) is applicable, by virtue of Finance Act 2018, only with effect from 1st April 2019, and, as for the permissible variation of 10% as against variation of 5% originally enacted the third proviso to Section 50C, this enhancement in permissible variation, by virtue of Finance Act 2020, is effective from 1st April 2021. It was submitted that the insertion of the third proviso to Section 50C could not be treated as retrospective in nature, as there is a specific date, as set out in the related amendment itself, from which the amendment in law is effective. We then requested the learned Departmental Representative to address us on the question as to whether these amendments by the Finance Act, 2018 and Finance Act, 2020 could be said to be retrospective in effect and could be treated as relating back to the time when the legal provision, which this amendment seeks to modify, was introduced. We have heard the learned Departmental Representative on this issue and have also benefited from the detailed submissions made by him, on this point, by way of a written note filed later in the day. It is in this background that we deem it fit and proper to first deal with the implications of insertions of third proviso to Section 50C(1)- as also amendments thereto. We have heard the learned Departmental Representative on this point, perused the material on record, and duly considered facts of the case in the light of the applicable legal position. 4. To adjudicate on this issue, only a few material facts need to be taken note of. The assessee before us is non-resident assessee. During the relevant financial period, she sold her flat, being
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that the anti-avoidance deeming rule in section 50C, which substitutes stamp-duty value for actual sale consideration in computing capital gains on transfer of immovable property, should not be applied where the stamp-duty valuation exceeds the stated consideration by no more than 10%. In this case, the assessee, a non-resident, sold a flat in the relevant financial year for A.Y. 2011-12, and the difference between the declared sale price and the stamp-duty authority’s valuation was 6.55%; the Tribunal therefore found the assessee entitled to the benefit of the third proviso to section 50C(1).

The Revenue argued that the third proviso to section 50C, inserted by the Finance Act 2018, was effective only from 1 April 2019 and that the increase in the tolerance band from 5% to 10%, made by the Finance Act 2020, was effective only from 1 April 2021, so neither could be applied to this earlier year. The Tribunal rejected that narrow prospective reading, holding that these amendments are curative in nature and should relate back to the original insertion of section 50C on 1 April 2003. On that reasoning, if the stamp-duty value is within 10% of the actual consideration, the actual sale consideration must be accepted and section 50C cannot be invoked to substitute the higher stamp-duty value.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that transfers of property where the stamp-duty value exceeds the agreed price by up to 10% should not trigger a section 50C adjustment under this ruling, even for earlier assessment years, according to this ITAT decision. The decision specifically affects capital-gains computations on sale of immovable property by taxpayers subject to section 50C, and it confirms that a 6.55% variance in this case was insufficient to justify an addition.

On 27.03.2015, SBI issued a loan-recall notice to the corporate debtor in its capacity as the lenders’ agent. On 31.03.2015, some of the original lenders of the corporate debtor, namely, India Infrastructure Finance Company Limited, SBI, State Bank of Hyderabad, State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur, State Bank of Patiala, and State Bank of Travancore assigned the debts owed to them by the corporate debtor to the appellant, the Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited. On 20.06.2015, the appellant issued a notice under Section 13(2) of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Securities Interest Act, 2002 [“SARFAESI Act”] on behalf of itself and other consortium lenders to the corporate debtor. On 01.06.2016, the appellant took actual physical possession of the project assets of the corporate debtor under the SARFAESI Act. On 26.12.2018, the appellant filed an application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 [“IBC”] before the National Company Law Tribunal, Calcutta [“NCLT”] for a default amounting to Rs.5997,80,02,973/- from the corporate debtor. As the relevant form indicating the date of default did not indicate any such date, this was made up by the appellant on 08.11.2019 by filing a supplementary affidavit before the NCLT, specifically mentioning the date of default and annexing copies of balance sheets of the corporate debtor, which, according to the appellant, acknowledged periodically the debt that was due. On 19.02.2020, the Section 7 application was admitted by the NCLT, observing that the balance sheets of the corporate debtor, wherein it acknowledged its liability, were signed before the expiry of three years from the date of default, and entries in such balance sheets being acknowledgements of the debt due for the purposes of Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 [“Limitation Act”], the Section 7 application is not barred by limitation. In an appeal filed to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal [“NCLAT”], the corporate debtor relied upon the Full Bench judgment of the NCLAT in V. Padmakumar v. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund, Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 57 of 2020 (decided on 12.03.2020) [“V.Padmakumar”], in which a majority of four members [Justice (Retd
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that the Limitation Act applies to proceedings under section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, because section 238A of the IBC makes the Limitation Act applicable “as far as may be.” In particular, section 18 of the Limitation Act can extend limitation for an insolvency application if there is a written acknowledgment of debt signed by the corporate debtor within the limitation period; the Court expressly rejected the contrary Full Bench view in **V. Padmakumar v. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund**.

The dispute arose from Corporate Power Ltd.’s thermal power project in Jharkhand, where SBI and other lenders had extended facilities; SBI classified the account as an NPA on **31 July 2013**, issued a loan-recall notice on **27 March 2015**, and several lenders assigned their debts to Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited on **31 March 2015**. ARCIL then issued a **Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice on 20 June 2015** and took physical possession of the assets on **1 June 2016**. ARCIL filed its **Section 7 IBC application on 26 December 2018** seeking to recover **Rs. 5,997,80,02,973/-**; because the original form did not clearly state the date of default, it filed a supplementary affidavit on **8 November 2019** identifying the default date and relying on the corporate debtor’s balance sheets as acknowledgments of liability.

The Court confirmed that an entry in the books of account, including a balance sheet, can amount to an acknowledgment of liability under **section 18 of the Limitation Act**, provided it is written and signed by the debtor within the relevant limitation period. It further held that the notes annexed to, or forming part of, the balance sheet and the auditor’s report must be read together with the balance sheet to determine whether there is an acknowledgment. Applying this rule, the Court upheld the NCLT’s admission order dated **19 February 2020**, which had treated the balance-sheet acknowledgments as keeping the Section 7 application within limitation.

For compliance purposes, the key practical consequence is that corporate debtors cannot assume insolvency exposure ends merely because the original default is older than three years; if their signed balance sheets, accompanying notes, or auditor-linked disclosures acknowledge the debt, that may restart/extend limitation under section 18. Lenders and asset reconstruction companies can therefore rely on properly signed financial statements and related disclosures to support limitation in IBC recovery actions, while corporate debtors should treat balance-sheet drafting, approval, and sign-off as legally significant events that may revive debt claims.

The emphasis is on disputed tax and not on disputed income. From a plain reading of the provisions of the DTVSV Act, 2020 and the Rules set out above, it emerges that the Designated Authority would have to issue Form 3 as referred to in section 5(1) specifying the amount payable in accordance with section 3 of the DTVSV Act. [ S.154, 264 Art , 226 ] SadruddinTejani vs. ITO Circle [WP No: 611, 606, 626, 590, 612, 601, 638, 593, 592,596, 625 of 2021]Order dated 09.04.2021 )(Bom) HC ) The Hon’ble High Court directed the Designated Authority to act upon the declaration of the Petitioner in Form 1 as per law within a period of two weeks. Honourable Justice Mr . Sunil .P. Deshmukh & Honourable Justice Mr. Abhay Ahuja Mr .K. Gopal with Ms. Neha Paranjape Advocates for the Petitioners Mr . Sham Valve Advocate for the Respondents Petitioners filed eleven writ petitions challenged the arbitrary and unreasonable action of the Pr. CIT [Designated Authority] of rejecting the declaration filed under section 4(1) of the Direct Tax Vivad Se Vishwas Act, 2020 [DTVSV Act] for the AYs 1988-89 to 1998-99 with the remark as ‘Rejected’ without giving any justification for the same. Facts: The Petitioner is an Individual and had filed return of income for the AY 1987-88 to 1998-99. The assessments for the AY 1987-88 to 1995-96 were reopened u/s 147 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 [hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act’] and the assessment orders were passed u/s 143(3) r.w.s 147 of the Act. For the AYs 1996-97 to 1998-99, the assessments were finalised u/s 143(3) of the Act by raising substantial demand. The additions made in the said assessments were challenged in appeals before CIT(A), who confirmed the action of the AO. Further, the appeal was preferred before ITAT contesting the additions confirmed in the appellate proceedings. The ITAT set aside the order of CIT(A) and directed the AO to grant relief. Pending the appellate proceedings, the TRO initiated the recovery proceedings and the Petitioner to avoid any coercive action handed over the cheques totalling to an amount of Rs.12,43,000/- against the demand raised for the AYs 1986-87 to 1998-99. However, while preparing the challans, the TRO wrongly mentioned only AY 1986-87 in all the challans and adjusted the said amount only against the demand for AY 1986-87 and not for the AYs 1987-88 to 1998-99. After the ITAT order, when the AO gave effect to the same, the demand for all the assessment years had substantially reduced. But, the credit for the taxes recovered was given only in the AY 1987-88, which resulted into refund in theAY 1987-88. Consequently, huge tax and interest demand was created in all the other years i.e AY 1988-1989 to 1998-99. Thus, the Petitioner sought rectification of the same by moving an application u/s 154 of the Act. However, the same was rejected.The Petitioner therefore, moved an application u/s 264 of the Act for all the AYs 1987-88 to 1998-99. Pending the application u/s 264 of the Act, the Petitioner preferred to settle the litigation under DTVSV Act, 2020. On filing the declaration u/s 4(1) of DTVSV Act, 2020, the Petitioner was asked to justify his claim that there is a ‘disputed tax’ when there is no ‘disputed income’ as per the relief sought in the applications filed u/s 264 of the Act. The Petitioner responded to the same and submitted that as per section 2 (1)(a)(v), an assessee whose application is pending on the specified date is an ‘appellant’ for the purpose of DTVSV Act, 2020. The
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that under the Direct Tax Vivad Se Vishwas Act, 2020 (DTVSV Act), the focus is on **“disputed tax,” not “disputed income,”** and therefore the Designated Authority cannot reject a declaration under section 4(1) merely because the taxpayer’s underlying claim is framed as a rectification or revision issue rather than a classic appellate dispute. In this case, the taxpayer had multiple income-tax disputes for AYs 1987-88 through 1998-99, including assessments reopened under section 147 and assessment orders passed under section 143(3) read with section 147, plus finalized assessments under section 143(3) for AYs 1996-97 to 1998-99; after appellate proceedings and a tax recovery sequence involving cheques totaling **Rs. 12,43,000**, the tax credits were allegedly misapplied by the department, creating large tax and interest demands in later years. The taxpayer first sought rectification under section 154, which was rejected, and then filed a revision application under section 264 for AYs 1987-88 to 1998-99; while that revision was pending, he filed a DTVSV declaration, but the Designated Authority marked it simply as **“Rejected”** without giving any reasons.  

The Court found this rejection to be arbitrary and unlawful. It held that, so long as the declarant is an **eligible appellant** and does not fall within the exclusions in **section 4(6)** or the disqualifications in **section 9** of the DTVSV Act, the Designated Authority must process the declaration and issue **Form 3** under section 5(1) stating the amount payable in accordance with section 3 of the Act. The Court specifically ruled that the Designated Authority cannot reject a valid declaration under section 4(1) unless the case is barred by those statutory exceptions; here, the relevant exclusion/disqualification did not apply on the facts presented.  

As a result, the Court **quashed the rejection order** and directed the Designated Authority to **act upon the petitioner’s Form 1 declaration in accordance with law within two weeks** from the date of the order (dated **9 April 2021**). For compliance teams, the key practical point is that under the DTVSV framework, a pending section 264 revision can still support “appellant” status for settlement purposes where the statutory conditions are otherwise met, and tax authorities must follow the Act’s procedure rather than summarily rejecting declarations without justification.

Sinha, Sachit Jolly, Vikramjit Banerjee ASG DATE: April 6, 2021 (Date of pronouncement) DATE: April 7, 2021 (Date of publication) AY: - FILE: Click here to download the file in pdf format CITATION: S. 254(2A) Stay by ITAT: Since the object of the 3rd proviso to s. 254(2A) is the automatic vacation of a stay that has been granted on the completion of 365 days, whether or not the assessee is responsible for the delay caused in hearing the appeal, such object being itself discriminatory, is liable to be struck down as violating Article 14 of the Constitution of India. Also, the said proviso would result in the automatic vacation of a stay upon the expiry of 365 days even if the Appellate Tribunal could not take up the appeal in time for no fault of the assessee. Further, vacation of stay in favour of the revenue would ensue even if the revenue is itself responsible for the delay in hearing the appeal. In this sense, the said proviso is also manifestly arbitrary being a provision which is capricious, irrational and disproportionate so far as the assessee is concerned. Consequently, the third proviso to s. 254(2A) will now be read without the word “even” and the words “is not” after the words “delay in disposing of the appeal”. Any order of stay shall stand vacated after the expiry of the period or periods mentioned in the Section only if the delay in disposing of the appeal is attributable to the assessee. rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that the **third proviso to Section 254(2A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961**, which caused an **automatic vacation of stay after 365 days**, was unconstitutional to the extent it operated **regardless of who caused the delay in disposing of the appeal**. The Court found that this produced an arbitrary and discriminatory result because an assessee could lose stay protection even when the Appellate Tribunal could not hear the matter in time for reasons entirely beyond the assessee’s control, and even where the Revenue itself was responsible for the delay.

As a result, the proviso is to be **read down**: the words **“even”** and **“is not”** are to be removed from the phrase dealing with delay in disposal of the appeal. Practically, this means a stay granted by the ITAT will **not automatically vacate merely because 365 days have passed**; it will vacate only if the **delay in disposing of the appeal is attributable to the assessee**. This ruling directly affects taxpayers and tax litigation teams seeking or maintaining stay of demand before the ITAT, and it limits the Revenue’s ability to insist on vacation of stay solely on the basis of the passage of time. The decision was pronounced on **April 6, 2021** and published on **April 7, 2021**.

Respondent No.2 i.e., Central Board of Direct Taxes issued Circular No.2 of 2020 dated 03.01.2020 empowering the Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions) to condone the delay in filing Form No.10B for a period upto 365 days from the assessment year 2018-19 onwards. However, vide the impugned order dated 19.02.2020, Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions), Mumbai rejected the application of the petitioner for condonation of delay for the assessment year 2018-19. Held: That being the position and having regard to the mandate of section 119(2)(b), we feel that even at this stage, petitioner may approach CBDT under the aforesaid provision seeking a special order to the Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions), Mumbai to condone the delay in filing Form No.10B for the assessment year 2018-19 which isbeyond 365 days and thereafter to deal with the said claim on merit and in accordance with law. Petitioner shall file an application before the CBDT under section 119(2)(b) of the Act to authorize the Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions), Mumbai to condone the delay in filing Form No.10B for the assessment year 2018-19 and to deal with the same on merit in accordance with law; If such application is filed by the petitioner within a period o
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that, under CBDT Circular No. 2/2020 dated 03.01.2020, the Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions) could condone delay in filing Form No. 10B only up to 365 days for AY 2018–19 and onward, and the Commissioner was therefore not wrong in refusing condonation beyond that period in the ordinary course. However, the Court also clarified that section 119(2)(b) of the Income Tax Act still allows the CBDT to pass a special order in an individual case condoning a delay beyond 365 days, so the existence of the general 365-day limit does not bar exceptional relief. The petitioners were charitable trusts running schools and claiming exemption under sections 11 and 12; because they had mistakenly uploaded Form No. 10BB instead of Form No. 10B, the CPC processed the return under section 143(1) and raised a demand of Rs. 1,46,01,489 by denying those exemptions for AY 2018–19. The Court did not itself direct condonation; instead, it directed the petitioners to apply to the CBDT under section 119(2)(b) within three weeks from the date of the judgment, and required the CBDT to decide that application on merits and in accordance with law within four weeks of receipt, with intimation to the petitioners.

From a compliance perspective, the practical takeaway is that charitable institutions seeking section 11/12 benefits must ensure the correct filing of Form No. 10B for the relevant assessment year, because filing the wrong form can trigger denial of exemption and a tax demand even where the error is clerical. For AY 2018–19 and later, a delay in filing Form No. 10B can be condoned by the CIT(E) only up to 365 days under Circular No. 2/2020; delays beyond that require recourse to the CBDT under section 119(2)(b) for a special, case-specific order. The Court expressly found no arbitrariness in the 365-day general limit, so organizations should not assume automatic relief for late filings beyond that period.

rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that CBDT Circular No. 21/2020 dated 4 December 2020, specifically the answer to Question 73, was inconsistent with the Direct Tax Vivad se Vishwas Act, 2020 (“VSVA”) and set it aside/quashed it. The dispute arose because the petitioner, Macrotech Developers Limited, had an appeal pending before the ITAT for AY 2015-16 on additions/disallowances made in assessment under section 143(3), while a separate prosecution had been initiated against it under section 276-C(2) for alleged wilful attempt to evade tax due to delayed payment of the balance self-assessment tax after deducting TDS. CBDT’s clarification said that if prosecution had been initiated for that assessment year, the taxpayer would be ineligible to file a VSVA declaration even for issues in appeal that were unrelated to the prosecution issue.

The Court rejected that interpretation. It held that section 9(a)(ii) of the VSVA excludes eligibility only where prosecution has been instituted in respect of the tax arrear relating to that assessment year on or before the date of filing the declaration; in other words, the prosecution must relate to the same tax arrear sought to be settled under VSVA. A prosecution for a different issue within the same assessment year does not bar settlement of the appealed tax dispute. The Court emphasized that the legislative purpose of the Act was to reduce direct tax litigation, and that CBDT’s broader reading would be illogical, irrational, and contrary to the statute’s text and object.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that tax teams evaluating whether a case is eligible under VSVA cannot disqualify an assessee merely because there is any prosecution pending for the same assessment year. The correct test is whether the prosecution is tied to the specific tax arrear sought to be resolved, and whether it was already instituted by the declaration date. This ruling is particularly relevant where a taxpayer has mixed issues for one AY—some under appeal and others subject to prosecution—because only a prosecution connected to the relevant arrear blocks use of the settlement scheme.

He has to explain with sufficient detail the source of all the deposits in his accounts as well as the corresponding destination of all payments from the accounts. The assessee should be able to show that money has been transferred through banking channels from the bank account of creditors to the bank account of the assessee, the identity of the creditors and that the money paid from the accounts of the assessee has returned to the bank accounts of the creditors. The assessee has to discharge the primary onus of disclosure in this regard (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); (i) There have been numerous cases before the AO, CIT (A), the ITAT and for that matter even before this Court, where the question involved concerns the treatment of ‘accommodation entries’. Basically, what an accommodation entry provider does is to accept cash from an Assessee and arranges to have a cheque issued from his own account or some other account, usually of ‘paper’ or fake entities, to make it appear to be a loan or an investment in share capital. The accommodation entry provider usually charges a commission which is deducted upfront. Where the Assessee is unable to explain the source of such credit in his account – i.e. by demonstrating the identity of the provider of the credit, the creditworthiness of such entity, and the genuineness of the transaction – the credit entry is treated as unexplained and the income is treated under Section 68 of the Act as the income of the Assessee. (ii) In cases where the Assessee discharges the initial onus of establishing the identity and creditworthiness of the credit provider and the genuineness of the transaction, be it one of loan or subscribing to share capital, the onus shifts to the revenue to show the contrary. Where, for instance, an Assessee furnishes the complete details of the entity like its certificate of incorporation, PAN number, income tax returns, bank accounts, names and addresses of the directors and so on, the Courts have insisted on the AO to make a proper enquiry to examine the identity and creditworthiness of such companies and the genuineness of the transactions in question. Where the AO fails to make such an enquiry, a Court might delete the additions made by the AO. (iii) The present case, however, is of a different nature. Here, we are dealing with an Assessee who does not deny that he is an accommodation entry provider. He, in fact, makes no bones of the fact that he either owned or floated ‘paper companies’ only for that purpose. He also does not dispute the fact that he has not been able to explain the source of all the deposits in his accounts or the ultimate destination of all the outgo from his accounts. (iv) The Assessee’s plea that he should be taxed only on a composite ‘peak credit’ is based entirely on principles of accountancy. He questions the logic behind allowing peak credits for some of the credit entries by way of cheques and denying it for the other entries in cash. He also questions the practice of working out separate peak credits for cheque and cash transactions. (v) The premise underlying the concept of peak credit is the squaring up of the deposits in the account with the corresponding payments out of the account to the same person. In Bhaiyalal Shyam Bihari v. CIT (supra), the Allahabad High Court explained that benefit of peak can be given only when the assessee owns up all the cash credits in the books of accounts. It was further held: “For adjudicating upon the plea of peak credit the factual foundation has to be laid by the assessee. He has to own all cash credit entries in the books of account and only thereafter can the question of peak credit be raised.” (vi) In that case, it was held that as the amount of cash credits stood in the names of different persons which the Assessee had all along been claiming to be genuine deposits, withdrawals/payments to different persons during the previous years, the Assessee was, therefore, not entitled to c
rows.summary:
This Delhi High Court decision under Section 68 concerns taxation of accommodation entry operations and the availability of “peak credit” treatment. The Court explained that an accommodation entry provider typically takes cash from an assessee and routes it back through cheques from his own or paper/fake entities’ bank accounts so it appears to be a loan or share-capital investment, usually after deducting commission; if the assessee cannot prove the identity of the credit provider, the provider’s creditworthiness, and the genuineness of the transaction, the credit can be treated as unexplained income under Section 68. Where a regular assessee does furnish full identity and banking details of the lender/investor and the genuineness of the transaction, the burden shifts to the Revenue to investigate further, and failure by the Assessing Officer to conduct proper inquiry can justify deletion of the addition.

In this case, however, the assessee did not dispute that he himself was an accommodation entry provider and that he had floated or owned paper companies for that purpose; he also could not explain the source of all deposits into his accounts or the destination of all outflows. The assessee argued that he should be taxed only on a composite “peak credit” basis and questioned why peak credit should be allowed for cheque entries but denied for cash entries, and why separate peaks should be computed for cash and cheque transactions. The Court rejected that broad approach in principle, noting that peak credit is based on squaring up deposits against corresponding payments to the same person and can be claimed only when the assessee lays a proper factual foundation and owns up all cash credit entries in the books.

The judgment relies on the rule that, for peak-credit treatment, the assessee must make a full and candid disclosure of all facts within his knowledge regarding the credit entries, including the source of every deposit and the destination of every payment, and must be able to show the banking trail from creditors’ accounts to the assessee’s account, the identity of the creditors, and that money paid out from the assessee’s account returned to those creditors’ bank accounts. The practical compliance takeaway is that entities involved in lending, investing, or routing funds through bank accounts must be able to substantiate each credit with documentary proof of identity, source, and genuineness; where the taxpayer is effectively running accommodation-entry transactions, the court indicates that partial or selective peak-credit claims are not available unless the assessee fully admits and explains the entire cycle of transactions. No specific statutory amendment, filing deadline, or monetary threshold is prescribed in the excerpt, but the ruling materially affects how unexplained credits and peak-credit claims are assessed in income-tax scrutiny for AY 1995–96 and similar cases.

The fact that there is close association and dependence between the US company and the Indian companies is irrelevant. The functions performed, assets used and risk assumed, is not a proper and appropriate test to determine whether there is a location PE (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The assessing authority decided that the assessees had a permanent establishment (hereinafter referred to as PE) as they had a fixed place where they carried on their own business in Delhi, and that, consequently, Article 5 of the India U.S. Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement of 1990 (hereinafter referred to as DTAA) was attracted. Consequently, the assessees were liable to pay tax in respect of what they earned from the aforesaid fixed place PE in India. The CIT (Appeals) dismissed the appeals of the assessees holding that Article 5 was attracted, not only because there was a fixed place where the assessees carried on their business, but also because they were “service PEs” and “agency PEs” under Article 5. In an appeal to the ITAT, the ITAT held that the CIT (Appeals) was right in holding that a “fixed place PE” and “service PE” had been made out under Article 5, but said nothing about the “agency PE” as that was not argued by the Revenue before the ITAT. However, the ITAT, on a calculation formula different from that of the CIT (Appeals), arrived at a nil figure of income for all the relevant assessment years. The appeal of the assessees to the High Court proved successful and the High Court in e-Funds IT Solutions/ e-Funds Corp vs. DIT (Delhi High Court), by an elaborate judgment, set aside the findings of all the authorities referred to above, and further dismissed the cross-appeals of the Revenue. On appeal by the Revenue to the Supreme Court HELD dismissing the appeal: (i) The Income Tax Act, in particular Section 90 thereof, does not speak of the concept of a PE. This is a creation only of the DTAA. By virtue of Article 7(1) of the DTAA, the business income of companies which are incorporated in the US will be taxable only in the US, unless it is found that they were PEs in India, in which event their business income, to the extent to which it is attributable to such PEs, would be taxable in India. Article 5 of the DTAA set out hereinabove provides for three distinct types of PEs with which we are concerned in the present case: fixed place of business PE under Articles 5(1) and 5(2)(a) to 5(2)(k); service PE under Article 5(2)(l) and agency PE under Article 5(4). Specific and detailed criteria are set out in the aforesaid provisions in order to fulfill the conditions of these PEs existing in India. The burden of proving the fact that a foreign assessee has a PE in India and must, therefore, suffer tax from the business generated from such PE is initially on the Revenue. With these prefatory remarks, let us analyse whether the respondents can be brought within any of the sub-clauses of Article 5. (ii) Since the Revenue originally relied on fixed place of business PE, this will be tackled first. Under Article 5(1), a PE means a fixed place of business through which the business of an enterprise is wholly or partly carried on. What is a “fixed place of business” is no longer res integra. In Formula One World Championship Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, International Taxation-3, Delhi and others, (2017) SCC Online SC 474, this Court, after setting out Article 5 of the DTAA, held as follows: “32. The principal test, in order to ascertain as to whether an establishment has a fixed place of business or not, is that such physically located premises have to be ‘at the disposal’ of the enterprise. For this purpose, it is not necessary that the premises are owned or even rented by the enterprise. It will be sufficient if the premises are put at the disposal of the enterprise. However, merely giving access to such a place to the enterprise for the purposes of the project would not suffice. The place would be treated as ‘at the disposal’ of the enterprise when t
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **ADIT v. e-Funds IT Solution Inc.** held that the US parent companies were **not taxable in India on business profits** under the India–US DTAA because the Revenue failed to prove that they had a **permanent establishment (PE) in India**. The Court emphasized that the concept of PE is **not found in the Indian Income-tax Act itself**; it arises only under **Article 5 of the DTAA**, and under **Article 7(1)** a US enterprise is taxable in India only to the extent its business profits are attributable to an Indian PE. The Court identified the relevant PE tests as **fixed place PE** under Article 5(1) and 5(2)(a)–(k), **service PE** under Article 5(2)(l), and **agency PE** under Article 5(4), and stated that the **initial burden is on the Revenue** to prove that a foreign enterprise has such a PE in India.

On the facts, the lower authorities had taken different views: the Assessing Officer treated the assessees as having a **fixed place PE in Delhi**; the CIT(A) also held that they had **fixed place, service, and agency PEs**; and the ITAT agreed there was a **fixed place PE and service PE**, though it said nothing on agency PE because that argument was not pressed before it. The Delhi High Court reversed those findings, and the Supreme Court agreed, dismissing the Revenue’s appeal. The Court reiterated that for a **fixed place PE**, the key requirement is that the premises be **“at the disposal” of the foreign enterprise**—mere access to a place for performing a project is not enough, and ownership or lease is not required, but the place must be available for the enterprise’s business in a meaningful way.

A major compliance takeaway is that the Court rejected the idea that **close association, dependence, common group relationships, or outsourced support functions** between the US company and Indian affiliates automatically create a PE. It also rejected the notion that **functions performed, assets used, and risks assumed** by the Indian entities is, by itself, the correct test for determining a location PE. In short, where an Indian affiliate performs support services for a foreign group company, that alone does not establish taxable presence unless the statutory and treaty conditions for a PE are actually met.

The decision is important for multinational groups using Indian subsidiaries for back-office, IT, or support functions: the group should still assess whether any Indian premises are truly **at the disposal** of the foreign entity, whether employees or dependent agents in India satisfy the treaty’s **service PE or agency PE thresholds/conditions**, and whether any portion of profits can properly be attributed to an established PE. No new filing deadline or rate change was announced in this judgment; the ruling is instead a substantive interpretation of **Article 5 and Article 7 of the India–US DTAA** that narrows the circumstances in which foreign companies are exposed to Indian business-income taxation.

No. 349/58/2017-GST Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue Central Board of Excise and Customs *** New Delhi, the 21 st September, 2017 Order No. 03/2017-GST Subject: Extension of time limit for submitting the declaration in FORM GST TRAN-1 under rule 117 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 In exercise of the powers conferred by rule 117 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 read with section 168 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, on the recommendations of the Council, the period for submitting the declaration in FORM GST TRAN-1 is extended till 31 st October, 2017. -sd- (Upender Gupta) Commissioner (GST)
rows.summary:
This Government of India order, issued by the Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, Central Board of Excise and Customs on **21 September 2017** as **Order No. 03/2017-GST**, extends the deadline for filing the transitional credit declaration in **FORM GST TRAN-1** under **rule 117 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017**. The order was made under the authority of **rule 117 read with section 168 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017**, and was issued on the **recommendation of the GST Council**.

The only substantive change is the **extension of the filing period**: taxpayers required to submit **FORM GST TRAN-1** now had time **until 31 October 2017** to do so. This affects entities that were eligible or required to file the TRAN-1 declaration to carry forward transitional GST-related entitlements under the CGST framework. No other procedural changes, thresholds, rates, or filing conditions are stated in this order; the compliance implication is simply that the deadline for submission was moved to the new date.

No. 349/164/2017/-GST Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue Central Board of Excise and Customs GST Policy Wing New Delhi, Dated the 01 st September, 2017 To, The Principal Chief Commissioners/Chief Commissioners/Principal Commissioners/ Commissioners of Central Tax (All) The Principal Director Generals/ Director Generals (All) Subject: System based reconciliation of information furnished in FORM GSTR-1 and FORM GSTR-2 with FORM GSTR-3B - regarding Sections 37, 38 and section 39 of the CGST Act, 2017(hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act’) read with rules 59, 60 and 61 of the CGST Rules, 2017(hereinafter referred to as ‘the Rules’) require every registered person to furnish details of outward supplies made in a month in FORM GSTR-1, details of inward supplies received in a month in FORM GSTR-2 and a return in FORM GSTR-3 by the 10 th , 15 th and 20 th of the next month respectively. Keeping in view that taxpayers may face certain issues in the initial days after the introduction of GST, the GST Council extended the date for filing of FORM GSTR-1 and FORM GSTR-2 for the months of July and August, 2017 and approved the filing of a simplified return in FORM GSTR-3Bfor these two months by the notified due dates after making the due payment of tax. 2. Registered persons opting to utilize transitional credit available under section 140 of the Act read with the rules made there under for discharging the tax liability for the month of July, 2017 were required to file FORM GST TRAN -1 on or before 28 th August,2017. This transitional credit was to be credited to the electronic credit ledger and be available for discharging the tax liability. 3. As per the provisions of sub-rule (5) of rule 61 of the Rules, the return in FORM GSTR-3B was required to be furnished when the due dates for filing of FORM GSTR-1 and FORM GSTR-2 have been extended. After the return in FORM GSTR-3B has been furnished, the process of reconciliation between the information furnished in FORM GSTR- 3B with that furnished in FORM GSTR-1 and FORM GSTR-2 would be carried out in accordance with the provisions of sub-rule (6) of rule 61 of the Rules. 4. The detailed procedure for reconciliation of information furnished in FORM GSTR-3 and FORM GSTR-3B is detailed in succeeding paras. Furnishing of information in FORM GSTR- 1 & FORM GSTR-2: 5. It may be noted that after the registered person has filed his return in FORM GSTR- 3B and the statement of outward supplies in FORM GSTR-1, the inward supplies shall be Page 2 of 4 auto drafted for all registered persons (corresponding recipients of supply) and made available to them in FORM GSTR-2A as per sub-rule (3) of rule 59 of the Rules. FORM GSTR-2A is the exact replica of FORM GSTR-2 containing only those details that are auto- populated from the details furnished in FORM GSTR-1 by the corresponding suppliers. Based on the details communicated in FORM GSTR-2A, the registered person shall prepare the statement of inward supplies in FORM GSTR-2 by:- a. adding, deleting or modifying the invoice level details communicated in FORM GSTR-2A; b. adding information pertaining to details that are required to be furnished in GSTR-2 but are not part of FORM GSTR-2A like details of imports, details of supplies attracting reverse charge that have been received by registered person; c. providing details of supplies received from composition suppliers and exempt, nil-rated & non GST inward supplies; d. providing details of advances paid on inward supplies attracting reverse charge, if any, along with adjustments; e. providing details of reversal of ITC as per the provisions of rules 37, 39, 42 and 43 of the Rules, if any; and f. providing HSN wise summary details of inward supplies. Correction of erroneous details furnished in FORM GSTR-3B: 6. In case the registered person intends to amend any details furnished in FORM GSTR- 3B, it maybe done in the FORM GSTR-1 or FORM GSTR-2, as the case may be. For example, while preparing and furnishing the details in FORM GSTR-1, if the outward supplies have been under reported or excess reported in FORM GSTR-3B, the same maybe correctly reported in the FORM GSTR-1. Similarly, if the details of inward supplies or the eligible ITC have been reported less or more than what they should have been, the same maybe reported correctly in the FORM GSTR-2. This will get reflected in the revised output tax liability or eligible ITC, as the case may be, of the registered person. The details furnished in FORM GSTR-1 and FORM GSTR-2 will be auto-populated and reflected in the return in FORM GSTR-3 for that particular month. Action on the system-based reconciliation: 7. After the registered person has furnished the statement of inward supplies in FORM GSTR-2 by the extended date, the common portal shall auto-draft Part-A of the return in FORM GSTR-3 for the said month based on the information furnished in FORM GSTR-1 and FORM GSTR-2. B
rows.summary:
This circular explains how GST data will be reconciled electronically for the initial return period under GST, specifically between FORM GSTR-1 (outward supplies), FORM GSTR-2 (inward supplies), and FORM GSTR-3B, in light of the GST Council’s extension of the filing deadlines for July and August 2017. It confirms that, under sections 37, 38, and 39 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with rules 59, 60, and 61 of the CGST Rules, registered persons were ordinarily required to file GSTR-1 by the 10th of the next month, GSTR-2 by the 15th, and GSTR-3 by the 20th, but for July and August 2017 the Council allowed filing of a simplified GSTR-3B by the notified due dates after payment of tax. It also notes that taxpayers using transitional input tax credit under section 140 for July 2017 had to file FORM GST TRAN-1 on or before 28 August 2017 so that the credit would be posted to the electronic credit ledger and could be used to pay July tax liability.

On reconciliation mechanics, once a taxpayer files GSTR-3B and then files GSTR-1, the recipient-side inward supply details are auto-drafted in FORM GSTR-2A from supplier-reported GSTR-1 data under rule 59(3). GSTR-2A is described as a replica of GSTR-2 containing only the auto-populated supplier-supplied invoice details, and the registered person must use that draft to prepare GSTR-2 by adding, deleting, or modifying invoice-level information; adding items not captured in GSTR-2A such as imports and reverse charge supplies received; reporting supplies from composition taxpayers and exempt, nil-rated, or non-GST inward supplies; reporting advances paid on reverse-charge inward supplies and related adjustments; reporting ITC reversals under rules 37, 39, 42, and 43; and providing HSN-wise inward supply summaries. In practical compliance terms, this means GSTR-2 is not just a passive acceptance of GSTR-2A but requires active completion and correction of all relevant inward supply and ITC information.

The circular also clarifies how taxpayers should correct errors already made in GSTR-3B: if outward supplies were under-reported or over-reported in GSTR-3B, the corrected figures should be reported in GSTR-1; if inward supplies or eligible ITC were under- or over-reported, the corrected figures should be reported in GSTR-2. Those corrections will flow into the revised output tax liability or eligible input tax credit, as applicable, and the information furnished in GSTR-1 and GSTR-2 will then auto-populate the monthly GSTR-3. Finally, after the taxpayer files GSTR-2 by the extended deadline, the common portal will auto-draft Part A of FORM GSTR-3 for that month based on the information in GSTR-1 and GSTR-2, so compliance teams needed to ensure that the GSTR-1/GSTR-2 data was accurate and reconciled because it directly drives the final return computation.

rows.title:
CGST dated 27.08.2017 is issued to clarify classification and GST
                            rate on lottery
rows.desc: Circular No.06/06/2017-CGST F. No. 354/149/2017-TRU Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue Tax Research Unit ***** New Delhi, the 27 th August, 2017 To, The Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioners/ Principal Commissioner/ Commissioner of Central Tax (All) / Director General of Systems Madam/Sir, Subject: - Issue related to classification and GST rate on lottery tickets – regarding Supply of lottery has been treated as supply of goods under the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017. 2. Accordingly, based on the recommendation of the GST Council, the GST rate for supply of lottery has been notified under relevant GST rate notification relating to CGST/IGST/UTGST/SGST. However, entries in the respective notifications mention classification for lottery as “-”. 3. In this connection, references have been received, inter-alia, stating that due to discrepancy in code allotted, i.e., lottery is defined as goods but code allotted for lottery is under services, the assessees are not able to upload return or deposit tax in time. 4. The matter has been examined. It should be noted that the process of filing return is linked with rate of tax specified for supply. Further, there is complete clarity about rate of tax on lotteries. As mentioned above, in GST, lottery is goods and the classification indicated in relevant notification for lottery is “-”, which means any chapter. 5. That being so, it is clarified that the classification for lottery in respective CGST, IGST, UTGST and SGST notifications shall be ‘Any Chapter’ of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (51 of 1975) and tax on lottery should be paid accordingly at prescribed rates, 12% or 28%, as the case may be. (Ruchi Bisht) Under Secretary (TRU)
rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the GST classification and applicable tax rate for lottery tickets under the CGST regime, effective from 27 August 2017, and is addressed to central tax field officers and systems personnel for implementation. It states that the supply of lottery is treated as a supply of goods under the CGST Act, 2017, but the rate notifications had shown the classification entry for lottery as “-,” which had caused confusion because the allotted code appeared to be under services and some assessees reported difficulty uploading returns or depositing tax on time. The circular resolves this by clarifying that, for purposes of the CGST, IGST, UTGST, and SGST notifications, lottery should be classified under “Any Chapter” of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, meaning the entry is not limited to a particular chapter. 

For compliance purposes, the key obligation is that tax on lottery tickets must be paid at the prescribed GST rate applicable to lotteries, namely 12% or 28% as applicable, and return filing should align with that rate-based classification. The circular indicates there is already “complete clarity” on the rate of tax on lotteries, so the practical change is not the rate itself but the formal classification used in notifications and return/tax-payment systems to prevent filing or payment issues. Entities dealing in lottery supplies should ensure their GST reporting and payment processes reflect this classification correction and continue applying the notified rate corresponding to the lottery transaction.

A large number of communications have been received from the field formations and exporters citing variation in the interpretation of above referred notification and circulars. 2. Therefore, in exercise of powers conferred under section 168 (1) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, for the purpose of uniformity in the implementation of the Act, following issues are being clarified hereunder: a. Eligibility to export under LUT: Notification No. 16/2017 – Central Tax dated 7 th July, 2017 specifies conditions to be fulfilled for export under Letter of Undertaking (LUT) in place of bond. In the extant Central Excise provisions, LUTs were limited to manufacturer exporters only. The intent of the said notification is to liberalize the facility of LUT and extend it to all kind of suppliers. It is hereby clarified that any registered person who has received a minimum foreign inward remittance of 10% of export turnover in the preceding financial year is eligible for availing the facility of LUT provided that the amount received as foreign inward remittance is not less than Page 2 of 5 Rs. one crore. This means that only such exporters are eligible to LUT facilities who have received a remittance of Rs. one crore or 10% of export turnover, whichever is a higher amount, in the previous financial year. A few illustrations are as follows: i. An exporter had a turnover of Rs. 15 crore in the previous financial year. He would be eligible for LUT facility if remittance received against this export is Rs. 1.5 crore or more (10% of export turnover is more than Rs. 1 crore) ii. An exporter had a turnover of Rs. 5 crore in the previous financial year. He would be eligible for LUT facility if remittance received against this export is Rs. 1.0 crore or more (10% of export turnover is less than Rs. 1 crore) iii. An exporter has an export turnover of Rs. 2 crore. He has received Rs. 80 lacs as foreign inward remittances in FY 2016-17 which is 40% of the export turnover. He will not be eligible for LUT facility as remittance received is less than Rs. 1 crore. iv. An exporter has export turnover of Rs. 40crore. He has received Rs. 2 Crores as foreign inward remittances in FY 2016-17 which is 5% of the export turnover. He will not be eligible for LUT facility as remittance received is less than 10% of export turnover, even though it is in excess of Rs. 1 crore. v. An exporter has received Rs. 1 Crore 10 lacs as foreign inward remittances in FY 2016-17 which is 20% of the export turnover. In this scenario, he will be eligible for LUT facility. It may however be noted that a status holder as specified in paragraphs 3.20 and 3.21 of the Foreign Trade Policy 2015-2020 is eligible for LUT facility regardless of whether he satisfies the above conditions. b. Form for LUT: Bonds are furnished on non-judicial stamp paper, while LUTs are generally submitted on the letterhead containing signature and seal of the person or the person authorized in this behalf as provided in said Notification. c. Page 3 of 5 d. The scheme holds no relevance under GST since transaction between a manufacturer and a merchant exporter is in the nature of supply and the same has not been exempted under GST even on submission of LUT/bond. rows.summary:
This circular, issued on 11 August 2017 by the Central Board of Excise and Customs (GST Policy Wing) under section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, clarifies how exporters may furnish a Bond or Letter of Undertaking (LUT) when making exports without payment of integrated tax (IGST), in order to ensure uniform implementation of Notification No. 16/2017-Central Tax and the earlier circulars cited. The main substantive change is that the LUT facility is liberalized beyond manufacturer-exporters and is available to **any registered person** exporting without payment of tax, but only if the person has received foreign inward remittances in the preceding financial year equal to **at least 10% of export turnover and not less than Rs. 1 crore**; in other words, the practical threshold is the **higher of Rs. 1 crore or 10% of export turnover**. The circular gives examples showing that an exporter with Rs. 15 crore turnover needs Rs. 1.5 crore remittance to qualify, an exporter with Rs. 5 crore turnover needs at least Rs. 1 crore, an exporter with Rs. 2 crore turnover and Rs. 80 lakh remittance does **not** qualify, and an exporter with Rs. 40 crore turnover and Rs. 2 crore remittance also does **not** qualify because the remittance is below 10% of turnover; however, a **status holder** under paragraphs 3.20 and 3.21 of the Foreign Trade Policy 2015–2020 is exempt from these conditions and may use LUT regardless.

The circular also specifies the form and processing rules for the documentation: **bonds** are to be furnished on **non-judicial stamp paper**, while **LUTs** are generally to be submitted on the relevant **letterhead** with the signature and seal of the authorized person. It further requires tax authorities to treat the LUT/bond as a **pre-condition for export** and to process and accept it on a priority basis within **three working days** from submission, provided the exporter has submitted complete documents; this timing applies to exports generally, including **supplies to SEZ developers or SEZ units**.

On legacy procedures, the circular states that the earlier **CT-1 form** regime used under central excise for merchant exporter purchases from manufacturers without duty no longer applies under GST. Supplies from a manufacturer to a merchant exporter remain a taxable **supply under GST**, and GST is payable on those transactions even if LUT/bond is furnished; zero-rating applies only to the **actual export supply** under LUT/bond or on payment of IGST, not to the preceding domestic supply chain. Finally, the circular clarifies that **supplies to EOUs are not zero-rated** and there is **no special exemption or dispensation** for them, so such supplies are taxable like any other taxable supply, while EOUs themselves retain zero-rating only for their own exports.

rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the procedure for exporting goods or services without payment of integrated tax under rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017, and applies to exports on or after 1 July 2017. It requires any registered exporter making zero-rated exports without IGST to furnish either a bond or a Letter of Undertaking (LUT) in FORM GST RFD-11; exporters eligible under Notification No. 16/2017-Central Tax dated 1 July 2017 may use an LUT, while all others must furnish a bond. The bond must be on non-judicial stamp paper of the value applicable in the State where it is executed.

A major change is that bonds are to be furnished as a running bond, not a separate bond for each consignment. The bond amount should cover the exporter’s estimated tax liability on exports as self-assessed, and the exporter must ensure the outstanding liability remains within the bond amount; if the bond becomes insufficient for exports yet to be completed, a fresh bond must be furnished to cover the shortfall. Form RFD-11 also contemplates a bank guarantee, but the jurisdictional Commissioner has discretion to set the amount based on the exporter’s track record; if the Commissioner is satisfied with the exporter’s track record, the bond may be accepted without any bank guarantee. Where a bank guarantee is required, it should normally not exceed 15% of the bond amount.

The circular also clarifies that an LUT is valid for 12 months, and if the exporter fails to comply with LUT conditions, the exporter can be required to furnish a bond instead. Existing LUTs and bonds may continue to be used until 31 July 2017, and all exporters must submit the revised-format LUTs/bonds by that date. Bond/LUT acceptance is to be handled by the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner having jurisdiction over the exporter’s principal place of business, although exporters may submit to either Central Tax or State Tax authorities until the administrative mechanism for taxpayer assignment is implemented; if a State Commissioner of State Tax issues a general direction, all such submissions are to be accepted by Central tax officers until that mechanism is in place.

Finally, the circular preserves the then-existing customs sealing procedure for export containers: bottle sealing under Central Excise supervision or otherwise continues until 1 September 2017, and sealing must be done under the supervision of the officer having physical jurisdiction over the place where sealing occurs. A copy of the sealing report must be sent to the Deputy/Assistant Commissioner having jurisdiction over the exporter’s principal place of business. The circular also directs field formations to issue trade notices to publicize these instructions.

rows.summary:
This circular, dated 5 July 2017, allocates “proper officer” powers under the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and related rules for provisions other than registration and composition. It is issued under section 2(91) of the CGST Act read with section 20 of the IGST Act, and subject to section 5(2) of the CGST Act, and it formally designates which central tax officers may exercise specified statutory functions. For compliance purposes, this matters because only the officers listed below are authorized to act for the listed sections/rules, so notices, orders, inspections, seizures, recoveries, assessments, refunds, penalties, and other actions must be handled by the correct rank of officer.

The circular assigns **Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of Central Tax** as proper officers only for **section 67(7)** and the **proviso to section 78**. It assigns **Additional/Joint Commissioners of Central Tax** for **section 67(1), (2), (5), and (9)**; **section 71(1) and (2)**; the **proviso to section 81**; the **proviso to section 129(6)**; and **rules 139(1)–(4)** and **140(2)**. It assigns **Deputy/Assistant Commissioners of Central Tax** for a broad set of operational functions, including refund matters under **section 54(5), (6), (7), and (10)**; scrutiny and inquiries under **section 60(1)–(3), section 63, section 64(1), section 65(6), section 74(1),(2),(3),(5),(6),(7),(9),(10), section 76(2),(3),(6),(8), section 79(1), section 123, section 127, section 129(3), section 130(6),(7), section 142(1)**; and multiple procedural rules covering refunds, recovery, bonds, seizures, inspection, and related processes, including **rules 82(2), 86(4) and its Explanation, 87(11) and Explanation 2, 90(2),(3), 91(2),(3), 92(1)–(5), 93 Explanation, 94, 96(6), 97(2), 98(2)–(5),(7), 100(2), 101(2)–(5), 143, 144(1),(3)–(7), 145(1),(2), 146, 147(1),(2),(3),(5),(6),(7),(8),(10)–(12),(14),(15), 151(1)–(3), 152, 153, 155, and 156**.

The circular further designates **Superintendents of Central Tax** as proper officers for **section 35(6)**, **section 61(1) and (3)**, **section 62(1)**, **section 65(7)**, **section 66(6)**, **section 67(11)**, **section 70(1)**, **section 73(1),(2),(3),(5),(6),(7),(9),(10)**, and **rules 56(6), 99(1)–(3), 132(1), 142(1)–(3),(7), and 150**. It assigns **Inspectors of Central Tax** only for **section 68(3)**, **rule 56(17)**, and **rule 58(5)**. The practical compliance implication is that field-verification, inspection, search-related, adjudication, demand/recovery, and refund activities must be issued or handled by officers at the correct rank for the specific statutory provision, otherwise the action may be procedurally defective.

There is no separate implementation date beyond the circular’s date of **5 July 2017**, so the assignments take effect from issuance. The only operational instruction to the department is to issue **suitable trade notices** to publicize the circular, and any implementation difficulties are to be reported to the Board.

rows.title:
Issues related to furnishing of Bond/ Letter of Undertaking for
                            Exports–Reg
rows.desc: Circular No. 2/2/2017-GST F. No. 349/82/2017-GST Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue Central Board of Excise and Customs GST Policy Wing New Delhi, Dated the 4 th July, 2017 To, The Principal Chief Commissioners/Chief Commissioners/Principal Commissioners/ Commissioners of Central Tax (All) Madam/Sir, Subject: Issues related to furnishing of Bond/ Letter of Undertaking for Exports–Reg. Various communications have been received from the field formations and exporters on the issue of difficulties being faced while supplying the goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax and filing the FORM GST RFD -11 on the common portal (www.gst.gov.in), because of which exports are being held up. 2. Whereas, as per rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017, any registered person availing the option to supply goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax shall furnish, prior to export, a bond or a Letter of Undertaking. This bond or Letter of Undertaking is required to be furnished in FORM GST RFD-11 on the common portal. Further, Circular No. 26/2017- Customs dated 1 st July, 2017 has clarified that the procedure as prescribed under rule 96A of the said rules requires to be followed for the export of goods from 1 st July, 2017. 3. Another issue being raised by various stakeholders is that the Bond/Letter of Undertaking is required to be given through the proper officer which is to be furnished to the jurisdictional Commissioner as per sub-rule (1) of rule 96A of the said rules. Taking cognizance of the fact that a large number of such Bonds/Letter of Undertakings would be required to be filed by the registered exporters who would be located at a distance from the office of the jurisdictional Commissioner, it is understood that the furnishing of such bonds/undertakings before the jurisdictional Commissioner may cause hardship to the exporters. 4. Thus, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (3) of section 5 of the CGST Act, 2017, it is hereby stated that the acceptance of the Bond/Letter of Undertaking required to be furnished by the exporter under rule 96A of the said rules shall be done by the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner. 5. Further, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 168 of the said Act, for the purpose of uniformity in the implementation of the said Act, the Bond/Letter of Undertaking required to be furnished under rule 96A of the said rules may be furnished manually to the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner in the format specified in FORM RFD-11 till the module for furnishing of FORM RFD-11 is available on the common portal. The exporters may download the FORM GST RFD-11 from the website of the Central Board of Excise and Customs (www.cbec.gov.in) and furnish the duly filled form to the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner. 6. The above specified provisions shall be applicable to all applications which have been filed on or after 1 st July, 2017. It is requested that suitable trade notices may be issued to publicize the contents of this circular. 7. Difficulty, if any, in the implementation of the above instructions may please be brought to the notice of the Board. Hindi version would follow. Sd/- (Upender Gupta) Commissioner (GST)
rows.summary:
This circular addresses the temporary procedure for exporters who want to supply goods or services for export without paying integrated tax by furnishing a Bond or Letter of Undertaking (LUT) under rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017. The Board acknowledges that exporters were facing difficulties because FORM GST RFD-11 had to be filed on the GST common portal, and exports were being delayed as a result. It also notes that, under the rules, the bond/LUT must be furnished before export, and that the export procedure under rule 96A applies from 1 July 2017.

The key change is that acceptance of the bond or LUT is not to be handled by the jurisdictional Commissioner as originally contemplated; instead, it must be accepted by the jurisdictional Deputy Commissioner or Assistant Commissioner. Until the RFD-11 module becomes available on the common portal, exporters may furnish the bond/LUT manually in FORM RFD-11 to the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner. Exporters are instructed to download FORM GST RFD-11 from the CBEC website (www.cbec.gov.in), complete it, and submit it to the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner.

These arrangements apply to all applications filed on or after 1 July 2017. The circular instructs field officers to issue suitable trade notices so the trade is informed, and asks that any implementation difficulties be reported to the Board.
