rows.summary:
This circular amends paragraph 7.1 of Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST, as already amended by Circular No. 169/01/2022-GST, to align the adjudication mechanism for DGGI-issued show cause notices with the expanded all-India adjudication powers granted to specified Central Tax officers. The underlying change is that Notification No. 27/2024-Central Tax, dated 25 November 2024, substituted Table V in Notification No. 02/2017-Central Tax to empower additional Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners of Central Tax in specified commissionerates with all-India jurisdiction for adjudicating show cause notices issued by DGGI officers; that notification took effect on 1 December 2024.  

For compliance purposes, the key rule is that DGGI show cause notices involving multiple noticees—whether they have the same PAN or different PANs—or multiple notices on the same issue to multiple noticees with the same PAN, where the principal places of business fall under different Central Tax Commissionerates, may now be adjudicated by one of the empowered Additional/Joint Commissioners of Central Tax regardless of the amount involved in the notice(s). The Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of the specified commissionerates are responsible for allocating adjudication charge for these “DGGI cases” to one or more Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners posted in their commissionerates.  

The circular also clarifies the jurisdictional routing rule: where multiple noticees are involved, the relevant commissionerate for adjudication is determined by the principal place of business of the noticee against whom the highest tax demand is raised in the show cause notice(s). In those cases, the DGGI should make the notices answerable to the concerned Additional/Joint Commissioner of Central Tax in the corresponding adjudicating commissionerate identified in the table.  

The table in paragraph 7.1.1 maps the commissionerate/zone where the highest-demand noticee’s principal place of business is located to the commissionerate whose Additional Commissioner or Joint Commissioner will adjudicate the DGGI notices. The mappings listed are: Ahmedabad Zone → Ahmedabad South; Vadodara Zone → Surat; Bhopal Zone → Bhopal; Nagpur Zone → Nagpur-II; Chandigarh Zone → Chandigarh; Panchkula Zone → Faridabad; Chennai Zone → Chennai South; Bengaluru Zone → Bengaluru East; Thiruvananthapuram Zone → Thiruvananthapuram; Delhi North and Delhi East Commissionerates of Delhi Zone → Delhi North; Delhi West and Delhi South Commissionerates of Delhi Zone → Delhi West; Jaipur Zone → Jaipur; Guwahati Zone → Guwahati; Hyderabad Zone → Rangareddy; and Visakhapatnam (Amaravathi) Zone → Visakhapatnam.  

For a corporate compliance team, the practical effect is on DGGI enforcement proceedings: if your group entities have notices spanning multiple registrations, PANs, or commissionerates, adjudication may be centralized before the specific all-India empowered officer linked to the highest-demand noticee’s jurisdiction under this mapping. No new tax rate, penalty formula, filing deadline, or return obligation is introduced here; the change is procedural/jurisdictional, but it directly affects which officer will hear and decide DGGI show cause notice matters and how the notices should be answered.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST ITC on Immovable Property: Eligibility & Risks
rows.desc: Summary: The article examines the restriction of input tax credit under Section 17(5)(c) and (d) of the CGST Act on works contract services, goods and services used for constructing immovable property, and the statutory exceptions for plant and machinery and construction not undertaken on a taxable person’s own account. It explains the meaning of immovable property through the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act and judicial tests concerning the nature, object, intention, functionality, permanency and marketability of annexation. It also discusses ITC eligibility for movable installations, HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems and other business equipment, and recommends separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery and movable goods to reduce the risk of denial of otherwise eligible credit. Table of Contents▸ Background: Blocked credit under section 17(5)(c/d) Comments: What is immovable property? Movable vs immovable property test-various judgements The principles laid down by the Apex Court in the case of Bharti Airtel Limited v The Commissioner of Central Excise, Pune Eligibility to Input tax credit and immovable property under GST Way ahead and conclusion Possible issues when there is a Single contract for construction of building and supply of machineries, other moveable goods: ACTION POINTS FOR ITC OPTIMISATION: Show all 10 sections Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background: It is being observed that the assesses are receiving notices requiring to reverse/pay back ITC availed pertaining to newly constructed building projects used for business operations[such as factory premise/warehouses], alleging such credit is restricted being of nature of “immovable property”. However in addition to civil works, such projects involve installation of electrical fittings, cabling, STP, security, fire fighting, machines for manufacture of finished goods etc. In this backdrop, paper writer has examined what is “immovable property” and ITC related to immovable property. Upon satisfaction of the basic conditions for availing the Input tax credit specified in Section 16, there comes a non-obstante clause under Section 17(5) that restricts input tax credit availed even if it is used in the course or furtherance of business. One such restriction has been set out under GST by way of the list of blocked credits under Section 17(5)(c)/(d) which is discussed as under. Blocked credit under section 17(5)(c/d) Section 17(5)(c) sets out that credit is blocked on works contract services for construction of an immovable property (other than plant and machinery) except where it is an input service for further supply of works contract service; Construction includes reconstruction, renovation, additions or alterations or repairs to the extent of capitalization, to the said immovable property; Works contract service is material plus labour contract, for building, construction, completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, renovation alteration of immovable property, which involves transfer of property in goods, in course of executing contract. Plant and machinery means apparatus, equipment, and machinery fixed to earth by foundation or structural support that are used for making outward supply of goods or services or both and includes such foundation and structural supports but excludes- (i) land, building or any other civil structures; (ii) telecommunication towers; and (iii) pipelines laid outside the factory premises. The restriction set out denies credit on works contract services used in the construction of immovable property. However, the said restriction has 2 exceptions (which means in the following instances ITC can be taken on the works contract services); When the works contract services, is received by a taxable person for the construction of “plant and machinery” as defined in Explanation to Section 17 of CGST Act [eg: when the contract is material and labour works contract resulting in HVAC plant, being immovable property]. Where the works contract service supplied for the construction of immovable property is an input service for further supply of the works contract. Eg: Developer of mall, selling units in course of construction to buyers of units in mall. Developer gives contract of material plus labour for construction works to a contractor, who executes such works contract. The developer can avail credit to extent related to units sold during construction. Further, Section 17(5)(d) restricts credit on goods or services or both received by a taxable person for construction of an immovable property (other than plant “and”* machinery)[*replaced in place of “plant or machinery” with retrospective effect from 1.7.2017, vide notification no. Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax dated 17.09.2025] on his own account including when such goods or services
rows.summary:
The document explains that GST input tax credit is commonly being disputed for newly constructed business premises such as factories and warehouses, where tax authorities are issuing notices to reverse ITC on the ground that the spending relates to “immovable property.” It states that, although a taxpayer may satisfy the basic ITC conditions under Section 16 of the CGST Act, Section 17(5) is a non-obstante restriction that still blocks credit in specified cases even when the goods or services are used in the course or furtherance of business.

The core restriction discussed is Section 17(5)(c), which blocks ITC on works contract services used for the construction of immovable property other than plant and machinery, except where the works contract service is itself an input service for further supply of works contract service. “Construction” is described broadly to include reconstruction, renovation, additions, alterations, and repairs to the extent they are capitalized, and “works contract service” is described as a material-plus-labour contract involving building, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, renovation, or alteration of immovable property where property in goods is transferred in the course of execution. The article also notes the statutory definition of “plant and machinery” as apparatus, equipment, and machinery fixed to earth by foundation or structural support and used for making outward supplies, including those foundations and structural supports, but expressly excluding land, buildings and other civil structures, telecommunication towers, and pipelines laid outside the factory premises.

The article identifies two important exceptions where ITC on works contract services is still allowed: first, where the taxable person receives works contract services for construction of plant and machinery as defined under the CGST Act; and second, where the works contract service for construction of immovable property is an input service used for further supply of works contract service, such as a real estate developer engaging a contractor for construction work in relation to units sold during construction. It gives the example that credit may be available to the developer to the extent attributable to units sold during construction. 

The document then discusses Section 17(5)(d), which blocks ITC on goods or services received by a taxable person for construction of immovable property other than plant and machinery “on his own account,” including where such goods or services are used in the course or furtherance of business. It specifically notes a retrospective amendment that replaced the phrase “plant or machinery” with “plant and machinery” effective from 1 July 2017, through Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax dated 17 September 2025. 

A significant portion of the article is devoted to distinguishing immovable property from movable property, because that distinction determines whether ITC is blocked. It says the meaning of immovable property must be understood using the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act, and judicial tests focusing on the nature of annexation, the object and intention of attachment, functionality, permanency, and marketability. Based on those principles, the article says movable installations and business equipment such as HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, and fire-safety systems may be eligible for ITC if they are not treated as blocked civil construction or otherwise qualify as movable/plant and machinery rather than immovable property.

From a compliance and documentation standpoint, the document recommends structuring projects through separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery, and movable goods to reduce the risk that otherwise eligible credit will be denied or challenged. The practical compliance message is that businesses constructing or fitting out facilities should not assume all project-related spending is blocked; instead, they should analyze each component against the immovable-property tests and the plant-and-machinery carve-out, because the GST treatment can differ materially depending on how the asset is classified and how the contract is documented.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Vague Fraud Allegation Cannot Invoke GST Section 74: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court: Mere Words “Fraud” or “Suppression of Facts” in a GST Show Cause Notice Are Not Enough to Invoke Section 74 Summary: The Supreme Court in M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. held that merely using the expressions “fraud” or “suppression of facts” in a GST show cause notice is insufficient to invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act. M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam challenged an SCN dated 13.06.2025 concerning FY 2018-19 and raising a demand of Rs.1,52,56,431/-. The company argued that the ordinary limitation period applicable under Section 73 had expired on 28.02.2025 and that the department had mechanically invoked Section 74 without identifying any conduct constituting fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Although the department sought to explain the allegations through its counter affidavit, the Court refused to consider those subsequent explanations. It reiterated that the legal validity of a notice must be determined from the notice itself and that deficiencies affecting jurisdiction cannot be cured through pleadings filed later before a court. The SCN contained only a bland reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” without explaining how fraud was inferred or concealment detected. The use of the expression “or” also indicated uncertainty regarding the allegation being made. Holding that the foundational facts and reasoning supporting the invocation of the extended limitation period must be disclosed in the notice, the Supreme Court set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order as well as the SCN and restrained the department from proceeding further on its basis. Table of Contents▸ Background of the Case What the Company Argued What the Department Argued What the Supreme Court Held Key Takeaways for Practitioners Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background of the Case This case deals with a Show Cause Notice (SCN) issued to a Ratlam-based infrastructure company for the assessment year 2018-19. The department issued the SCN on 13.06.2025 under Section 74 of the CGST Act read with the MPGST Act, raising a total demand of Rs. 1,52,56,431/-. The matter first went before the Madhya Pradesh High Court at Indore, where the company had challenged the SCN by way of a writ petition. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on 29.10.2025, holding that the petitioner should participate in the SCN proceedings and raise its objections before the proper officer, rather than approach the writ court directly. The company then went in appeal before the Supreme Court. What the Company Argued The company’s main argument was about limitation. Under Section 73 of the CGST Act, a notice for a normal (non-fraud) case has to be issued within three years, counted from the due date of filing the annual return. For FY 2018-19, after accounting for various notifications extending the annual return due date, and after excluding the COVID limitation period as directed by the Supreme Court in its Suo Motu Writ Petition (Re: Cognizance for Extension of Limitation), the extended limitation period under Section 73 worked out to 28.02.2025. Since the SCN was issued only on 13.06.2025, it was clearly beyond the three-year period applicable under Section 73. The department could still act within a five-year period, but only if the case genuinely involved fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts, since that is what Section 74 requires. The company’s case was that the SCN merely used the words “fraud or suppression of facts” without explaining what the actual fraud or suppression was. According to the company, such vague and mechanical wording cannot justify invoking the extended five-year period under Section 74. What the Department Argued The department, through its counsel, tried to rely on the counter affidavit filed before the Court to explain and elaborate on the allegations of fraud and suppression, arguing that these details justified proceeding under Section 74. What the Supreme Court Held The Supreme Court refused to look at the counter affidavit for this purpose. It reiterated a well-settled principle: if a notice or order is under challenge for being invalid—for example, for non-application of mind or for not meeting statutory requirements—then whatever is needed to make that notice valid must be found within the notice itself. It cannot be supplied later through a counter affidavit filed in court. Coming to the SCN itself, the Court observed that it only contained a bland statement referring to “fraud or concealment of facts”, without stating how the fraud was inferred or how the concealment was detected. The Court even pointed out that the use of the word “or” between fraud and concealment showed that the department itself was not clear about which allegation actually applied. rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that a GST show cause notice cannot validly invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act merely by using the words “fraud” or “suppression/concealment of facts”; the notice itself must set out the foundational facts showing how fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression was discovered and why the case falls outside the normal Section 73 period. In this case, M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited, Ratlam challenged an SCN dated 13.06.2025 issued under Section 74 of the CGST Act read with the MPGST Act for FY 2018-19, proposing a demand of Rs. 1,52,56,431/-. The company argued that the ordinary limitation period under Section 73 had expired on 28.02.2025 after accounting for return-due-date extensions and the Supreme Court’s COVID limitation exclusions, so the department could proceed only if it genuinely established the fraud-based elements required for Section 74.

The Supreme Court rejected the department’s attempt to cure the notice by relying on explanations later given in its counter affidavit. It reiterated that jurisdictional defects and deficiencies in the notice cannot be repaired after the fact in court; the legal validity of the SCN must stand or fall on the wording and reasons contained in the SCN itself. Here, the notice contained only a vague reference to “fraud or concealment of facts,” without explaining the basis for that allegation, and the use of “or” suggested uncertainty as to which statutory ground was actually being invoked. On that basis, the Court set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order dated 29.10.2025, quashed the SCN, and restrained the department from proceeding further on the basis of that notice.

For compliance teams, the practical point is that a Section 74 notice should be scrutinized for specific, articulated facts showing fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression; a bare label is not enough to sustain the extended five-year exposure. If the department issues a fraud-based notice after the normal limitation period, the notice must itself explain the conduct alleged and the reasoning for invoking Section 74, because later pleadings will not rescue a vague or mechanically drafted SCN. This decision is particularly relevant for companies facing late-issued GST demands for historical periods, because it confirms that limitation and jurisdiction objections can be fatal where the notice fails to plead the statutory basis with sufficient specificity.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Restores Section 129 Penalty for Iron Scrap Moved Without E-Way Bill
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12632 Case Name Santosh Mani Mishra Vs PROP (GSTAT Lucknow) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GST Appellate Authority Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Santosh Mani Mishra Vs PROP (GSTAT Lucknow) Summary: The GST Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow Bench considered an appeal arising from detention of goods transported without an E-Way Bill and examined whether the surrounding circumstances established an intention to evade tax. The source order contains a party-description inconsistency: its cause title identifies Santosh Mani Mishra as the appellant and the Islam Trading Company-related party as respondent, while paragraph 1 describes the appellant as Revenue and paragraph 1.2 refers to M/s Islam Trading Company as the appellant. The proceedings arose from transportation of 132.90 cubic feet of iron goods by M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly, under Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018. The vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018. The E-Way Bill was not available with the driver at the time of interception. Tax of Rs. 47,844/- and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844/- were imposed under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017. The first appellate authority, however, set aside the tax and penalty by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018. The Department contended that transportation without the mandatory E-Way Bill violated Rule 138 of the GST Rules and that subsequent production of the tax invoice, books of account, GST returns and proof of tax payment could not retrospectively cure the statutory violation. It further argued that the interception of the vehicle, nature of the goods, route and subsequent production of documents cumulatively indicated an intention to evade tax. The authorised representative also submitted that an E-Way Bill is generated online whereas the tax invoice is manually issued, leaving scope for subsequent manipulation of books of account. No one appeared for the respondent despite adequate opportunity. The Tribunal identified the central issue as whether the alleged intention to evade tax was merely a presumption despite the availability of relevant documents, or whether the facts and circumstances established such intention when the goods were transported without an E-Way Bill. The Tribunal examined the judicial precedents relied upon by the First Appellate Authority, including Sarva Shri Singh Tire v. State of U.P., Shri KL Industries v. State of U.P., Harley Foods Products Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 others, M/s Modern Traders v. State of UP and 2 others, and M/s Rai Prexim India Private Limited v. State of Kerala. The Tribunal distinguished those decisions on facts. It emphasised that generation of the E-Way Bill is an online process, whereas the tax invoice is manually issued by the taxpayer. In its view, non-generation of the E-Way Bill left scope for subsequent manipulation of books of account and therefore constituted substantive non-compliance which, in the circumstances of the case, established an intention to evade tax. The Tribunal also noted that the goods were loaded at Baheri, Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh and were shown for delivery at Kichha, Uttarakhand, approximately 25 km away. It considered this circumstance, along with the absence of the E-Way Bill, interception and nature of the goods, as further supporting the finding of intent to evade tax. The Tribunal additionally relied upon its own order dated 20.08.2026 in Appeal No. APL/79/LKC/2026, Om Prakash v. M/s Islam Trading Company, involving the same nature of goods, the same destination and a similar modus operandi in which the E-Way Bill was produced only after interception by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly. The Tribunal treated the repetition of the same lapse as significant in determining that the conduct could not be regarded merely as a procedural or technical lapse. Accordingly, the Tribunal held that the First Appellate Authority erred in interfering with the order passed under Section 129(3). The appeal filed by the Appellant (Revenue) was allowed. The first appellate authority’s order dated 24.09.2021 was set aside, and the order dated 09.03.2018 passed by the Proper Officer under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017 imposing tax and penalty was restored. The Tribunal’s reasoning turns on the cumulative circumstances and the repeated post-interception production of the E-Way Bill, rather than treating the absence of the E-Way Bill as an isolated technical lapse. Cases Discussed Sarv Shri Harley Foods Products Pvt Ltd. V. State of U.P. & 3 others (2018) 37 VLI-UP M/s Modern Traders Vs. State of UP and 2 others 2018 NTN(Vol-67)-71 M/s Rai Prexim India Private Limited Vs. State of Kerala 2019 NTN (Vol.70)-29 FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF GSTAT 1.This appe
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow Bench held that moving goods without carrying an E-Way Bill can justify detention and penalty under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017 where the surrounding facts show an intention to evade tax, and it restored the original tax-and-penalty order. The case concerned 132.90 cubic feet of iron goods transported by M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly under Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018; the vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018, and the driver did not have the E-Way Bill at the time of interception. The Proper Officer had imposed tax of Rs. 47,844 and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844 under Section 129(3), but the First Appellate Authority later set that order aside by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018.

On appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal disagreed with the appellate authority and reinstated the detention order dated 09.03.2018. It accepted the Department’s position that the absence of the E-Way Bill was a substantive violation of Rule 138 of the GST Rules, and that later production of the invoice, books of account, GST returns, and tax-payment evidence did not cure the defect after interception. The Tribunal emphasized that E-Way Bills are generated online while tax invoices are manually issued, so the failure to generate and produce the E-Way Bill before interception created room for post-facto manipulation and supported a finding of tax evasion intent. It also relied on the fact that the goods were moving only about 25 km from Baheri, Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh to Kichha, Uttarakhand, and viewed that short route, the nature of the goods, and the interception circumstances as additional indicators of evasion.

The Tribunal distinguished the cases cited by the First Appellate Authority, including Sarva Shri Singh Tire, Shri KL Industries, Harley Foods Products, Modern Traders, and Rai Prexim India, and also noted its own recent decision in Om Prakash v. M/s Islam Trading Company, Appeal No. APL/79/LKC/2026 dated 20.08.2026, involving the same type of goods, the same destination, and a similar pattern where the E-Way Bill was produced only after interception. The Tribunal treated the repeated post-interception production of the E-Way Bill as significant and rejected the view that this was merely a technical or procedural lapse. For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that transporting goods without an E-Way Bill exposes the consignee/consignor and transporter to detention and Section 129 tax-plus-penalty exposure, and subsequent document production after interception may not avoid liability if the authorities infer evasion from the facts.

rows.summary:
This Tribunal order addresses whether real-estate developers can be taxed under “construction of complex/commercial construction” service, or whether post-1.6.2007 their activity falls under “works contract service,” with important consequences for tax base, composition-scheme eligibility, and penalties. The order covers three appeals: Real Value Promoters Pvt. Ltd. (commercial and residential projects), Ceebros Property Development, and Prime Developers; all were initially subjected to service tax demands by the department for amounts collected from both buyers and landowners in development arrangements.

For Real Value Promoters, the department issued one show cause notice dated 23.10.2008 covering the period 1.4.2007 to 31.3.2008 and proposing a total service tax demand of Rs. 2,06,20,252/-, broken down as Rs. 34,38,337/- for the commercial project PRGT (services to buyers), Rs. 1,07,33,392/- for residential projects The Lords, Sananda Brindavan, Sujeet, and Surya Skanda (services to buyers), Rs. 48,98,579/- for commercial project PRGT Amarasri (services to landowners), and Rs. 15,49,944/- for residential project Sai Brindavan (services to landowners). The department also issued another notice dated 20.10.2009 for the period 1.4.2008 to 31.3.2008 proposing Rs. 1,05,99,978/- on PRGT, again on the basis that the developer was liable under construction service categories. The department’s theory was not only that the activity was taxable, but also that after 1.6.2007 the appellants could not validly pay tax under the works contract composition scheme because, in the department’s view, these were not works contracts and the appellants had not exercised the required option/intimation to the department under the Works Contract (Composition Scheme for Payment of Service Tax) Rules, 2007.

The common adjudication order dated 16.8.2010 confirmed the proposed demands with interest, imposed a penalty of Rs. 2,06,20,252/- under section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994, and also imposed penalties under sections 76 and 77. Prime Developers’ case involved a joint development agreement dated 17.1.2005 with Prime Textiles Ltd. for a residential complex of 432 apartments; units were sold under separate agreements to buyers. A show cause notice dated 10.8.2009 covered January 2005 to August 2008 and resulted in a confirmed demand of Rs. 1,16,42,448/-, with the adjudicating authority taking the view that for the period prior to 1.6.2007 the activity was taxable under construction of complex service, not works contract.

A key compliance point from the dispute is that the department attempted to tax both the buyer-facing construction receipts and the amounts attributable to landowners under development/joint-development structures, while also challenging the availability of works contract composition treatment from 1.6.2007 onward absent a formal option/intimation. The Tribunal’s order is therefore material for developers and real-estate companies using separate sale agreements and joint development arrangements: it directly concerns how such contracts are characterized for service tax purposes, whether tax should be paid under works contract composition after 1.6.2007, and whether penalties can be sustained where the classification is disputed.

rows.summary:
The Allahabad High Court granted bail to Waseem Akram @ Monu in Case Crime No. 539 of 2025, arising from allegations of GST fraud involving a purportedly non-existent firm, M/s Super Power Industries. The criminal case was registered at Police Station Brahampuri, District Meerut, under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, and 120-B of the IPC, and the court noted that the FIR itself did not name the applicant; his involvement surfaced later through the statement of Sakeel Khan. The applicant argued that he had no connection with the firm, was not its owner, was not a beneficiary of the alleged fraud, and that the firm had already been declared bogus in November 2021, while the FIR was lodged much later on 04.11.2025. He also stated that he had no other criminal history and had been in jail since 05.04.2026, and the court accepted that prolonged trial delay was likely given the heavy pendency of cases.

The Court allowed bail without expressing any view on the merits of the allegations. It directed release on execution of a personal bond and furnishing two sureties of the like amount to the satisfaction of the trial court. The bail is conditional: the applicant must not tamper with evidence, must not pressurize or intimidate prosecution witnesses, must appear before the trial court on every date fixed unless exempted, must not commit a similar offence, and must not induce, threaten, or promise any person acquainted with the facts to prevent them from disclosing those facts to the court or police. The trial court was instructed to verify the identity, status, and residence proof of the sureties before accepting them, and it was given liberty to cancel bail if any condition is breached. The High Court also clarified that its observations are only for deciding the bail request and will not affect the trial on the merits.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Holds Municipal Hoarding Space Taxable, But Quashes Extended-Period Service Tax Demand
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12629 Case Name Chief Municipal Officer Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Chief Municipal Officer Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Delhi) Summary: The CESTAT New Delhi considered whether a municipality was liable to service tax on two activities: providing space for display of advertisements through hoardings and renting/licensing its immovable properties, including vacant land, to agencies, persons and traders. The disputed period was 2009-10 to 2014-15, covering both the pre-negative-list and post-negative-list service tax regimes. The appellant had received Rs. 3,06,738/- from hoarding rent during April 2009 to June 2012 and Rs. 3,39,22,974/- as rent from various immovable properties during April 2009 to July 2014. The Department proposed service tax of Rs. 39,22,945/- together with interest, penalties and late fee for non-filing of ST-3 returns. The demand was confirmed by the adjudicating authority and Commissioner (Appeals), leading to the appeal before the Tribunal. The appellant contended that the expression “Renting of Immovable Property Service” had been incorrectly interpreted. It argued, relying particularly on Cuddalore Municipality Vs Joint Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, that the expression “any other person” meant a person other than the owner. It also argued that vacant land was excluded from the relevant definition and that arrears of rent had been taxed at an incorrect service tax rate. On advertisement receipts, the appellant maintained that it merely collected statutory licence fees under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 for allotting land on which advertisers erected hoardings, rather than selling advertising space. It further challenged penalties on the ground that there was no intention to evade tax. For the period before 01.07.2012, the Tribunal held that providing space for hoardings was covered by section 65(105)(zzzm) of the Finance Act, 1994. Since the statutory explanation expressly included providing space for display, advertising or showcasing products or services on billboards and public places, the demand under “Sale of Space or Time for Advertisement Services” was upheld for the period up to 01.07.2012. The Tribunal also rejected the appellant’s interpretation of “Renting of Immovable Property” for the pre-01.07.2012 period. It examined the definitions under sections 65(90a) and 65(105)(zzzz) and held that the vacant land supplied for market places was being used for commercial purposes and did not fall within the claimed exclusion. The Tribunal further held that “any other person” in the taxable-service provision meant any person other than the recipient and did not require the service provider to be a person other than the owner. For the period after 01.07.2012, the Tribunal examined section 65B(44), which broadly defined “service”, together with section 66D containing the negative list. The relevant negative-list provision excluded specified services by Government or local authorities but carved out services provided to business entities. The Tribunal found that the appellant had rented immovable property, including vacant land, for organising “Flee Markets” for consideration. Regardless of whether the receipts were described as licence fees, the activity was undertaken for commerce and provided to traders/business entities. In reaching this conclusion, the Tribunal relied upon the Supreme Court decision in Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti, New Mandi Yard, Alwar, which distinguishes mandatory statutory/sovereign functions from activities undertaken for consideration. The Tribunal applied that distinction and found the appellant’s commercial renting activity taxable. The Department’s reliance on that decision was therefore accepted in substance. On limitation, however, the Tribunal granted substantial relief. It observed that the appellant was a government authority and that there was no evidence establishing any positive act of suppression with intent to evade service tax. Referring to Anand Nishikawa Co. Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Excise, Meerut, the Tribunal held that mere failure to declare or pay tax does not by itself constitute wilful suppression and that a positive act is required for invoking the extended period. Accordingly, the Tribunal held that both activities were taxable and that service tax was payable on the value received for those services. However, the extended-period demand was set aside. The demand for the normal period was confirmed with proportionate reduction in the penalty. The appeal was therefore partly allowed. Cases Discussed Cuddalore Municipality Vs Joint Commissioner of GST & Central Excise — 2021 (55) G.
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Delhi held that a municipality’s activities relating to hoarding space and certain immovable-property rentals could fall within service tax, but it materially limited the Department’s recovery by quashing the extended-period demand. For the period **before 1 July 2012**, the Tribunal found that granting space for hoardings was taxable under **section 65(105)(zzzm) of the Finance Act, 1994** as “sale of space or time for advertisement,” because the statutory explanation expressly covered providing space for display, advertising, or showcasing products/services on billboards and public places. It therefore upheld taxability on the hoarding receipts of **Rs. 3,06,738** received from **April 2009 to June 2012**.

On the property-rental issue, the Tribunal rejected the municipality’s argument that the phrase **“any other person”** in the renting provision excluded the owner from being the service provider, and it also rejected the claim that **vacant land** used for market places was outside the taxable definition. For the **pre-1 July 2012** regime, it held under **sections 65(90a) and 65(105)(zzzz)** that the land/property was being put to **commercial use**, so rent/license income from those immovable properties was taxable. The Tribunal also noted the municipality’s contention that some arrears had been taxed at an incorrect rate, though the summary outcome is that the activity was still held taxable.

For the period **from 1 July 2012 onward**, the Tribunal applied the negative-list regime under **section 65B(44)** and **section 66D** and held that the municipality’s renting/licensing of immovable property, including vacant land used for **“Flee Markets,”** remained taxable because it was provided **for consideration to traders/business entities** and was a commercial activity rather than a sovereign/statutory function. The Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court’s distinction in **Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti, New Mandi Yard, Alwar** between mandatory governmental functions and activities undertaken for consideration, and concluded that the municipality’s conduct fell on the taxable side of that line.

The Department had demanded **Rs. 39,22,945** in service tax, along with **interest, penalties, and late fee for non-filing of ST-3 returns**, for the dispute period **2009-10 to 2014-15**. The Tribunal upheld taxability on the substantive activities, but on limitation it found no evidence of a **positive act of suppression with intent to evade tax**, emphasizing that mere non-payment or non-declaration is not enough to invoke the **extended limitation period**. As a result, the **extended-period demand was set aside**, the demand was sustained only for the **normal period**, and the penalty was **reduced proportionately**; the appeal was therefore **partly allowed**.

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court dealt with a writ petition by Sankaran Mekala relating to AY 2015-16, where the petitioner challenged a demand communication/order dated 16.07.2026 arising from earlier proceedings under sections 147, 271(1)(b), and 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The background was that in an earlier writ petition (W.P. No. 1242 of 2026), the Court had on 09.02.2026 directed the petitioner to file the return of income for AY 2015-16 and to respond to the section 148 notice; the petitioner stated that she complied in part by depositing Rs. 5 lakhs, but could not upload the return because of technical problems on the income-tax e-filing portal. In support, she produced proof of the Rs. 5 lakh deposit, other documents she had filed, and a screenshot showing the portal upload failure.

The Court accepted that the portal issue prevented compliance and held that, in the interests of justice, the petitioner should be given an opportunity to file the return. It therefore set aside the impugned demand notice dated 16.07.2026 and directed the Revenue to take necessary steps to provide access to the income-tax portal so the petitioner could upload the return for AY 2015-16. The petitioner was directed to file the return within three weeks from receipt of the order, and the Assessing Officer/Rsvenue was directed to complete the assessment by issuing an assessment order within six weeks from receipt of the return, after giving the petitioner a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The connected miscellaneous petitions were closed, and there was no order as to costs.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the Court treated documented technical inability to upload a return on the tax portal as a valid basis to preserve filing rights and require the department to facilitate portal access, rather than enforce the demand notice immediately. The decision reinforces that where a taxpayer can substantiate attempted compliance—here via a screenshot and proof of partial compliance such as the Rs. 5 lakh deposit—the authorities may be compelled to reopen the practical ability to file and must then proceed quickly with assessment within the court-imposed timelines.

Chessman Impex Private Limited Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Chennai) Summary: CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017, holding that the customs duty demand of Rs.2,16,93,068/- against Chessman Impex Pvt. Ltd., consequential interest, penalties of Rs.20 lakh each under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962 and penalties imposed on the co-appellants could not be sustained in the absence of reliable and corroborative evidence. Chessman Impex had obtained a DEEC licence under the EXIM Policy 1997-2002 permitting duty-free import of 5350 MTs of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against export obligation of 5000 MTs of non-alloy steel bars and rods. Revenue alleged that the imported scrap was diverted in the domestic market and maize was fraudulently exported to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export instead of the stipulated steel products. The Tribunal found material support for the appellant’s case in the special permission for exports through Ghojadanga LCS, Customs examination of export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, DRI Chennai’s confirmation regarding manufacture by Goyal Ispat Ltd., the foreign buyer’s permission for segregation and export of unprocessed scrap, undisputed realisation of export proceeds and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority. Significantly, the CBI had investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and filed a final report recording that the available evidence indicated that the disputed exports to Bangladesh had actually taken place; the report was accepted by the competent Criminal Court. The adjudicating authority had not identified additional material or specific evidence not considered by the CBI. The Tribunal further held that Revenue produced no independent evidence of buyers of the allegedly diverted material, cash trail, procurement or transportation of maize, domestic disposal or seizure of offending goods. Mere “grey areas” or suspicion could not substitute cogent evidence necessary for penal action under Sections 112 and 114 of the Customs Act. The adjudicating authority had also travelled beyond the Show Cause Notice by introducing issues concerning classification of CTD bars, availability of 16 mm bars and amendment of the DEEC licence. The Tribunal found material discrepancies in the statements relied upon by Revenue, some of which had been retracted, and observed that statements recorded under Section 108 had been relied upon without examining the statutory requirements of Section 138B. Since the allegations against the principal noticee failed for want of reliable and corroborative evidence, allegations of connivance or abetment and consequential penalties against the co-appellants also could not survive. All appeals were accordingly allowed with consequential relief and the impugned Order-in-Original was set aside. Cases Discussed Commissioner of Customs, Trichy v. rows.summary:
CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals filed by Chessman Impex Private Limited and co-appellants and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017 in full. The Customs demand of Rs. 2,16,93,068, along with consequential interest, and the penalties of Rs. 20 lakh each imposed on Chessman Impex under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, as well as the penalties imposed on the co-noticees, were all quashed because the Tribunal found the Revenue’s case was not supported by reliable, corroborative evidence.

The underlying allegation was that Chessman Impex had obtained a DEEC licence under the EXIM Policy 1997-2002 allowing duty-free import of 5,350 MT of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against an export obligation of 5,000 MT of non-alloy steel bars and rods, but instead diverted the imported goods into the domestic market and fraudulently exported maize to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export. The Tribunal rejected this theory, emphasizing that the record actually contained supporting material for the appellant: special permission for exports through Ghojadanga LCS, Customs examination of export consignments, Central Excise certification on AR-4s/ARE-1s, DRI Chennai confirmation that the goods were manufactured by Goyal Ispat Ltd., the foreign buyer’s permission for segregation and export of unprocessed scrap, undisputed realization of export proceeds, and an Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority.

A particularly important point for compliance purposes is that the CBI had already investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and filed a final report stating that the available evidence indicated the exports to Bangladesh had actually taken place, and that report had been accepted by the criminal court. The Tribunal noted that the adjudicating authority did not produce any additional material beyond what CBI had already considered, and also failed to show independent evidence such as identified domestic buyers of the allegedly diverted material, a cash trail, procurement or transport evidence for maize, seizure of offending goods, or proof of domestic disposal. The Tribunal held that suspicion, inconsistencies, or “grey areas” cannot replace the cogent evidence required for penal action under Sections 112 and 114 of the Customs Act.

The Tribunal also held that the adjudicating authority had gone beyond the Show Cause Notice by introducing new issues, including the classification of CTD bars, availability of 16 mm bars, and amendment of the DEEC licence, which could not be used to sustain the demand. It found material discrepancies in the statements relied on by Revenue, noted that some had been retracted, and observed that statements recorded under Section 108 were relied upon without proper compliance with Section 138B. Since the allegations against the principal noticee failed, the related allegations of connivance or abetment against the co-appellants also failed, and all appeals were allowed with consequential relief.

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court disposed of three connected writ petitions filed by Reckitt Benckiser (India) Private Limited concerning GST matters for the tax period 2019–2020. One petition challenged a show cause notice in Form GST DRC-01 dated 31.05.2024, another challenged an order/reply dated 29.05.2024, and the third challenged Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023 and the related State/Government orders issued under Section 168A of the GST laws that extended limitation periods. The limitation-extension issue was the key compliance point in the case, but the Court did not rule on the substantive validity of that notification or on the underlying tax dispute.

At admission, the Court had granted interim protection on 13.08.2024. After that, the jurisdictional State Tax Officer submitted a detailed report dated 27.01.2026, and the Court recorded that the report’s conclusion prima facie supported the petitioner’s position. Based on that report and the subsequent developments, the petitioner stated that no further adjudication was necessary for the DRC-01 challenge, and the Court accepted that position.

As a result, the Court held that the challenge in W.P. No. 20657 of 2024 no longer required adjudication, and the challenges in W.P. Nos. 20652 and 20655 of 2024 had become academic. The Court therefore closed W.P. Nos. 20652 and 20655 of 2024 and disposed of W.P. No. 20657 of 2024. No costs were awarded, and the connected miscellaneous petitions were also closed.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is procedural rather than substantive: this order does not create a new GST rule or invalidate the limitation-extension notifications on the merits, but it shows that limitation-related GST challenges can be rendered moot by later departmental developments and officer reports. Entities facing GST notices for older tax periods, especially where limitation extension under Section 168A and Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax is involved, should note the dates involved here—31.03.2023 for the notification, 29.05.2024 for the order/reply, 31.05.2024 for the DRC-01, 13.08.2024 for interim protection, and 27.01.2026 for the officer’s report—because the court treated those later developments as decisive in closing the litigation.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd Vs State of Rajasthan (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd and set aside the appellate order dated 27.02.2026, which had rejected the petitioner’s GST appeal on limitation. The Court directed the Appellate Authority to consider and decide the appeal on its own merits, subject to the petitioner firm depositing late fees, penalty and other statutory deposits as admissible. The petitioner had sought quashing of the order dated 07.02.2024 and restoration of its GST registration, besides setting aside the appellate order dated 27.02.2026 and a direction for adjudication of the appeal on merits. The petitioner relied principally on the Rajasthan High Court’s Division Bench judgment in M/s. Pratap Power Spares Vs. Union of India & Ors., D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 9882/2024, decided on 28.07.2026. In that case, the Court had condoned a 99-day delay after granting relaxation of 120 days under Section 107 of the CGST Act and directed the Appellate Authority to entertain the appeal and adjudicate it on merits if filed within 30 days. The petitioner also relied upon M/s. Molana Construction Company Vs. Central Goods and Service Tax Department & Ors., Man Singh Tanwar v. Commissioner, Central Goods and Services Tax Department & Ors., and the two decisions in RPC PSIPL JV Vs. State of Rajasthan & Ors. The petitioner additionally referred to M/s. Kakar Automobiles Vs. Union of India & Ors. The respondents relied upon Sharwan Singh Devda Vs. The Union of India & Ors., D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 15910/2026. The relevant passage recognised that there was no absolute bar on invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226/227 after expiry of the statutory appellate period, but cautioned that such jurisdiction could not ordinarily be exercised to circumvent the statutory limitation scheme. It stated that intervention may be justified in exceptional circumstances, including complete disregard of natural justice or clearly established inherent lack of jurisdiction. The petitioner submitted that the medical circumstances in the present matter constituted such exceptional circumstances and that the judgments relied upon were consistent in permitting consideration of delayed GST appeals where circumstances beyond the taxpayer’s control had prevented timely filing. The High Court accepted this submission. It held that although the Appellate Authority is bound by the statutory limitation provisions under Section 107 of the RGST/CGST Act, the medical reasons which resulted in the petitioner not submitting the appeal within the stipulated time were beyond the petitioner’s control. The Court further found that non-adjudication of the appeal on merits would cause grave injury and prejudice to the petitioner. Consequently, the Court exercised its writ jurisdiction, set aside the appellate order dated 27.02.2026 and directed the Appellate Authority to consider and decide the petitioner’s appeal on merits in accordance with law. The relief was made subject to the petitioner firm depositing late fees, penalty and other statutory deposits required for entertaining the appeal, as admissible. All pending applications were also disposed of. Cases Discussed M/s. Pratap Power Spares Vs. Union of India & Ors. — D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 9882/2024, decided on 28.07.2026. M/s. rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST appeal should not be rejected solely as time-barred where the delay was caused by medical circumstances beyond the taxpayer’s control. In this case, Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd. challenged the rejection of its GST appeal by the appellate authority’s order dated 27.02.2026, and also sought quashing of the underlying order dated 07.02.2024 as well as restoration of its GST registration. The Court set aside the appellate authority’s limitation-based rejection and directed that the appeal be entertained and decided on its merits in accordance with law.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Court recognized that although appellate authorities remain bound by the limitation rules under Section 107 of the Rajasthan/CGST GST framework, writ jurisdiction under Articles 226/227 may be used in exceptional cases where strict adherence to limitation would cause grave prejudice and the delay arose from reasons outside the taxpayer’s control. The judgment relied on prior Rajasthan High Court cases, especially M/s. Pratap Power Spares, where a 99-day delay was condoned after the Court granted relaxation of the 120-day statutory appeal window under Section 107 and directed the appeal to be heard if filed within 30 days. The Court also referred to other decisions supporting delayed GST appeals in exceptional circumstances, while acknowledging the general rule that writ jurisdiction should not be used to bypass statutory limitation.

The relief was not unconditional: the Court made it subject to the petitioner depositing the late fee, penalty, and other statutory amounts required for entertaining the appeal, “as admissible.” The appellate authority must now consider the appeal on merits rather than refuse it on limitation alone. All pending applications were disposed of. From a compliance perspective, this decision underscores that delayed GST appeals may still be pursued where there is documented, compelling hardship such as medical incapacity, but the taxpayer should expect to satisfy all statutory deposit requirements and should not assume that ordinary limitation deadlines will be excused absent exceptional facts.

The reliefs sought included a declaration that the blocking of IGST ITC with negative balance was illegal, inoperative and void, a direction to re-credit the Electronic Credit Ledger for any ITC unlawfully set off against the impugned demand, and other appropriate relief. At the hearing, the petitioner submitted that the blocking had already ceased to operate by operation of the statute on expiry of one year and that the Electronic Credit Ledger had consequently been reactivated with the credit. The surviving issue, according to the petitioner, was whether the respondents could have blocked the ITC without complying with the mandatory requirements of Rule 86A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017. The respondents fairly conceded that the Electronic Credit Ledger was operational, but were unable to demonstrate compliance with Rule 86A before the ITC was blocked. In response to the Court’s query as to why the Rule had not been complied with, the respondents submitted that it was a bona fide mistake. They further acknowledged that, although the concerned authority had reasons for taking the action, no proper and reasoned order had been passed and no opportunity of hearing had been afforded to the petitioner before the blocking. The respondents undertook that any future blocking would be carried out only through a proper and reasoned order by the competent authority and strictly in conformity with Rule 86A, and tendered an unconditional apology on behalf of the concerned officer. The Court identified the narrow issue as whether anything further survived for adjudication once the Electronic Credit Ledger containing the ITC had become operational and was no longer blocked. It nevertheless recorded that Rule 86A prescribes mandatory preconditions before an Electronic Credit Ledger can be blocked. The Court reproduced Rule 86A(1), read with Rule 86A(1)(d), including the requirement that the competent authority have reasons to believe that the ITC had been fraudulently availed or was ineligible and, in the circumstances specified by the Rule, could, for reasons to be recorded in writing, disallow debit of an equivalent amount from the Electronic Credit Ledger for discharge of liability under section 49 or for a refund of unutilised amount. On the record before it, the Court found that the mandatory requirements contemplated under Rule 86A had not been complied with. However, treating the matter as an exceptional case and accepting the unconditional apology tendered on behalf of the concerned officer, the Court disposed of the writ petition with a clear and categorical warning. It held that if the respondents in future take action without due compliance with Rule 86A, such action would render them liable to pay appropriate compensation to the aggrieved party. Pending applications, if any, were also disposed of. The decision therefore records non-compliance with the mandatory Rule 86A safeguards, while disposing of the present petition after the ITC restriction had already ceased and the Electronic Credit Ledger had become operational. The Rajasthan High Court considered a writ petition by M/s Jagdish Prasad Agrawal, a partnership firm, challenging the blocking of Input Tax Credit (ITC) in its Electronic Credit Ledger, specifically an IGST ITC block shown with a negative balance. The petitioner asked for the blocking action to be declared illegal, inoperative, and void, for the ledger to be re-credited with any ITC that had been wrongly set off against the disputed demand, and for other appropriate relief. By the time of hearing, the blocking had already automatically ceased to operate because the statutory one-year period had expired, and the Electronic Credit Ledger had been reactivated; as a result, the live dispute narrowed to whether the ITC could have been blocked at all without following Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017.

The respondents conceded that the ledger was operational again, but they could not show that the mandatory preconditions under Rule 86A had been satisfied before the block was imposed. The Court noted that Rule 86A requires the competent authority to have “reasons to believe” that ITC was fraudulently availed or was ineligible, and then, for reasons recorded in writing, to disallow debit of an equivalent amount from the Electronic Credit Ledger for payment of tax liability under section 49 or for refund of unutilised credit; the Court also specifically referred to Rule 86A(1)(d). The respondents admitted the omission was a bona fide mistake, acknowledged that no proper reasoned order had been passed, and conceded that the petitioner had not been given an opportunity of hearing before the blocking. They undertook that any future blocking would be done only by the competent authority through a proper, reasoned order and strictly in accordance with Rule 86A, and an unconditional apology was tendered on behalf of the concerned officer.

Although the Court found on the record that the mandatory requirements of Rule 86A had not been complied with, it treated the matter as exceptional because the restriction had already lapsed and the ledger had been restored. The writ petition was therefore disposed of rather than decided on broader merits, and pending applications were also disposed of. Importantly for compliance purposes, the Court issued a clear warning that if the respondents in future block ITC without due compliance with Rule 86A, they may be liable to pay appropriate compensation to the aggrieved party. The practical compliance takeaway is that any ITC-blocking action under Rule 86A must be supported by recorded reasons, based on the statutory “reasons to believe” standard, and carried out by the proper authority with a reasoned order; otherwise, the action risks being treated as non-compliant and exposing the department to compensation claims.

The appellant was a 100% export unit providing Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas entities under specific service agreements and exported those services without payment of service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005. It had claimed refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. Refund of ₹78,79,939 was rejected in respect of General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services on the ground that the services lacked nexus with exported output services. Before the Tribunal, the appellant contended that availment of CENVAT credit, its utilisation and its refund were distinct aspects and that, where the Department had not challenged availment under Rule 14, refund could not subsequently be denied under Rule 5 by questioning the credit’s eligibility. It further submitted that the disputed services fell within the definition of “input service” under Rule 2(l), relying on numerous judicial decisions, and that direct nexus with the final output services was not necessary in view of Circular No. 120/1/2010-ST dated 19.01.2010 and the decision in Reliance Corporate IT Park Ltd. The Tribunal held that it was settled by various decisions that where availment of CENVAT credit had not been challenged by the Department under Rule 14, refund could not be denied by resorting to Rule 5. It further found that, during the disputed period, the definition of input service was exhaustive and that General Insurance Service, Commercial or Industrial Construction Services and Works Contract Service had been held to be input services by various decisions. Ltd., a 100% export-oriented service provider, was entitled to refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The company provided Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas clients under service agreements and exported those services without payment of service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005. The specific refund claim rejected by the department was ₹78,79,939, and the rejection related only to credit taken on General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services, and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services on the theory that those services lacked nexus with the exported output services.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that where the Department has not first challenged the availment of CENVAT credit under Rule 14, it cannot later deny refund of the accumulated credit under Rule 5 by questioning whether the credit was eligible in the first place. The Tribunal treated availment, utilisation, and refund of credit as distinct issues and relied on prior case law to conclude that refund proceedings are not the proper stage to re-litigate the underlying eligibility of credit that was never put in dispute under Rule 14. It also reaffirmed that, during the relevant period, the definition of “input service” under Rule 2(l) was broad/exhaustive enough to cover General Insurance Service, Commercial or Industrial Construction Service, and Works Contract Service, and that a strict direct nexus with the exported output service was not required.

The Tribunal specifically relied on Circular No. 120/1/2010-ST dated 19.01.2010 and the decision in Reliance Corporate IT Park Ltd. for the proposition that direct one-to-one linkage between each input service and the exported output service is not necessary for refund eligibility. Accordingly, the impugned order rejecting the refund was set aside and the appeal was allowed with consequential relief, if any, as per law. The practical compliance takeaway is that exporters claiming Rule 5 refunds should ensure credits are properly availed and documented as input services, but if the department intends to dispute eligibility, it should do so at the credit-availment stage under Rule 14; otherwise, a later refund denial on nexus grounds is vulnerable.

Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Hyderabad considered an appeal by M/s Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. against an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 confirming Service Tax demands, interest and penalties principally under “Banking and Other Financial Services” and “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” for 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The first dispute concerned charges deducted by foreign/intermediary banks while export proceeds were transmitted from foreign buyers through banking channels. The appellant, a manufacture-exporter of pharmaceutical products, contended that the foreign buyers remitted consideration through their banking arrangements and that the foreign/intermediary banks deducted charges before the balance reached the appellant’s Indian bank. The Department proceeded on the basis that, because the deductions economically reduced the amount received by the appellant, the appellant was the recipient of banking services and was liable to Service Tax under Reverse Charge Mechanism. The Tribunal rejected that approach. It found no evidence that the appellant had engaged the foreign banks, entered into contractual arrangements with them, or was otherwise obliged to pay consideration to them for services rendered to it. Merely bearing the economic impact of deductions did not establish a service provider-service recipient relationship. The Tribunal also relied on the appellant’s own earlier decision, Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020, where the same issue for the earlier period had been decided in the appellant’s favour, and on Eastman Exports Global Clothing Pvt Ltd. The demand under Banking and Other Financial Services was accordingly held unsustainable. The second dispute concerned payments made to M/s DADA Consultancy and M/s Pharpe Dr. D.R. Iban for preparation and compilation of clinical and non-clinical overviews and regulatory documentation required for obtaining overseas pharmaceutical product approvals. Revenue classified the activities as “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” because the consultants possessed scientific and technical expertise and the documentation involved scientific and technical product particulars. The appellant submitted that the agencies merely compiled already available data and published material and prepared regulatory dossiers/forms; they did not undertake independent scientific research, experimentation or technical studies, nor did they provide advice in a discipline of science or technology. The Tribunal followed the appellant’s earlier decision and the decision in IPCA Laboratories Ltd., holding that regulatory services connected with obtaining permissions/registrations and meeting overseas regulatory requirements cannot merely on that account be classified as Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services. It emphasised that the essential character of a service must be determined from the activity actually undertaken, rather than merely from the professional qualifications of the persons rendering it. The CESTAT Hyderabad allowed Aurobindo Pharma Ltd.’s appeal and set aside service tax, interest, and penalties confirmed by the Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 for the periods 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The dispute involved two categories of alleged taxability: first, deductions made by foreign/intermediary banks from export remittances received by the company from overseas buyers; and second, payments to overseas/regulatory consultancy vendors M/s DADA Consultancy and M/s Pharpe Dr. D.R. Iban for preparing clinical/non-clinical overviews and regulatory documents to obtain foreign pharmaceutical product approvals. For the bank charges, the Tribunal held that Aurobindo was not the recipient of “Banking and Other Financial Services” merely because the banks’ fees reduced the net remittance amount; there was no evidence of any contract, engagement, or obligation by Aurobindo to pay those foreign banks, so reverse charge liability did not arise.

For the regulatory documentation work, the Tribunal rejected Revenue’s attempt to classify the services as “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services.” It found that the consultants were mainly compiling existing data, published materials, and dossier/form submissions for regulatory filings, not performing independent scientific research, experimentation, technical studies, or giving advice in a scientific discipline. The Tribunal emphasized that classification must be based on the actual nature of the work performed, not simply on the scientific/technical background of the personnel doing it, and held that services rendered to obtain overseas registrations/permissions do not become scientific or technical consultancy just because they relate to regulated pharma approvals. It also relied on Aurobindo’s own earlier favorable order (Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020) and on the IPCA Laboratories line of cases, noting that no material change in facts or service nature had been shown.

A further point important for compliance is that Aurobindo had already discharged service tax on these consultancy payments under “Management or Business Consultant Service,” and the Department had appropriated that amount in the impugned order while simultaneously reclassifying the same services under another taxable head; once the reclassification failed, the demand could not stand. Because the underlying tax demands were set aside, the related interest and penalties were also cancelled. The Tribunal did not separately decide the appellant’s argument about penalty computation under Section 76 of the Finance Act, 1994, in light of the amendment effective 08.04.2011, because that issue became moot after the substantive liabilities were deleted. For compliance teams, the case reinforces that export-remittance bank deductions are not automatically reverse-charge taxable absent a direct service relationship, and that pharma regulatory dossier preparation/compilation for foreign approvals is not, by itself, scientific or technical consultancy.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ranjita Rajendra Bane Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Mumbai) Summary: The Customs, Excise & Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai considered the appeal filed by Ranjita Rajendra Bane, widow and successor in interest of deceased Rajendra Bane, challenging personal penalties of ₹2,50,000/- and ₹1,00,000/- imposed under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962. Rajendra Bane had been serving as a Customs Hawaldar. The penalties arose from an investigation into smuggled gold recovered from the gent’s toilet at Pune International Airport after passengers travelled from Dubai by Spice Jet Flight No. SG 52 on 16.08.2018. The allegation was that although Rajendra Bane was on sanctioned leave and staying at his native place near Ratnagiri, he had facilitated the smuggling of gold and assisted the smugglers. The material relied upon against him included statements recorded under Section 108 of the Customs Act, 1962, particularly statements of co-accused/accomplices, call records received from the telephone operator, and recovery of gold from the airport toilet and from a passenger. The defence completely denied involvement. It admitted that Rajendra Bane was on leave and at his native place on the relevant day, but contended that the seizure had actually followed information transmitted by him to the Superintendent on duty at Pune International Airport. The defence claimed that the information involved privileged communication with an informer and therefore its source could not be disclosed. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, rejected this explanation. He considered the statements of co-accused to have been corroborated by SDRs/CDRs and the recovery of gold, and relied upon the Supreme Court decision in Naresh J. Sukhwani Vs. UOI [1996 (83) ELT 258 (S.C)] concerning the evidentiary value of statements recorded under Section 108. The Commissioner (Appeals) also treated the phone call made by Rajendra Bane to the Superintendent as an afterthought intended to camouflage his role. A further adverse inference was drawn because, when the Superintendent did not respond to the first call, Rajendra Bane had allegedly not approached another departmental officer. The Tribunal found that the reliance on Naresh J. Sukhwani was made in a materially different factual context. It noted that nothing incriminating, including the allegedly relevant SIM card, had been seized from Rajendra Bane. The Tribunal referred to the principle concerning accomplice evidence under Section 114, illustration (b), of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and held that where nothing incriminating had been seized from the deceased Appellant, he could not be implicated solely on the statement of a co-accused or accomplice. The Tribunal also examined the call evidence more closely. According to the record considered by the Tribunal, the Superintendent, Shri D.G. Nandanwar, had called Rajendra Bane back and was informed that gold brought in the Spice Jet flight had been dumped in the gent’s lavatory of the Immigration Hall. The investigation also revealed several calls between 03:04:03 A.M. and 05:33 A.M. from the mobile number of Rajendra Bane’s son, Prathmesh Rajendra Bane. The CDR shown to the Superintendent for the period from 5 A.M. to 6 A.M. did not reveal that number. The Tribunal considered this relevant because the seizure was effected at 05.15 A.M. The Tribunal found two contradictory theories regarding Rajendra Bane’s role. According to the substituted Appellant, he was an informer whose tip resulted in recovery of more than 13 Kgs. of smuggled gold, including 10 Kgs. placed in the dustbin of the gent’s toilet. According to the Department, he was allegedly acting in connivance with smugglers and the phone call informing the Superintendent was an afterthought because DRI already had intelligence regarding the transaction. The Tribunal observed that the circumstances did not establish the latter theory. It noted that no seizure had been made from passengers inside the airport and one passenger had allegedly left with more than 3 Kgs. of gold, while another was apprehended in the retiring area after becoming ill because gold was present in his rectum. According to the Tribunal, these circumstances indicated that DRI did not have definite information concerning the exact transaction and that such information had been supplied by the deceased Appellant. The Tribunal also rejected the Commissioner (Appeals)’ reasoning concerning the failure to contact another senior officer after the Superintendent did not answer the first call.
