rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai deleted the personal penalties of ₹2,50,000 and ₹1,00,000 imposed under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962 on the deceased Customs Hawaldar, Rajendra Bane, whose widow carried the appeal. The penalties had been imposed on the theory that he had aided a gold-smuggling operation connected to passengers arriving from Dubai on SpiceJet Flight SG 52 on 16.08.2018, but the Tribunal found that the Department had not established his involvement with reliable evidence. In particular, the Tribunal held that he could not be implicated solely on the basis of co-accused/accomplice statements recorded under Section 108, especially where nothing incriminating—including the allegedly relevant SIM card—had been seized from him, and the factual context differed from the Supreme Court decision in Naresh J. Sukhwani on which the Commissioner (Appeals) had relied.

The Tribunal gave significant weight to the call evidence and the sequence of events around the seizure at about 05:15 A.M. It noted that the Superintendent, Shri D.G. Nandanwar, had called Rajendra Bane back and was told that gold brought on the SpiceJet flight had been dumped in the gent’s lavatory of the Immigration Hall, and it also examined the call detail record showing multiple calls between 03:04:03 A.M. and 05:33 A.M. from the mobile number of Rajendra Bane’s son, Prathmesh Rajendra Bane. The Tribunal found it material that the CDR shown to the Superintendent for the 5 A.M. to 6 A.M. period did not reflect that number, and it treated this as supporting the view that the Department’s theory of prior intelligence/connivance was not proved.

The Department’s case was that Rajendra Bane, while on sanctioned leave at his native place near Ratnagiri, had facilitated the smuggling and later tried to camouflage his role by making a phone call to the Superintendent; the Tribunal rejected that as unproven. It also rejected the adverse inference drawn by the Commissioner (Appeals) from the fact that Rajendra Bane allegedly did not contact another officer after the Superintendent did not answer the first call. On the Tribunal’s assessment, the surrounding circumstances were more consistent with Rajendra Bane acting as an informer whose tip led to recovery of more than 13 kg of smuggled gold, including 10 kg placed in the dustbin of the gent’s toilet, rather than as a participant in the smuggling.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that Section 112(a) personal penalty cannot be sustained on conjecture, accomplice statements alone, or inferred involvement where there is no direct incriminating seizure from the person concerned and the call/electronic evidence does not clearly establish participation. The case also shows that authorities must reconcile call detail records and other documentary evidence with the alleged timeline of interception before treating a call to customs officers as an “afterthought” or using silence/failure to contact another officer as proof of culpability.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Patna HC Remits Nukkad Natak GST Exemption Issue to Appellate Authority
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12611 Case Name Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal Vs State of Bihar (Patna High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Patna High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal Vs State of Bihar (Patna High Court) Summary: The Patna High Court considered a writ petition filed by M/S Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal, a registered GST person engaged in conducting Nukkad Natak (street plays) for public awareness programmes primarily assigned by Government Departments. The petitioner challenged the Appellate Authority’s order dated 28.02.2026 in Appeal Case No. GST/PTC-2—2025-26 and the underlying demand dated 20.08.2025 raising tax, interest and penalty of Rs. 1,63,452/-. The dispute arose for the financial year 2022-23. A notice had been issued against the petitioner under Section 73 of the CGST Act, 2017 on the basis of gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100/- received from the District Public Relations Officer, Gaya. The Adjudicating Authority subsequently imposed a liability of tax, interest and penalty amounting to Rs. 1,63,452/- on 20.08.2025. The petitioner thereafter filed an appeal under Section 107(1) of the CGST Act, 2017. The appeal was dismissed on 28.02.2026 because it was filed with a delay of 21 days. The petitioner, however, relied upon a subsequent memo issued by the Collectorate, Gaya, Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025. According to the petitioner, that communication stated that GST was not applicable to receipts against sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in the profession of Nukkad Natak and that Nukkad Natak teams comprising (4-6-8-10) members were exempted from the GST regime. Before the High Court, the petitioner therefore contended that the underlying issue was not merely the delay in filing the appeal but whether the petitioner, being a registered person performing Nukkad Natak, was exempt from GST liability. The State opposed the petition on limitation grounds, submitting that the Appellate Authority had rightly dismissed the appeal after expiry of the statutory period by 21 days. It was also submitted that the alleged exemption communication had been issued by the District Public Relation Officer, Gaya, and did not identify the statutory provision or any decision of the GST Council under which the Nukkad Natak team was claimed to be exempt. The High Court focused on the nature of the issue raised by the petitioner. It observed that the exemption question went to the root concerning the jurisdiction of the authority which had imposed the tax liability. The Court further noted that the Appellate Authority had dismissed the appeal as time barred instead of deciding the substantive exemption issue raised by the petitioner. In these circumstances, the High Court held that the Appellate Authority must decide the petitioner’s contention that, as a registered person performing Nukkad Natak, it was exempted from GST liability. The Court accordingly set aside the appellate order dated 28.02.2026 and remitted the matter to the Appellate Authority for deciding the exemption issue in accordance with law within two months from receipt or production of the High Court’s order. The writ petition was disposed of with further procedural directions. The petitioner was directed to produce a copy of the High Court order and appear before the Appellate Authority for fixing the hearing date within one week. Upon production of the order, the Appellate Authority was directed to fix the hearing and dispose of the appeal after granting personal hearing to the petitioner within a maximum period of two months. The judgment therefore does not finally determine that Nukkad Natak is exempt from GST. Instead, the High Court set aside the dismissal on limitation and required the competent Appellate Authority to examine and decide the exemption claim in accordance with law. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that a notice was issued under Section 73 of GST against petitioner for the financial year 2022-23 on the basis of gross receipt of Rs. 4,98,100/-, received from the District Public Relations Officer, Gaya and the order has been passed by the Adjudicating Authority on 20.08.2025, imposing a liability of tax/interest/penalty against the pet
rows.summary:
The Patna High Court did **not** finally decide whether Nukkad Natak services are exempt from GST; instead, it sent the issue back to the appellate authority for a merits decision. The petitioner, **M/s Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal**, is a **GST-registered entity** that performs **Nukkad Natak (street plays)** for government public-awareness programmes, and the tax dispute arose for **FY 2022–23** based on **gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100** received from the **District Public Relations Officer, Gaya**. An adjudication order dated **20.08.2025** had imposed **tax, interest, and penalty totaling Rs. 1,63,452**, after a notice was issued under **Section 73 of the CGST Act, 2017**.  

The petitioner appealed under **Section 107(1)**, but the Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on **28.02.2026** solely because it was filed **21 days late**. Before the High Court, the petitioner argued that a later government communication, **Collectorate, Gaya Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025**, stated that **GST was not applicable to receipts from sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in Nukkad Natak** and that **Nukkad Natak teams comprising 4, 6, 8, or 10 members were exempt from GST**; the State objected that this memo did not cite any statutory basis or GST Council decision and that the appeal was time-barred. The High Court held that the exemption question went to the root of the tax demand and that the Appellate Authority should have decided that substantive issue rather than disposing of the matter only on limitation.  

Accordingly, the Court **set aside the appellate order dated 28.02.2026** and **remitted the matter to the Appellate Authority** to decide, in accordance with law, whether the petitioner as a registered person performing Nukkad Natak is exempt from GST liability. Procedurally, the petitioner must **produce a copy of the High Court’s order and appear before the Appellate Authority within one week** for fixing a hearing date, and the Appellate Authority must then provide a **personal hearing** and **dispose of the appeal within two months** from receipt/production of the High Court order. For compliance purposes, the decision means the demand remains under challenge and the key open issue is whether the asserted Nukkad Natak exemption has any lawful basis under GST law; the High Court expressly did **not** affirm the exemption, only required a proper adjudication of it.

Builders Vs Commissioner of commercial taxes (GSTAT Bengaluru) Summary: The Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, allowed the appeal of M/s. N. R. Builders by way of remand in a dispute concerning alleged excess Input Tax Credit (ITC) of ₹2,33,502/- for Financial Year 2018–19. The disputed amount comprised CGST of ₹1,16,751/- and SGST of ₹1,16,751/-. Interest of ₹2,03,730/- and penalty of ₹23,350/- had also been imposed, resulting in a total demand of ₹4,60,582/-. The Appellant, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, contended that the apparent mismatch between FORM GSTR-3B and FORM GSTR-2A did not represent excess ITC. According to the Appellant, the disputed credit related to Financial Year 2017–18 invoices but was availed in Financial Year 2018–19 within the permissible period under Section 16(4). The Appellant also challenged the proceedings on the ground that no personal hearing was granted and that no notice in FORM GST ASMT-10 had preceded the proceedings. A pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A was issued on 22.01.2024, followed by a Show Cause Notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 under Section 73. The Show Cause Notice itself recorded the date, time and venue of personal hearing as “NA”. The Proper Officer subsequently confirmed the entire demand ex parte. The First Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal and upheld the demand. The Tribunal first considered whether the GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A difference could be treated as inadmissible ITC without examining the Appellant’s explanation concerning Financial Year 2017–18 invoices. It noted that, during the transition period, Section 16(4) permitted the relevant ITC to be claimed within the applicable extended period. The Tribunal also relied upon CBIC Circular No. 183/15/2022-GST, which specifically addresses differences between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A for FY 2017–18 and 2018–19 and requires verification rather than summary disallowance. The Tribunal held that non-appearance of an invoice in GSTR-2A for Financial Year 2018–19 did not, without verification, establish that the supplier had failed to pay tax. It found that the Appellate Authority had proceeded on an assumption and had not undertaken invoice-wise verification of the Appellant’s explanation. The Tribunal therefore answered Issue No. 1 in favour of the Appellant, holding that the demand could not be sustained on the existing record without such verification. The Tribunal also examined the authorities relied upon by the First Appellate Authority, namely Mahalakshmi Cotton Ginning Processing and Oil Industries v. State of Maharashtra, ALD Automotive Private Limited v. CTO and Microqual Techno Ltd. v. State of Karnataka. It distinguished all three decisions on the basis that their statutory provisions and factual circumstances materially differed from the present dispute, including the absence here of any finding that the underlying purchases were non-genuine. On natural justice, the Tribunal found a clear infirmity. Section 75(4) requires an opportunity of hearing where an adverse decision is contemplated. Since the Show Cause Notice recorded the personal hearing details as “NA” and the record contained no evidence that a hearing had actually been granted, the Tribunal held that the absence of personal hearing itself justified setting aside the Order-in-Original. The Tribunal, however, rejected the Appellant’s contention concerning FORM GST ASMT-10. It held that Section 61 and Section 73 are independent provisions. Where proceedings are initiated directly under Section 73 pursuant to a specific assignment and not by invoking the scrutiny mechanism under Section 61, absence of FORM GST ASMT-10 does not by itself invalidate the proceedings. ([TaxGuru][3]) As to interest and penalty, the Tribunal held that their sustainability would abide by the fresh determination of the principal tax liability. It relied upon the proposition concerning the compensatory character of interest in Prathibha Processors v. Union of India, while observing that final determination of tax, interest and penalty would be premature until fresh adjudication. The Proper Officer was directed to verify the reconciliation invoice-wise with reference to FY 2017–18 GSTR-2A, suppliers’ GSTR-1, the Appellant’s ITC register, books of account and GSTR-9/GSTR-9C returns for FY 2017–18 and 2018–19. rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, remanded the case of **M/s. N. R. Builders v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes** for fresh adjudication after finding that the alleged **ITC mismatch between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A** for **FY 2018–19** had not been properly verified. The disputed ITC was **₹2,33,502** in total, split equally into **CGST ₹1,16,751** and **SGST ₹1,16,751**; the department had also levied **interest of ₹2,03,730** and **penalty of ₹23,350**, making the total demand **₹4,60,582**. The taxpayer, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, argued that the credit related to **FY 2017–18 invoices** but was lawfully availed in **FY 2018–19** within the time allowed under **Section 16(4)**, so the mismatch did not automatically mean excess or inadmissible ITC.

On procedure, the Tribunal found a serious **natural justice defect** because the **show-cause notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024** recorded the personal hearing as **“NA”**, and there was no evidence that any hearing was actually granted; this violated **Section 75(4)**, which requires an opportunity of hearing when an adverse order is contemplated. The proceedings had begun with a **pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A on 22.01.2024**, followed by the Section 73 notice, and the Proper Officer ultimately confirmed the demand **ex parte**. However, the Tribunal rejected the argument that the absence of **FORM GST ASMT-10** invalidated the case, holding that **Section 61 scrutiny and Section 73 adjudication are independent**, and if the matter is directly assigned under Section 73, ASMT-10 is not a precondition.

Substantively, the Tribunal held that a mismatch between **GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A** cannot be summarily treated as inadmissible ITC without **invoice-wise verification** of the taxpayer’s explanation. It relied on **CBIC Circular No. 183/15/2022-GST**, which specifically deals with GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A differences for **FY 2017–18 and FY 2018–19** and requires verification rather than automatic disallowance. The Tribunal noted that the mere fact that invoices did not appear in GSTR-2A for FY 2018–19 did not, by itself, prove that the suppliers had not paid tax, and it faulted the lower authorities for not checking the taxpayer’s claim that the invoices belonged to FY 2017–18 but were availed within the permissible extended period.

The Tribunal also distinguished the precedents relied upon by the department/first appellate authority—**Mahalakshmi Cotton Ginning Processing and Oil Industries v. State of Maharashtra**, **ALD Automotive Private Limited v. CTO**, and **Microqual Techno Ltd. v. State of Karnataka**—because those cases involved different statutory settings and factual situations, including the absence here of any finding that the underlying purchases were non-genuine. It therefore set aside both the **Order-in-Original dated 20.04.2024** and the **Order-in-Appeal dated 07.11.2024**, and remanded the matter for **de novo adjudication**. The Proper Officer must now verify the reconciliation **invoice by invoice** with reference to **FY 2017–18 GSTR-2A, suppliers’ GSTR-1 returns, the assessee’s ITC register, books of account, and GSTR-9/GSTR-9C returns for FY 2017–18 and FY 2018–19**; the Tribunal also observed that the final position on **interest and penalty** will depend on the fresh determination of the principal tax liability.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative & Judicial Developments
rows.desc: Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative and Judicial Developments – Period covered: September 2025 to September 2026 Summary: The period from September 2025 to September 2026 witnessed substantial changes in India’s GST framework across legislation, tax rates, refunds, return filing, appellate remedies and judicial interpretation. The Finance Act, 2026 amended provisions governing post-supply discounts, credit notes, provisional refunds and appellate arrangements, while omitting Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act concerning intermediary services. Commencement differs across provisions, and the amendments to Sections 15, 34 and 54 of the CGST Act await notification. Rate rationalisation was completed through the withdrawal of compensation cess and migration of specified tobacco and pan masala products to the 40 per cent slab. Risk-based provisional refunds were expanded, GSTAT benches became operational and revised limitation dates were prescribed for legacy appeals. The return architecture increasingly requires verification and reconciliation before filing, supported by GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B and the Invoice Management System. Judicial developments clarified buyer exposure where suppliers fail to deposit tax, statutory timelines for detention orders and the prospective application of penalty-related pre-deposit requirements. With the 57th GST Council meeting scheduled for 12 September 2026, further proposals concerning ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds and small-business compliance remain under consideration but cannot be treated as operative law until formally implemented. The twelve months preceding the 57th meeting of the GST Council have produced the densest concentration of change since the levy was introduced in July 2017. Three distinct layers moved at once. The rate architecture recommended by the 56th Council was completed with the withdrawal of compensation cess and the migration of tobacco and pan masala into the 40 per cent slab. The Finance Act, 2026 rewrote four operative provisions of the CGST Act and deleted one of the most litigated provisions of the IGST Act. And the Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, dormant for eight years, began passing orders. For a practitioner, the practical consequence is that positions taken as recently as FY 2024–25 now require re-examination — on valuation of post-sale discounts, on the export status of intermediary services, on the availability of input tax credit where a supplier defaults, and on the forum in which a demand is contested. This article sets out the position as it stands, identifies which amendments are in force and which await notification, and flags the points on which the law is still unsettled. Table of Contents▸ 1. rows.summary:
This document reviews major GST developments in India from September 2025 to September 2026 and is especially relevant for businesses dealing with discounting, refunds, exports, intermediary services, appellate litigation, and return compliance. The most important legislative change is the Finance Act, 2026, which received Presidential assent on 30 March 2026 and made five GST-related changes: it rewrote Section 15(3)(b) of the CGST Act so that post-supply discounts can be excluded from transaction value only if a credit note is issued and the recipient reverses the related input tax credit; it amended Section 34(1) so such discounts are now an express basis for issuing a credit note; it expanded Section 54 to allow 90% provisional refund in inverted duty structure cases and removed the minimum threshold for refunds on exports made with payment of tax; it inserted Section 101A(1A) to allow the Central Government to authorise an existing tribunal to hear appeals until the National Appellate Authority is set up; and it omitted Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act, which had deemed intermediary services to be supplied at the supplier’s location.  

The commencement dates are not uniform and are critical for compliance: Sections 2 to 129, clause (b) of Section 152, and Section 156 came into force on 1 April 2026, but the amendments to Sections 15, 34 and 54 do not automatically apply until the Central Government notifies them; Section 157 is treated separately and, as described in the document, the deletion of Section 13(8)(b) is in force through that provision’s commencement mechanism. In practical terms, companies should not assume the amended discount and refund rules apply until the relevant notification is issued, while the intermediary-service position must be reassessed because the old place-of-supply deeming rule has been removed.  

On rates, the GST Council completed the long-running rate rationalisation by withdrawing compensation cess and moving specified tobacco and pan masala products into the 40% GST slab. The document treats this as a completed change to the rate architecture, so affected manufacturers, distributors, and importers of those products need to update pricing, classification, invoicing, and tax computations accordingly.  

Refund and appellate processes also changed materially. Administratively, risk-based provisional refunds were expanded ahead of the statutory amendment, so taxpayers seeking refunds should expect greater use of system-driven checks, especially where claims are linked to inverted duty structure or exports. The GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT), which had been dormant for eight years, became operational and started issuing orders, and the document notes that revised limitation dates were prescribed for legacy appeals; importantly, a relaxation date of 31 December 2026 is not a general extension of limitation, so old appeals still need to be checked against the specific rules rather than treated as broadly revived.  

The return and portal architecture is becoming more verification-heavy before filing. The document highlights the growing role of GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B, and the Invoice Management System in pre-filing reconciliation and matching, meaning businesses should tighten vendor data review and internal controls before filing returns. Judicially, the courts clarified that buyers can remain exposed when suppliers fail to deposit tax, that detention orders must meet statutory timelines, and that penalty-related pre-deposit rules apply prospectively rather than retroactively. Finally, the 57th GST Council meeting was scheduled for 12 September 2026, with proposals under discussion on ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds, and small-business compliance, but none of those proposals are operative until formally implemented.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaulting Sellers
rows.desc: Why Does the GST Department Chase Bona Fide Buyers Under Section 16(2)(c) Instead of Defaulting Sellers Under Section 76? Summary: Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act makes a recipient’s entitlement to Input Tax Credit conditional upon the tax charged by the supplier having actually been paid to the government. Consequently, even a bona fide buyer who possesses a genuine invoice, receives the goods or services, pays the entire consideration including GST and files returns correctly may be required to reverse ITC if the supplier defaults. Section 76, however, independently empowers the GST department to recover tax collected but not deposited from the person who collected it, together with applicable interest and penalty. Despite this direct remedy, enforcement action is frequently taken against compliant buyers because they are easier to trace, possess identifiable assets and remain active within the GST system, whereas defaulting suppliers may have closed operations, disappeared or operated through shell entities. Automated GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B mismatch identification also makes buyer-side proceedings administratively easier than investigation and recovery against sellers. The Supreme Court’s decision in Bhandari Scrap Traders upheld the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c), recognising ITC as a statutory benefit subject to legislative conditions, including supplier payment of tax. Nevertheless, questions of fairness and enforcement sequencing remain. A balanced approach would prioritise recovery under Section 76 from the defaulting supplier and reserve ITC denial for transactions involving collusion, fraud or failure to establish genuineness. Until legislation or binding precedent clarifies the sequencing of these provisions, buyers should maintain comprehensive evidence of supplier verification, invoices, receipt of supplies, e-way bills, transport records, banking payments and return reconciliation. Anyone who has dealt with a GST department notice in the last few years has probably come across this pattern: a buyer who paid the full invoice value, including GST, to a registered supplier, files his returns properly, claims Input Tax Credit, and then months later gets a notice asking him to reverse that credit and pay the tax again — this time out of his own pocket. The reason given is almost always the same one line: the supplier did not deposit the tax with the government. At first glance this seems backwards. The seller collected the money. The seller had a legal duty to pay it over to the exchequer. So common sense says the department should go after the seller. Yet in practice, it is the buyer’s door that gets knocked on far more often. This article looks at why that happens, what the law actually allows, and whether the current approach is fair. Table of Contents▸ What the Law Actually Says The Bhandari Scrap Traders Position Why the Department Leans on Section 16(2)(c) Compliant Buyers Are Easier to Trace Automated Return-Mismatch Proceedings Burden Shifted to the Buyer The Fairness Question Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); What the Law Actually Says Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act lays down one of the conditions a taxpayer must satisfy before he can claim ITC — that the tax charged on the supply has actually been paid to the government, either in cash or through utilisation of admissible credit. On paper this looks like a routine anti-fraud safeguard. In practice, it has become the single most litigated condition in the entire ITC framework, because it puts the buyer in the position of guaranteeing his supplier’s conduct — something he has no real way to control once the transaction is complete and the invoice is genuine. Section 76, on the other hand, deals with a completely different situation: a person who has collected tax “as representing tax” but not paid it to the government. This provision gives the department a direct, standalone route to recover that amount from the person who collected it, along with interest and penalty, regardless of whether any assessment proceedings are pending. In other words, the law already gives the department a tool designed specifically for the defaulting seller. The question is why this tool is used so sparingly compared to the far more frequent invocation of Section 16(2)(c) against the buyer. The Bhandari Scrap Traders Position The debate around Section 16(2)(c) was pushed further by the ruling in the Bhandari Scrap Traders matter, where the constitutional validity of the provision was upheld. The reasoning offered was that claiming ITC is a statutory concession, not a vested or absolute right, and Parliament is free to attach conditions to it — including a condition that depends on the conduct of a third party, the supplier. Once that principle is accepted, a buyer who has done everything right — genuine invoice, actual payment, proper filing — can still end up losing his credit purely because someone else in the chain
rows.summary:
The document explains that under **Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act**, a buyer’s right to claim **Input Tax Credit (ITC)** depends on the supplier having **actually paid the tax to the government**; as a result, even a bona fide purchaser who has a genuine invoice, receives the goods or services, pays the full amount including GST, and files returns correctly can still be forced to **reverse ITC** if the supplier defaults. It contrasts this with **Section 76**, which gives the GST department a **direct recovery route against the person who collected tax but failed to deposit it**, allowing recovery of the unpaid tax **plus interest and penalty** from the defaulting seller itself. The article’s core point is that, despite Section 76, the department often proceeds against the buyer because buyers are usually easier to find, still active in the GST system, and have identifiable assets, while defaulting suppliers may have shut down, vanished, or operated through shell entities; automated **GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B mismatch** checks also make buyer-side action simpler and more routine than tracing and enforcing against sellers.

The document notes that the Supreme Court in **Bhandari Scrap Traders** upheld the constitutional validity of **Section 16(2)(c)**, treating ITC as a **statutory benefit rather than an absolute right** and accepting that Parliament can condition ITC on the supplier’s payment of tax. At the same time, the article criticizes the fairness of routinely shifting the loss to compliant buyers and argues that enforcement should, as a matter of policy, **prioritize recovery under Section 76 from the defaulting supplier** and reserve ITC denial for cases involving **collusion, fraud, or failure to prove the genuineness of the transaction**. There is **no new statutory deadline or rate change** stated in the document, but the practical compliance message is clear: until the law or binding precedent clarifies sequencing, buyers should preserve strong evidence of due diligence and transaction genuineness, including **supplier verification records, tax invoices, proof of receipt of goods/services, e-way bills, transport documents, banking/payment records, and GST return reconciliations** to defend against notices requiring ITC reversal.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12594 Case Name Pankaj Kumar Singhal Vs Shailendra Ajmera (Karnataka High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Karnataka High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pankaj Kumar Singhal Vs Shailendra Ajmera (Karnataka High Court) Summary: The petitioner, who is the Resolution Professional of Byju’s K3 Education Private Limited (Byju’s K3), approached the High Court seeking, inter alia, setting aside of the order dated 13.08.2026 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench in I.A. No. 768/2026 in C.P. (IB) No. 29/2025, and quashing of the public announcement dated 02.08.2026 concerning sale of certain assets at IndoSpace Logistics Complex, Bommasandra, Bengaluru. The petitioner apprehended that Respondent No.1, being the Resolution Professional of Think and Learn Private Limited, a subsidiary or related company of Byju’s K3, was proposing to sell properties allegedly belonging to Byju’s K3, which could adversely affect the insolvency resolution process being conducted by the petitioner. The High Court noted that the matter was already seized of by the National Company Law Tribunal and that the assets of both companies were in the custody of the Tribunal. The Court therefore held that the petitioner should pursue the matter before the NCLT and that parallel proceedings could not be initiated before the High Court, particularly when the dispute was between two Resolution Professionals. The writ petition was accordingly disposed of by reserving liberty to the petitioner to move the pending proceedings before the NCLT on 20.08.2026 and directing the NCLT to take up the matter and pass appropriate orders. The High Court further permitted the petitioner to produce documents that subsequently came into his possession and to file such other applications as may be considered necessary before the NCLT, including a copy of the writ petition. The NCLT was directed to consider the matter as expeditiously as possible and, in any event, within 15 days from the following day. The Court also observed that, if necessary, the NCLT could exercise its discretion to protect the assets of the companies in the manner it considered appropriate. The decision underscores the principle that disputes concerning assets forming part of an ongoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP), particularly disputes between Resolution Professionals, should ordinarily be addressed before the Adjudicating Authority already seized of the insolvency proceedings rather than through parallel writ proceedings. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF KARNATAKA HIGH COURT 1. The petitioner is before this Court seeking for the following reliefs: A. Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of certiorari setting aside the order dated 13.08.2026 (Annexure-A) passed by the Hon’ble National Company Law Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench in 1.A No. 768/2026 (Annexure-S) filed in C.P (IB) 29 of 2025, in so far as it declines to halt the sale of the assets lying at the at IndoSpace Logistics Complex, Bommasandra, 2nd Floor, Plot Nos. 183 to 187 and 254 to 258, Bommasandra Jigani Link Road, Bengaluru, Karnataka – 562106; B. Issue a writ, order or direction quashing the public announcement dated 02.08.2026 (Annexure-V) for the sale of the allegedly identified assets of Think & Learn Private Limited issued under Regulation 29 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 as being illegal, arbitrary and violative of principles of natural justice; C. Set aside/cancel the sale of the assets (if any) to an alleged successful bidder pursuant to the public announcement dated 02.08.2026 (Annexure-V) and restrain Respondent No.1 from concluding, confirming, or giving effect to any sale of the said assets, and from executing any sale certificate or other document of transfer, and from effecting delivery of possession of any part of the said assets in favour of Respondent No.2 or any other bidder; D. Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of mandamus directing a joint physical verification of the said warehouse by the Petitioner or his nominees and Respondent No.1 or his nominees, with liberty to photograph and video-record, including but not limited to: open cartons, to record device serial numbers and carton identifiers and to inspect the server room, and to file a joint inventory before the Hon’ble Tribunal; E. Direct the Hon’ble Tribunal to take up and dispose of I.A. (IBC) No. 768 of 2026 (Annexure-S) in a time-bound manner; F. Award costs in favour of the Petitioner And pass any such other further orders that this Hon’ble Court may deem fit in the interests of justice and equity 2. Petitioner is a Resolution Professional of Byju’s K3
rows.summary:
This Karnataka High Court decision does not create a new corporate rule; rather, it deals with a dispute during ongoing insolvency proceedings over whether certain assets at the IndoSpace Logistics Complex, Bommasandra, Bengaluru, belonged to Byju’s K3 Education Private Limited or were being wrongfully treated as assets of Think and Learn Private Limited. The petitioner, who is the Resolution Professional of Byju’s K3, challenged an NCLT Bengaluru order dated 13.08.2026 in I.A. No. 768/2026 in C.P. (IB) No. 29/2025, and also sought to quash a public announcement dated 02.08.2026 issued under Regulation 29 of the CIRP Regulations for sale of the disputed assets. The petitioner alleged that the Resolution Professional of Think and Learn Private Limited was attempting to sell property at the warehouse site—specifically the premises at IndoSpace Logistics Complex, Bommasandra, 2nd Floor, Plot Nos. 183 to 187 and 254 to 258, Bommasandra Jigani Link Road, Bengaluru, Karnataka 562106—despite the assets allegedly belonging to Byju’s K3, and asked for a halt to any sale, cancellation of any sale already completed, a joint physical verification of the warehouse, access to open cartons and server rooms, and a joint inventory.

The High Court declined to entertain the writ petition as a parallel proceeding, emphasizing that the NCLT was already seized of the insolvency matter and that the relevant assets were under the Tribunal’s custody. The Court held that disputes of this kind, especially disputes between two Resolution Professionals over assets connected with a corporate insolvency resolution process, should be pursued before the Adjudicating Authority rather than through separate writ proceedings in the High Court. It therefore disposed of the petition while granting liberty to the petitioner to pursue the pending proceedings before the NCLT on 20.08.2026 and to file additional applications and documents before that forum, including documents that came into his possession after the writ filing and a copy of the writ petition itself.

Importantly for compliance teams handling CIRP asset sales, the High Court directed the NCLT to take up the dispute and pass appropriate orders as expeditiously as possible, and in any event within 15 days from the following day. The Court also noted that the NCLT could, if necessary, exercise its discretion to protect the companies’ assets in whatever manner it considered appropriate. The practical takeaway is that where there is an asset-title or ownership dispute within an ongoing CIRP, especially between resolution professionals, the forum already supervising the insolvency should be approached immediately, and sale actions should not be assumed to be beyond challenge until the NCLT resolves the matter.

Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The two appeals concern a common dispute regarding the levy of Service Tax on charges collected by M/s Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) towards certification of SOFTEX forms and issuance of No Objection Certificates (NoCs). The Department classified these activities under “Business Support Service” under the Finance Act, 1994. In appeal no. ST/20226/2014, the dispute covered the period from 2007-08 to 2011-12 and involved Service Tax of Rs. 5,15,53,520/- along with interest and penalties. Appeal no. ST/30531/2016 concerned the period April 2012 to June 2012 and involved Service Tax of Rs. 2,06,792/- along with interest and penalties. The Commissioner (Appeals), in the latter appeal, upheld the demand while extending cum-tax benefit. STPI contended that it is an autonomous society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 and functioning under the administrative control of the Department of Electronics and Information Technology, Government of India. It was established, inter alia, to administer and facilitate implementation of the Software Technology Park Scheme. STPI was separately registered with the Service Tax Department and admittedly paid Service Tax on various services including renting of immovable property, bandwidth services, co-location services and project consultancy. The controversy was confined to charges connected with activities under the STP Scheme, particularly SOFTEX certification and issuance of NoCs. The appellant argued that certification of SOFTEX forms and issuance of NoCs were statutory functions entrusted to STPI under the Foreign Trade Policy, FEMA and relevant RBI Circulars. According to STPI, such functions could not be regarded as services rendered in relation to business or commerce. Reliance was placed on Board Circular Nos. 89/2006-ST dated 18.12.2006 and 96/07/2007-ST dated 23.08.2007, contending that activities performed by a foreign or Public authority in discharge of statutory duties against collection of statutory fees were not liable to Service Tax. STPI further submitted that its constitution as a Society did not take away the statutory character of the functions performed by it. It also contended that the charges were prescribed and controlled by its Governing Council headed by the concerned Minister of the Government of India. Several judicial decisions were relied upon by the appellant in support of its submissions. The Department, on the other hand, contended that STPI was an autonomous society and not a department of the Central Government. According to the Department, the services were rendered to STP units for facilitating and supporting their export business and the charges were collected from those units in consideration of services rendered. The Department also submitted that the charges were neither a tax nor a compulsory statutory levy deposited into the Consultation Fund or Government Treasury. The amounts were retained by STPI and utilised towards administrative and establishment expenditure. Consequently, according to the Department, the conditions contemplated by the Board circular relied upon by STPI were not satisfied. The Tribunal identified the principal issue as whether the activities undertaken by STPI constituted taxable Business Support Services or sovereign/statutory functions outside the scope of Service Tax. The Tribunal observed that STPI was incorporated and registered as a society under the Societies Registration Act. Although it functioned under the administrative control of the Central Government and performed functions under the STP Scheme, it did not thereby become a Department of the Government. The mere fact that an activity was regulated by law or that an organisation had been authorised by the Government to perform the activity did not convert every such activity into a sovereign function. The Tribunal distinguished between an activity which could only be performed by the State in exercise of sovereign authority and a service rendered by an autonomous body for facilitating business operations of its clients or members. It found that certification of SOFTEX forms, issuance of NoCs and other assistance rendered to STP units were intrinsically connected with the business activities of software exporters. Such certification and approvals facilitated exports, foreign exchange realisation and compliance with the regulatory framework. rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that charges collected by Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) for certifying SOFTEX forms and issuing No Objection Certificates (NoCs) are taxable under Service Tax as “Business Support Service” under the Finance Act, 1994, rather than being treated as exempt sovereign/statutory functions. The dispute covered two appeal periods: 2007-08 to 2011-12, involving Service Tax demand of Rs. 5,15,53,520 plus interest and penalties, and April 2012 to June 2012, involving Service Tax demand of Rs. 2,06,792 plus interest and penalties; in the later matter, the Commissioner (Appeals) had already upheld the demand while granting cum-tax benefit. STPI argued that it is an autonomous society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, operating under the Department of Electronics and Information Technology, and that SOFTEX certification/NoC issuance were statutory functions under the Foreign Trade Policy, FEMA, and RBI circulars, so they should not be taxed; it relied on Board Circulars No. 89/2006-ST dated 18.12.2006 and No. 96/07/2007-ST dated 23.08.2007, which it claimed exempted statutory-fee activities performed by public authorities. The Department countered that STPI is not a Central Government department, that the charges were collected from STP units as consideration for facilitating their export business, and that the amounts were retained by STPI and used for administrative and establishment expenses rather than being collected as a compulsory statutory levy paid into the Government treasury or a consultation fund.

The Tribunal accepted the Department’s position and emphasized that merely because an activity is regulated by law or an organization is authorized by the Government does not make every such activity a sovereign function. It distinguished between truly sovereign acts that only the State can perform and services provided by an autonomous body to support business operations; it found that SOFTEX certification, NoCs, and related assistance are directly connected with software exporters’ business, foreign exchange realization, and regulatory compliance. On that basis, the Tribunal concluded STPI was providing business facilitation/support to STP units and that the resulting charges were taxable as Business Support Service. Practically, the ruling means STPI’s SOFTEX certification and NoC charges for the relevant periods remain liable to Service Tax, along with the associated interest and penalties, and the earlier cum-tax relief in the 2012 period did not alter the underlying taxability finding.

rows.title: Service Tax | SVLDRS Discharge Certificate Bars Revenue Appeal on Same Dispute: CESTAT Hyderabad
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12586 Case Name Commissioner of Central Tax Vs Big C Mobiles Pvt. Ltd. (CESTAT Hyderabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Commissioner of Central Tax Vs Big C Mobiles Pvt. Ltd. (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: CESTAT Hyderabad dismissed the Revenue’s appeal against an Order-in-Original which had confirmed service tax of Rs.1,43,75,615/- for the normal period while dropping the demand attributable to the extended period. The respondent, Big C Mobiles Pvt. Ltd., was engaged in sale of mobile phones through retail outlets in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. Proceedings had been initiated through Show Cause Notice No.20/2018-19 dated 21.12.2018 alleging non-payment of service tax on insurance coverage charges collected from customers during 2013-14 to June 2018. After adjudication, the Commissioner confirmed the demand only for the normal period and dropped the extended-period demand. Thereafter, the respondent opted for settlement under the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme, 2019. Its declaration was accepted, the amount determined was paid and Form SVLDRS-4 dated 10.02.2020 was issued as a discharge certificate for full and final settlement. The Tribunal held that the legal effect of such certificate, particularly under Section 129 of the Finance Act, 2019, was to bring finality to the matter and period covered by the declaration. It relied upon Astute Valuers and Consultants Pvt. Ltd. Vs Union of India (Bombay High Court), where continuation of proceedings after issuance of a discharge certificate was held inconsistent with the object and statutory finality of the Scheme. The Tribunal also independently examined limitation. The Show Cause Notice dated 21.12.2018 was the fifth notice involving substantially similar issues, and earlier notices had already been adjudicated. Therefore, the Department was fully aware of the respondent’s accounting method, collection of insurance charges and service-tax treatment. Relying upon Nizam Sugar Factory Vs Collector of Central Excise, A.P., the Tribunal held that once relevant facts were already within the Department’s knowledge through earlier notices, suppression could not be alleged again for invoking the extended period. The Tribunal consequently held that the SVLDRS discharge certificate rendered the departmental appeal unsustainable and, even otherwise, the Commissioner had correctly restricted the demand to the normal period. Revenue’s appeal was dismissed. Cases Discussed / Relied Upon Astute Valuers and Consultants Pvt. Ltd. Vs Union of India (Bombay High Court) — relied upon for the proposition that issuance of an SVLDRS discharge certificate brings finality to the matter and period covered and proceedings on the same dispute cannot thereafter continue. Nizam Sugar Factory Vs Collector of Central Excise, A.P. [2006 (197) E.L.T. 465 (S.C.)] — relied upon for the principle that where earlier show-cause notices on identical facts have already placed the Department in possession of the relevant facts, extended limitation cannot subsequently be invoked on the allegation of suppression. FULL TEXT OF THE CESTAT HYDERABAD ORDER The present appeal has been filed by the Revenue against the Order-in-Original No. HYD-EXCUS-004-COM-005-19-20 dated 18.12.2019, whereby, the Learned Commissioner confirmed Service Tax demand only to the extent of Rs. 1,43,75,615/- falling within the normal period while dropping the demand pertaining to the extended period along with consequential relief. 2. The Revenue is aggrieved by the dropping of the demand relatable to the extended period and has preferred the present appeal. 3. The respondent has opposed the appeal by submitting that after passing the impugned Order-in-Original, the entire dispute stood finally settled under the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme, 2019 (SVLDRS) and a discharge certificate under Section 127 of the Finance Act, 2019 was issued on 10.02.2020. It is further submitted that the appeal itself is not maintainable in view of Section 129 of the scheme. The respondent has also relied upon the recent judgments of the Hon’ble Bombay High Court in Astute Valuers and Consultants Pvt Ltd., Vs Union of India [2026 (39) Centax 98 (Bom.)] and the decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Nizam Sugar Factory Vs Collector of Central Excise, A.P. [2006 (197) E.L.T. 465 (S.C.)]. 4. The fact, in brief, is that the respondent is engaged in the business of sale of Mobile Phones through its retail outlets situated in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. 5. Proceedings were initiated by issuances of Show Cause Notice No. 20/2018-19 dated 21.12.2018 alleging non-payment of Service Tax on insurance coverage charges collected from customers
rows.summary:
The Revenue appealed an Order-in-Original dated 18.12.2019 that had confirmed service tax only for the normal limitation period and had dropped the demand for the extended period. The underlying dispute arose from Show Cause Notice No. 20/2018-19 dated 21.12.2018, issued to Big C Mobiles Pvt. Ltd., which sells mobile phones through retail outlets in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, alleging non-payment of service tax on insurance coverage charges collected from customers during the period 2013-14 through June 2018. The Commissioner ultimately confirmed service tax of Rs. 1,43,75,615/- only for the normal period and granted consequential relief by rejecting the extended-period allegation.

After that adjudication, the taxpayer opted into the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme, 2019 (SVLDRS). Its declaration was accepted, the determined amount was paid, and Form SVLDRS-4 was issued on 10.02.2020 as a discharge certificate signifying full and final settlement. The CESTAT held that once a discharge certificate is issued under Section 127 of the Finance Act, 2019, Section 129 gives finality to the dispute for the period covered by the declaration, so the Department cannot continue pursuing an appeal on the same dispute; the Tribunal relied on Astute Valuers and Consultants Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India for that proposition. Independently, the Tribunal also agreed with the Commissioner on limitation: this was the fifth show-cause notice on substantially the same issue, earlier notices had already been adjudicated, and the Department therefore already knew the relevant facts about the company’s accounting method, collection of insurance charges, and service-tax treatment. Because those facts were already within the Department’s knowledge, the Tribunal applied the Supreme Court’s ruling in Nizam Sugar Factory to hold that suppression could not be alleged again to invoke the extended period. On both grounds—the SVLDRS discharge certificate and the merits of the limitation finding—the Revenue’s appeal was dismissed.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12584 Case Name Jaswant Singh @ Rolly Babu Vs Union of India (Patna High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Patna High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Jaswant Singh @ Rolly Babu Vs Union of India (Patna High Court) Summary: The Patna High Court considered the regular bail application of Shri Jaswant Singh @ Rolly Babu in connection with Complaint Case No. 49 of 2026, arising from allegations under Section 132(1)(a), (b), (c) and (d) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017. The petitioner was arrested following summons/interrogation in a CGST complaint concerning alleged tax evasion and fraudulent transactions. The prosecution alleged that the petitioner issued tax invoices to multiple beneficiary firms without actual physical movement or supply of goods, fraudulently availed input tax credit without actual receipt of goods or services and without corresponding e-way bills, falsified accounts and financial records, and abetted and operated shell entities by controlling GST credentials, banking operations, passwords and compliance activities. The alleged revenue implication was approximately Rs. 73.75 crores. The petitioner denied the allegations and contended that his arrest was based merely on suspicion and without the requisite “reason to believe”. He argued that the allegations principally rested upon statements of proprietors of other firms and co-accused persons, without giving him an opportunity for cross-examination. He also submitted that the allegation concerning control of GST credentials was incorrect, that no incriminating material, notebook or diary was found during the search of his residence, and that the filing of returns and other forms had been handled by his accountant. According to the petitioner, investigation of the relevant IP address would be necessary before attributing responsibility for electronic filings. Reliance was placed on Section 69 of the CGST Act, 2017, under which the Commissioner must have reasons to believe that the person has committed specified offences under Section 132 before authorising arrest. The petitioner argued that the arrest authorisation and arrest memo did not disclose the requisite reason to believe or the monetary threshold relevant to the alleged offence. He also relied upon Section 132 of the CGST Act, 2017 concerning offences and punishment. The petitioner relied upon Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Anr. and reproduced the Supreme Court’s directions requiring arrest to be preceded by consideration of necessity and appropriate reasons and requiring Magistrates to scrutinise the basis for detention. Reliance was also placed on Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Anr., including the principles concerning arrest under Section 35 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. The petitioner further relied upon State of Punjab v. Davinder Pal Singh Bhullar, Radhika Agarwal v. Union of India, Andaman Timber Industries v. CCE, Shri Mukesh Agarwal v. UOI and Sanket Mittal v. Central GST Department. He emphasised that the investigation had been completed and the charge sheet filed, that there was no possibility of tampering with evidence, and that he had remained in judicial custody since 26.05.2026. The Union of India opposed bail, submitting that the matter involved an economic offence which should be dealt with sternly. It referred to the punishment prescribed under Section 132 for wrongly availed or utilised input tax credit or refund exceeding the statutory thresholds, submitting that where the amount exceeded Rs. 5 crores, the punishment could extend to five years. Having heard the parties and considered the facts and circumstances, the Patna High Court was inclined to enlarge the petitioner on bail. The Court directed his release in Complaint Case No. 49 of 2026 upon furnishing a bail bond of Rs.10,000/- with two sureties of the like amount each to the satisfaction of the learned Special Judge, Economic Offence, Patna/Concerned Court, Patna. The order therefore resulted in grant of regular bail to the petitioner; it did not finally adjudicate the allegations concerning fake invoices, fraudulent input tax credit, falsification of records or operation of shell entities. rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Notice Only Under Additional Notices Tab Violates Natural Justice: Calcutta HC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12582 Case Name Subhra Baral Vs Deputy Commissioner of Revenue (Calcutta High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Calcutta High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Subhra Baral Vs Deputy Commissioner of Revenue (Calcutta High Court) Summary: The Calcutta High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Subhra Baral challenging the adjudication order dated 28.07.2024 and the appellate order dated 29.05.2025 passed under Section 107 of the West Bengal Goods and Services Tax Act and Section 107 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, whereby the petitioner’s appeal had been dismissed solely on limitation. The petitioner submitted that Show Cause Notice in Form GST DRC-01 No. ZD190524017416E dated 12.05.2024, demanding tax, interest and penalty, had been uploaded on the GST portal only under the “Additional Notice and Orders” tab. According to the petitioner, no separate intimation was received, due to which the notice remained unnoticed and no reply could be filed. The petitioner stated that the adjudication order dated 28.07.2024 came to his knowledge only when his accountant checked the common portal in March 2025. The appeal filed thereafter under Section 107 was dismissed on limitation without examination on merits. The State contended that ample opportunities had been granted and the appeal was correctly rejected as time-barred. The High Court, however, found that the petitioner had made out a prima facie case. It specifically observed that uploading the show cause notice only under the “Additional Notice and Orders” tab without separate intimation had prevented the petitioner from replying and constituted a violation of natural justice. Since the appellate authority had dismissed the appeal only on limitation and had not considered the merits, the Court held that interference was warranted in the peculiar facts of the case. The High Court consequently quashed and set aside both the appellate order dated 29.05.2025 and the adjudication order dated 28.07.2024, and also quashed the consequential bank attachment. Respondent No.1 was directed to revisit the issue by considering on merits the grounds taken in the petitioner’s appeal, grant an opportunity of hearing and pass a fresh reasoned adjudication order in accordance with law within 12 weeks. The decision was directed to be communicated to the petitioner within one week thereafter. The writ petition was accordingly disposed of. FULL TEXT OF THE CALCUTTA HIGH COURT ORDER 1. Affidavit of service filed in Court today be kept with the record. 2. The present petition has been filed challenging inter alia, the legality and validity of the adjudication order dated 28.07.2024 passed by the respondent No.1 and the appellate order dated 29th May, 2025 passed by the respondent no.2 under Section 107 of the West Bengal Goods and Services Tax Act(hereinafter referred to as the said ‘WBGST Act’) and the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (hereinafter referred to as the said ‘CGST Act’), whereby the appeal of the petitioner has been dismissed on ground of limitation. 3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits as follows; i. That a show cause notice in Form DRC 01 No. ZD190524017416E dated 12.05.2024 has been issued to the petitioner demanding tax, interest and penalty. ii. That said notice has been uploaded on the GST portal under the tab ‘Additional Notice and Orders’. Due to this, the petitioner did not get any actual intimation and hence could not respond to the show cause notice. iii. That the petitioner came to know above the adjudication order dated 28.07.2024 only after the accountant checked the common portal in the month of March, 2025. iv. That the petitioner preferred an appeal before the appellate authority under Section 107 of the said Act but the same has been dismissed solely on the ground of limitation, without considering the merits. v. That the entire proceedings and the impugned order are contrary to law and have been passed in violation of principles of natural justice and without due compliance with the procedure prescribed under the said Act. 4. Learned counsel appearing for the State respondents opposed the writ petition and submitted since the petitioner has been granted ample opportunities to defend his case, the appeal has been rightly dismissed on limitation. 5. Having heard the parties and upon perusing the records made available this Court observes as follows; i. The petitioner has been able to make a prima facie case. ii. The fact that show cause notice has been only uploaded under the ‘tab Additional Notice and Orders’ and no separate intimation has been given therefore the petitioner has been unable to reply to the same. This constitutes a violation of natural justice. 6. Since
rows.summary:
This Calcutta High Court decision concerns GST adjudication and appeal proceedings under Section 107 of the West Bengal GST Act and the Central GST Act, 2017. The petitioner challenged an adjudication order dated 28.07.2024 and an appellate order dated 29.05.2025, after the appeal was rejected solely as time-barred. The underlying dispute began with a show cause notice in Form GST DRC-01 No. ZD190524017416E dated 12.05.2024, proposing tax, interest, and penalty; the petitioner argued that the notice was uploaded only in the GST portal’s “Additional Notice and Orders” tab and no separate intimation was sent, so it was never seen in time and no reply could be filed. The court accepted that this portal-only upload, without separate notice, prevented a response and amounted to a violation of natural justice, and it noted that the appellate authority had not examined the merits at all, but had dismissed the appeal only on limitation.

As a result, the High Court quashed both the appellate order dated 29.05.2025 and the adjudication order dated 28.07.2024, and also set aside the consequential bank attachment. The matter was sent back to respondent no. 1 to reconsider the case on the merits of the grounds raised in the appeal, give the petitioner an opportunity of hearing, and pass a fresh reasoned adjudication order in accordance with law within 12 weeks. The court further directed that the decision be communicated to the petitioner within one week after the fresh order is passed. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that GST notices placed only in the portal’s “Additional Notice and Orders” section, without effective intimation, may be vulnerable to challenge on natural justice grounds, especially where the taxpayer is deprived of any chance to respond before adjudication.

(Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court allowed the writ petition filed by M/s Mayur Timber challenging the show-cause notice dated 13.06.2024 and consequential order dated 15.10.2024 passed under Section 74 of the CGST Act, 2017, whereby GST demand of Rs.3,13,894, interest of Rs.4,26,002 and penalty of Rs.3,13,894 had been confirmed on the allegation of ITC availment without actual receipt of goods. The Court found that the show-cause notice, reminder and adjudication order bore neither digital nor physical signatures. Examining Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules, 2017, the Court held that electronic issuance and authentication are distinct and cumulative requirements and that mere generation of a document on the GST portal or allotment of a reference number cannot substitute authentication by signature. A signature authenticates the document, fixes accountability on the issuing officer and safeguards against arbitrariness by evidencing application of mind. Consequently, an unsigned show-cause notice or order is no notice or order in the eyes of law, and the defect is not a curable irregularity but goes to the root of the authority to proceed. The Court further noted that the documents had been uploaded only under “Additional Notices and Orders”, the petitioner learnt about the demand only upon bank recovery proceedings, and no effective personal hearing had been afforded contrary to Section 75(4). The plea of alternative remedy was therefore rejected. The show-cause notice, consequential order dated 15.10.2024 and recovery notice in FORM GST DRC-13 dated 20.08.2025 were set aside, while liberty was granted to the respondents to proceed afresh through a duly authenticated show-cause notice and after providing an effective opportunity of hearing. The Court expressly left all issues on the merits of the tax demand open. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF RAJASTHAN HIGH COURT 1. Prior thereto, an unsigned (as alleged) FORM GST DRC-01 (Summary of Show Cause Notice) along with the Show Cause Notice dated 13.06.2024 was issued on the GST portal. The allegation was that the petitioner had availed ITC of Rs.3,13,894 without actual receipt of goods. 2.1 The impugned order was uploaded on the GST portal on 15.10.2024. It was uploaded under the head “Additional Notices and Orders” and not under “Notices and Orders”. It is stated that the order was never served upon the petitioner manually or in hard copy. Learned counsel for the petitioner argues that the impugned order dated 15.10.2024 was passed without proper communication of the show cause notice. rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST show-cause notice and adjudication order issued under Section 74 of the CGST Act, 2017 are invalid if they are not authenticated by signature. In this case, M/s Mayur Timber challenged a show-cause notice dated 13.06.2024 and the consequential order dated 15.10.2024 confirming GST demand of Rs. 3,13,894, interest of Rs. 4,26,002, and penalty of Rs. 3,13,894, all based on the allegation that the taxpayer had wrongly availed ITC of Rs. 3,13,894 without actual receipt of goods. The Court found that the show-cause notice, reminder, and order bore neither digital nor physical signatures; under Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules, electronic issuance and authentication are separate and cumulative requirements, so mere upload on the GST portal or allotment of a reference number does not amount to lawful authentication. Because a signature is what shows the issuing officer applied mind and takes responsibility for the document, the Court treated an unsigned notice or order as no notice or order in law, not a curable technical defect.

The Court also noted serious service and hearing defects: the order was uploaded only under “Additional Notices and Orders,” not the normal “Notices and Orders” section; it was never manually served; and the taxpayer first learned of it only when its bank informed it on 21.08.2025 that recovery had been initiated. The department had issued FORM GST DRC-13 on 20.08.2025 under Section 79(1)(c) to Kotak Mahindra Bank, directing recovery of Rs. 9,00,820 from the taxpayer’s account, and the bank account was provisionally attached before being released after the taxpayer filed an affidavit dated 22.08.2025. The Court further held that no effective personal hearing had been granted, contrary to Section 75(4), so the alternative-remedy objection was rejected. As a result, the Court set aside the show-cause notice dated 13.06.2024, the order dated 15.10.2024, and the recovery notice in FORM GST DRC-13 dated 20.08.2025, but it expressly allowed the department to start again with a duly authenticated show-cause notice and by giving an effective opportunity of hearing; the merits of the alleged tax demand were left open.

(Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by M/s. Saudi Arabian Airlines and set aside the penalty imposed for delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax (FTT), holding that delayed payment of FTT cannot be equated with failure or non-payment of tax for the purposes of Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979. The Court held that while Section 38(3) deals with non-payment of FTT, delayed deposit falls within Section 38(4) read with the Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979. It further held that imposition of penalty under Section 38 is not automatic merely because a statutory timeline has been breached. The dispute arose from six instances of delayed deposit of FTT collected by the appellant airline. In five instances, the delay ranged from one day to eleven days, though the demand drafts had been purchased before the respective due dates. The appellant explained that the drafts could not be deposited because of security restrictions. In the sixth instance, involving December 1995, there was a delay of 63 days, which was attributed to the concerned employee being on emergency leave. The initial adjudication order had imposed a penalty of Rs.12,000 for the six cases of late payment, but after remand the penalty was enhanced drastically to Rs.71,29,140. Examining Section 38(3), the Supreme Court emphasised the expressions “fails to pay the foreign travel tax” and “the amount of the tax not so paid”. The Court held that “failure to pay” means non-payment and cannot be equated with delay in making payment. If Parliament intended Section 38(3) to cover delayed payment, it could have used language to that effect. In interpreting fiscal statutes, courts cannot expand statutory expressions by importing meanings not used by the legislature. The Court drew support from U.S. Technologies International Private Limited Vs Commissioner of Income Tax, where the Supreme Court had interpreted Section 271C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and held that mere belated remittance of TDS after its deduction did not amount to failure to deduct TDS and therefore did not attract penalty under Section 271C. Applying the same interpretative approach, the Court held that delayed payment of FTT could not be treated as non-payment for invoking Section 38(3). The Supreme Court thereafter examined Section 38(4) of the Finance Act along with Rules 4 and 9 of the Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979. Rule 4 required FTT collected by a carrier to be deposited within 30 days from the end of the month but empowered the Collector of Customs, on sufficient cause being shown and having regard to the carrier’s accounting system, to allow a longer period. Rule 9 similarly prescribed the timeline for filing monthly returns while permitting extension of time. The Court held that this statutory framework demonstrated that the timelines were not inflexible. The Court explained that payment made before issuance of a show-cause notice would constitute delayed payment rather than non-payment. It further observed that where delay was condoned under the proviso to Rule 4, no question of penalty for such delay would arise. Consequently, the view of the authorities below and the Bombay High Court that penalty followed automatically upon breach of the prescribed timeline was held to be incorrect. On the question whether penalty was mandatory, the Supreme Court examined Rule 12, which requires a written show-cause notice, opportunity to make a representation and reasonable opportunity of hearing before penalty can be imposed. According to the Court, such an adjudicatory mechanism necessarily gives the authority discretion to decide whether penalty should be imposed. Treating penalty as automatic would render the statutory opportunity of representation and hearing largely meaningless. The Supreme Court clarified that exclusion of mens rea and automatic imposition of penalty are separate concepts. Certain statutory penalties may not require proof of mens rea, but it does not follow that penalty must automatically be imposed whenever a statutory breach occurs. Whether penalty is automatic depends upon the statutory scheme and the adjudicatory process prescribed by the legislation. The power to impose penalty includes, in an appropriate case, the power not to impose it. Referring to Hindustan Steel Ltd.
