rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax (FTT) by a carrier is **not the same as non-payment or failure to pay tax** for purposes of **Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979**. In this case, Saudi Arabian Airlines had six delayed remittances of collected FTT: in five instances the delay was only **1 to 11 days** and the demand drafts had been purchased before the due dates but could not be deposited because of security restrictions; in the sixth instance, relating to **December 1995**, the delay was **63 days** because the relevant employee was on emergency leave. An initial penalty of **Rs. 12,000** was later drastically enhanced after remand to **Rs. 71,29,140**, but the Supreme Court set aside the penalty and allowed the airline’s appeal.

The Court interpreted the statutory language in Section 38(3) — “**fails to pay the foreign travel tax**” and “**the amount of the tax not so paid**” — to mean **actual non-payment**, not mere late payment. It held that if Parliament intended delayed payment to be covered by Section 38(3), it would have used express language to that effect, and courts cannot expand fiscal penalty provisions by implication. Instead, the Court said delayed deposit falls within **Section 38(4)** read with the **Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979**, which specifically address delayed compliance and allow flexibility.

Under **Rule 4**, collected FTT had to be deposited **within 30 days from the end of the month**, but the **Collector of Customs** could extend that period on **sufficient cause** and having regard to the carrier’s accounting system. **Rule 9** similarly required monthly returns within the prescribed time but also allowed extension. The Court emphasized that this framework shows the deadlines are **not inflexible**; where delay is explained and condoned under the rules, the situation is not one of punishable non-payment. The Court further stated that payment made **before a show-cause notice is issued** is to be treated as **delayed payment**, not failure to pay.

On penalty, the Court relied on **Rule 12**, which requires a **written show-cause notice**, an opportunity to make a **representation**, and a **reasonable opportunity of hearing** before any penalty can be imposed. That procedural structure means the authority must exercise **discretion**; penalty is **not automatic** merely because a deadline was missed. The Court distinguished between cases where mens rea is not required and cases where penalty still remains discretionary, and it reaffirmed the principle from **Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa** that penalty for breach of a statutory obligation depends on the facts and surrounding circumstances. The decision therefore protects carriers and other entities subject to the FTT regime from automatic penalty exposure for late deposit where the tax was in fact collected and the delay is explainable or otherwise dealt with under the rules.

rows.title: Income Tax | PMS Charges Deductible Under Section 48 Amid Divergent Views: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12573 Case Name Ameeta Jagdish Thackersey Vs ITO (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ameeta Jagdish Thackersey Vs ITO (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the assessee’s appeal concerning the allowability of Portfolio Management Service (PMS) charges while computing capital gains under section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The appeal arose from the order of the Ld. CIT(A), dated 28.08.2025, which had sustained the disallowance made by the Assessing Officer under section 143(3) for Assessment Year 2011-12. The assessee had returned total income of Rs. 72,26,297/- from salary, short term capital gain and income from other sources. In computing capital gains, the assessee claimed Rs. 8,42,360/- towards fees and charges paid to Trust Investment Advisors Pvt. Ltd. for portfolio management services. The Assessing Officer disallowed the amount on the ground that the expenditure could not be regarded as expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer of the capital asset within the meaning of section 48. The CIT(A) sustained the disallowance, relying principally upon the Mumbai Tribunal decision in ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah, where PMS fees and performance-linked charges had been held not deductible under section 48. Before the Tribunal, the assessee contended that the issue was unsettled because different coordinate Benches had adopted divergent views. Reliance was placed upon KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT, where PMS fees were allowed as a deduction while computing capital gains. The assessee also submitted that although the Revenue had challenged KRA Holding and Trading before the Bombay High Court, the substantial question raised before the High Court concerned whether PMS income was assessable under the head “capital gains” or “profit and gains of business or profession”; the allowability of PMS charges under section 48 was not raised as a substantial question of law. The assessee further relied upon Zarah Rafik Malik v. ITO and ACIT v. Vireet Investment Pvt. Ltd., both of which had taken a view favourable to deduction of PMS expenses in the circumstances considered by those Benches. The Revenue, on the other hand, relied upon ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah and contended that PMS charges were composite in nature, relating to advisory, management and consultancy services rather than being directly relatable to acquisition or transfer of particular securities. The Tribunal noted that divergent views existed. The Mumbai Bench in Apurva Mahesh Shah had held PMS fees not deductible under section 48, whereas the Pune Bench in KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd., the Mumbai Bench in Zarah Rafik Malik and the Delhi Bench in Vireet Investment Pvt. Ltd. had allowed such deduction on the facts before them. The Tribunal then applied the principle laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd. [(1973) 88 ITR 192 (SC)]. It held that where two reasonable and plausible constructions of a taxing provision are possible, the interpretation favourable to the assessee should be adopted, particularly where no binding decision of the jurisdictional High Court or Supreme Court directly settles the controversy. The Tribunal found that the Revenue had not brought to its notice any binding decision of the Hon’ble Bombay High Court or the Hon’ble Supreme Court specifically holding that PMS charges were not deductible under section 48. Accordingly, following the assessee-favouring principle, it adopted the favourable view and held that the PMS charges of Rs. 8,42,360/- were allowable as a deduction while computing capital gains under section 48. The orders of the revenue authorities were set aside on this issue and the Assessing Officer was directed to allow the assessee’s claim. The appeal was consequently allowed. Cases Discussed KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT — Pune ITAT decision allowing PMS fees as deduction while computing capital gains. ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah — Mumbai ITAT decision holding PMS and performance-linked fees not deductible under section 48. Zarah Rafik Malik v. ITO — Mumbai ITAT decision relied upon for allowing PMS expenses in the circumstances discussed. ACIT v. Vireet Investment Pvt. Ltd. — Delhi ITAT decision allowing PMS-related expenditure on the facts considered. CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd. [(1973) 88 ITR 192 (SC)] — Supreme Court principle that where two reasonable constructions of a taxing provision are possible, the construction favourable to the assessee should be adopted. FULL TEXT OF THE ORDER OF ITAT MUMBAI The instant appeal of the assessee filed against the order of the Ld. Assistant Commissioner
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that Portfolio Management Service (PMS) fees are deductible while computing capital gains under section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, at least on the facts of this case, where the assessee had paid **Rs. 8,42,360** to **Trust Investment Advisors Pvt. Ltd.** for PMS. The assessee, **Ameeta Jagdish Thackersey**, had returned **total income of Rs. 72,26,297** for **Assessment Year 2011-12**, comprising salary, short-term capital gains, and income from other sources; the Assessing Officer disallowed the PMS charges in a **section 143(3)** assessment on the ground that they were not expenditure incurred “wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer” of capital assets under section 48. The **CIT(A) order dated 28.08.2025** upheld that disallowance, relying mainly on **ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah**, where the Mumbai Bench had held PMS fees and performance-linked charges not deductible under section 48.

On appeal, the assessee argued that the law was unsettled because different ITAT Benches had taken different views, citing **KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT** (Pune ITAT), **Zarah Rafik Malik v. ITO** (Mumbai ITAT), and **ACIT v. Vireet Investment Pvt. Ltd.** (Delhi ITAT), all of which had accepted deduction of PMS-related expenses in the circumstances before them. The assessee also pointed out that although the Revenue had challenged **KRA Holding** before the Bombay High Court, the substantial question there concerned whether the income was taxable as **capital gains** or **business income**; it did **not** specifically raise the deductibility of PMS charges under section 48. The Revenue maintained that PMS charges were composite advisory/management/consultancy fees and not directly linked to the acquisition or transfer of any particular security, so they should not qualify under section 48.

The Tribunal noted the existence of divergent coordinate Bench rulings and found no binding judgment of either the **Bombay High Court** or the **Supreme Court** squarely holding that PMS charges are not deductible under section 48. Applying the Supreme Court’s rule in **CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd. (88 ITR 192)**—that where two reasonable interpretations of a taxing provision exist, the interpretation favorable to the assessee should be adopted—the Tribunal chose the assessee-favouring view. It therefore **allowed the deduction of Rs. 8,42,360 as PMS charges** in computing capital gains, **set aside the revenue authorities’ orders on this issue, and directed the Assessing Officer to allow the claim**. The appeal was consequently allowed.

Ltd. challenging an assessment order dated 15.10.2018 to the extent it disallowed refund of input tax credit lying in the Electronic Credit Ledger under the head SGST credit. The respondents also objected to maintainability of the writ petition because the petitioner had not exhausted the statutory remedy and had approached the High Court after expiry of the limitation period for appeal. The petitioner argued that an appeal would be futile because the adjudicating authority had acted on a departmental circular that would also bind the appellate authority. It observed that transitional credit representing the closing balance of eligible taxes lying in the last return under the erstwhile regime as on 30.06.2017 would be carried forward as credit in the Electronic Credit Ledger as on 01.07.2017. Consequently, unutilised input tax credit under the erstwhile regime as on 30.06.2017 would be available as the opening balance of unutilised ITC on 01.07.2017. The petitioner had not produced a copy of the declaration in Form GST TRAN-1 required to be filed within the prescribed period and had not produced satisfactory material proving the credit in its Electronic Credit Ledger as on 01.07.2017. The adjudicating authority could allow the refund only upon proof that the amount claimed stood credited in the Electronic Credit Ledger as on 01.07.2017. In the absence of such satisfactory material, the Court found no reason to interfere with the impugned adjudication order. The High Court also dealt with the belated invocation of its writ jurisdiction. The Kerala High Court dismissed AVT McCormick Ingredients Pvt. Ltd.’s writ challenge to an assessment order dated 15.10.2018 that had disallowed its GST refund claim to the extent of SGST input tax credit lying in the Electronic Credit Ledger. The company, an exporter of spice extracts and oleoresins, had earlier been registered under the Kerala VAT regime and had filed Form GST TRAN-1 in November 2017 to transition excess pre-GST input tax credit into the GST Electronic Credit Ledger; it claimed that this transitional credit was reflected in the ledger on 27.12.2017 and used that balance to support a refund claim for November 2017. The Department rejected the refund on the ground that transitional credit is not “Net ITC” for purposes of Rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017, as clarified by Circular No. 37/11/2018-GST dated 15.03.2018, and therefore could not be included in the refund computation.

On the legal position, the Court accepted that Section 140 of the CGST Act and Rule 117 of the CGST Rules permit eligible closing credit under the pre-GST regime as on 30.06.2017 to be carried forward into the Electronic Credit Ledger on 01.07.2017, so that unutilised ITC under the earlier regime could form the opening balance under GST. However, the petitioner failed on proof: it did not produce a copy of the TRAN-1 declaration filed within the prescribed period and did not produce satisfactory evidence showing the credit standing in its Electronic Credit Ledger as on 01.07.2017. The Court held that refund could be allowed only if the claimant proves that the amount claimed was actually credited in the ledger as of 01.07.2017, and in the absence of such material, there was no basis to interfere with the adjudication order.

The Court also rejected the writ petition on maintainability grounds because the company had not exhausted statutory remedies and had approached the High Court only after the limitation period for appeal had expired. It noted that Sections 107 and 108 of the CGST Act provide appeal and revision mechanisms against adjudication orders, and that a taxpayer cannot let the statutory appeal period lapse and then use that lapse as a basis to invoke Article 226. The Court relied on Supreme Court authority, including A.V. Venkateswaran, Rikhab Chand Jain, and Glaxo Smith Kline Consumer Health Care, to emphasize that writ jurisdiction must be exercised promptly and consistently with the legislative scheme; it also noted that the petitioner’s reliance on Moriroku UT India was undermined because that High Court decision had been set aside by the Supreme Court. In practical compliance terms, the decision underscores that refund claims based on transitional credit must be supported by timely filed TRAN-1 documentation and evidence of the exact ledger position as on 01.07.2017, and that missed statutory appeal deadlines are unlikely to be cured by later filing a writ petition.

Vs Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The CESTAT Hyderabad partly allowed the appeal of Lahari Holiday Homes Ltd. against an Order-in-Original confirming service tax of Rs.1,63,15,458/- with interest under “Club or Association Service”, besides penalties under Sections 76, 77 and 78 of the Finance Act, 1994 and smaller demands under Mandap Keeper Service, Internet Café Service, Rent-a-Cab Scheme Operator Service and Renting of Immovable Property Service. The appellant operated Lahari Resorts and had introduced a Time Share Holiday Scheme under which customers acquired a contractual right to occupy specified accommodation for one week every year for 12 years against predetermined consideration. The Tribunal examined whether persons enrolled under the Time Share Scheme could be regarded as “members” of a club or association merely because the agreement used that terminology. It held that taxability must depend upon the real legal and commercial character of the arrangement rather than nomenclature. The customers acquired no proprietary, voting, management or shareholding rights in the appellant company. Their relationship with the appellant remained that of customer and service provider, and they merely purchased accommodation rights for specified periods. The Tribunal also noted that the appellant was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and that the time-share customers did not become members of the company in accordance with that Act. They neither subscribed to the memorandum, became shareholders, nor had their names entered in the register of members. Therefore, the foundation for treating them as members of a “Club or Association” was held to be legally unsustainable. The Tribunal relied heavily upon State of West Bengal Vs Calcutta Club Ltd. and noted that the Supreme Court had explained that incorporated clubs and associations constituted under statutory enactments stood on a different footing and that charging provisions must be interpreted strictly. The Tribunal further observed that commercial hospitality arrangements could not become “Club or Association Service” merely because customers were described as members. It also relied upon Bharat Hotels Ltd. and Adarsh Realty & Hotel Pvt. Ltd., where loyalty or membership programmes of hotels were treated as commercial hospitality arrangements rather than club membership. A further significant factor was the introduction of “Short Term Accommodation Service” under Section 65(105)(zzzzw) of the Finance Act, 1994 with effect from 01.05.2011. According to the Tribunal, creation of this specific taxable category supported the conclusion that hotel and resort accommodation was not intended to be taxed earlier under “Club or Association Service”. The dominant object of the appellant’s Time Share Scheme was accommodation, not the provision of club facilities or privileges. On the facts, the consideration paid by each customer was directly linked to the category of accommodation selected. Customers acquired only a contractual right to occupy accommodation for one week each year during the tenure of the scheme. rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that Lahari Holiday Homes Ltd.’s time-share holiday scheme was **not taxable as “Club or Association Service”** under the Finance Act, 1994, because the customers were not actually members of a club or association in the legal sense. The company operated Lahari Resorts and offered customers a contractual right to occupy specified accommodation for **one week every year for 12 years** in exchange for predetermined consideration; although the agreement used “member”-type language, the Tribunal said taxability depends on the **real legal and commercial substance**, not labels.

The Tribunal emphasized that the time-share customers had **no proprietary, voting, management, or shareholding rights** in the company and did not become members of the company under the Companies Act, 1956. They did not subscribe to the memorandum, become shareholders, or have their names entered in the register of members, so the legal basis for treating them as “members” of a club/association was absent. The relationship was therefore one of **customer and service provider**, not members of a mutual club or association, and the dominant object of the scheme was **accommodation**, not club privileges, sports, recreation, or similar facilities.

A significant point in the decision was the Tribunal’s reliance on the later introduction of **“Short Term Accommodation Service” under Section 65(105)(zzzzw)** of the Finance Act, 1994, effective **1 May 2011**. The Tribunal viewed this as supporting the conclusion that hotel/resort accommodation was not meant to be taxed earlier under the “Club or Association Service” head merely because it involved a membership-style arrangement. It also relied on the Supreme Court’s reasoning in **State of West Bengal v. Calcutta Club Ltd.** and on prior hospitality-sector cases such as **Bharat Hotels Ltd.** and **Adarsh Realty & Hotel Pvt. Ltd.**, which treated similar membership/loyalty arrangements as commercial hospitality transactions rather than club services.

On the tax demand side, the original order had confirmed **service tax of Rs. 1,63,15,458/-** along with interest under “Club or Association Service,” plus smaller demands under **Mandap Keeper Service, Internet Café Service, Rent-a-Cab Scheme Operator Service, and Renting of Immovable Property Service**, and penalties under **Sections 76, 77, and 78** of the Finance Act, 1994. The Tribunal set aside the entire **Club or Association Service** demand, but upheld the view that the smaller category-wise liabilities had already been **voluntarily paid in full along with applicable interest before the show-cause notice was issued**. Because the Department did not dispute the payment or quantum, and there was no evidence of fraud, wilful suppression, or clandestine conduct, the Tribunal held the appellant was entitled to the protection of **Section 73(3)**, and therefore the penalties under Sections 76, 77, and 78 were not sustainable. The Tribunal also noted that the appellant had maintained regular books, the time-share receipts were disclosed in audited financial statements, and the Department’s case was built on the appellant’s own records, showing that the dispute was about **classification and interpretation**, not concealment.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Customs Cannot Indefinitely Detain Imported Car Without Seizure Order: Gujarat HC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12569 Case Name Pranavbhai Ambalal Patel Vs Additional Director General (Gujarat High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Gujarat High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pranavbhai Ambalal Patel Vs Additional Director General (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court allowed a writ petition challenging the prolonged detention and subsequent seizure of a Toyota Land Cruiser imported from Japan. The petitioner purchased the vehicle for USD 54,000, filed Bill of Entry No.7472252 dated 26.12.2024 and paid customs duty of Rs.99,78,795. Out-of-charge was granted on 02.01.2025. On 07.02.2025, however, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the petitioner’s residence, prepared a Panchnama and directed him not to deal with or part with the vehicle. No contemporaneous seizure order under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 was passed. During pendency of the writ petition, the DRI ultimately issued a seizure memo only on 17.04.2026, more than one year after the original detention, followed by a show-cause notice dated 08.05.2026 under Section 124 read with Section 28(4). The Department also passed a provisional release order on 18.05.2026 requiring a bond for Rs.85,95,860 and a bank guarantee of Rs.1.20 crore by relying upon paragraph 2 of Circular No.35/2017-Customs dated 16.08.2017. The High Court noted that the relied-upon part of the Circular had already been struck down by the Delhi High Court in Shanus Impex Vs Union of India & Ors. to the extent it curtailed the adjudicating authority’s discretion. The Gujarat High Court strongly deprecated the Department’s continued reliance upon that paragraph. The Court rejected the Department’s attempt to attribute the delay in initiating Section 110 proceedings to pendency of the writ petition. It examined the sequence of interim orders and found that the High Court had never restrained the DRI from investigating or proceeding under the Customs Act. On the contrary, the Court repeatedly directed completion of the investigation. The High Court characterised the statement that pendency of the writ petition prevented initiation of Section 110 proceedings as a bald assertion and observed that the record showed that time had instead been consumed by the Department. The Court relied substantially upon Union of India & Ors. Vs Jatin Ahuja, where the Supreme Court held that where goods are seized under Section 110(1), notice under Section 124(a) must be given within six months, subject to a permissible extension of another six months under Section 110(2); absent such notice even within the extended period, the seized goods have to be released. The Gujarat High Court emphasised the legal distinction between “detention” and “seizure”. Merely recording in a Panchnama that the owner should not remove, part with or otherwise deal with the goods cannot substitute for an order contemplated by Section 110. Where seizure is undertaken, the proper officer must record reasons to believe that the goods are liable to confiscation. Where physical seizure is not practicable, the statutory provisos themselves prescribe the manner in which custody or restrictions are to be imposed. Relying upon Worldline Tradex Pvt. Ltd., the Court reiterated that detention through a Panchnama cannot automatically be treated as a seizure under Section 110(1). The Court also examined Instruction No.01/2017-Cus. dated 08.02.2017, which specifically directs field formations that whenever goods are seized, an appropriate seizure memo/order must be passed in addition to the Panchnama and must clearly record the reasons to believe that the goods are liable to confiscation. Where immediate seizure is impracticable, an appropriate statutory order restricting dealings with the goods has to be served and investigation must be fast-tracked. Construing these statutory requirements together, the High Court held that the seizure order must be coterminous with, or follow the Panchnama without permitting indefinite detention. Customs authorities cannot keep goods detained for an unlimited period and subsequently issue a Section 110(1) seizure order merely to restart the six-month limitation period under Section 110(2). In the present case, time began running from the actual detention of the vehicle under the Panchnama dated 07.02.2025. The seizure memo issued on 17.04.2026, after more than one year, could not enable the DRI to reap the benefit of its own inaction by thereafter issuing the Section 124 notice on 08.05.2026. The Court further declared the provisional release order dated 18.05.2026 illegal because its conditions were based upon paragraph 2 of Circular No.35/2017-Customs, already struck down in Shanus Impex. rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court held that customs authorities cannot keep imported goods—here, a Toyota Land Cruiser imported from Japan—under indefinite “detention” through a Panchnama and then much later issue a seizure memo under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 in an attempt to restart the limitation clock for notice and confiscation proceedings. In this case, the importer filed Bill of Entry No. 7472252 dated 26.12.2024 and paid customs duty of Rs. 99,78,795; out-of-charge was granted on 02.01.2025. The DRI searched the importer’s residence on 07.02.2025, recorded a Panchnama, and directed him not to deal with or part with the vehicle, but did not contemporaneously pass a seizure order; only on 17.04.2026 did it issue a seizure memo, followed by a show-cause notice on 08.05.2026 under Section 124 read with Section 28(4).

The Court emphasized the legal distinction between detention and seizure: a Panchnama restraining the owner from dealing with the goods is not, by itself, a valid Section 110 seizure, and if seizure is intended the proper officer must record “reasons to believe” that the goods are liable to confiscation. The Court relied on Supreme Court authority in Union of India v. Jatin Ahuja, reiterating that where goods are seized under Section 110(1), notice under Section 124(a) must be issued within six months, extendable by another six months under Section 110(2), and absent timely notice the goods must be released. It also relied on Worldline Tradex Pvt. Ltd. and Instruction No. 01/2017-Cus. dated 08.02.2017, which require an actual seizure memo/order in addition to the Panchnama and require that, where immediate seizure is impracticable, an appropriate statutory order restricting dealings be served and the investigation fast-tracked.

The Court rejected the Department’s argument that pendency of the writ petition prevented it from initiating proper Section 110 action, noting that the record showed no court order restraining investigation; instead, the Court had repeatedly directed completion of the investigation. It treated the Department’s claim as a bald assertion and found that the delay was attributable to the Department’s own inaction. Critically, the Court held that customs cannot hold goods indefinitely and then issue a Section 110(1) seizure later merely to reset the six-month period under Section 110(2); time ran from the actual detention under the 07.02.2025 Panchnama, so the 17.04.2026 seizure memo could not validate the later notice.

The Court also set aside the provisional release order dated 18.05.2026 because it required a bond of Rs. 85,95,860 and a bank guarantee of Rs. 1.20 crore based on paragraph 2 of Circular No. 35/2017-Customs dated 16.08.2017, which the Delhi High Court had already struck down in Shanus Impex to the extent it curtailed the adjudicating authority’s discretion. The Gujarat High Court strongly deprecated continued departmental reliance on that paragraph and held the provisional release conditions unlawful. In practical compliance terms, the decision warns customs officers that if imported goods are to be restrained or seized, the statutory seizure process must be followed promptly and cannot be backfilled later to extend limitation periods; for importers, it strengthens the position that prolonged detention without a valid seizure order is challengeable and that release conditions must have a lawful statutory basis.

rows.title: Excise Duty | CENVAT Credit Cannot Be Denied When Manufacturer’s Invoice Names Assessee as Consignee: CESTAT Kolkata
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12568 Case Name Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. Vs Commissioner of CGST & C.Ex. (CESTAT Kolkata) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Kolkata Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. Vs Commissioner of CGST & C.Ex. (CESTAT Kolkata) Summary: CESTAT Kolkata allowed the appeal filed by Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. and set aside the demand for reversal of CENVAT credit of Rs.83,839. The appellant had availed credit on the basis of three invoices, two issued in 2011 and one dated 22.01.2014. The Department sought reversal on the ground that the appellant had purchased the goods through M/s Ashis Enterprise, which did not possess dealer registration. The appellant contended that the invoices issued by M/s Roshanlal Bhagirathmal specifically showed Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. as the consignee, while Ashis Enterprise was shown as the buyer. The goods were directly dispatched to the appellant and were duly accounted for in RG 23A Part I. Ashis Enterprise separately issued a commercial invoice to facilitate payment, which could be correlated with the invoice issued by Roshanlal Bhagirathmal. On examining the invoices, the Tribunal found that the appellant was expressly shown as the consignee and that all particulars required for an invoice under Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 were fulfilled. The Tribunal further noted that there was no allegation that the goods had not actually been received by the appellant. The goods had also been accounted for in RG 23A Part I after receipt at the appellant’s factory. In these circumstances, the Tribunal held that the Revenue had failed to establish any contravention of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The demand was accordingly set aside, the appeal was allowed and the appellant was held eligible for consequential relief, if any, in accordance with law. FULL TEXT OF THE CESTAT KOLKATA ORDER The appellant has taken the Cenvat Credit of Rs.83,839 on the basis of the Dealer’s invoice. The credit was taken in respect of of 2 invoices issued in the year 2011 and one invoice issued on 22.01.2014. 2. On the ground that the appellant has bought goods from a Dealer, who did not have Dealer’s Registration, a Show Cause Notice was issued to the appellant seeking reversal of Rs.83,839. After due process, the lower authorities have confirmed the demand. Hence, the appellant is before the Tribunal. 3. The Ld. Consultant appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that the appellant has received the invoices clearly showing the present appellant as the Consignee and the dealer M/s. Ashis Enterprise, as the Buyer. The goods have been directly despatched by M/s. Roshanlal Bhagirathmal with proper Dealer’s Invoice, based on which the appellant has taken the Cenvat Credit. The appellant has also properly accounted for the inputs in the RG 23A Part I as can be observed from the Invoices. The Dealer Ashish Enterprise has issued a separate Invoice so that the payment can be made by the appellant to him. The Invoice issued by Ashish can be correlated with the Dealer’s Invoice issued by Roshanlal Bharatmal. Therefore, it is prayed that the appeal may be allowed. 4. The Ld. Authorized Representative submits that the Ashish Enterprise has not taken the Dealer’s registration. The goods have been received from Roshanlal with this invoice, who is the main seller and the buyer is Ashsish, who has not issued the Dealer’s Invoice. Therefore, it is submitted that the appellant has taken irregular cenvat credit. Therefore, he justifies the confirmed the demand. 5. Heard both the sides. 6. I have gone through the copy of the Invoices produced by the appellant. The sample copy is produced below: 7. From the above Invoice issued by Roshanlal Bhagirathmal, I find that the present appellant is shown as the Consignee. The buyer of the goods is mentioned as Ashis Enterprise. I observe that all the details required under an invoice to issued in terms of Rule 9 of CCR, 2004 have been fulfilled in the invoice raised by the Roshanlal Bhagirathmal. 8. Further, there is no allegation that the goods in question have not been received by the appellant. It is seen that the appellant has accounted for the goods received in RG 23A part I, after the same is received at his factory. 9. Therefore, I do not find any case has been made out by the Revenue towards any contravention of provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules 2004. Hence, I set aside the demand and allow the appeal. 10. The appellant would be eligible for consequent relief if any, as per law. (Dictated & Pronounced in the open court) Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Filed under CENVAT CreditCestat judgments Author Info Name: CA Sandeep Kanoi
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Kolkata held that CENVAT credit cannot be denied merely because the seller’s commercial chain involved a party that did not hold dealer registration, so long as the invoice on which credit is taken satisfies the Rule 9 requirements and the goods were actually received by the assessee. In this case, Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. had taken CENVAT credit of **Rs. 83,839** based on **three invoices**—**two from 2011** and **one dated 22.01.2014**—and the department demanded reversal after alleging the goods were purchased through **M/s Ashis Enterprise**, which allegedly lacked dealer registration. The Tribunal found that the invoice issued by **M/s Roshanlal Bhagirathmal** specifically named the appellant as the **consignee**, while **Ashis Enterprise** was shown as the buyer; it also accepted the appellant’s explanation that Ashis Enterprise issued a separate commercial invoice only to facilitate payment and that this invoice could be correlated to the main seller’s invoice.

The key compliance point is that the Tribunal treated the main seller’s invoice as valid for credit because it contained all particulars required under **Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004**, and there was **no allegation that the goods were not actually received** by the appellant. The appellant also had the goods recorded in **RG 23A Part I** after receipt at its factory, which supported the legitimacy of the credit. Because the Revenue could not establish any contravention of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, the Tribunal **set aside the confirmed demand** and allowed the appeal.

For compliance teams, the case reinforces that when taking credit on third-party procurement arrangements, companies should preserve invoice chains that clearly show the consignee, buyer, and correlation between commercial documents and the tax invoice, and should maintain contemporaneous receipt records such as RG 23A Part I or equivalent inventory/credit records. The decision does **not** create a new deadline or procedural filing requirement, but it underscores the importance of being able to prove actual receipt of goods and documentary compliance under Rule 9 if credit is challenged. The appellant was also held eligible for **consequential relief, if any, in accordance with law**.
