rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12567 Case Name ECI BJCL JV Vs Commissioner of Central Excise and Service Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); ECI BJCL JV Vs Commissioner of Central Excise and Service Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: CESTAT Hyderabad dismissed the appeal filed by ECI BJCL JV and upheld the Commissioner (Appeals)’ order dismissing its service tax appeal for failure to comply with a direction requiring pre-deposit of 50% of the adjudged demand. The appellant had executed EPC/works contracts relating to construction of dams, reservoirs, canals and allied structures for the Government of Andhra Pradesh during June 2007 to March 2012. A show-cause notice dated 23.10.2012 demanded service tax of Rs.43,86,471/- under Works Contract Service, which was confirmed by the adjudicating authority on 09.01.2014. The appellant challenged the order and sought waiver of pre-deposit. The Commissioner (Appeals) fixed the stay application for hearing on 12.06.2014; although the appellant sought an adjournment, the request was declined and, by order dated 13.06.2014, it was directed to deposit 50% of the service tax demand. The appellant subsequently requested a speaking order considering its legal submissions and precedents, but did not comply with the pre-deposit condition. Its appeal was consequently dismissed on 23.07.2014. Before the Tribunal, the appellant argued that its appeal had been dismissed without adjudication on merits and that the Commissioner (Appeals) had failed to consider its prima facie case, balance of convenience and financial hardship. It relied, inter alia, upon Lanco Infratech Ltd., Badve Helmets India Pvt. Ltd., DSM Sugar, Pennar Industries Ltd., Amber Anuruddha Mufti, Surya Pharmaceutical Ltd., B. Rama Rao & Company and Thermopads Pvt. Ltd. The Revenue maintained that adequate opportunity had been provided, the adjournment request had been considered and declined for recorded reasons, and failure to satisfy the pre-deposit condition justified dismissal. The Tribunal found that the Commissioner (Appeals) had granted an opportunity of personal hearing and had expressly considered the appellant’s request for an adjournment of about one month. The request was declined having regard to the statutory requirement of expeditious disposal, and the stay order recorded reasons for directing a 50% pre-deposit. It therefore rejected the contention that the stay order had been passed mechanically or without reasons. The decisions relied upon by the appellant concerning absence of adequate hearing or reasoned orders were held factually distinguishable. The Tribunal further held that the amended provisions of Section 35F of the Central Excise Act, 1944 prescribing a mandatory 10% pre-deposit came into force only from 06.08.2014 and operated prospectively. Since the impugned appellate order had been passed before that amendment, the parties’ rights and obligations continued to be governed by the unamended provision. Consequently, a subsequent deposit of 10% could not cure the appellant’s earlier failure to comply with the 50% conditional stay order. The Tribunal reiterated that the right of appeal is statutory and subject to conditions prescribed by the statute. Under the then applicable Section 35F, the Commissioner (Appeals) could insist upon an appropriate pre-deposit while considering waiver, and once such a condition was imposed, the appellant had either to comply or seek appropriate relief from a competent forum. The Tribunal also rejected the plea of violation of natural justice, observing that a request for adjournment did not create an indefeasible right to obtain it and that the Commissioner (Appeals) had exercised discretion judicially by recording reasons. Subsequent compliance with the amended 10% requirement could not retrospectively validate an appeal already dismissed under the earlier statutory regime. The Tribunal accordingly held that the Commissioner (Appeals) committed no legal error in dismissing the appeal for non-compliance with the pre-deposit condition under the unamended Section 35F and dismissed ECI BJCL JV’s appeal. Cases Discussed / Relied Upon Lanco Infratech Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Excise, Belapur [2011 (271) E.L.T. 75 (Tri.-Mumbai)] — relied upon by the appellant in support of its claimed prima facie case concerning service tax on construction of dams, canals and EPC projects. Badve Helmets India Pvt. Ltd. Vs CCE, Aurangabad [2012 (28) STR 403 (Tri.-Mumbai)] — relied upon by the appellant; distinguished by the Tribunal because the factual background concerning opportunity of hearing/reasoned order was materially different. DSM Sugar Vs Commissioner of Central Excise Appeals [2009 (248) ELT 49
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that a service tax appeal can be dismissed for non-compliance with a pre-deposit condition, and it upheld the Commissioner (Appeals)’ dismissal of ECI BJCL JV’s appeal on that basis. The underlying dispute arose from EPC/works contracts for construction of dams, reservoirs, canals, and related structures executed for the Government of Andhra Pradesh during June 2007 to March 2012; a show-cause notice dated 23.10.2012 proposed service tax of Rs. 43,86,471 under Works Contract Service, and the demand was confirmed by the adjudicating authority on 09.01.2014. The appellant appealed and sought waiver of pre-deposit, but after a hearing date of 12.06.2014 and a rejected adjournment request, the Commissioner (Appeals) issued an order on 13.06.2014 directing deposit of 50% of the adjudged service tax demand; when the appellant did not comply, the appeal was dismissed on 23.07.2014.

Before the Tribunal, the appellant argued that the appeal had been thrown out without merits consideration and that the Commissioner (Appeals) had not properly evaluated prima facie case, balance of convenience, or financial hardship; it relied on several cited decisions, including Lanco Infratech Ltd., Badve Helmets India Pvt. Ltd., DSM Sugar, Pennar Industries Ltd., Amber Anuruddha Mufti, Surya Pharmaceutical Ltd., B. Rama Rao & Company, and Thermopads Pvt. Ltd. The Revenue responded that the appellant had been given an opportunity to be heard, the adjournment request was considered and denied for recorded reasons, and failure to make the required deposit justified dismissal. The Tribunal accepted the Revenue’s position, finding that the Commissioner (Appeals) had exercised discretion judicially, had recorded reasons for requiring a 50% pre-deposit, and had not acted mechanically or in violation of natural justice.

A key legal point in the ruling was that the amended Section 35F of the Central Excise Act, 1944, which introduced a mandatory 10% pre-deposit, came into force only on 06.08.2014 and applied prospectively. Because the appellate order under challenge was passed before that amendment, the Tribunal held that the parties’ rights and obligations were governed by the unamended law, under which the Commissioner (Appeals) could insist on a pre-deposit as a condition for stay/waiver. The Tribunal specifically held that a later deposit of 10% could not cure the earlier failure to comply with the 50% condition, and that subsequent compliance with the new statutory regime could not revive an appeal already dismissed under the old one. For compliance purposes, the decision reinforces that when an appellate authority imposes a conditional pre-deposit under the applicable statutory framework, the appellant must either comply with that condition or seek relief from a competent forum; failure to do so can result in dismissal of the appeal without a merits ruling.

rows.title: Income Tax | Delhi HC Orders Rs.53 Crore TDS Refund with Interest Without Form 26B
rows.desc: Delhi High Court directs Rs.53.09 crore TDS refund with interest, holding Form 26B and Rule 31A inapplicable after Section 201 assessment.The post Delhi HC Orders Rs.53 Crore TDS Refund with Interest
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court has ordered the income-tax department to refund **₹53.09 crore of TDS** to the taxpayer **with interest**, and held that **Form 26B** and **Rule 31A** could not be used to deny the refund once a **Section 201 assessment** had already been completed. The core compliance point is that, in this case, the court treated the matter as one where the tax liability and TDS position had already been adjudicated under Section 201, so the department could not insist on a separate procedural filing in Form 26B as a condition for issuing the refund.

For corporate taxpayers and withholding agents, the decision is significant because it limits the tax department’s ability to impose additional procedural hurdles after a Section 201 determination has settled the issue. The ruling implies that where excess TDS has been deposited and the taxpayer’s entitlement is established through assessment, the refund should follow along with applicable interest, rather than being withheld for non-submission of Form 26B. Compliance teams should therefore note that refund claims tied to TDS may turn on the status of the Section 201 proceedings and the court’s view that procedural forms cannot override a completed assessment.

rows.title: Income Tax | Delhi HC Orders TDS Refund as Form 26B Inapplicable after Section 201 assessment
rows.desc: Chhattisgarh High Court held that interest on excess self-assessment tax refund is payable from the date of tax payment till refund, subject to statutory provisions.The post Delhi HC Orders TDS Refund
rows.summary: The document reports that the Chhattisgarh High Court held that when a taxpayer has paid excess self-assessment tax, interest on the resulting refund is payable from the date the tax was originally paid until the date the refund is actually issued, but only to the extent allowed under the applicable statutory provisions. In practical terms, this means taxpayers who overpay self-assessment tax may be entitled not just to the principal refund but also to interest for the entire period the government retained the excess amount, rather than interest starting from a later point in time. The note is framed as a tax-court ruling rather than a legislative amendment, so there is no new compliance deadline or filing form requirement stated in the text itself. The key compliance takeaway for corporate tax teams is to review refund claims for excess self-assessment tax and assess whether interest should be claimed from the original payment date, while confirming the claim is consistent with the governing statute.

rows.title: Income Tax | RFCTLARR Compensation Exempt from Income Tax: Andhra Pradesh HC
rows.desc: Andhra Pradesh High Court holds RFCTLARR compensation exempt from income tax and remands TDS issue for fresh consideration.The post RFCTLARR Compensation Exempt from Income Tax: Andhra Pradesh HC appe
rows.summary:
The Andhra Pradesh High Court held that compensation paid under the RFCTLARR framework is exempt from income tax, meaning such compensation should not be treated as taxable income for the recipient. The court’s ruling is significant for land acquisition and compensation payments made under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, because it confirms tax exemption status for those amounts. In the same decision, the court did not finally resolve the tax-deduction-at-source question; instead, it remanded the TDS issue for fresh consideration, so the withholding treatment must be re-examined rather than assumed settled.

For compliance purposes, entities involved in RFCTLARR compensation disbursements should distinguish between the underlying compensation amount, which the court says is exempt, and any separate withholding analysis, which remains open and subject to further determination. Until the TDS issue is reconsidered, payors should not treat the judgment as a blanket confirmation that no withholding obligations can ever arise in connection with such payments; the specific facts and the fresh ruling on remand will matter.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Chhattisgarh HC Quashes GST Cancellation for Failure to Specify Date & Time of Personal Hearing
rows.desc: Chhattisgarh High Court quashes GST registration cancellation where REG-17 omitted personal hearing date/time and physical verification report was not uploaded.The post Chhattisgarh HC Quashes GST Can
rows.summary: The document reports a Chhattisgarh High Court decision holding that a GST registration cancellation was invalid because the department’s REG-17 notice did not specify the date and time of the personal hearing, and because the physical verification report was not uploaded as required. For compliance teams, the key point is that GST cancellation proceedings must strictly follow prescribed procedural safeguards: taxpayers must receive a proper opportunity of hearing with the hearing date and time clearly stated, and the department must complete and upload the required verification record before proceeding. The ruling indicates that cancellation orders issued without these procedural details are vulnerable to being quashed on challenge, even if the department believes substantive grounds for cancellation exist. Although the excerpt does not provide a statutory amendment, rate, threshold, or fixed deadline, it materially reinforces that GST authorities must comply with notice and hearing requirements in cancellation cases, and businesses facing cancellation should review whether the REG-17 notice and verification process were properly completed before treating the cancellation as final.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Rule 43 Amendment Excluding Duty Scrips From ITC Reversal Is Prospective: GSTAT
rows.desc: GSTAT Kolkata holds Notification No. 14/2022 amending Rule 43 to exclude duty credit scrips from exempt turnover is prospective, but Section 74 cannot apply without fraud, wilful misstatement or suppr
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT), Kolkata held that Notification No. 14/2022, which amended Rule 43 of the CGST Rules to exclude duty credit scrips from the calculation of exempt turnover for input tax credit (ITC) reversal purposes, applies only prospectively and not retrospectively. For compliance teams, this means businesses cannot be required to reopen earlier periods and recalculate ITC reversals on the basis of this amendment for periods before the notification took effect; the exclusion of duty scrips from exempt turnover is a forward-looking change only.

The decision also addresses penalty/recovery proceedings under Section 74 of the CGST Act, stating that Section 74 cannot be invoked unless there is fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression of facts. In practical terms, if the department seeks to recover alleged short ITC reversal or related tax dues merely because of a later interpretive change in Rule 43, it must still establish the statutory elements required for Section 74; absent those elements, Section 74 is not the proper basis for action.

For affected entities, the ruling is relevant to taxpayers that have generated or accounted for duty credit scrips and have historically included them in exempt turnover for ITC reversal computations. Compliance teams should verify that post-notification ITC reversal calculations reflect the amended Rule 43 treatment going forward, while keeping prior-period positions supportable under the law as it stood then.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | IGST Refund on Exports: Madras High Court Directs Consideration of Claim
rows.desc: Madras HC permits Kuntal Granites to submit documents for IGST export refund and directs GST authority to decide the claim on merits.The post IGST Refund on Exports: Madras High Court Directs Consider
rows.summary:
The document reports a Madras High Court order concerning **IGST refund on exports** for **Kuntal Granites**. The Court has **allowed the exporter to submit the necessary documents** in support of its refund claim and has **directed the GST authority to examine and decide the claim on its merits**, rather than rejecting it without such consideration.

For a compliance team, the key point is that this is a **judicial directive affecting an export refund claim under GST/IGST**, and it confirms that the taxpayer must be given an opportunity to cure/document the claim before a decision is made. The excerpt does **not specify any statutory change, monetary threshold, refund rate, or new general compliance rule** for all exporters; it is a **case-specific order** involving one exporter’s pending IGST refund on exports.

Operationally, the order means that if an exporter’s refund claim is pending or has been blocked for documentation reasons, the taxpayer may be permitted to **file additional supporting papers**, and the tax authority is expected to **reassess the claim substantively**. No deadline or effective date is stated in the provided text.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Madras HC Grants Retrospective ITC Benefit Where Return Filed Before 30.11.2021
rows.desc: Madras HC quashes GST ITC demand for FY 2018-19 as return was filed before the Section 16(5) cut-off of 30.11.2021.The post Madras HC Grants Retrospective ITC Benefit Where Return Filed Before 30.11.2
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court has held that a taxpayer cannot be denied input tax credit (ITC) for FY 2018-19 when the relevant GST return was filed before the statutory cut-off date of 30.11.2021 under section 16(5) of the CGST Act. In practical terms, the court quashed the GST ITC demand raised for that year because the filing had been completed within the period that the retrospective benefit was intended to protect.  

For compliance teams, the key point is that this decision reinforces the retrospective application of the section 16(5) relief for eligible returns filed on or before 30 November 2021, even if the underlying FY is 2018-19. Entities facing ITC denial notices for that period should review whether their returns were timely filed before the cut-off, because such cases may now be defensible or eligible for challenge. The ruling does not announce a new filing procedure or rate change, but it does create an important legal precedent affecting GST ITC claims and dispute handling for taxpayers with pre-30.11.2021 filings.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Bombay HC Quashes Consolidated GST Notice Covering Multiple Financial Years
rows.desc: Bombay High Court quashes a Section 73 GST notice clubbing FY 2021-22 to 2023-24, allowing fresh notice strictly under law.The post Bombay HC Quashes Consolidated GST Notice Covering Multiple Financia
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court has quashed a GST notice issued under Section 73 that attempted to club together multiple financial years—FY 2021-22, FY 2022-23, and FY 2023-24—into a single consolidated proceeding. The court held that this combined notice was not permissible and directed that any further action must be taken only by issuing a fresh notice strictly in accordance with the GST law. This matters for registrants facing tax-demand proceedings because the ruling reinforces that the department cannot bundle multiple assessment periods into one Section 73 notice if the statute requires period-specific action.

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is procedural rather than substantive tax-rate or threshold change: if a GST demand or adjudication notice covers more than one financial year in a manner inconsistent with the law, it may be challengeable and potentially set aside. The ruling does not change GST rates, registration thresholds, or filing obligations, but it does affect how tax authorities must structure demand notices and recovery proceedings. Businesses should review any pending Section 73 notices to confirm whether they are year-specific and otherwise issued within the statutory framework, and be prepared to contest consolidated notices that improperly combine multiple periods.

rows.title: Company Law | Kerala HC Rejects Limitation Objection Against Official Liquidator’s Recovery Claim
rows.desc: Kerala High Court held that Official Liquidator’s claim under Section 446 can be filed within four years from the winding-up order.The post Kerala HC Rejects Limitation Objection Against Official Liqu
rows.summary: The Kerala High Court held that an Official Liquidator’s recovery claim under Section 446 of the Companies Act may be filed within **four years from the date of the winding-up order**, rejecting the limitation objection raised against the claim. In practical terms, the court confirmed that the liquidator’s application was not time-barred so long as it was brought within that four-year period, thereby preserving the liquidator’s ability to pursue recovery actions on behalf of the company in liquidation. This ruling is significant for companies in liquidation, their officers, creditors, and other parties facing claims from an Official Liquidator, because it clarifies the outer limitation period that may be relied upon for Section 446 recovery proceedings. No other procedural changes, thresholds, or filing requirements are described in the text provided beyond the four-year timing rule tied to the winding-up order.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Bengaluru Denies Section 128A Waiver for December 2020 ITC Demand
rows.desc: GSTAT Bengaluru holds Section 128A waiver unavailable where excess ITC was first availed in December 2020.The post GSTAT Bengaluru Denies Section 128A Waiver for December 2020 ITC Demand appeared firs
rows.summary:
The document reports a GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT), Bengaluru decision holding that the Section 128A waiver is **not available** for an input tax credit (ITC) demand where the excess ITC was **first availed in December 2020**. In other words, the tribunal treated the timing of the initial wrongful/excess ITC availment as outside the scope of the waiver relief being claimed, so the taxpayer could not use Section 128A to eliminate the demand.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that businesses should not assume Section 128A relief applies automatically to all GST ITC disputes; eligibility depends on the **specific tax period in which the excess credit was first taken** and the facts of the demand. Companies with GST litigation or assessments involving ITC should review the period of first availment carefully, because a demand tied to December 2020 ITC was found ineligible for waiver in this case.

No further numerical thresholds, deadlines, filing procedures, or additional compliance steps are provided in the text excerpt.

rows.title: Service Tax | Microsoft software licence royalty not taxable as IPR service before 16.05.2008: CESTAT Allahabad
rows.desc: CESTAT Allahabad sets aside service tax, interest and penalties on software royalty, holding pre-16.05.2008 software services not taxable under IPR service.The post Microsoft software licence royalty
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Allahabad ruling holds that royalty paid for Microsoft software licences was **not liable to service tax under the “Intellectual Property Right (IPR) service” category for periods before 16.05.2008**. The tribunal set aside the **service tax demand, interest, and penalties**, confirming that the tax department could not retrospectively treat software-licensing royalty as taxable IPR service for the pre-16 May 2008 period.

For compliance purposes, the key point is the **effective date**: only **services/royalties arising on or after 16.05.2008** would fall to be examined under the relevant service-tax framework for IPR service, whereas **pre-16.05.2008 software licence royalty receipts/payments were held non-taxable** under that head. This affects businesses that paid or received software licence royalties and had exposure to service-tax notices or audits on those amounts, especially where the department attempted to levy tax, interest, and penalties for earlier periods.

The decision is relevant for companies with software licensing arrangements because it confirms that **characterization of the payment as “royalty” for software use did not, by itself, make it taxable as IPR service before the statutory date**. If a company has historical assessments or pending disputes for software licence royalty relating to periods before 16.05.2008, this ruling supports contesting those demands and the related interest/penalty exposure.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Condonation of 968-Day Customs Appeal Delay Denied for Prolonged Inaction: Delhi HC
rows.desc: Delhi HC upholds CESTAT’s refusal to condone 968-day delay, finding no substantial question of law or sufficient cause.The post Condonation of 968-Day Customs Appeal Delay Denied for Prolonged Inactio
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court upheld the CESTAT’s refusal to condone a **968-day delay** in filing a customs appeal, holding that there was **no substantial question of law** and that the appellant had not shown **sufficient cause** for the prolonged delay. In practical terms, the ruling confirms that customs litigants cannot rely on vague or unsupported explanations to excuse nearly three years of lateness; they must be able to demonstrate a concrete, credible reason for missing the appeal deadline. The decision reinforces strict compliance with appellate timelines in customs matters and signals that **extended inaction will not be treated leniently** absent compelling justification.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that any entity involved in customs disputes must have tight internal controls for monitoring notices, adverse orders, and appeal filing deadlines, because failure to act promptly may permanently forfeit appellate remedies. The court’s reasoning indicates that delay-condonation requests will be scrutinized closely, especially where the record shows prolonged inactivity rather than a short, explainable lapse.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Telangana HC Quashes Section 226(3) Attachment of BIOSOT Bank Accounts
rows.desc: Telangana High Court holds BIOSOT entitled to Article 289 immunity and quashes Section 226(3) bank-account attachment.The post Telangana HC Quashes Section 226(3) Attachment of BIOSOT Bank Accounts ap
rows.summary: The Telangana High Court held that BIOSOT is entitled to constitutional immunity under Article 289, and on that basis quashed the Income Tax Department’s attachment of BIOSOT’s bank accounts under Section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act. The decision means the garnishee/attachment action taken against the bank accounts could not be sustained where the entity is protected by Article 289 immunity, which generally shields State property from Union taxation unless a valid constitutional exception applies. For compliance purposes, the immediate practical effect is that the specific bank-account attachment order is invalidated and any similar recovery action against BIOSOT would need to account for its constitutional status before being pursued. The document does not describe any new filing deadline, monetary threshold, rate change, or procedural rule of general application; it is a case-specific judicial ruling affecting the enforceability of tax recovery measures against BIOSOT’s accounts.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST ITC on Immovable Property: Eligibility & Risks
rows.desc: Summary: The article examines the restriction of input tax credit under Section 17(5)(c) and (d) of the CGST Act on works contract services, goods and services used for constructing immovable property, and the statutory exceptions for plant and machinery and construction not undertaken on a taxable person’s own account. It explains the meaning of immovable property through the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act and judicial tests concerning the nature, object, intention, functionality, permanency and marketability of annexation. It also discusses ITC eligibility for movable installations, HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems and other business equipment, and recommends separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery and movable goods to reduce the risk of denial of otherwise eligible credit. Table of Contents▸ Background: Blocked credit under section 17(5)(c/d) Comments: What is immovable property? Movable vs immovable property test-various judgements The principles laid down by the Apex Court in the case of Bharti Airtel Limited v The Commissioner of Central Excise, Pune Eligibility to Input tax credit and immovable property under GST Way ahead and conclusion Possible issues when there is a Single contract for construction of building and supply of machineries, other moveable goods: ACTION POINTS FOR ITC OPTIMISATION: Show all 10 sections Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background: It is being observed that the assesses are receiving notices requiring to reverse/pay back ITC availed pertaining to newly constructed building projects used for business operations[such as factory premise/warehouses], alleging such credit is restricted being of nature of “immovable property”. However in addition to civil works, such projects involve installation of electrical fittings, cabling, STP, security, fire fighting, machines for manufacture of finished goods etc. In this backdrop, paper writer has examined what is “immovable property” and ITC related to immovable property. Upon satisfaction of the basic conditions for availing the Input tax credit specified in Section 16, there comes a non-obstante clause under Section 17(5) that restricts input tax credit availed even if it is used in the course or furtherance of business. One such restriction has been set out under GST by way of the list of blocked credits under Section 17(5)(c)/(d) which is discussed as under. Blocked credit under section 17(5)(c/d) Section 17(5)(c) sets out that credit is blocked on works contract services for construction of an immovable property (other than plant and machinery) except where it is an input service for further supply of works contract service; Construction includes reconstruction, renovation, additions or alterations or repairs to the extent of capitalization, to the said immovable property; Works contract service is material plus labour contract, for building, construction, completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, renovation alteration of immovable property, which involves transfer of property in goods, in course of executing contract. Plant and machinery means apparatus, equipment, and machinery fixed to earth by foundation or structural support that are used for making outward supply of goods or services or both and includes such foundation and structural supports but excludes- (i) land, building or any other civil structures; (ii) telecommunication towers; and (iii) pipelines laid outside the factory premises. The restriction set out denies credit on works contract services used in the construction of immovable property. However, the said restriction has 2 exceptions (which means in the following instances ITC can be taken on the works contract services); When the works contract services, is received by a taxable person for the construction of “plant and machinery” as defined in Explanation to Section 17 of CGST Act [eg: when the contract is material and labour works contract resulting in HVAC plant, being immovable property]. Where the works contract service supplied for the construction of immovable property is an input service for further supply of the works contract. Eg: Developer of mall, selling units in course of construction to buyers of units in mall. Developer gives contract of material plus labour for construction works to a contractor, who executes such works contract. The developer can avail credit to extent related to units sold during construction. Further, Section 17(5)(d) restricts credit on goods or services or both received by a taxable person for construction of an immovable property (other than plant “and”* machinery)[*replaced in place of “plant or machinery” with retrospective effect from 1.7.2017, vide notification no. Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax dated 17.09.2025] on his own account including when such goods or services
rows.summary:
The document explains that GST input tax credit can be denied even where expenses are otherwise incurred for business if they fall within the blocked-credit rules in Section 17(5)(c) and 17(5)(d) of the CGST Act. In particular, Section 17(5)(c) blocks credit on works contract services used for the construction of immovable property, except when the same works contract service is taken as an input service for further supply of works contract service; “construction” for this purpose includes reconstruction, renovation, additions, alterations, and repairs to the extent capitalized to the immovable property. The article also clarifies that “plant and machinery” is a key carve-out: it means apparatus, equipment, and machinery fixed to earth by foundation or structural support and used for making outward supplies, including those foundations/supports, but excluding land, buildings or other civil structures, telecommunication towers, and pipelines laid outside factory premises.

A separate exception under Section 17(5)(c) allows ITC where the works contract service is received for construction of “plant and machinery.” The article gives the example of a material-and-labour works contract that results in HVAC plant, stating that such a case can qualify for credit because the contract is tied to plant and machinery rather than blocked civil construction. It also notes the second exception for further supply of works contract service, illustrated by a developer constructing mall units for sale during construction: the developer may take credit to the extent the work relates to units sold during construction.

Section 17(5)(d) is described as blocking credit on goods or services received for construction of immovable property other than plant and machinery when the construction is for the taxpayer’s own account, including use in the course or furtherance of business. The text specifically notes an amendment replacing the phrase “plant or machinery” with “plant and machinery” retrospectively from 1 July 2017 through Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax dated 17.09.2025. This means compliance teams should treat the plant-and-machinery carve-out as applying consistently back to GST’s start date, and review any prior positions or disputes in light of that retrospective correction.

The article highlights a recurring compliance problem: taxpayers are receiving notices to reverse or repay ITC claimed on newly constructed business premises such as factories and warehouses, on the theory that the underlying project is immovable property. It emphasizes that such projects often include more than civil construction and may also involve electrical fittings, cabling, sewage treatment plants, security systems, fire-fighting systems, and manufacturing equipment, so the tax treatment depends on whether each component is truly part of blocked immovable property or is separate movable/plant-and-machinery equipment eligible for ITC. The document recommends structuring transactions through separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery, and movable goods/services so that eligible credits are less likely to be denied in an audit or notice proceeding.

Finally, the document explains that whether something is “immovable property” is not determined just by attachment to land; the analysis depends on statutory definitions and judicial tests such as the nature of annexation, intention, functionality, permanency, and marketability. It specifically discusses movable-vs-immovable treatment for installations like HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems, and other business equipment, implying that compliance teams should assess each item separately rather than assuming all fitters, systems, or equipment embedded in a facility are automatically blocked. The practical takeaway is that businesses constructing operational facilities should document classification carefully, segregate contracts and invoices, and retain evidence showing which items are civil construction, which are plant and machinery, and which are movable business assets to support ITC eligibility.

rows.title: Income Tax | Builder Delay Can Trigger TDS Interest for Homebuyers
rows.desc: How Home Buyers Get Trapped into Paying TDS Interest When Builders Delay Telling Them About TDS on Installments Summary: Homebuyers purchasing property from builders through construction-linked installments may incur substantial interest liability if tax is not deducted at source from each payment. Under Section 194-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, a buyer acquiring qualifying immovable property from a resident seller must deduct TDS at 1% at the time of payment or credit, whichever is earlier. For transactions governed by the 1961 Act, the buyer must furnish Form 26QB within 30 days from the end of the month of deduction and issue Form 16B to the seller. From 1 April 2026, the corresponding obligation continues under Section 393(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with Form 141 replacing Form 26QB for applicable transactions. Problems arise when builders raise installment demands without informing buyers about TDS and communicate the requirement only near possession or final payment. Earlier installments may consequently remain subject to delayed deduction. Interest is then payable from the date on which tax should have been deducted, even if the buyer was unaware of the obligation. Under Section 201(1A) of the 1961 Act, interest applies at 1% per month or part thereof for delayed deduction and 1.5% per month or part thereof for delayed deposit after deduction. Buyers should independently monitor every installment, deduct TDS within the applicable timeline and complete the prescribed statement and certificate requirements without waiting for instructions from the builder. Table of Contents▸ Introduction What the Law Actually Says Where the Problem Starts Why This Creates an Interest Liability What Buyers Should Actually Do Final Thought Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Introduction Buying a flat or property from a builder is usually done in installments—some amount at booking, some at various construction stages, and the balance near possession. Very few buyers know that under income tax law, TDS has to be deducted on every single installment, not just on the final payment. This small but important compliance requirement is where most buyers unknowingly land themselves in trouble. What the Law Actually Says Under Section 194-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, if you are buying an immovable property (other than agricultural land) worth Rs. 50 lakh or more, you, as the buyer, are required to deduct TDS at 1% on the amount paid or credited to the seller—whichever happens earlier. This TDS has to be deducted at the time of each payment, whether that payment is Rs. 5 lakh, Rs. 10 lakh, or any partial installment. After deducting the TDS, the buyer has to deposit it with the government using Form 26QB, within 30 days from the end of the month in which the deduction was made, and issue Form 16B to the seller (builder) as proof of TDS deducted. With the Income-tax Act, 2025 (which replaces the 1961 Act with effect from 1 April 2026), this requirement of deducting TDS on transfer of immovable property continues in substance under the corresponding renumbered provision in the new Act. The underlying obligation, however—deduct 1% TDS at the time of every payment where the transaction value is Rs. 50 lakh or more—remains unchanged in principle. So if you are paying in, say, 8 installments over 2 years, technically you are supposed to deduct TDS and file Form 26QB 8 separate times—once for every installment—under the old or Form 141 under the new Act. Where the Problem Starts Most buyers, especially first-time home buyers, have no idea about this requirement. They assume TDS on property is something to be handled only once, at the time of final payment or registration—the way it works for outright property purchases. Builders, on their part, often do not explain this to buyers at the time of booking or during construction-linked payments. Many simply raise demand notes for each installment for the full amount, without mentioning that 1% TDS needs to be deducted before paying them. It is only near the last installment—sometimes at the possession stage—that some builders suddenly intimate the buyer to deduct TDS, and that too, sometimes on the entire sale value in one go, or just on the remaining balance. By this time, several earlier installments have already been paid in full, without any TDS having been deducted at all. Why This Creates an Interest Liability Once the buyer realizes (usually very late) that TDS should have been deducted on each installment, they end up deducting and depositing TDS much after the actual due dates. Each installment is treated as a separate point at which TDS ought to have been deducted. If TDS is deducted or deposited late, interest is payable under Section 201(1A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (carried forward in substance under the corresponding provision of the Income-tax Act, 2025): 1% per month for the period between the date TDS was deductible and the date it
rows.summary:
The document explains that homebuyers purchasing immovable property from builders under construction-linked installment plans can unknowingly trigger TDS default interest if they do not deduct tax on each installment as required. Under Section 194-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, where the property is not agricultural land and the purchase price is Rs. 50 lakh or more, the buyer must deduct TDS at 1% from each payment or credit to the resident seller, whichever is earlier; this applies installment by installment, not only at possession or final settlement. After deduction, the buyer must deposit the TDS using Form 26QB within 30 days from the end of the month in which the deduction was made, and must also issue Form 16B to the seller as evidence of deduction.

The document highlights a change in the governing statute: from 1 April 2026, the corresponding obligation continues under Section 393(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with Form 141 replacing Form 26QB for applicable transactions. Substantively, however, the duty remains the same: buyers still must deduct 1% TDS at each installment payment where the transaction value is Rs. 50 lakh or more. If a buyer pays, for example, eight installments over two years, the compliance expectation is eight separate TDS deductions and filings, one for each installment, rather than a single deduction at the end.

The compliance risk arises when builders do not tell buyers about the TDS requirement until late in the project, often near possession or final demand. By then, earlier installments may already have been paid in full without TDS, and the buyer is then forced to make delayed deductions and filings. The document states that ignorance of the obligation does not avoid the tax consequence: interest becomes payable from the date on which TDS should originally have been deducted.

Under Section 201(1A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the interest rates are 1% per month or part of a month for delayed deduction and 1.5% per month or part of a month for delayed deposit after deduction. The practical compliance instruction for buyers is to monitor every installment independently, deduct and deposit TDS on time for each payment, and complete the prescribed statement and certificate process without waiting for the builder to prompt them. The key operational issue for corporate compliance teams handling employee housing benefits, real estate payments, or advising customers is that each construction-linked installment is a separate TDS event, and late awareness does not protect against interest exposure.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Vague Fraud Allegation Cannot Invoke GST Section 74: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court: Mere Words “Fraud” or “Suppression of Facts” in a GST Show Cause Notice Are Not Enough to Invoke Section 74 Summary: The Supreme Court in M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. held that merely using the expressions “fraud” or “suppression of facts” in a GST show cause notice is insufficient to invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act. M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam challenged an SCN dated 13.06.2025 concerning FY 2018-19 and raising a demand of Rs.1,52,56,431/-. The company argued that the ordinary limitation period applicable under Section 73 had expired on 28.02.2025 and that the department had mechanically invoked Section 74 without identifying any conduct constituting fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Although the department sought to explain the allegations through its counter affidavit, the Court refused to consider those subsequent explanations. It reiterated that the legal validity of a notice must be determined from the notice itself and that deficiencies affecting jurisdiction cannot be cured through pleadings filed later before a court. The SCN contained only a bland reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” without explaining how fraud was inferred or concealment detected. The use of the expression “or” also indicated uncertainty regarding the allegation being made. Holding that the foundational facts and reasoning supporting the invocation of the extended limitation period must be disclosed in the notice, the Supreme Court set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order as well as the SCN and restrained the department from proceeding further on its basis. The department issued the SCN on 13.06.2025 under Section 74 of the CGST Act read with the MPGST Act, raising a total demand of Rs. 1,52,56,431/-. The matter first went before the Madhya Pradesh High Court at Indore, where the company had challenged the SCN by way of a writ petition. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on 29.10.2025, holding that the petitioner should participate in the SCN proceedings and raise its objections before the proper officer, rather than approach the writ court directly. The company then went in appeal before the Supreme Court. What the Company Argued The company’s main argument was about limitation. Under Section 73 of the CGST Act, a notice for a normal (non-fraud) case has to be issued within three years, counted from the due date of filing the annual return. For FY 2018-19, after accounting for various notifications extending the annual return due date, and after excluding the COVID limitation period as directed by the Supreme Court in its Suo Motu Writ Petition (Re: Cognizance for Extension of Limitation), the extended limitation period under Section 73 worked out to 28.02.2025. Since the SCN was issued only on 13.06.2025, it was clearly beyond the three-year period applicable under Section 73. The department could still act within a five-year period, but only if the case genuinely involved fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts, since that is what Section 74 requires. The company’s case was that the SCN merely used the words “fraud or suppression of facts” without explaining what the actual fraud or suppression was. According to the company, such vague and mechanical wording cannot justify invoking the extended five-year period under Section 74. What the Department Argued The department, through its counsel, tried to rely on the counter affidavit filed before the Court to explain and elaborate on the allegations of fraud and suppression, arguing that these details justified proceeding under Section 74. What the Supreme Court Held The Supreme Court refused to look at the counter affidavit for this purpose. It reiterated a well-settled principle: if a notice or order is under challenge for being invalid—for example, for non-application of mind or for not meeting statutory requirements—then whatever is needed to make that notice valid must be found within the notice itself. It cannot be supplied later through a counter affidavit filed in court. Coming to the SCN itself, the Court observed that it only contained a bland statement referring to “fraud or concealment of facts”, without stating how the fraud was inferred or how the concealment was detected. The Court even pointed out that the use of the word “or” between fraud and concealment showed that the department itself was not clear about which allegation actually applied. rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that a GST show cause notice cannot validly invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act merely by reciting the words “fraud,” “wilful misstatement,” or “suppression of facts.” In **M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.**, the department had issued an SCN dated **13.06.2025** for **FY 2018-19** demanding **Rs. 1,52,56,431**, and the taxpayer argued that the normal Section 73 limitation had already expired on **28.02.2025** after applying the relevant return-due-date extensions and the COVID-related limitation exclusions. The Court agreed that if the department wants to rely on the **five-year** period under Section 74 instead of the ordinary **three-year** period under Section 73, the notice itself must set out the specific foundational facts showing how fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression occurred; a bare or mechanical reference to those terms is not enough.

The Court rejected the department’s attempt to cure the defect by relying on explanations in its counter affidavit, holding that a notice’s legal validity must be tested on the face of the notice itself and that jurisdictional defects cannot be repaired later in litigation. Here, the SCN contained only a vague reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” without explaining what conduct constituted fraud, how concealment was discovered, or why Section 74 was being invoked; the Court also noted that the use of the word “or” suggested uncertainty about the actual allegation. As a result, the Supreme Court set aside the **Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order** and also quashed the **SCN itself**, and it restrained the department from proceeding further on the basis of that notice.

For compliance teams, the key point is procedural and jurisdictional: where the department seeks to use Section 74 rather than Section 73, the SCN must contain concrete facts and reasoning supporting the fraud/suppression allegation at the time of issuance. A notice that simply uses statutory buzzwords without particulars may be vulnerable to challenge, even if the department later supplies details in court filings. This decision reinforces the importance of scrutinizing GST notices for limitation and for whether the jurisdictional basis for invoking the extended period is actually pleaded in the notice itself.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12632 Case Name Santosh Mani Mishra Vs PROP (GSTAT Lucknow) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GST Appellate Authority Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Santosh Mani Mishra Vs PROP (GSTAT Lucknow) Summary: The GST Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow Bench considered an appeal arising from detention of goods transported without an E-Way Bill and examined whether the surrounding circumstances established an intention to evade tax. The source order contains a party-description inconsistency: its cause title identifies Santosh Mani Mishra as the appellant and the Islam Trading Company-related party as respondent, while paragraph 1 describes the appellant as Revenue and paragraph 1.2 refers to M/s Islam Trading Company as the appellant. The proceedings arose from transportation of 132.90 cubic feet of iron goods by M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly, under Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018. The vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018. The E-Way Bill was not available with the driver at the time of interception. Tax of Rs. 47,844/- and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844/- were imposed under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017. The first appellate authority, however, set aside the tax and penalty by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018. The Department contended that transportation without the mandatory E-Way Bill violated Rule 138 of the GST Rules and that subsequent production of the tax invoice, books of account, GST returns and proof of tax payment could not retrospectively cure the statutory violation. It further argued that the interception of the vehicle, nature of the goods, route and subsequent production of documents cumulatively indicated an intention to evade tax. The authorised representative also submitted that an E-Way Bill is generated online whereas the tax invoice is manually issued, leaving scope for subsequent manipulation of books of account. No one appeared for the respondent despite adequate opportunity. The Tribunal identified the central issue as whether the alleged intention to evade tax was merely a presumption despite the availability of relevant documents, or whether the facts and circumstances established such intention when the goods were transported without an E-Way Bill. The Tribunal examined the judicial precedents relied upon by the First Appellate Authority, including Sarva Shri Singh Tire v. State of U.P., Shri KL Industries v. State of U.P., Harley Foods Products Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 others, M/s Modern Traders v. State of UP and 2 others, and M/s Rai Prexim India Private Limited v. State of Kerala. The Tribunal distinguished those decisions on facts. It emphasised that generation of the E-Way Bill is an online process, whereas the tax invoice is manually issued by the taxpayer. In its view, non-generation of the E-Way Bill left scope for subsequent manipulation of books of account and therefore constituted substantive non-compliance which, in the circumstances of the case, established an intention to evade tax. The Tribunal also noted that the goods were loaded at Baheri, Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh and were shown for delivery at Kichha, Uttarakhand, approximately 25 km away. It considered this circumstance, along with the absence of the E-Way Bill, interception and nature of the goods, as further supporting the finding of intent to evade tax. The Tribunal additionally relied upon its own order dated 20.08.2026 in Appeal No. APL/79/LKC/2026, Om Prakash v. M/s Islam Trading Company, involving the same nature of goods, the same destination and a similar modus operandi in which the E-Way Bill was produced only after interception by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly. The Tribunal treated the repetition of the same lapse as significant in determining that the conduct could not be regarded merely as a procedural or technical lapse. Accordingly, the Tribunal held that the First Appellate Authority erred in interfering with the order passed under Section 129(3). The appeal filed by the Appellant (Revenue) was allowed. The first appellate authority’s order dated 24.09.2021 was set aside, and the order dated 09.03.2018 passed by the Proper Officer under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017 imposing tax and penalty was restored. The Tribunal’s reasoning turns on the cumulative circumstances and the repeated post-interception production of the E-Way Bill, rather than treating the absence of the E-Way Bill as an isolated technical lapse. State of UP and 2 others 2018 NTN(Vol-67)-71 M/s Rai Prexim India Private Limited Vs. State of Kerala 2019 NTN (Vol.70)-29 FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF GSTAT 1.This appe
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow Bench, restored a detention-cum-penalty order under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017 for movement of iron goods without an E-Way Bill, holding that the facts showed an intention to evade tax rather than a mere technical lapse. The case involved 132.90 cubic feet of iron goods transported by M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly under Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018; the vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018, and the driver did not have the E-Way Bill at the time of interception. On that basis, the Proper Officer had imposed tax of Rs. 47,844 and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844 under Section 129(3).  

The First Appellate Authority had later set aside both the tax and penalty by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018, but the Department appealed, arguing that transportation without a mandatory E-Way Bill violated Rule 138 of the GST Rules and that producing the tax invoice, books of account, GST returns, and proof of tax payment only after interception could not cure the violation. The Department also stressed that the E-Way Bill is generated online while the invoice is manually issued, creating scope for later manipulation of records, and that the route, nature of goods, and post-interception documents together indicated evasion; no one appeared for the respondent despite opportunity.  

The Tribunal accepted the Department’s position and distinguished the precedents relied upon by the first appellate authority, including Sarva Shri Singh Tire, Shri KL Industries, Harley Foods Products, Modern Traders, and Rai Prexim India, on the facts. It specifically noted that the goods were loaded at Baheri, Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh for delivery to Kichha, Uttarakhand, about 25 km away, and treated the short-distance movement, the absence of the E-Way Bill, and the interception circumstances as supporting an inference of intent to evade tax. The Tribunal also relied on its own later order dated 20.08.2026 in Appeal No. APL/79/LKC/2026, Om Prakash v. M/s Islam Trading Company, involving the same goods, same destination, and a similar pattern where the E-Way Bill was produced only after interception, and held that the repeated post-interception production of the E-Way Bill showed a recurring modus operandi rather than a harmless procedural lapse.  

As a result, the Tribunal held that the First Appellate Authority erred in interfering with the Section 129(3) detention order, allowed the Revenue’s appeal, set aside the appellate order dated 24.09.2021, and restored the original order dated 09.03.2018 imposing the Rs. 47,844 tax and Rs. 47,844 penalty. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that transporting goods without the E-Way Bill at the time of interception can sustain Section 129 detention and penalty where the authorities infer evasive intent from the surrounding facts, and post-interception production of supporting documents may not be enough to avoid penalty.

This common CESTAT Chennai order (pronounced 18.09.2018) disposed of three appeals involving real-estate developers and the levy of service tax on property-construction transactions. The core dispute was whether the appellants’ arrangements should be taxed as “construction of complex / commercial or industrial construction services” under the Finance Act, 1994, or as “works contract service” after 1.6.2007; the department also argued that, even where works contract composition was claimed, the assessees had not validly opted into the composition scheme by notifying the department as required under the Works Contract (Composition Scheme for Payment of Service Tax) Rules, 2007. In the Real Value Promoters matter, the department issued SCN No. 351/2008 dated 23.10.2008 for the period 1.4.2007 to 31.3.2008, proposing service tax of Rs. 2,06,20,252 plus interest and penalties under sections 76 and 78, split across buyer-facing and landowner-facing development projects: commercial PRGT (Rs. 34,38,337), residential The Lords / Sananda Brindavan / Sujeet / Surya Skanda (Rs. 1,07,33,392), commercial PRGT Amarasri (Rs. 48,98,579), and residential Sai Brindavan (Rs. 15,49,944). A second SCN, No. 570/2009 dated 20.10.2009, covered amounts received for construction of residential apartments and commercial complexes and proposed an additional Rs. 1,05,99,978 on Commercial PRGT for the allegation of non-payment on services provided to buyers.

The adjudicating authority’s common order dated 16.8.2010 confirmed the entire demand raised in those notices, with interest, imposed a penalty equal to Rs. 2,06,20,252 under section 78, and also imposed penalties under sections 76 and 77. In the Prime Developers appeal, the developer had entered into a Joint Development Agreement dated 17.1.2005 with the landowner (Prime Textiles Ltd.) for a 432-apartment residential complex, and sold units to ultimate buyers under separate agreements; SCN dated 10.8.2009 covered the period January 2005 to August 2008 and the original authority confirmed Rs. 1,16,42,448, holding that service tax was payable under CICS at least for the period before 1.6.2007. For compliance teams, the practical issue is that the department treated the construction activity as taxable both where developers contracted with buyers and where they received consideration from landowners in JDA-style structures, and it specifically challenged the availability of works-contract classification and the procedural validity of the composition option. The final outcome of the Tribunal’s legal analysis is not fully shown in the excerpt provided, so the safe compliance takeaway from the document content alone is that these construction/JDA arrangements were under active tax scrutiny for the stated periods, with large confirmed demands, interest exposure, and section 76/77/78 penalty risk, particularly where no documented works-contract composition option had been exercised before the department.

(Allahabad High Court) Summary: The Allahabad High Court has granted bail to Waseem Akram @ Monu in a case concerning an alleged GST fraud involving non-existing firm M/s Super Power Industries. The applicant sought bail in Case Crime No. 539 of 2025 registered under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471 and 120-B IPC at Police Station Brahampuri, District Meerut. The applicant’s counsel submitted that he was innocent and had been falsely implicated. It was argued that the FIR concerning the alleged GST fraud did not name the applicant and that he had no connection with the allegations. The applicant also asserted that he was not the owner of M/s Super Power Industries, which had allegedly been declared bogus in November 2021, whereas the FIR was lodged approximately four years later on 04.11.2025. It was further submitted that the applicant’s name surfaced in the matter through the statement of Sakeel Khan and that he was not a beneficiary in any manner. The applicant was stated to have no criminal history apart from the present case and had been in jail since 05.04.2026. It was also submitted that, considering the heavy pendency of cases, there was no likelihood of an early conclusion of the trial. The prayer for bail was opposed by the learned A.G.A. as well as the counsel appearing for the GST Department. After considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the record, evidence, nature of allegations and submissions of the parties, the Court held that the applicant was entitled to be enlarged on bail during pendency of the trial. Accordingly, without expressing any opinion on the merits of the case, the High Court allowed the bail application and directed that Waseem Akram @ Monu be released on bail on execution of a personal bond and furnishing two sureties of the like amount to the satisfaction of the concerned court. The bail was made subject to conditions including that the applicant would not tamper with evidence, pressurise or intimidate prosecution witnesses, and would appear before the trial court on the dates fixed unless his personal presence was exempted. He was also prohibited from committing a similar offence and from making any inducement, threat or promise to persons acquainted with the facts of the case for the purpose of dissuading them from disclosing such facts to the Court or police. The Court further directed verification of the identity, status and residence proof of the sureties before their acceptance. In case of breach of any of the conditions, the trial court was given liberty to cancel the bail. The Court clarified that its observations were confined to disposal of the bail application and would have no bearing on the merits of the case during trial. This is an Allahabad High Court bail order in a criminal prosecution arising out of an alleged GST fraud connected to a non-existing/bogus firm, M/s Super Power Industries, and it does **not** announce any new GST rule, filing requirement, tax rate, or compliance deadline. The underlying case is Case Crime No. 539 of 2025 at Police Station Brahampuri, District Meerut, registered under Sections **420, 467, 468, 471, and 120-B of the IPC**. The applicant, **Waseem Akram @ Monu**, argued that he was not named in the FIR, had no connection with the alleged fraud, was not the owner of the firm, and was not a beneficiary; his name allegedly surfaced only from the statement of **Sakeel Khan**. He also pointed out that the firm had been declared bogus in **November 2021**, while the FIR was filed on **04.11.2025**, and that he had no criminal history apart from this case and had been in custody since **05.04.2026**.

The State and GST Department opposed bail, but the Court held that, based on the record, allegations, and submissions, the applicant was entitled to bail during trial. The Court ordered release on bail upon execution of a **personal bond** and furnishing **two sureties of like amount**, subject to standard compliance conditions: he must not tamper with evidence, threaten or influence prosecution witnesses, commit a similar offence, or make inducements/threats/promises to persons connected with the case to prevent disclosure of facts to the Court or police. He must appear before the trial court on all dates unless exempted, and the trial court must verify the **identity, status, and residence proof** of the sureties before accepting them. If any condition is breached, the trial court may cancel bail. The Court expressly said its observations were limited to the bail decision and would not affect the merits of the case at trial.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12629 Case Name Chief Municipal Officer Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Chief Municipal Officer Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Delhi) Summary: The CESTAT New Delhi considered whether a municipality was liable to service tax on two activities: providing space for display of advertisements through hoardings and renting/licensing its immovable properties, including vacant land, to agencies, persons and traders. The disputed period was 2009-10 to 2014-15, covering both the pre-negative-list and post-negative-list service tax regimes. The appellant had received Rs. 3,06,738/- from hoarding rent during April 2009 to June 2012 and Rs. 3,39,22,974/- as rent from various immovable properties during April 2009 to July 2014. The Department proposed service tax of Rs. 39,22,945/- together with interest, penalties and late fee for non-filing of ST-3 returns. The demand was confirmed by the adjudicating authority and Commissioner (Appeals), leading to the appeal before the Tribunal. The appellant contended that the expression “Renting of Immovable Property Service” had been incorrectly interpreted. It argued, relying particularly on Cuddalore Municipality Vs Joint Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, that the expression “any other person” meant a person other than the owner. It also argued that vacant land was excluded from the relevant definition and that arrears of rent had been taxed at an incorrect service tax rate. On advertisement receipts, the appellant maintained that it merely collected statutory licence fees under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 for allotting land on which advertisers erected hoardings, rather than selling advertising space. It further challenged penalties on the ground that there was no intention to evade tax. For the period before 01.07.2012, the Tribunal held that providing space for hoardings was covered by section 65(105)(zzzm) of the Finance Act, 1994. Since the statutory explanation expressly included providing space for display, advertising or showcasing products or services on billboards and public places, the demand under “Sale of Space or Time for Advertisement Services” was upheld for the period up to 01.07.2012. The Tribunal also rejected the appellant’s interpretation of “Renting of Immovable Property” for the pre-01.07.2012 period. It examined the definitions under sections 65(90a) and 65(105)(zzzz) and held that the vacant land supplied for market places was being used for commercial purposes and did not fall within the claimed exclusion. The Tribunal further held that “any other person” in the taxable-service provision meant any person other than the recipient and did not require the service provider to be a person other than the owner. For the period after 01.07.2012, the Tribunal examined section 65B(44), which broadly defined “service”, together with section 66D containing the negative list. The relevant negative-list provision excluded specified services by Government or local authorities but carved out services provided to business entities. The Tribunal found that the appellant had rented immovable property, including vacant land, for organising “Flee Markets” for consideration. Regardless of whether the receipts were described as licence fees, the activity was undertaken for commerce and provided to traders/business entities. In reaching this conclusion, the Tribunal relied upon the Supreme Court decision in Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti, New Mandi Yard, Alwar, which distinguishes mandatory statutory/sovereign functions from activities undertaken for consideration. The Tribunal applied that distinction and found the appellant’s commercial renting activity taxable. The Department’s reliance on that decision was therefore accepted in substance. On limitation, however, the Tribunal granted substantial relief. It observed that the appellant was a government authority and that there was no evidence establishing any positive act of suppression with intent to evade service tax. Referring to Anand Nishikawa Co. Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Excise, Meerut, the Tribunal held that mere failure to declare or pay tax does not by itself constitute wilful suppression and that a positive act is required for invoking the extended period. Accordingly, the Tribunal held that both activities were taxable and that service tax was payable on the value received for those services. However, the extended-period demand was set aside. The demand for the normal period was confirmed with proportionate reduction in the penalty. The appeal was therefore partly allowed. Cases Discussed Cuddalore Municipality Vs Joint Commissioner of GST & Central Excise — 2021 (55) G.
rows.summary:
The CESTAT, New Delhi held that a municipality’s activity of giving space on hoardings for advertisements was taxable as “sale of space or time for advertisement services” for the period up to 01.07.2012 under section 65(105)(zzzm) of the Finance Act, 1994, because the statutory explanation expressly covered space used for display, advertising, or showcasing products or services on billboards and in public places. The Tribunal also held that the municipality’s leasing/licensing of immovable property, including vacant land, for commercial use was taxable both before and after 01.07.2012: for the pre-negative-list period, it rejected the argument that “any other person” meant only a person other than the owner and found that the vacant land used as market space was not within the claimed exclusion; for the post-01.07.2012 period, it found the activity fell within the broad definition of “service” in section 65B(44) and was not covered by the negative list because the property was provided to business entities for commercial activities such as “Flee Markets.”

The dispute covered the period 2009-10 to 2014-15. The municipality had received Rs. 3,06,738 from hoarding rent during April 2009 to June 2012 and Rs. 3,39,22,974 as rent from various immovable properties during April 2009 to July 2014. The Department had proposed service tax of Rs. 39,22,945, along with interest, penalties, and a late fee for failure to file ST-3 returns, and the adjudicating authority and Commissioner (Appeals) had upheld the demand before the matter reached the Tribunal.

A key compliance outcome is that the Tribunal accepted the Department’s substantive position on taxability of both revenue streams, including amounts described as “licence fee” rather than rent, because the underlying activity was commercial and for consideration. However, it granted major relief on limitation: because the appellant was a government authority and there was no evidence of a positive act of suppression with intent to evade tax, the extended limitation period could not be invoked. The Tribunal relied on the principle from Anand Nishikawa Co. Ltd. that mere non-payment or non-declaration is not enough to establish wilful suppression; a positive act is required.

For compliance purposes, the practical result is that similar municipal or local-authority monetization of hoardings, advertising space, vacant land, market space, or other immovable property for commercial use can be subject to service tax/GST-era successor analysis depending on the period and facts, especially where the recipient is a trader or business entity and the arrangement is for consideration. In this case, the demand survived only for the normal limitation period, with proportionate reduction in penalty, while the extended-period demand was set aside. The appeal was therefore partly allowed.

(ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The ITAT Mumbai Special Bench was constituted to decide whether the amount received by the assessee under the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015 is taxable as a revenue receipt in view of the amendment to Section 2(24) of the Income-tax Act by insertion of clause (xviii) with effect from Assessment Year 2016-17. The assessee, engaged in manufacturing specialty chemicals and bulk drugs, had initially claimed the MEIS assistance as a revenue receipt, but subsequently contended before the CIT(A) that it was a capital receipt. The CIT(A) accepted the assessee’s contention for AYs 2016-17 and 2017-18, leading to the Revenue’s appeals. The Revenue argued that MEIS constitutes government assistance and falls within the amended definition of income under Section 2(24)(xviii), irrespective of the nomenclature of the benefit as a “reward”. It relied upon the objective of the Foreign Trade Policy, the expression “by whatever name called”, the Supreme Court’s decisions in Sahney Steel Press Works Ltd. and Ponni Sugars & Chemicals Ltd., and various Tribunal decisions. The assessee, on the other hand, contended that MEIS was a reward intended to improve the export competitiveness of the country and did not constitute the forms of assistance contemplated by Section 2(24)(xviii). It relied, among others, upon Ponni Sugars, CIT v. Chaphalkar Brothers, DCIT v. Munjal Auto Industries and Shree Balaji Alloys. The Special Bench first examined the “purpose test” laid down by the Supreme Court. In Sahney Steel, incentives linked to carrying on business and production were held to be revenue in nature, whereas Ponni Sugars established that where the object of the subsidy was to enable setting up a new unit or expansion of an existing unit, the receipt could be capital in nature. The Special Bench found that MEIS was designed to offset infrastructural inefficiencies and associated costs involved in exports and to enhance India’s export competitiveness. It was not linked to setting up a new unit, capacity expansion or capital investment. Applying that test, the Bench held that MEIS rewards were intended to compensate exporters for costs associated with ordinary export operations and to improve their competitiveness. The duty credit scrips were freely transferable, could be used for payment of various duties and taxes, and were not subject to any obligation requiring their utilisation for acquisition of capital assets or repayment of capital borrowings. The reward was calculated with reference to the FOB value of exports and was available to qualifying exporters, including manufacturer and merchant exporters. These features distinguished MEIS from the capital-oriented incentive scheme considered in Ponni Sugars. The Bench also considered the particular circumstances of the pharmaceutical industry and noted the export challenges arising from non-tariff barriers and other regulatory and market-related difficulties. Since MEIS was intended to address export-related costs and enhance competitiveness rather than facilitate creation or expansion of manufacturing capacity, the Bench concluded under the purpose test that the MEIS rewards were revenue receipts forming part of the assessee’s business income. The Special Bench then examined Section 2(24)(xviii), which includes within “income” assistance in the form of subsidy, grant, cash incentive, duty drawback, waiver, concession or reimbursement “by whatever name called”, subject to specified exclusions. The Bench held that the wording was deliberately broad and was intended to cover not merely the specifically enumerated forms of assistance but other forms of government assistance irrespective of nomenclature. It therefore rejected the assessee’s argument based on ejusdem generis. According to the Special Bench, the term “reward” used in MEIS could fall within the statutory expression “by whatever name called”.
