rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai Special Bench held that incentives received under the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015 are taxable as revenue receipts and therefore form part of business income, beginning with AY 2016-17, because of the amendment to section 2(24) of the Income-tax Act inserting clause (xviii). The dispute arose in the case of Aarti Drugs Ltd., a manufacturer of specialty chemicals and bulk drugs, which had initially treated the MEIS benefit as revenue receipt, later argued before the CIT(A) that it was a capital receipt, and succeeded before the CIT(A) for AYs 2016-17 and 2017-18; the Revenue appealed. The Revenue’s position was that MEIS is government assistance covered by section 2(24)(xviii), and that the label “reward” does not matter because the statute includes assistance “by whatever name called.”

The Special Bench applied the Supreme Court’s “purpose test” and concluded that MEIS was designed to offset export-related infrastructural inefficiencies and other ordinary export costs, and to improve India’s export competitiveness, not to help set up a new unit, expand capacity, or make capital investment. It noted that MEIS duty credit scrips are freely transferable, can be used to pay various duties and taxes, and do not carry any condition that they be used to acquire capital assets or repay capital borrowings; the benefit is computed with reference to the FOB value of exports and is available to qualifying manufacturer and merchant exporters. On that basis, the Bench held MEIS rewards are revenue in nature and are taxable as business income.

The Bench also held that section 2(24)(xviii) is drafted broadly enough to include assistance in the form of subsidy, grant, cash incentive, duty drawback, waiver, concession, reimbursement, or other similar government assistance “by whatever name called,” and rejected the assessee’s attempt to narrow the provision through ejusdem generis. It specifically found that the term “reward” used under MEIS falls within this broad language and that the MEIS benefit is, in substance, a cash incentive because it is linked to a percentage of FOB exports. The two statutory exclusions in section 2(24)(xviii) did not apply: MEIS was not an amount linked to the actual cost of a depreciable asset, and it was not a corpus donation to a trust or institution.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that, for AY 2016-17 onward, MEIS receipts should be treated as taxable income and included in business income rather than booked as a capital receipt. The decision also signals that exporters and other recipients of similar government export incentives should review their tax positions, accounting treatment, and return disclosures for periods covered by the amended definition of income, particularly where benefits are structured as duty credit scrips or “rewards” rather than explicitly labeled subsidies or grants.

rows.title: Income Tax | Gujarat HC Dismisses Reassessment Appeal Where Recorded Reasons Produced No Addition
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12627 Case Name PCIT Vs NK Proteins Pvt. Ltd (Gujarat High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Gujarat High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); PCIT Vs NK Proteins Pvt. Ltd (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court considered the Revenue’s appeal under section 260A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 arising from the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal order dated 12.11.2024 for A.Y. 2009-10. The assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing edible and non-edible oil products and byproducts. The original assessment under section 143(3) was completed on 29.12.2011. The source records total income at Rs. 22,55,48,605/- in paragraph 3.1, while paragraph 7 records Rs. 22,55,48,602/-. A notice under section 148 was issued on 09.03.2015 beyond four years from the end of the relevant assessment year. The recorded reasons concerned two matters: an alleged short computation of disallowance under section 14A read with Rule 8D, and an alleged income of Rs.244.98 crores said to have been received from National Stock Exchange Ltd. (NSEL) through so-called paper trade. In reassessment, however, the Assessing Officer made a disallowance of Rs.13,89,08,810/- under section 43(5) read with section 73 and section 40A(2)(b), along with excess disallowance of Rs.1,04,652/- under section 14A. The assessee challenged the reopening before the CIT(Appeals), pointing out that no addition had ultimately been made on either recorded reason. The CIT(Appeals) found that the NSEL figure of Rs.244.98 crores related to an addition in the assessee’s own case for A.Y. 2011-12 and that the assessee had not carried out NSEL transactions in the year under consideration. The CIT(Appeals) also noted that the original section 14A disallowance had been deleted by the Ahmedabad ITAT because the assessee had not received exempt dividend income. On the second reopening reason, the CIT(Appeals) found that the notice was issued beyond four years, the recorded reasons did not allege failure by the assessee to disclose truly and fully all material facts, and no new tangible material had been brought on record. The reassessment was therefore treated as invalid. The CIT(Appeals) relied, among other decisions, on CIT v. Mohmed Juned Dadani and decisions concerning the scope of reassessment under sections 147 and 148. The Tribunal dismissed the Revenue’s appeal, upheld the quashing of the reassessment as without jurisdiction, and consequently quashed the Rs.13,89,08,810/- addition under sections 43(5), 73 and 40A(2)(b). Before the High Court, the Revenue contended that once an assessment was reopened, the Assessing Officer could examine other issues arising during reassessment and defended the additions under sections 43(5), 73 and 14A. The assessee relied on the jurisdictional High Court’s decision in Mohmed Juned Dadani, as well as Jet Airways (I) Ltd. and other decisions. It was submitted that the Rs.244.98-crore figure belonged to A.Y. 2011-12 and that the special auditor had accepted that there was no NSEL transaction in the year under consideration. The High Court held that no addition had been made for either of the reasons recorded for reopening. Since the notice was issued beyond four years, the Court held that there was no failure by the assessee to disclose truly and fully the income said to have escaped assessment so as to confer jurisdiction under the substantive provisions of section 147. In considering Explanation 3 to section 147, the Court relied on the principle stated in Mohmed Juned Dadani that although, after a valid reopening, the Assessing Officer may assess or reassess other escaped income which comes to notice during the proceedings, the position is different where the very ground on which reopening was based fails. The Court reproduced the reasoning that if the foundation of reopening is knocked out, further proceedings cannot survive. It also considered the explanatory memorandum to Explanation 3, which described the amendment as clarificatory and retrospective from 01.04.1989. Relying on S. Sundaram Pillai v. V.R. Pattabiraman, the Court reiterated that an Explanation cannot expand the scope and sweep of the main statutory provision. The Court further noted that Explanation 3 permits assessment or reassessment of an issue not included in the recorded reasons when that issue subsequently comes to the Assessing Officer’s notice, but it does not override the substantive conditions of section 147. Where no income has escaped assessment on the recorded reasons and no addition is made on those reasons, the retrospective Explanation 3 does not cure the jurisdictional defect. The Court also noted that the Supreme Court had dismissed the SLP arising from the Delhi High Court judgment in Jakhotia Pla
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court dismissed the Revenue’s section 260A appeal in **PCIT v. NK Proteins Pvt. Ltd.** for A.Y. **2009-10**, upholding the Tribunal’s order that had quashed the reassessment as **without jurisdiction**. The reassessment notice under **section 148** had been issued on **09.03.2015**, which was **beyond four years** from the end of the assessment year, so the reopening could stand only if the Revenue could show that income had escaped assessment because of the assessee’s **failure to disclose truly and fully all material facts**. The recorded reasons for reopening were limited to two alleged escapement items: an alleged under-disallowance under **section 14A read with Rule 8D**, and an alleged **Rs. 244.98 crore** receipt from **National Stock Exchange Ltd. (NSEL)** through a supposed paper trade.

The reassessment ultimately did **not** make any addition on either of those recorded reasons. Instead, the Assessing Officer made a different addition of **Rs. 13,89,08,810/-** under **sections 43(5), 73, and 40A(2)(b)**, plus an alleged excess disallowance of **Rs. 1,04,652/-** under **section 14A**. The CIT(A) and Tribunal both held that this could not sustain the reassessment because the NSEL figure related to an addition made in the assessee’s **A.Y. 2011-12** proceedings and the assessee had **not carried out NSEL transactions in the year under review**, while the original section 14A disallowance had already been deleted by the Ahmedabad ITAT on the ground that the assessee had **not earned exempt dividend income**. The Court agreed that the reopening failed at the threshold because the recorded reasons produced **no addition**, there was **no allegation of failure to disclose fully and truly all material facts**, and the Revenue had brought **no new tangible material** on record.

The High Court also rejected the Revenue’s reliance on **Explanation 3 to section 147**, holding that while that Explanation may allow the Assessing Officer, after a **valid** reopening, to assess other income that comes to notice during reassessment, it does **not** override the basic jurisdictional requirements of section 147. The Court applied the principle from **CIT v. Mohmed Juned Dadani** that if the **foundation** for reopening collapses, the reassessment cannot survive; it also reiterated that an Explanation cannot enlarge the scope of the main statutory provision. Practically, the ruling means that where a reassessment is initiated **after four years** and the recorded grounds themselves do not result in any addition, the Revenue cannot salvage the reassessment by making unrelated additions discovered later in the process.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 272A(2)(e) Penalty Cannot Continue Beyond Section 139(4): Chennai ITAT
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12626 Case Name Swamy Vivekanandha Vidhyala Trust Vs ITO (ITAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2013-14 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Chennai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Swamy Vivekanandha Vidhyala Trust Vs ITO (ITAT Chennai) Summary: The appeal concerned levy of penalty under section 272A(2)(e) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for failure by a charitable trust to furnish its return of income. The assessee, a charitable trust running an educational institution and registered under section 12A, had not filed its return for AY 2013-14. The Assessing Officer received information that the assessee had deposited cash of Rs. 75,55,200/- into its bank account. Consequently, assessment proceedings were reopened by issuing notice under section 147. In response, the assessee filed a return declaring Nil income after claiming exemption under section 10(23C)(iiiad). The assessment under section 147 accepted the returned income. Subsequently, penalty proceedings under section 272A(2)(e) were initiated. The assessee explained that the return had not been filed because of a bona fide belief that no return was required where the income was exempt. It also contended that there was no loss to the Revenue and no intention to conceal income. The Assessing Officer rejected these submissions and levied penalty of Rs. 3,04,300/-. The CIT(A) confirmed the penalty, holding, among other things, that the assessee had failed to comply with section 139(4C), that ignorance of law was not an acceptable excuse, absence of revenue loss and mens rea was irrelevant, and that the penalty was mandatory in the absence of reasonable cause under section 273B. At the hearing before the Tribunal, the assessee pressed only ground No.8 and did not press the remaining grounds. The assessee argued that penalty under section 272A(2)(e) should be calculated only for the period during which it could legally furnish the return. According to the assessee, the period after expiry of the time prescribed under section 139(4), until issuance of notice under section 148, could not be treated as a continuing default because the assessee could no longer voluntarily furnish a valid return. The assessee relied upon section 139(4) and section 139(4A), and relied particularly upon Bethany Seva Sangam vs. ITO [2023] 155 taxmann.com 352 (Raipur-Trib.). The Departmental Representative contended that the default continued until the assessee actually furnished the return in response to the notice under section 148. According to the Revenue, because section 272A(2)(e) imposes penalty for every day during which the failure continues, the entire period up to the filing of the return was liable to be considered. The Tribunal examined whether the expression “during which the failure continues” in section 272A(2)(e) could extend beyond the period in which the assessee had a statutory right to voluntarily furnish a valid return. It held that the obligation under section 139(4A) had to be understood within the statutory scheme of section 139. Once the period prescribed under section 139(4) expired, the assessee was no longer empowered to voluntarily furnish a valid return. Therefore, the statutory obligation became incapable of voluntary compliance and the default could not continue indefinitely. The Tribunal followed the reasoning of the Raipur Bench in Bethany Seva Sangam, which had considered the interplay between sections 139(4A), 139(4) and 272A(2)(e), and held that penalty could not be imposed for the period after expiry of the time available for filing a belated return. The Tribunal also noted the Hyderabad Bench decision in G. Pulla Reddy v. JCIT (2010) 47 DTR 1 (Hyd.), where the period of default under section 272A(2)(e) was held to be restricted to the time limit prescribed under section 139(4). The Tribunal observed that accepting the Revenue’s interpretation would result in penalty for a period during which the assessee had no statutory right to voluntarily furnish a valid return. Accordingly, the Tribunal held that penalty under section 272A(2)(e) was liable to be computed only up to the last date prescribed under section 139(4), and not up to the date on which the assessee subsequently filed the return in response to the section 148 notice. The matter was remitted to the Assessing Officer for the limited purpose of recomputing the penalty by restricting the period of default to the period available under section 139(4). The appeal was partly allowed. Cases Discussed Bethany Seva Sangam vs. ITO [2023] 155 taxmann.com 352 (Raipur-Trib.) G. Pulla Reddy v. JCIT (2010) 47 DTR 1 (Hyd.) Sri Dadar (W.Rly) Sidhachakra Vardhaman Tap Ayambil Khata v. Dy. Director of Investigation (E) (59 ITD 253 (SMC)) FULL TEXT OF THE ORDER OF ITAT CHENNA
rows.summary:
The Chennai ITAT held that a penalty under section 272A(2)(e) of the Income-tax Act for failure to furnish a return cannot run indefinitely past the point at which the assessee was still legally able to file a valid voluntary return under section 139(4). The case involved a charitable trust registered under section 12A and running an educational institution, which had not filed its return for AY 2013-14; the Assessing Officer reopened the case under section 147 after finding cash deposits of Rs. 75,55,200 in the trust’s bank account, and the trust then filed a return declaring nil income and claiming exemption under section 10(23C)(iiiad). Although the assessment was completed on the returned income, the Assessing Officer levied penalty of Rs. 3,04,300 under section 272A(2)(e), and the CIT(A) upheld it, taking the view that the trust had failed to comply with section 139(4C), that ignorance of law and absence of revenue loss were irrelevant, and that no relief was available absent “reasonable cause” under section 273B.

Before the Tribunal, the trust pressed only the issue that the penalty period should stop when the time for filing a valid belated return under section 139(4) expired, rather than continuing until the return was actually filed in response to notice under section 148. The Revenue argued that because section 272A(2)(e) applies for every day during which the failure continues, the default should be treated as continuing up to the eventual filing date. The Tribunal rejected that approach, holding that once the section 139(4) deadline passed, the assessee no longer had the statutory ability to voluntarily furnish a valid return, so the failure could not be treated as continuing beyond that point for purposes of section 272A(2)(e).

Relying on Bethany Seva Sangam v. ITO [2023] 155 taxmann.com 352 (Raipur Tribunal) and also noting G. Pulla Reddy v. JCIT (2010) 47 DTR 1 (Hyd.), the Tribunal ruled that the penalty must be restricted to the period up to the last date permitted under section 139(4), and not extended to the date of filing in response to the section 148 notice. It therefore set aside the penalty computation and remanded the matter to the Assessing Officer solely to recompute the penalty by limiting the default period to the section 139(4) window. The appeal was partly allowed.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12625 Case Name Sankaran Mekala Vs ITO (Madras High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2015-16 Courts All High Courts, Madras High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Sankaran Mekala Vs ITO (Madras High Court) Summary: The writ petition was filed by Sankaran Mekala challenging the impugned demand order dated 16.07.2026 issued under sections 147, 271(1)(b) and 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for Assessment Year 2015-16. The petitioner sought quashing of the demand and a direction to reopen the income-tax e-filing portal so that she could file her return in accordance with an earlier order of the Madras High Court dated 09.02.2026 in W.P. No.1242 of 2026. The petitioner submitted that she had earlier challenged the assessment order dated 16.01.2024 and notice dated 12.04.2022 in W.P. No.1242 of 2026. That writ petition was disposed of on 09.02.2026 with a direction to the petitioner to file the return of income for AY 2015-16 and reply to the notice issued under section 148. The petitioner complied with the direction to the extent of depositing Rs.5 lakhs, but was unable to upload the return because of technical issues with the income-tax portal. She therefore sought another opportunity to comply with the earlier order. The Revenue accepted notice. The petitioner placed before the Court proof of the Rs.5 lakh deposit made pursuant to the earlier order and evidence of various documents filed by her. She also produced a screenshot showing that she had been unable to upload the return of income on the portal. The High Court held that, in these circumstances, the interest of justice required that the petitioner be provided an opportunity to file the return. The Court accordingly disposed of the writ petition by setting aside the impugned demand notice dated 16.07.2026. The respondent was directed to take necessary steps to provide the petitioner access to the income-tax portal for uploading the return for AY 2015-16. The petitioner was directed to file the return within three weeks from receipt of a copy of the order. Thereafter, the respondent was directed to conclude the assessment by issuing an assessment order within six weeks from receipt of the return, after providing a reasonable opportunity to the petitioner. The connected miscellaneous petitions were closed and there was no order as to costs. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF MADRAS HIGH COURT 1. A communication demanding payment of tax and penalty in terms of earlier assessment order dated 16.01.2024 is assailed in this writ petition. 2. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that W.P.No.1242 of 2026 was filed earlier by the petitioner challenging the assessment order dated 16.01.2024 and notice dated 12.04.2022. He also points out that said writ petition was disposed of on 09.02.2026 directing the petitioner to file return of income for the assessment year 2015-2016 and reply to the Section 148 notice. While the petitioner was able to deposit the sum of Rs.5 lakhs, as directed by said order, he submits that the petitioner was unable to upload the return of income due to technical issues in the portal. Therefore, he seeks another opportunity. 3. Ms.Sheela, learned Senior Standing Counsel and Mr.H.Siddarth, learned Junior Standing Counsel, accept notice for the respondent. 4. The petitioner has placed on record the proof of deposit of the sum of Rs.5 lakhs in compliance with the earlier order. There is also evidence that the petitioner filed various documents. As regards the return of income, the petitioner has placed on record the screenshot indicating that he was unable to upload said return of income. Therefore, the interest of justice requires that an opportunity be provided to the petitioner. 5. This Madras High Court order concerns **AY 2015-16** and a taxpayer, **Sankaran Mekala**, who challenged a **demand communication/order dated 16.07.2026** issued in connection with an earlier reassessment matter under **sections 147, 271(1)(b), and 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961**. The taxpayer had already filed **W.P. No. 1242 of 2026** against the underlying **assessment order dated 16.01.2024** and **notice dated 12.04.2022**; that earlier writ was disposed of on **09.02.2026** with directions to file the return of income for AY 2015-16 and respond to the section 148 notice. The petitioner stated she had complied in part by depositing **Rs. 5 lakhs** pursuant to the earlier order, but could not upload the return because of technical issues on the income-tax e-filing portal, and she produced a **screenshot** evidencing the upload failure along with proof of other filings.

The Court accepted that the portal issue prevented compliance and held that, in the interests of justice, the taxpayer should be given another opportunity to file the return. It therefore **set aside the impugned demand notice dated 16.07.2026** and directed the Revenue to **take necessary steps to provide access to the income-tax portal** so the return for AY 2015-16 could be uploaded. The taxpayer was ordered to **file the return within three weeks from receipt of the order**, and the department was then required to **complete the assessment by issuing an assessment order within six weeks from receipt of the return**, after granting a **reasonable opportunity** to the taxpayer. The connected miscellaneous petitions were closed, and **no costs** were awarded.  

From a compliance perspective, the order is significant because it shows the Court will treat **documented portal/access failures** as a valid basis for relief where the taxpayer has otherwise attempted to comply, and it reinforces that the department must provide a functional means of electronic filing when a court has directed the taxpayer to file a return.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DCIT-2(1)(1) Vs Bank of Baroda (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal dismissed the Revenue’s appeals concerning the manner in which refunds payable to M/s. Bank of Baroda were required to be adjusted between the interest component and the principal tax component. The consolidated order covered AYs 2003-04, 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10, 2016-17 and 2005-06, with ITA No.5707/Mum/2025 for AY 2003-04 taken as the lead case. The Revenue challenged the order of the CIT(A), NFAC, contending that where a refund comprised both tax and interest under section 244A, any refund payment should first be appropriated towards the principal tax component rather than the interest component. According to the Revenue, section 244A contained no express provision prescribing that interest should be adjusted first. It was also argued that adjusting the refund against interest would result in further interest liability on the unpaid tax component and would effectively amount to charging interest on interest. The assessee contended that the issue had already been settled by various judicial decisions and by decisions of the Tribunal in its own case. It relied on the principle of consistency and submitted that, in the absence of any change in facts or circumstances, the earlier view should be followed. The assessee also relied upon decisions concerning Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, Bank of India, IDBI Bank, Reliance Industries Limited, State Bank of India and Tata Sons Limited, among others. The Tribunal noted that section 244A provides for simple interest on refunds due to an assessee and contains mechanisms for increasing or reducing such interest when the refundable tax component changes pursuant to subsequent assessment or appellate orders. The Tribunal observed that the legislative purpose was to compensate the assessee for the hardship caused by excess payment and delayed refund and to require the Revenue to refund the amount due within the prescribed framework. The Tribunal relied particularly on the Delhi High Court’s decision in India Trade Promotion Organisation Vs. CIT, which interpreted the expression “any amount” in section 244A broadly enough to include the interest element accrued and payable with the refund. The Tribunal also considered the Supreme Court’s decision in Sandvik Asia Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Income Tax-I, which had criticised the Revenue’s differing approaches to appropriation when collecting interest from assessees and when making refunds. The Tribunal further referred to the principle recognised in decisions including Narendra Doshi and CIT Vs. HEG Ltd., under which an amount of interest that remains unpaid along with the refundable tax can itself form part of the amount due to the assessee. The Tribunal held that the expression “amount due” was not confined merely to the principal tax component. On this reasoning, the Tribunal held that the Revenue ought to adjust the interest component first before appropriating the principal tax amount while crediting refunds to the assessee. According to the Tribunal, such sequential adjustment was consistent with equitable treatment because interest represented compensation for the time value of money retained by the Revenue. Adjusting tax first could leave the interest component unpaid and thereby dilute the compensation contemplated by section 244A. The Tribunal therefore dismissed the Revenue’s grounds in the lead appeal. It directed that the same finding would apply mutatis mutandis to ITA Nos.5709, 5710 and 5711/Mum/2025 and ITA Nos.5659 and 5708/Mum/2025. Consequently, all the Revenue’s appeals were dismissed. rows.summary:
The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal held that, when the Income Tax Department issues a refund that includes both the principal tax amount and interest payable under section 244A, the refund must be adjusted **interest first and principal tax second**. The Revenue had argued the opposite—that the refund should first be appropriated toward the tax component because section 244A does not expressly say interest must be paid first, and that paying interest first could create further interest on the unpaid tax. The Tribunal rejected that position and, relying on the purpose of section 244A, said the provision is meant to compensate the taxpayer for excess payment and delay in refund through **simple interest**, not to leave the interest component unpaid while only the principal is returned.

The ruling was based on prior judicial authorities, especially **India Trade Promotion Organisation v. CIT** and **Sandvik Asia Ltd. v. CIT**, along with other cases including **CIT v. H.E.G. Ltd.** and **Narendra Doshi**, which support the view that the “amount due” on refund is not limited to the principal tax alone and can include the interest element. The Tribunal emphasized that, where later assessment or appellate orders change the refundable tax amount, section 244A contains its own mechanism for adjusting the interest accordingly; however, that does not permit the Department to reverse the order of appropriation so that tax is satisfied before interest. It viewed interest as compensation for the time value of money retained by the government, so paying tax first would undercut the statutory compensation scheme.

This decision arose in the case of **DCIT-2(1)(1) v. Bank of Baroda (ITAT Mumbai)** and covered multiple assessment years: **AY 2003-04, 2005-06, 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10, and 2016-17**. The Tribunal dismissed the Revenue’s lead appeal for **AY 2003-04 (ITA No. 5707/Mum/2025)** and applied the same reasoning to the related appeals, including **ITA Nos. 5709, 5710 and 5711/Mum/2025 and 5659 and 5708/Mum/2025**, so all Revenue appeals were dismissed. For compliance purposes, this means that in refund processing where section 244A interest is part of the amount payable, the Department’s adjustment sequence is expected to prioritize **interest before tax**, and taxpayers receiving such refunds may rely on this precedent in similar Mumbai ITAT matters unless and until a higher court says otherwise.

Chessman Impex Private Limited Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Chennai) Summary: CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017, holding that the customs duty demand of Rs.2,16,93,068/- against Chessman Impex Pvt. Ltd., consequential interest, penalties of Rs.20 lakh each under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962 and penalties imposed on the co-appellants could not be sustained in the absence of reliable and corroborative evidence. Chessman Impex had obtained a DEEC licence under the EXIM Policy 1997-2002 permitting duty-free import of 5350 MTs of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against export obligation of 5000 MTs of non-alloy steel bars and rods. Revenue alleged that the imported scrap was diverted in the domestic market and maize was fraudulently exported to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export instead of the stipulated steel products. The Tribunal found material support for the appellant’s case in the special permission for exports through Ghojadanga LCS, Customs examination of export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, DRI Chennai’s confirmation regarding manufacture by Goyal Ispat Ltd., the foreign buyer’s permission for segregation and export of unprocessed scrap, undisputed realisation of export proceeds and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority. Significantly, the CBI had investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and filed a final report recording that the available evidence indicated that the disputed exports to Bangladesh had actually taken place; the report was accepted by the competent Criminal Court. The adjudicating authority had not identified additional material or specific evidence not considered by the CBI. The Tribunal further held that Revenue produced no independent evidence of buyers of the allegedly diverted material, cash trail, procurement or transportation of maize, domestic disposal or seizure of offending goods. Mere “grey areas” or suspicion could not substitute cogent evidence necessary for penal action under Sections 112 and 114 of the Customs Act. The adjudicating authority had also travelled beyond the Show Cause Notice by introducing issues concerning classification of CTD bars, availability of 16 mm bars and amendment of the DEEC licence. The Tribunal found material discrepancies in the statements relied upon by Revenue, some of which had been retracted, and observed that statements recorded under Section 108 had been relied upon without examining the statutory requirements of Section 138B. Since the allegations against the principal noticee failed for want of reliable and corroborative evidence, allegations of connivance or abetment and consequential penalties against the co-appellants also could not survive. All appeals were accordingly allowed with consequential relief and the impugned Order-in-Original was set aside. Cases Discussed Commissioner of Customs, Trichy v. CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals filed by Chessman Impex Private Limited and co-appellants and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017. The adjudication had demanded customs duty of Rs. 2,16,93,068 along with consequential interest and imposed penalties of Rs. 20 lakh each on Chessman Impex under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, as well as penalties on the co-appellants, on the allegation that duty-free DEEC imports were misused and that the export obligation was fraudulently fulfilled through export of maize rather than the permitted steel products.

The Tribunal noted that Chessman Impex had obtained a DEEC licence under the EXIM Policy 1997–2002 for duty-free import of 5,350 MT of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against an export obligation of 5,000 MT of non-alloy steel bars and rods. Revenue’s theory was that the imported scrap had been diverted into the domestic market and that maize was exported to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export instead of the required steel goods, but the Tribunal found the record insufficient to support that case. It relied on multiple pieces of evidence supporting the assessee, including special permission for exports through Ghojadanga LCS, Customs examination of export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, DRI Chennai’s confirmation that the goods were manufactured by Goyal Ispat Ltd., permission from the foreign buyer to segregate and export unprocessed scrap, realization of export proceeds, and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority.

A key factor was that the CBI had already investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and filed a final report stating that the available evidence indicated the disputed exports to Bangladesh had actually taken place; that report had been accepted by the competent criminal court. The Tribunal held that the customs adjudicating authority had not brought any additional reliable material beyond what the CBI had examined, and Revenue had produced no independent proof of buyers for the allegedly diverted material, cash trail evidence, procurement or transport of maize, domestic disposal, or seizure of offending goods. It emphasized that suspicion or “grey areas” cannot replace cogent evidence for imposing penalties under Sections 112 and 114 of the Customs Act.

The Tribunal also held that the adjudicating authority went beyond the scope of the Show Cause Notice by raising new issues such as classification of CTD bars, availability of 16 mm bars, and amendment of the DEEC licence. It found discrepancies in the witness statements relied upon by Revenue, noted that some statements had been retracted, and criticized the reliance on Section 108 statements without proper consideration of Section 138B requirements. Because the allegations against the principal noticee failed for lack of reliable and corroborative evidence, the derivative allegations of connivance or abetment against the co-appellants also failed, and all penalties were set aside with consequential relief.

(Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered a challenge to a customs penalty of Rs. 425,27,99,100/- imposed on Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962. The penalty arose from an allegation that a consignment of natural diamonds had been mis-declared as lab-grown diamonds to pay a lower tariff. The Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025 was challenged before the Gujarat High Court, but the challenge failed when the High Court dismissed the appeal on 20.01.2026. The matter then reached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court did not enter into the merits of the underlying customs dispute. Instead, the appellant contended that several judgments and articles relied upon by the second respondent in the Order-in-Original had been generated using Artificial Intelligence. The Court independently verified the material relied upon in the customs order and found that the second respondent had relied upon case laws that were either non-existent or had fake citations. The Court further found that some case laws which did exist did not lay down the legal propositions attributed to them. The Court observed that the material appeared to be a hallucination of AI. This discovery led the Supreme Court to rely upon its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh Vs Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd., where the Court had adopted a zero-tolerance approach towards producing, citing or relying upon artificial-intelligence-generated precedents without verification. The Supreme Court reiterated that presenting or relying upon fake or hallucinated material as a court precedent undermines the integrity of adjudication. The Court also made broader observations concerning the use of Artificial Intelligence in adjudicatory processes. It noted that the Supreme Court had recently released draft Regulations for Use of Artificial Intelligence in Courts, 2026, inviting comments and suggestions. Although those regulations had not yet been finalised, the Court acknowledged that AI could be used as an assistive tool to speed up decision-making processes. However, it emphatically distinguished assistance from adjudication, observing that AI may serve as “training wheels” but cannot be entrusted with the “pilot’s seat”. Applying these principles to the case, the Supreme Court held that the use of AI had resulted in reliance by the second respondent on dubious material and that this was fatal to the sustainability of the penalty order. The Court therefore found it necessary to interfere without determining the substantive merits of the customs dispute. The Supreme Court consequently set aside the Gujarat High Court order confirming the penalty as well as the Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025. The proceedings against the appellant before the second respondent were revived for fresh adjudication by an officer of the same rank other than the officer who had passed the original order. The civil appeal was allowed. The Court also disposed of any pending applications and left it to the wisdom of the appointing authority to initiate such action against the author of the Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025 as may be warranted in accordance with law. The Supreme Court set aside a customs penalty order after finding that the adjudicating officer appears to have relied on fake or AI-generated legal authorities. The underlying Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025, issued by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat, had imposed a penalty of ₹425,27,99,100 under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962 on Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya for allegedly misdeclaring a consignment of natural diamonds as lab-grown diamonds in order to pay a lower tariff; the Gujarat High Court had upheld/dismissed the challenge on 20.01.2026, but the Supreme Court reversed that outcome without deciding the substantive customs merits.

The Court said it independently verified the judgments and articles cited in the customs order and found that some were non-existent or carried fake citations, while others existed but did not support the propositions attributed to them. It described the material as appearing to be an AI “hallucination” and relied on its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd. (2026 SCC OnLine SC 1258), reaffirming a zero-tolerance approach to producing, citing, or relying on artificial-intelligence-generated precedents without verification.

The Court acknowledged AI may be used only as an assistive tool to speed decision-making, but emphasized that AI cannot be put in the “pilot’s seat” of adjudication. Because the penalty order was tainted by reliance on dubious and unverified authorities, the Supreme Court held the order unsustainable and set it aside, along with the Gujarat High Court order that had confirmed it.

Procedurally, the Court revived the proceedings before the customs authority for fresh adjudication by another officer of the same rank, expressly requiring that the new officer be different from the one who issued the original order. It allowed the civil appeal, disposed of pending applications, and left it to the appointing authority to decide whether any action should be taken against the author of the original order in accordance with law.

The petitioner sought a direction to the respondent to lift the blockage and permit free utilisation of the Input Tax Credit available in the electronic credit ledger. An assessment order dated 17.03.2023 had been issued for the assessment period 2017-2020. Primarily challenging the clubbing of assessments relating to multiple assessment periods, the petitioner had filed W.P.No.41890 of 2025. An interim stay concerning recovery measures was granted on 25.02.2026. The electronic credit ledger, however, had already been blocked on 04.02.2025, and that blocking order was challenged in the present writ petition. The petitioner contended that the blocking could not survive in view of the interim order dated 25.02.2026. It was further argued that the blocking travelled beyond the scope of Section 79 of the CGST Act. Comparing Section 79 with Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, learned counsel contended that negative blocking was impermissible under Section 79. The Revenue submitted that there was no infirmity in the blocking. It also contended that the interim order dated 25.02.2026 merely directed that recovery proceedings be kept in abeyance and did not affect the earlier blocking order. The Court accepted the Revenue’s interpretation of the interim order. It held that the limited impact of the interim order was that amounts lying in the electronic credit ledger could not be debited for purposes of recovering the dues. The interim order did not otherwise affect the earlier blocking order. On the scope of Section 79, the Court examined Section 79(1), which permits the proper officer to recover amounts payable to the Government through one or more specified modes. These include deduction from money under the control of the proper officer, recovery through detention and sale of goods, garnishee proceedings, distraint and sale of movable or immovable property, recovery through the Collector, and recovery through the appropriate Magistrate. The Court held that the width of Section 79 is evident from sub-section (1), with the proper officer entitled to recover amounts payable by adopting one or more of the modes specified in clauses (a) to (f). The Court specifically concluded that blocking of the credit ledger, including negative blocking, clearly falls within the scope of those clauses. The Court distinguished Rule 86A from Section 79. It observed that Rule 86A is a provisional measure typically undertaken at the pre-determination-of-liability stage, whereas Section 79 provides wider powers because the measures under it operate at the post-determination stage for recovery of amounts due and payable to the Government. The Madras High Court upheld the blocking of M/s. Zigma Machinery & Equipment Solutions’ electronic credit ledger and rejected the argument that the blockage had to be lifted because of an interim stay in a related case. The ledger had been blocked by reference No. BL3302250000152 dated 04.02.2025, and the petitioner asked for permission to freely use the input tax credit in that ledger; the Court held that the later interim order dated 25.02.2026 only paused recovery proceedings and did not undo or invalidate the earlier blocking order. The Court also confirmed that the underlying assessment order dated 17.03.2023 covered the assessment period 2017–2020, and that the related writ challenge to clubbing of multiple assessment periods did not change the effect of the blocking order being challenged here.

On the legal issue, the petitioner argued that “negative blocking” of the electronic credit ledger was beyond the power granted by Section 79 of the CGST Act and compared that provision with Rule 86A of the CGST Rules. The Court disagreed and held that Section 79(1) is broad enough to authorize recovery of amounts payable to the Government through the specified recovery modes in clauses (a) to (f), and that blocking the credit ledger — including negative blocking — falls within that recovery framework. The Court specifically distinguished Rule 86A as a provisional, pre-determination safeguard, whereas Section 79 operates after liability has been determined and permits recovery of dues already payable. As a result, the Court found no legal infirmity in the blocking of the electronic credit ledger, held that amounts in the ledger could not be debited for recovery while the interim stay remained in effect, and disposed of the writ petition with no order as to costs.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12620 Case Name Nahas Kakkattummal Vs ITO (Kerala High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Kerala High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Nahas Kakkattummal Vs ITO (Kerala High Court) Summary: The appellant approached the Kerala High Court in a writ appeal after the learned Single Judge declined to exercise writ jurisdiction and relegated him to the alternative statutory remedy under the Income Tax Act, 1961. The dispute concerned amounts received by the appellant while pursuing postgraduate medical studies. According to the appellant, the amounts were stipend and not salary. The appellant’s counsel contended that the assessment order had been issued by relying “blindly” on documents supplied by the University where the appellant was studying and drawing stipend, in which the sums were shown as salary. It was submitted that the appellant was admittedly a postgraduate student and that the amount received was stipend statutorily paid under law and in accordance with mandatory guidelines of the National Medical Commission. On that basis, it was argued that the Assessing Authority could not assess the receipts as salary. Alternatively, the appellant sought liberty to produce additional documents before the Assessing Authority. Counsel pointed out that even the University communication relied upon by the Assessing Authority categorically certified that the appellant had been admitted to an MD/MS postgraduate course as a Junior Resident. It was submitted that such students were covered by the regulations of the NMC, which prohibited payment of salary but mandated stipend. The appellant also relied upon Ext.P5, which certified that he was a bona fide PG student of the University, and contended that the letters relied upon by the Assessing Authority were contrary to that certificate. The Income Tax Department opposed the appeal. Its Senior Standing Counsel submitted that, when information was sought from the University, the Department received an intimation stating that the appellant had been paid salary “in lieu of the work tendered” (sic). The University letter had been extracted in the Assessment Order and, according to the Department, clearly showed that the payments were treated as salary. TDS had also been deducted and remitted. It was therefore argued that the matter involved disputed questions of fact and that the learned Single Judge had correctly relegated the appellant to the statutory remedy. The Division Bench accepted that, where an alternative efficacious remedy exists, a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution would normally be untenable. However, the Court noted that established exceptions exist, particularly where the impugned order has been issued without adverting to relevant facts and law and consequently stands vitiated. In the present case, the Assessing Officer had proceeded solely on the basis of the letters stated to have been received from the University, without adverting to the other documents relied upon by the appellant, including Ext.P5 and the Government Order under which he had been admitted to the course. The Court clarified that this did not necessarily mean that the Assessing Officer was at fault, since the assessee also had the responsibility of placing relevant material before the authority. At the same time, the appellant’s case was that he had not been given such an opportunity. The Court considered it significant that the “stipend” paid to a student was admitted to be fully exempted from the ambit of the Act. The Assessment Order did not address this aspect and instead treated the sums as “salary” solely on the basis of certain documents obtained from the University. The Court held that whether the receipts were actually stipend was a vital question of fact which the assessee had to be given an opportunity to establish cogently before a conclusive view could be taken against him. TaxGuru has also discussed the taxation of student scholarships/stipends in its post Tax on scholarship/Stipends to students. Accordingly, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside both the impugned judgment of the learned Single Judge and Ext.P12 order. Full liberty was left with the Assessing Officer to reconsider the matter after affording the appellant the necessary opportunity to produce documents and other germane inputs, culminating in an appropriate fresh Assessment Order as expeditiously as possible. The Court expressly clarified that it had not entered into the merits of the rival contentions. Its observations were confined to guiding the decision to set aside the existing order and provide the appellant an opportunity for fresh consideration. rows.summary:
The Kerala High Court remanded a tax dispute involving a postgraduate medical student’s receipts, holding that the Assessing Officer had assessed the amounts as “salary” without adequately considering the taxpayer’s claim that they were a statutory stipend paid to an MD/MS junior resident under National Medical Commission (NMC) rules. The assessee argued that the university documents relied on by the department were being read too literally, that a separate government order and certificate showed he was a bona fide postgraduate student, and that under the applicable medical education framework stipend — not salary — is what such students are to receive; he also asked for permission to submit additional records. The Income Tax Department countered that the university had informed it the payment was salary “in lieu of the work tendered,” and that TDS had been deducted and remitted, so the issue was factual and should be pursued through the ordinary statutory remedy rather than writ jurisdiction.

The High Court held that while writ jurisdiction is normally avoided where an effective alternative remedy exists, an exception applies where the assessment order is said to have been made without considering relevant facts and law. Here, the Court found that the Assessing Officer had relied only on certain university letters and had not addressed the taxpayer’s other materials, including Ext. P5 and the government order under which he was admitted to the course; the Court also noted that the assessment order did not deal with the taxpayer’s central contention that stipend paid to students is outside the tax net. The Court emphasized that whether the receipts were actually stipend was a material factual question that should be tested on a complete record, and that the taxpayer should be given a proper opportunity to produce supporting documents before any final adverse conclusion is reached.

As a result, the High Court set aside both the Single Judge’s order and the impugned assessment-related order (Ext. P12), and sent the matter back to the Assessing Officer for fresh consideration. The department was given full liberty to reconsider the issue after allowing the assessee to place all relevant documents and other material, and the Court directed that a new assessment order be passed as expeditiously as possible. The Court expressly did not decide the merits of whether the payments were stipend or salary; it only ruled that the prior decision could not stand because the assessee had not been afforded a fair opportunity to establish his case.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Sandhya Roy Vs ITO (ITAT Kolkata) Summary: The appeal before the Kolkata ‘SMC’ Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal arose from the order of the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), National Faceless Appeal Centre, dated 16.02.2026 for AY 2015-16. The assessee had not originally filed a return of income and also did not file a return in response to the notice issued under section 148 on 31.03.2022. The reassessment concerned a Joint Development Agreement dated 22.01.2015 entered into by the assessee with a co-owner/developer arrangement. The Assessing Officer treated the JDA as a transfer of property under section 2(47), determined the total sale consideration at ₹48,68,542/- based on fair market value and cash consideration, took the cost of acquisition at NIL and completed assessment under sections 147, 144 and 144B at total income of ₹48,68,542/-, including long-term capital gains of the same amount. Before the CIT(A), the assessee challenged both the validity of reassessment and the capital-gains addition. On limitation, the assessee relied upon the Supreme Court decisions concerning the reassessment transition regime, including Union of India vs. Ashish Agarwal and Union of India & Ors. Vs Rajeev Bansal. The CIT(A), however, held that the notice dated 31.03.2022 was issued before 01.04.2022 and therefore did not fall within the category of notices which the Department had conceded before the Supreme Court to be time-barred. It consequently applied the directions in Ashish Agarwal to the case and rejected the limitation challenge. On the capital-gains issue, the CIT(A) accepted the Assessing Officer’s position that execution of the JDA resulted in extinguishment of the assessee’s rights in the capital asset and therefore constituted a transfer under section 2(47). The CIT(A) further observed that section 45(5A) was not applicable to the assessment year under consideration and that, in the absence of documentary evidence establishing the cost of acquisition, the cost was rightly taken as NIL. The assessee’s contention that possession was to be handed over only after obtaining the sanctioned plan, and therefore that no effective transfer occurred during FY 2014-15, was held to be unsubstantiated. Before the Tribunal, the assessee’s authorised representative principally sought restoration of the matter to the CIT(A). It was submitted that the valuation report concerning the two properties had never been communicated to the assessee and that she could not properly respond to the show-cause notice. The property had been inherited in 1994 from the assessee’s father along with her mother, and the assessee contended that the cost of acquisition ought to have been considered while computing long-term capital gains. The assessee also relied upon the purchase deed of her father and explained the JDA arrangement, including the proposed allocation of a first-floor flat and car-parking space, together with monetary consideration. The Tribunal considered the rival submissions, the facts, the record and the CIT(A)’s order. Rather than finally adjudicating the disputed valuation, cost of acquisition and merits of the capital-gains computation, it deemed it appropriate to set aside the CIT(A)’s order and restore the appeal to the CIT(A) for disposal of the assessee’s grounds on merits by passing a speaking order. The assessee was to receive a reasonable opportunity of being heard and to make further submissions in support of her grounds, while unnecessary adjournments were to be avoided. The Tribunal also directed that Rule 46A of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 be followed and that an opportunity of hearing be provided to the Assessing Officer, if required. Accordingly, the assessee’s appeal was partly allowed for statistical purposes. The Tribunal’s order therefore does not finally delete or confirm the ₹48,68,542/- capital-gains addition on the merits; instead, the CIT(A)’s order was set aside and the appeal was restored for fresh disposal on merits. Cases Discussed Union of India vs. Ashish Agarwal — considered in relation to reassessment notices issued during the transition to the amended reassessment regime. Union of India & Ors. Vs Rajeev Bansal — considered in relation to limitation of reassessment notices and the Revenue’s concession concerning AY 2015-16. FULL TEXT OF THE ORDER OF ITAT KOLKATA This appeal filed by the assessee is against the order of the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), National Faceless Appeal Centre (NFAC) [hereinafter referred to as Ld. ‘CIT(A)’] passed u/s 250 of the Act for AY 2015-16 dated 16.0
rows.summary:
The ITAT Kolkata’s SMC Bench did not finally decide the tax liability in this case; instead, it set aside the CIT(A)’s order and sent the matter back for fresh adjudication on the merits. The dispute arose from AY 2015-16 and concerned a Joint Development Agreement dated 22.01.2015 entered into by Sandhya Roy, under which the Assessing Officer treated the arrangement as a “transfer” of a capital asset under section 2(47) and assessed long-term capital gains of ₹48,68,542, using fair market value plus cash consideration as the sale consideration and taking the cost of acquisition at nil. The reassessment was initiated through a notice under section 148 dated 31.03.2022; the assessee had not filed a return originally or in response to that notice, and the assessment was completed under sections 147, 144 and 144B.

Before the CIT(A), the assessee challenged both the reopening and the capital-gains addition. On limitation, the CIT(A) rejected the challenge, holding that because the section 148 notice was issued before 01.04.2022, it was not one of the notices treated as time-barred in the reassessment transition cases; it applied the Supreme Court’s directions in Union of India vs. Ashish Agarwal and Union of India & Ors. vs. Rajeev Bansal. On merits, the CIT(A) agreed with the Assessing Officer that execution of the JDA extinguished the assessee’s rights and therefore amounted to a transfer, and it held that section 45(5A) did not apply to this assessment year. It also upheld the nil cost basis because, in its view, the assessee had not produced documentary evidence of cost of acquisition.

The Tribunal, however, did not affirm that merits determination. The assessee argued that the valuation report for the properties had never been communicated, that she therefore could not properly respond to the show-cause process, and that the property had been inherited in 1994 from her father along with her mother, so the cost of acquisition should have been taken into account; she also pointed to the father’s purchase deed and explained the agreed allotment of a first-floor flat, car parking space, and monetary consideration under the JDA. The Tribunal accepted that the matter required further factual examination and restored the appeal to the CIT(A) with directions to pass a speaking order after giving the assessee a reasonable opportunity of hearing, avoiding unnecessary adjournments, following Rule 46A of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 if additional evidence is involved, and giving the Assessing Officer an opportunity to be heard if needed. As a result, the ₹48,68,542 capital-gains addition remains unresolved on the merits and was neither deleted nor sustained by the Tribunal; the appeal was allowed only for statistical purposes.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12618 Case Name Ved Enterprises Unnao Vs State of U.P (Allahabad High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Allahabad High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ved Enterprises Unnao Vs State of U.P (Allahabad High Court) Summary: The petitioner challenged the order dated May 28, 2022 passed by the Deputy Commissioner, State Tax, Sector-1, District Unnao under Section 74 of the Uttar Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017. The writ petition was filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The petitioner’s registration under the Act had been cancelled on 16.11.2021. Thereafter, the petitioner did not carry on any business. A show cause notice was uploaded on the GST portal and, subsequently, the impugned order was passed under Section 74. The Court held that once the registration had been cancelled, the petitioner was not obligated to check the GST portal. The Court observed that the mode of service of any show cause notice had to be by way of alternative means to the petitioner. The petitioner relied upon the coordinate Bench decision in M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others, Neutral Citation No.2024:AHC:23697-DB. The Court stated that it was essentially in agreement with the principle enunciated by the coordinate Bench. Finding a violation of the principle of natural justice, the Allahabad High Court quashed and set aside the impugned order dated May 28, 2022. The Department was left at liberty to issue a proper notice to the petitioner and act in accordance with law. The writ petition was accordingly disposed of. Cases Discussed M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others, Neutral Citation No.2024:AHC:23697-DB FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF ALLAHABAD HIGH COURT 1. Heard Sri Mukesh Kumar Tewari, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner and Sri Sanjay Sarin, learned Additional Chief Standing Counsel appearing on behalf of the State-respondents. 2. This is a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India wherein the petitioner is aggrieved by the order dated May 28, 2022 passed by the respondent No.2/Deputy Commissioner, State Tax, Sector-1, District Unnao under Section 74 of the Uttar Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”). 3. Factual matrix in the matter is that the petitioner’s registration under the Act was cancelled on 16.11.2021. Subsequent to the same, no business was carried out by the petitioner. It appears that a show cause notice was uploaded on the GST portal and subsequent to the same, the order impugned was passed under Section 74 of the Act. 4. Once the registration has been cancelled, the petitioner is not obligated to check GST portal. The mode of service of any show cause notice has to be by way of alternative means to the petitioner. 5. Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner relies upon an order passed by the coordinate Bench of this Court in M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others, Neutral Citation No.2024:AHC:23697-DB. We are essentially in agreement with the said principle enunciated by the coordinate Bench in the said order. 6. We find that there has been violation of the principle of natural justice, and accordingly, the impugned order dated May 28, 2022 passed by the respondent No.2 is quashed and set aside. The Department shall be at liberty to issue a proper notice to the petitioner and act in accordance with law. 7. With the above direction, the writ petition is disposed of. rows.summary:
The Allahabad High Court quashed a GST demand/order passed under Section 74 of the Uttar Pradesh GST Act, 2017 because the department served the show-cause notice only by uploading it on the GST portal after the taxpayer’s registration had already been cancelled. In this case, Ved Enterprises Unnao’s registration was cancelled on 16.11.2021, it stopped carrying on business thereafter, and the impugned order was passed on 28.05.2022 by the Deputy Commissioner, State Tax, Sector-1, District Unnao. The Court held that once registration is cancelled, the taxpayer is not expected to keep checking the GST portal, so service of notice must be made by an alternative/appropriate means that actually reaches the taxpayer.

The Court agreed with the principle laid down in the coordinate Bench decision in M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others (Neutral Citation No. 2024:AHC:23697-DB), and found that failure to serve notice properly amounted to a violation of natural justice. As a result, the Section 74 order dated 28.05.2022 was set aside. The department was, however, expressly given liberty to issue a fresh, proper notice and proceed in accordance with law. For compliance teams, the key point is that after GST registration cancellation, portal-only service of show-cause notices may be legally insufficient; tax authorities must use a mode of service that reasonably informs the former registrant before passing adverse orders.

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court issued a common order on 24.04.2026 disposing of three interconnected writ petitions filed by Reckitt Benckiser (India) Private Limited concerning GST proceedings for the tax period 2019–2020. One petition challenged a show cause notice in Form GST DRC-01 dated 31.05.2024; another challenged an order/reply dated 29.05.2024; and the third challenged Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023, along with consequential Government Orders issued under Section 168A of the GST enactments that extended the limitation period. The dispute therefore centered on whether the limitation period for GST actions had been validly extended and whether the resulting notice and related proceedings for 2019–2020 could survive.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Court did not decide the merits of the limitation-extension notification or the underlying GST liability. At admission, the Court had granted interim protection on 13.08.2024, and afterward the jurisdictional State Tax Officer filed a detailed report dated 27.01.2026. The Court recorded that this report prima facie supported the petitioner’s position, and on that basis the petitioner stated that no further adjudication remained necessary in respect of the DRC-01 proceeding.

As a result of those subsequent developments, the Court treated the challenge to the show cause notice as no longer requiring adjudication and held that the challenges to the limitation-extension notification and the related order/reply had also become academic. Accordingly, W.P. Nos. 20652 and 20655 of 2024 were closed, and W.P. No. 20657 of 2024 was disposed of. No costs were awarded, and the connected miscellaneous petitions were also closed. The practical takeaway is that this order ends this particular litigation pathway without resolving the substantive validity of Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax or establishing a general rule on limitation extension under Section 168A for other taxpayers.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd Vs State of Rajasthan (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd and set aside the appellate order dated 27.02.2026, which had rejected the petitioner’s GST appeal on limitation. The Court directed the Appellate Authority to consider and decide the appeal on its own merits, subject to the petitioner firm depositing late fees, penalty and other statutory deposits as admissible. The petitioner had sought quashing of the order dated 07.02.2024 and restoration of its GST registration, besides setting aside the appellate order dated 27.02.2026 and a direction for adjudication of the appeal on merits. The petitioner relied principally on the Rajasthan High Court’s Division Bench judgment in M/s. Pratap Power Spares Vs. Union of India & Ors., D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 9882/2024, decided on 28.07.2026. In that case, the Court had condoned a 99-day delay after granting relaxation of 120 days under Section 107 of the CGST Act and directed the Appellate Authority to entertain the appeal and adjudicate it on merits if filed within 30 days. The petitioner also relied upon M/s. Molana Construction Company Vs. Central Goods and Service Tax Department & Ors., Man Singh Tanwar v. Commissioner, Central Goods and Services Tax Department & Ors., and the two decisions in RPC PSIPL JV Vs. State of Rajasthan & Ors. The petitioner additionally referred to M/s. Kakar Automobiles Vs. Union of India & Ors. The respondents relied upon Sharwan Singh Devda Vs. The Union of India & Ors., D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 15910/2026. The relevant passage recognised that there was no absolute bar on invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226/227 after expiry of the statutory appellate period, but cautioned that such jurisdiction could not ordinarily be exercised to circumvent the statutory limitation scheme. It stated that intervention may be justified in exceptional circumstances, including complete disregard of natural justice or clearly established inherent lack of jurisdiction. The petitioner submitted that the medical circumstances in the present matter constituted such exceptional circumstances and that the judgments relied upon were consistent in permitting consideration of delayed GST appeals where circumstances beyond the taxpayer’s control had prevented timely filing. The High Court accepted this submission. It held that although the Appellate Authority is bound by the statutory limitation provisions under Section 107 of the RGST/CGST Act, the medical reasons which resulted in the petitioner not submitting the appeal within the stipulated time were beyond the petitioner’s control. The Court further found that non-adjudication of the appeal on merits would cause grave injury and prejudice to the petitioner. Consequently, the Court exercised its writ jurisdiction, set aside the appellate order dated 27.02.2026 and directed the Appellate Authority to consider and decide the petitioner’s appeal on merits in accordance with law. The relief was made subject to the petitioner firm depositing late fees, penalty and other statutory deposits required for entertaining the appeal, as admissible. All pending applications were also disposed of. Cases Discussed M/s. Pratap Power Spares Vs. Union of India & Ors. — D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 9882/2024, decided on 28.07.2026. M/s. Union of India & Ors. — D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 13403/2026, decided on 13.07.2026. Sharwan Singh Devda Vs. The Union of India & Ors. — D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 15910/2026. rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST appeal rejected as time-barred could still be revived in exceptional circumstances where the delay was caused by medical reasons beyond the taxpayer’s control. In this case, Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd. challenged the order dated 07.02.2024 and also sought restoration of its GST registration; it further sought quashing of the appellate authority’s order dated 27.02.2026, which had refused to entertain the GST appeal on limitation grounds. The Court accepted the petitioner’s reliance on prior Rajasthan High Court decisions, including **Pratap Power Spares**, **Molana Construction Company**, **Man Singh Tanwar**, **RPC PSIPL JV**, and **Kakar Automobiles**, and distinguished the respondents’ reliance on **Sharwan Singh Devda**, noting that Article 226/227 relief is not barred after expiry of the statutory appeal period but should be used only in exceptional cases such as natural justice failures or clear lack of jurisdiction.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that although the appellate authority remains bound by the limitation provisions under **Section 107 of the RGST/CGST Act**, the High Court can intervene where the taxpayer shows that non-filing within time resulted from circumstances outside its control, here specifically medical reasons. The Court found that refusing to decide the appeal on merits would cause grave injury and prejudice to the petitioner, so it exercised writ jurisdiction to set aside the appellate order dated **27.02.2026** and ordered the appellate authority to hear and decide the appeal on merits in accordance with law. This relief was not unconditional: the petitioner must first deposit the **late fees, penalty, and other statutory deposits “as admissible”** for the appeal to be entertained. The judgment does not create a general extension of limitation, but it confirms that delayed GST appeals may be considered where a taxpayer can prove exceptional, uncontrollable circumstances, subject to compliance with the monetary/statutory pre-deposit requirements.

The Rajasthan High Court considered a writ petition by M/s Jagdish Prasad Agrawal, a partnership firm, challenging the blocking of its Input Tax Credit (ITC) in the Electronic Credit Ledger, including an alleged blocking of IGST ITC with a negative balance. The petitioner asked the Court to declare the blocking illegal, inoperative, and void, to quash it, and to direct re-credit of any ITC unlawfully set off against the disputed demand. By the time of hearing, the blocking had already ceased automatically by operation of law after one year, and the Electronic Credit Ledger had been reactivated, so the dispute had narrowed to whether the ITC could lawfully have been blocked in the first place without following Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017.

The respondents conceded that the ledger was now operational, but they could not show that the mandatory conditions under Rule 86A had been satisfied before blocking the credit. They admitted that the action was a bona fide mistake and that, although the officer had reasons for action, no proper reasoned order had been passed and the petitioner had not been given an opportunity of hearing before the blockage. The Court specifically noted that Rule 86A requires the competent authority to have “reasons to believe” that ITC has been fraudulently availed or is ineligible, and to record those reasons in writing before disallowing debit of an equivalent amount from the Electronic Credit Ledger for payment of tax liability under section 49 or for a refund of unutilised credit. The Court found, on the record before it, that these mandatory preconditions were not complied with.

Because the restriction had already expired and the ledger had been restored, the Court did not grant further substantive relief in the petition; instead, it disposed of the matter after accepting the unconditional apology tendered on behalf of the concerned officer. However, the Court issued a clear warning for future cases: if the department blocks ITC without due compliance with Rule 86A, it may become liable to pay appropriate compensation to the affected taxpayer. For compliance purposes, the key point is that Rule 86A safeguards are mandatory before ITC blocking—specifically, a recorded written basis and proper legal satisfaction by the competent authority are required, and a failure to follow those steps can expose the department to compensation exposure and judicial censure.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Agilent Technologies International Pvt Ltd Vs Commissioner of Central Goods & Service Tax (CESTAT Chandigarh) Summary: The Chandigarh Bench of the Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal of M/s Agilent Technologies International Pvt Ltd against denial of refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The appellant was a 100% export unit providing Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas entities under specific service agreements and exported those services without payment of service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005. It had claimed refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. Refund of ₹78,79,939 was rejected in respect of General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services on the ground that the services lacked nexus with exported output services. Before the Tribunal, the appellant contended that availment of CENVAT credit, its utilisation and its refund were distinct aspects and that, where the Department had not challenged availment under Rule 14, refund could not subsequently be denied under Rule 5 by questioning the credit’s eligibility. It further submitted that the disputed services fell within the definition of “input service” under Rule 2(l), relying on numerous judicial decisions, and that direct nexus with the final output services was not necessary in view of Circular No. 120/1/2010-ST dated 19.01.2010 and the decision in Reliance Corporate IT Park Ltd. The Tribunal held that it was settled by various decisions that where availment of CENVAT credit had not been challenged by the Department under Rule 14, refund could not be denied by resorting to Rule 5. It further found that, during the disputed period, the definition of input service was exhaustive and that General Insurance Service, Commercial or Industrial Construction Services and Works Contract Service had been held to be input services by various decisions.
