The CESTAT Chandigarh allowed Agilent Technologies International Pvt. Ltd.’s appeal against denial of refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Agilent was a 100% export unit providing Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas customers under service agreements and exporting those services without paying service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005; it had claimed refund of accumulated credit under Rule 5 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The refund amount at issue was ₹78,79,939, which the department had rejected on the ground that credit taken on General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services, and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services allegedly had no nexus with the exported output services.  

The Tribunal held that the department could not deny a Rule 5 refund by re-litigating the eligibility of credit where the availment of that CENVAT credit had never been challenged under Rule 14 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. In other words, the decision treats credit availment, its utilisation, and refund of unutilised credit as distinct issues, and says a refund objection under Rule 5 cannot be used as a substitute for an untimely or absent challenge to credit admissibility itself. The Tribunal also reiterated that, for the relevant period, the definition of “input service” under Rule 2(l) was exhaustive and that the disputed services had been accepted in various precedents as qualifying input services; it further accepted the appellant’s position that direct one-to-one nexus with the exported output services was not necessary, relying on Circular No. 120/1/2010-ST dated 19.01.2010 and case law including Reliance Corporate IT Park Ltd.  

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that exporters claiming Rule 5 refunds should retain documentation showing that the underlying credits were validly availed and not previously disputed, because the Tribunal emphasized that once the department has not invoked Rule 14 to challenge availment, it cannot later deny refund merely by questioning nexus at the refund stage. The order ultimately set aside the impugned denial and granted the refund with consequential relief, if any, as per law.

Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Hyderabad considered an appeal by M/s Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. against an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 confirming Service Tax demands, interest and penalties principally under “Banking and Other Financial Services” and “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” for 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The first dispute concerned charges deducted by foreign/intermediary banks while export proceeds were transmitted from foreign buyers through banking channels. The appellant, a manufacture-exporter of pharmaceutical products, contended that the foreign buyers remitted consideration through their banking arrangements and that the foreign/intermediary banks deducted charges before the balance reached the appellant’s Indian bank. The Department proceeded on the basis that, because the deductions economically reduced the amount received by the appellant, the appellant was the recipient of banking services and was liable to Service Tax under Reverse Charge Mechanism. The Tribunal rejected that approach. It found no evidence that the appellant had engaged the foreign banks, entered into contractual arrangements with them, or was otherwise obliged to pay consideration to them for services rendered to it. Merely bearing the economic impact of deductions did not establish a service provider-service recipient relationship. The Tribunal also relied on the appellant’s own earlier decision, Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020, where the same issue for the earlier period had been decided in the appellant’s favour, and on Eastman Exports Global Clothing Pvt Ltd. The demand under Banking and Other Financial Services was accordingly held unsustainable. The second dispute concerned payments made to M/s DADA Consultancy and M/s Pharpe Dr. D.R. Iban for preparation and compilation of clinical and non-clinical overviews and regulatory documentation required for obtaining overseas pharmaceutical product approvals. Revenue classified the activities as “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” because the consultants possessed scientific and technical expertise and the documentation involved scientific and technical product particulars. The appellant submitted that the agencies merely compiled already available data and published material and prepared regulatory dossiers/forms; they did not undertake independent scientific research, experimentation or technical studies, nor did they provide advice in a discipline of science or technology. The Tribunal followed the appellant’s earlier decision and the decision in IPCA Laboratories Ltd., holding that regulatory services connected with obtaining permissions/registrations and meeting overseas regulatory requirements cannot merely on that account be classified as Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services. It emphasised that the essential character of a service must be determined from the activity actually undertaken, rather than merely from the professional qualifications of the persons rendering it. rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad set aside the Service Tax demands raised against Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. in an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 for the periods 2011-12 and up to June 2012, along with the related interest and penalties. Two categories of demand were in dispute: first, amounts deducted by foreign/intermediary banks from export remittances before the net proceeds reached the appellant’s Indian bank; and second, payments to overseas regulatory consultants for preparing clinical/non-clinical overviews and other documentation for foreign pharma product approvals.  

On the banking issue, the Tribunal held that Aurobindo was not the recipient of a taxable banking service merely because bank charges were economically borne through reduced export proceeds. The record did not show that the company had contracted with, engaged, or owed consideration to the foreign banks, so the reverse charge demand under “Banking and Other Financial Services” was unsustainable; the Tribunal also relied on its own earlier favourable order for an earlier period and the Eastman Exports decision.  

On the consultancy issue, the Tribunal rejected Revenue’s attempt to classify regulatory dossier preparation and compilation work performed by M/s DADA Consultancy and M/s Pharpe Dr. D.R. Iban as “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services.” It held that compiling already available information and published material for regulatory submissions, without independent scientific research, experimentation, technical studies, or actual advice in a scientific/technical discipline, does not become scientific/technical consultancy simply because the service providers have technical expertise or the documentation relates to scientific product particulars. The Tribunal emphasized that the true nature of the activity controls classification, and it followed the appellant’s earlier case and IPCA Laboratories Ltd. for the proposition that services connected with obtaining regulatory approvals/registrations abroad are not automatically taxable under that head.  

The order also noted that Aurobindo had already discharged Service Tax on these consultant payments under “Management or Business Consultant Service,” and the impugned order had appropriated that tax while simultaneously reclassifying the same activity under another taxable heading; once the reclassification failed, the demand could not survive. Because the substantive tax demands were set aside, the associated interest and penalties were also quashed, and the Tribunal did not separately rule on the appellant’s Section 76 penalty-computation argument tied to the amendment effective 08.04.2011.

Rajendra Bane had been serving as a Customs Hawaldar. The penalties arose from an investigation into smuggled gold recovered from the gent’s toilet at Pune International Airport after passengers travelled from Dubai by Spice Jet Flight No. SG 52 on 16.08.2018. The allegation was that although Rajendra Bane was on sanctioned leave and staying at his native place near Ratnagiri, he had facilitated the smuggling of gold and assisted the smugglers. The material relied upon against him included statements recorded under Section 108 of the Customs Act, 1962, particularly statements of co-accused/accomplices, call records received from the telephone operator, and recovery of gold from the airport toilet and from a passenger. The defence completely denied involvement. It admitted that Rajendra Bane was on leave and at his native place on the relevant day, but contended that the seizure had actually followed information transmitted by him to the Superintendent on duty at Pune International Airport. The defence claimed that the information involved privileged communication with an informer and therefore its source could not be disclosed. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, rejected this explanation. He considered the statements of co-accused to have been corroborated by SDRs/CDRs and the recovery of gold, and relied upon the Supreme Court decision in Naresh J. Sukhwani Vs. UOI [1996 (83) ELT 258 (S.C)] concerning the evidentiary value of statements recorded under Section 108. The Commissioner (Appeals) also treated the phone call made by Rajendra Bane to the Superintendent as an afterthought intended to camouflage his role. A further adverse inference was drawn because, when the Superintendent did not respond to the first call, Rajendra Bane had allegedly not approached another departmental officer. The Tribunal found that the reliance on Naresh J. Sukhwani was made in a materially different factual context. It noted that nothing incriminating, including the allegedly relevant SIM card, had been seized from Rajendra Bane. The Tribunal referred to the principle concerning accomplice evidence under Section 114, illustration (b), of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and held that where nothing incriminating had been seized from the deceased Appellant, he could not be implicated solely on the statement of a co-accused or accomplice. The Tribunal also examined the call evidence more closely. According to the record considered by the Tribunal, the Superintendent, Shri D.G. rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai set aside the personal penalties of ₹2,50,000 and ₹1,00,000 imposed under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962 on late Rajendra Bane, a Customs Hawaldar, and deleted the penalties entirely for lack of proof that he knowingly aided the smuggling operation. The case arose from the recovery of smuggled gold from a men’s toilet at Pune International Airport after SpiceJet Flight SG 52 from Dubai arrived on 16.08.2018, with the Department alleging that Bane—though on sanctioned leave and at his native place near Ratnagiri—had facilitated the smuggling through statements of co-accused, call records, and the recovery of gold from the airport and a passenger.  

The Tribunal held that the Department’s case rested too heavily on accomplice/co-accused statements and that, under the evidentiary principle reflected in Section 114 illustration (b) of the Indian Evidence Act, a person cannot be implicated solely on such statements where no incriminating material was seized from him. It specifically noted that no incriminating article, including the allegedly relevant SIM card, had been recovered from Bane, and it distinguished the Commissioner (Appeals)’ reliance on the Supreme Court’s Naresh J. Sukhwani precedent as being in a materially different factual setting. The Tribunal also found weaknesses in the call-record theory: the Superintendent, Shri D.G. Nandanwar, had called Bane back and was told that the gold had been dumped in the Immigration Hall men’s lavatory, and the investigation showed calls from Bane’s son Prathmesh Rajendra Bane’s number between 03:04:03 A.M. and 05:33 A.M., whereas the CDR produced to the Superintendent for 5:00 A.M. to 6:00 A.M. did not show that number; the seizure itself occurred at 05:15 A.M.  

On the facts, the Tribunal concluded that the Department failed to establish that the later call to the Superintendent was a fabricated afterthought or that Bane was acting in connivance with the smugglers. It also rejected the adverse inference drawn by the lower authority from Bane’s alleged failure to contact another officer when the Superintendent did not answer the first call, finding that such reasoning did not overcome the absence of direct incriminating evidence. The Tribunal viewed the surrounding circumstances as more consistent with Bane having provided an actionable tip that led to recovery of more than 13 kg of smuggled gold, including about 10 kg found in the dustbin of the men’s toilet, rather than with his being part of the smuggling network. As a result, the Section 112(a) penalties were deleted in full.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal Vs State of Bihar (Patna High Court) Summary: The Patna High Court considered a writ petition filed by M/S Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal, a registered GST person engaged in conducting Nukkad Natak (street plays) for public awareness programmes primarily assigned by Government Departments. The petitioner challenged the Appellate Authority’s order dated 28.02.2026 in Appeal Case No. GST/PTC-2—2025-26 and the underlying demand dated 20.08.2025 raising tax, interest and penalty of Rs. 1,63,452/-. The dispute arose for the financial year 2022-23. A notice had been issued against the petitioner under Section 73 of the CGST Act, 2017 on the basis of gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100/- received from the District Public Relations Officer, Gaya. The Adjudicating Authority subsequently imposed a liability of tax, interest and penalty amounting to Rs. 1,63,452/- on 20.08.2025. The petitioner thereafter filed an appeal under Section 107(1) of the CGST Act, 2017. The appeal was dismissed on 28.02.2026 because it was filed with a delay of 21 days. The petitioner, however, relied upon a subsequent memo issued by the Collectorate, Gaya, Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025. According to the petitioner, that communication stated that GST was not applicable to receipts against sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in the profession of Nukkad Natak and that Nukkad Natak teams comprising (4-6-8-10) members were exempted from the GST regime. Before the High Court, the petitioner therefore contended that the underlying issue was not merely the delay in filing the appeal but whether the petitioner, being a registered person performing Nukkad Natak, was exempt from GST liability. The State opposed the petition on limitation grounds, submitting that the Appellate Authority had rightly dismissed the appeal after expiry of the statutory period by 21 days. It was also submitted that the alleged exemption communication had been issued by the District Public Relation Officer, Gaya, and did not identify the statutory provision or any decision of the GST Council under which the Nukkad Natak team was claimed to be exempt. The High Court focused on the nature of the issue raised by the petitioner. It observed that the exemption question went to the root concerning the jurisdiction of the authority which had imposed the tax liability. The Court further noted that the Appellate Authority had dismissed the appeal as time barred instead of deciding the substantive exemption issue raised by the petitioner. In these circumstances, the High Court held that the Appellate Authority must decide the petitioner’s contention that, as a registered person performing Nukkad Natak, it was exempted from GST liability. The Court accordingly set aside the appellate order dated 28.02.2026 and remitted the matter to the Appellate Authority for deciding the exemption issue in accordance with law within two months from receipt or production of the High Court’s order. The writ petition was disposed of with further procedural directions. The petitioner was directed to produce a copy of the High Court order and appear before the Appellate Authority for fixing the hearing date within one week. Upon production of the order, the Appellate Authority was directed to fix the hearing and dispose of the appeal after granting personal hearing to the petitioner within a maximum period of two months. The judgment therefore does not finally determine that Nukkad Natak is exempt from GST. Instead, the High Court set aside the dismissal on limitation and required the competent Appellate Authority to examine and decide the exemption claim in accordance with law. The Patna High Court did **not** decide the merits of whether Nukkad Natak services are exempt from GST, but it held that the **exemption question must be examined on the merits** rather than being rejected solely as time-barred. The petitioner, **M/s Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal**, is a **GST-registered entity** engaged in **Nukkad Natak (street plays)** for public awareness programs assigned mainly by government departments; for **FY 2022–23**, it received **gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100** from the **District Public Relations Officer, Gaya**, leading to a **Section 73 CGST Act notice** and an adjudication order dated **20.08.2025** imposing **tax, interest, and penalty totaling Rs. 1,63,452**. The petitioner appealed under **Section 107(1)** of the CGST Act, but the Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on **28.02.2026** because it was filed **21 days late**.  

The petitioner relied on **Collectorate, Gaya Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025**, which allegedly stated that **GST is not applicable to receipts against sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in Nukkad Natak** and that **Nukkad Natak teams of 4–6–8–10 members are exempt from GST**; however, the State argued that this communication did not identify any statutory exemption provision or GST Council decision and that the appeal was simply out of time. The High Court treated the exemption issue as one going to the **root of tax jurisdiction** and faulted the Appellate Authority for dismissing the appeal on limitation without deciding the substantive claim. Accordingly, the Court **set aside the 28.02.2026 appellate order** and **remitted the matter back to the Appellate Authority** to decide whether the petitioner, as a registered person performing Nukkad Natak, is actually **exempt from GST liability**, in accordance with law.  

For procedure, the petitioner must **produce a copy of the High Court order and appear before the Appellate Authority within one week** for fixation of a hearing date. Upon production, the Appellate Authority must provide a **personal hearing** and dispose of the appeal **within a maximum of two months** from receipt/production of the High Court order. Compliance takeaway: this ruling does **not** create a general GST exemption for Nukkad Natak teams; it only requires the appellate forum to determine the exemption claim on its legal merits in this case.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 54 Shortfall Not Taxable in Original Year: Mumbai ITAT Deletes Penalty
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12610 Case Name Rajesh Parasram Nichani Vs ITO (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2014-15 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Rajesh Parasram Nichani Vs ITO (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The appeal was filed by the assessee against the order dated 19.02.2026 passed by the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals)/National Faceless Appeal Centre, Delhi under section 250 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for Assessment Year 2014-15. The dispute concerned a penalty of Rs.5,25,923/- levied under section 271(1)(c) in relation to an exemption claimed under section 54. The assessee had sold a residential house for Rs.1,35,00,000/- and computed long-term capital gain of Rs.72,19,588/-. He claimed exemption under section 54 for the entire long-term capital gain and filed his return under section 139(1). During scrutiny proceedings, the assessee explained that Rs.68,25,500/- had been invested with M/s Damodar Suruchi Developers in respect of a proposed residential project and Rs.10,00,000/- had been deposited in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme maintained with the State Bank of India. The project undertaken by M/s Damodar Suruchi Developers was subsequently stalled for reasons beyond the assessee’s control. The assessee entered into a compromise transaction and purchased another residential property for Rs.49,95,000/-. The resulting shortfall of Rs.24,40,579/- was admitted by the assessee as chargeable to tax. The Assessing Officer accordingly brought that amount to tax in AY 2014-15 and simultaneously levied penalty of Rs.5,25,923/-, being 100% of the tax sought to be evaded, under section 271(1)(c). The CIT(A) confirmed the penalty. According to the CIT(A), the assessee had furnished inaccurate particulars by claiming excess exemption under section 54 and had not voluntarily disclosed the shortfall before scrutiny. The CIT(A) relied upon the Supreme Court decision in MAK Data (P.) Ltd. and held that disclosure after issuance of a scrutiny notice could not be treated as voluntary. The CIT(A) also rejected the assessee’s contention based on section 54(2), holding that the funds had not been utilised in accordance with the investment plan disclosed in the return. Before the Tribunal, the assessee primarily relied upon section 54(2) and contended that the shortfall could become taxable only in the assessment year relevant to expiry of the statutory period prescribed under that provision, and not in AY 2014-15. The Revenue relied upon the orders of the lower authorities. The Tribunal examined the proviso to section 54(2), which provides that where an amount deposited in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme remains unutilised for the purchase or construction of a new residential house within the prescribed period, the unutilised amount is charged under section 45 in the previous year in which the three-year period expires. The Tribunal noted that, strictly speaking, the proviso applies to amounts deposited in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme, whereas the substantial amount in the present case had been invested with M/s Damodar Suruchi Developers. Nevertheless, the Tribunal considered the underlying legislative intent relevant. The Tribunal noted that the assessee entered into a fresh purchase agreement on 28.05.2015, relevant to AY 2016-17, and ultimately invested Rs.49,95,000/- in the new residential property instead of the originally proposed investment of Rs.68,25,500/- and Rs.10,00,000/- in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme. Consequently, Rs.24,40,579/- of the capital gain ultimately remained liable to tax. The Tribunal held that the shortfall could not have been subjected to tax in AY 2014-15. At the time of filing the original return, the assessee was still within the statutory period available for making the investment under section 54. Further, by the time it became apparent that the entire proposed investment would not materialise, the time limit for filing a revised return under section 139(5) had expired, while the statutory investment period had not. The Tribunal therefore held that the assessee could not have revised the return to offer the shortfall to tax in AY 2014-15. Accordingly, once the amount of Rs.24,40,579/- was held not liable to tax in the impugned assessment year, the very basis for alleging concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars for AY 2014-15 disappeared. The Tribunal therefore held that the penalty under section 271(1)(c) could not be sustained and directed the Assessing Officer to delete the penalty of Rs.5,25,923/-. The appeal was allowed. Cases Discussed MAK Data (P.) Ltd. — relied upon by the CIT(A) for the proposition concerning disclosure made after scrutiny proceedings. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF IT
rows.summary: This ITAT Mumbai decision concerns an AY 2014-15 penalty dispute under section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, arising from the assessee’s claim of section 54 capital gains exemption after selling a residential house for Rs.1,35,00,000 and computing long-term capital gain of Rs.72,19,588. The assessee initially claimed exemption for the full capital gain, stating that Rs.68,25,500 had been invested with M/s Damodar Suruchi Developers for a proposed residential project and Rs.10,00,000 had been deposited in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme with SBI; when the project stalled, he later entered into a compromise and purchased another residential property for Rs.49,95,000, leaving a shortfall of Rs.24,40,579 that was ultimately admitted to be taxable. The Assessing Officer taxed that Rs.24,40,579 in AY 2014-15 and imposed a penalty of Rs.5,25,923, equal to 100% of the tax sought to be evaded, and the CIT(A)/NFAC upheld the penalty on the theory that the assessee had furnished inaccurate particulars by claiming excess exemption and had not voluntarily disclosed the shortfall before scrutiny, relying on MAK Data (P.) Ltd. The Tribunal disagreed and held that, under section 54(2), the shortfall could not be taxed in AY 2014-15 because the statutory investment period had not yet expired when the original return was filed, and by the time it became clear that the full investment would not materialize, the time limit for filing a revised return under section 139(5) had already lapsed; the Tribunal also noted that a fresh purchase agreement was entered into on 28.05.2015, relevant to AY 2016-17. Although the proviso to section 54(2) technically applies to unutilised amounts in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme, the Tribunal treated the legislative intent as supporting the view that taxability arises only in the year of expiry of the prescribed period, not immediately in the original assessment year. Because the Rs.24,40,579 was held not taxable in AY 2014-15, the Tribunal found that there was no basis for alleging concealment or furnishing of inaccurate particulars for that year and deleted the entire penalty of Rs.5,25,923; the assessee’s appeal was allowed.

Builders by way of remand in a dispute concerning alleged excess Input Tax Credit (ITC) of ₹2,33,502/- for Financial Year 2018–19. The disputed amount comprised CGST of ₹1,16,751/- and SGST of ₹1,16,751/-. Interest of ₹2,03,730/- and penalty of ₹23,350/- had also been imposed, resulting in a total demand of ₹4,60,582/-. The Appellant also challenged the proceedings on the ground that no personal hearing was granted and that no notice in FORM GST ASMT-10 had preceded the proceedings. A pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A was issued on 22.01.2024, followed by a Show Cause Notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 under Section 73. The First Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal and upheld the demand. The Tribunal first considered whether the GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A difference could be treated as inadmissible ITC without examining the Appellant’s explanation concerning Financial Year 2017–18 invoices. It noted that, during the transition period, Section 16(4) permitted the relevant ITC to be claimed within the applicable extended period. The Tribunal also relied upon CBIC Circular No. 183/15/2022-GST, which specifically addresses differences between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A for FY 2017–18 and 2018–19 and requires verification rather than summary disallowance. The Tribunal held that non-appearance of an invoice in GSTR-2A for Financial Year 2018–19 did not, without verification, establish that the supplier had failed to pay tax. It found that the Appellate Authority had proceeded on an assumption and had not undertaken invoice-wise verification of the Appellant’s explanation. The Tribunal therefore answered Issue No. 1 in favour of the Appellant, holding that the demand could not be sustained on the existing record without such verification. The Tribunal, however, rejected the Appellant’s contention concerning FORM GST ASMT-10. It held that Section 61 and Section 73 are independent provisions. rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, remanded a GST input tax credit dispute involving M/s. N. R. Builders, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, after setting aside both the Order-in-Original dated 20.04.2024 and the Order-in-Appeal dated 07.11.2024. The case involved an alleged excess ITC of ₹2,33,502 for FY 2018–19, split equally into CGST of ₹1,16,751 and SGST of ₹1,16,751, with related interest of ₹2,03,730 and penalty of ₹23,350, taking the total demand to ₹4,60,582. The department had issued a pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A on 22.01.2024 and then a show cause notice in FORM GST DRC-01 on 30.01.2024 under Section 73; the notice recorded the personal hearing details as “NA,” and the Proper Officer confirmed the demand ex parte. The Tribunal held that the dispute could not be resolved merely by pointing to a GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A mismatch, because the assessee’s explanation was that the credit related to FY 2017–18 invoices but was lawfully availed in FY 2018–19 within the period permitted by Section 16(4). It relied on CBIC Circular No. 183/15/2022-GST, which requires verification of such mismatches for FY 2017–18 and 2018–19 instead of automatic disallowance, and specifically found that non-appearance of an invoice in GSTR-2A does not by itself prove that the supplier failed to pay tax.

On facts, the Tribunal concluded that neither the adjudicating authority nor the first appellate authority had conducted the necessary invoice-wise verification of the appellant’s explanation, and therefore the demand could not be sustained on the existing record. It also rejected the first appellate authority’s reliance on Mahalakshmi Cotton Ginning Processing and Oil Industries v. State of Maharashtra, ALD Automotive Private Limited v. CTO, and Microqual Techno Ltd. v. State of Karnataka, holding that those cases were distinguishable because the statutory provisions and factual circumstances differed and there was no finding here that the underlying purchases were non-genuine. On natural justice, the Tribunal found a procedural defect: Section 75(4) requires an opportunity of hearing when an adverse decision is proposed, and since the notice itself showed “NA” for personal hearing and there was no evidence that any hearing was actually granted, the ex parte order was unsustainable. The Tribunal rejected the appellant’s argument that FORM GST ASMT-10 was mandatory, holding that Section 61 scrutiny and Section 73 demand proceedings are independent and that failure to issue ASMT-10 does not invalidate a directly initiated Section 73 proceeding. Interest and penalty were left to follow the outcome of the reassessment, with the Tribunal noting their dependence on the final tax determination and citing the compensatory nature of interest.

For compliance purposes, the remand order requires the Proper Officer to redo the adjudication de novo and specifically verify the ITC invoice-wise against FY 2017–18 GSTR-2A, suppliers’ GSTR-1, the assessee’s ITC register, books of account, and GSTR-9/GSTR-9C for both FY 2017–18 and FY 2018–19. The practical takeaway is that where a taxpayer claims that ITC appearing mismatched in GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A was actually eligible because it related to prior-year invoices booked and availed within the Section 16(4) time limit, the department must examine the underlying invoices and reconciliation before disallowing credit, and must also provide a genuine opportunity of hearing before confirming liability.

rows.title: Income Tax | Gujarat HC Allows Section 11(1A) Exemption to Charitable Trust, Quashes Section 264 Rejection
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12608 Case Name Sheth Shree Karshandas Halu Dharamshala Jamnagar VS CIT (Exemption) & Anr. (Gujarat High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Gujarat High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Sheth Shree Karshandas Halu Dharamshala Jamnagar VS CIT (Exemption) & Anr. (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court has allowed the writ petition filed by Sheth Shree Karshandas Halu Dharamshala Jamnagar and quashed the order dated 19.11.2020 passed under Section 264 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, rejecting the Trust’s claim for exemption under Section 11(1A) in respect of capital gains reinvested in a fixed deposit. The petitioner, a public charitable trust registered under the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950 and under Section 12A of the Income-tax Act with effect from 01.04.2007, had sold its immovable property for Rs.4,87,50,000/- under a registered sale deed dated 11.07.2011. The entire sale proceeds were thereafter invested in a two-year Fixed Deposit Receipt with Canara Bank, Jamnagar, in accordance with the conditions imposed by the Joint Charity Commissioner. For A.Y. 2012-13, the Trust inadvertently failed to claim the exemption under Section 11(1A) for the reinvestment of the capital gains, although the capital gains were fully disclosed and tax was paid. The return was processed under Section 143(1), resulting in a demand of Rs.19,44,180/-. The Trust subsequently invoked Section 264. The High Court relied upon the principles laid down in C. Parikh & Co., Ramdev Exports and S.R. Koshti, holding that revisional jurisdiction under Section 264 is sufficiently wide to grant relief where an assessee has been over-assessed because of a mistake or omission. The fact that the assessee itself had disclosed the income in the original return did not prevent the Commissioner from considering the lawful exemption. The Court further held that the question relevant to the claim was whether the Trust satisfied the requirements of Section 11(1A) read with CBDT Instruction No. 883 dated 24.09.1975. Since the sale proceeds were invested in an FDR with a scheduled bank for more than six months, the investment qualified for the treatment contemplated under Section 11(1A). The Court held that Section 11(1A) was a standalone provision and could not be interjected with Section 36(1)(a) of the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950 for denying the capital gains exemption. Following the Bombay High Court decision in Swaminarayan Mandir Trust, the Court also held that Section 264 could cover a situation where an assessee commits an error or mistake in the return. The decision of the Supreme Court in Goetze (India) Ltd. was held to be inapposite because it concerned a claim made before the Assessing Officer otherwise than through a revised return and did not govern the Commissioner’s revisional jurisdiction under Section 264. The High Court concluded that the petitioner had acted bona fide, had disclosed the entire capital gains, had paid the tax and had not suppressed any material. It therefore quashed the impugned order dated 19.11.2020, allowed the Section 264 application and held that the petitioner was entitled to exemption under Section 11(1A). The Court directed payment of excess tax of Rs.1,00,27,295/- for A.Y. 2012-13 together with applicable interest under Section 244A, with necessary orders to be passed within four weeks. List of Cases Discussed / Relied Upon Chandrakant J. Patel vs. V.N Srivastava, [2012] 20 taxmann.com 513 (Guj.) — considered regarding the exercise of revisional powers under Section 264. C. Parikh & Co. vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, [1980] 4 Taxman 224 (Guj.) — referred to for the proposition that revisional powers can grant relief where an assessee detects a mistake after assessment. S.R. Koshti vs. CIT, 276 ITR 165 (Guj.) — referred to for the proposition that only legitimate tax due under law should be collected. Ramdev Exports vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, 251 ITR 873 — referred to regarding the revisional authority’s power to consider deductions claimed for the first time. Swaminarayan Mandir Trust vs. Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions), Mumbai & Ors., [2026] 182 taxmann.com 209 (Bom.) — referred to regarding the scope of Section 264 where an assessee commits an error or mistake in the return. Goetze (India) Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, [2006] 157 Taxman 1 / 284 ITR 323 (SC) — considered and held inapposite to a revision under Section 264. Bahar Infocons Pvt. Ltd. Vs PCIT — referred to in considering the distinction between Goetze (India) Ltd. and the revisional jurisdiction under Section 264. Hapag Lloyd India Pvt. Ltd. Vs PCIT — referred to regarding the width of revisional jurisdiction under Section 264. Geekay Security Services (P) Ltd. v
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court held that a charitable trust could obtain exemption under Section 11(1A) of the Income-tax Act even though it had not claimed the exemption in its original return, and it quashed the Commissioner’s rejection of the trust’s Section 264 revision application dated 19.11.2020. The assessee, Sheth Shree Karshandas Halu Dharamshala Jamnagar, was a public charitable trust registered under the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950 and registered under Section 12A of the Income-tax Act with effect from 01.04.2007; it sold immovable property for Rs. 4,87,50,000 under a registered sale deed dated 11.07.2011 and then invested the entire sale consideration in a two-year fixed deposit receipt with Canara Bank, Jamnagar, pursuant to conditions imposed by the Joint Charity Commissioner. For A.Y. 2012-13, the trust inadvertently omitted the Section 11(1A) claim in its return, although the capital gains were fully disclosed and tax was paid, and the return was processed under Section 143(1) resulting in a tax demand of Rs. 19,44,180.

The Court accepted that Section 264 revisional jurisdiction is broad enough to grant relief where an assessee has been over-assessed because of a bona fide omission or mistake, even if the income was already disclosed in the original return. It relied on Gujarat and other precedents, including C. Parikh & Co., Ramdev Exports, S.R. Koshti, and Swaminarayan Mandir Trust, and held that the Commissioner should have examined whether the trust satisfied the substantive conditions for Section 11(1A) relief rather than refusing relief because the claim had not been made at the assessment stage. The Court specifically held that the relevant test was compliance with Section 11(1A) read with CBDT Instruction No. 883 dated 24.09.1975, and that because the sale proceeds were placed in an FDR with a scheduled bank for more than six months, the transaction qualified for the intended exemption treatment.

The Court also rejected the attempt to deny exemption by linking Section 11(1A) with Section 36(1)(a) of the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950, holding that Section 11(1A) is a standalone income-tax provision and cannot be curtailed by that state-law provision. It further held that the Supreme Court’s decision in Goetze (India) Ltd. was not controlling because that case dealt with claims before the Assessing Officer otherwise than by revised return, not the Commissioner’s powers under Section 264. Finding that the trust had acted bona fide, fully disclosed the capital gains, paid the tax, and suppressed nothing material, the Court allowed the Section 264 application, held that the trust was entitled to the Section 11(1A) exemption, and directed refund/payment of excess tax of Rs. 1,00,27,295 for A.Y. 2012-13 together with applicable interest under Section 244A, with consequential orders to be passed within four weeks. From a compliance perspective, the case reinforces that charitable trusts with qualifying reinvestment of sale proceeds should not assume a lost exemption claim is irrecoverable: if the facts and statutory conditions are satisfied, relief may still be available through revision, particularly where the omission was inadvertent and the tax position was otherwise fully disclosed.

The Tribunal first upheld the validity of reassessment proceedings initiated after four years, holding that the subsequent survey conducted on 30.11.2018 revealed information regarding allegedly bogus transactions which had not been examined in the original assessment. The original assessment order itself recorded that the assessee had no business activity, despite substantial purchases, sales and disclosed profit. The Tribunal therefore found that the reopening was based on subsequent information and was not merely a change of opinion. On merits, however, the Tribunal held that the Assessing Officer could not simply treat the entire purchases of Rs.5,81,57,000/- as undisclosed income when the corresponding sales of Rs.5,94,91,966/- had also been treated as bogus. The Tribunal rejected the assessee’s contention that banking-channel transactions alone established genuineness, since physical movement of goods and existence of the parties had not been established. It is also mentioned by the Ld. It is further recorded that the physical movement of purchase and sold goods was not evidenced and the supplier’s names and customers’ names were also not in evidence. However, the Ld. CIT(A) upheld the action of Ld. AO in adding the entire allegedly bogus purchases amounting to Rs.5,81,57,000/- as undisclosed income. 1.3 Further aggrieved, the assessee has approached the ITAT with grounds challenging the addition on merits, on the basis that once both purchases and sales are held to be undisclosed then the purchases simply alone cannot be added. It has also been raised as a ground that the case was reopened through issue of notice u/s 148 of the Act after four years from the end of the relevant assessment year even when there was no failure on the part of the assessee to disclose material facts. 2. Before us the Ld. AR argued that in the present case the sales and purchases were bogus and therefore it was not fair on the part of the assessing authorities to simply choose the purchases for disallowance in entirety. The Ld. AR submitted that the assessee had disc
rows.summary:
The Delhi ITAT dealt with AY 2012-13 in the case of HSB Home Solutions Ltd. and first upheld the validity of reopening under section 148 even though the notice was issued after four years from the end of the assessment year. The Tribunal accepted the Revenue’s position that the reassessment was based on fresh information from a survey conducted on 30.11.2018 under section 133A in the case of Shri Ashok Kumar Gupta and others, which allegedly exposed accommodation-entry activity through M/s Gayatri Maa Enterprise; this was not treated as a mere change of opinion because the original assessment had not examined the bogus-transaction issue and the survey material surfaced later. The original assessment record also noted that the assessee had no business activity despite reporting substantial purchases, sales, and profit, which supported the reopening.

On the merits, the Assessing Officer had treated the entire alleged bogus purchases of Rs. 5,81,57,000 as undisclosed income, and the CIT(A) upheld that full addition. The ITAT disagreed with the approach of taxing the entire purchases when the corresponding sales of Rs. 5,94,91,966 were also found to be bogus, holding that the Revenue could not simply select the purchase side for a 100% addition. At the same time, the Tribunal rejected the assessee’s argument that payments through banking channels alone proved genuineness, because the actual movement of goods and even the existence of the parties from whom purchases were allegedly made had not been established.

Instead of sustaining the full purchase disallowance, the ITAT directed the AO to apply a 5% gross profit rate on the turnover of Rs. 5,94,91,966, with credit allowed for profit already disclosed by the assessee. In practical compliance terms, the decision confirms that reassessment after four years can still be sustained where later survey material reveals previously unexamined bogus-entry activity, and it also confirms that in cases where both purchases and sales are treated as non-genuine, the tax addition should be based on a reasonable profit estimate rather than automatically adding the entire purchase figure.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Ahmedabad Dismisses Revenue Appeals on Goodwill, Electricity & Steam Valuation
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12606 Case Name DCIT Vs Nirma Limited (ITAT Ahmedabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2018-19 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Ahmedabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DCIT Vs Nirma Limited (ITAT Ahmedabad) Summary: The Ahmedabad Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal dismissed both Revenue appeals, ITA Nos. 1569 and 1570/AHD/2026, concerning Assessment Years 2018-19 and 2020-21. The appeals challenged orders dated 09.02.2026 passed by the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), Ahmedabad-13 under Section 250 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Since the appeals involved identical issues, they were heard together and disposed of through the common order pronounced on 21.08.2026. For AY 2018-19, the Revenue challenged deletion of an addition of Rs. 4,09,94,465/- relating to depreciation on goodwill arising from amalgamation of Saurashtra Chemicals Ltd. The Revenue contended that the amalgamating company was a sick, loss-making entity with negative net worth and that the goodwill was merely an accounting entry. The CIT(A), however, had relied upon earlier decisions of the Tribunal in the assessee’s own case for AYs 2012-13 to 2016-17. The Tribunal upheld the CIT(A)’s order and dismissed the corresponding Revenue grounds. The Revenue also challenged deletion of Rs. 1,73,64,613/- relating to depreciation on brands and names transferred from the demerged unit. Again, the CIT(A) had relied upon the Tribunal’s earlier decisions in the assessee’s own case. The Tribunal followed the same earlier decisions and dismissed the Revenue’s grounds. The major transfer-pricing dispute for AY 2018-19 concerned inter-unit sale of electricity. The Assessing Officer/TPO had made an adjustment of Rs. 1,17,72,05,188/-, taking the position that electricity generated by the captive power plant should not be benchmarked at the rate at which the manufacturing unit purchased electricity, but at the rate at which power generating companies supplied electricity to distribution companies. The CIT(A) relied upon the jurisdictional Gujarat High Court decision in CIT vs. Gujarat Alkalies & Chemicals Ltd., reported at 395 ITR 247, and earlier Tribunal decisions in the assessee’s own case. The Tribunal upheld the CIT(A)’s conclusion and dismissed the Revenue’s grounds. For AY 2020-21, the Revenue challenged depreciation of Rs. 97,67,598/- on brands and trade marks transferred pursuant to a demerger and depreciation of Rs. 2,30,59,386/- on goodwill arising from amalgamation of Saurashtra Chemicals Limited. The Revenue argued, among other things, that the valuation of the intangible assets had not attained finality and that the goodwill was artificially created. The Tribunal held that these grounds were covered by its earlier decisions in the assessee’s own case and dismissed them. The Revenue also challenged deletion of Rs. 20,17,23,105/- relating to inter-unit electricity benchmarking. Following its decision on the corresponding AY 2018-19 issue, the Tribunal dismissed these grounds as well. The remaining substantive issue concerned valuation of steam transferred between eligible and non-eligible units. The AO/TPO had made an adjustment of Rs. 1,06,55,75,141/- by treating steam generated as a by-product of the captive power plant and determining its arm’s length price at nil. The CIT(A) rejected this approach. The CIT(A) relied, among other decisions, upon Vishal Fabrics Ltd. and Star Paper Mill Ltd. v. DCIT, as well as the Gujarat High Court decision in Gujarat Alkalies & Chemicals Ltd. The CIT(A) reasoned that the fact that steam was generated as a by-product did not automatically make its value nil for arm’s length pricing purposes. External market prices could constitute an appropriate benchmark where reliable data and suitable adjustments were available. The Tribunal agreed, holding that steam being a by-product did not mean that it had no cost or market value. It found no infirmity in the CIT(A)’s reliance on the prevailing market rate for electricity and the relevant judicial precedents. The Revenue’s grounds challenging the deletion of the Rs. 1,06,55,75,141/- adjustment were therefore dismissed. The Tribunal consequently dismissed both Revenue appeals. The order’s epilogue expressly concludes that ITA Nos. 1569 and 1570/AHD/2026 filed by the Revenue are dismissed. The substantive reasoning principally concerns depreciation on goodwill and brands and the arm’s length valuation of captive electricity and steam under the transfer-pricing framework, including Section 80IA and Rule 10B. Cases Discussed CIT vs. Gujarat Alkalies & Chemicals Ltd., 395 ITR 247 (Guj.) Vishal Fabrics Ltd., ITA No. 1820/Ahd/2019 Star Paper Mill Ltd. v. DCIT, 134 Taxmann.com 177 (2022) Nandan Denim Ltd., 156 Taxmann.com 287 (2023) Earlier

The Ahmedabad ITAT dismissed both Revenue appeals in **DCIT v. Nirma Limited**, being **ITA Nos. 1569 and 1570/AHD/2026**, which covered **Assessment Years 2018-19 and 2020-21** and arose from CIT(A), Ahmedabad-13 orders dated **09.02.2026** under **Section 250 of the Income-tax Act, 1961**. The Tribunal heard the matters together because they involved substantially identical issues and issued a common order on **21.08.2026**, ultimately confirming the CIT(A)’s relief to the taxpayer on every contested point.

For **AY 2018-19**, the Revenue’s challenge to deletion of **Rs. 4,09,94,465** of depreciation on **goodwill** created on amalgamation of **Saurashtra Chemicals Ltd.** was rejected; the Tribunal accepted that the issue was already covered by earlier Tribunal orders in the assessee’s own case for **AYs 2012-13 to 2016-17**. The Revenue’s challenge to deletion of **Rs. 1,73,64,613** of depreciation on **brands and names** transferred from a demerged unit was also dismissed on the same basis. The major transfer-pricing dispute for this year was the inter-unit sale of **electricity** from a captive power plant, where the AO/TPO had made an adjustment of **Rs. 1,17,72,05,188** by valuing the electricity not at the rate charged to the manufacturing unit, but at the price at which power-generating companies sell to distribution companies; the Tribunal upheld the CIT(A)’s reliance on **CIT v. Gujarat Alkalies & Chemicals Ltd. (395 ITR 247, Gujarat High Court)** and earlier assessee-favourable decisions, and sustained deletion of the adjustment.

For **AY 2020-21**, the Revenue again failed on depreciation claims: the Tribunal upheld deletion of **Rs. 97,67,598** on **brands and trade marks** transferred under demerger and **Rs. 2,30,59,386** on **goodwill** arising from the amalgamation of Saurashtra Chemicals Ltd., rejecting arguments that the intangible valuation had not attained finality and that the goodwill was artificially created. The Revenue also lost on inter-unit electricity benchmarking, where the CIT(A)’s deletion of **Rs. 20,17,23,105** was affirmed by following the Tribunal’s ruling on the AY 2018-19 issue.

The remaining substantive issue was valuation of **steam** transferred between eligible and non-eligible units for **AY 2020-21**. The AO/TPO had treated steam generated as a by-product of the captive power plant as having **nil arm’s length price** and made an adjustment of **Rs. 1,06,55,75,141**. The CIT(A) rejected that approach, relying on **Vishal Fabrics Ltd.**, **Star Paper Mill Ltd. v. DCIT (134 Taxmann.com 177 (2022))**, and **Gujarat Alkalies & Chemicals Ltd.**, holding that the fact steam is a by-product does not mean it has no cost or market value and that external market prices can be used as a benchmark if reliable data and appropriate adjustments are available. The Tribunal agreed, upheld the CIT(A)’s use of the prevailing market rate approach, and dismissed the Revenue’s ground challenging deletion of the steam adjustment.

In practical compliance terms, the order reinforces that, for this taxpayer and similar transfer-pricing fact patterns, **captive electricity and steam transfers cannot automatically be benchmarked at nil or at a generically higher external supply rate without regard to the actual inter-unit transaction and judicial precedent**, and that depreciation on **goodwill, brands, and trademarks** arising from amalgamation/demerger remains allowable where prior year rulings in the assessee’s own case have already settled the issue. The final outcome is that **both Revenue appeals were dismissed in full**.

The appeals arose from orders of the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals) concerning, among other matters, disallowances relating to payments made to motor vehicle dealers. The Tribunal, however, decided the batch on a preliminary legal issue arising from a subsequent insolvency resolution process and did not adjudicate the merits of the individual additions or disallowances. The assessee, now IndusInd General Insurance Company Limited and formerly Reliance General Insurance Company Limited, was an unlisted subsidiary of Reliance Capital Limited (RCL), which held approximately 99.83% of its equity share capital during the relevant period. RCL was admitted into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. A Resolution Plan submitted by IndusInd International Holdings Limited was approved by the Committee of Creditors in June 2023 and subsequently approved by the NCLT on 27.02.2024 under Section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The plea was that the approved Resolution Plan rendered pending tax proceedings relating to periods preceding its approval date incapable of continuation. The Tribunal first considered maintainability of the additional ground and the Rule 27 plea. It held that the issue was a pure question of law arising from undisputed subsequent events and did not require fresh factual investigation. Referring to the width of the Tribunal’s appellate powers under section 254 of the Income-tax Act, and the principles recognised in Peter Vaz and CIT v. Hazarimal Nagji & Co., the Tribunal admitted the additional grounds and accepted the Rule 27 plea. The substantive issue was whether pending proceedings under the Income-tax Act concerning periods before the NCLT approval date could continue after approval of the Resolution Plan. The Tribunal emphasised the statutory binding effect of Section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, including its application to governmental authorities. It also examined Clauses 9.1.8 and 9.1.9 of the Resolution Plan. Clause 9.1.8 expressly dealt with pending, threatened, present or future tax proceedings and other proceedings relating to periods before the approval date concerning the corporate debtor, affiliates, subsidiaries and associate companies, while Clause 9.1.9 restrained governmental, judicial and quasi-judicial authorities from acting contrary to the approved Resolution Plan. The Tribunal further relied upon the NCLT’s order dated 27.02.2024, particularly paragraph 49, and the subsequent correction order dated 13.03.2024, which clarified that the approval extended to Clauses 9.1.8 to 9.1.13. It also noted that the NCLT had declined a subsequent attempt by SEBI to confine the relief to RCL and exclude its subsidiaries. The Tribunal regarded the Income-tax Department’s participation in the NCLT proceedings and rejection of its objections as particularly significant. The subsequent conduct of GST authorities was treated only as a surrounding circumstance. The Tribunal held that the legal position was authoritatively settled by Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons (P.) Ltd. v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd., under which claims not forming part of an approved Resolution Plan stand extinguished and proceedings concerning such claims cannot thereafter be initiated or continued. rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that once an insolvency resolution plan is approved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, pending income-tax proceedings relating to periods before the plan’s approval generally cannot be continued if the claims were not preserved in the approved plan. This ruling came in the consolidated appeals of the Revenue and the assessee (IndusInd General Insurance Company Limited, formerly Reliance General Insurance Company Limited) for Assessment Years 2011-12 to 2018-19 and 2020-21, but the Tribunal did not decide the underlying merits of the tax additions/disallowances; it disposed of the matters on the legal effect of the approved resolution plan.

The facts the Tribunal relied on were that Reliance Capital Limited, which held about 99.83% of the assessee’s equity, went into CIRP, the NCLT Mumbai admitted the insolvency petition on 06.12.2021 and imposed the Section 14 moratorium, and a resolution plan submitted by IndusInd International Holdings Limited was approved by the Committee of Creditors in June 2023 and then approved by the NCLT on 27.02.2024 under Section 31 of the IBC. The Income-tax Department had already participated in the NCLT process and objected mainly on Section 79 loss-carryforward issues, but those objections were considered and rejected. The assessee’s later name change effective 22.09.2025 did not alter the Tribunal’s analysis.

Procedurally, the Tribunal admitted additional grounds raised by the assessee and allowed the Revenue matter to be argued under Rule 27 of the ITAT Rules because the issue was a pure question of law based on undisputed later events, and no fresh fact-finding was needed. Substantively, the Tribunal placed weight on Section 31 of the IBC, which makes an approved resolution plan binding on the corporate debtor and its stakeholders, including governmental authorities, and on Clauses 9.1.8 and 9.1.9 of the approved plan. Clause 9.1.8 specifically addressed pending, threatened, present, or future tax proceedings and other proceedings relating to periods before the approval date for the corporate debtor and related entities, while Clause 9.1.9 barred governmental, judicial, and quasi-judicial authorities from acting contrary to the plan.

The Tribunal also relied on the NCLT’s approval order dated 27.02.2024, its corrective order dated 13.03.2024 clarifying that approval extended to Clauses 9.1.8 through 9.1.13, and the NCLT’s refusal to accept SEBI’s later attempt to limit relief only to Reliance Capital and exclude subsidiaries. Citing the Supreme Court’s decision in Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons and Bombay High Court decisions such as Uttam Value Steels and AMNS Gandhidham, the Tribunal held that claims not included in an approved resolution plan stand extinguished and cannot be pursued afterward. It rejected the Revenue’s reliance on S. V. Kondaskar as distinguishable because that case involved winding-up under the Companies Act, 1956, not the post-approval consequences of an IBC resolution plan. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that once a resolution plan with express tax-claim treatment is approved under the IBC, pre-approval tax proceedings against the corporate debtor covered by the plan may be barred from continuation, including proceedings involving subsidiary/affiliate periods if the plan and NCLT order expressly extend that far.

rows.summary:
For Assessment Year 2017–18, the ITAT Jodhpur dismissed the Revenue’s appeal in **ITO v. Varsha Mills** and upheld deletion of two major additions: **₹2,79,03,981** relating to alleged undervaluation of damaged guar gum stock and **₹3,36,49,500** added under **Section 69A** for cash deposits made during the demonetization period. The assessee was in the business of manufacturing and trading agricultural products, mainly guar gum and its by-products Churi and Korma; its Phalodi account had turned into an NPA, the bank took possession of the factory and residential premises on **29.09.2016**, and the stock was allegedly damaged by rain, germs, bacteria, and lack of proper care while in the bank’s possession. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee’s closing stock valuation and substituted a market-based **net realisable value (NRV) of ₹82.58 per kg** sourced from an internet website, but the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position that under **Accounting Standard 2 (AS-2)** inventories are valued at the **lower of cost and NRV**, and that damaged inventory must be written down rather than valued as normal stock. The Tribunal also relied on the fact that the damaged guar gum had actually been processed into **Churi/Korma** and sold for **₹2,02,69,593**, with that amount already offered to tax, so the stock addition was not sustainable.  

On the Section 69A issue, the disputed cash deposits were made in Mumbai bank accounts during **09.11.2016 to 25.11.2016**, and the Revenue objected because the assessee had a Phalodi account and questioned why cash from Phalodi sales was deposited elsewhere. The assessee explained that because the Phalodi account had become an NPA and the premises had been taken over, he and his family had shifted to Mumbai and therefore deposited the cash there instead. The Tribunal accepted this explanation and, importantly for compliance purposes, noted that the cash deposits were already recorded in the audited books as **cash sales**, supported by **sale bills, delivery challans, the sale register, and the stock register** produced before the Assessing Officer. Because the cash receipts had been duly recorded in the regular books and the related income had already been offered to tax, the same money could not be taxed again as unexplained under **Section 69A** absent contrary evidence. The practical takeaway is that properly documented, recorded cash sales—especially in exceptional circumstances like bank possession, relocation, and demonetization-era banking constraints—were sufficient here to defeat an unexplained-money addition, while damaged inventory supported by accounting policy, audit disclosure, and evidence of actual disposal at reduced value was also protected from arbitrary revaluation.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Delhi Upholds LIBOR Plus 300 Basis Points for Foreign-Currency Loans
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi dismisses both appeals, upholding LIBOR+300 for foreign-currency loans, excluding unsuitable comparables and deleting receivables and Section 14A adjustments.The post ITAT Delhi Upholds LIB
rows.summary:
The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Delhi decision that dismisses both appeals and upholds the transfer pricing approach of benchmarking foreign-currency loans at **LIBOR plus 300 basis points**. The Tribunal agreed that **unsuitable comparables should be excluded**, meaning the arm’s-length analysis for such loans must be based on comparables that are actually relevant to the foreign-currency lending context rather than on weak or mismatched data.

The decision also states that the Tribunal **deleted adjustments relating to receivables and Section 14A**. For compliance purposes, this means the tax position accepted by the Tribunal does **not** support making those additional upward adjustments on the facts of this case, and taxpayers with similar fact patterns may cite this outcome when defending against receivable-related transfer pricing adjustments or Section 14A disallowances. No new filing deadline, implementation date, or procedural timetable is mentioned in the excerpt; the material point is the substantive tax treatment endorsed by the ITAT for **foreign-currency loans** and the rejection of the two additional adjustments.

The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Delhi ruling in favor of PNB Gilts that removes a ₹4.26 crore disallowance made under Section 14A of the Income Tax Act. The practical takeaway for corporate tax teams, especially for entities holding securities as trading stock and claiming deductions related to exempt income, is that the tribunal accepted the taxpayer’s position on the treatment of these items in this instance. rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Jodhpur Restores 12AB Registration Application for RPT Act Exemption Examination
rows.desc: ITAT Jodhpur restores 12AB and 80G applications, directing CIT(E) to examine exemption from Rajasthan Public Trust Act registration.The post ITAT Jodhpur Restores 12AB Registration Application for RPT
rows.summary:
The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Jodhpur decision affecting a charitable entity’s tax exemption registrations. The Tribunal restored the assessee’s applications for registration under Section 12AB and approval under Section 80G, which had been rejected or not granted at the Commissioner (Exemptions) level, and directed the Commissioner (Exemptions) to re-examine the matter on the merits.

A key issue in the order is whether the entity’s registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act (RPT Act) should be examined as part of the exemption eligibility review. The ITAT instructed the tax authority to consider the exemption position in light of the RPT Act registration requirement, rather than disposing of the application without that examination. The practical effect is that the charitable organization gets another opportunity to establish eligibility for income tax exemption and donor deduction approval, which are essential for continuing tax-exempt operations and for enabling donors to claim benefits under Section 80G.

No specific monetary thresholds, rates, or filing deadlines are provided in the document. The compliance significance is procedural: charitable trusts and institutions seeking or maintaining Section 12AB registration and Section 80G approval should ensure their state-law registration status and related exemption claims are properly documented, because the tax authority is expected to review those facts when deciding eligibility.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 263 Cannot Import Later Restrictions into AY 2022-23: ITAT Chennai
rows.desc: ITAT Chennai quashes Section 263 revision, holding later Finance Act 2023 restrictions cannot govern AY 2022-23 loan repayment application.The post Section 263 Cannot Import Later Restrictions into AY
rows.summary:
The document reports an ITAT Chennai ruling that quashed a Section 263 revision order and held that restrictions introduced later by the Finance Act, 2023 cannot be applied retrospectively to Assessment Year 2022–23. In substance, the Tribunal found that the tax authority could not revise the assessment by relying on a rule limitation or disallowance framework that did not exist for the relevant assessment year, because the taxpayer’s loan repayment application had to be judged under the law in force for AY 2022–23.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the decision protects taxpayers from having later statutory restrictions “imported” into prior-year assessments through revision proceedings under Section 263. The affected matter involved an application of loan repayment-related tax treatment, and the Tribunal’s reasoning means that the tax position for AY 2022–23 must be assessed using the pre-Finance Act 2023 legal regime, not the amended restrictions that came later. The ruling therefore limits the Commissioner’s revisionary power where the original assessment is consistent with the law applicable at the time, and it underscores the need to verify the exact assessment year and effective date of any amendment before applying new disallowance or eligibility conditions.

rows.title: CA, CS, CMA | How Underpriced Audits Weaken Anti-Corruption Controls
rows.desc: Low fees, limited time and market concentration weaken audit quality. Here is how stronger audits can help India prevent corruption and protect savings.The post How Underpriced Audits Weaken Anti-Corr
rows.summary:
The document argues that underpriced audit engagements can undermine anti-corruption controls by reducing audit quality, because very low fees, limited auditor time, and concentration of work in a small market can all weaken the independence, depth, and effectiveness of audits. Its core compliance message is that when audits are priced too cheaply, auditors may not devote sufficient resources to properly test controls, scrutinize transactions, or identify warning signs of corruption and misuse of funds, which in turn increases risk for companies, investors, and depositors. It emphasizes that stronger, better-resourced audits are important for protecting savings and improving India’s broader anti-corruption environment.

For a corporate compliance team, the practical implication is that audit pricing and scope should not be treated as a purely commercial issue: if an audit is materially underpriced, management should consider whether the fee level could impair audit quality or signal that planned procedures may be too shallow to detect control failures. The document does not appear to announce a new legal deadline, filing requirement, numerical threshold, or formal regulatory rule; rather, it is a policy-oriented warning about the compliance risk created by low-fee audit arrangements and market concentration. Organizations using external auditors should therefore ensure the engagement is resourced adequately for the complexity and risk profile of the business, and should be alert to whether budget pressure could compromise the auditor’s ability to perform a credible anti-corruption review.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaulting Sellers
rows.desc: Why are bona fide buyers denied GST input tax credit when sellers fail to deposit tax? Analysis of Sections 16(2)(c) and 76 of the CGST Act.The post Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaul
rows.summary:
The document is a commentary on a recurring GST compliance issue rather than a new statutory amendment: it examines why bona fide purchasers can be denied input tax credit (ITC) when their suppliers collect GST but fail to deposit it with the government. The discussion focuses on the interaction between Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act, which conditions ITC on tax actually being paid to the government, and Section 76, which allows recovery of tax from a person who has collected it but not remitted it. The key compliance message is that, under this framework, the tax department may target the buyer’s ITC claim even where the buyer acted in good faith, if the seller did not discharge the tax liability.

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that invoice possession and payment to the vendor are not enough to secure ITC unless the supplier has also properly reported and paid the tax. Businesses therefore need stronger vendor-due-diligence and invoice-validation controls, because the risk of ITC denial can arise from counterparty non-compliance rather than the buyer’s own error. The document’s emphasis is on the policy and legal rationale behind this enforcement approach, namely that GST law prioritizes tax actually reaching the exchequer and gives the department a route to recover from the person who collected the tax but defaulted on payment. No new filing deadline, rate change, or numerical threshold is set out in the excerpt provided.

rows.title: Income Tax | Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (FAST-DS 2026)
