It specifically flags the need to understand **eligibility**, **Section 133 payments**, **Rule 5**, **Form 1**, **valuation**, **deadlines**, **immunity**, and the **consequences of exceeding the permitted limit**, which suggests the scheme imposes a formal disclosure and payment process rather than an informal amnesty.

From the text provided, the key compliance points are that affected taxpayers must determine whether they qualify as **small taxpayers** under the scheme, complete the required disclosure in **Form 1**, and comply with the prescribed **valuation rules** for foreign assets. The mention of **Section 133 payments** indicates there is a required payment component tied to the disclosure, and **Rule 5** appears to govern one or more procedural or substantive conditions for access to the scheme. The document also indicates there are **deadlines** that must be met, and that the scheme offers some form of **immunity** if the disclosure is made properly and on time, while failure to stay within the scheme’s limits may trigger **excess-limit consequences**, meaning the benefits may be lost or additional liabilities may arise.

Because the excerpt is truncated and does not include the underlying operative text, it does not provide the actual numeric thresholds, payment rates, filing dates, or the exact scope of immunity. For compliance purposes, the material takeaway is that any taxpayer with foreign assets who may fall within the “small taxpayer” category should review the full FAST-DS 2026 rules immediately, confirm eligibility, prepare the Form 1 disclosure with the required valuation methodology, and ensure the associated payment and filing deadlines are met to preserve the scheme’s protections.

rows.title: Income Tax | Non-Registration under Rajasthan Public Trust Act Cannot Alone Defeat Section 12AB Renewal: ITAT Jodhpur
rows.desc: ITAT Jodhpur directs fresh examination of Section 12AB renewal application of Urban Improvement Trust, Pali, holding that non-registration under Rajasthan Public Trust Act cannot justify rejection wit
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur held that an assessee’s failure to obtain registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, by itself, cannot be used as a ground to reject renewal of registration under Section 12AB of the Income-tax Act. The case concerned Urban Improvement Trust, Pali, whose Section 12AB renewal application had been rejected; the Tribunal did not finally grant renewal on the merits but directed the tax authorities to conduct a fresh examination of the application.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that renewal under Section 12AB must be evaluated on the statutory income-tax criteria, and a separate state-law registration deficiency cannot automatically defeat the application. Any authority reviewing a Section 12AB renewal request must therefore base its decision on the requirements of the Income-tax Act and the relevant facts of the trust’s activities and eligibility, rather than relying solely on absence of Rajasthan Public Trust Act registration.

rows.title: Income Tax | Corpus Donations Not Taxable Merely Due to Section 10(23C)(vi) Claim: ITAT Jodhpur
rows.desc: ITAT Jodhpur held ₹26.50 lakh corpus contributions cannot be taxed merely because exemption was claimed under section 10(23C)(vi).The post Corpus Donations Not Taxable Merely Due to Section 10(23C)(vi
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur held that corpus donations totaling ₹26.50 lakh cannot be treated as taxable income merely because the recipient institution had claimed exemption under section 10(23C)(vi) of the Income-tax Act. In other words, the tax authority cannot deny corpus-donation treatment or automatically tax these receipts solely on the basis that the entity is claiming a particular exemption provision.  

For compliance purposes, this ruling is relevant to educational or other institutions receiving donations intended to form part of their corpus, because it confirms that the tax characterization of the receipt depends on the nature and purpose of the donation, not just on the fact that the institution has sought exemption under section 10(23C)(vi). The decision does not announce a new filing deadline, rate, or numeric threshold beyond the specific amount involved in the case, but it reinforces that corpus contributions documented as such should not be added to taxable income simply due to the exemption claim.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai sets aside ISKCON 12AB rejection and grants 80G renewal
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai held ISKCON's charitable activities outside section 2(15)'s proviso, set aside 12AB rejection and directed 80G renewal.The post ITAT Mumbai sets aside ISKCON 12AB rejection and grants 80G
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai ruled in favor of ISKCON, holding that its charitable activities do not fall within the restrictive proviso to section 2(15) of the Income-tax Act, which is often used to deny charitable status where an organization is seen as carrying on “advancement of any other object of general public utility” with commercial elements. As a result, the tribunal set aside the tax authority’s rejection of ISKCON’s registration under section 12AB, meaning ISKCON’s charitable registration should not be denied on that ground. The tribunal also directed renewal of ISKCON’s approval under section 80G, which is the provision that allows donors to claim tax deduction benefits for contributions made to the organization.  

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the tribunal found ISKCON’s activities to remain within the charitable framework and not to be disqualified merely because of the nature of its operations. The decision affects entities with similar religious/charitable structures that seek or rely on section 12AB registration and section 80G approval, especially where the tax department has challenged charitable status by invoking the section 2(15) proviso. No specific monetary thresholds, procedural deadlines, or new filing timelines are mentioned in the document excerpt; the operative change is the appellate relief reversing the rejection of 12AB registration and requiring renewal of 80G approval.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Karnataka HC Directs Sale of Hazardous Goods Under GST Section 129(6)
rows.desc: Karnataka HC directs authorities to sell hazardous seized goods under Section 129(6) after notice, following transporter’s payment of Rs.1 lakh.The post Karnataka HC Directs Sale of Hazardous Goods Un
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court held that hazardous goods seized under GST enforcement may be sold by the authorities under section 129(6) after the required notice process, rather than being left in custody indefinitely. The case arose after a transporter paid ₹1 lakh, and the court directed the authorities to proceed with sale of the hazardous seized goods in accordance with section 129(6), indicating that the enforcement mechanism can extend to disposal/sale where the goods are hazardous and continued retention would be impractical or unsafe.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that seizure of hazardous goods does not necessarily mean they will remain stored until a prolonged adjudication is completed; instead, authorities may move to sale after issuing notice under the statute. This decision is relevant to taxpayers, transporters, and logistics operators handling hazardous consignments under GST because it underscores the need to respond promptly to detention/seizure notices, address any demanded payment or penalty exposure quickly, and recognize that the goods themselves may be liquidated by the department if statutory procedures are followed. No broader rate, deadline, or industry-wide threshold is stated in the summary beyond the ₹1 lakh payment noted in the case.

rows.title: Income Tax | GP Rate Cannot Be Uniform Across Pre and Post Survey Periods: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi held that books could not be rejected under Section 145(3) and deleted the GP addition based on an adhoc rate.The post GP Rate Cannot Be Uniform Across Pre and Post Survey Periods: ITAT Del
rows.summary: The ITAT Delhi held that the Assessing Officer could not reject the taxpayer’s books of account under Section 145(3) merely to make a gross profit (“GP”) addition on an ad hoc basis, and it deleted the GP addition made in this case. The key point of the ruling is that a GP rate cannot be mechanically applied as a uniform benchmark across pre-survey and post-survey periods without proper justification and factual support, so an assessment cannot rest solely on a generalized rate comparison. For compliance purposes, this means tax authorities must have a defensible basis before discarding books or imposing estimated profit adjustments, and companies should preserve books, inventory records, and supporting explanations for any margin changes around survey periods to rebut arbitrary GP extrapolations. No new statutory rate, threshold, filing deadline, or procedural change was announced in the document itself; the significance is the limitation it places on ad hoc profit estimation and the need for evidence-based assessments under Section 145(3).

rows.title: Corporate Law | Karnataka HC Directs NCLT to Expeditiously Consider Dispute Over Sale of Byju’s K3 Assets
rows.desc: Karnataka High Court declines parallel proceedings against NCLT and directs the Tribunal to expeditiously consider the Resolution Professional’s plea concerning proposed sale of assets allegedly belon
rows.summary:
The document reports a Karnataka High Court order in a corporate insolvency dispute involving Byju’s, where the court declined to continue parallel proceedings against the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and instead directed the NCLT to promptly hear and decide the Resolution Professional’s application concerning the proposed sale of the company’s “K3 assets.” The key issue is whether those assets were already sold under an earlier process or whether the Resolution Professional can lawfully proceed with the proposed sale; the article indicates the assets are “allegedly” subject to dispute, which makes their ownership/status central to any transaction. For compliance purposes, the practical implication is that any contemplated sale, transfer, or related action involving these assets should be treated as legally uncertain until the NCLT rules, because the High Court has pushed the matter back to the insolvency forum rather than adjudicating it itself.

The order does not announce a new statutory rule, threshold, fee, or general compliance deadline. Instead, it imposes a procedural direction: the NCLT must consider the Resolution Professional’s request expeditiously, meaning parties affected by the insolvency proceedings should monitor the tribunal case closely and be prepared for a quick decision that could authorize, restrict, or invalidate a proposed asset sale. If a corporate compliance team is involved with the borrower, resolution process, bidders, or creditors, it should ensure no transaction steps assume clear title to the K3 assets until the tribunal’s decision is issued and any resulting legal constraints are reviewed.

rows.title: Service Tax | STPI’s SOFTEX Certification Charges Taxable as Business Support Service: CESTAT Hyderabad
rows.desc: CESTAT Hyderabad holds STPI’s SOFTEX certification and NoC charges taxable as Business Support Service under the Finance Act, 1994.The post STPI’s SOFTEX Certification Charges Taxable as Business Supp
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad has held that charges collected by the Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) for SOFTEX certification and issuance of No Objection Certificates (NoCs) are taxable as “Business Support Service” under the Finance Act, 1994. In practical terms, the tribunal treated these services as taxable support services rather than as non-taxable or merely regulatory/administrative charges, meaning the amounts recovered by STPI for these certifications can fall within the service tax net.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the ruling affects entities that pay for or provide such certification-related services in the STPI context, particularly where the charges are linked to business facilitation for software exporters or similar regulated activities. No specific effective date, rate, threshold, exemption, or procedural deadline is stated in the provided text, but the legal consequence is that these SOFTEX certification and NoC fees are characterized as taxable consideration for service tax purposes under the pre-GST regime. Companies dealing with STPI certifications should therefore review whether historical service tax was charged, paid, or accounted for correctly on such fees and assess any exposure for past periods, credits, or disclosures.

rows.title: Income Tax | Madras HC Upholds Deletion of Penny Stock Gains Addition under Section 68
rows.desc: Madras HC upholds deletion of Section 68 additions on penny-stock gains, holding suspicion cannot replace evidence linking assessee to price manipulation.The post Madras HC Upholds Deletion of Penny S
rows.summary:
The document reports a Madras High Court decision affirming the deletion of an income-tax addition made under Section 68 in relation to alleged “penny stock” gains. The court held that the tax authority cannot sustain an addition merely on suspicion or on the general view that the scrip was associated with price manipulation; there must be concrete evidence connecting the specific assessee to the alleged manipulation or to an unexplained credit scheme. In other words, the fact that a stock is low-priced or suspected of being a penny stock is not enough by itself to tax the gains as unexplained income.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is evidentiary: if an assessee has reported gains from share transactions, the Revenue must establish a direct link between that taxpayer and the fraud/manipulation before invoking Section 68. The decision reinforces that documentation of genuine transactions—such as purchase/sale records, contract notes, demat entries, payment trails, and other corroborating records—remains critical in defending against penny-stock related additions. The document does not announce a new statutory amendment, rate change, threshold, filing deadline, or procedural rule; it describes a judicial ruling that narrows the practical basis on which Section 68 additions can be made in penny-stock cases.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Jodhpur Deletes 115BBE Rate on Survey Surrender Without Deeming Provision
rows.desc: ITAT Jodhpur held that Section 115BBE cannot apply to survey surrender income without bringing it within Sections 68 to 69D.The post ITAT Jodhpur Deletes 115BBE Rate on Survey Surrender Without Deemin
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur held that income surrendered during a survey cannot automatically be taxed at the punitive rate under Section 115BBE unless the Revenue first brings that income within one of the deeming provisions in Sections 68 to 69D. In other words, a mere voluntary surrender in a survey does not, by itself, make the amount “deemed income” of the kind that triggers Section 115BBE’s higher tax treatment. The practical compliance point is that taxpayers who disclose income during a survey should not be assumed to face 115BBE taxation unless the tax authority can specifically classify the surrendered amount under the statutory deeming rules for unexplained cash credits, investments, money, bullion, expenditures, etc.

For affected entities, this ruling is relevant to businesses and individuals subject to tax surveys under the Income-tax Act, especially where income is offered to settle survey findings. It signals that the department must establish the legal basis for applying Section 115BBE rather than relying solely on the fact of surrender. There is no new statutory deadline or procedural filing requirement announced here; the key change is interpretive, limiting when the higher 115BBE rate can be imposed on survey-related surrendered income. Compliance teams should still document the source and nature of any surrendered amounts carefully, because if the income does fall within Sections 68 to 69D, Section 115BBE can still apply.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Co-operative Bank Conversion Mid-Recovery: Forum, Composite Notice & Cost of Delay
rows.desc: Analyse forum, limitation, guarantor liability, SARFAESI notices, delayed asset sales and attachment after a co-operative bank converts.The post Co-operative Bank Conversion Mid-Recovery: Forum, Compo
rows.summary:
The document addresses legal and recovery-process implications when a co-operative bank converts during an ongoing enforcement/recovery matter, with a focus on what happens to the proper forum, limitation, guarantor liability, SARFAESI notices, delayed asset sales, and attachment actions after conversion. The core compliance issue is that a bank’s conversion mid-recovery can change the legal characterization of the institution and may affect which authority or court has jurisdiction over the dispute or enforcement action, so recovery teams must confirm the correct forum before proceeding further. It also emphasizes the need to review whether previously issued notices remain valid after conversion, especially composite notices under recovery law and SARFAESI-based demand or enforcement notices, because a procedural defect in notice/service can later be used to challenge the recovery steps.

The document also highlights that guarantor liability remains a material issue in mid-recovery conversion cases, meaning compliance teams should not assume that a change in the bank’s structure automatically extinguishes or weakens enforcement rights against guarantors. Delays in asset sale or attachment are treated as legally significant, and the document suggests that postponement can create additional risk, including arguments about delay, prejudice, or invalidity of the enforcement timeline. In practical terms, the bank or recovery team should document the conversion date, map it against each recovery step already taken, verify whether any fresh or amended notices are needed, and reassess the legal basis for continued SARFAESI action, sale of secured assets, and attachment proceedings after the conversion event.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Deletes ₹48.09 Lakh Addition on BSNL Receipts; Form 26AS Alone Cannot Decide Nature of Income
rows.desc: Chennai ITAT deletes ₹48.09 lakh addition in Sri Balaji Shopping World, holding that BSNL trade discount cannot be treated as commission merely because the gross receipts were reported in Form 26AS.Th
rows.summary:
The document reports a Chennai Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) ruling in **Sri Balaji Shopping World** in which the Tribunal **deleted an addition of ₹48.09 lakh** made by the tax authorities. The disputed amount related to **receipts from BSNL**, which the Assessing Officer had treated as **commission income** largely because the **gross receipts appeared in Form 26AS**; the ITAT held that **Form 26AS alone is not determinative of the true nature of income**.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Tribunal recognized the taxpayer’s position that the BSNL amounts were in the nature of a **trade discount** rather than commission, and it rejected the revenue’s attempt to recharacterize the receipts solely on the basis of tax-reporting data. The ruling reinforces that **third-party reporting in Form 26AS does not by itself establish the legal character of a payment or receipt**; the substance of the underlying arrangement and supporting evidence matter. No new statutory deadline, filing date, or rate change is announced in the document, but the decision is relevant to entities dealing with **BSNL or similar commercial arrangements** where receipts may be reflected in Form 26AS under a label that could later be challenged by tax authorities.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 35(2AB) Deduction Cannot Be Denied Due to Later DSIR Approval: Gujarat HC
rows.desc: Gujarat HC admits Revenue’s appeal on six tax issues but dismisses challenge to Section 35(2AB) deduction for AY 2013-14.The post Section 35(2AB) Deduction Cannot Be Denied Due to Later DSIR Approval:
rows.summary:
The document reports a Gujarat High Court decision involving AY 2013-14 in which the Revenue’s appeal was admitted on six tax issues, but the Court rejected the Revenue’s challenge to the taxpayer’s claim of a deduction under Section 35(2AB) of the Income-tax Act. The key holding is that the deduction for in-house research and development expenses cannot be denied merely because DSIR approval was granted later, so long as the underlying claim otherwise satisfies the statutory conditions; in other words, a delayed approval from the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research does not by itself defeat the deduction.  

For a compliance team, the practical implication is that taxpayers claiming Section 35(2AB) relief should still maintain full support for the R&D expenditure, the eligible in-house facility, and the linkage between the spend and the approved scientific research activity, because the court’s ruling addresses timing of DSIR approval rather than eliminating the need for documentation or substantive eligibility. The document does not provide any new monetary threshold, rate change, filing deadline, or procedural amendment; its significance is judicial confirmation that later DSIR approval, by itself, is not a valid basis for disallowance of the deduction for AY 2013-14.

rows.title: Income Tax | Shares Issued as Business Acquisition Consideration Outside Section 56(2)(viib): ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi grants relief to C L Educate Ltd on share premium, bad debts, Section 14A, liabilities written back and loan processing charges.The post Shares Issued as Business Acquisition Consideration
rows.summary:
The document is a short tax-law update reporting that the ITAT Delhi granted relief to C L Educate Ltd across several income-tax disputes, specifically on share premium, bad debts, Section 14A disallowance, liabilities written back, and loan processing charges. The key point for compliance purposes is the ruling on shares issued as business acquisition consideration: the tribunal held that where shares are issued in connection with acquiring a business, the issue is treated as consideration for the acquisition and falls outside the scope of Section 56(2)(viib), which is the anti–share premium provision often used to tax excessive premium received by closely held companies. In practical terms, this means a company issuing shares as part of a bona fide business acquisition structure should not automatically be taxed under Section 56(2)(viib) merely because the shares are issued at a premium, provided the transaction is genuinely acquisition-linked rather than a disguised capital infusion.

The update does not describe any new statutory amendment, rate change, filing deadline, or numeric threshold; instead, it summarizes a judicial interpretation that may be relied on in similar fact patterns. Compliance teams should therefore focus on whether share issuances in acquisition transactions are properly documented as acquisition consideration, with board approvals, acquisition agreements, valuation support, and transaction records showing commercial substance. The same article also notes the tribunal’s favorable outcome for the taxpayer on the other contested items, but it does not provide the detailed reasoning or operative compliance standards for those issues.

rows.title: Income Tax | Object-Modification Delay Alone Cannot Deny Section 12AB Registration: ITAT Chennai
rows.desc: ITAT Chennai restores Section 12AB and 80G applications, holding object-modification delay alone cannot justify rejection without merits examination.The post Object-Modification Delay Alone Cannot Den
rows.summary:
The ITAT Chennai held that a mere delay in filing an amended trust deed or modifying objects, by itself, cannot be treated as a valid ground to reject applications for registration under Section 12AB or approval under Section 80G. In this matter, the tribunal restored the assessee’s applications and found that the authorities were not justified in denying registration/approval solely because the object modification was filed late, without first examining the merits of the trust’s objects and eligibility under the law.

For compliance teams, the practical point is that charitable or religious entities seeking Section 12AB registration or Section 80G approval should not be denied relief automatically on a procedural timing issue relating to object amendments alone. The tax authority is expected to look at the substance of the application—namely, whether the entity’s stated objects and activities satisfy the statutory requirements—rather than relying only on the timing of the deed modification.

No specific monetary thresholds, rates, or hard filing deadlines are stated in the document excerpt. The key compliance implication is that entities should still keep object clauses, trust deeds, and related amendments properly documented and aligned with their actual activities, but a late amendment, without more, should not by itself defeat a Section 12AB or 80G application.

rows.title: Service Tax | SVLDRS Discharge Certificate Bars Revenue Appeal on Same Dispute: CESTAT Hyderabad
rows.desc: CESTAT Hyderabad dismissed Revenue’s appeal after SVLDRS discharge certificate and also rejected extended limitation in the fifth SCN.The post SVLDRS Discharge Certificate Bars Revenue Appeal on Same
rows.summary:
The document reports a CESTAT Hyderabad decision holding that once a taxpayer has received a valid discharge certificate under the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme (SVLDRS), the Revenue cannot continue or revive an appeal on the same settled dispute. In this case, the Tribunal dismissed the Department’s appeal because the underlying tax dispute had already been resolved through SVLDRS, and the discharge certificate operated as final settlement for that matter. For compliance teams, the key point is that an SVLDRS discharge certificate has binding finality with respect to the covered issue, so any later departmental challenge on the same demand should be barred.

The decision also addresses limitation in a fifth show-cause notice (SCN): the Tribunal rejected the Revenue’s attempt to invoke the extended period of limitation for that notice. This means the Department could not justify the additional time window for raising the demand, which is important where allegations depend on suppression, wilful misstatement, or similar grounds typically needed to extend the normal limitation period. Although the summary provided does not include the underlying tax amount, dates, or the exact factual basis for the fifth SCN, the ruling is significant for entities that have concluded disputes under SVLDRS or are facing late-issued service tax notices, because it reinforces both the finality of the SVLDRS settlement and the need for the Department to meet strict legal standards before relying on extended limitation.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 153C Time Limit Runs From Material Receipt: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi holds AYs 2010-11 and 2011-12 outside Section 153C limitation as the block period runs from receipt of seized material by the other person’s AO.The post Section 153C Time Limit Runs From Ma
rows.summary:
This document reports an ITAT Delhi ruling on **Section 153C of the Income-tax Act** concerning the **time limit for completing assessments** in cases involving seized material belonging to “the other person” (i.e., a person other than the one searched). The key holding is that the **limitation period for Section 153C proceedings starts from the date the Assessing Officer (AO) of the other person receives the seized material**, not from the date of the original search or seizure. Based on that rule, the Tribunal held that the assessments for **Assessment Years (AYs) 2010-11 and 2011-12** were **outside the permissible Section 153C limitation period** and therefore could not be sustained.

For compliance purposes, the practical significance is that when a company or related entity becomes subject to Section 153C proceedings because materials were found in someone else’s search, the department must be able to show **when the receiving AO actually got the seized material**, since that date governs the statutory block-period timeline. If the notice or assessment is issued beyond the limitation calculated from that receipt date, the assessment may be vulnerable to challenge as time-barred. The decision underscores the need to preserve records of the **date of transfer/receipt of seized documents between AOs**, because that date can determine whether the income-tax department’s action is valid.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Patna High Court Grants Bail in ₹73.75 Crore GST Evasion Case
