rows.summary: The document reports that the Patna High Court granted bail in a GST evasion matter involving alleged tax evasion of ₹73.75 crore, and that the court was examining the legality of an arrest made under Sections 69 and 132 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act. From a compliance perspective, the only substantive information provided is that the case concerns a large-scale GST evasion allegation and that enforcement action included arrest powers under those two provisions. No rule change, new compliance obligation, filing deadline, effective date, threshold, or procedural amendment is described in the text. The document therefore functions as a litigation/enforcement update rather than a regulatory change notice, and it does not state any specific operational requirement for businesses beyond highlighting the continued use of arrest provisions in serious GST evasion cases.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Recovery Demand Alone Does Not Require Custodial Interrogation: Bombay HC
rows.desc: Bombay HC confirmed anticipatory bail after investigation was completed and State stated custodial interrogation was no longer required.The post GST Recovery Demand Alone Does Not Require Custodial In
rows.summary: The Bombay High Court held that a GST recovery demand by itself does not justify custodial interrogation, and on that basis it confirmed anticipatory bail for the accused once the investigation had been completed. The State itself stated that custodial interrogation was no longer required, which the Court treated as an important factor in deciding that arrest-related custody was unnecessary. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that a recovery proceeding or demand under GST, standing alone, was not treated here as enough to support custodial detention where the investigative phase had already ended. The decision is relevant to businesses and individuals facing GST enforcement because it indicates that, at least on these facts, coercive custody was not warranted merely because tax recovery was being pursued. No specific monetary threshold, deadline, or new filing procedure is stated in the provided text.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Notice Only Under Additional Notices Tab Violates Natural Justice: Calcutta HC
rows.desc: Calcutta HC quashed GST adjudication and appellate orders where SCN was uploaded only under Additional Notice and Orders without separate intimation.The post GST Notice Only Under Additional Notices T
rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court held that a GST adjudication order and the related appellate order could not stand where the department uploaded the show cause notice (SCN) only under the “Additional Notices” tab on the GST portal and did not separately intimate the taxpayer. The court found this mode of service violated natural justice because the taxpayer was deprived of a proper and effective opportunity to see and respond to the notice before adverse orders were passed. As a result, the HC quashed both the adjudication order and the appellate order.

For compliance purposes, the key point is procedural: GST authorities cannot rely on a buried portal upload alone if it does not reasonably alert the registered person to the SCN. Taxpayers should therefore monitor the GST portal carefully, including the “Additional Notices” section, and maintain internal controls to detect portal communications promptly. At the same time, if an SCN or order was issued without separate intimation and the taxpayer can show it was not effectively brought to its attention, this decision supports a challenge on natural justice grounds. The document does not state any new tax rate, threshold, or substantive GST liability change; it is a service/procedure ruling affecting how notices and orders must be communicated.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Sports Centre Building Tax Exemption Claim Requires Reconsideration: Kerala HC
rows.desc: Kerala HC directed reconsideration of Sports Centre’s building tax exemption claim based on principal use and charitable activities.The post Sports Centre Building Tax Exemption Claim Requires Reconsi
rows.summary:
The Kerala High Court has directed that Sports Centre’s claim for exemption from building tax be reconsidered, focusing on the centre’s **principal use** and whether its activities qualify as **charitable**. The court did not appear to grant the exemption outright in the document provided; instead, it required the relevant authority to re-examine the claim on the merits under the applicable tax-exemption standards.

For compliance purposes, the key issue is that tax exemption entitlement for a building will depend on the **actual dominant use of the premises**, not merely on how the entity describes itself. The decision indicates that if an organization is seeking building tax relief on the basis of charitable status or charitable use, it should be prepared to substantiate that the property is primarily used for that exempt purpose and that its activities genuinely fit within the charitable category recognized by law.

No specific effective date, filing deadline, tax rate, or numerical threshold is stated in the document excerpt. The practical compliance takeaway is that entities claiming building tax exemptions should maintain clear records demonstrating the building’s primary use, the nature of the organization’s activities, and the legal basis for exemption, because authorities may be required to reassess such claims if the factual basis is disputed.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Unsigned GST Show Cause Notice & Order Invalid: Rajasthan High Court
rows.desc: Rajasthan HC quashes unsigned GST SCN and order, holding digital or physical authentication mandatory under Rule 26(3) of CGST Rules.The post Unsigned GST Show Cause Notice & Order Invalid: Rajas
rows.summary: The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST show cause notice and the resulting order were invalid because they were unsigned, emphasizing that either digital authentication or physical signature is mandatory under Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules. In practical terms, the court found that GST notices/orders issued without proper authentication do not satisfy the legal requirement for validity, so taxpayers can challenge such documents on the ground that they were not duly signed. This ruling directly affects GST-registered entities that receive departmental notices or adjudication orders, because they should verify that any SCN, demand notice, or order is properly authenticated before treating it as enforceable. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is to check every GST communication for valid signature or digital authentication and to preserve a copy of any unsigned document as a potential ground for objection or appeal.

rows.title: Income Tax | Stale Investigation Material Cannot Justify Reassessment: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi quashes reassessment based on stale material already available in earlier proceedings; Section 151 approval held mechanical.The post Stale Investigation Material Cannot Justify Reassessment
rows.summary:
This document reports an ITAT Delhi decision holding that a reassessment under the Income-tax Act cannot be sustained where it is based on stale investigation material that was already available to the tax department in earlier proceedings. In the case described, the tribunal found that the reassessment was improperly initiated because the “reasons to believe” did not rest on fresh, live information or a valid new basis; instead, the department attempted to reopen an assessment using the same information it had previously possessed and could have acted on earlier.

A key compliance takeaway is that the tribunal also held the approval under Section 151 to be mechanical, meaning the sanctioning authority had not applied independent, meaningful scrutiny before approving the reopening. That matters because reassessments require proper statutory approval, and the decision reinforces that such approval cannot be a rubber-stamp exercise; it must reflect real consideration of the facts and legal basis for reopening.

For companies and tax teams, the practical implication is that if the department issues a reassessment notice relying on old investigation material or information already on record, the notice may be challengeable as invalid, especially if the approval process appears perfunctory. This is not a substantive change in tax rates or filing deadlines, but a procedural ruling affecting the validity of reassessment actions under the Income-tax Act and the standards for Section 151 approval.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Delhi Allowed Section 80G Approval as Religious Spending Stayed Within 5% Limit
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi directs grant of Section 80G registration where spiritual and satsang expenditure remained below the permissible 5% limit.The post ITAT Delhi Allowed Section 80G Approval as Religious Spend
rows.summary:
The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) Delhi decision directing the tax authority to grant Section 80G approval/registration to an applicant despite some spiritual or satsang-related expenditure, because that religious spending stayed within the statutory tolerance limit of 5%. The key compliance point is that charitable institutions seeking or maintaining Section 80G status are not disqualified merely because they incur some religious expenditure, so long as that spending does not exceed the permitted threshold. In this case, the Tribunal treated the applicant’s expenditure as acceptable because it was below the 5% cap, and therefore approved the Section 80G registration rather than denying it on the basis of religious use of funds. 

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that organizations applying for or relying on Section 80G recognition should monitor any spending that could be characterized as religious or spiritual and ensure it remains within the 5% limit referenced by the Tribunal. The document does not describe a new rule, effective date, or broader procedural change; it reflects an adjudicated application of the existing Section 80G standard to a specific fact pattern.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Penalty Not Automatic for Delayed Foreign Travel Tax Payment: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court rules delayed Foreign Travel Tax payment is not non-payment under Section 38(3) and penalty cannot be imposed automatically.The post Penalty Not Automatic for Delayed Foreign Travel Tax
rows.summary:
The document reports a Supreme Court holding that a **delay in paying Foreign Travel Tax (FTT) does not amount to “non-payment” under Section 38(3)** of the relevant law, and therefore **penalty cannot be imposed automatically solely because the tax was paid late**. In other words, the Court distinguished between **late payment** and **failure to pay**, limiting the automatic use of penalty provisions where the tax was eventually paid rather than wholly omitted.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that entities responsible for collecting/remitting Foreign Travel Tax should still **pay on time to avoid disputes**, but a delayed remittance by itself is **not treated as an outright default equivalent to non-payment** under Section 38(3). Any penalty action must be assessed in light of this ruling rather than assumed to follow mechanically from lateness. The document does not specify any new filing deadline, rate change, or revised procedure; it is primarily a **judicial clarification restricting automatic penalty imposition** for delayed FTT payment.

rows.title: Income Tax | Telangana HC Dismisses ITTA as ₹10 Lakh Tax Effect Falls Below CBDT Monetary Limit
rows.desc: Telangana HC dismissed ITTA No. 4 of 2026 as ₹10 lakh tax effect was below the CBDT monetary limit under Circular No. 5 of 2024.The post Telangana HC Dismisses ITTA as ₹10 Lakh Tax Effect Falls Below
rows.summary: The document reports that the Telangana High Court dismissed Income Tax Appeal (ITTA) No. 4 of 2026 because the tax effect involved was only ₹10 lakh, which is below the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) monetary limit for filing appeals under Circular No. 5 of 2024. The practical compliance point is that the tax authority did not pursue the appeal since the amount in dispute did not meet the minimum threshold set by the CBDT for litigation. This is not a change in substantive tax law, but it confirms the operational effect of the CBDT’s litigation-management policy: appeals should generally not be filed or continued where the tax effect is below the prescribed limit. For corporate taxpayers and tax teams, the key takeaway is that small-value disputes may be vulnerable to dismissal on monetary-limit grounds, so appeal strategy should be reviewed against the current CBDT threshold before proceeding.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Karnataka HC Directs Reimbursement of Differential GST to Government Contractor
rows.desc: Karnataka HC directs PWD to determine and reimburse differential GST to contractor within six weeks, subject to verification of records.The post Karnataka HC Directs Reimbursement of Differential GST
rows.summary:
The document reports that the Karnataka High Court has directed the Public Works Department (PWD) to determine and reimburse the **differential GST** payable to a government contractor. The court’s order requires the PWD to complete this exercise **within six weeks**, and the reimbursement is expressly **subject to verification of the relevant records**, meaning the contractor’s claim is not automatic and must be checked against supporting documentation.

For a compliance team, the key point is that this is a **contractor-specific GST reimbursement direction** arising in a government contracting context, and it creates an immediate administrative obligation for the PWD to review the tax difference and process payment within the court-imposed timeline. The document does not provide the underlying GST rate difference, the contract details, or the amount involved, but it does establish that differential GST claims in such matters may need to be examined and settled based on records rather than denied outright.

rows.title: Income Tax | Madras HC Directs Fresh Section 148 Notice to Legal Representatives of Deceased Assessee
rows.desc: Madras HC directs fresh Section 148 notice to legal representatives where reassessment notice was issued in deceased assessee's name.The post Madras HC Directs Fresh Section 148 Notice to Legal Repres
rows.summary:
The document reports a Madras High Court ruling on reassessment procedure under the Income-tax Act: where the Income Tax Department had issued a Section 148 reassessment notice in the name of a deceased assessee, the court directed that a fresh notice must be issued to the deceased person’s legal representatives instead. The key compliance point is that a notice addressed only to a deceased individual is not sufficient to validly initiate or continue reassessment proceedings; the department must instead serve the legally responsible representatives of the deceased taxpayer.

For taxpayers and their estates, this means reassessment proceedings cannot be pursued mechanically against a dead person’s name, and legal heirs/executors must be properly identified and notified before the reassessment can proceed. The ruling is specifically relevant to notices under Section 148, i.e. notices for income escaping assessment, and it reinforces that procedural validity depends on issuing the notice to the correct legal person. The document does not mention any new monetary thresholds, tax rates, filing deadlines, or substantive tax changes; its significance is procedural and relates to proper service of reassessment notices after a taxpayer’s death.

rows.title: Income Tax | PMS Charges Deductible Under Section 48 Amid Divergent Views: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai allows Rs. 8.42 lakh PMS charges as deduction under Section 48, following the assessee-favouring rule amid divergent Tribunal views.The post PMS Charges Deductible Under Section 48 Amid Di
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai has held that portfolio management service (PMS) charges of Rs. 8.42 lakh are deductible while computing capital gains under Section 48 of the Income-tax Act. In this case, the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position and allowed the PMS fees to be treated as an expenditure incurred in connection with the transfer of capital assets, despite the fact that there have been divergent views among different Tribunal decisions on this issue. The practical effect is that taxpayers who have incurred PMS charges in relation to managing investments and then realized capital gains may be able to claim those charges as a deduction from capital gains, reducing taxable gains, subject to the facts of their case and the applicable judicial view.  

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that this is a favorable appellate ruling, but it is not described as a statutory amendment or a universal rule change; rather, it reflects a tribunal-level interpretation in a contested area. Entities or individuals using PMS should therefore preserve documentation showing the PMS fees paid, the link between those charges and the management/transfer of capital assets, and the basis on which the deduction is claimed under Section 48, because the deductibility position may still depend on jurisdictional precedent and case-specific facts.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Belated Writ Cannot Revive Time-Barred GST Refund Challenge: Kerala HC
rows.desc: Kerala HC dismissed a belated writ against rejection of transitional ITC refund, holding Article 226 cannot revive a remedy lost by limitation.The post Belated Writ Cannot Revive Time-Barred GST Refun
rows.summary: The Kerala High Court held that a taxpayer cannot use a delayed writ petition under Article 226 to resurrect a GST refund challenge that has already become time-barred. The case involved rejection of a transitional input tax credit (ITC) refund, and the court dismissed the writ on the ground that the claimant had missed the legally available time to pursue the remedy. In practical compliance terms, the decision reinforces that GST refund and transitional credit disputes must be raised within the prescribed limitation period, because courts may refuse to entertain stale challenges even if the underlying grievance concerns tax credit or refund denial. The ruling does not announce a new GST filing requirement or change any statutory deadline, but it is an important procedural warning: once the statutory or otherwise available challenge window closes, Article 226 will generally not be available as a fallback to reopen the matter.

rows.title: Income Tax | Kerala HC Quashes Reassessment Order for Ignoring Taxpayer’s Prior-Year Tax Claim
rows.desc: Kerala HC quashes a Section 148A(3) order for failing to examine the assessee’s claim that the disputed amount was already taxed in AY 2019-20.The post Kerala HC Quashes Reassessment Order for Ignorin
rows.summary: The document reports a Kerala High Court ruling on an income tax reassessment matter in which the court quashed an order passed under Section 148A(3) because the assessing authority did not properly consider the taxpayer’s claim that the disputed amount had already been taxed in Assessment Year (AY) 2019-20. In practical terms, the court held that before initiating or sustaining reassessment proceedings, the department must meaningfully examine the assessee’s explanation and tax history, especially where the taxpayer asserts that the same income has already been offered to tax in an earlier year. The decision appears to affect taxpayers facing reassessment notices under Section 148A and the tax authorities handling them, reinforcing that a reassessment order cannot be sustained if it ignores a material factual contention raised by the assessee. No specific tax rate, monetary threshold, or filing deadline is mentioned in the excerpt, but the compliance takeaway is that companies should preserve and be prepared to produce prior-year tax computations, return disclosures, and supporting records whenever the department questions whether an amount has been taxed already.

rows.title: Service Tax | Time Share Accommodation Not Taxable as Club or Association Service: CESTAT Hyderabad
rows.desc: CESTAT Hyderabad set aside service tax on time-share accommodation, holding customers were not club members and penalties were unsustainable.The post Time Share Accommodation Not Taxable as Club or As
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that service tax could not be levied on time-share accommodation by treating it as a “club or association” service, and it set aside the tax demand. The tribunal’s reasoning was that the customers using the time-share accommodation were not members of a club or association in the legal sense required for that tax category, so the arrangement did not fit the taxable service definition relied on by the department. As a result, the related penalties were also struck down as unsustainable.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that this decision narrows the department’s ability to classify time-share accommodation receipts as club/association service merely because customers pay for access or use over time; the legal form of the relationship matters. The ruling indicates that businesses offering time-share accommodation should review how their service is categorized for indirect tax purposes, especially where the tax position was based on the customers being treated as members. No effective date, rate change, or prospective compliance deadline is stated in the text provided; the document reflects a judicial determination on a disputed tax classification and penalty exposure.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Customs Cannot Indefinitely Detain Imported Car Without Seizure Order: Gujarat HC
rows.desc: Gujarat HC ordered release of an imported Land Cruiser, holding Customs cannot bypass Section 110 limitation by keeping goods under prolonged detention.The post Customs Cannot Indefinitely Detain Impo
rows.summary:
The document reports a Gujarat High Court ruling that Customs authorities cannot avoid the statutory seizure framework under Section 110 of the Customs Act by simply keeping imported goods under prolonged detention without issuing a proper seizure order. The specific case involved an imported Land Cruiser that had been held by Customs, and the court directed its release, indicating that indefinite retention of imported goods is not permissible when Customs has not lawfully completed the seizure process.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that once Customs takes possession or control of imported goods, it must act within the legal limits and cannot continue detaining the property indefinitely as a substitute for seizure. The ruling reinforces that Customs enforcement actions must follow the prescribed statutory procedure, including timely issuance of a seizure order where required, rather than relying on open-ended detention. No specific monetary thresholds, deadlines, or rate changes are mentioned in the provided text, but the decision is significant for importers, customs brokers, and compliance teams handling detained shipments because it strengthens the ability to challenge prolonged detention that is not backed by formal seizure action.

rows.title: Excise Duty | CENVAT Credit Cannot Be Denied When Manufacturer’s Invoice Names Assessee as Consignee: CESTAT Kolkata
rows.desc: CESTAT Kolkata allows CENVAT credit where manufacturer’s invoice named assessee as consignee and goods were received and accounted for.The post CENVAT Credit Cannot Be Denied When Manufacturer’s Invoi
rows.summary:
The document reports a CESTAT Kolkata ruling on excise/CENVAT credit, holding that CENVAT credit cannot be denied merely because the manufacturer’s invoice named the assessee as the **consignee**, so long as the goods were actually received by the assessee and properly entered in its records/accounts. In other words, the tribunal recognized that the invoice description and consignee designation were sufficient to support credit when the underlying transaction was genuine and the receipt of goods was evidenced.  

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that credit eligibility should be evaluated based on **substance and documentation of receipt/use**, not only on rigid invoice-form terminology, where the assessee is clearly identified as the consignee and the goods are traced into inventory or accounting records. The ruling does not announce a new rate, threshold, or filing deadline; it is a judicial interpretation affecting how manufacturers and recipients defend CENVAT credit claims in excise audits or disputes. Firms should still retain invoices, goods receipt evidence, stock/accounting entries, and any supporting transport or inward records to substantiate that the goods were received and accounted for, because those facts were central to the credit being allowed.

rows.title: Service Tax | Non-Compliance With Pre-Deposit Justifies Dismissal of Service Tax Appeal: CESTAT Hyderabad
rows.desc: CESTAT Hyderabad upheld dismissal of appeal for failure to comply with 50% pre-deposit ordered under unamended Section 35F.The post Non-Compliance With Pre-Deposit Justifies Dismissal of Service Tax A
rows.summary: The document reports a CESTAT Hyderabad ruling that upheld dismissal of a service tax appeal because the appellant did not comply with a pre-deposit direction. The tribunal had ordered a deposit of 50% of the disputed amount under the **unamended Section 35F**, and the appeal was dismissed when that condition was not satisfied. For compliance purposes, the key point is that, at least for appeals governed by the pre-amendment regime, failure to make the required pre-deposit can be a complete bar to appellate relief and can result in dismissal of the case without a merits hearing. The decision reinforces that companies contesting service tax demands must strictly track and meet any court/tribunal-ordered pre-deposit requirement within the prescribed time, because non-compliance can forfeit the appeal.

rows.title: Income Tax | Delhi HC Orders Rs.53 Crore TDS Refund with Interest Without Form 26B
rows.desc: Delhi High Court directs Rs.53.09 crore TDS refund with interest, holding Form 26B and Rule 31A inapplicable after Section 201 assessment.The post Delhi HC Orders Rs.53 Crore TDS Refund with Interest
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court has directed the income tax department to refund **Rs. 53.09 crore of TDS, together with applicable interest**, and held that the department could not insist on **Form 26B** or rely on **Rule 31A** in this situation. The key point is that, **after a Section 201 assessment has already been completed**, the court treated the request as one that did not require the payer to go through the usual Form 26B process for correction or refund processing.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that this ruling limits the tax department’s ability to reject or delay a TDS refund merely because **Form 26B was not filed**, where the liability issue has already been determined under **Section 201**. The decision appears to affect **deductors/payers seeking TDS refund after an adverse or completed Section 201 proceeding**, and it reinforces that procedural requirements under **Rule 31A** should not be applied mechanically to defeat a refund once the substantive assessment has been concluded.

The document does not provide any broader statutory amendment, rate change, or general new filing deadline; it is a **court-directed refund order** with interest, based on the facts of the case. Compliance officers should read it as a signal to review refund positions in Section 201 matters, especially where the department may attempt to insist on Form 26B even though the assessment record already resolves the tax position.

rows.title: Income Tax | Delhi HC Orders TDS Refund as Form 26B Inapplicable after Section 201 assessment
rows.desc: Chhattisgarh High Court held that interest on excess self-assessment tax refund is payable from the date of tax payment till refund, subject to statutory provisions.The post Delhi HC Orders TDS Refund
rows.summary:
The document reports a court ruling that affects the timing of interest on refunds of excess self-assessment tax. The Chhattisgarh High Court held that where a taxpayer has paid excess self-assessment tax and is later entitled to a refund, interest is payable on that refund for the period beginning on the date the tax was paid and continuing until the date the refund is actually issued, but only to the extent permitted by the applicable statutory provisions.

For a corporate compliance team, the key point is that this decision reinforces that refund interest is not limited merely to a later administrative date or to the date of claim processing; the interest period can run from the original tax payment date itself. This matters for companies tracking tax credits, refund claims, and cash-flow impact, because the ruling supports claiming interest for the full overpayment period when excess self-assessment tax has been remitted.

The title also references a separate Delhi High Court issue concerning TDS refund and the inapplicability of Form 26B after a Section 201 assessment, but the provided document content does not supply the underlying facts, holding, dates, thresholds, or procedural requirements for that matter. Based on the text provided, the only clearly stated substantive rule is the Chhattisgarh High Court’s position on interest for excess self-assessment tax refunds, subject to the statute governing such interest.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Jodhpur Quashes TDS Demands on SBI for Foreign-Leg LFC Payments
rows.desc: ITAT Jodhpur quashes TDS demands and penalty against SBI, holding no Section 201 default where judicial orders restrained TDS deduction on LFC.The post ITAT Jodhpur Quashes TDS Demands on SBI for Fore
rows.summary:
The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Jodhpur ruling in which the Tribunal quashed TDS demands and the related penalty imposed on State Bank of India (SBI) in connection with Leave Fare Concession (LFC) payments for the “foreign-leg” portion. The core holding is that SBI was **not** to be treated as an assessee in default under **Section 201** for not deducting tax at source on these payments, because prior judicial orders had already restrained TDS deduction on the relevant LFC amounts. In other words, the Tribunal accepted that SBI’s non-deduction was covered by court protection and therefore could not trigger the usual TDS default consequences.

From a compliance perspective, the decision is relevant to employers and payers handling employee travel-related reimbursements or benefits, especially where court orders or other binding judicial restraints exist that alter ordinary withholding obligations. The ruling indicates that where a competent court has specifically restrained deduction of TDS on a payment, failure to deduct tax on that payment should not automatically result in Section 201 demand or penalty exposure for the payer. No new statutory rate, threshold, or deadline is announced in the document; the material point is the Tribunal’s affirmation that judicial protection can override ordinary TDS collection consequences for the covered payments.

rows.title: Income Tax | RFCTLARR Compensation Exempt from Income Tax: Andhra Pradesh HC
rows.desc: Andhra Pradesh High Court holds RFCTLARR compensation exempt from income tax and remands TDS issue for fresh consideration.The post RFCTLARR Compensation Exempt from Income Tax: Andhra Pradesh HC appe
rows.summary:
The Andhra Pradesh High Court held that compensation paid under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (RFCTLARR) is exempt from income tax, meaning such compensation should not be treated as taxable income for the recipient. This ruling is significant for land acquisition payments made under the RFCTLARR framework and affects taxpayers receiving compensation under that statute, as well as any entity responsible for withholding tax on such payments.

The court also remanded the related TDS issue for fresh consideration, so the question of whether tax was properly deducted at source on the compensation was not finally resolved in this decision. Practically, this means the withholding position on RFCTLARR compensation remains subject to further review in the specific matter, and payors should not assume the TDS issue has been conclusively settled by this judgment alone.

No specific effective date, monetary threshold, or rate change is stated in the provided text. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that RFCTLARR compensation is to be treated as income-tax exempt, while the proper TDS treatment must be re-examined in light of this ruling and any subsequent proceedings.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Chhattisgarh HC Quashes GST Cancellation for Failure to Specify Date & Time of Personal Hearing
rows.desc: Chhattisgarh High Court quashes GST registration cancellation where REG-17 omitted personal hearing date/time and physical verification report was not uploaded.The post Chhattisgarh HC Quashes GST Can
rows.summary:
The document reports a Chhattisgarh High Court ruling quashing a GST registration cancellation because the cancellation process was procedurally defective. The key defect was that the REG-17 notice did not specify the date and time for the personal hearing, which meant the taxpayer was not properly informed of when to appear or respond. The court also noted that the physical verification report was not uploaded, indicating another lapse in the administrative record/process supporting the cancellation.

For compliance purposes, the decision reinforces that GST authorities must follow the prescribed cancellation procedure strictly before cancelling registration. In practical terms, any cancellation action relying on a show-cause notice or hearing process should include a clearly stated hearing date and time, and relevant verification materials should be properly uploaded and maintained in the record. The ruling does not announce a new tax rate or filing deadline, but it is important for registered taxpayers because it can be used to challenge cancellations that are issued without full procedural compliance.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Rule 43 Amendment Excluding Duty Scrips From ITC Reversal Is Prospective: GSTAT
rows.desc: GSTAT Kolkata holds Notification No. 14/2022 amending Rule 43 to exclude duty credit scrips from exempt turnover is prospective, but Section 74 cannot apply without fraud, wilful misstatement or suppr
rows.summary:
The GSTAT Kolkata has held that Notification No. 14/2022, which amended Rule 43 of the GST Rules to exclude duty credit scrips from the computation of exempt turnover for input tax credit (ITC) reversal purposes, applies **prospectively only** and not to prior periods. For compliance teams, this means businesses cannot be required to retroactively reverse ITC on the basis of this amendment for periods before the notification took effect; any such reversal should be tested against the pre-amendment Rule 43 position applicable at the time. The ruling is particularly relevant to taxpayers that receive, use, or account for **duty credit scrips** in their indirect tax computations and determine exempt turnover/ITC reversal under Rule 43.

The Tribunal also stated that **Section 74** of the CGST Act cannot be invoked unless there is evidence of **fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression of facts**. In other words, the department cannot use the extended demand/recovery mechanism under Section 74 merely because it disagrees with the taxpayer’s ITC reversal treatment or classification of duty scrip proceeds unless those higher-threshold ingredients are present and supported by facts. From a practical compliance standpoint, entities should review historical ITC reversals relating to duty scrips, preserve documentation supporting the treatment taken for pre-Notification No. 14/2022 periods, and ensure that any future reversals reflect the amended Rule 43 methodology going forward.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | IGST Refund on Exports: Madras High Court Directs Consideration of Claim
rows.desc: Madras HC permits Kuntal Granites to submit documents for IGST export refund and directs GST authority to decide the claim on merits.The post IGST Refund on Exports: Madras High Court Directs Consider
rows.summary:
The document reports a Madras High Court order allowing Kuntal Granites to submit the documents needed to support its claim for an IGST refund on exports and directing the GST authorities to examine the claim on its merits rather than rejecting it on a procedural basis. For compliance purposes, the key point is that export refund claims under GST may still be considered if the exporter is given an opportunity to cure/document its claim, and the authority must make a substantive decision based on the supporting records. The order does not announce a new statutory rule, rate, threshold, or blanket deadline; instead, it addresses one exporter’s refund application and the procedural handling of that claim by the GST department.  

What this means operationally is that exporters seeking IGST refunds should ensure all export documentation is complete and ready to be produced if the department queries the claim, because the court has signaled that the authority should consider the claim on merits when the necessary papers are filed. The affected entity in the reported matter is Kuntal Granites, but the practical compliance implication is broader for any GST-registered exporter claiming refund of IGST paid on exports. There is no indication in the summary of any change to the refund formula or any new compliance deadline; the requirement is simply that the GST authority must now review the claim after allowing submission of the supporting documents.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Indore Remands Agricultural Land Capital Gains Dispute for De Novo Adjudication
rows.desc: ITAT Indore condones 575-day delay, sets aside CIT(A) order and remands rural agricultural land capital gains dispute to AO for fresh adjudication.The post ITAT Indore Remands Agricultural Land Capita
rows.summary:
The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Indore has condoned a **575-day delay** in filing the appeal, set aside the order of the **Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) [CIT(A)]**, and **remanded the matter back to the Assessing Officer (AO) for de novo adjudication**. The dispute concerns the **capital gains treatment of rural agricultural land**, which is relevant to whether the land qualifies for exemption or is taxable as a capital asset under income-tax law.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is procedural rather than a new substantive tax rule: the Tribunal did **not finally decide the taxability** of the land transaction, but instead ordered a **fresh review** by the AO, meaning the underlying exemption/tax treatment remains unresolved and will be reassessed. Any taxpayer or entity with similar agricultural land transactions should ensure that supporting facts and records establishing the land’s rural/agricultural character, location, and use are fully documented and available for the fresh adjudication. Because the CIT(A) order has been overturned, the outcome will now depend on the AO’s re-examination of the evidence and applicable law.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai Deletes Notional Interest on Unconventional Exclusivity Payment
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai partly allows Tech Mahindra’s AY 2008-09 appeal, deleting major transfer-pricing interest adjustments and remanding section 14A computation.The post ITAT Mumbai Deletes Notional Interest o
rows.summary:
The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Mumbai decision in Tech Mahindra’s assessment year 2008–09 appeal, with the tribunal partly allowing the taxpayer’s case. The main compliance-relevant outcome is that the tribunal deleted a major transfer-pricing adjustment involving **notional interest** that had been proposed in relation to an **unconventional exclusivity payment**, reducing the income adjustment exposure on that issue. It also indicates that the tribunal **remanded the section 14A disallowance computation** for reconsideration, meaning the tax authority must redo the exempt-income expense disallowance analysis rather than relying on the original calculation.

For a corporate compliance team, the practical significance is that this decision limits the tax authority’s ability to impute interest on certain non-standard commercial arrangements where an exclusivity payment is involved, at least on the facts of this case. The ruling does **not** appear to create a new filing deadline, rate, or statutory amendment; rather, it is a judicial outcome affecting how existing transfer-pricing and section 14A rules were applied to Tech Mahindra for AY 2008–09. Companies with similar intercompany or related-party arrangements, especially those involving upfront or exclusivity-based payments, should review whether any transfer-pricing positions depend on assumed notional interest income, and should also ensure their section 14A expense disallowance computations are supportable and properly documented if exempt income is involved.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Madras HC Grants Retrospective ITC Benefit Where Return Filed Before 30.11.2021
rows.desc: Madras HC quashes GST ITC demand for FY 2018-19 as return was filed before the Section 16(5) cut-off of 30.11.2021.The post Madras HC Grants Retrospective ITC Benefit Where Return Filed Before 30.11.2
rows.summary:
The document reports a Madras High Court ruling granting retrospective input tax credit (ITC) relief under GST for FY 2018–19 where the taxpayer had filed the relevant return before the statutory cut-off date of 30.11.2021 under Section 16(5). The court quashed the GST department’s ITC demand on the basis that the taxpayer’s claim was not time-barred because the return had already been filed within the period that the retrospective amendment intended to protect. For compliance teams, the key point is that this judgment recognizes that ITC claims linked to FY 2018–19 may still be available if the return was filed before 30 November 2021, even if the department had previously raised a denial based on the earlier limitation position.

This is not a new filing requirement or rate change, but a legal clarification affecting businesses that claimed or were denied ITC for FY 2018–19. Companies with pending GST disputes or notices involving FY 2018–19 ITC should check whether their returns were filed on or before 30.11.2021, because this ruling may support reopening or defending those claims. The practical compliance implication is to retain evidence of the filing date of the relevant GST returns and to reassess any ITC demands, disallowances, or litigation positions that were based solely on the pre-amendment time bar.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Chennai Allows Enhanced ₹25 Lakh Leave Encashment Exemption for Retired Bank Employee
rows.desc: ITAT Chennai condones 1,221-day delay and allows ₹11.27 lakh leave encashment exemption under the enhanced ₹25 lakh limit.The post ITAT Chennai Allows Enhanced ₹25 Lakh Leave Encashment Exemption for
rows.summary:
The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Chennai ruling that is relevant to payroll, tax withholding, and employee retirement-benefit compliance, especially for banks and other employers handling leave encashment payments to retired employees. In the case described, the Tribunal condoned a **1,221-day delay** in filing and held that a retired bank employee was entitled to an **₹11.27 lakh leave encashment exemption** under the **enhanced ₹25 lakh exemption limit**. The practical significance is that, where leave encashment is paid on retirement, the higher **₹25 lakh cap** can be applied rather than an older lower limit, reducing the taxable portion of the retirement payout for eligible employees.

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that employers and payroll/tax functions should ensure that leave encashment paid to retiring employees is tested against the **current statutory exemption ceiling of ₹25 lakh** when determining TDS and taxable salary treatment. The ruling indicates that if a payment falls within the exemption framework, the exempt amount should be recognized accordingly, and only any excess over the applicable limit should be treated as taxable. Because the article is framed as a tribunal allowance for a specific retired bank employee, it does not appear to create a new filing deadline or procedural requirement for employers, but it reinforces the need to apply the revised exemption limit correctly in retirement settlements and tax reporting.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Bombay HC Quashes Consolidated GST Notice Covering Multiple Financial Years
rows.desc: Bombay High Court quashes a Section 73 GST notice clubbing FY 2021-22 to 2023-24, allowing fresh notice strictly under law.The post Bombay HC Quashes Consolidated GST Notice Covering Multiple Financia
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court has quashed a GST show-cause notice issued under Section 73 that had improperly clubbed multiple financial years together—FY 2021-22, FY 2022-23, and FY 2023-24—in a single consolidated proceeding. The court held that this manner of issuing the notice was not compliant with the statutory framework, and therefore set it aside.  

For compliance teams, the key point is that GST authorities cannot use one combined Section 73 notice to cover multiple assessment periods if the law requires year-wise or otherwise period-specific proceedings; notices must be issued strictly in accordance with the procedural requirements under GST law. The ruling does not eliminate the department’s ability to proceed: it expressly allows the tax authority to issue fresh notices, but only in a manner that is legally valid and confined to the proper periods.  

Operationally, businesses should review any pending or received GST notices to confirm whether different financial years have been improperly aggregated, because such notices may be vulnerable to challenge on procedural grounds. The decision is especially relevant for taxpayers facing Section 73 allegations relating to tax short payment, non-payment, or wrongful input tax credit issues over multiple years, since it reinforces that each relevant tax period must be handled within the bounds of the statute.

rows.title: Company Law | Kerala HC Rejects Limitation Objection Against Official Liquidator’s Recovery Claim
rows.desc: Kerala High Court held that Official Liquidator’s claim under Section 446 can be filed within four years from the winding-up order.The post Kerala HC Rejects Limitation Objection Against Official Liqu
rows.summary: The Kerala High Court held that an Official Liquidator’s recovery claim under Section 446 is subject to a four-year limitation period running from the date of the winding-up order, and therefore a limitation objection could not defeat the claim in this case. The ruling confirms that where a company has been ordered to be wound up, the Official Liquidator may initiate recovery proceedings within four years of that order, rather than being barred by a shorter or earlier limitation period argued by the opposing party. For compliance purposes, this means entities dealing with a company in liquidation should treat claims brought by the Official Liquidator as potentially timely for up to four years after the winding-up order and should not assume such claims are time-barred merely because more time has passed from the underlying transaction or default. The decision is relevant to companies, counterparties, and legal/compliance teams involved in insolvency, liquidation, or legacy recovery disputes, because it reinforces the Liquidator’s ability to pursue recovery actions during that four-year window.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Calcutta HC Accepted ED Officer’s Unconditional Apology in Stay Order Contempt
rows.desc: Calcutta HC accepts ED officer’s unconditional apology for prima facie violation of a subsisting stay order and closes contempt proceedings.The post Calcutta HC Accepted ED Officer’s Unconditional Apo
rows.summary:
The document reports a Calcutta High Court contempt matter involving an Enforcement Directorate (ED) officer who was found to have prima facie acted in violation of an existing stay order. The court accepted the officer’s unconditional apology and, as a result, closed the contempt proceedings. From a compliance perspective, the key point is that the court treated the conduct as a serious potential breach of a subsisting judicial stay, but resolved the matter through the officer’s apology rather than further sanction in this instance.

No new regulatory rule, filing deadline, monetary threshold, or formal procedure is announced in the text provided. The practical compliance takeaway is limited to the reminder that orders of court—especially stay orders—must be strictly observed by government officers and enforcement personnel, because even prima facie noncompliance can trigger contempt proceedings.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Bengaluru Denies Section 128A Waiver for December 2020 ITC Demand
rows.desc: GSTAT Bengaluru holds Section 128A waiver unavailable where excess ITC was first availed in December 2020.The post GSTAT Bengaluru Denies Section 128A Waiver for December 2020 ITC Demand appeared firs
rows.summary:
The document reports a GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT), Bengaluru decision holding that the Section 128A waiver is **not available** for a demand involving **excess input tax credit (ITC) first availed in December 2020**. In practical terms, this means a taxpayer cannot use the Section 128A relief mechanism to extinguish or reduce liability for that ITC demand if the disputed credit originated in that period, and the tribunal’s view narrows the availability of the waiver based on the **date the excess ITC was first claimed**.

For compliance teams, the key point is that **timing of the original ITC availment matters**: if the excess credit was first taken in **December 2020**, this ruling indicates the taxpayer may remain exposed to the underlying GST demand, along with the associated consequences under the normal assessment/enforcement process. The summary provided does not include additional procedural directions, monetary amounts, or filing deadlines beyond the December 2020 date and the conclusion that Section 128A relief was denied, so the immediate compliance takeaway is to review any pending or historical ITC disputes to confirm whether the credit was first availed during a period that may fall outside Section 128A waiver eligibility.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Gujarat HC Quashes GST Notices and Orders Issued Against Deceased Proprietor
rows.desc: Gujarat HC quashes GST proceedings initiated against deceased proprietor, allowing fresh proceedings against the legal heir in accordance with law.The post Gujarat HC Quashes GST Notices and Orders Is
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court held that GST notices and consequential orders issued in the name of a deceased sole proprietor are invalid, because proceedings cannot validly continue against a non-existent person. In the case described, the GST department had initiated and completed proceedings against a proprietorship after the proprietor had died, and the Court quashed those notices and orders on that ground.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that when a proprietor dies, the tax authorities must follow the legal route for proceeding against the estate or legal heir rather than continuing or issuing fresh notices in the deceased proprietor’s name. The Court permitted the department to start fresh proceedings against the legal heir, but only in accordance with law, meaning the authority must identify and proceed against the correct successor/legal representative and comply with the applicable procedural requirements. This is especially relevant for GST registrations and assessments involving sole proprietorships, where the proprietor’s death can create a defect in jurisdiction or party identity if notices are still addressed to the deceased.

There is no change to GST rates, thresholds, filing deadlines, or tax liability rules in this item; the material point is procedural validity of enforcement actions. Compliance teams should therefore ensure that, upon learning of a proprietor’s death, any ongoing GST dispute, show-cause notice, assessment, demand, or appeal is reviewed promptly for whether the proper party has been substituted and whether notices need to be reissued to the legal heir or representative under the governing legal procedure.

rows.title: Income Tax | Jharkhand HC Quashes GST Orders Passed Against Deceased Proprietor, Allows Fresh Legal Action
rows.desc: Jharkhand HC quashes GST orders against deceased proprietor and leaves department free to pursue claims against legal representative in accordance with law.The post Jharkhand HC Quashes GST Orders Pas
rows.summary:
The Jharkhand High Court held that GST assessment/orders passed against a sole proprietorship after the proprietor’s death are not sustainable, and it quashed those orders. The key compliance point is that the tax department cannot validly continue proceedings or issue enforceable orders in the name of a deceased proprietor; once death occurs, any recovery or adjudication action must be taken in accordance with law against the proper legal representative or successor, rather than against the deceased individual. 

The court also made clear that its ruling does not bar the department from pursuing the underlying tax claim itself. Instead, it left the authorities free to initiate fresh legal action against the deceased proprietor’s legal representative, provided they follow the correct statutory procedure. For compliance teams, this means that if a business is a sole proprietorship and the proprietor has died, all pending GST notices, orders, or recovery steps must be reviewed immediately to confirm whether they were issued to a non-existent party and whether fresh proceedings need to be commenced against the estate/legal heir under applicable law.

rows.title: Income Tax | ₹1.80 Crore Cash During Demonetisation; ITAT Delhi Restricts Section 68 Addition to ₹5 Lakh
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi restricts demonetisation cash deposit addition to Rs. 5 lakh and directs normal-rate taxation instead of Section 115BBE.The post ₹1.80 Crore Cash During Demonetisation; ITAT Delhi Restricts
rows.summary:
This document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) Delhi decision concerning cash deposits made during the demonetisation period. The taxpayer had deposited ₹1.80 crore in cash, and the tax department sought to treat the entire amount as unexplained cash credit under Section 68, which would ordinarily trigger taxation under Section 115BBE at the punitive rate applicable to unexplained income. The ITAT, however, restricted the Section 68 addition to only ₹5 lakh, rather than the full ₹1.80 crore, materially reducing the exposure.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the tribunal directed that the deposit be taxed at normal rates rather than under Section 115BBE, meaning the harsher special-tax regime for unexplained income was not upheld on the full amount. The decision specifically arose in the context of demonetisation-era cash deposits, so it is relevant to entities or individuals with large cash holdings and deposits during that period. No statutory amendment is described; the document is summarizing a tribunal ruling that narrows the tax addition and the applicable tax rate in this fact pattern.

rows.title: Income Tax | NRI Assessee Was Abroad During ₹58.50 Lakh Cash Deposit in Joint Account: ITAT Deletes Addition
rows.desc: ITAT Chandigarh deletes Rs.58.50 lakh cash deposit addition after finding the assessee was abroad and deposits were made by her husband.The post NRI Assessee Was Abroad During ₹58.50 Lakh Cash Deposit
rows.summary:
This document is not a regulation or rulemaking; it is an ITAT Chandigarh tax appellate decision addressing an income-tax addition made on account of cash deposits. The Tribunal deleted the addition of ₹58.50 lakh that had been made in the assessee’s hands because the evidence showed she was an NRI and was abroad at the time the cash was deposited into a joint account. The key factual finding was that the deposits were made by her husband, not by her, and therefore the cash could not be attributed to her as unexplained income merely because the account was jointly held.  

For compliance purposes, the case reinforces that tax authorities must establish actual ownership/source of cash deposits before treating them as taxable income in the hands of a joint-account holder, especially where the person is absent from India and another joint holder controls the funds. There are no new deadlines, filing changes, thresholds, or procedural obligations announced in this item; it is an adjudication limited to the facts of this assessee’s case.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Delhi Directs 25% Tax Rate for Rajasthan Pulses Despite Denial of Section 115BAA
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi holds Rajasthan Pulses taxable at 25% where FY 2017-18 turnover was below Rs.400 crore, despite failure to file Form 10-IC.The post ITAT Delhi Directs 25% Tax Rate for Rajasthan Pulses Desp
rows.summary:
The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Delhi ruling involving Rajasthan Pulses on the applicability of the concessional corporate tax regime under Section 115BAA. The key holding is that Rajasthan Pulses was directed to be taxed at 25% because its financial year 2017–18 turnover was below Rs. 400 crore, even though the company had failed to file Form 10-IC, which is ordinarily the procedural filing associated with opting into the lower tax regime.

For compliance purposes, the material point is that the tribunal treated the turnover condition as decisive for the lower rate, and the absence of Form 10-IC did not prevent application of the 25% tax rate on the facts of this case. The affected entity type is a corporate taxpayer eligible for the Section 115BAA regime, with the relevant factual threshold being prior-year turnover under Rs. 400 crore. The decision signals that companies in similar circumstances should review whether they qualify for the reduced rate based on turnover and should not assume that a procedural lapse alone necessarily disqualifies them, although filing obligations remain important to avoid disputes.

No other deadlines, numerical rates, or procedural changes are provided in the excerpt beyond the 25% rate, the Rs. 400 crore turnover benchmark, and the missed Form 10-IC filing.

rows.title: Service Tax | Microsoft software licence royalty not taxable as IPR service before 16.05.2008: CESTAT Allahabad
rows.desc: CESTAT Allahabad sets aside service tax, interest and penalties on software royalty, holding pre-16.05.2008 software services not taxable under IPR service.The post Microsoft software licence royalty
rows.summary:
The document reports a CESTAT Allahabad ruling that **service tax, interest, and penalties were set aside** on amounts paid as **Microsoft software licence royalty**, because the tribunal held that **software-related services were not taxable as “Intellectual Property Right (IPR) service” for the period before 16.05.2008**. In practical compliance terms, this means that **royalty or licence payments for software use made prior to 16 May 2008** should not be treated as falling within the service tax net under the IPR service category on the basis applied in this case.

The affected activity is the **licensing/royalty arrangement for Microsoft software**, and the key legal cutoff is **16.05.2008**. For transactions or tax positions involving **pre-16.05.2008 software licence royalty**, the tribunal’s decision indicates that service tax demands, along with related interest and penalty exposure, were not sustainable under the IPR service classification used by the department. Compliance teams should therefore distinguish between **software royalty/licence payments before and after 16 May 2008**, since the ruling turns on that date and does not state that all software royalty is universally non-taxable.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Condonation of 968-Day Customs Appeal Delay Denied for Prolonged Inaction: Delhi HC
rows.desc: Delhi HC upholds CESTAT’s refusal to condone 968-day delay, finding no substantial question of law or sufficient cause.The post Condonation of 968-Day Customs Appeal Delay Denied for Prolonged Inactio
rows.summary: The Delhi High Court upheld the CESTAT’s refusal to condone a **968-day delay** in filing a customs appeal, concluding that there was **no sufficient cause** shown for such prolonged inaction and **no substantial question of law** warranting interference. The ruling is important for customs compliance because it reinforces that appellate deadlines in customs matters are enforced strictly, and long periods of inactivity cannot be excused merely by seeking leniency after the fact. The court’s decision confirms that where an appellant fails to act diligently for an extended period, the tribunal is entitled to reject the appeal as time-barred rather than reopen the matter on equitable grounds. For companies handling customs disputes, the practical compliance takeaway is to monitor filing timelines closely, document any reasons for delay contemporaneously, and ensure appeals are lodged well within the prescribed limitation period to avoid dismissal without merits review.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Gauhati HC Grants Bail to Woman Accused in GST Case Subject to Investigation Conditions
rows.desc: Gauhati HC grants bail to woman accused in GST case on Rs. 75,000 bond, with sureties and conditions for investigation cooperation.The post Gauhati HC Grants Bail to Woman Accused in GST Case Subject
rows.summary:
The document reports a Gauhati High Court bail order in a GST-related criminal matter, not a new tax rule or regulatory amendment. The court granted bail to a woman accused in a GST case, but the release is conditional: she must furnish a bond of Rs. 75,000 and provide sureties, and she must comply with investigation-related conditions imposed by the court. The key compliance-relevant point is that the order preserves the investigating authority’s ability to continue its inquiry while the accused remains on bail, so the accused is required to cooperate with investigation proceedings rather than simply being released without restriction. 

For a corporate compliance team, this is relevant only as a procedural enforcement development in GST litigation: it signals that the court is willing to grant bail in GST matters, but only with financial security and ongoing cooperation obligations. No broader GST rate, filing, or reporting requirement is announced in the document, and there is no indication of a change in GST law or compliance deadlines. The material details are limited to the bail amount, the requirement for sureties, and the condition that the accused assist with the investigation.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Telangana HC Quashes Section 226(3) Attachment of BIOSOT Bank Accounts
rows.desc: Telangana High Court holds BIOSOT entitled to Article 289 immunity and quashes Section 226(3) bank-account attachment.The post Telangana HC Quashes Section 226(3) Attachment of BIOSOT Bank Accounts ap
rows.summary:
The Telangana High Court held that BIOSOT was entitled to constitutional immunity under Article 289 and therefore quashed the tax department’s attachment of BIOSOT’s bank accounts under Section 226(3). The practical effect is that the revenue authorities cannot proceed with this mode of recovery against BIOSOT’s accounts on the facts of this case, because the court found the attachment itself invalid. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that if an entity can establish Article 289 protection, bank-account garnishment/attachment under Section 226(3) should not be used against it for the relevant tax demand. 

The document does not provide the underlying tax amount, the specific nature of the demand, or any broader rule change beyond this court ruling, and it does not set any new filing deadline, rate, or threshold. It is therefore best read as a case-specific judicial ruling affecting BIOSOT’s accounts rather than a general legislative amendment.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai Deletes Notional Rent Addition and Allows Related Expense Claims
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai deletes Rs. 475.73 lakh notional rent addition, allows related expenses, and grants depreciation on moulds and dies.The post ITAT Mumbai Deletes Notional Rent Addition and Allows Related E
rows.summary:
The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Mumbai decision in which the Tribunal removed a **Rs. 475.73 lakh notional rent addition** from the taxpayer’s assessment. The key compliance takeaway is that the tax authority’s attempt to tax an imputed rental value did not stand, so the assessed income was reduced by that amount. In addition, the Tribunal **allowed the related expense claims** tied to the disputed property/arrangement, meaning those expenditures were accepted as deductible rather than being disallowed alongside the notional rent adjustment.

The decision also **granted depreciation on moulds and dies**, confirming that these assets qualified for depreciation treatment under the applicable tax rules. For compliance and tax reporting purposes, this outcome supports the position that where a taxpayer has incurred actual, supportable expenses and holds depreciable assets such as moulds and dies, those claims may be sustainable even if the tax authority seeks to make an imputed income adjustment. No specific statutory amendment, filing deadline, or future effective date is mentioned in the provided text; the document is a case outcome rather than a rule change.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai Allows 12AB Renewal and 80G Approval Despite No Formal Trust Deed
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai allows 12AB renewal and 80G approval, holding that absence of a formal trust deed cannot alone defeat registration.The post ITAT Mumbai Allows 12AB Renewal and 80G Approval Despite No Form
rows.summary:
The document reports an ITAT Mumbai ruling that a charitable organization’s request for renewal of registration under section 12AB and approval under section 80G cannot be rejected solely because it does not have a formal trust deed. In other words, the tribunal held that the absence of a written trust deed, by itself, is not enough to deny tax-exempt charitable status or donor-deduction approval if the organization otherwise meets the legal requirements. This matters for charitable trusts, societies, and other nonprofit entities seeking or renewing income-tax registrations, because it clarifies that the tax authority must look at the substance of the organization’s constitution and activities rather than treating a missing deed as automatically disqualifying.

There is no new statutory deadline, rate, or numeric threshold announced in the text; the key compliance point is the evidentiary standard for registration renewals and approvals. For compliance teams, the practical implication is that organizations without a formal trust deed should still be prepared to demonstrate their governing structure, charitable objects, and actual operations through other founding documents and records when applying for or renewing 12AB and 80G status. The ruling is favorable to applicants, but it does not eliminate the need to satisfy the substantive conditions for registration and approval under the income-tax law.

rows.desc: CompaniesLIC Gets RBI Approval To Raise ICICI Bank Stake To 9.99%; Key DetailsEdited by: Priya RaghuvanshiUpdated Sep 5, 2026, 17:52 ISTLIC has received Reserve Bank of India approval to acquire up to 9.99 per cent in ICICI Bank, with the permission valid for one year from September 4.According to the exchange filing, ICICI Bank received the RBI’s approval letter dated September 4, 2026. (File Photo)follow usfollow us.Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) has secured approval from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to acquire up to 9.99 per cent of the paid-up share capital or voting rights in ICICI Bank, according to a regulatory filing by the private sector lender. The approval gives the state-owned insurer one year from the date of the RBI’s letter to complete the proposed acquisition. The permission will cease to remain valid if LIC does not acquire the stake within the prescribed period.ICICI Bank said it received the RBI communication on September 4, 2026, at 9:09 pm. The proposed stake purchase will also have to comply with all applicable statutory and regulatory requirements.According to ICICI Bank’s exchange filing, the RBI has permitted LIC to build an “aggregate holding” of as much as 9.99 per cent in the bank.“On September 4, 2026 at 9:09 pm, ICICI Bank Limited (the Bank) has received a copy of Reserve Bank of India (RBI ) letter dated the same day addressed to Life Insurance Corporation of India (the applicant) that it has accorded its approval to the applicant to acquire ‘aggregate holding’ of up to 9.9 9 per cent of the paid -up share capital or voting rights in the Bank within one year from the date of RBI approval letter, failing which RBI approval shall stand cancelled.”The filing further clarified that the regulatory permission comes with conditions governing the transaction.“The approval is subject to certain conditions including compliance with the relevant statutory and regulatory provisions,” the filing read.This means any increase in LIC’s holding will remain subject to the broader rules applicable to shareholding in regulated banking entities.LIC Expands Presence Across Major BanksThe RBI approval for ICICI Bank comes shortly after LIC received clearance to increase its holding in another major private lender, HDFC Bank.In an August 19 regulatory filing, HDFC Bank disclosed that the RBI had approved LIC’s application to acquire up to 9.99 per cent of its paid-up share capital or voting rights.The filing stated that the regulator had “accorded its approval to Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC)” to acquire the additional stake in the bank.HDFC Bank also disclosed LIC’s existing ownership position, stating that LIC "holds 4.11% of the total share capital of the Bank."The latest approvals underline LIC’s growing presence as a significant institutional investor in India’s banking sector, particularly among the country’s largest private lenders.What The ICICI Bank Approval MeansThe RBI clearance does not by itself indicate that LIC will immediately purchase the entire 9.99 per cent permitted stake. Instead, it provides the insurer with regulatory authorisation to build its holding up to that level during the one-year approval period.The final extent and timing of any acquisition will therefore depend on LIC’s investment decisions and compliance with applicable regulations.For ICICI Bank, the approval provides clarity on LIC’s ability to increase its ownership in the lender while placing the transaction within the regulatory framework governing significant shareholdings in banks.The development also comes as institutional investors continue to play a prominent role in India’s financial sector, with large insurers and other long-term investors holding stakes in leading banking companies.(With Agency Inputs)Latest News worldWhat Did Sarah Khalifa Do? rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has approved Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) to acquire up to 9.99% of the paid-up share capital or voting rights in ICICI Bank, giving LIC a one-year window from the date of the RBI’s approval letter to complete the purchase. ICICI Bank said it received the RBI’s letter on September 4, 2026 at 9:09 pm, so the approval will lapse if LIC does not make the acquisition within one year from that date.  

The approval is not unconditional: the bank’s filing states that the transaction is subject to compliance with all applicable statutory and regulatory requirements, meaning LIC’s eventual shareholding increase must still fit within the broader rules governing ownership in regulated banking entities. The filing specifically refers to LIC’s permitted “aggregate holding” of up to 9.99%, making clear that the cap applies to LIC’s total holding/voting rights in the bank rather than a separate or incremental carve-out.  

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that this is only a regulatory authorization, not a completed share purchase. LIC may buy up to the approved limit during the one-year validity period, but any actual increase in its stake must be executed in accordance with the banking, securities, and other applicable legal requirements, or the RBI approval will stand cancelled.  

The document also notes a recent similar approval involving HDFC Bank, where the RBI had already cleared LIC to acquire up to 9.99% of paid-up share capital or voting rights; HDFC Bank disclosed that LIC already held 4.11% of its total share capital. This reinforces that LIC is expanding its potential shareholding positions in major private banks, but each transaction remains separately subject to RBI approval and ongoing regulatory compliance.

The case follows a complaint filed by LICHFL, which has accused Chandra, Pankaj Suroliya, Amish Pandya and Rajeev Dholakia of allegedly cheating the housing finance company and conspiring to secure credit facilities on the basis of disputed financial disclosures.According to the complaint, Chandra submitted a net worth certificate in 2018 declaring his net worth at Rs 59,113 crore. LICHFL has alleged that the certificate was used to obtain loan facilities for M/s Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt Ltd and other companies linked to him.Relying on the financial certificate, LICHFL subsequently extended credit facilities to three companies associated with Chandra, the complaint stated.The housing finance company has now raised objections over Chandra's statements made during subsequent insolvency proceedings, particularly his denial that he had ever possessed a net worth of Rs 50,000 crore, as reflected in the certificates submitted to LICHFL.LICHFL has alleged cheating, criminal breach of trust and conspiracy in its complaint to the investigating agency.The complaint given to the CBI Head Office reads, "A loan facility of Rs. 500 Crores to Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt. Ltd. and Pan India Infra projects Pvt. Ltd. (Co-borrower) as a Home Entity Loan (Takeover & Top-up for Business Expansion) under Loan Account No. 610700003341 secured by a Letter of Continuing Guarantee dated 28th March 18 executed by Subhash Chandra (Vasant Sagar Loan Facility) and a loan facility of Rs. 480 Crores to Digital Subscriber Management and Consultancy Services Pvt. Ltd. and Spirit Infra power and Multi Ventures Pvt. Ltd. Chartered Accountants on 06.07.2018, certifying that his networth was Rs. 40,562 Crores," it added."Thereafter, defaults have occurred in the Vasant Sagar Loan Facility and Digital Loan Facility. In the course of the subsequent proceedings under the Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code, 2016 for the personal insolvency resolution of Subhash Chandra, he categorically denied having the Net Worth as stated in the Net Worth Certificates, which he had submitted to LICHFL to cause approval and disbursal of the loan detailed above," the complaint states."In the course of the proceedings. he has stated that his net worth in 2024 is Rs. 31.79 crore and stated that, even in 2017-18. he did not have the net worth of more than Rs. 40.000 Crores," it noted.Subhash Chandra’s Statement In Insolvency ProceedingsMeanwhile, on 27th August, Zee Group founder Subhash Chandra, in a statement, claimed he has not borrowed any money from any lender and is only a personal guarantor.
