rows.summary:
The CBI has registered a criminal case against Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra, along with Pankaj Suroliya, Amish Pandya, and Rajeev Dholakia, based on a complaint from LIC Housing Finance Ltd. (LICHFL) alleging cheating, criminal breach of trust, and conspiracy in connection with housing finance loans exceeding Rs 1,322 crore. The complaint says the loans were obtained on the basis of disputed net worth certificates and related financial disclosures, including a March 28, 2018 certificate from DIM & Co. stating Chandra’s net worth was US$ 6,197.62 million (about Rs 59,113.21 crore) as of March 31, 2017, and a July 6, 2018 certificate from MPJ & Co. stating net worth of Rs 40,562 crore. Based on those disclosures and Chandra’s continuing guarantees, LICHFL extended at least two named facilities: a Rs 500 crore home entity loan to Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt. Ltd. and Pan India Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. (co-borrower) under Loan Account No. 610700003341, secured by a continuing guarantee dated March 28, 2018; and a Rs 480 crore rental discounting facility to Digital Subscriber Management and Consultancy Services Pvt. Ltd. and Spirit Infra Power and Multi Ventures Pvt. Ltd. (co-borrower) under Loan Account No. 610700003500, secured by a continuing guarantee dated August 10, 2018.

According to LICHFL, defaults later occurred in both facilities, and during later proceedings under the Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code, 2016 relating to Chandra’s personal insolvency resolution, he allegedly denied that he ever had the net worth reflected in the certificates submitted to secure the loans. The complaint specifically says he stated his net worth in 2024 was Rs 31.79 crore and that even in 2017–18 he did not have a net worth above Rs 40,000 crore, which LICHFL says undermines the basis on which the credit was granted and disbursed. For compliance purposes, the document highlights a fraud-risk pattern centered on materially inconsistent net worth representations to a lender, use of those representations to obtain large credit facilities for linked entities, and subsequent disputes in insolvency proceedings over the truth of those statements. There is no new regulatory rule or industry-wide deadline announced here; the operative development is the filing of a criminal case and the continuation of investigation into the alleged loan fraud.

Separately, in a statement dated August 27, Chandra said he has not borrowed money from any lender and is only a personal guarantor. He said the total claim against him as a personal guarantor in the personal insolvency proceedings is Rs 3,992 crore from creditors who rejected the resolution plan, not Rs 22,000 crore overall; he also said Rs 21,696 crore was admitted by the Resolution Professional, Rs 620 crore has been settled, and another Rs 1,063 crore was offered to be paid by the borrower entities. He further stated that the borrowing entities for which he provided personal guarantees have repaid Rs 43,000 crore to date and have assured settlement of any remaining amount due.

rows.title: RBI May Resume Rate Hikes In H2 FY27; Union Bank Sees Repo Rate Rising To 6%Sep 4, 2026, 14:10 IST
rows.desc: EconomyRBI May Resume Rate Hikes In H2 FY27; Union Bank Sees Repo Rate Rising To 6%Edited by: Priya RaghuvanshiUpdated Sep 4, 2026, 14:10 ISTUnion Bank expects RBI to raise the repo rate to 5.75-6 per cent in FY27 as liquidity surges and inflation risks rise, with hikes possible from December.Reserve Bank of India (File Photo)Photo : iStockfollow usfollow usThe Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may have to return to monetary tightening in the second half of FY27 as strong economic activity, elevated inflation risks and a surge in banking-system liquidity create fresh policy challenges, according to an assessment by Union Bank of India (UBI). UBI expects the central bank to potentially lift the repo rate by 50-75 basis points from its current 5.25 per cent level. The anticipated increase could come through two or three hikes of 25 basis points each, taking the benchmark rate to a range of 5.75-6 per cent.The bank's base-case view places the beginning of the potential tightening cycle in December, although it has not completely ruled out an earlier move depending on global developments and domestic liquidity conditions.The outlook reflects a combination of factors that could put pressure on the RBI to recalibrate its monetary policy stance. Strong economic growth, a possible pickup in inflation and tighter financial conditions globally are among the key considerations highlighted by UBI.“Rate hikes are back on the table for H2 FY27,” the report said, adding that December appears to be the more likely starting point in its base-case scenario.The assessment marks a shift in the interest-rate outlook, particularly as the RBI has been dealing with a substantial increase in system liquidity. If excess funds remain within the banking system for an extended period, managing liquidity could become increasingly important for the central bank.Forex Inflows Fuel Surge In Banking LiquidityA major factor behind the liquidity build-up has been the significant foreign exchange inflows associated with the RBI's special swap facility.As of August 31, these inflows had reached around USD 136 billion. FCNR(B) deposits accounted for approximately USD 127.23 billion, while overseas foreign currency borrowings and external commercial borrowings made up the balance.The resulting increase in liquidity has been visible in core liquidity levels. According to UBI, core liquidity climbed from Rs 4.82 lakh crore in mid-June to Rs 8.05 lakh crore by mid-August, with the foreign exchange impact accounting for almost all of the increase.The bank's illustrative scenario points to an even sharper rise, with core liquidity potentially reaching around Rs 14.17 lakh crore by September 11.“After getting dollar flows, now Rupee liquidity management is key policy challenge for RBI,” the report said.RBI May Use Liquidity Tools Before Raising RatesUBI expects the RBI to first focus on absorbing surplus liquidity rather than immediately relying on the repo rate as its primary tool.The central bank could announce liquidity-absorption measures ahead of its October monetary policy review. Among the options identified by UBI are short-duration and longer-duration variable rate reverse repo operations (VRRR), along with an incremental cash reserve ratio (I-CRR).The RBI could also consider bond sales and foreign exchange swaps as additional ways of managing the surplus.UBI believes temporary measures may initially be preferable because they can be rolled back as credit demand improves during the second half of FY27. The bank estimates that the RBI could use a roughly 50:50 combination of short-term VRRR operations and longer-duration measures to tackle the projected liquidity surplus.October Rate Increase Still PossibleAlthough December is UBI's preferred starting point for a rate-hike cycle, an October increase remains possible under certain circumstances.The bank said an earlier hike could come into consideration if the US Federal Reserve increases interest rates in September and the RBI has already addressed excess domestic liquidity through more durable measures.Oil prices are another factor that could influence the central bank's decision. UBI noted that crude prices above USD 90 per barrel could intensify inflationary pressures and put additional strain on the rupee.At the same time, a reduction in geopolitical tensions could provide the RBI with greater room to manoeuvre on monetary policy.Get Latest News Live on Times Now along with Breaking News and Top Headlines from Business, Economy and around the World.Latest News world‘Berlin Is Forgetting WWII’: Medvedev Accuses German Leadership Of ‘Nazi’ Behaviourentertainment newsWhy Did Blackpink Lisa Name Her New Song SaWaDiKa? rows.summary:
Union Bank of India’s assessment says the Reserve Bank of India may reverse course and resume repo rate hikes in the second half of FY27 if strong growth, rising inflation risks, and excess banking-system liquidity persist. UBI’s base case is for the repo rate to rise by 50–75 basis points from the current 5.25% through two or three 25-basis-point hikes, reaching about 5.75% to 6.0%, with December identified as the most likely start date; however, an October hike is still possible if the US Federal Reserve raises rates in September and the RBI has already absorbed enough liquidity through more durable tools.  

The document is not a new regulation, but it signals likely RBI policy actions that compliance and treasury teams should monitor because they affect funding costs, liquidity management, and interest-rate risk. UBI says the immediate policy focus is likely to be liquidity absorption before any repo increase, using short-duration and longer-duration variable rate reverse repo operations (VRRR), an incremental cash reserve ratio (I-CRR), bond sales, and foreign exchange swaps; it expects a roughly 50:50 mix of short-term VRRR and longer-duration measures.  

The liquidity build-up is driven largely by RBI’s special swap facility and related foreign exchange inflows, which had reached about USD 136 billion as of August 31. Of that amount, roughly USD 127.23 billion was FCNR(B) deposits, with the remainder coming from overseas foreign currency borrowings and external commercial borrowings. Core liquidity rose from Rs 4.82 lakh crore in mid-June to Rs 8.05 lakh crore by mid-August, and UBI’s illustrative scenario shows it could climb further to around Rs 14.17 lakh crore by September 11 if the inflows continue.  

For compliance planning, the practical takeaway is that monetary conditions may tighten in FY27 even before the repo rate moves, because the RBI may first deploy liquidity-absorption measures at or before its October policy review. UBI flags crude oil above USD 90 per barrel as an additional inflation and rupee-risk trigger that could accelerate tightening, while easing geopolitical tensions could delay or soften the response.

rows.summary:
HDFC Bank’s report says India’s balance of payments is still expected to remain in surplus in FY27, with a projected surplus of USD 60–65 billion, even though the current account deficit is expected to widen. The bank’s forecast is that the CAD will rise to about 1.1–1.3% of GDP in FY27, and that the second quarter CAD could be even wider at 1.5–1.7% of GDP; despite that, HDFC Bank says it is keeping an upside bias to its BoP surplus estimate.

The key offsetting factor is large foreign exchange inflows mobilized through RBI special schemes, especially FCNR(B) deposits and overseas borrowing channels, which the bank says should more than compensate for weaker capital flows seen in the first quarter. As of August 31, total foreign exchange inflows under the RBI’s special USD-INR swap facility had reached USD 136.38 billion, comprising USD 127.23 billion through FCNR(B) deposits, USD 5.26 billion through overseas foreign currency borrowings (OFCBs), and USD 3.89 billion through external commercial borrowings (ECBs).

The document also notes that India’s BoP was in deficit by USD 8.1 billion in Q1, versus a surplus of USD 4.5 billion in the same quarter a year earlier. Within that quarter, the capital account slipped to a USD 5.5 billion deficit, and foreign portfolio investors were net sellers with outflows of USD 9.6 billion. From a compliance or treasury perspective, the material takeaway is that the RBI-supported deposit and borrowing channels remain a significant source of inflows that can materially affect external-liquidity planning and foreign exchange funding assumptions, while capital-account weakness and FPI outflows remain a risk factor.

The first-of-its-kind, day-long interactions saw deputy governors and the executive directors of the Department of Supervision, Department of Regulation and Department of Enforcement take up issues relating to governance, ethics, the role of the boards and supervisory expectations. (The exercise was repeated in 2024.) Three years on, HDFC Bank is in the headlines — caught up in the swirl of the issues flagged back then. First, Atanu Chakraborty quit as the bank’s chairman. “Certain happenings and practices within the bank, that I have observed over the last two years, are not in congruence with my personal values and ethics,” he said in his resignation letter. On its part, Mint Road held that: Based on “our periodical assessment, there are no material concerns on record as regards its conduct or governance. The bank remains well-capitalised and the financial position of the bank remains satisfactory with sufficient liquidity.” Then, HDFC Bank’s board under a new chairman Rajiv Kumar, in July this year, slapped a fine of ₹1 lakh each on Sashidhar Jagdishan, the lender’s managing director (MD) and chief executive officer (CEO), and two of his senior colleagues: Srinivasan Vaidyanathan, chief financial officer, and Arvind Vohra, group head, retail assets. It was the first such action in India Inc. Even as it was clarified that based on the findings and recommendation of the Special Disciplinary Committee of Independent Directors, the board had concluded that “the conduct of the employees involved constituted business overreach rather than any mala fide action, personal enrichment, or improper motive.” Jagdishan did not resign and there was nothing to suggest (in the public domain) that he had not offered himself for a third term (his second is to conclude next month: on October 26). rows.summary:
The document is a news analysis, not a formal regulation, but it highlights governance and leadership-continuity expectations in India’s banking sector using HDFC Bank as the case study. It says the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had already pressed boards of both public and private banks in May 2023, and again in 2024, on governance, ethics, the role of boards, and supervisory expectations during day-long meetings led by the governor, deputy governors, and senior supervision/regulation/enforcement officials. Against that backdrop, HDFC Bank has become the focal point because chairman Atanu Chakraborty resigned, stating that certain happenings and practices he observed over the previous two years were “not in congruence” with his personal values and ethics; the RBI publicly said it had no material concerns on record regarding the bank’s conduct or governance and that the bank remained well-capitalized with satisfactory financial position and sufficient liquidity.

The article also reports a significant board-level disciplinary action taken in July under new chairman Rajiv Kumar: the board imposed a fine of ₹1 lakh each on managing director and CEO Sashidhar Jagdishan, chief financial officer Srinivasan Vaidyanathan, and group head, retail assets Arvind Vohra. The board said, based on the findings and recommendation of the Special Disciplinary Committee of Independent Directors, the conduct involved was “business overreach” rather than mala fide intent, personal enrichment, or improper motive. This appears to be the first such board action in India Inc. mentioned in the piece, and it underscores that even where conduct does not amount to fraud or self-dealing, boards may still impose monetary penalties for overstepping authority or process.

From a compliance perspective, the key operational concern is leadership continuity and orderly handover at the top tier. The article notes that Jagdishan did not resign after the penalty and that, as publicly reported, there was nothing to indicate he had not sought a third term; his current second term was set to end on October 26 (year implied by the article context). The piece does not announce any new legal filing requirement or industry-wide rule, but it strongly signals that banks should expect closer scrutiny of board governance, succession planning, executive conduct, and the handling of senior-management transitions, especially where board actions, disciplinary findings, or chairmanship changes could affect regulatory comfort with the institution’s governance framework.

The government has intervened in the onion market by selling about 4,000 tonnes of buffer stock across 17 cities during the first ten days of a subsidised retail sale program intended to bring down sharply rising prices. The intervention is being carried out by the Centre through its agencies NCCF and Nafed, which together are holding a buffer stock of 1.21 lakh tonnes of onions for 2026. These agencies are moving onions from producing states to consuming centres using either a dedicated rail rake called the “Kanda Express” or trucks, indicating an active logistics-backed price stabilization effort rather than a one-off release.

The onions are being sold at a subsidised retail price of Rs 35 per kg in selected price-sensitive cities. According to Consumer Affairs Secretary Nidhi Khare, the 4,000-tonne figure reflects sales completed so far, not the total planned release, so additional quantities may still be deployed depending on market conditions. Bulk consignments have already reached Delhi and Chennai via the Kanda Express, and a third rake is currently being loaded for dispatch to Guwahati in the coming days. For compliance purposes, the key point is that this is a government supply intervention affecting onion procurement, transport, and retail pricing in multiple cities, with the current operational benchmark being Rs 35/kg and a 1.21 lakh-tonne buffer inventory available for further market action.

rows.title: ARCIL seeing fastest growth in NBFC originated retail bad loans: CEO Phanindranath Kakarla
rows.desc: Articles 5 min read ARCIL seeing fastest growth in NBFC originated retail bad loans: CEO Phanindranath Kakarla Asset Reconstruction Company India Ltd (ARCIL) is seeing the fastest growth in retail assets originated by NBFCs, even as bank originated, corporate and other retail portfolios continue to grow, with CEO Phanindranath Kakarla and CFO Pramod Kumar Gupta saying retail and SME assets are likely to gain a larger share of the portfolio as they grow faster than corporate assets. The company, which is set to become the first standalone asset reconstruction company to list in India, is also open to acquisitions of smaller ARCs. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Published On Sep 6, 2026 at 11:03 PM IST var news_msid = 133846109; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook INTERVIEW | ARCIL CEO Phanindranath Kakarla & CFO Pramod Kumar Gupta* ARCIL expects retail and SME assets to gain share as they grow faster than corporate assets.* The fastest growth in ARCIL’s portfolio is currently coming from retail assets originated by NBFCs.* Retail and SME together accounted for a little over 31% of ARCIL’s portfolio in FY26, while corporate assets accounted for around 69%.* ARCIL’s retail and SME portfolio has grown at a CAGR of close to 56% over the last couple of years.* Currently handles around 32 lakh NPA accounts on the retail side and operates across around 24 states.* Resolves close to 25% of its opening AUM every year, supported by low leverage and cash flows generated through resolutions.* Around Rs 5.5 lakh crore of corporate assets written off by banks and NBFCs are returning to the resolution ecosystem.* Sees NARCL as both a competitor and a complement, with NARCL largely focused on very large-ticket stressed assets.* ARCIL is open to acquiring smaller ARCs where there is a willing seller, the right valuation and a strategic fit.Q. The overall credit base is now more than Rs 200 lakh crore, and even if around 2 per cent of that gets stressed in a year, that still creates a very large pool of assets.There is also incremental lending of around Rs 30 lakh crore every year. So, while the percentage of stressed assets may be lower, the absolute opportunity remains significant.We are seeing a shift in the composition of the assets available to us. Retail and SME are growing faster than corporate, and we expect their share of our portfolio to increase going forward. Advt Q. Within retail, where are you seeing the strongest growth?Phanindranath Kakarla: The fastest growth has come from retail assets originated by NBFCs. That does not mean that bank-originated assets are not growing. They are also growing, as are corporate assets and other retail portfolios.It is just that NBFC-originated retail assets are growing faster compared with the other asset classes.Q. How significant are retail and SME assets in ARCIL’s portfolio now?Phanindranath Kakarla: In FY26, corporate assets accounted for around 69 per cent of our portfolio, while SME was around 8 per cent and the balance was retail. So retail and SME together were a little over 31 per cent.Over the last couple of years, the retail and SME portfolio has grown at a CAGR of close to 56 per cent. Given the availability of assets and the growth opportunity, we expect retail and SME to continue gaining share.Q. Are you seeing greater opportunity in secured or unsecured retail bad loans?Phanindranath Kakarla: We are seeing opportunities in both secured and unsecured assets. We are not seeing a sharp divergence between the two at this point. What is changing is that smaller-ticket secured and unsecured assets are increasing as a share of the opportunity. That requires us to strengthen our systems, processes and operating capabilities because the volumes are much higher. Advt Q. Retail resolution is much more technology-led compared with corporate resolution, and we have invested significantly in building those capabilities.Q. Five years ago, we had fewer than one lakh retail borrowers or accounts; today, that number is around 32 lakh. Advt AI is already being used in our operations. It is not merely at the pilot stage. We will conti
rows.summary:
This is not a regulatory rulemaking or financial filing; it is an interview-style business article about ARCIL’s current portfolio mix, market outlook, and operating scale. The main substantive point is that ARCIL says the fastest growth in its stressed-asset pipeline is coming from **retail assets originated by NBFCs**, even though bank-originated retail assets, corporate assets, and other retail portfolios are also growing. Management expects **retail and SME assets to take a larger share of ARCIL’s portfolio** over time because they are growing faster than corporate assets, and says the overall stressed-asset opportunity remains large despite banking NPAs being at **decadal lows** because India’s credit base is now **more than Rs 200 lakh crore** and annual incremental lending is about **Rs 30 lakh crore**.

On the portfolio composition figures the company gave for **FY26**, **corporate assets were around 69%**, **SME around 8%**, and the balance was retail, meaning **retail plus SME together were a little over 31%** of the portfolio. ARCIL said its **retail and SME portfolio has grown at a CAGR of close to 56% over the last couple of years**, and it expects that segment to keep gaining share. Within retail, the company said the strongest growth is specifically in **NBFC-originated retail bad loans**, not because other asset types are declining, but because this category is expanding faster than bank-originated retail and other portfolios.

Operationally, ARCIL said it currently handles about **32 lakh NPA accounts** on the retail side and operates across around **24 states**. It described retail resolution as far more technology-led than corporate resolution and said it has invested significantly in systems and capabilities because smaller-ticket secured and unsecured assets are rising as a share of the opportunity, which increases transaction volume and operational complexity. The company also said it resolves about **25% of its opening AUM every year**, supported by relatively low leverage and cash flows from resolutions.

The article also notes a broader market development: around **Rs 5.5 lakh crore** of corporate assets written off by banks and NBFCs are reportedly returning to the resolution ecosystem. ARCIL said it views **NARCL** as both a competitor and a complement, with NARCL mainly focused on very large stressed assets. Finally, ARCIL said it is open to **acquiring smaller ARCs** if there is a willing seller, appropriate valuation, and strategic fit, and that **AI is already being used in operations** rather than remaining at the pilot stage.

rows.title: Credit cards set for wider UPI-led adoption, says report
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Credit cards set for wider UPI-led adoption, says report The integration of credit cards with UPI is expected to increase utilisation, particularly in ecommerce and higher-value spending, while UPI-powered digital wallets continue to be widely used for day-to-day transactions. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Sep 5, 2026 at 08:41 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133785799; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook India’s credit card usage is expected to grow as integration with the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) expands the use of cards, allowing consumers to make payments through widely accepted UPI QR codes and at merchants without traditional point-of-sale infrastructure, according to a GlobalData report.The integration of credit cards with UPI is expected to increase utilisation, particularly in ecommerce and higher-value spending, while UPI-powered digital wallets continue to be widely used for day-to-day transactions. Credit cards also offer consumers rewards, discounts and instalment payment options, supporting their adoption. Advt India had 122.9 million outstanding credit cards as of July, compared with 1.03 billion debit cards, according to the latest Reserve Bank of India data. Debit cards remain the most widely held card type, supported by financial inclusion initiatives and the expansion of formal banking access.Credit and charge card adoption remains comparatively low because of limited formal credit histories, particularly in rural areas, as well as concerns over interest costs and debt. However, rising incomes, greater awareness and promotional campaigns by banks are supporting increased adoption.The integration with UPI could widen the range of transactions where credit cards can be used by enabling payments through UPI QR codes, including at merchants that do not accept cards through traditional point-of-sale infrastructure. This could make cards more relevant in areas where conventional card acceptance remains limited.Riding on e-commerceEcommerce expansion is also supporting wider adoption of electronic payments and is expected to contribute to card usage. Credit cards are likely to remain relevant for higher-value spending, where consumers can use credit while accessing rewards, discounts and instalment options.The expansion of formal financial services is creating a broader base for electronic payment adoption. More than 590 million accounts and over 410 million RuPay cards had been issued under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana as of August, highlighting the role of bundled debit cards in bringing first-time users into the formal financial system. Advt The Financial Inclusion Index rose to 70 as of March-end from 67 a year earlier, reflecting continued progress in access to financial services, financial literacy and consumer protection.Going ahead, credit card utilisation is expected to benefit from wider UPI integration, particularly as UPI provides a broader acceptance network for card-linked payments. Continued ecommerce expansion, rising incomes and greater adoption of credit products could further support card usage, according to the GlobalData report. rows.summary:
The document is a market-report article, not a new rule or circular, and it does not announce a binding regulatory change. It says that India’s credit card usage is expected to rise as credit cards become integrated with the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), because this will let consumers pay through widely accepted UPI QR codes and at merchants that do not have traditional point-of-sale card infrastructure. The practical effect described is broader card acceptance and higher card utilization, especially for ecommerce and higher-value purchases, while UPI-based digital wallets are expected to remain the main tool for everyday transactions.  

For compliance teams at banks, card issuers, payment aggregators, merchants, and fintechs, the key point is that the article signals an expanding payment ecosystem rather than a new obligation: credit-linked UPI payments may need to be supported across QR-based acceptance points and non-POS merchants, and products may need to be positioned for rewards, discounts, and installment features that are driving adoption. The article notes that India had 122.9 million outstanding credit cards as of July, versus 1.03 billion debit cards, underscoring that credit card penetration is still relatively low. It also states that more than 590 million accounts and over 410 million RuPay cards had been issued under Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana as of August, and that the Financial Inclusion Index increased to 70 at March-end from 67 a year earlier.  

The reasons given for slower credit and charge card adoption are limited formal credit histories, especially in rural areas, plus consumer concerns about interest costs and debt; rising incomes, greater awareness, and bank promotional campaigns are cited as offsetting factors. No effective date, deadline, threshold for compliance action, or mandated procedure is provided. The main takeaway for compliance is to monitor product, merchant-acquisition, QR acceptance, and disclosure practices as UPI-linked credit card use expands, particularly in ecommerce and higher-value spending, but the article itself does not impose a new legal requirement.

rows.title: GDP growth debate: Is the deflator making India’s 7.8% growth look stronger?
rows.desc: Articles 7 min read GDP growth debate: Is the deflator making India’s 7.8% growth look stronger? Critics have questioned whether the combination of a new base year, changes in price measures and revisions to previous estimates has resulted in an unusually high real growth rate. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Sep 5, 2026 at 08:40 AM IST var news_msid = 133785757; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook India’s 7.8% real GDP growth in the April-June quarter has triggered a debate over the methodology behind the latest national accounts series, with questions focusing particularly on the GDP deflator and revisions to earlier estimates. The government has defended the numbers, saying the changes reflect the new 2022-23 base year, improved data sources and methodological changes rather than an attempt to inflate growth.Here is what the controversy is about and how the GDP deflator affects the growth calculation.What exactly is the controversy over the 7.8% GDP growth rate?India’s real GDP grew 7.8% year-on-year in Q1 FY27, compared with 6.9% a year earlier. Nominal GDP grew 10.3%, while real GVA grew 8.2%. The growth was stronger than the Reserve Bank of India’s earlier 7% forecast and market expectations of around 7.1%. Advt The controversy arose because the new GDP series has also significantly revised earlier data. Critics have questioned whether the combination of a new base year, changes in price measures and revisions to previous estimates has resulted in an unusually high real growth rate.The government has rejected that interpretation, saying the new series incorporates improved data sources and methodological changes in line with national accounting practices.What is the GDP deflator?The GDP deflator is the implicit price index obtained by comparing GDP at current prices with GDP at constant prices. It captures the price changes associated with the goods and services included in domestic output.In simple terms, it helps separate the change in the value of economic output into its price and volume components.For Q1 FY27, nominal GDP grew 10.3%, while real GDP grew 7.8%. The relationship between the two implies an increase of roughly 2.3% in the implicit GDP deflator.Why has the GDP deflator become central to the issue?Because the gap between nominal and real GDP growth is relatively small.A 10.3% increase in nominal GDP and 7.8% real growth implies an implicit GDP deflator increase of roughly 2.3%. Critics argue that if the relevant economy-wide price increase were higher, the resulting real GDP growth would be lower. Advt This is why the debate has focused on whether the price measures used in the new GDP series adequately capture price changes across the economy.However, it would be incorrect to conclude that a low GDP deflator automatically means real GDP growth is overstated. The deflator is derived from the prices and weights relevant to different components of national output. It is not simply another measure of CPI or WPI inflation.Why doesn’t the GDP deflator simply use CPI inflation?Because the GDP deflator and consumer price inflation measure different things.CPI measures changes in the prices of a basket of goods and services consumed by households. The GDP deflator captures price changes across the goods and services included in domestic output and also reflects changes in the composition of production. Advt WPI, meanwhile, measures wholesale prices of selected goods. Neither CPI nor WPI can therefore simply be substituted for the GDP deflator.The new national accounts series has introduced more granular price data and expanded the range of deflators used in the national accounts, including the use of producer price data in relevant areas.What has changed in the new GDP series?The latest national accounts series uses 2022-23 as the base year, replacing the earlier base year. MoSPI released the new series in February 2026.The latest estimates incorporate the new Output PPI, a revised Index of Industrial Production series with 2022-23 as its base and updated administrative data. MoSPI has also revised quarterly estimates from Q1 FY23 through Q4 FY26. Advt This means comparisons with older GDP estimates need to be made carefully because the underlying methodology and data sources have changed.What is “double deflation” and why is it being discussed?Double deflation is particularly important for manufacturing.Under the new methodology, MoSPI separately deflates output and intermediate consumption, rather than applying the same deflator to both. Real manufacturing GVA is then calculated as real output minus real intermediate consumption.The objective is to capture changes in both selling prices and input costs more accurately.For example, if manufacturers’ input costs rise faster than their output prices, their real value added can behave differently from their nominal valu
rows.summary:
This article is not a regulation or rule change, but a policy-methodology explanation about India’s national accounts that compliance teams in finance, economics, or public-policy functions may need to understand when interpreting reported macro data. The main issue is India’s reported **7.8% year-on-year real GDP growth for Q1 FY27 (April–June quarter)**, which came alongside **10.3% nominal GDP growth** and **8.2% real GVA growth**; critics argue the growth number may appear elevated because of the **new 2022-23 base year**, revised price measures, and revisions to prior estimates. The government’s position is that the higher growth rate reflects **improved data sources and methodological changes** under the updated national accounts series, not an attempt to overstate growth.

A central technical point is the **GDP deflator**, which is the implicit price index used to convert nominal GDP into real GDP. Because nominal GDP rose **10.3%** while real GDP rose **7.8%**, the implied GDP deflator increase is only about **2.3%**; that narrow gap is what has triggered scrutiny, since a higher economy-wide price increase would mechanically reduce the real growth rate. The article emphasizes that the GDP deflator is **not interchangeable with CPI or WPI**: CPI tracks household consumption prices, WPI tracks a selected basket of wholesale goods, while the GDP deflator reflects prices across domestic output and changes in the production mix.

The article identifies the concrete methodological changes in the new GDP series: **MoSPI released the revised series in February 2026**, using **2022-23 as the new base year**, and incorporated the **new Output PPI**, a **revised Index of Industrial Production series with 2022-23 as its base**, and **updated administrative data**. MoSPI has also **revised quarterly estimates from Q1 FY23 through Q4 FY26**, meaning historical comparisons to earlier GDP series are not directly comparable and must be treated cautiously for forecasting, disclosure, and commentary purposes.

Finally, the article explains a key methodological change in manufacturing: **“double deflation.”** Under the new approach, MoSPI separately deflates **output** and **intermediate consumption** rather than applying one deflator to both, and then calculates real manufacturing GVA as **real output minus real intermediate consumption**. The stated purpose is to better capture situations where input costs rise faster than output prices, so compliance or reporting teams relying on India macro data should avoid using old-series assumptions, should reference the revised base year and revised quarterly history, and should recognize that the new deflator methodology can materially affect apparent real-growth outcomes.

rows.title: AU SFB seen sustaining 20%+ credit growth as universal-bank transition advances
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read AU SFB seen sustaining 20%+ credit growth as universal-bank transition advances The bank's Rs 1.34 lakh crore loan book as of March 2026 would place it among the top-10 private sector banks following the transition, while its nearly 90% retail asset mix gives it a distinct positioning among large private lenders. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Sep 5, 2026 at 08:43 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133785840; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook AU Small Finance Bank is poised to sustain credit growth of more than 20% over FY26-FY28 as it transitions towards becoming a universal bank, potentially allowing it to continue gaining market share even as private sector lenders have lost momentum against public sector banks.The bank's Rs 1.34 lakh crore loan book as of March 2026 would place it among the top-10 private sector banks following the transition, while its nearly 90% retail asset mix gives it a distinct positioning among large private lenders. AU has also delivered more than 30% loan and profit CAGR over the past decade, with average credit costs of around 1% and RoE above 15%, according to a report by ICICI Securities. Advt The Reserve Bank of India had granted AU SFB in-principle approval to transition into a universal bank in August 2025. The move is expected to provide a platform for the lender to scale its franchise further as it seeks to gain both credit and deposit market share.AU's incremental credit market share stood at 1% in FY26, compared with 0.6% on a period-end basis, indicating that the lender has been growing faster than the system and gaining share from existing players. This comes at a time when private sector banks have seen their pace of market-share gains moderate, while public sector banks have captured a larger share of incremental credit.Selected private sector banks recorded average credit growth of about 14% between FY23 and FY26, compared with more than 20% during FY15-FY19. AU, in contrast, has maintained loan growth of more than 30% over the past decade, supported by its retail franchise, distribution network and underwriting capabilities in semi-urban and rural markets.Retail strengthRetail assets accounted for nearly 90% of AU's loan portfolio as of June 2026, one of the highest proportions among the top-10 private sector banks. Large private sector peers typically have retail asset shares of 50-75%, with unsecured loans accounting for around 10-20% of their portfolios. Advt AU has focused on expanding secured retail lending while keeping unsecured exposure below 15%. Despite its relatively lower unsecured loan share and higher cost of deposits, its net interest margin leads the pack among the top-10 private sector banks, the report said.The bank's growth has also been accompanied by contained credit costs. Its average credit cost over the past decade was around 1%, with a peak of 1.9% and a low of 0.3%. This has enabled AU to maintain a cross-cycle RoE of around 15% while delivering substantially higher loan growth than many private-sector peers.The lender is expected to benefit from further expansion of its retail distribution, including through Fincare touch points in south India. Growth could also be supported by a recovery in microfinance, credit cards and personal loans, along with stronger traction in gold loans from a relatively low base. Advt AU has simultaneously been strengthening its deposit franchise. Deposits grew 23% year-on-year in FY26, while CASA deposits increased 20%. Overall deposits expanded at a 34% CAGR between FY21 and FY26, helping reduce the premium AU pays over larger private sector banks for term deposits.AU's peak term-deposit rate premium over the top three private sector banks, which exceeded 100 basis points in FY23, had declined to 80 basis points by August 2026. Excluding the top three private banks, the premium had fallen to around 25 basis points, pointing to an improvement in its liability franchise.The share of CASA, retail term deposits and non-callable bulk term deposits increased to around 79% of deposits by June 2026 from about 65% in March 2024. More than 80% of AU's deposits are mobilised from urban markets, with Maharashtra accounting for 23%, Rajasthan 20% and Delhi 14% as of March 2026. Advt AU has more than 500 urban branches within its total network of 703 branches and plans to add 80-100 branches annually, with a focus on the top 20 cities that already account for around 57% of its deposits.The bank's deposit market share stood at 0.6% as of March 2026. While it has built a strong savings-account proposition through digital channels, developing a stronger current-account franchise remains a longer-term challenge as it seeks to deepen relationships with individual and retail customers. By ETBFSI Research , ETBFSI Published On Sep 5, 2026 at 08:43 AM IST Telegram
rows.summary:
The document is a market/industry article about AU Small Finance Bank’s expected growth trajectory and balance-sheet mix as it prepares to transition into a universal bank; it is not a new regulation or rule, but it does describe developments relevant to compliance and strategic planning. RBI granted AU SFB in-principle approval to convert into a universal bank in August 2025, and the article says this transition is expected to support continued scale-up in credit and deposits. ICICI Securities is cited as expecting AU to sustain credit growth of more than 20% across FY26–FY28, with the bank’s loan book projected at about Rs 1.34 lakh crore as of March 2026, which would put it among the top-10 private sector banks after conversion.

From a risk/profile standpoint, AU’s business remains highly retail-focused: retail assets were about 90% of the loan book as of June 2026, one of the highest retail concentrations among large private banks. The bank has deliberately kept unsecured lending below 15% of the portfolio, while expanding secured retail lending, and the article says this, together with relatively contained credit costs, has supported strong profitability and market-share gains. Over the past decade, AU reportedly delivered more than 30% CAGR in both loans and profit, with average credit costs around 1% (peaking at 1.9% and bottoming at 0.3%) and return on equity above 15%.

On the liability side, the article highlights that AU has been strengthening deposits and gradually reducing its funding-cost disadvantage versus larger private banks. Deposits grew 23% year-on-year in FY26, CASA deposits rose 20%, and total deposits grew at a 34% CAGR from FY21 to FY26. The premium AU pays on term deposits versus the top three private sector banks fell from more than 100 basis points in FY23 to 80 basis points by August 2026; versus all private banks other than the top three, the premium was down to about 25 basis points. The mix of CASA, retail term deposits, and non-callable bulk term deposits increased to about 79% of deposits by June 2026, up from roughly 65% in March 2024.

The article also notes geographic concentration and expansion plans that may matter for compliance monitoring and branch governance. More than 80% of deposits are mobilized from urban markets, with Maharashtra contributing 23%, Rajasthan 20%, and Delhi 14% as of March 2026. AU had more than 500 urban branches out of 703 total branches and plans to add 80–100 branches per year, focused on the top 20 cities, which already account for around 57% of deposits. Deposit market share was 0.6% as of March 2026, and the article says building a stronger current-account franchise remains a longer-term challenge even though the bank has developed a strong savings-account proposition through digital channels.

rows.title: FCNR inflows to dilute bank margins, but could add Rs 10,000 crore to bank earnings
rows.desc: Articles 4 min read FCNR inflows to dilute bank margins, but could add Rs 10,000 crore to bank earnings The record USD 127.2 billion FCNR-B mobilisation is set to reshape banks’ funding mix, with Jefferies expecting near term NIM compression but an annual Rs 10,000-11,000 crore addition to the banking sector’s profit pool. CareEdge, meanwhile, estimates core banking-system liquidity could swell to Rs 13-14 lakh crore by December, potentially accelerating the decline in wholesale funding costs. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Updated On Sep 4, 2026 at 06:19 PM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133763281; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The record mobilisation of FCNR(B) deposits is likely to create a near term squeeze on banks’ net interest margins (NIMs), the scale of inflows which happened to be four times of 2013, could ultimately add around Rs 10,000-11,000 crore annually to the banking sector’s earnings, according to Jefferies.The brokerage estimates that FCNR-B deposits could create an additional profit pool of Rs 100-110 billion a year, equivalent to around 2 per cent of the banking sector’s profit before tax. While the deposits are structurally a lower-NIM business and are likely to dilute both NIM and return on assets (ROA), they are expected to be accretive to net interest income (NII) and return on equity (ROE). Advt The concessional swap window for FCNR-B deposits closed on August 31, with FCNR-B inflows reaching USD 127.2 billion. The document reports that the RBI’s concessional swap window for FCNR-B deposits closed on **31 August**, after driving **record FCNR-B inflows of USD 127.2 billion**. When combined with **USD 5.3 billion** of overseas foreign currency borrowings and **USD 3.9 billion** of ECBs, total inflows under the broader RBI scheme reached **USD 136.4 billion** by the same date. For compliance and treasury teams, the practical implication is that banks have already locked in this foreign-currency funding and now need to manage the downstream impact on balance-sheet mix, funding costs, and margin reporting rather than any further inflow processing under the closed concessional window.

Jefferies expects these inflows to **compress net interest margins (NIMs) in the near term**, with the first visible impact likely in **Q2**, because many banks raised bonds and loans in advance of actually receiving and deploying the FCNR-B funds, creating a timing mismatch between funding cost and asset deployment. The brokerage says the effect may be treated as **non-recurring** in short-term earnings analysis, but structurally the product is lower-margin: it describes FCNR-B deposits as involving a “double-counting” of deposits and assets, with the first leg generating only a **10–15 basis point spread**, which mechanically dilutes average margins even though absolute interest income rises. Jefferies nevertheless expects FCNR-B deposits to be **accretive to net interest income (NII) and return on equity (ROE)** and estimates they could add **Rs 100–110 billion** annually to the sector’s earnings, or about **Rs 10,000–11,000 crore**, equal to roughly **2% of banking-sector profit before tax**.

Over the **next two to four quarters**, Jefferies expects margins to normalize as banks use the foreign-currency funding to reduce reliance on **high-cost wholesale deposits**, trim the amount of **government securities held for liquidity coverage requirements**, and cut exposure to **low-margin overseas trade financing**. It also notes that wholesale funding rates are already easing: **3-month certificate of deposit rates fell 90 bps to 5.9%**, and **6-month CD rates fell 50 bps to 6.46%** in the last month. From a compliance and liquidity-risk perspective, this means banks may see a rapid change in funding mix and pricing, and should ensure internal transfer pricing, ALM, and margin attribution models reflect the shift in liability costs and the temporary versus structural impact of the inflows.

CareEdge separately warns that the liquidity effect could be very large: core banking-system liquidity, which was **Rs 8.1 lakh crore in mid-August**, could rise to **Rs 13–14 lakh crore by end-December** if the RBI does not intervene with liquidity-management operations, equivalent to about **4.5–5% of net demand and time liabilities**. Its estimate already subtracts expected offsets, including about **Rs 1.1 lakh crore** of currency-in-circulation growth during the festive season, around **Rs 3 lakh crore** from maturity of the RBI’s short dollar-forward position, and about **Rs 70,000 crore** of CRR accretion from deposit growth. The compliance takeaway is that banks should be prepared for a broader system-wide decline in wholesale funding costs and should monitor RBI liquidity operations, CRR effects, and internal funding migrations closely, as the article suggests the system surplus could still rise sharply even after these offsets.

rows.desc: Articles 7 min read Niva Bupa hikes premiums 8-9% annually to keep pace with medical inflation: CFO Vishwanath Mahendra Niva Bupa Health Insurance is prioritising profitable growth even as medical inflation continues to push up the cost of health cover, with the insurer raising premiums by around 8-9% annually and expecting this trend to continue. CFO Vishwanath Mahendra said smaller annual increases are preferable to sharp hikes every few years, while the insurer targets a 98-99% combined insurance service ratio by FY29 and mid-to-high teens ROE. Overall premium grew 32%, while profit after tax nearly doubled 93% to Rs 138 crore, even as the insurer remained selective in group health amid an unfavourable pricing environment.But the growth is coming against a persistent challenge for the health insurance industry: rising medical inflation and the resulting pressure on premiums. Niva Bupa CFO Vishwanath Mahendra said the insurer has already raised premiums by 8-9% annually, and expects this to continue as medical costs rise, arguing that smaller, regular hikes are preferable to a sharp increase every few years. Advt Mahendra also said Niva Bupa is targeting profitable growth, with a medium-term goal of a 98-99% combined insurance service ratio by FY29 and mid-to-high teens ROE, while its retail market share has crossed 11%.Here are the edited excerpts from the interview:Q. By how much has Niva Bupa raised its premiums this year to tackle rising medical inflation. Rather than increasing premiums once in three years by a big number, our preference is to increase them by only single digits every year, so that it is not as much of a pinch for policyholders.So, when I say 8-9%, I mean 8-9% per annum, which will be experienced by policyholders. And yes, this is something we expect to continue next year as well.Of course, we are also doing many other things, discussions with hospitals on treatment protocols, industry initiatives and care pathways, to ensure there are no unnecessary admissions, abuse or wastage. Is that growth coming at healthy economics or are you sacrificing margins to gain market share?Vishwanath: It is coming from healthy economics. Our newly launched product, ReAssure 3.0, has also been received very well by distributors and customers.Our claim settlement ratio is close to 96%, and we are not compromising on underwriting or profitability to drive growth. Advt Q. You have also kept group health growth largely flat. Was that a conscious decision because pricing was not attractive?Vishwanath: Yes. We generally write business only if it is value-accretive. The pricing environment in group health was not very supportive, so we decided to stay away from business that was not economically attractive.We continue to focus on segments within group health which are good businesses from a profitability perspective. The approach is very clear, we want profitable growth, not growth at any cost.Q. With 32% overall growth and 93% growth in profit after tax, how close are you to consistently generating underwriting profits? Advt Vishwanath: We are very much there. We are very much on that trajectory.Our post-tax ROE was 11.8% for the last four rolling quarters, so the trajectory is very much there.Q. Retail market share has crossed 11%. How much further do you want to take it?Vishwanath: Our target is to keep growing retail health at least 8-10% higher than the industry and keep gaining market share ever

The document is an interview-style business article about Niva Bupa Health Insurance’s pricing and growth strategy, and it contains no formal regulation or legal filing, but it does disclose material operating and compliance-relevant practices. The key change/continuing practice is that Niva Bupa is raising health insurance premiums by about 8–9% per year, and the CFO says this is expected to continue next year as well, because the company views annual single-digit increases as preferable to infrequent sharp hikes and believes medical inflation must ultimately be passed through to policyholders to keep products sustainable. This is relevant to any policyholder communication, product governance, and pricing oversight functions because the insurer is explicitly linking premium increases to medical-cost inflation, while also saying it is working with hospitals on treatment protocols, industry initiatives, and care pathways to reduce unnecessary admissions, abuse, and wastage.

Operationally, the company says its retail health business grew 47% year-on-year in Q1 versus 32% industry growth, while overall premium grew 32% and profit after tax rose 93% to Rs 138 crore. It says this growth is being pursued without sacrificing underwriting discipline: claim settlement ratio is around 96%, the company says it is not compromising on underwriting or profitability, and it is deliberately avoiding or limiting group health business where pricing is unattractive. The CFO said the firm writes group business only if it is “value-accretive,” because the group health pricing environment has been weak, so the company is choosing profitable growth rather than growth at any cost.

From a financial target standpoint, Niva Bupa says its combined insurance service ratio improved by 300 basis points from 103.2% to 100.2%, and management says it is “very much” close to underwriting profitability, saying only about 20 basis points remain to reach that point. Its medium-term guidance remains a 98–99% combined insurance service ratio by FY29 and mid-to-high-teens return on equity; the most recent post-tax ROE cited is 11.8% for the last four rolling quarters. The company also said its retail market share has crossed 11% and that it aims to keep retail health growth at least 8–10% above industry growth going forward.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has proposed draft restrictions that would ban or sharply limit revolving credit facilities offered by non-bank lenders (NBFCs), but the latest industry consultation suggests the final rule may be narrower than the original draft. RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu has already met with NBFCs and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) to hear concerns, and the RBI has reportedly received about 350 responses directly, while around 30–40 lenders have submitted feedback through FIDC; the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) is expected to forward the suggestions discussed to the RBI as well.  

The key compliance issue is that the RBI originally appeared to believe the impact would be limited to only three or four NBFCs, but industry feedback indicates the definition could affect a much broader segment of the NBFC sector, including products and lending structures that are not intended to function as perpetual rollovers. Because of that, the RBI is now considering a partial restriction rather than an outright blanket ban, and the final contours have not yet been finalized. Industry participants said the draft is particularly concerning because some products involve limited redraw or replenishment within an existing sanctioned facility, which NBFCs argue should not automatically be treated as prohibited revolving credit.  

The RBI’s policy objective, as described in the article, is to curb evergreening and strengthen borrower credibility and repayment discipline by preventing credit lines from remaining continuously available on a revolving basis. NBFCs are warning that if the definition is written too broadly, it could sweep in working-capital products and other lending structures that are operationally similar to revolving credit but are not intended to be captured by the regulation. The article also notes that the issue has been discussed with RBI in the past, but putting the proposal into writing has made the grey areas more significant from a compliance standpoint because firms would need to follow the precise regulatory wording.  

No final exemption list or revised threshold has been published yet, but supply chain financing has been repeatedly raised during the discussions as a possible area for exemption, suggesting some carve-out may be considered. Sources quoted in the article said the final guidelines may take another two months to be issued, so affected NBFCs should expect the current draft to remain in flux until then and should monitor whether the RBI adopts a blanket prohibition, a partial restriction, or specified exemptions.

rows.summary:
Ujjivan Small Finance Bank’s key leadership change is the early retirement of Managing Director and CEO Sanjeev Nautiyal on health grounds, effective September 1, 2026, after which he ceased to serve as MD & CEO and as a key managerial personnel; he will remain on leave during his three-month notice period ending November 30, 2026. The Reserve Bank of India has approved the appointment of Executive Director Carol Furtado as interim MD & CEO for three months, and the bank is expected to accelerate its succession process and submit shortlisted permanent candidates to the RBI within the next three to four months, with both internal and external candidates under consideration.

From a compliance and governance perspective, the bank states that Nautiyal’s departure is unrelated to strategy, governance, or operations, and that its near-term FY27 guidance and strategic priorities remain unchanged. Management says MSME growth remains in line with guidance and asset quality is broadly in line with Q1 performance, with no material deviations currently visible, so there is no indicated need for a near-term reset of disclosed operating targets.

The longer-term roadmap still being executed is substantial and remains the key continuity issue for oversight: Ujjivan is targeting a gross loan book of Rs 1 lakh crore by FY30, along with a secured-loan mix of 65–70% by FY30, up from about 50% in June 2026 and about 31% in June 2024. The bank’s FY30 plan also includes CASA of 35%, deposits at three times the Q1FY26 level, a branch network of 1,150 branches, a cost-to-income ratio of 55%, and a credit-to-assets ratio below 5%; the strategy centers on strengthening the liability franchise, expanding digital and physical distribution, and continuing the shift toward secured lending.

The article also notes an additional management change: Vikas Agarwal has been appointed head of the MSME business to strengthen leadership bandwidth, and he brings more than 25 years of experience across MSME, business banking, retail banking, credit, product, and distribution. Ujjivan remains non-committal on when it will reapply for a universal banking licence, so compliance and governance focus should remain on execution of the current business plan, succession continuity, deposit-franchise strengthening, and MSME expansion under the interim leadership until the RBI-cleared permanent CEO is chosen.

rows.title: September set for IPO boom as Jio, NSE could drive record fundraising
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read September set for IPO boom as Jio, NSE could drive record fundraising Jio's proposed Rs 37,700-crore issue has already received Sebi approval, while NSE's proposed Rs 30,000-crore issue could significantly add to September's fundraising if launched. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Sep 1, 2026 at 01:02 PM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133672651; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook JIO, NSE ఐపీఓలు.. ఇండియా స్టాక్ మార్కెట్ చరిత్ర తిరగరాయడం ఖాయమా?September’s IPO calendar has opened with mainboard issues from Purple Style Labs, Deepa Jewellers and Rays of Belief, alongside SME offerings.More than 25 companies are expected to tap the IPO market, with Zepto, PhonePe and Manipal Health among the larger names in the broader pipeline.Improved market sentiment and stronger listing gains have revived IPO activity after a subdued first half of CY26.Despite strong average IPO returns, wide variations in post-listing performance underline the need for selective stock picking.September could emerge as one of the biggest months for India’s primary market, with more than 25 companies expected to tap the IPO market and potential mega issues from Jio Platforms and the National Stock Exchange (NSE) capable of pushing monthly fundraising towards Rs 70,000 crore.The month has opened with a busy primary-market calendar. Purple Style Labs, Deepa Jewellers and Rays of Belief are among the mainboard offerings around the start of September, while Farm Peace, Phychem Technologies, Shanti Inorganics and Ashutosh Fibre are among the SME issues. The seven issues identified in the opening-week calendar together are looking to raise more than Rs 1,400 crore. Advt The biggest potential trigger, however, is Jio Platforms. The company has received Sebi approval for a proposed IPO of around Rs 37,700 crore, which would make it India's largest IPO if launched at that size. NSE is also considering a public issue of around Rs 30,000 crore, although its launch timing has not been confirmed.If either of the two mega issues comes to market in September, fundraising could rise sharply, with the month's total potentially approaching Rs 70,000 crore depending on the issue launched, its final size and the broader IPO pipeline.The possibility of a record September comes after a sharp revival in primary-market activity in July and August. Companies raised more than Rs 28,000 crore through IPOs in July, while 22 companies raised over Rs 23,000 crore in August. The August fundraising was the highest in a year in terms of the number of companies accessing the market.The revival follows a subdued first half of CY26, when market volatility, valuation concerns, foreign investor outflows and geopolitical tensions weighed on IPO activity. The Nifty 50 fell around 9% during H1 CY26, prompting several companies to defer their fundraising plans.Primary market boomMarket conditions improved in July and August, helping restore investor appetite. The Nifty 50 gained around 1.8% from the end of June through the first two months of the second half, while IPO listing performance improved substantially.The average listing-day gain of 25 IPOs that debuted between July 1 and August 19 stood at 20.9%, compared with 1.72% in H1 CY26. Across 47 mainboard IPOs during the year, the average listing gain was 11.9%. Advt The stronger listing performance has provided a more favourable backdrop for September's IPO pipeline. Companies that had held back their plans amid weaker market conditions now have greater incentive to proceed, while merchant bankers have a sizeable pool of approved and filed offerings to bring to market.The broader pipeline includes large companies such as Zepto, PhonePe and Manipal Health, among others. However, these companies should not be treated as confirmed September IPOs, as their launch dates have not been announced.The pipeline remains sizeable. Since March 2025, 146 companies have received Sebi approval, while 67 are awaiting regulatory approval, 65 have filed DRHPs and another 33 have filed confidential DRHPs. This gives the primary market a substantial pool of potential issuers beyond the current September calendar. Advt The surge in IPO activity will nevertheless test the market's ability to absorb a large supply of new equity. Large offerings from Jio Platforms and potentially NSE could compete for institutional and retail liquidity with smaller mainboard and SME issues coming to market at the same time.Investor returns also remain uneven despite the improvement in sentiment. The average gain from issue price across 407 IPOs stood at 66% as of July 31, but 17% of companies were trading 25-50% below their issue price and another 9% were more than 50% below the issue price. By ETBFSI Research , ETBFSI Published On Sep 1, 2026 at 01:02 PM IST Telegram Facebook Copy Link Comments What are you
rows.summary:
The document is a market commentary, not a rulemaking notice, and it does not impose new legal or compliance obligations. Its main point is that September 2026 is expected to be a very heavy month for Indian IPO activity, potentially becoming one of the biggest months ever for the primary market, with more than 25 companies expected to access the IPO market. The month has already begun with mainboard IPOs from Purple Style Labs, Deepa Jewellers, and Rays of Belief, plus SME issues including Farm Peace, Phychem Technologies, Shanti Inorganics, and Ashutosh Fibre; the seven issues in the opening-week calendar are together targeting more than Rs 1,400 crore.

The biggest anticipated drivers are Jio Platforms and the National Stock Exchange (NSE). Jio has already received SEBI approval for a proposed IPO of about Rs 37,700 crore, which would be India’s largest IPO if launched at that size, while NSE is considering a public issue of about Rs 30,000 crore, though its launch timing has not yet been confirmed. If either mega issue launches in September, total monthly fundraising could approach Rs 70,000 crore, depending on which issue comes, its final size, and the rest of the pipeline.

The article explains that IPO activity rebounded strongly in July and August after a weak first half of calendar year 2026. Companies raised more than Rs 28,000 crore in July and over Rs 23,000 crore in August, with August notable for the highest number of companies accessing the market in a year. The earlier slowdown was attributed to market volatility, valuation concerns, foreign investor outflows, geopolitical tensions, and a roughly 9% decline in the Nifty 50 during H1 CY26, which caused several issuers to delay fundraising plans.

Market conditions improved in the second half of the year, supporting a stronger IPO environment. The Nifty 50 rose about 1.8% from the end of June through the first two months of H2 CY26, and average listing-day performance improved materially: the 25 IPOs that debuted between July 1 and August 19 delivered an average first-day gain of 20.9%, versus 1.72% in H1 CY26. Across 47 mainboard IPOs in the year so far, the average listing gain was 11.9%, but post-listing performance remains uneven, with 17% of companies trading 25% to 50% below issue price and another 9% trading more than 50% below issue price even though the average gain across 407 IPOs was 66% as of July 31.

From a compliance-monitoring perspective, the broader pipeline remains large: since March 2025, 146 companies have received SEBI approval, 67 are awaiting regulatory approval, 65 have filed DRHPs, and 33 have filed confidential DRHPs. The article names larger pipeline candidates such as Zepto, PhonePe, and Manipal Health, but explicitly says they are not confirmed September IPOs because launch dates have not been announced. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is to watch for potential concentration and liquidity pressure in September as a large wave of mainboard and SME offerings competes for investor attention, especially if Jio and/or NSE come to market.

rows.title: Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules Non-banking finance companies have sought clarity from the Reserve Bank of India on whether recovery calls fall under the service-call category permitted through the 1600 numbering series, amid concerns that customers increasingly block calls originating from the series, sources part of the discussion told ETBFSI. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Updated On Sep 4, 2026 at 11:31 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133737944; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The issue was raised by NBFC CEOs and industry representatives during a meeting with RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu on Thursday, where the industry flagged concerns around the implementation of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India’s (TRAI) mandatory 1600-series framework for regulated financial entities.“Sales calls should be outside the 1600 series. We fully agree with that. But whether recovery calls fall under service calls is still a question. That needs to be clarified,” a source told ETBFSI.The 1600 series was allocated by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) for service and transactional voice calls by Government and BFSI entities. TRAI, in November 2025, subsequently mandated a phase-wise migration of RBI-, SEBI- and PFRDA-regulated entities to the series, with the objective of allowing consumers to distinguish legitimate calls from regulated financial institutions from spam, promotional and potentially fraudulent calls. Advt For RBI-regulated entities, commercial banks were required to adopt the 1600 series by January 1, 2026, while large NBFCs with asset size above Rs 5,000 crore, payments banks and small finance banks were given a February 1, 2026 deadline. Remaining NBFCs, co-operative banks, regional rural banks and other entities were required to migrate by March 1, 2026.RBI regulated entities covered by the mandate are not permitted to initiate service or transactional voice calls from numbers other than those allocated under the 1600 series, even where they have explicit or inferred customer consent.TRAI's stated objective is to prevent promotional calls from being made under the guise of service or transactional calls and to give BFSI entities a distinct identity that allows consumers to make informed decisions about whether to answer a call.However, NBFCs said the framework does not clearly address recovery communications. Lenders typically make large volumes of calls to borrowers regarding overdue payments, repayment schedules and other recovery-related matters, and the industry wants to know whether such calls qualify as service calls under the 1600 framework.“The distinction between a sales call, a service call and a recovery call is important. I agree that a sales call should not be made through 1600. But whether a recovery call is considered a service call is not clear,” the NBFC CEO said.The concern is compounded by the possibility of customers blocking calls originating from the 1600 series. Industry participants said that while the dedicated series is intended to help consumers identify genuine financial-sector calls, borrowers may still block such numbers as unwanted or spam, particularly when they receive repeated recovery calls. Advt “If you are doing mass recovery calls and people are blocking those numbers, the whole purpose is lost,” the source said.According to the industry, the problem becomes particularly acute when a borrower does not respond to repeated calls from a lender’s 1600 number.“Imagine a 1600 call. If the customer does not pick up, how will a banker communicate? If we try once or twice and the number is blocked, can we then call from our normal number? That is the question,” the CEO said. rows.summary:
This article reports that NBFCs and other industry participants have asked the Reserve Bank of India for clarification on whether loan recovery and collections calls can be treated as “service calls” under TRAI’s mandatory 1600-series calling framework. The immediate compliance issue is that, while the industry agrees sales/promotional calls should not use the 1600 series, it says the rules do not clearly state whether calls made to remind borrowers about overdue payments, repayment schedules, and other recovery matters must also be routed through 1600 numbers.

TRAI had previously allocated the 1600 series by the Department of Telecommunications for service and transactional voice calls by government and BFSI entities, and in November 2025 it made migration mandatory in phases for RBI-, SEBI- and PFRDA-regulated entities to help consumers distinguish legitimate financial-sector calls from spam, promotional, and fraudulent calls. For RBI-regulated entities, commercial banks had to migrate by January 1, 2026; large NBFCs with asset size above Rs 5,000 crore, payments banks, and small finance banks by February 1, 2026; and remaining NBFCs, co-operative banks, regional rural banks, and other covered entities by March 1, 2026. The rule also says regulated entities covered by the mandate may not initiate service or transactional voice calls from numbers outside the 1600 series, even if the customer has expressly or impliedly consented.

The main operational concern raised by NBFCs is that borrowers may block calls from 1600 numbers because repeated recovery calls can be perceived as spam, which could undermine the whole purpose of the dedicated series. Industry participants are worried that if a customer does not answer, or blocks the 1600 number after one or two attempts, lenders will not know whether they are allowed to switch back to ordinary numbers for further contact. The article does not report any change to the rules themselves, only that RBI is being asked to clarify the treatment of recovery calls and the permitted fallback procedures.

LIC Housing Finance said it would file an appeal along with other public financial institutions. HDFC Bank, which had a 3.17 per cent voting share, said it had opposed and voted against the resolution and was exploring an appeal. Advt The repayment plan, submitted by Chandra on October 16, 2024, was approved with 80.814 per cent of the voting share. The largest votes in favour came from World Crest Advisors (28.49 per cent), Lemonade Capital Advisors (16.85 per cent), Catalyst Trusteeship (11.85 per cent), Corpcall Capital Advisors (10.30 per cent) and Veena Investments (4.99 per cent).Among those voting against were LIC Housing Finance (6.09 per cent), IDBI Trusteeship representing Franklin Templeton (3.36 per cent), HDFC Bank (3.17 per cent), Axis Bank (2.86 per cent), Canara Bank (1.60 per cent), Union Bank of India (UK) (0.76 per cent) and RBL Bank (0.55 per cent). Creditors representing another 4.10 per cent did not vote.The dissenting lenders had argued that five entities - Veena Investments, Direct Media Distribution Ventures, World Crest Advisors, Lemonade Capital Advisors and Corpcall Capital Advisors, were associates of Chandra and should therefore not have been allowed to vote. Together, the five represented about 61.78 per cent of the voting share.They also raised concerns over the speed of the process. Chandra submitted the plan on October 16, the Resolution Professional filed his report on October 17, and the creditors’ meeting was held on October 24. Creditors were asked to evaluate claims of around Rs 21,697 crore, with the voting period later extended to October 31. Advt The lenders had also questioned the adequacy of Chandra’s asset disclosures and sought an independent forensic audit and asset-tracing exercise. They pointed to earlier net-worth certificates showing his wealth at Rs 45,888 crore in 2017 and Rs 40,562 crore in 2018, compared with a current net worth of around Rs 31.79 crore cited in the proceedings.The NCLT itself saw a split in the matter. The Technical Member had found procedural violations, including the shortened timeline for the creditors’ meeting, and questioned the participation of alleged associates in the voting process.The Judicial Member, however, held that the creditors had sufficient practical opportunity to examine the plan, noting that the voting period had been extended and that the creditors ultimately approved the plan by the requisite majority. Advt The matter was subsequently referred to a Third Member because of the difference between the two members. The Third Member backed approval of the repayment plan, subject to certain directions including exclusion of specified claims from the final creditor list.
