rows.summary:
The document reports that several lenders are preparing to challenge the National Company Law Tribunal’s approval of Zee founder Subhash Chandra’s repayment plan before the NCLAT. The plan, submitted on October 16, 2024, was approved by creditors with 80.814% of the voting share, but HDFC Bank, LIC Housing Finance, and Union Bank of India (UK) say they opposed the plan and object to both the voting process and the inclusion of certain creditors they believe were not eligible to vote.

The principal compliance issue raised by the dissenting lenders is that five entities — Veena Investments, Direct Media Distribution Ventures, World Crest Advisors, Lemonade Capital Advisors, and Corpcall Capital Advisors — were alleged to be associates of Chandra and therefore should not have been permitted to vote; together, those entities accounted for about 61.78% of the voting share. The creditors were asked to evaluate claims totaling around Rs 21,697 crore, and the voting window was later extended to October 31. The lenders also challenged the pace of the process, noting that Chandra’s plan was filed on October 16, the resolution professional’s report was filed on October 17, and the creditors’ meeting was held on October 24, which they say did not give adequate time for review.

The article also says lenders sought a forensic audit and asset-tracing exercise because they believe Chandra’s asset disclosures may be incomplete or inconsistent. They pointed to earlier net-worth certificates showing assets of Rs 45,888 crore in 2017 and Rs 40,562 crore in 2018, while the proceedings reportedly relied on a current net worth of about Rs 31.79 crore. Within the NCLT, the Technical Member found procedural violations, including the shortened timeline and the participation of alleged associates, while the Judicial Member held that creditors had enough practical opportunity to assess the plan and that the required majority had approved it after the voting period was extended.

Because the two NCLT members disagreed, the matter was referred to a Third Member, who ultimately supported approval of the repayment plan, but with directions to exclude specified claims from the final creditor list. The lenders now intend to move promptly against that approval before the NCLAT, with Union Bank of India (UK) saying it would challenge the decision “immediately” and LIC Housing Finance saying it would appeal together with other public financial institutions. HDFC Bank, which held a 3.17% voting share, said it voted against the plan and was exploring an appeal.

rows.title: Master Circular for Stock Exchange - Cash Market
rows.summary:
This document is SEBI’s **Master Circular for Stock Exchanges on the Trading Part (Part I)**, which is a compilation of all then-applicable circulars issued by SEBI’s Market Regulation Department **up to March 31, 2010**. It applies to **stock exchanges** and came into force **from the date of its issue**; for a compliance team, the key point is that it consolidates prior operative requirements rather than creating a single new standalone rule, so exchanges and connected market participants must treat the circular as the current reference point for the covered topics.

Substantively, the circular organizes the cash-market trading framework into several compliance areas that exchanges must implement and supervise: **bulk deals and block deals**, **index-based market-wide circuit filters and scrip-wise price bands**, and **uniform security-specific action across stock exchanges**. It also contains detailed requirements for **margin trading**, including which securities are eligible, the conditions brokers must satisfy to offer the facility, the need for **no-objection certificates**, required client agreements, funding sources and **maximum borrowing limits for brokers**, prescribed **margin requirements**, and the process for **liquidating securities if a client defaults**. The circular further requires brokers to maintain records, disclose exposure to margin trading, provide for arbitration, and handle the use of the **Investor Protection Fund** and **Trade/Settlement Guarantee Fund** in the manner specified.

The document also sets out a separate framework for **market makers**, including the criteria for selecting scrips for market making, whether market makers have exclusivity, how many market makers may be appointed per share, the qualifications for registration, and the specific obligations and rights of a market maker. It addresses **voluntary and compulsory de-registration**, information dissemination requirements, the number of shares each market maker must support, and risk-containment/monitoring measures. In addition, it includes provisions for **negotiated deals** and **odd-lot trading and settlement** in dematerialised securities, indicating that exchanges must ensure these transaction types are handled under the prescribed special procedures rather than under ordinary continuous trading rules.

For compliance purposes, the document should be read as an exchange-level operating manual covering the cash market trading infrastructure: exchanges must ensure their rules, surveillance, settlement processes, broker onboarding, disclosure controls, and risk-management arrangements align with the circular’s requirements, and because it is a master circular, it is intended to capture and supersede the scattered prior circulars on these topics as of its cutoff date.

rows.title: Master Circular on Anti Money Laundering and Combating Financing of Terrorism (AML and CFT) Standards-PDF
rows.summary:
This SEBI master circular, issued on 19 December 2008, consolidates all anti-money laundering and countering financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) requirements applicable to SEBI-registered intermediaries up to 15 December 2008. It applies to all intermediaries registered under section 12 of the SEBI Act, 1992—specifically including stock brokers, sub-brokers, share transfer agents, bankers to an issue, trustees to a trust deed, registrars to an issue, merchant bankers, underwriters, portfolio managers, investment advisers, depository participants, and other securities-market intermediaries—and, to the extent local law permits, to their foreign branches and subsidiaries, especially those in jurisdictions that do not or insufficiently apply FATF recommendations. Where host-country law conflicts with SEBI’s standards, the foreign branch/subsidiary must apply the stricter of the two regimes; if local law prevents implementation, that fact must be reported to SEBI.

The circular restates the core transaction-reporting obligations under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), which came into force on 1 July 2005. Intermediaries must maintain records of: all cash transactions above Rs. 10 lakhs (or equivalent in foreign currency); all series of cash transactions that are individually below Rs. 10 lakhs but are integrally connected and occur within one calendar month; and all suspicious transactions, whether or not they involve cash. The document also confirms that the earlier SEBI AML guidelines from 18 January 2006 and the detailed procedure/reporting circular from 20 March 2006 remain the framework being consolidated here.

The circular requires intermediaries to maintain a proper AML policy framework tailored to their business and to put in place client disclosures beyond the minimum where needed to address money laundering and suspicious-transaction risks. Each intermediary must designate a “Principal Officer” responsible for ensuring compliance with PMLA obligations, and the name, designation, and full address including email address of that officer must be communicated immediately to the Director, FIU, at the specified New Delhi address. The circular is issued under SEBI’s powers under section 11(1) of the SEBI Act and Rule 7 of the PMLA record-keeping rules, so it is not merely advisory: it is intended to impose enforceable compliance obligations on securities-market intermediaries.

rows.summary:
SEBI’s Nodal Co-ordination Cell issued an informal guidance letter dated March 2, 2026 in response to Maithan Alloys Limited’s December 26, 2025 request for an interpretive letter under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2025. The request asked SEBI to interpret the phrase “related to promoters or directors” in Regulation 16(1)(b)(iii) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, in the context of whether a proposed Independent Director candidate could be considered eligible.

The company stated that it is a listed issuer incorporated on September 19, 1985, with shares listed on the Calcutta Stock Exchange Limited and the National Stock Exchange of India Limited, and traded on BSE Limited in the permitted category. It described its business as ferro alloys manufacturing for the iron and steel sector and real estate activities. The promoter is Mr. Subhas Chandra Agarwalla, who is also the Chairman and Managing Director, and the company listed several members of the promoter group who are employees receiving remuneration: Mr. Subhas Chandra Agarwalla (Chairman and Managing Director), Mr. Subodh Agarwalla (Whole-time Director and CEO), Mr. Sudhanshu Agarwalla (President and CFO), and Mr. Siddhartha Shankar Agarwalla (Vice President).

The key proposed appointment was Mr. Siddhartha Shankar Agarwalla’s cousin as an Independent Director. SEBI recorded that Mr. Siddhartha Shankar Agarwalla is the son of the promoter’s cousin, is included in the promoter group under the ICDR Regulations, is a person acting in concert with the promoter, and serves as a director in two subsidiaries of the company. SEBI also noted that the proposed Independent Director candidate is the daughter of Mr. Siddhartha Shankar Agarwalla’s father’s sister, has advanced academic qualifications, and has worked as an Assistant Professor at Praxis Business School and Head of the Corporate Branding Team, with publications on consumer behavior and branding topics. The company’s stated rationale was that the word “related” in Regulation 16(1)(b)(iii) should be read narrowly to cover only relatives (as defined in Regulation 2(1)(zd)) of promoters or directors of the listed entity and its holding, subsidiary, and associate companies, and that the explanation in Regulation 17(1)(b) about being “related to any promoter” applies only to that regulation and not to Regulation 16(1)(b)(iii).

The excerpt provided stops at the beginning of paragraph 3, so the actual SEBI conclusion or any formal interpretive answer is not visible in the supplied text. Based on the material shown, the compliance issue is whether the proposed cousin relationship disqualifies the nominee from being treated as “not related to promoters or directors” for purposes of Independent Director eligibility under Regulation 16(1)(b)(iii), but the final SEBI determination is not included in the excerpt.

rows.summary:
SEBI’s informal guidance says that securities purchased under a Non-Discretionary Portfolio Management Services (ND-PMS) arrangement may be pledged by the client, because the client remains the beneficial owner of those securities even though they are held in the client’s demat account under the ND-PMS structure. SEBI clarified that, under Regulation 23(1) of the SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2020, a non-discretionary portfolio manager must act according to the client’s directions, so the final decision to pledge rests entirely with the client; accordingly, a pledge initiated solely by the client, or at the client’s discretion through an instruction routed via the portfolio manager to the custodian, is permissible. SEBI further stated that this kind of client-initiated pledge is not treated as the portfolio manager “borrowing funds or securities on behalf of the client” under Regulation 23(8), so the borrowing prohibition is not breached merely because the client uses PMS-held securities as collateral for the client’s own borrowing arrangement. 

The letter also addresses reporting and AUM treatment: although the securities remain in the client’s beneficial ownership, SEBI said it is a matter for the portfolio manager to determine whether the market value of pledged securities should continue to be included in the portfolio manager’s Assets Under Management (AUM) and reflected in regulatory reporting. However, SEBI did not provide a blanket approval on that point and instead left it to the portfolio manager’s own assessment under the applicable PMS reporting framework. The request also asked whether SEBI or the custodian must be informed of such pledges; the provided text does not yet show SEBI’s final position on that query, so any compliance team should treat notification obligations as unresolved from the excerpt alone and verify the remainder of the guidance or applicable circulars before implementing a process. 

From a compliance perspective, the key operational point is that the pledge must be truly client-driven and not undertaken for the portfolio manager’s benefit; the portfolio manager should not appear to be arranging leverage for itself or using the client’s assets to circumvent the PMS borrowing restriction. The request also asked about disclosures and risk warnings, including the risk of invocation of pledge and loss of securities, but the visible portion of the document does not yet state SEBI’s response on whether specific warnings are mandatory. The letter is dated May 18, 2026 and references the client’s request dated March 17, 2026; no new effective date or implementation deadline is stated in the excerpt.

rows.summary:
SEBI’s informal guidance letter, dated April 20, 2026, was issued in response to First Water Capital Advisory LLP’s questions about the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 (“MF Regulations 2026”) under the Informal Guidance Scheme, 2025. The applicant had stated that under Regulation 5(1)(e), an AMC registered under Route 2 must have a minimum net worth of ₹150 crore at the time of registration, to be contributed by the sponsor, and must continuously maintain at least ₹100 crore invested in assets specified by SEBI; the applicant also noted that this ongoing net worth requirement can reduce to ₹50 crore if the company earns profits for five consecutive years, and that the sponsor is responsible for ensuring compliance with these net worth requirements.

Two queries were raised: first, whether a sponsor can apply for a mutual fund licence under Route 2 by contributing net worth of ₹150 crore, structured as ₹50 crore equity share capital and ₹100 crore preference shares redeemable only after the AMC achieves profits for five consecutive years; and second, whether a family trust can be a sponsor of a mutual fund. SEBI declined to provide a response to Query 1 for policy reasons under paragraph 11(h) of the Informal Guidance Scheme, 2025, so no compliance position or approval was given on using redeemable preference shares to satisfy the sponsorship net-worth contribution. For Query 2, SEBI stated that Regulation 2(1)(xx) defines a “sponsor” as any person who, acting individually or in concert with another body corporate, establishes a mutual fund or mutual fund lite, and SEBI interpreted this to mean the sponsor must be a body corporate; therefore, a family trust, not being a body corporate, cannot be a sponsor of a mutual fund.

SEBI emphasized that the letter was issued with competent authority approval and is based only on the facts represented in the application; different facts or conditions could lead to a different outcome. The letter reflects only the department’s enforcement position and does not constitute a Board decision on the questions posed. SEBI also stated that the guidance is limited to the MF Regulations 2026 and does not affect obligations under other applicable laws, including the SEBI Act, 1992, or any rules, regulations, guidelines, or circulars administered by SEBI or other authorities.

rows.summary:
SEBI has issued an informal guidance letter to UTI Alternatives Private Limited (UAPL), the investment manager of three SEBI-registered Category II AIFs: UTI Emerging India Opportunities Fund (IN/AIF2/18-19/0576), UTI SDOF Growth Theme Fund (IN/AIF2/22-23/1044), and UTI Multi Opportunities Fund (IN/AIF2/21-22/0994). The guidance concerns the newly cited SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026, specifically the restriction that an AMC must not undertake any business other than management/advisory services to pooled assets, together with the definition of a “broad based fund” as a fund having at least 20 investors and no single investor holding more than 25% of corpus. SEBI states that this broad-based requirement applies not only to mutual funds but also to management/advisory services provided by AMCs or their subsidiaries to AIFs and their schemes, because AIFs are treated as pooled assets for this purpose.

On the second question, SEBI clarifies that compliance must be tested at the individual scheme level, not at the overall fund level. The reason given is that under Regulation 10 of the AIF Regulations each AIF scheme is a separate investment vehicle for purposes such as investor limits, corpus requirements, and compliance obligations, so the “actual investor composition” relevant to the broad-based test is the composition of each scheme that receives the management/advisory services.

On the third question, SEBI indicates that in a master-feeder structure it is not enough for only the master fund to be broad based if the feeder funds are not doing standalone investments and the active management sits at the master level; the analysis still turns on the scheme-level structure described above. The letter also refers to Regulation 15 of the AIF Regulations, which permits an AIF, if its fund documents authorize it, to invest in units of another AIF, but the guidance ties that fact back to the conclusion that each scheme remains a distinct vehicle for broad-based compliance. 

On the fourth question, SEBI has not yet provided the substantive answer in the text supplied here—the document cuts off immediately after beginning the response to Query 3—so no guidance on the claimed exemption under paragraph 17.3 of the SEBI Master Circular for Mutual Funds dated June 27, 2024 is visible in the provided excerpt. From what is visible, the key compliance takeaway is that UAPL and similarly situated AMCs/subsidiaries managing AIFs should assess broad-based status separately for each AIF scheme, and ensure each such scheme meets the 20-investor / 25% single-investor concentration test where the MF regulation is being applied to those pooled assets.

SEBI issued an informal guidance letter dated **March 20, 2026** in response to **FRR Shares and Securities Limited’s** request under the **SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2025**. FRR is a SEBI-registered intermediary, operating as a **trading member of NSE and BSE (SEBI Reg. No. INZ000279232)** and a **CDSL depository participant (IND 12068100)**. The company asked whether **client trade instructions sent via WhatsApp chat from a client’s registered mobile number** could count as evidence of client order placement under SEBI’s requirements for preventing unauthorized trading.

SEBI stated that the older circular on unauthorized trading, **CIR/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD2/CIR/P/2017/108 dated September 26, 2017**, has been **superseded** by the **SEBI Master Circular for Stock Brokers, SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/90 dated July 17, 2025**. Under **paragraph 35.2** of that Master Circular, a stock broker must retain **evidence of pre-trade confirmation from the client**, and that evidence may include **email, logs for internet transactions, SMS messages, or any other legally verifiable record**. SEBI’s interpretive position is that a **WhatsApp instruction from the client’s registered mobile number may qualify as a legally verifiable record**, but only if the broker’s logs/records are **retrievable and legally verifiable for investigation or legal proceedings**.

SEBI also made clear that, if there is a dispute, the broker must be able to **prove the legal verifiability of the WhatsApp communication under the applicable law governing electronic evidence** and must comply with **all other applicable requirements of the SB Master Circular**. This guidance is **fact-specific** and based only on FRR’s representation; SEBI expressly said different facts or conditions could lead to a different result, and the letter reflects the department’s **enforcement position only**, not a binding Board decision. The guidance also does **not override any other SEBI regulations, circulars, guidelines, or any other law** that may apply.

rows.desc: Page 1 of 5 GENERAL MANAGER DEPARTMENT OF DEBT AND HYBRID SECURITIES POLICY AND DEVELOPMENT – 1 SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS-RACPOD1/P/OW/2025/0000025190/1 September 23, 2025 To, Ms. Rashmi Jain, Company Secretary and Compliance Officer, Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited, E Block, Valtas Premises, TB Kadam Marg, Chichpokli, Mumbai-400 033 Ma’am, Subject: Request for informal guidance by way of an interpretative letter on applicability of Chapter IV and Chapter VA of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 under the provisions of SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 by Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited 1. This has reference to your letter dated June 09, 2025, seeking an interpretative letter under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003. 2. Vide the said letter it has been inter-alia stated that Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited is a public limited company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and is a wholly owned subsidiary of Tata Sons Private Limited, having only Non-Convertible debentures (‘NCDs’) listed on BSE; with no other listed specified securities. Further, based on your audited financial statements, the value of outstanding listed NCDs as on March 31, 2025 is Rs.535 crores. Page 2 of 5 3. In view of the above, you have sought an interpretive letter under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 from SEBI on the following: 3.1. Query 1: As on March 31, 2025, the outstanding value of the listed NCDs of the Company were Rs.535 Crores. Hence, would the company be classified as a HVDLE w.e.f April 01, 2025? 3.2. Query 2: As on March 31, 2025, the outstanding value of the listed NCDs of the company were Rs.535 crores. Hence, would the company be under statutory obligations to comply with Regulation 3(3) of SEBI Listing Regulations which mandates the company to comply with the provision of Chapter IV of the SEBI Listing Regulations or considering that regulation 15(1A) restricts its applicability to only listed entities which have listed its non-convertible debt securities and has an outstanding value of listed non-convertible debt securities of Rupees One Thousand Crore and above, the same is not applicable to the Company. 3.3. Query 3: As on March 31, 2025, the outstanding value of the listed NCDs of the Company were Rs.535 Crores. Hence, would the Company be under statutory obligations to comply with the provisions of Chapter VA of SEBI Listing Regulations? The company has not listed any new debt securities on or after April 01, 2025. If the company is classified as HVDLE, obtaining prior No Objection Certificate from the Debenture Trustee will not be applicable. Comments: The submissions made in your letter have been considered. Without necessarily agreeing with your analysis, our response on the queries raised in your communications, are as under: 4.1. In regards to query 1, the following is informed: Since the outstanding value of listed NCDs of the applicant as on March 31, 2025 is Rs.535 crores, which is less than the specified threshold of Rs.1000 crore, as specified under Regulations 15(1A) and 62C(1) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“SEBI (LODR) Regulations”), the applicant is not classified as HVDLE on March 31, 2025, under Chapter IV and Chapter VA of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations. rows.summary:
SEBI has responded to Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited’s informal guidance request on whether it became a “high value debt listed entity” (HVDLE) and whether Chapters IV and VA of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 apply to it. The company stated that it is a public limited company and wholly owned subsidiary of Tata Sons Private Limited, with only non-convertible debentures (NCDs) listed on BSE and no listed specified securities; its audited financials showed outstanding listed NCDs of **Rs. 535 crore as of March 31, 2025**.

SEBI’s response is that the company is **not classified as an HVDLE as on March 31, 2025**, because the relevant threshold under **Regulations 15(1A) and 62C(1)** is **Rs. 1,000 crore** of outstanding listed debt securities, and Tata Realty’s amount is below that level. SEBI also clarified that **Chapter IV is not applicable** to the applicant, and **Chapter VA is likewise not applicable as on March 31, 2025**, because the new Chapter VA framework inserted by the **amendment notification dated March 28, 2025** applies only to entities that have **only listed NCDs of Rs. 1,000 crore and above** and **no listed specified securities**.

SEBI did note an important trigger-based compliance obligation: if, during a financial year, the company’s outstanding listed NCDs become **equal to or greater than Rs. 1,000 crore**, the company must **comply with the relevant provisions within six months from the date of that trigger**. The letter therefore does not create immediate Chapter IV/VA obligations for the company on the facts provided, but it does impose a future compliance timeline if the threshold is crossed. The response also specifically references that high value debt listed entity status is determined on the basis of the **principal outstanding of listed debt securities as on March 31, 2025**.

rows.summary:
SEBI issued an informal guidance letter to ISK Advisors Private Limited on 22 August 2025 in response to its 19 March 2025 request regarding how the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 (PIT Regulations) apply to a merchant banker’s obligation to maintain a restricted list when acting for an issuer. The core issue was whether a merchant banker that is advising on a transaction must keep a “restricted list” only for the issuer and its connected persons, or whether that list must also include the “all entities with whom unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI) is shared” in connection with the assignment, including prospective investors, consultants, lawyers, accountants, and other advisers involved in the transaction.

SEBI’s response indicates that the compliance obligation is broader than a narrow issuer-only list: where UPSI is shared for the purpose of a transaction or assignment, the merchant banker should treat the recipients of that UPSI as part of the restricted-list/control framework so that trading restrictions and information barriers can be imposed on those persons while the information remains unpublished. In practical terms, the guidance implies that a merchant banker cannot limit controls to the client company alone if it has disclosed UPSI to other parties in the course of execution; it must identify and manage access by all such recipients to prevent misuse of the information under the PIT Regulations.

The document is an informal guidance letter, so it reflects SEBI’s interpretive position on the specific facts presented rather than a new regulation or amendment with a universal effective date. No monetary penalty, filing deadline, or numerical threshold is set out in the text provided, but the compliance takeaway for merchant bankers is that they should review internal insider-trading controls, restricted-list procedures, and transaction-team access protocols to ensure that every external party receiving UPSI in a deal is covered by appropriate restrictions and monitoring.

rows.summary:
SEBI’s informal guidance letter, dated **July 9, 2025**, responds to Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited’s request regarding whether a **close-ended Alternative Investment Fund (AIF)** can continue investing during an **extended tenure** or may only liquidate existing holdings. The applicant stated it is the investment manager for a **Category III AIF (registration no. IN/AIF3/16-17/0291)** and a **Category II AIF (registration no. IN/AIF2/17-18/0340)**, and asked specifically whether, during the extended period, the fund may make new portfolio investments or only liquidate existing portfolio investments.

SEBI points first to **Regulation 13(5)** of the AIF Regulations: a close-ended AIF’s tenure may be extended by **up to two years** with approval of **two-thirds of unit holders by value**; a **large value fund for accredited investors** may be extended by **up to five years**, also with **two-thirds by value** approval, subject further to any conditions SEBI may specify for existing schemes. Under **Regulation 13(6)**, if unit-holder consent is not obtained under Regulation 13(5), or once the extended tenure expires, the AIF/scheme must be wound up under **Regulation 29**.

SEBI then explains the winding-up framework: under **Regulation 29(7)**, during the **liquidation period**—defined as the **one-year period following expiry of the tenure or extended tenure**—assets must be liquidated and proceeds distributed to investors after all liabilities are met. If unliquidated investments remain after the liquidation period and the scheme enters the **dissolution period** (as contemplated by **Regulation 29B**), then under **Regulation 29(10)** those remaining investments must be **mandatorily distributed in-specie** to investors in the manner specified by SEBI. During the dissolution period, **Regulation 29B(4)** prohibits the scheme from accepting any **fresh commitment** and from making any **new investment**.

On the core question, SEBI states that because the liquidation and dissolution periods are part of the **winding-up** process, an AIF/scheme **cannot make any fresh investments during the liquidation period or the dissolution period**. However, SEBI also states that the AIF Regulations **do not expressly prohibit new investments during the extended tenure itself**; winding up begins only after the extended tenure expires. Accordingly, SEBI’s interpretive position is that the **extended tenure is not itself part of winding up**, so the restrictions applicable to liquidation/dissolution do **not automatically apply** during that extended period.

For compliance purposes, the key practical takeaway is that a close-ended AIF with a validly approved extension may continue operating during the extension period, and SEBI’s guidance indicates that new investments are **not expressly barred** during that time; but once the extended tenure ends, the scheme enters winding-up, which triggers a **one-year liquidation period**, possible **dissolution period**, and a strict ban on **fresh commitments** and **new investments**. The fund must then either liquidate assets and distribute proceeds, or, if necessary, distribute remaining unliquidated investments in-specie to investors.

Madam, Kind attention: Ms. Surbhi Jain, Company Secretary and Compliance Officer Sub: Request for Informal guidance by way of an interpretive letter under the provisions of SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 received from InfoBeans Technologies Limited (“Company”) seeking interpretation of the provisions of regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 1. This is with reference to your letter dated February 25, 2025 read with clarification dated March 21, 2025 (“Application”) seeking interpretative letter under SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme 2003 in respect of the term “material pecuniary relationship” used in regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“LODR Regulations”) in the context of an Independent Director. 2. The following information is gathered from your Application: a. InfoBeans Technologies Limited (“Company” / “Applicant”) is an entity having its registered office at Indore, Madhya Pradesh. The shares of the Company are listed on National Stock Exchange of India Limited and BSE Limited. Page 2 of 5 b. The Company has appointed an Independent Director and pays sitting fees/commission as per the permissible limit under the Companies Act. Subsequently, the Company intends to engage the same individual (Ms. Opal Perry) as a consultant to its US-based subsidiary, InfoBeans INC. As a consultant, the individual will receive compensation from InfoBeans INC for services rendered. c. Ms. Opal’s responsibilities in the US subsidiary will be advisory in nature, focusing on strategic guidance, risk management, and business development. She will not have executive authority or direct involvement in the day-to-day operations. d. The aggregate consultancy fees payable to the Independent Director, excluding sitting fees/commission, will not exceed 10% of the director's total annual income. e. The US subsidiary's company structure does not formally define designation as “Independent Director”. Despite this, you have stated that you will ensure compliance with the Companies Act limits regarding her pecuniary relationship and total income. f. In this background, you have requested for clarification on the expression “material pecuniary relationship” mentioned in Regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the LODR Regulations in the context of an Independent Director. 3. In view of the above facts and circumstances, you have sought confirmation that the appointment of Ms. Opal in the US subsidiary, as described above, and the proposed consultancy arrangement with InfoBeans INC, would not conflict with SEBI’s regulatory framework concerning Independent Directors under the LODR Regulations. 4. With respect to your query, we have considered the submissions made by you in your Application and without necessarily agreeing with your analysis, our views on the queries are given below: Page 3 of 5 4.1. The term “independent director” has been defined under Regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the LODR Regulations inter-alia as a non-executive director who does not have any material pecuniary relationship with the listed entity and its related entities. The provision is reproduced for reference as under- “Definitions. 16. (1) For the purpose of this chapter, unless the context otherwise requires – (a)... (b) “independent director" means a non-executive director, other than a nominee director of the listed entity: (i)... (ii).... (iii).... (iv) who, apart from receiving director's remuneration, has or had no material pecuniary relationship with the listed entity, its holding, subsidiary or associate company, or their promoters, or directors, during the three immediately preceding financial years or during the current financial year;” It may be noted that no quantitative limits have been specified in the regulations for determining whether a pecuniary relationship between an independent director and listed entity, its holding, subsidiary or associate company, or their promoters, or directors is ‘material’ or not. 4.2. However, regulation 16(1)(b) specifies various parameters to determine the independence of a director. For example, such director should not be a promoter of the listed entity or its holdings or subsidiary or associate companies and not be related to such promoter, shall not hold the position of key managerial personnel in such entities, shall not be a non-independent director of another company on the board of which any non-independent director of the listed entity is an independent director, shall neither himself nor his relatives be a material supplie
rows.summary:
SEBI has issued an informal interpretive letter to InfoBeans Technologies Limited on May 14, 2025, in response to the company’s February 25, 2025 application (with a March 21, 2025 clarification) concerning Regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 and the meaning of “material pecuniary relationship” for an Independent Director. The facts presented were that InfoBeans, whose shares are listed on NSE and BSE, already pays an Independent Director sitting fees/commission within Companies Act limits and now wants to engage the same individual, Ms. Opal Perry, as a consultant to its US subsidiary, InfoBeans INC; the consultancy would be advisory in nature (strategic guidance, risk management, business development), would not involve executive authority or day-to-day operational control, and the consultancy fees would be capped so that the aggregate amount excluding sitting fees/commission does not exceed 10% of the director’s total annual income.  

SEBI’s response states that under Regulation 16(1)(b)(iv), an independent director is a non-executive director who, apart from director’s remuneration, has had no material pecuniary relationship with the listed entity, its holding, subsidiary or associate company, or their promoters or directors, during the three immediately preceding financial years or the current financial year. SEBI emphasized that the regulation does **not** prescribe any quantitative threshold for determining when a pecuniary relationship is “material,” so the fact that compensation is below 10% of annual income does not itself establish compliance or non-compliance under the LODR definition. SEBI also noted that independence must be assessed against the broader set of parameters in Regulation 16(1)(b), not only the pecuniary relationship test; the letter references other independence conditions such as not being a promoter, not being related to a promoter, and not holding key managerial personnel positions, among other criteria.  

The practical compliance takeaway is that the proposed consultancy arrangement with the US subsidiary is not automatically disqualified under SEBI’s framework solely because the individual is already an Independent Director and would receive separate consultancy compensation from a group entity, but InfoBeans must independently ensure that the arrangement does not create a “material pecuniary relationship” under Regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) and does not otherwise impair the director’s independence under the full regulation. The letter is informational/interpretive in nature, based on the company’s stated facts, and SEBI expressly says it is not necessarily agreeing with the company’s analysis.

rows.title: Consultation Paper on Review of Voluntary Delisting norms under SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021  Addendum- Executive Summary
rows.summary:
This SEBI addendum is not itself a final rule change, but an executive summary of a consultation paper issued on 14 August 2023 proposing revisions to the voluntary delisting framework under the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021. For compliance teams, the key proposed change is to the counter-offer trigger in reverse book building (RBB): under current regulations, a counter-offer is allowed only if the acquirer’s existing shareholding plus shares tendered by public shareholders reaches at least 90% of paid-up capital; the proposal would lower that trigger so a counter-offer could be made when the cumulative holding/tendered shares are below 90% but at or above 75% of paid-up capital. If that counter-offer route is used after the 90% threshold is not reached, the proposed floor price for the counter-offer would be the volume-weighted average price of the shares tendered by willing shareholders in the delisting offer.

The consultation paper also proposes to expand the floor-price methodology by adding “Adjusted Book Value” as an additional factor, and it states this would apply to both frequently traded and infrequently traded shares. Another major proposal is to allow delisting at a fixed price as an alternative to the current RBB-only exit-price discovery mechanism, but only for companies whose shares are frequently traded. In parallel, the reference date for calculating the floor price would move from the date of board approval to the date of the initial public announcement; for delisting of a subsidiary’s equity shares under a scheme of arrangement under Regulation 37, the reference date would instead be the date prior intimation is given to the stock exchanges.

The paper also proposes a special delisting framework for investment holding companies (IHCs) through a scheme of arrangement involving selective capital reduction under Section 66 of the Companies Act. Under this mechanism, underlying shares that the IHC holds in other listed companies would be transferred to public shareholders in proportion to their holdings in the IHC, while public shareholders would receive cash for the IHC’s investments in unlisted companies and other assets. This alternative to RBB would be available only to listed IHCs in which at least 75% of total value consists of investments in other listed companies. As this is only an executive summary, the document does not set final operative deadlines or implementation dates beyond the consultation-paper publication date; firms should treat these as proposed changes pending SEBI’s finalization.

However, the document content provided here does not include the exact percentage, the specific trade categories covered, implementation timetable, or any exemptions, so those details would need to be checked in the full consultation text or final regulatory action before assessing operational impact.

rows.title: Consultation Paper on framework for mandating additional disclosures from Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) that fulfil certain objective criteria, to 1) guard against possible circumvention of Minimum Public Shareholding (“MPS”), and 2) to guard against possible misuse of the FPI route to circumvent the requirements of Press Note 3 (“PN3”)

Until the final rules are published, there is no confirmed filing obligation from this document alone, but compliance teams should treat the proposal as a signal that FPI structures with concentrated ownership, related-party links, or India-sensitive investor connections may come under enhanced scrutiny.

rows.summary:
This document is primarily a promotional and investor-information page for **MFCentral / MITRA**, described as a unified, secure, all-in-one mutual fund services gateway created by **KFintech and CAMS**. It states that investors can use a single service request to make changes across **all mutual fund folios** (for example, updating bank mandates, personal contact details, or IDCW-related instructions), and that the platform is intended to provide a single view of an investor’s mutual fund portfolio across all fund houses. From a compliance perspective, the document’s main operational message is that mutual fund service requests are increasingly expected to be handled digitally through this centralized platform rather than by paper-based or fund-by-fund processing.

The document then flags several specific regulatory or industry changes. First, it announces the **Positive Pay System (PPS)** for cheques, noting that the **Reserve Bank of India introduced PPS in September 2020** as an additional security layer for cheques **above Rs. 50,000**, and that banks indicated enforcement beginning **1 September 2021**. Investors are warned that mutual fund investment cheques may be rejected during clearing if PPS requirements are not met, so compliance teams should ensure cheque-based subscription processes and customer instructions align with the PPS rule for high-value cheques.

Second, it summarizes the **realization-based NAV** rule under **SEBI Circular SEBI/HO/IMD/DF2/CIR/P/2020/253**. Effective **1 February 2021**, the **closing NAV of the day when funds become available for utilization** applies to mutual fund purchases, and this applies **regardless of scheme category or investment amount**; the document expressly says this also covers **systematic transactions registered before 1 February 2021**. This means any processing, cut-off, and payment realization controls must ensure NAV allocation is based on actual fund availability, not merely when an order was placed, and that legacy systematic investments were brought under the same treatment from the effective date.

Third, it notes SEBI’s change to dividend nomenclature: under the **5 October 2020 SEBI communication** on review of dividend options/plans, all existing and proposed mutual fund schemes’ **Dividend Option/Plan** are to be renamed and reflected as **“Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal Plan (IDCW)”** in statements and transaction descriptions. Compliance teams should confirm that investor communications, transaction confirmations, statements, scheme documentation, and internal systems use the IDCW terminology consistently, because the old dividend naming is no longer the required label.

Overall, the document does not impose a new rule on the platform itself so much as it highlights the main investor-service and transaction-processing obligations relevant to mutual fund operations: centralized digital servicing through MFCentral, PPS compliance for cheque-based investments over **Rs. 50,000**, NAV determination based on **fund realization as of 1 February 2021**, and mandatory **IDCW** terminology for dividend-like mutual fund distributions.

rows.summary:
The document is a SEBI “Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)” listings page, not a single substantive rule text, and it functions as a regulatory docket of AIF-related papers, circulars, master circulars, and guidance items over time. For compliance purposes, the most material items visible in the excerpt are current and recent regulatory actions affecting AIF managers, trustees, and related market participants: SEBI issued a **Master Circular for AIFs on 3 June 2026**; a **circular on regulatory reporting by AIFs on 4 March 2026**; and a **GARUDA “Green-Channel” mechanism on 30 July 2026** for processing AIF placement memoranda filed with SEBI upon document acknowledgement, indicating a new/streamlined filing workflow for placement memorandum processing. The page also shows that on **9 September 2025** SEBI issued a circular establishing a **framework for AIFs to make co-investment within the AIF structure**, which is relevant to how co-investment opportunities are structured and offered through the fund vehicle itself rather than outside it.

The listing also reflects several consultation papers that signal likely or proposed rule changes affecting compliance obligations, even though the page itself does not state the final rule text. These include a **30 June 2026 consultation paper** on rationalizing when investor consent is required and the scope of conflicted transactions that require such consent under the SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012; an **8 August 2025 consultation paper** proposing flexibilities for **Large Value Funds for Accredited Investors (LVFs)**; and another **8 August 2025 consultation paper** proposing a separate AIF scheme type for **only Accredited Investors**. There is also a **9 May 2025 consultation paper** on providing flexibility for AIFs to offer co-investment opportunities to investors within the AIF structure, which aligns with the later September 2025 circular and is relevant for funds considering co-investment mechanics, allocation policies, and conflicts controls.

A compliance team should also note the **13 March 2025 informal guidance request from FirstPort Capital Angel Fund**, which specifically concerns provisions for **Angel Funds** under the SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012; while not a rule itself, this suggests there were interpretive issues requiring regulatory clarification. Likewise, the **3 March 2025 circular on relaxation in the timeline for reporting differential rights issued by AIFs** is directly relevant to reporting calendars and internal controls around investor rights instruments. The **21 February 2025 consultation paper** seeks to expand the definition of **Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs)** under the SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018 to include **Accredited Investors** for the limited purpose of investments in **Angel Funds**, which would materially affect investor onboarding and eligibility verification if implemented.

More broadly, the page confirms the AIF regulatory stream is active and includes multiple compliance touchpoints across filings, reporting, investor classification, consent/conflict management, co-investment, angel fund treatment, and LVF/accredited investor structures. Because the content provided is a navigational listing rather than the full text of the circulars, it does not give the underlying thresholds, ratios, consent percentages, or detailed deadlines beyond the publication dates shown above; however, those dates are the operative dates to track for document issuance and potential effective compliance planning.

rows.summary:
The document is a SEBI “Bankers to an Issue” listing page that primarily functions as an index of regulatory actions, circulars, and master circulars applicable to bankers to an issue, rather than a standalone rule change. The most important current item shown is the **Master Circular for Bankers to an Issue dated 3 June 2024**, which consolidates the operative requirements for this category of intermediary; in a compliance context, this means firms should treat the 2024 master circular as the current reference point for obligations, while also checking the underlying older circulars and regulations listed on the page for historical amendments and any provisions not superseded. The listing also shows a related **master circular dated 22 May 2024 for issue and listing of non-convertible securities, securitised debt instruments, security receipts, municipal debt securities and commercial paper**, which may intersect with banker-to-an-issue responsibilities when those instruments are offered or listed.

The page reflects several earlier regulatory changes that remain relevant to compliance oversight. SEBI issued amendments to the **SEBI (Bankers to an Issue) Regulations, 2011** on **5 July 2011** and earlier on **7 September 2006**, indicating that the regulatory framework has been updated over time and that firms should ensure their internal controls align with the amended regulations as incorporated in the current master circular. The listing also includes a **2010 circular reducing the time between issue closure and listing**, which is material for issuers and bankers because it creates a tighter post-issue operational timeline for completing listing formalities and related coordination. In addition, SEBI repeatedly issued circulars beginning in **2009 and 2010** on **Applications Supported by Blocked Amount (ASBA)** in public issues and rights issues, showing that bankers to an issue have compliance responsibilities connected to ASBA processing where they participate in or facilitate application handling, fund blocking, and related issue workflows.

The page also points to ongoing reporting and supervisory obligations. A **30 March 2008 circular** requires **periodic reporting of information** by bankers to an issue, and a **20 June 2011 circular** requires a **periodic report on the grant of prior approval to bankers to an issue**, which implies a continuing obligation to monitor and report approval status or changes to SEBI in the prescribed format and frequency. Separate circulars from **29 March 2012** on **review of regulatory compliance and periodic reporting** and from **2 August 2011** on **processing investor complaints in SCORES** indicate that bankers to an issue are expected to maintain complaint-handling mechanisms and ensure investor grievances are tracked and escalated through SEBI’s SCORES system as required. The page also references a **9 July 1999 requirement to submit an annual statement of activities undertaken as bankers to issues**, which remains important as a baseline filing obligation unless specifically superseded, and the duplicate listing of that item suggests it is a formal recurring compliance requirement rather than an optional disclosure.

This document is not a substantive CIS rule, circular, or notice itself; it is a SEBI “Collective Investment Schemes (C.I.S)” page that functions as an index of CIS-related regulatory materials, enforcement items, reports, and public notices. The most recent listed item is a **26 Feb 2026 circular** titled **“Ease of Doing Investment (EoDI)- Disclosure of registered name and registration number by SEBI regulated entities and their agents on Social Media Platforms (SMPs)”**—this appears to be the only current item in the CIS listing and is likely the most operationally relevant for compliance teams, although the underlying circular text is not included here. The page also references older CIS materials, including **court judgments in CIS-related prosecution matters (17 Apr 2012)**, **prosecution cases launched by SEBI against CIS entities (31 Jul 2009)**, **status of CIS (31 Jul 2003)**, **list of appraising agencies and auditors (1 Oct 2002)**, multiple **CIS public notices (1 Oct 2002 and 31 Mar 2002)**, a **CIS public notice dated 10 Dec 1999**, and the **Dr. S.A. Dave Committee final and interim reports** on CIS dated **5 Apr 1999** and **31 Dec 1998**. 

For compliance purposes, the only identifiable new requirement from the page content is that SEBI-regulated entities and their agents must, under the Feb. 26, 2026 circular, disclose their **registered name** and **registration number** on **social media platforms**; however, the page does not provide implementation mechanics, deadlines, or any penalties, so those details would need to be confirmed from the circular itself. No thresholds, rates, filing forms, or effective dates beyond the listing dates are stated on this page, and there is no indication here of a direct CIS-specific operational obligation beyond the indexed materials and the social-media disclosure circular. If your compliance team is reviewing CIS exposure, the key takeaway is that this page is a document repository and pointer to historical enforcement/public notice material, with the only clearly signaled current compliance topic being SEBI’s social-media disclosure requirement for registered name and registration number.

rows.summary:
This listing shows recent SEBI commodity derivatives regulatory materials and indicates that firms active in the commodity derivatives market need to monitor multiple updates across trading, clearing, settlement, and risk management obligations. The document itself is a search/listing page rather than a full circular, so it does not provide the detailed text of each rule change; however, it identifies the most material current items and their publication dates.

The newest items are a **12 Aug 2026 circular** on the **review of inclusion of historical scenarios in stress testing for the commodity derivatives segment**, and **11 Aug 2026 consultation papers** on both **expanding the scope of the SEBI (Vault Managers) Regulations, 2021** and **FPI participation in exchange traded commodity derivatives (ETCDs)**. These are currently consultation-stage items, meaning they are not yet operative rules, but they are important because they may affect how risk is modeled, how warehoused commodities are handled, and whether foreign portfolio investors can participate in commodity derivative products under revised conditions.

On **19 Jun 2026**, SEBI issued a circular on **clarification regarding the applicability of the benefit of early pay-in in the commodity derivatives segment**. Any exchange member, clearing member, or participant relying on early pay-in treatment should review this because it clarifies when the benefit applies and therefore affects margin, settlement, and operational processing.

On **16 Mar 2026**, SEBI issued a circular on the **coverage of the Settlement Guarantee Fund (SGF) for the commodity derivatives segment**, and on **5 Feb 2026** it released a related **consultation paper on draft circulars covering both historical scenario inclusion in stress testing and SGF coverage**. Together, these items indicate a broader review of default-risk backstops and stress-testing methodology for clearing corporations and commodity derivatives market infrastructure. Compliance teams at clearing corporations and exchanges should treat these as likely to affect risk parameter calibration, default fund coverage, and the documentation used for internal and regulatory risk controls.

The 2024 items are operationally significant and directly relevant to market infrastructure and members. On **30 May 2024**, SEBI issued a circular on **comprehensive guidelines for the Investor Protection Fund (IPF) and Investor Services Fund (ISF) for stock exchanges having a commodity derivatives segment**, and another circular on **revision of eligibility criteria for launching commodity futures contracts**. These affect exchanges that list commodity derivatives and may change the conditions that must be satisfied before a new commodity futures contract can be introduced, as well as the contribution/use framework for investor protection and services funds. On the same date, SEBI also modified the **requirement for inspection of accredited warehouses by clearing corporations**, which affects warehouse accreditation and ongoing supervision over deliverable inventory used in physical settlement.

Also on **27 May 2024**, SEBI issued a **standard operating procedure for handling stock exchange outages and extending trading hours in the commodity derivatives segment**, and a circular setting **eligibility criteria for launching options on commodity futures as underlying** for stock exchanges with commodity derivative segments. These require exchanges and members to have explicit outage-response procedures and could impose conditions on listing new options products, including product-launch controls, risk checks, and operational readiness. On **24 May 2024**, SEBI modified the **staggered delivery period in commodity futures contracts**, which is directly relevant to delivery-cycle planning, warehouse coordination, and member/client settlement processes.

Finally, the listing includes earlier 2024 and 2023 framework items such as **cross-margin benefits for offsetting positions with different expiry dates** (23 Apr 2024), a **notification of goods under the SCRA, 1956** (5 Mar 2024), a **Master Circular for the Commodity Derivatives Segment** (4 Aug 2023), a **revision in computation of the Core Settlement Guarantee Fund** (23 May 2023), and **direct market access (DMA) to SEBI-registered…** (10 May 2023, truncated in the listing). For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that commodity derivatives participants should check whether they are an exchange, clearing corporation, broker, FPI, warehouse/vault operator, or other market intermediary because different updates affect different parts of the market stack, and several of the newest items may still be under consultation rather than final implementation.

The document is not a substantive regulatory circular or rule text; it is a Securities and Exchange Board-style “Corp. Debt Market” listing page showing recent debt offer documents filed/published in the corporate debt market section. The content primarily consists of a searchable index with filters for date, department, section, and “Info For” categories, and it does not itself announce a new requirement, amendment, threshold, fee, deadline, or compliance procedure. In other words, there is no rule change or obligation stated in the text itself; it is a document repository/navigation page.

What the page does show is a chronological listing of debt offer filings, which may be relevant for monitoring issuer disclosures and prospectus activity. The visible records include, among others, KLM Axiva Finvest Ltd. (Draft Prospectus on Aug. 3, 2026; Prospectus on Aug. 14, 2026; Addendum-cum-corrigendum on Aug. 18, 2026), Kosamattam Finance Ltd. The document is not itself a single rule text; it is a SEBI “Credit Rating Agencies” page listing the regulatory instruments currently associated with credit rating agencies. For compliance purposes, the key point is that the operative framework includes the SEBI Credit Rating Agencies Regulations, 1999, as amended over time in 2006, 2010, 2011 (two amendment sets), with a later operational circular issued on 6 January 2023 and a master circular issued on 3 July 2023. These are the core documents a CRA, and in some cases market participants interacting with CRAs, would need to follow.  

The 3 July 2023 Master Circular for Credit Rating Agencies consolidates the regulatory requirements applicable to CRAs; it supersedes or compiles the earlier operational directions into one reference document for ongoing compliance. The 6 January 2023 Operational Circular for Credit Rating Agencies is the more immediate operational instruction set for CRAs and should be read together with the Regulations, because it governs day-to-day compliance implementation.  

A separate 4 September 2023 circular specifically addresses the mechanism for sharing information by CRAs with debenture trustees, meaning CRAs must follow prescribed information-sharing arrangements with DTs where relevant to debt issues and surveillance of instruments. This is directly relevant where a company has rated debt securities backed by a debenture trustee structure, since the circular affects what rating-related information is shared and the process/timing for such exchange.  

The page also lists a 22 May 2024 master circular covering the issue and listing of non-convertible securities, securitised debt instruments, security receipts, municipal debt securities, and commercial paper, and a 18 December 2025 circular on modification of conditions for reduction in denomination of debt securities, plus a 27 February 2026 circular on revised norms for appointment of an independent third-party reviewer/certifier for green debt securities. Those later items are not CRA-specific in the narrow sense, but they matter to entities issuing rated debt or green debt because they affect issuance/listing mechanics and, for green debt, third-party review/certification expectations.  

The document does not contain the substantive text of the requirements, deadlines, fees, thresholds, or detailed procedures; it is essentially a regulatory index showing the current legal/regulatory touchpoints for CRAs. From a compliance standpoint, the actionable takeaway is to monitor the 2023 CRA master/operational circulars and the underlying CRA Regulations as the governing framework, and to review the 4 September 2023 debenture-trustee information-sharing circular if your organization is involved in rated debt securities or trustee reporting.

This document is a SEBI “COVID-19 Measures” listing page, not a single substantive rule text. It shows a sequence of COVID-related circulars, press releases, and relaxation measures issued across 2020–2021, indicating that SEBI repeatedly extended or modified compliance timelines and procedural requirements because of the pandemic. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these were temporary regulatory relief measures affecting multiple market participants, and the firm would need to identify which of these circulars applied to its regulated activities and whether any extended deadlines or relaxed procedural requirements were still operative or had already expired.

The listed measures cover several regulated segments: Investment Advisers, AIFs and VCFs, Debenture Trustees, Debt and Hybrid Securities issuers and related disclosure requirements, issuer/listing procedures, valuation of debt and money market instruments, portfolio segregation, and other general regulatory compliance timelines. The page specifically references “relaxation in timelines for compliance with regulatory requirements” on multiple dates in 2020 and 2021, showing that SEBI continued to defer deadlines as the pandemic evolved. It also references an “addendum” to the April 13, 2020 COVID-19 timeline-relaxation circular, a further extension for “creation of security in issuance of listed debt securities and due diligence by debenture trustee(s),” and a circular on “relaxation from compliance with certain provisions of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 / other applicable circulars,” which signals that both statutory/regulatory obligations and SEBI circular-based obligations were affected.

The page provides specific dated entries that compliance teams should map against internal obligations: May 31, 2021 (AIFs/VCFs relaxation), May 3, 2021 (debenture trustees’ compliance timeline relaxation), April 29, 2021 (general timeline relaxation and addendum), April 29, 2021 (LODR/circular compliance relaxation for debt and hybrid securities), January 19, 2021 (procedural relaxations relating to issues and listing), December 31, 2020 (general timeline relaxation and extension of implementation timeline for creation of security and debenture trustee due diligence), December 1, 2020 (general timeline relaxation), October 1, 2020 (valuation of debt and money market instruments due to COVID-19 and another general timeline relaxation), September 29, 2020 (validity of SEBI observations and revision in issue size), September 18, 2020 (regulatory measures to continue), September 2, 2020 (segregation of portfolio review), and September 30, 2021 (extension of timelines for investment advisers).

Because the content is only a listing index, it does not contain the actual deadline lengths, numeric thresholds, or the precise revised dates in the text shown here. A compliance officer should treat this as an alert to review each linked circular/press release individually, confirm the exact relaxations granted, check whether any requirements were extended again or lapsed, and verify whether the firm had to file, disclose, maintain records, or implement procedures differently during the applicable COVID-19 relief period.

This document is a listing of SEBI materials relevant to **Debenture Trustees** rather than a single rule change. The most recent items show an active regulatory focus on how debenture trustees manage listed debt issuance, security creation, monitoring, defaults, reporting, and the scope of activities they may perform.

The newest listed item is a **circular dated April 28, 2026** titled **“Extension of timeline for compliance with terms and conditions by Debenture Trustees for carrying out activities outside the purview of SEBI.”** Although the underlying text is not provided here, the title indicates SEBI has extended a compliance deadline relating to debenture trustees undertaking activities that are outside SEBI’s regulatory scope, so firms relying on any such permissions or conditional relaxations should verify the revised timeline and ensure their activity set still conforms to the conditions attached to that extension. The listing also includes a **December 18, 2025 circular** on **modification in conditions for reduction in denomination of debt securities**, which would be relevant where listed debt securities are being re-denominated or subdivided and would require compliance with whatever revised conditions SEBI has imposed for that process.

The most operationally important items in the listing are the **2024 master circular** and the **2022/2021/2020 circulars** dealing with **security creation, due diligence, monitoring, and default procedures** for listed debt securities. The **May 22, 2024 Master Circular for issue and listing of non-convertible securities, securitised debt instruments, security receipts, municipal debt securities and commercial paper** consolidates the operative framework for debt-market issuance and listing and would be the primary reference document for ongoing compliance. The **August 4, 2022 circular** introduced **enhanced guidelines for debenture trustees and listed issuers on security creation and initial due diligence**, and the **December 19, 2022 clarification** interprets or supplements that framework; together these require trustees to carry out more robust pre-issuance checks and security-verification steps before relying on the issuance structure. The **May 19, 2022 circular** revised the **format of the security cover certificate** and also changed **monitoring and revision timelines**, so issuers and trustees must use the updated certificate format and meet the revised reporting/monitoring schedule rather than older versions. There is also a **December 31, 2020 circular** extending the implementation timeline for **creation of security in issuance of listed debt securities and due diligence by debenture trustees**, which indicates that SEBI had previously deferred the effective date for those obligations and that compliance teams should confirm whether later circulars have superseded those deadlines.

The list also includes SEBI’s **default-management and investor-protection measures**. The **October 13, 2020 circular** standardized the procedure debenture trustees must follow when an issuer of listed debt securities defaults, meaning trustees must follow a prescribed sequence of actions rather than ad hoc responses when payment or covenant failures occur. The **October 22, 2020 circular** requires issuers of listed or proposed-to-be-listed debt securities to contribute to a **“Recovery Expense Fund,”** which creates a specific funding obligation that needs to be built into issuance documentation and compliance tracking. The **August 13, 2021 circular** on **“Security and Covenant Monitoring” using Distributed Ledger Technology** indicates SEBI approved/encouraged a technology-based monitoring mechanism for covenant and security compliance, so trustees using that framework would need to ensure their systems and reporting processes align with the DLT-based monitoring model.

Several items affect periodic reporting and internal governance. The **December 19, 2011 circular** on **review of regulatory compliance, periodic reporting, and contents of trust deed** implies trustees must maintain an ongoing compliance-review process, submit periodic reports, and ensure the trust deed contains mandated provisions. The **June 20, 2011 circular** addressed **periodical reports and grant of prior approval to debenture trustees**, indicating that some actions require prior regulator approval rather than post-facto reporting. Earlier foundational rules appear as well, including the **SEBI (Issue and Listing of Debt Securities) Regulations, 2008**, the **SEBI (Debenture Trustees) Regulations, 1993** as amended, and older circulars on **dissemination of information on debentures** and the **simplified listing agreement for debt securities**, all of which remain relevant as the baseline framework unless specifically overridden.

For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that this page signals a regulatory environment where debenture trustees must stay current on: the **latest master circular**, the **updated security-cover certificate format**, the **enhanced pre-issuance due diligence and security-creation requirements**, the **prescribed default-handling procedure**, any **Recovery Expense Fund contribution requirement**, and any **deadline extensions** granted for activities outside SEBI’s core remit. Because several entries are amendments, clarifications, or extensions, compliance should not rely on legacy processes or old timeline assumptions without confirming the latest circular text and effective dates.

rows.summary:
This document sets out the rights and obligations of a Beneficial Owner (account holder) and a Depository Participant (DP) under the Depositories Act, 1996, SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 1996, SEBI rules/circulars/guidelines, and the relevant depository bye-laws, business rules, operating instructions, and government notifications in force from time to time. A DP may open or activate a demat account only after receiving a complete account-opening form, KYC, and supporting documents as specified by SEBI, and it must keep all beneficial owner information confidential except where disclosure is required by a legal, statutory, or regulatory authority. The beneficial owner must promptly notify the DP in writing of any change in the details originally provided in the account-opening documents.

On costs, the beneficial owner must pay the charges agreed with the DP as reflected in the DP’s tariff sheet for holding and transferring securities in dematerialized form and for depository services, and the document explicitly notes that no charges are payable for opening a demat account. For Basic Services Demat Accounts, the DP must follow the charge structure prescribed by SEBI and/or the depository through applicable circulars, directions, or notifications. Any increase in agreed charges or tariff requires at least 30 days’ prior written notice to the beneficial owner.

The beneficial owner has the right to dematerialize securities admitted on the depository, and the DP must maintain separate accounts for each beneficial owner so that securities are segregated and not mixed with other clients’ securities or the DP’s own dematerialized holdings. The DP may not facilitate any pledge, hypothecation, or other encumbrance over securities except in the manner specifically permitted under the Depositories Act, SEBI regulations, and depository rules. Transfers into or out of the demat account can be made only on the basis of a duly authorized order, instruction, direction, or mandate from the beneficial owner, and the DP must preserve the original authorization documents and an audit trail.

For account statements, the DP must provide statements in the format and at the times agreed with the beneficial owner and as required by SEBI or the depository. If there are no transactions during the year, or the balance becomes nil, the DP must send one physical holding statement annually and then restart transaction statements once activity resumes. Electronic statements are allowed if the beneficial owner wants them, and the DP may issue them under its digital signature in accordance with the Information Technology Act, 2000; if the DP lacks electronic statement capability, it must send physical statements instead. For Basic Services Demat Accounts, the DP must send transaction statements as specifically mandated by SEBI and/or the depository from time to time.

The excerpt cuts off at the beginning of the “Manner of Closure of Demat account” section, so any closure requirements are incomplete in the provided text and cannot be summarized reliably from this excerpt alone.
