This document is not a substantive regulatory circular itself, but a listing page for SEBI’s **Derivatives** communications, showing the historical universe of circulars and master circulars in this area. The entries indicate that, over time, SEBI has issued requirements affecting **stock brokers, trading members, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs), mutual funds, banks, clearing members, and other market participants** in exchange-traded derivatives, including equity derivatives, currency derivatives, interest rate futures, and derivatives linked to indices and foreign markets.

The listed materials include several major rule changes and product introductions, such as: a **review of position limits** for stock brokers, FPIs Category I & II, and mutual funds in **stock derivatives contracts**; introduction of **exchange-traded cross-currency derivatives** on **EUR-USD, GBP-USD, and USD-JPY** and option contracts on **EUR-INR, GBP-INR, and JPY-INR**; and introduction of **cash-settled interest rate futures** on **6-year, 10-year, and 13-year Government of India securities**. Earlier entries also reference position limits for mutual funds in **10-year IRF**, revised position limits for banks trading **USD/INR derivative contracts**, and the introduction of IRFs on **2-year and 5-year Government of India securities**.

The listing also reflects compliance-related operational rules covering **client margin short-collection/non-collection**, **post-trade modification of client codes**, **self-clearing membership in the currency derivatives segment**, **liquidity enhancement schemes for illiquid securities in equity derivatives**, and **physical settlement of stock derivatives**. Other product/eligibility changes shown include **mini index derivatives on Sensex and Nifty**, **revision of eligibility criteria for stocks in the derivatives segment**, **European-style stock options**, **options on USD-INR spot rate**, **index options with tenure up to 5 years**, and **derivative contracts on volatility indices** and **foreign stock indices**.

The page also shows that SEBI periodically issued **master circulars** consolidating requirements relating to exchange-traded derivatives, including versions dated **Apr. 1, 2013**, **Jan. 2, 2012**, and **Dec. 31, 2010**. Because the content is only an index of documents and not the full text of any one circular, it does **not provide the operative deadlines, thresholds, margin percentages, or exact effective dates for each rule change** beyond the publication dates shown in the list; a compliance team would need to open the specific circulars referenced here to determine the exact obligations, implementation dates, and numeric limits that apply to its activities.

rows.title: Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI)
rows.desc: Proposal No Comment Rationale Level of Agreement Rationale for rejection 2 Identification of SWAGT-FIs – requirement for validation of SWAGAT-FI status for existing FPIs will increase burden on investors and lead to operational inconvenience. Request to relook at the proposal regarding providing proof. FPIs will need to prove diversification, independen ce of fund managers, regulator confirmation, blind pool, absen ce of segregated portfolios, which are burdensome and wil l increase paperwork. Existing subcategory framework should be applied instead of the FPIs having to pro vide additional documents to meet the specified criteria . Disagree To reduce operational burden, the verification requirements shall be on similar lines to the existing exemption criteria under Additional Disclosure Framework, which has already been implemented by the industry. 4 No the periodicity of re-KYC should be maintained as at present. The periodicity of payment is also to be maintained as is currently practiced. The need to do a re-KYC is to be maintained for FPI s similar to other types of investors. Any material change e. g. UBO, if not reported on time will be found while conduct ing the re- KYC. The payment of yearly fees should be maintained as at the current periodicity or manner of payment. The propo sal to get payments at say a period of every 10 years woul d restrict the ability of SEBI to increase or decrease the yea rly fees. In view of retaining flexibility of being able to m anage the yearly fees far more easily it is suggested that th e current system is to be maintained. Disagree Requirements regarding material change shall continue. Proposal for removal of additional re-KYC requirement was made on the basis of a risk vs convenience assessment. There is no yearly fee requirement even today. Only the block period for fee is being increased from 3 years to 10 years, to coincide with the re-KYC requirement. 6 Many commenters were of the opinion to not facilitate single demat account for different modes of foreign investment. Foreign investors generally rely on custodian repor ts rather than depository statements for tracking and reconci ling their holdings. While consolidated custodian reports can be used for an overall view, FPI and FVCI holdings must be distinctly identifiable as required by RBI NDI Rules. A single demat account combining both routes prevent issuers and regulators from distinguishing between FPI and FVCI investments, leading to monitoring and compliance challenges. Recording unlisted FVCI investments in an FPI- tagged account would also create regulatory and rep orting issues. Maintaining separate demat accounts ensures accurate record-keeping, prevents co-mingling of se curities, facilitates data retrieval, and preserves confident iality— whereas a single account complicates segregation, s lows data collection, and increases compliance risks. Disagree Single demat account is proposed on optional basis, so investors can choose as per their convenience. Requisite clarification on operational matters shall be provided under the respective notification or Standard Operating Procedure to be issued for implementation of SWAGAT-FI framework.
rows.summary:
The document summarizes stakeholder comments and SEBI’s responses on the proposed **SWAGAT-FI / FPI framework**. On the proposal to require **existing FPIs to prove SWAGAT-FI status**, commenters objected that this would force investors to provide extensive evidence of diversification, fund-manager independence, regulator confirmation, blind-pool status, and absence of segregated portfolios, creating unnecessary paperwork and operational burden. SEBI **disagreed with the objection** and said the verification approach will instead be aligned with the **existing exemption criteria under the Additional Disclosure Framework**, which the industry already uses, in order to reduce operational burden while still validating eligibility.

On the proposal to change the **re-KYC cadence and fee-payment periodicity**, commenters argued that the current periodicity should remain unchanged and that existing re-KYC should continue for FPIs, with material changes such as **UBO changes** caught through that process; they also objected that moving to a 10-year payment cycle would reduce SEBI’s flexibility to change annual fees. SEBI **disagreed**, stating that the requirement to report **material changes** will continue and that the earlier removal of additional re-KYC was based on a **risk-versus-convenience assessment**. SEBI clarified that there is **no annual fee requirement today**; rather, the **fee block period is being extended from 3 years to 10 years**, and this change is intended to **coincide with the re-KYC requirement**.

On the proposal relating to a **single demat account for different modes of foreign investment**, commenters warned that combining investment routes would obscure the distinction between **FPI** and **FVCI** holdings, complicate reporting, and create monitoring and compliance problems, especially for **unlisted FVCI investments** recorded in an FPI-tagged account. SEBI **disagreed** with the objection and stated that a **single demat account is optional**, meaning investors may choose it if convenient. SEBI also said that the **operational details** for implementation of the **SWAGAT-FI framework** will be provided in the relevant **notification or Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)**.

The most recent listed item is a **March 25, 2026 circular** clarifying the **eligibility of members of the Institute of Cost Accountants of India to conduct the annual audit of Investment Advisers**, which indicates a compliance issue around who may perform the required audit. Another recent item, dated **February 26, 2026**, concerns **Ease of Doing Investment (EoDI)** and requires **SEBI-regulated entities and their agents** to disclose their **registered name and registration number on social media platforms**, which is a specific external disclosure obligation.

The page also shows a **February 6, 2026 Master Circular for Investment Advisers**, which would consolidate existing obligations for IAs, and an earlier **May 21, 2024 Master Circular for Investment Advisers**, plus a **May 7, 2024 circular** on the **periodic reporting format for Investment Advisers**. From that, compliance teams should understand that periodic reporting requirements were formalized/updated and that the reporting format is a specific operational obligation for registered advisers. The page further lists an **October 10, 2023 circular** extending the timeline for compliance with the **qualification and experience requirements under Regulation 7(1) of the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013**, which is important because it shows SEBI granted additional time to meet adviser qualification/experience norms.

Several 2023–2021 items show the ongoing substantive compliance framework for IAs: a **June 15, 2023 Master Circular**, an **April 6, 2023 circular** on the **use of brand name/trade name by Investment Advisers and Research Analysts**, an **April 5, 2023 circular** on the **advertisement code** for both IAs and RAs, and a **November 28, 2022 circular** on the **procedure for seeking prior approval for change in control**. For a compliance officer, these titles indicate specific operational controls: branding/trade name usage must conform to SEBI rules, advertisements must follow a prescribed code, and any change in control requires prior SEBI approval rather than post-facto notification. The page also references **December 13, 2021** guidance requiring IAs to **publish an Investor Charter and disclose investor complaints on their websites/mobile applications**, which creates an ongoing public disclosure requirement.

The remaining listed items establish additional compliance and registration context: **December 21, 2021** permits **investment advisory services for Accredited Investors**, **August 26, 2021** concerns implementation modalities for the **Accredited Investors framework**, **June 18, 2021** sets the **framework for administration and supervision of Investment Advisers** under the 2013 regulations, **September 28, 2020** amends **operating guidelines for IAs in IFSC**, **September 23, 2020** provides the **Guidelines for Investment Advisers**, and **August 6, 2020** covers **administration and supervision of Investment Advisers**. The page also includes a **September 30, 2021 extension of timelines**, an **August 31, 2021 extension of time for seeking membership of BSE Administration & Supervision Limited**, and a **June 2021 framework for administration/supervision**, all of which suggest that membership, supervisory arrangements, and implementation deadlines were being phased in over time. Finally, the page shows there are **36 records** total and that it is organized by date/type/title for the Investment Advisers regulatory category, so a compliance team should use it as a change-log index and review the underlying circulars for exact operative requirements.

rows.title: Settlement Application
rows.summary:
This document is the online **SEBI Settlement Application** form and its filing instructions, and the key compliance requirement is that once the applicant successfully pays the **non-refundable settlement application fee online**, the applicant must **physically submit the settlement application together with all required documents, including proof of payment, to the SEBI Settlement Division within 7 calendar days** from the date of successful payment. The form specifically directs applicants to review the **SEBI Circular dated June 18, 2019** before filing, and it is designed for multiple settlement pathways, including **Summary Settlement (SS), Suo Motu (SM), Pre-SCN, Post-SCN, Post-Appeal, Post-SAT Order, and Settlement with Confidentiality (SC)**. The application requires the applicant to identify the relevant proceeding by entering items such as the **Show Cause Notice number/date, Summary Settlement Notice number/date, SAT Appeal number, and Appeal number**, depending on the application type.

For the applicant details section, the form requires entry of the **name, PAN, applicant type (Individual or Body Corporate), and proposed settlement amount**, and it expressly states that the **settlement amount cannot be less than Rs. 3 lakhs** under the Settlement Regulations. The applicant must upload **certified true copies** of supporting tax and identity documents, including **ITRs for the last 3 financial years** in PDF format up to **20 MB** and a **PAN card copy** in PDF format up to **500 KB**. It also requires correspondence details such as **GST number, state/territory, phone number (must be 10 digits), primary email address, and alternate email addresses**; the form notes that the **primary email address will be used for all communications** with the entity.

The attachments section requires certified true copies of the principal case documents, including **Form-A**, the **Summary Settlement Notice**, the **Show Cause Notice**, the **SAT Appeal**, **any orders passed**, and **any other relevant document**, with each upload limited to **PDF files up to 20 MB**. The form also includes fields for **Settlement Application UID**, **Type of Category**, and fee/payment fields such as **Application Fees (in Rs.), CGST, SGST, IGST, and Payment Status**, indicating that tax components are calculated or recorded as part of the filing process. In practical compliance terms, this means the filing is not complete upon payment alone: the applicant must ensure the online submission is followed promptly by the hard-copy package, all prescribed documents are included, the minimum settlement amount threshold is met, and the required identifiers and jurisdiction/contact details are accurately provided to avoid rejection or processing delays.

rows.title: Settlement Calculator BETA
rows.summary:
This document is a “Settlement Calculator BETA” intended to help applicants estimate an indicative settlement amount under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Settlement Proceedings Regulations, 2018, using the computation matrix in Schedule II and the factors in Regulation 10. It makes clear that the calculator is only advisory: the final settlement amount can be modified by the Internal Committee (IC), the High Powered Advisory Committee (HPAC), or the Panel of Whole Time Members (WTMs), and in some cases non-monetary settlement terms may also be imposed under Regulation 9. The settlement amount is made up of the indicative amount (IA), and the IA must not be less than ₹3 lakh for a first-time applicant or ₹7 lakh for any other applicant; a “first-time applicant” is defined as someone against whom no order has ever been passed by SEBI’s adjudicating officer or Board and who has never obtained a settlement order from SEBI as of the date of the current application.

The document requires the IA to be calculated using a proceeding conversion factor (PCF) based on the stage of the case when the application is made, and the IA is computed per count of default, either jointly or separately depending on the facts. If a person’s business has been corporatized, converted into an LLP or partnership, or merged/taken over by new management, the record of the old entity is treated as the record of the new entity; related issues such as insolvency, name changes, or changes in management/ownership are to be handled according to any SEBI guidance issued from time to time. For voluntary applications or applications seeking confidentiality, an entity can obtain a lower PCF only if, before receiving any show-cause notice, it itself informs SEBI of the default (“intimation defaults”) and cooperates in any investigation, inquiry, inspection, or audit; in that case the application is treated as if made “pre-issue of notice to show cause” for PCF purposes.

The calculator and settlement process rely on the alleged defaults described in the relevant inspection report, investigation report, report of the designated authority, show-cause notice, supplementary show-cause notice, or in the findings/order of a Designated Member, Whole Time Member, Adjudicating Officer, or Securities Appellate Tribunal, as applicable. However, the IC/HPAC/WTM panel may conclude that the facts show a different default and may seek modification of the charge(s), and it can also re-categorize alleged defaults based on the facts and circumstances. The document also gives these bodies broad discretion to accept or reject an application and to recommend a settlement amount either lower or higher than the amount produced by the calculator, but they must record reasons and act consistently with securities law and the gravity of the charges.

For body corporates, the IC/HPAC/WTM panel may require the settlement amount to be paid by officers in default, including persons in charge, so that the burden is not placed on investors holding the issuer’s securities. The same principle may be applied, mutatis mutandis, to the sponsor, manager, or trustee of a trust, the karta of a Hindu Undivided Family, and office bearers of an association of persons. Finally, if the formulae in the schedule cannot be applied or adapted because of the peculiar nature of the default or because the default is not covered by the tables in the calculator, the settlement authority has discretion to deal with the matter outside the standard formula framework.

rows.title: Adjudication Order in the matter of Fast Track Finsec Private Limited
rows.summary:

INM000012500), covering the period April 1, 2020 to December 31, 2021, to test compliance with the Merchant Bankers Regulations, CAPSM Regulations, SAST Regulations, ICDR Regulations, and related SEBI circulars. Based on prima facie findings, SEBI initiated adjudication on July 22, 2024 and appointed an Adjudicating Officer on March 18, 2025 under Sections 15-I, 15A(a), and 15HB of the SEBI Act and the SEBI Adjudication Rules. The show-cause notice dated April 21, 2025 alleged violations across ten areas: irregularities in the IPO of Trekkingtoes.com Limited; irregularities in five open offers/takeovers involving KD Leisures Limited, AKM Lace and Embrotex Limited, Spaceage Products Limited, Specular Marketing and Finance Limited, and Oracle Credit Limited; irregularities in periodic reports; failure to disclose track record on the company’s website; non-compliance with merchant banker certification requirements; and deficiencies in the internal code of conduct.

In its reply dated May 3, 2025, the noticee said it had already given a detailed response in a prior letter dated May 10, 2022 and asked that it be treated as reiterated. It also argued that penalties had already been imposed in related matters under Adjudicating Order No. Order/MC/RM/2021-22/14794 dated January 27, 2022 (penalty of INR 2,00,000, paid on January 28, 2022) and Order No. Order/SM/DD/2021-22/15644 dated March 28, 2022 (penalty of INR 6,00,000, paid on June 17, 2022). The noticee further pointed to an interim order dated January 24, 2022 restraining it from taking up any new merchant banking assignment in the securities market until further orders, stating that it had already remained under restraint for one year and implying that additional punishment would be duplicative. rows.title: Deposits and Accounts – Accounts of Non-resident banks
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/251 A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 20 September 02, 2026 To All Authorised Dealer Category-I banks Madam / Sir Deposits and Accounts – Accounts of Non-resident banks Please refer to Para B.2(ii) and B.8(i) of Part B of the A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No.92, dated April 4, 2003, in terms of which AD banks were required to: a. Furnish an up-to-date list of all its offices/branches maintaining Rupee accounts of non-resident banks, as at the end of December each year before 15th January of the following year to the Central Office of Reserve Bank, and b. Report temporary overdrawals by overseas branches/ correspondents over permissible limit, if not adjusted within five days, to the Central Office of Reserve Bank. 2. On a review, it has been decided to dispense with the above reporting requirements with immediate effect. 3. The directions contained in this circular have been issued under sections 10(4) and 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (42 of 1999) and are without prejudice to permissions/approvals, if any, required under any other law. Yours faithfully (N. Senthil Kumar) Chief General Manager
rows.summary: This RBI circular, issued to all Authorised Dealer Category-I banks on September 2, 2026, removes two reporting obligations that previously applied under Para B.2(ii) and B.8(i) of A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 92 dated April 4, 2003. First, AD banks no longer need to furnish to the Reserve Bank’s Central Office an annual up-to-date list of all offices/branches maintaining rupee accounts of non-resident banks as of the end of December by January 15 of the following year. Second, AD banks no longer need to report temporary overdrawals by overseas branches/correspondents beyond the permissible limit if those overdrawals are not adjusted within five days. The change takes effect immediately, meaning the reporting requirements are dispensed with as of September 2, 2026, and no new substitute filing, threshold, or approval process is introduced in this circular. The circular is issued under sections 10(4) and 11(1) of the FEMA, 1999, and it states that the change is without prejudice to any permissions or approvals that may still be required under other applicable laws.

rows.title: Relief Measures in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities - Reporting through Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) Portal - Introduction of Half-Yearly Return
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/250 CO.FIDD.FSD.No.S544/05-10-001/2026-27 September 02, 2026 The Chief Executive Officer / Managing Director All Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks) All Local Area Banks/ Urban Cooperative Banks/ Rural Cooperative Banks/ Non- Banking Financial Companies / AIFIs Madam / Dear Sir, Relief Measures in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities - Reporting through Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) Portal - Introduction of Half- Yearly Return The regulatory framework governing the relief measures to be extended by the Regulated Entities (REs) in areas affected by natural calamities has been revised vide the amendment directions on Resolution of Stressed Assets dated April 29, 2026 (list enclosed), which came into effect from July 1, 2026. 2. These directions require REs to submit data relating to relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities through the CIMS portal on a half-yearly basis. Accordingly, in order to align the existing reporting mechanism with the revised regulatory framework, REs shall furnish the required information in the revised reporting format through the CIMS portal. 3. The return shall be submitted within 30 days from the end of each half-year, i.e., by October 30 for the half-year ending September 30, and by April 30 for the half-year ending March 31. 4. REs shall ensure that the information submitted through the CIMS portal is accurate, complete, and duly validated. Appropriate internal systems and processes may be 2 established to facilitate timely collection, verification, consolidation, and submission of the required information. 5. Further, the existing monthly return which was applicable to all Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Small Finance Banks and excluding Regional Rural Banks) on relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities stands discontinued with effect from July 1, 2026. Yours sincerely, (R Giridharan) Chief General Manager 3 The detailed guidelines on the Amendments Directions on Resolution of Stressed Assets with respect to Relief Measures by Banks in Areas affected by Natural Calamities may be accessed through the following links: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Amendment Directions, 2026 479 kb Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Amendment Directions, 2026 437 kb Reserve Bank of India (Rural Cooperative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Amendment Directions, 2026 467 kb Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Amendment Directions, 2026 463 kb Reserve Bank of India (Urban Cooperative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Second Amendment Directions, 2026 436 kb Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Amendment Directions, 2026 467 kb Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Amendment Directions, 2026 467 kb Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Second Amendment Directions, 2026 443 kb
rows.summary:
The RBI has revised the reporting framework for relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities, following the amendment directions on Resolution of Stressed Assets issued on April 29, 2026, which became effective on July 1, 2026. Regulated entities (REs) must now report this information through the Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) portal using a revised reporting format, and the reporting frequency has been changed to a half-yearly return.

The new return must be filed within 30 days after the end of each half-year: by October 30 for the half-year ending September 30, and by April 30 for the half-year ending March 31. RBI specifically requires that the data submitted through CIMS be accurate, complete, and duly validated, and expects institutions to put in place appropriate internal systems and processes for timely collection, verification, consolidation, and submission of the information.

This applies to all Regulated Entities covered by the revised framework, including Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks), Local Area Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, Rural Cooperative Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies, and All India Financial Institutions. A key compliance change is that the existing monthly return requirement for Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Small Finance Banks, but excluding Regional Rural Banks) on relief measures in natural calamity-affected areas has been discontinued effective July 1, 2026.

In practical terms, compliance teams should ensure their reporting processes are updated to the new half-yearly CIMS submission cycle, confirm the revised format is in use, and retire any legacy monthly reporting workflow that was previously applicable to the covered commercial banks. The notice also points readers to the relevant amended RBI directions for each entity type, which form the underlying substantive framework for the relief measures being reported.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Second Amendment Directions, 2026
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/249 DOR.MRG.REC.No.217/00-00-011/2026-27 September 2, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Second Amendment Directions, 2026 Please refer to Chapter VIII of Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025, on Investment in non-SLR securities. In view of the establishment of Indian Digital Payment Intelligence Corporation (IDPIC) as the nation's central digital payment fraud intelligence platform and to enable UCBs to acquire its membership, there is a need to amend the extant instructions. 2. Accordingly, in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (hereinafter called the Act), read with Section 56 thereof, and all other laws enabling the Reserve Bank in this regard, the Reserve Bank, being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in the public interest so to do, hereby, issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. (i) These Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Second Amendment Directions, 2026. (ii) These Amendment Directions shall come into effect from the date of issue. 4. The Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025, are amended as provided below. (i) Paragraph 101.(5) shall be substituted by the following, namely:- “101.(5) Equity shares of Umbrella Organization (UO) of UCB sector and Indian Digital Payment Intelligence Corporation (IDPIC) for acquiring membership;”. (ii) Paragraph 107.(1) shall be substituted by the following, namely:- “107.(1) Equity shares of Market Infrastructure Companies (MICs), Umbrella Organization (UO) of UCB Sector, IDPIC, and CCBs / StCBs, if it becomes necessary to do so for acquiring membership of these entities;”. (Sunil T S Nair) Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Second Amendment Directions, 2026** update the **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio Directions, 2025**, specifically the provisions dealing with **investment in non-SLR securities**. The change is made because the RBI notes the establishment of the **Indian Digital Payment Intelligence Corporation (IDPIC)** as the country’s central digital payment fraud intelligence platform, and the amendment is intended to allow **UCBs to acquire membership in IDPIC**.

The amendment takes effect **immediately from the date of issue, September 2, 2026**. It is issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and it formally amends the 2025 Directions.

Substantively, **paragraph 101(5)** is replaced so that UCBs may invest in **equity shares of the Umbrella Organization (UO) of the UCB sector and of IDPIC, but only for the purpose of acquiring membership**. This is a narrower, membership-linked permission rather than a general investment authorization.

In addition, **paragraph 107(1)** is replaced to permit **equity shares of Market Infrastructure Companies (MICs), the UO of the UCB sector, IDPIC, and CCBs/StCBs**, again **only if necessary to acquire membership of those entities**. For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that UCBs now have an explicit RBI-sanctioned basis to make limited equity investments in IDPIC, and the existing investment rules must be applied with the condition that the holding is tied to membership acquisition rather than ordinary portfolio investment.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Second Amendment Directions, 2026**, effective **immediately on August 25, 2026**. This amendment applies to the prior **Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025** (updated as of June 17, 2026) and changes the end date of a temporary deposit-rate relaxation from **September 30, 2026** to **August 31, 2026**.

Substantively, the temporary measure being shortened is the RBI’s **withdrawal of the interest rate ceiling on fresh FCNR(B) deposits with 3–5 year tenors** and the associated **restriction on interest rates for NRE deposits of 3 years and above, including renewals upon maturity**, which had been granted starting **June 17, 2026**. Under this amendment, those relaxed rules continue to apply only **through August 31, 2026**, instead of through the end of September.

The amendment specifically revises **paragraph 24(4) footnote (1)** and **paragraph 29(7) footnote (2)** of the 2025 Directions by replacing the phrase **“with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until September 30, 2026”** with **“with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until August 31, 2026.”** No other substantive changes are stated in the text.

For compliance purposes, rural co-operative banks that are relying on this temporary relaxation must ensure their deposit-rate offering and renewal practices for the affected **FCNR(B)** and **NRE** tenors are aligned to the shortened expiry date, and they should cease applying the temporary treatment after **August 31, 2026** unless further RBI relief is issued.

Specifically, the earlier temporary measure that had applied **from June 17, 2026 until September 30, 2026** is now revised to run **only until August 31, 2026**.

This change affects **urban co-operative banks** and relates to two deposit categories already covered in the 2025 Directions: **fresh FCNR(B) deposits of 3–5 year tenors** and **NRE deposits of 3 years and above tenors, including renewals upon maturity**. The document does not change the substance of those temporary relaxations themselves; it only **advances the end date** of the relaxation period by one month, from **September 30, 2026 to August 31, 2026**.

Specifically, under the underlying **Directions dated November 28, 2025 (updated June 17, 2026)**, local area banks had been allowed a temporary withdrawal of the interest rate ceiling on **fresh FCNR(B) deposits with 3–5 year tenors** and a restriction on interest rates on **NRE deposits with tenors of 3 years and above**, including deposits renewed at maturity, effective **June 17, 2026** and originally continuing until **September 30, 2026**.

This amendment shortens that temporary period by replacing **“September 30, 2026” with “August 31, 2026”** in the relevant provisions of the Directions. The change is made in **paragraph 26(4), subscript (1)** and **paragraph 31(7), subscript (2)**, both of which now state that the relaxation applies **from June 17, 2026 through August 31, 2026** instead of through September 30, 2026.

The amendment is issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and takes **immediate effect** on **August 25, 2026**. The change applies in two places in the 2025 Directions: **paragraph 27(4) footnote (1)** and **paragraph 32(7) footnote (2)**, both of which now read that the temporary measure is effective **from June 17, 2026, until August 31, 2026** instead of until September 30, 2026.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/242 DOR.RET.REC.209/12.01.001/2026-27 August 25, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026 Please refer to the Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (updated as on June 19, 2026) wherein exemption from CRR and SLR maintenance have been provided to fresh FCNR(B) deposits of minimum tenor of three years and maximum tenor of five years and fresh Non-Resident (External) Rupee (NRE) term deposits of tenor of three years or more mobilized (including deposits that are renewed upon maturity) by the banks between June 8, 2026 to September 30, 2026 and June 19, 2026 to September 30, 2026 respectively. On review, it has been decided to amend the date “September 30, 2026” to the date “August 31, 2026” for the aforesaid exemptions. 2. Accordingly, in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and pursuant to Section 42 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and Sections 18 and 24, read with section 56 (AACS), of Banking Regulation Act, 1949, as amended from time to time, and all other provisions / laws enabling the Reserve Bank of India in this regard, the Reserve Bank being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in the public interest so to do, hereby, issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. These Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026. 4. The provisions shall come into force with immediate effect. 2 5. These Amendment Directions modify the Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 as under: i. In paragraph 21(5), the words “between June 8, 2026 and September 30, 2026” shall be substituted with “between June 8, 2026 and August 31, 2026”. ii. In paragraph 21(6), the words “between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026” shall be substituted with “between June 19, 2026 and August 31, 2026”. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** for **rural co-operative banks** revise the earlier **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) Directions, 2025** (updated June 19, 2026) by **shortening the availability window** for certain CRR/SLR exemptions on specified fresh deposits. Specifically, the RBI had previously exempted from CRR and SLR maintenance: **fresh FCNR(B) deposits** with a minimum tenor of **3 years** and maximum tenor of **5 years** mobilized by banks **between June 8, 2026 and September 30, 2026**, and **fresh NRE term deposits** with a tenor of **3 years or more** (including deposits renewed on maturity) mobilized **between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026**.

Under this amendment, the end date for both exemption windows is moved earlier from **September 30, 2026** to **August 31, 2026**. As a result, only deposits mobilized within the amended periods—**June 8, 2026 to August 31, 2026** for FCNR(B) deposits and **June 19, 2026 to August 31, 2026** for NRE term deposits—continue to qualify for the exemption from CRR and SLR maintenance.

The amendment is issued under the RBI’s statutory powers, including **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, **Section 42 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**, and **Sections 18 and 24 read with section 56(AACS) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. It is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** and states that it takes effect **immediately** upon issuance, dated **August 25, 2026**.

For compliance purposes, rural co-operative banks must therefore ensure that only deposits meeting the original tenor conditions **and** placed within the revised dates through **August 31, 2026** are treated as exempt for CRR/SLR calculation purposes. Any FCNR(B) or NRE deposits mobilized after **August 31, 2026** will no longer fall within the exemption window created by the 2025 Directions as amended.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026**, effective **immediately on August 25, 2026**. This amendment applies to **urban co-operative banks** subject to the RBI’s CRR/SLR framework under the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025**.

The only substantive change is a **shortening of the qualifying period** for the existing CRR and SLR exemptions on certain new deposits. For **fresh FCNR(B) deposits** with a **minimum tenor of 3 years and maximum tenor of 5 years**, including deposits renewed on maturity, the exemption window is changed from deposits mobilized **between June 8, 2026 and September 30, 2026** to deposits mobilized **between June 8, 2026 and August 31, 2026**. For **fresh NRE term deposits** with a tenor of **3 years or more**, including deposits renewed on maturity, the exemption window is similarly changed from **June 19, 2026 to September 30, 2026** to **June 19, 2026 to August 31, 2026**.

Practically, banks covered by these directions must apply the CRR/SLR exemption only to qualifying deposits booked within the revised date ranges; deposits mobilized after **August 31, 2026** will not qualify under these exemption provisions. No other thresholds, rates, or procedural changes are introduced in this amendment.

Specifically, the exemption from both Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio maintenance for fresh FCNR(B) deposits with a minimum tenor of three years and maximum tenor of five years now applies only to deposits mobilized between June 8, 2026 and August 31, 2026, instead of through September 30, 2026. For compliance purposes, regional rural banks must ensure their CRR/SLR calculations and deposit classification systems reflect the revised cutoff date, and they should stop treating any FCNR(B) or qualifying NRE deposits mobilized after August 31, 2026 as eligible for these specific exemptions.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** for **Small Finance Banks’ Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** shortens the eligibility window for certain deposit exemptions. Under the underlying 2025 Directions, RBI had granted **exemption from CRR and SLR maintenance** for **fresh FCNR(B) deposits** with a **minimum tenor of 3 years and maximum tenor of 5 years** and for **fresh NRE term deposits** with a **tenor of 3 years or more**, including deposits renewed on maturity, if mobilized within specified periods. This amendment changes the end date for those exemption windows from **September 30, 2026** to **August 31, 2026**.

Specifically, the exemption period for the **FCNR(B)** category is now **June 8, 2026 through August 31, 2026** (instead of through September 30, 2026), and the exemption period for the **NRE term deposit** category is now **June 19, 2026 through August 31, 2026** (instead of through September 30, 2026). The change is made by amending paragraphs **20(6)** and **20(7)** of the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025**.

The amendment was issued under RBI’s powers, including **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934**, and **Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. It took effect **immediately upon issuance on August 25, 2026**. For compliance purposes, small finance banks should treat **August 31, 2026** as the final date for deposits to qualify for the CRR/SLR exemption under these two categories, and deposits mobilized after that date will not fall within the amended exemption window.

rows.summary: The Reserve Bank of India’s Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026, issued on August 25, 2026, shorten the temporary CRR and SLR exemption window previously granted to commercial banks for certain fresh long-term NRI deposits. Under the underlying 2025 Directions, fresh FCNR(B) deposits with a minimum tenor of three years and a maximum tenor of five years were exempt from cash reserve ratio and statutory liquidity ratio maintenance if mobilized by banks between June 8, 2026 and September 30, 2026, and fresh NRE term deposits with a tenor of three years or more were similarly exempt if mobilized (including renewals upon maturity) between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026. The change is made under the RBI’s powers under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, read with Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934 and Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, and it applies specifically to commercial banks subject to the CRR and SLR Directions, 2025. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** on **August 25, 2026**, and they take **immediate effect**. The amendment was made under the RBI’s statutory powers and specifically revises the **large exposure framework** for **Infrastructure Debt Fund–Non-Banking Financial Companies (IDF-NBFCs)** that fall within the **Upper Layer** regulatory category.  

The sole substantive change is the insertion of a new **paragraph 39A** after paragraph 39 in Chapter IV of the existing **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025**. This new paragraph states that the **large exposure limits applicable to NBFC-IFCs** will also apply to **IDF-NBFCs subject to Upper Layer regulation**, as determined under **paragraph 60A of the RBI (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025**, read with **paragraph 18(4)(i) of the RBI (Commercial Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025**.  

For compliance purposes, this means affected IDF-NBFCs in the Upper Layer must now monitor and comply with the same concentration-risk / large-exposure caps and related controls that already apply to NBFC-IFCs, effective immediately, with no transition period stated in the amendment. The document does not introduce new numeric thresholds in the text itself; instead, it imports the existing NBFC-IFC large exposure limits by reference into the IDF-NBFC Upper Layer framework.

rows.title: Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1267/ 1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List: Amendment of 21 Entries
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/236 DOR.AML.REC.204/14.06.001/2026-27 August 19, 2026 The Chairpersons/ CEOs of the Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, Rural Co-operative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Local Area Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, All India Financial Institutions Madam/Dear Sir, Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1267/ 1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List: Amendment of 21 Entries Please refer to Chapter IX on “Requirements/obligations under International Agreements - Communications from International Agencies” of the Reserve Bank of India - Know Your Customer, Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025 (amended as on December 29, 2025) (“Directions”), as applicable, as per which, regulated entity shall ensure that in terms of section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) (UAPA) Act, 1967 and amendments thereto, it does not have any account in the name of individuals / entities appearing in the lists of individuals and entities, suspected of having terrorist links, which are approved by and periodically circulated by the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). 2. In this connection, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Government of India has informed about the UNSC press release SC/16435, dated August 18, 2026 wherein the Security Council pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da’esh), Al‑Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities enacted the amendments specified with strikethrough and underline in the entries mentioned in Annexure 1 on its ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List of individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2734 (2024), and adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations. 2 3. Press release dated August 18, 2026 regarding the above can be found at https://press.un.org/en/2026/sc16435.doc.htm Further, in accordance with paragraph 61 of resolution 2734 (2024), the Committee has made accessible on its website the narrative summaries of reasons for listing of the above entries at the following URL: https://main.un.org/securitycouncil/en/sanctions/1267/aq_sanctions_list/summaries 4. The details of the sanction measures and exemptions are available at the following URL: https://www.un.org/securitycouncil/sanctions/1267#further_information 5. In view of the above, regulated entities are advised to take appropriate action in terms of Chapter IX of the aforementioned Directions and strictly follow the procedure as laid down in the UAPA Order dated February 02, 2021 (amended on April 22, 2024) annexed to the Directions. 6. Updated lists of individuals and entities linked to ISIL (Da'esh), Al-Qaida and Taliban are available at: www.un.org/securitycouncil/sanctions/1267/aq_sanctions_list https://www.un.org/securitycouncil/sanctions/1988/materials 7. Further, as per the instructions from the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), any request for de-listing received by any bank is to be forwarded electronically to Joint Secretary (CTCR), MHA for consideration. Individuals, groups, undertakings or entities seeking to be removed from the Security Council’s ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List can submit their request for delisting to an independent and impartial Ombudsperson who has been appointed by the United Nations Secretary-General. More details are available at the following URL: https://www.un.org/securitycouncil/ombudsperson/application 8. Regulated entities are advised to take note of the aforementioned UNSC communications and ensure meticulous compliance. Yours faithfully, (Sirin Kumar) General Manager
rows.summary:
This RBI circular instructs all regulated entities covered by the RBI KYC Directions, 2025 — including commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, urban and rural co-operative banks, regional rural banks, local area banks, NBFCs, asset reconstruction companies, and all India financial institutions — to continue enforcing the section 51A UAPA, 1967 obligations that prohibit maintaining accounts in the names of persons or entities appearing on the UNSC-approved terrorist sanctions lists. The specific update being communicated is the UN Security Council press release SC/16435 dated August 18, 2026, which amended 21 entries on the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al‑Qaida Sanctions List under UNSC resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015), with those individuals/entities subject to asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo measures under resolution 2734 (2024).

Compliance teams are directed to act immediately in accordance with Chapter IX of the RBI KYC Directions, 2025, and to strictly follow the UAPA Order dated February 2, 2021 as amended on April 22, 2024. Practically, this means institutions must screen against the updated UNSC lists, ensure no accounts are held in the names of listed persons/entities, and take appropriate sanctions-response action whenever a match or new listing is identified. RBI also points institutions to the UNSC narrative summaries and sanctions detail pages for identifying information and the scope of the measures/exemptions.

On de-listing, the circular reflects MHA guidance that any delisting request received by a bank must be forwarded electronically to the Joint Secretary (CTCR), Ministry of Home Affairs for consideration. It also notes that listed persons or entities may submit delisting requests to the UN Secretary-General’s independent Ombudsperson. No separate RBI deadline is given for filing actions in this circular, but the operative expectation is immediate and ongoing compliance with the updated UNSC designations and the prescribed UAPA/RBI procedures.

The RBI is reminding regulated entities that, under Chapter IX of the RBI KYC Directions, 2025 (as amended on December 29, 2025), they must continue to ensure compliance with Section 51A of the UAPA, 1967 by not maintaining accounts in the name of any individual or entity appearing on the UNSC-approved sanctions lists circulated under that law. This circular, dated August 18, 2026 (RBI/2026-27/235), specifically conveys a Ministry of External Affairs communication about UNSC press release SC/16433 dated August 14, 2026, which updated the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida sanctions list under resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015), and the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo regime under UNSC resolution 2734 (2024).

The material change is that four list entries have been amended, so compliance teams must ensure their screening systems reflect the updated particulars immediately and that any existing or prospective relationships are re-screened against the revised data. The first amended entry is QDi.002, Amin Muhammad Ul Haq Saam Khan (also known as Amin Al-Haq / Muhammad Amin / Dr. Amin / Dr. Amin Ul-Haq), an Afghan national born on either 30 April 1963 or in 1960, associated with Kabul, Afghanistan as of June 2026; the entry notes his role as security coordinator for Usama bin Laden, that he was repatriated to Afghanistan in February 2006, was in Afghanistan as of August 2021, was arrested in Pakistan in 2024 and deported to Afghanistan in 2025, and that photo and fingerprints are available via the INTERPOL-UN Security Council Special Notice. The second amended entry is QDi.436, Abubakar Swalleh (also listed as Abubaker Swaleh / Tom Kiyurige; low-quality alias Isaac Mupeta), a Ugandan national born on 13 January 1992 or 16 March 1993, with Uganda passport number A00195974 expiring 16 December 2029, national ID CM920231090NZA, and an address at Luzira Prison, Kampala, Uganda; the entry states he provides financial, material, technological, and logistical support to ISIL (listed as Al-Qaida in Iraq/QDe.115), has acted since 2018 as an ISIL facilitator for East and Southern Africa, and includes a phone number (+963936016952) plus an INTERPOL notice reference. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued a directive dated **August 10, 2026** assigning **Lead Bank responsibility** for **five newly created districts in the Union Territory of Ladakh**, following the UT Administration’s **Gazette Notification SG-LD-E-27042026-1712 dated April 27, 2026**. The new districts are **Sham, Nubra, Changthang, Zanskar, and Drass**, and the RBI has designated **State Bank of India (SBI)** as the Lead Bank for **each** of these districts.  

The RBI also allotted a **District Working Code** to each new district for operational use: **Sham – 02Z** (read as zero-two-Z), **Nubra – 03B** (zero-three-B), **Changthang – 03A** (zero-three-A), **Zanskar – 03C** (zero-three-C), and **Drass – 03D** (zero-three-D). The circular does **not** alter the Lead Bank assignments for any of the **existing districts** in Ladakh; it specifically states that there is **no change** for the other districts.  

For compliance purposes, the key action is to ensure all Lead Bank-related records, district mappings, and any internal reporting or monitoring systems for Ladakh are updated to reflect the new district structure and SBI’s responsibility for these five districts, with the above working codes used exactly as specified.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Second Amendment Directions, 2026
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/232 FIDD.CO.PSD.BC.No.08/04.09.001/2026-27 August 07, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Second Amendment Directions, 2026 Please refer to the Governor’s Statement dated June 5, 2026, and RBI circular FMOD.MAOG.No.S-56/01.06.016/2026-27 dated June 08, 2026 on ‘Swap Facility for FCNR (B) Deposits’, wherein it has been decided to introduce a US Dollar-Rupee swap facility for fresh Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) [FCNR (B)] dollar funds, mobilised for a minimum tenor of three years and maximum tenor of five years. 2. Further, reference is also invited to the Reserve Bank of India (Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Second and Third Amendment Directions dated June 08, 2026 and June 19, 2026, as applicable to various banks, wherein exemption has been provided from maintenance of Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio on fresh FCNR (B) deposits of minimum tenor of three years and maximum tenor of five years mobilised (including deposits that are renewed upon maturity) between June 08, 2026 and September 30, 2026, and on fresh Non-Resident (External) Rupee (NRE) term deposits of tenor of three years or more mobilised (including deposits that are renewed upon maturity) between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026. 3. In this connection, please refer to the Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on January 19, 2026). It has been decided that the following advances extended in India will be excluded from calculation of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC): a) advances against the fresh FCNR (B) deposits of minimum tenor of three years and maximum tenor of five years mobilised (including deposits that are renewed upon maturity) by the banks between June 08, 2026 and September 30, 2026, and b) advances against NRE term deposits of three years or more mobilised (including deposits that are renewed upon maturity) by the banks between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026. 2 | Page 4. The Amendment Directions modify the Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Directions, 2025 as below: i. Item no. VI in the table at paragraph 6.1 shall be partially modified as below: Advances extended in India against the incremental fresh FCNR (B) / NRE deposits (including deposits that are renewed upon maturity), qualifying for exemption from Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements, as per the Reserve Bank’s circulars DBOD.No.Ret.BC.36/12.01.001/2013-14 dated August 14, 2013 read with DBOD.No.Ret.BC.93/12.01.001/2013-14 dated January 31, 2014, DBOD mailbox clarification issued on February 6, 2014 and UBD.BPD.(PCB).CIR.No.5/13.01.000/2013-14 dated August 27, 2013 read with UBD.BPD.(PCB).Cir.No.72/13.01.000/ 2013-14 dated June 11, 2014. Reserve Bank of India (Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Second and Third Amendment Directions dated June 08, 2026 and June 19, 2026, as applicable to various banks. Note: The amount to be excluded from ANBC for computation of priority sector targets shall not exceed the fresh FCNR (B) / NRE deposits eligible for exemption from maintenance of CRR / SLR in terms of the above Amendment Directions. ii. Foot note no.3 shall be deleted: The incremental advances extended out of the resources generated from the eligible incremental FCNR(B)/NRE deposits is calculated as the difference between outstanding advances in India as on March 7, 2014 (June 13, 2014, in case of UCBs) and the Base Date (July 26, 2013). The amount to be excluded from ANBC for computation of priority sector targets will not exceed incremental FCNR (B) / NRE deposits eligible for exemption from maintenance of CRR / SLR in terms of the circulars mentioned above. In case, the difference in the amount outstanding is zero or negative, no amount would be eligible for deduction from ANBC for the purpose of arriving at the priority sector lending targets. 5. The above amendment shall come into force with immediate effect. Yours faithfully, (Nisha Nambiar) Chief General Manager-in-Charge
rows.summary:
This RBI amendment revises the Priority Sector Lending (PSL) classification rules so that certain advances made in India against eligible fresh foreign currency/non-resident deposits will be excluded from the calculation of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC), which is the base used for computing priority sector lending targets. Specifically, advances against fresh FCNR(B) dollar deposits with a minimum tenor of 3 years and a maximum tenor of 5 years, mobilised or renewed between June 8, 2026 and September 30, 2026, and advances against NRE term deposits of 3 years or more, mobilised or renewed between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026, are to be excluded from ANBC. This exclusion is tied to the related CRR/SLR exemption regime introduced by the RBI’s June 8, 2026 and June 19, 2026 directions, meaning the amount excluded from ANBC cannot exceed the amount of fresh FCNR(B)/NRE deposits that actually qualify for CRR/SLR exemption under those circulars.

The amendment changes paragraph 6.1, item VI of the 2025 PSL Directions by replacing the prior language with a narrower rule focused on “incremental fresh FCNR(B) / NRE deposits” that are eligible for CRR/SLR exemption under the listed RBI circulars and amendment directions. It also deletes footnote 3, which had contained the earlier methodology for calculating incremental advances using a comparison to the bank’s outstanding advances on March 7, 2014 (or June 13, 2014 for UCBs) versus the base date of July 26, 2013; that prior formula and zero/negative-difference limitation are removed from the directions. In practical terms, banks should stop using the deleted footnote methodology and instead apply the new exclusion rule only to the eligible incremental deposit-linked advances described in the amended text, subject to the cap that excluded amounts cannot exceed the qualifying deposit base.

The amendment is effective immediately as of August 7, 2026. It applies to advances extended in India by banks that fall within the PSL framework and affects compliance calculations for priority sector target achievement by reducing ANBC to the extent of the eligible exclusions. Banks should ensure their PSL reporting, ANBC computation, and related deposit-linked advance tracking reflect the eligible date windows, tenor requirements, and the direct linkage to CRR/SLR-exempt FCNR(B)/NRE deposits.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) Third Amendment Directions, 2026** replace the existing HFC-specific recovery-agent guidance in Chapter X (“Fair Practices Code”) of the **RBI (Housing Finance Companies) Directions, 2025**. Specifically, **sub-section A.15 “Guidelines for engaging Recovery Agents” and paragraph 170 are deleted** and replaced with a new provision, **A.15A “Conduct of HFCs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agents”**, which directs every HFC to comply with **paragraphs 100A.2 to 100AB of Chapter III** of the **RBI (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025**.

The practical effect is that HFCs must now follow the RBI’s broader, comprehensive conduct standards for recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies that apply to NBFCs under the Responsible Business Conduct framework, rather than the prior standalone HFC recovery-agent instructions. The document also states that the earlier, more general instructions on recovery-agent conduct for HFCs had been reviewed in light of this broader framework.

These amendment directions are issued under **Section 30A of the National Housing Bank Act, 1987** and become **effective on January 1, 2027**. No numerical thresholds, rates, or deadlines beyond the commencement date are introduced in this amendment, but compliance teams should treat this as a mandatory incorporation by reference of the NBFC conduct requirements for HFC recovery practices and agent engagement from that date forward.

rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Responsible Business Conduct) Third Amendment Directions, 2026** overhaul the framework governing **recovery of loan dues and the use of recovery agencies/agents** by NBFCs. The RBI states that it has reviewed the existing recovery-agent instructions and is replacing them with **comprehensive conduct requirements** for all **NBFCs**, except **Mortgage Guarantee Companies, Core Investment Companies, NBFC-Account Aggregators, Standalone Primary Dealers, Non-Operating Financial Holding Companies, and NBFCs with no customer interface**. The amendment is issued under **Sections 45JA, 45L and 45M of the RBI Act, 1934** and **takes effect on January 1, 2027**.

The amendment adds formal definitions that matter for outsourcing governance: a **“recovery agency”** is any entity or individual other than the NBFC’s own employees that is engaged under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues from a defaulting borrower, **including taking possession of security**; a **“recovery agent”** is the representative of that agency who performs recovery-related activities **at the point of customer interface**. The text makes clear that if an **individual is directly engaged by an NBFC** under an outsourcing arrangement for recovery or possession-related work, then **all rules applicable to both the recovery agency and recovery agent apply to that individual**.

The amendment also removes earlier provisions in the 2025 Directions: **paragraphs 26, 27, and 89 to 97** in Chapter III are deleted, along with the prior **Section I on “Responsibilities of Recovery Agents of the NBFC”** and paragraphs **98 to 100** under it. In their place, RBI inserts a new **Section J: “Conduct of NBFCs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agencies”**, which applies to recovery of loan dues from borrowers in default, **including possession of security**. Where explicitly stated, it also applies **mutatis mutandis** to **normal-course collection from non-defaulting borrowers**. The new section also clarifies that it does **not override statutory enforcement rights** or any other recovery-related directions, including special recovery actions such as **one-time settlement**.

From a compliance standpoint, the new requirements begin with a mandatory **board-/management-level policy** on collection and recovery. Every affected NBFC must have a policy covering recovery by both **its own employees and recovery agents**, and that policy must address: the **triggers for starting recovery**, a **graded escalation matrix**, **codes of conduct** for employees and agents, handling recovery when the **borrower has died**, and a **structured framework for financially distressed customers**, including **documented pre-escalation engagement** and guidance on available resolution options. The policy must also set out the NBFC’s standards for **engaging recovery agencies**, including **eligibility and due diligence criteria**, **performance evaluation**, **inspection/audit/control mechanisms** for legal and regulatory compliance, and **procedures and penalties** for non-compliant agencies or agents. The new section continues beyond the excerpt, but the portions shown already make clear that NBFCs must tighten vendor oversight, document escalation and resolution processes, and ensure recovery practices are governed by a formal policy well before the **January 1, 2027** effective date.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Third Amendment Directions, 2026 revise the RBI’s existing “All India Financial Institutions – Responsible Business Conduct” framework and apply to all All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) from **January 1, 2027**. The key change is that RBI is replacing the prior, narrower instructions on recovery agents with a **comprehensive set of conduct requirements for recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies**, including both collection from defaulting borrowers and, where specifically stated, certain collection activities in the normal course from non-defaulting borrowers.

A new set of definitions is added to the RBI directions. A **“recovery agency”** is defined broadly as any entity or individual, other than the AIFI’s own employees, engaged under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues from a defaulting borrower, **including taking possession of security**, regardless of the contractual label used. A **“recovery agent”** is a representative of such a recovery agency who interacts with the customer on behalf of the AIFI. The amendment also makes clear that if an individual is directly engaged by the AIFI under outsourcing for recovery or possession-related work, then the rules for both recovery agencies and recovery agents apply to that individual.

Paragraph 32 of Chapter III is deleted and replaced with a new section on **“Conduct of AIFIs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agencies.”** This section applies to recovery from borrowers in default, including possession of security, and—only when expressly stated—also applies mutatis mutandis to certain collection activities from borrowers who are not in default. It is also stated to be **without prejudice to the AIFI’s statutory rights and obligations** relating to enforcement of security under other laws, and without affecting separate provisions on specific recovery actions such as one-time settlements contained in other RBI directions. For this section, “AIFI employees” is expanded to include employees deployed for recovery work, including possession of security.

Every AIFI must now have a **formal policy on collection/recovery of loan dues** by its own employees or recovery agents. That policy must address, at a minimum: when recovery actions are triggered; a **graded escalation matrix** for recovery; a **code of conduct** for employees and recovery agents; procedures for recovery in the event of a borrower’s death; and a **structured framework for financially distressed borrowers**, including documented pre-escalation engagement and guidance on available resolution options. The policy must also set out **eligibility and due diligence criteria** for appointing recovery agencies, performance standards, inspection/audit and control mechanisms to ensure statutory and regulatory compliance, and the procedures and penalties to be applied if recovery agencies or their agents are non-compliant.

The policy must further include rules for **compensation to borrowers and guarantors** for losses arising from recovery-related actions by the AIFI or its recovery agencies when those actions are not consistent with the RBI directions. In addition, where an AIFI uses a **technology-based recovery mechanism** under the later-referenced paragraph 32.1S, the institution must incorporate the related requirements and restrictions into this policy as well. Overall, the amendment is intended to make AIFIs responsible not just for appointing recovery intermediaries, but for governing their conduct, monitoring compliance, and remedying harm caused by improper recovery practices.

It replaces the earlier, narrower recovery-agent instructions by inserting a new dedicated section in Chapter VIII and deleting the prior paragraphs **369 to 378**.

A **“recovery agency”** is defined as any entity or individual, other than the RCB’s own employees, engaged under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues from a borrower in default, **including taking possession of security**, regardless of the contract label used. The circular expressly states that a **Business Correspondent (BC)** involved in recovery-related activities on behalf of an RCB is treated as a recovery agency. A **“recovery agent”** is defined as the representative of a recovery agency who performs recovery activities at the point of customer interface; where an individual is directly engaged by the RCB under outsourcing for recovery or possession-related work, the rules applying to both recovery agency and recovery agent apply to that person.

The new section applies to **recovery of loan dues from borrowers in default**, including possession of secured assets, and—where explicitly stated—also to **collection of dues in the normal course from borrowers who are not in default**. It is also made clear that these provisions do **not** override any statutory rights or obligations relating to security enforcement under other laws, and they are separate from other recovery frameworks such as one-time settlement provisions in other Directions. For these purposes, **“RCB employees”** includes employees deployed for recovery activities, including taking possession of security.

The amendment also makes clear that the new section applies to SFB employees involved in recovery and possession work, by defining **“SFB employees”** for this purpose to include employees deployed for those activities. In exercise of the powers conferred by Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act,1949, the Reserve Bank, being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in public interest so to do, hereby issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. Short Title and Commencement (1) These Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** applies to **all Commercial Banks except Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, Regional Rural Banks, and Local Area Banks**. It **comes into effect on January 1, 2027** and replaces the earlier piecemeal instructions on recovery agents with a more comprehensive framework governing **recovery of loan dues, possession of security, and engagement of recovery agencies**. The RBI has issued these changes under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.

The amendment first introduces two key defined terms into the Directions. A **“recovery agency”** is any entity or individual, other than the bank’s own employees, engaged by a bank under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovering loan dues from a borrower in default, including taking possession of security; the definition explicitly says that a **Business Correspondent (BC)** involved in recovery-related work for a bank is treated as a recovery agency for these purposes. A **“recovery agent”** is the representative of such a recovery agency who interacts directly with customers at the point of customer interface. If an individual is directly engaged by the bank under an outsourcing arrangement for recovery or possession-related work, that person is subject to the requirements applicable to both recovery agencies and recovery agents.

The amendment then **deletes paragraphs 408 to 416 and 442 to 454** of Chapter VIII on Responsible Lending Conduct and inserts a new section titled **“Conduct of Banks in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agencies.”** This new section applies to **recovery of loan dues from borrowers in default, including taking possession of security**, and, where expressly stated, also applies **mutatis mutandis to dues collection from borrowers who are not in default**. It also makes clear that these provisions are **without prejudice to any statutory enforcement rights or obligations under other laws** and do not override other Directions dealing with specific recovery actions such as **one-time settlement**.

Under the new section, a bank must have a formal **policy on collection/recovery of loan dues and possession of security** by both its own employees and recovery agents. That policy must specify, at minimum, the **trigger points for starting recovery**, a **graded escalation matrix** for recovery actions, a **code of conduct** for employees and recovery agents, procedures for cases involving the **death of a borrower**, and a **structured framework for dealing with financial distress**, including documented pre-escalation engagement and guidance on available resolution options. The policy must also cover the **eligibility and due diligence standards** for appointing recovery agencies, their **performance evaluation criteria**, **inspection/audit/control mechanisms** to ensure compliance with legal and regulatory requirements, and the **procedures and penalties** for dealing with non-compliant recovery agencies or their agents.

The amendment further requires the policy to include provisions for **compensating borrowers or guarantors for losses arising from recovery-related actions** of the bank or its recovery agencies that are not in compliance with applicable requirements, and it is clear from the structure of the inserted section that the RBI expects banks to tighten governance over outsourcing, borrower treatment, escalation discipline, and remedy mechanisms. Although the excerpt cuts off before the remainder of paragraph 454F and any additional paragraphs, the material change is already clear: banks will need to review and likely revise their recovery and outsourcing policies, staff and agent conduct rules, due diligence and monitoring processes, and borrower-redress/compensation arrangements so they are compliant by **1 January 2027**.
