rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they are stated to take **immediate effect**. The directions are issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (including **Sections 23 and 35A**) and apply specifically to **payments banks** in relation to branch and outlet authorisation, off-site service points, BC/BF arrangements, doorstep banking, and reporting. Although the excerpt provided cuts off before the full “Applicability” section, the title and chapter structure make clear that this is a sector-specific framework governing how payments banks may open and operate physical and service delivery touchpoints.

At a compliance level, the document replaces prior branch-authorisation rules for payments banks and organizes the rules around a required **board-approved policy** and the board’s oversight responsibilities. Payments banks must have board-approved governance covering where and how banking outlets, branches, offices, customer service points, and related service channels can be opened or operated, and management must ensure the bank follows the RBI’s prescribed process rather than treating outlet expansion as a purely operational decision. The directions also cover the use of **business facilitators (BFs)** and **business correspondents (BCs)**, which means a payments bank that uses third parties for customer acquisition or service delivery must ensure eligibility checks, engagement standards, and ongoing controls are in place.

The chapter on **banking outlet authorisation** indicates that RBI has prescribed when and how payments banks can open outlets, branches, offices, customer service points, and also how **off-site/mobile ATMs, cash deposit machines (CDMs), and bunch note acceptor machines (BNAMs)** are to be treated for authorisation purposes. This suggests that compliance teams must classify each physical or semi-physical customer interface correctly and ensure it is opened only in accordance with the RBI’s authorisation framework, rather than assuming all customer-facing infrastructure is treated the same. The directions also contemplate **doorstep banking**, meaning payments banks may be permitted to deliver certain services at a customer’s location, but only under the eligibility, service-scope, modality, delivery-process, risk-management, transparency, and grievance-redress rules set out in that chapter.

The document further requires ongoing **information reporting** to RBI on **banking outlets, branches, offices, customer service points, and related locations**, so compliance should expect periodic or event-based regulatory reporting obligations tied to each outlet/service point. Finally, the directions include **repeal and savings** provisions, plus a statement that other applicable laws are not barred and that RBI’s interpretations control. Because the supplied text stops before the substantive applicability and detailed operational clauses, the exact thresholds, distances, caps, or numerical limits are not visible in this excerpt; however, the document clearly establishes a comprehensive regulatory regime for payments banks’ physical presence, outsourced distribution, doorstep service models, and reporting, effective immediately from **28 November 2025**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights Directions, 2025** apply specifically to **payments banks** and are intended to ensure that major shareholders remain **“fit and proper” on a continuing basis**. The directions are issued under **Sections 12, 12B, and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and must be read together with the RBI’s existing **Guidelines on Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights in Banking Companies**. They take effect **on the date they are placed on the RBI’s official website**.

Substantively, the document establishes a regulatory framework for both **prior approval for acquisition** and **ongoing monitoring** of shareholding/voting rights in payments banks. “Acquisition” is defined broadly to include acquiring, or agreeing to acquire, shares or voting rights **directly or indirectly**, and “shares” includes both **equity and preference shares** under **Section 12(1)(ii)** of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The directions also set out detailed rules on **fit-and-proper criteria**, the **procedure for obtaining prior approval**, and the RBI’s expectations for **continuous due diligence** by banks to identify and report possible breaches.

A key compliance point is that payments banks must maintain **continuous monitoring arrangements** to detect violations of **Section 12B(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, which governs limits and restrictions on acquisition/holding of shares and voting rights. The directions require banks to perform ongoing due diligence over shareholders, identify potential violations, and comply with RBI **reporting requirements** when issues arise. The document also contains annexed provisions on **limits on shareholding**, **lock-in requirements**, and a **ceiling on voting rights**, indicating that compliance teams must track not only who holds shares, but also whether the amount and duration of holdings remain within permitted regulatory limits.

The directions repeal and replace prior instructions to the extent specified in the repeal-and-saving provisions, while preserving the effect of actions taken under the earlier framework where applicable. They also clarify that other applicable laws are **not barred**, meaning payments banks must continue to comply with company law, securities law, and other relevant legal/regulatory requirements alongside these RBI directions. The document includes prescribed **Forms A1, A2, A, and B** and an annexure setting out procedural and information requirements for both **prior approval** and **ongoing monitoring**, so affected banks should treat the forms and annexed thresholds as mandatory compliance inputs rather than optional guidance.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend) Directions, 2026** apply specifically to **Local Area Banks (LABs)** and take effect from **FY 2026–27**. The Directions are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and are intended to govern when and how LABs may declare dividends on equity shares, including interim dividends; they expressly **exclude dividends on Perpetual Non-Cumulative Preference Shares (PNCPS)**.

Under the new framework, a bank’s **Board of Directors** must review several prudential and supervisory factors before approving any dividend proposal. These include any **divergence in asset classification and provisioning for NPAs** observed in RBI supervisory findings, the **auditors’ report** for the relevant year (including any **modified opinion** or **Emphasis of Matter**), the bank’s **current and projected capital position** compared with applicable regulatory capital requirements, and the bank’s **long-term growth plans**. The definition of **Adjusted Profit After Tax (PAT)** is also important: it is the PAT for the year for which dividend is proposed **minus 50% of Net NPA as on March 31** of that financial year. The Directions also note that **“extra-ordinary profit / income”** has the same meaning as under applicable accounting standards.

Although the excerpt cuts off in the middle of the eligibility section, it makes clear that a bank must satisfy specified **prudential requirements** before it can declare dividends, and those requirements are tied to regulatory compliance, capital strength, and asset-quality discipline. The document also establishes further chapters on the **quantum of dividend payable**, **profits ineligible for dividend**, **reporting requirements**, **restrictions on payment**, and **penal consequences for non-compliance**, indicating that dividend distribution is being treated as a tightly controlled supervisory matter rather than a board-level discretion alone. It also contains provisions on **repeal and saving**, states that other laws continue to apply, and provides interpretation rules, meaning these Directions are meant to operate alongside—not in place of—other statutory or regulatory obligations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 27, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Miscellaneous Directions, 2025** (as updated **April 27, 2026**) consolidate a series of operating, compliance, and reporting requirements applicable to **local area banks (LABs)**. At a high level, the directions require LABs to maintain RBI-approved governance and compliance policies, follow the special treatment for **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF)** transfers/claims, observe limits and provisioning rules for **investments in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)**, conduct periodic **KYC updation outreach**, comply with legal/regulatory information and court-order requirements, register under **FATCA/IGA with the United States**, and avoid prohibited dealings such as certain donations, deposit mobilization through private financiers/unincorporated bodies, and associations with prize chit or lottery activities.

A compliance team should note that the document is organized as an omnibus rulebook for LABs, with Chapter II requiring the **Board** to approve relevant policies and periodically review them, and Chapter III setting out detailed DEAF obligations: what credits go into the fund, how refunds and interest are handled, how registration and claims are processed, what returns must be filed, how amounts are disclosed in the notes to accounts, and the audit/record-retention/information-furnishing standards tied to the scheme. The same chapter also requires the bank to maintain contact details and abide by RBI’s interpretation of the scheme’s provisions, so operational teams should expect procedural obligations around transfer, claim submission, record preservation, and reporting rather than just a passive accounting treatment.

The AIF chapter imposes a specific investment control framework for **bank investments in Alternative Investment Funds**. It defines the relevant terms, requires a general compliance framework before investing, and then limits exposure and provisioning in the manner set out in the directions, while also identifying certain **exemptions** and transitional treatment. From a compliance perspective, the key point is that LABs are not free to invest in AIFs without monitoring concentration, regulatory limits, and provisioning impact; any existing or proposed AIF exposure must be checked against the RBI-prescribed caps and the bank’s internal approval process.

The market-operations chapter requires LABs to run **camps and campaigns for periodic KYC updation**, which means the bank must actively organize customer outreach to refresh KYC records rather than waiting for individual customer requests. The regulatory-compliance chapter further requires implementation of RBI instructions, general legal compliance, adherence to court directives, and compliance with the **FATCA/IGA registration requirements** with the U.S. for cross-border tax transparency. Finally, the financial-conduct chapter prohibits LABs from making donations or contributions for public/charitable purposes except as permitted by the directions, from accepting deposits at the instance of **private financiers or unincorporated bodies**, and from associating with **prize chit schemes or lottery ticket sales**; these are direct prohibitions that should be reflected in customer/dealer onboarding, third-party arrangements, and staff conduct controls.

Because the excerpt is only the table of contents and not the chapter text, the document’s substantive specifics on rates, thresholds, deadlines, or exact procedural forms are not visible here beyond the chapter-level requirements and the effective/update date reference. However, the compliance significance is clear: LABs must treat this as a consolidated RBI compliance manual covering governance, fund transfers/claims, investment restrictions, customer KYC refresh, tax-information registration, and prohibited business conduct, with board oversight and reporting controls supporting each area.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025**, effective **immediately** on **November 28, 2025**, under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. These Directions apply specifically to **Local Area Banks**, and they govern how such banks must manage risks arising from **outsourcing arrangements**, with particular emphasis on outsourced **IT services** and certain specific outsourcing models covered later in the document. The excerpt indicates that existing arrangements are addressed by a saving/proviso, but the full transitional treatment is not shown in the provided text, so compliance teams should assume legacy contracts may need review against the new framework.

From a governance perspective, the Directions require the **Board** of each covered bank to approve a formal **outsourcing policy** and remain accountable for oversight of all outsourced activities. The Board is expected to ensure that outsourcing does not dilute the bank’s responsibility to customers, regulators, or supervisors, and that senior management and the IT function each have defined roles in implementing controls, monitoring providers, and maintaining security and resilience. The policy and governance structure must also cover how the bank evaluates service providers, executes agreements, monitors performance, maintains an inventory of outsourced services, and manages business continuity, disaster recovery, exit, and termination.

A substantial part of the Directions is devoted to **outsourcing of IT services**. Banks must establish a risk management framework that addresses confidentiality, information security, and operational risk throughout the outsourcing lifecycle, including pre-engagement assessment, contractual protections, ongoing supervision, and incident management. The bank remains responsible for the outsourced function and must ensure service providers are selected through due diligence, that outsourcing agreements contain enforceable terms, and that outsourced services are subject to monitoring and control sufficient to preserve compliance, security, and service quality.

The Directions also identify **special outsourcing arrangements** that require additional caution or controls, including outsourcing within a **group/conglomerate**, **offshore or cross-border outsourcing**, outsourcing of a **Security Operations Centre (SOC)**, and use of **cloud computing services**. Although the excerpt does not include the detailed conditions, these categories are expressly singled out, meaning banks must expect enhanced scrutiny, contractual safeguards, oversight, and likely business continuity and data protection requirements for such arrangements. The document also includes a dedicated section on **redressal of grievances related to outsourced services**, indicating that customer complaint handling cannot be delegated away and must remain operationally effective even when the underlying activity is outsourced.

Finally, the Directions include a **repeal and saving** chapter and a statement that other applicable laws are not barred, meaning compliance must be assessed not only against these RBI Directions but also against any other binding legal or regulatory obligations. For a compliance team, the immediate action items are to confirm whether the bank is a Local Area Bank in scope, inventory all outsourced arrangements, map them against the new policy and governance expectations, and review contracts, monitoring controls, grievance handling, continuity planning, and exit provisions against the RBI framework now in force.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025** consolidate and replace the RBI’s customer service and conduct instructions for **all Local Area Banks (LABs)**, and they took effect **immediately upon issuance on November 28, 2025**, unless a specific provision states otherwise. The document is framed under the RBI’s powers in the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and is intended to create one unified set of requirements covering customer service, fair conduct, financial inclusion, payments, deposits, lending conduct, and related miscellaneous obligations for LABs.

For compliance purposes, the most important threshold issue is scope: **every LAB is covered**, and the directions are not limited to specific branches or products unless a chapter says so. The document begins by defining key terms that will matter throughout the rules, including **accounts with survivorship clause** (such as “either or survivor,” “anyone or survivor,” etc.), **apostille**, and **Annual Percentage Rate (APR)** as the total annual cost of credit including interest and all other charges. This indicates the directions are meant to govern both deposit and credit conduct in a standardized way and to support customer-facing disclosures, especially where legal documentation or fee presentation is involved.

The chapter structure shows the operational areas that LABs must align with: **institutional framework**, **customer service in branches**, **customer guidance and protection**, **financial inclusion and accessibility**, **payment and remittance services**, **deposit and other liabilities**, **responsible lending conduct**, and **miscellaneous/repeal provisions**. Even from the introductory material, a compliance team should infer that the RBI expects LABs to implement formal policies, branch-level service standards, customer protection processes, inclusion/accessibility measures, payment/remittance controls, and lending practices that are “responsible” in the sense of clear pricing, fair treatment, and transparent disclosures.

Several annexes signal that the directions contain detailed procedural requirements for **claims settlement**, **nominee/survivorship account claims**, **accounts without nominee/survivorship clauses**, **indemnity/surety documentation**, **disclaimer/no-objection letters**, **affidavits**, **safe deposit locker inventory and acknowledgement forms**, **articles in safe custody inventory**, and a **Key Facts Statement**. Those annexes indicate that LABs must maintain documented claim-handling and custody processes, not just general customer-service principles. In particular, the presence of separate claim forms for accounts with and without nominee/survivorship clauses suggests that branches will need to verify account type and use the correct documentation pathway when a depositor dies or a claim is otherwise made.

Because the excerpt provided stops at the beginning of the definitions section, the detailed operative requirements and any numeric limits, timelines, disclosure formats, or product-specific thresholds are not visible here. However, based on the structure and annexes, a compliance officer should expect the full directions to impose mandatory procedures for customer grievance handling, deposit claim processing, locker/custody inventory, and lending disclosures, and should confirm whether any later chapters contain **specific deadlines, service turnaround times, or documentation standards** that require policy updates, staff training, branch process changes, or form redesign before implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 KYC Directions for Local Area Banks set the binding anti-money laundering / counter-terrorist financing framework that these banks must follow to prevent misuse of the banking system for money laundering or terrorist financing, and they expressly update and consolidate the KYC obligations applicable to Local Area Banks under RBI oversight. The document’s scope is limited to Local Area Banks, but it incorporates broad customer onboarding, identification, due diligence, ongoing monitoring, recordkeeping, and suspicious transaction reporting requirements, and it is tied to India’s AML legal framework under the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 and the PML Rules, 2005, as well as FATF standards.

At a policy level, the directions require the bank’s Board of Directors to approve and oversee a formal KYC/AML governance framework, including customer acceptance policy, risk management, customer identification procedures, customer due diligence procedures, record management, and reporting to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India. The bank must classify customers by risk and apply risk-based due diligence, with the ability to impose enhanced checks for higher-risk customers and simplified measures only where allowed by the directions; the requirements also extend to individuals, sole proprietorships, legal entities, and beneficial ownership identification, so compliance cannot be limited to retail accounts alone. The document also requires ongoing due diligence throughout the customer relationship, meaning banks must monitor transactions and update customer information when risk, activity, or circumstances change rather than treating KYC as a one-time onboarding exercise.

The directions further require specific customer identification procedures before account opening or relationship establishment, and they cover how banks must verify identity and address, identify and verify legal persons and their controllers, and determine the beneficial owner where the customer is acting through entities or complex ownership structures. The bank must maintain records of the information and documents used for identification and due diligence, preserve those records for the prescribed retention period, and make them available for regulatory and law-enforcement purposes as required. The directions also impose reporting obligations to the FIU-India, which means the bank must file the relevant cash, suspicious, and other mandated reports in the prescribed manner and within applicable deadlines.

The document additionally addresses compliance with international-agency communications and obligations arising under international agreements, meaning the bank must have controls for screening and responding to relevant notifications, restrictions, or directions connected to global sanctions / counter-terrorism or related cooperation frameworks. Finally, it contains repeal and savings provisions, indicating that prior RBI instructions covered by this issuance are superseded to the extent stated, while actions already taken under the earlier framework may be preserved. For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that Local Area Banks must operate a formal, board-approved, risk-based KYC program with documented onboarding checks, beneficial ownership verification, ongoing monitoring, record retention, FIU reporting, and controls for international obligations, all effective under the 2025 Directions as updated through December 29, 2025.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025** apply specifically to **Local Area Banks** and take effect **immediately**. They are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and are intended to govern how these banks prepare, present, and disclose items in their financial statements. For each accounting period, a Local Area Bank must prepare its **balance sheet and profit and loss account** in the **Forms in the Third Schedule of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, for all business transacted by the bank, as required under **Section 29** of the Act; the Forms referenced are the Government of India’s notified forms in **S.O. 240(E) dated March 26, 1992**, reproduced in Annex I to the Directions.

The Directions require banks to follow the general compilation instructions for the balance sheet and profit and loss account and to ensure **strict compliance with the Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, as amended from time to time**, except where RBI directions or guidelines require otherwise. In other words, accounting presentation must align with the statutory schedule format, but also with applicable accounting standards and any RBI-specific overrides or instructions. The document then adds further RBI guidance on specific accounting standard issues and detailed notes/disclosure requirements, which are mandatory for the financial statements of Local Area Banks.

Beyond the core balance sheet and profit and loss account format, the Directions include a separate chapter on **notes to accounts and disclosures**, plus a chapter on **other instructions** that cover compliance treatment for items such as inter-branch account net debit balances, reconciliation of Nostro accounts and outstanding entries, transfers to or appropriations from reserve funds, provisioning for fraud, unreconciled balances, deferred tax liability on special reserves under **Section 36(1)(viii) of the Income Tax Act, 1961**, and restrictions against window dressing. The document also contains a **repeal and saving** chapter, states that other laws are not barred unless expressly inconsistent, and reserves interpretive authority. For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that these Directions are a comprehensive, RBI-mandated financial statement presentation and disclosure framework for Local Area Banks, effective immediately, and banks must ensure their financial reporting templates, accounting policies, and disclosure controls are aligned accordingly.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters Directions, 2025** apply **immediately** and are issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. They apply to **all Local Area Banks**, but the restrictions on further finance to wilful defaulters and the provisions on large defaulters also apply more broadly to **all RBI-regulated entities**, even if those entities are not “lenders” as defined in the Directions. The stated objective is to ensure a **non-discriminatory, transparent, and natural-justice-based process** for classifying wilful defaulters and to create a credit-information system that warns lenders and prevents further institutional finance to such persons.

The Directions define key terms that drive compliance, including “credit facility” broadly to cover **fund-based and non-fund-based exposures, including off-balance sheet items such as derivatives, guarantees, and letters of credit**, and they adopt the definition of “default” from the RBI’s **Local Area Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets, 2025** Directions. They also define “diversion of funds” with specific examples that compliance teams must watch for: using short-term working capital for long-term purposes contrary to sanction terms, using borrowed funds to create assets other than those financed, moving funds to subsidiaries or group entities without approval, routing funds through other lenders without permission, investing borrowed funds in other companies or entities without approval, and any unexplained shortfall between disbursed/drawn amounts and actual deployment. The definition of “director” is specifically tied to a director of a company classified as a large defaulter or wilful defaulter who was associated with the company when the acts leading to default occurred, and “DIN” has the Companies Act meaning.

From a governance perspective, the Directions require banks to have an **identification committee** for wilful defaulters, to be constituted by the bank and comprised of a **Whole-Time Director** and other members as specified later in the document. The overall framework is designed to govern how a borrower is identified as a wilful defaulter, to ensure fair process, and to support later reporting to credit information systems. The document also anticipates separate chapters on the **function of the Board**, **treatment of wilful defaulters**, **reporting of wilful defaulters and large defaulters**, and **preventive measures and auditors’ role**, indicating that banks will have ongoing internal control, reporting, and governance duties beyond initial classification.

For compliance purposes, the most immediate operational point is that the Directions are **effective from November 28, 2025** with **immediate commencement**, so Local Area Banks need to align their internal classification, board oversight, reporting, and preventive controls right away. The document also includes annexed formats for **submission of lists of large defaulters** and **data on cases of wilful default**, which means banks will have prescribed reporting templates and data-submission obligations. Overall, the Directions create a tighter RBI framework for identifying, documenting, and reporting wilful and large defaulters and for preventing further credit exposure to them across the regulated financial system.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (LABs) – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025** (updated through **July 1, 2026**) create a consolidated framework for **early recognition, reporting, and time-bound resolution of stressed assets**, and they also **rationalize and harmonize rules for compromise settlements and technical write-offs**. The document expressly notes that some LABs may participate in **State Government Debt Relief Schemes (DRS)** that waive or sacrifice debt obligations for targeted borrower groups in return for fiscal support, and warns that frequent or poorly designed schemes can harm credit discipline, create moral hazard, delay recoveries, and cause mismatches between claims submitted by banks and amounts accepted by governments. Because of these concerns, the Directions also set out **broad principles for LAB participation in DRS** and a **model operating procedure** that was shared with State Governments to align expectations among governments, banks, and borrowers.

The Directions apply to **Local Area Banks**, and they establish requirements for **board-approved policies**, **early identification and reporting of stress**, and **disclosures**. The compliance emphasis is on having internal governance arrangements in place so that stressed exposures are identified quickly, reported in a structured manner, and resolved within prescribed timelines rather than allowed to deteriorate. The document also includes separate prudential norms for **restructuring of accounts**, special rules for **compromise settlements and technical write-offs**, and a distinct chapter for **accounts impacted by calamities**, showing that affected accounts are not handled under a single generic process but through issue-specific resolution pathways.

For calamity-impacted accounts, the Directions assign roles to the **State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC)**, **Union Territory Level Bankers’ Committee (UTLBC)**, and **District Consultative Committee (DCC)** in coordinating the response. Banks must then **implement the resolution plan** under the prescribed framework and follow additional **ancillary measures** and **reporting requirements** set out in the chapter. This means LABs need procedures not only for individual borrower relief but also for committee-based coordination and formal reporting whenever accounts are affected by floods, droughts, or other calamity-type events covered by the framework.

The Directions also include a specific chapter on **Government Debt Relief Schemes (DRS)**, which states that LABs’ participation is subject to prudential treatment designed to manage the risks of waiver-based relief programs. In addition, the document contains **special trade relief measures**, and it ends with **repeal and saving provisions**, a statement that application of other laws is **not barred**, and an **interpretation clause**. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that this is a comprehensive RBI framework governing how LABs must detect, report, restructure, settle, write off, and disclose stressed assets, while also constraining and standardizing how they may participate in government-sponsored debt relief and calamity-related relief programs.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Local Area Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances) Directions, 2025” were issued on November 28, 2025 and are stated as updated as of July 1, 2026. They apply specifically to Local Area Banks and set out binding prudential requirements for how those banks recognize income on advances, classify assets, make provisions, disclose related information, and handle recoveries, with the Reserve Bank emphasizing that these norms are intended to align Indian practice with international prudential standards and earlier Committee on the Financial System recommendations.

At a governance level, the directions assign responsibility to the bank’s Board for overseeing prudent lending, consumer education, and compliance with the prudential framework, and they impose disclosure requirements in the prescribed manner. The document then establishes detailed rules for asset classification, including when an account must be treated as a non-performing asset (NPA), how to classify accounts that are regularized close to the balance sheet date, and how to treat specific types of exposures under special circumstances. It also sets out the categories of NPAs and the conditions for upgrading NPA accounts back to standard status, which is critical for both financial reporting and supervisory compliance.

On provisioning, the directions prescribe the baseline provisioning framework for standard, substandard, doubtful, and loss assets, and they also address special provisioning situations, including a specific additional provisioning requirement where a resolution plan is implemented under Chapter IV-A of the Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025. The text further covers rules on floating provisions, the ability to create provisions above the prescribed minimums, treatment of provisions under special circumstances, and a separate requirement relating to the Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR). These provisions affect capital planning, impairment measurement, and the bank’s internal provisioning policies, and compliance teams will need to ensure accounting systems and board-approved policies reflect the prescribed rates and triggers.

For income recognition, the directions require advances to be treated consistently with prudential status: once an account is classified as NPA, any income previously recognized must be reversed, interest accrual after NPA classification is restricted, and recoveries from NPAs must be appropriated in the manner specified. The framework also contains special-case income-recognition rules and addresses the tax treatment of provisions, which may affect both statutory accounts and tax computations. Finally, the directions repeal prior inconsistent provisions while preserving anything done under the earlier framework to the extent saved, clarify that other applicable laws are not barred unless inconsistent, and reserve interpretive authority in the manner set out in the document.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. These Directions replace the prior framework for asset-liability management for local area banks, and they are intended to impose a formal ALM, liquidity risk, currency risk, and interest rate risk governance and reporting regime on the covered institutions. The document is specifically aimed at **Local Area Banks** and sets out board responsibilities, internal control expectations, reporting templates, and prescribed monitoring statements that must be prepared and periodically submitted.

For compliance purposes, the key obligation is that a Local Area Bank must maintain a structured **Asset-Liability Management (ALM) framework** with clear board oversight, approved policies, risk limits, and periodic review. The board is required to approve the bank’s ALM policy and the relevant risk limits, and management must implement information systems and organizational arrangements capable of measuring and monitoring structural liquidity, short-term dynamic liquidity, currency risk, and interest rate risk. The Directions require the bank to build and use formal statements and reports for these risks, including the **Structural Liquidity Statement (SLS)**, the **Short-Term Dynamic Liquidity (STDL) statement**, and the **Interest Rate Sensitivity (IRS) statement**, with annexed formats provided in the Directions. The document also refers to additional maturity profile schedules and interest-rate-sensitivity annexures, indicating that compliance is not merely policy-based but requires regular operational reporting in prescribed formats.

The Directions impose specific monitoring and control requirements around **liquidity risk management**, including ongoing monitoring of liquidity positions through the SLS and STDL frameworks, rather than ad hoc review. They also require **currency risk management** and **interest rate risk (IRR) management**, including use of **traditional gap analysis** and an **Interest Rate Sensitivity Statement** to assess exposure. The mention of behavioural patterns and embedded options means the bank must take account of non-contractual or option-like customer behaviors in measuring liquidity and interest-rate risk, rather than relying only on contractual maturities. The inclusion of **Internal Transfer Pricing (ITP)** signals that ALM must also be integrated into the bank’s internal pricing and funds transfer methodology, which is relevant for product pricing, business-line incentives, and risk attribution.

The Directions also create a formal compliance cadence for **preparation, review, and regulatory reporting** of the required statements and returns. Chapter VIII indicates that the prescribed statements must be prepared and reviewed internally and then reported to the RBI according to specified periodicity; while the excerpt does not list the exact filing intervals, the existence of a dedicated reporting chapter means periodic submissions are mandatory and should be treated as regulatory returns. Chapter IX provides a **repeal and saving** clause, meaning prior inconsistent directions are superseded to the extent covered, while the other-law and interpretation provisions preserve the RBI’s ability to apply other legal requirements and interpret the Directions. For a compliance team, the operational takeaway is that Local Area Banks must align board governance, ALM systems, liquidity monitoring, risk measurement, and regulatory reporting to the 2025 Directions immediately upon commencement, and must use the RBI’s annexed formats and prescribed review process for ongoing compliance.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions for Local Area Banks on classification, valuation, and operation of the investment portfolio set the regulatory framework these banks must follow for recognizing, measuring, trading, and reporting investments, with the document updated through May 18, 2026. They apply specifically to Local Area Banks and govern both investment policy design and day-to-day portfolio operations, including government securities, non-SLR securities, subsidiaries/associates/joint ventures, and derivatives. The directions require the board to approve and oversee an investment policy framework and establish internal controls, audit/review, and reporting processes that support compliance with RBI-prescribed classification and valuation rules.

A major requirement is that investments must be categorized into prescribed accounting buckets, including Held to Maturity (HTM), Available for Sale (AFS), and Fair Value through Profit and Loss (FVTPL), with a separate Held for Trading (HFT) treatment under FVTPL. The directions also address investments in subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures, and set out rules for initial recognition, subsequent measurement, and when and how reclassifications between categories are permitted. The document further restricts sale of HTM investments and lays down conditions under which such sales can occur without violating the HTM classification framework.

For valuation, the RBI prescribes how banks must determine fair value for quoted securities, unquoted SLR securities, and unquoted non-SLR securities, with a specific chapter devoted to fair-value methodology. Operational controls are required for government securities and non-SLR holdings, and banks must maintain internal control systems, use brokers only in accordance with RBI rules, and undergo audit, review, and reporting procedures. The directions also cover income recognition, including broken-period interest accounting, and specifically address non-performing investments (NPI), meaning banks must apply asset-classification-style discipline to investment assets that deteriorate in performance.

The document also requires creation and maintenance of an Investment Fluctuation Reserve, indicating a prudential buffer against market-value declines in the investment book. Derivatives are separately regulated under the same directions, so any local area bank using derivative instruments must follow the specific RBI framework in Chapter XII rather than relying on general treasury practice. Finally, Chapter XIII repeals prior instructions on the subject while preserving actions already taken under the superseded framework, so compliance teams should treat this as the controlling updated regime and verify that legacy policies, valuation methods, and reporting templates have been aligned to the 2025 directions as updated on May 18, 2026.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025** apply **only to Local Area Banks** and take effect **immediately upon issuance** on **November 28, 2025**. The directions are issued under Sections **21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and replace the prior framework for how these banks may price loans and advances. For compliance teams, the core requirement is that each bank must have a **comprehensive Board-approved policy** governing interest rates on advances, including **microfinance loan pricing**, and all floating-rate lending must generally be linked to a permitted benchmark.

The document defines the key pricing concepts that will govern compliance: **internal benchmark rates** are bank-set references; **external benchmark rates** include the **RBI policy repo rate**, **GOI 3-month and 6-month Treasury Bill yields published by FBIL**, and any other **FBIL-published benchmark market interest rate**. It also defines fixed-rate and floating-rate loans, “advance against own deposit,” short-term borrowing (tenor **up to but less than one year**), term loans, and other terms used in the pricing rules. Compliance officers should note that the benchmark used to price a loan must be stated in the **loan contract**, and the bank must determine the final lending rate by adding the applicable **spread components** to the chosen benchmark.

The directions require that, unless specifically exempted in paragraph 44, **all floating-rate loans** be priced with reference to a benchmark described in the later paragraphs (**9 to 26**). Banks retain the freedom to offer advances on either **fixed or floating rates**, but the floating-rate structure must follow the benchmark-plus-spread method set out in the directions. Interest on advances must be charged only in accordance with the new framework, and the bank’s policy must cover the pricing methodology as well as the treatment of different loan categories, including microfinance.

The document also indicates that there are further chapters dealing with the **benchmark framework, other aspects of lending rates, foreign currency advances, exemptions, and repeal/transition provisions**, so compliance review should focus on the later sections for any exceptions, transitional rules, or special treatment. Based on the text provided, there are no specific numerical rate caps in the excerpt beyond the benchmark definitions and the short-term borrowing threshold, but the operative compliance obligation is immediate alignment of pricing policies, loan documentation, and floating-rate structures with the RBI’s benchmark-based framework.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk Directions, 2025** are a new, self-contained framework governing permitted credit-risk transfer activity for **Local Area Banks (LABs)**. They are **effective on the date they are placed on the RBI’s official website** and apply specifically to **LABs**. The directions are issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and are intended to regulate loan transfers, including transfers by **novation or assignment**, with the key legal requirement that, where a loan is transferred, **legal ownership must be transferred to the transferee to the extent of the economic interest transferred**.

A critical restriction in the document is that **LABs are permitted to act only as transferors of stressed loans under Part A, Chapter III**; they are **not permitted to act as transferors or transferees in any other type of loan transfer**. More generally, a bank may undertake **only those loan transfers or acquisitions specifically permitted under Part A and only in the manner prescribed there**, and this prohibition is stated to be without prejudice to separately permitted RBI-regulated products such as **External Commercial Borrowings, trade credits, structured obligations, guarantees, or other products explicitly allowed under RBI guidelines**. The directions also state that **banks may acquire loans only from a transferor specified as a lender in paragraph 12(4), unless specifically permitted**.

The document begins defining the legal and operational scope for these transfers. For Part A, terms are defined as needed in the relevant chapters, and any undefined expressions are to take their meanings from the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**, other statutory modifications/re-enactments, or commercial parlance as appropriate. One defined term already visible in the excerpt is **“credit enhancement”**, which is a contractual arrangement providing added protection to other parties to mitigate credit risk on acquired exposures, and **“default”**, which is tied to the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016** as non-payment of debt when due; the excerpt also notes a special treatment for **revolving facilities such as cash credit**, indicating that default can also be triggered by continuing outstanding balances under those facilities.

Because the directions are framed as a comprehensive framework for the development of a credit risk market, a compliance team at a LAB should treat this as a **structural prohibition-plus-permission regime**: LABs are not general participants in loan secondary markets, but are confined to the specific stressed-loan transfer role set out later in the directions. Compliance should therefore verify that any contemplated transaction is expressly authorized by these Directions, confirm the counterparty’s status against the permitted transferor/transferee rules, and ensure the transfer mechanics satisfy the mandated **legal ownership/economic interest alignment**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance**. They apply specifically to **Local Area Banks (LABs)**, and they are intended to manage concentration risk on both the **asset side** (single borrower/group borrower exposures) and the **liability side** (inter-bank liabilities). The RBI states these directions are issued under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they replace/continue the RBI’s prudential approach to exposure limits in a proportionate way for LABs.

A key compliance point is the definition of **“capital funds for exposure norms,”** which consists of **Tier I and Tier II capital** as defined in the RBI’s **Local Area Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy, 2025**, using the figures from the **published accounts as of March 31 of the previous year**. Capital infused after the balance sheet date can also be counted for the exposure ceiling, but **only actual infusion**; banks may **not** count ordinary capital accretions such as quarterly profits, and they are expressly **prohibited from exceeding the regulatory ceiling in anticipation of future capital infusion**. In other words, exposure room must be supported by existing capital or completed capital infusion, not expected funding.

The directions define **“exposure”** broadly to include both **credit exposure** and **investment exposure**, and for limits the bank must generally use the **higher of the sanctioned limit or the outstanding amount**. An exception is made for **fully drawn term loans** with no re-drawal feature, where only the **outstanding balance** may be treated as exposure. Credit exposure includes all funded and non-funded limits, as well as leasing, hire purchase, and factoring; investment exposure covers **shares, debentures, PSU bonds, and commercial paper**, and also treats investments in **debentures/bonds/security receipts/PTCs issued by a securitisation company or reconstruction company as exposure on that SC/RC**. The directions also make clear that investments in **corporate bonds/debentures guaranteed by an RBI-regulated entity** must follow the separate **RBI (Local Area Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025**.

For derivatives, the document treats **interest rate, foreign exchange, and gold derivative transactions** as generating **credit exposure of derivative products**, which must be included in exposure measurement. The excerpt ends while introducing the methodology, but the compliance implication is that LABs must calculate derivative-related credit exposure using the prescribed RBI method and include it in concentration-risk limits alongside funded/non-funded lending and investment exposures. Overall, the document requires LABs to maintain exposure calculations and internal controls that prevent exceeding concentration ceilings based on defined capital funds, current sanctioned/outstanding exposures, and derivative exposure treatment, with no reliance on expected future capital.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (LABs) – Credit Risk Management Directions, 2025** are binding on all **Local Area Banks** and take effect **immediately upon issuance** (the document is an updated version noted as of **July 01, 2026**, but the operative directions begin on issuance). The RBI issues them under its powers in the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** to strengthen credit risk controls, including both prudential and restriction-based measures. For a compliance team, the key point is that these are not general principles only: they create enforceable requirements around lending governance, exposure limits, documentation, security creation, reporting, and related-party controls.

A major compliance obligation introduced in the opening provisions is that LABs must align lending and credit administration with RBI-defined terms and the scope of the directions; the document expressly applies to **Local Area Banks only**. The definitions section is important because it sets the regulatory meaning of products and exposures that will be used throughout the directions, including **bank guarantee**, **bills purchased and discounted**, and **cash credit (CC)**. In particular, a **cash credit facility** is defined as a running account backed by hypothecation/pledge of goods, book debts, standing crops, etc., with **drawing power (DP)** periodically fixed based on eligible current assets and the outstanding amount repayable on demand; this definition signals that CC account management and DP discipline are part of the regulated credit-risk framework.

The document also introduces governance architecture for credit decisions, including a **“Committee on lending to related parties”** as a Board-level committee entrusted with sanctioning loans to related parties. That means LABs must ensure related-party lending is not handled informally at management level but through the specified Board governance process. More broadly, the table of contents shows that the directions cover **Board-approved policies**, **credit risk evaluation**, **statutory and regulatory restrictions**, **unhedged foreign currency exposure (UFCE)**, **Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) requirements for borrowers**, **valuation of properties and empanelment of valuers**, **filing of security interests with CERSAI** for immovable, movable, and intangible assets, and **maintenance of cash credit/current/overdraft accounts**—so compliance is not limited to underwriting, but extends into post-sanction monitoring, collateral perfection, borrower identification, and account operation.

Because the text provided is only the introductory and preliminary portion of the full directions, it does **not yet state the numeric exposure limits, thresholds, or detailed filing deadlines** that may appear in the later chapters. However, it clearly establishes that LABs must treat credit risk management as a formal regulatory compliance function, with mandatory policy approval by the Board and adherence to RBI-prescribed restrictions across lending products and borrower categories. If you want, I can also turn this into a **chapter-by-chapter compliance checklist** once you provide the remaining text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
These Directions, issued under section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005, create the RBI’s dedicated framework for **Local Area Banks (LABs)** on **credit information reporting, dissemination, customer access, and grievance redressal**. They take effect **immediately** on issuance (unless a specific provision states otherwise), and the document is the **2025 Directions, updated as on July 1, 2026**. The core compliance objective is to standardize how LABs report borrower credit data to Credit Information Companies (CICs), protect the confidentiality and security of that data, and ensure consumers can obtain corrections and redress where credit-reporting errors occur.

For a compliance team, the main operational requirement is that LABs must become and remain compliant CIC members and must **report credit information in the prescribed formats and timelines**, keep the data **updated**, and follow RBI-prescribed guidelines for accuracy, rectification of rejected submissions, and monitoring of the **Data Quality Index (DQI)**. The Directions also require banks to use credit information reports in credit appraisal in the manner prescribed, and to follow the rules on **displaying credit information** and on **correction of credit information reports** when errors are identified. In addition, the Directions expressly extend to customer-service and grievance-handling obligations, including a framework for **compensation to customers** in appropriate cases and the applicability of the **Reserve Bank-Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021** where relevant.

The document is structured to also address governance and implementation: it provides for a **Technical Working Group**, sets out **best practices**, and clarifies the effect of **repeal and savings**, interaction with other laws, and interpretive principles. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed operational clauses, the compliance implication is that affected Local Area Banks must align internal systems, vendor/process controls, customer-facing procedures, and escalation mechanisms to the RBI’s specified reporting standards and remediation requirements. If your institution is a Local Area Bank, this is a direct and ongoing compliance framework governing every stage of credit information handling—from submission to CICs, to correction and customer grievance resolution.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Debit Card: Issuance and Conduct Directions, 2025** apply specifically to **Local Area Banks** and take **immediate effect** from **November 28, 2025**. They govern the general conduct, issuance, and associated controls for **debit cards, including co-branded debit cards**, and must be read together with any other RBI prudential, payment, technology, and cyber-security directions that apply to debit and co-branded cards. The RBI states that, for issuing debit cards, **prior RBI approval is not required**, but each bank must operate under a **Board-approved debit card issuance policy** and broader card-conduct framework.

A bank must maintain **Board-approved comprehensive policies and procedures** covering debit card issuance, co-branding arrangements where relevant, the standard operating procedure for **blocking, deactivating, or suspending cards at the bank’s discretion**, the **time period for completing formalities after a lost card is blocked**, and **grievance redressal plus compensation**. These policies are not optional or generic; the Directions expect the bank’s internal procedures to address the specific matters later set out in the Directions themselves.

On issuance, debit cards may be issued **only to customers holding Savings Bank or Current Accounts**. The document begins the restriction section by stating that **no bank shall issue debit cards to cash ...**, but the excerpt provided cuts off before the full restriction is visible, so the remaining wording cannot be safely reconstructed from this text alone. The definition of “debit card” includes both **physical and virtual payment instruments** linked to a savings or current account and usable for cash withdrawal, online payments, point-of-sale and QR-code transactions, fund transfers, and similar activities, subject to prescribed terms and conditions.

The Directions also define several compliance-relevant terms, including **cardholders**, **card-issuers**, **co-branded cards**, **convenience fees**, **form factors**, and **card loyalty/reward programmes**. A **co-branded card** is one issued jointly by a bank and a co-branding partner and bearing both names, while a **form factor** is any physical or virtual substitute instrument used instead of a card to carry out payment or banking transactions. A **card loyalty/reward programme** includes schemes tied to debit card usage that provide digital coupons, points, discounts, cash back, or other monetary-value benefits redeemable for the same or later transactions after accumulation.

For compliance purposes, the key operational takeaway is that Local Area Banks must ensure **board-level approval, documented controls, and customer-eligibility restrictions** are in place immediately, and must align all debit-card issuance and conduct practices—including any co-branding and any card-blocking and grievance procedures—with the RBI’s Directions and any other applicable RBI card-security and payment regulations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction set, issued on November 28, 2025 and updated as on April 01, 2026, establishes the credit-facility framework for Local Area Banks and replaces the earlier position on these matters, with the update date indicating the operative text to read as of April 1, 2026. The document is structured as a full credit administration code for local area banks and expressly covers board-approved policies, digital lending, lending against gold and silver collateral, microfinance, non-fund-based credit facilities, and credit to the real estate sector, so compliance teams should assume it applies to all such activities conducted by a Local Area Bank unless a chapter says otherwise. It also contains repeal/savings language and interpretive provisions, meaning prior inconsistent instructions on the covered topics are superseded to the extent repealed, while other applicable laws continue to apply.

A major part of the directions is the digital lending regime for bank–LSP arrangements and DLAs, which imposes conduct, customer-protection, technology, data, reporting, and loss-sharing obligations when the bank uses a lending service provider or a digital lending app. The bank must have board-approved policies and controls around these arrangements, including accountability for customer-facing conduct, data handling, reporting of credit information, and allocation of losses in default situations; compliance officers should treat the bank as remaining responsible for outsourced digital-lending activities rather than shifting compliance risk to the LSP. The chapter also covers general provisions for digital lending, so any new or renewed LSP/DLA arrangement should be checked against the RBI’s required operational, disclosure, and governance standards before launch.

For lending against gold and silver collateral, the directions impose separate restrictions and ceilings, valuation and assaying requirements, and an LTV framework that must be followed before sanction and during the life of the loan. The document signals that these loans are not to be treated as ordinary secured credit: the bank must follow prescribed collateral-handling and valuation processes, and lending limits must stay within RBI’s specified cap. Compliance teams should verify branch-level controls for acceptance, storage, valuation, renewal, and monitoring of precious-metal collateral, because these loans typically carry extra regulatory scrutiny.

The microfinance chapter defines what counts as microfinance, requires assessment of household income, and caps the total repayment obligations a household can take on. This means the bank must assess borrower household income before extending or revising such exposures and ensure that the household’s aggregate repayment obligations remain within the RBI-prescribed percentage threshold under the directions; the exact cap is not provided in the excerpt, but the requirement is clearly mandatory and household-based rather than borrower-only based. The bank therefore needs systems to aggregate all household debt obligations across lenders and product types before approving microfinance loans.

The non-fund-based credit chapter governs guarantees, e-guarantees, co-acceptances, and overseas current or capital account transaction-related guarantees, including the timing of payment when a guarantee is invoked. Compliance should note that the directions extend beyond funded loans and cover contingent liabilities and documentary/payment obligations, with specific rules on issuing, using electronic guarantees, and settling invoked guarantees in a timely manner. Finally, the real-estate chapter addresses the quantum of lending to the real estate sector, indicating that exposure sizing to that sector is regulated and must be checked against the RBI’s prescribed limits before origination or enhancement of facilities.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025** (as updated **August 25, 2026**) set the deposit-interest framework for **local area banks** and replace earlier RBI directions for this topic, with the document stating that it comes into force on the date specified in the directions and applies to deposit products and related interest-payment practices covered in the text. The directions require local area banks to follow RBI-prescribed rules for **domestic rupee deposits**, **rupee deposits of non-residents**, and **foreign currency deposits**, including how interest may be set, calculated, compounded, paid, forfeited, or continued after account events such as death, renewal, premature withdrawal, or a depositor’s return to India.

For **domestic current accounts, savings deposits, and term deposits**, the directions establish the permissible interest-rate framework and associated operational rules, including periodicity of interest payment on savings accounts, treatment of overdue deposits, floating-rate term deposits, and the manner in which additional interest may be paid in specified cases. They also prescribe the rule for **interest payable on the domestic deposit account of a deceased depositor**, and they specifically allow banks, at their discretion, to pay interest on the **minimum credit balance in the composite cash credit account of a farmer** under the conditions stated in the directions. The document also addresses **premature withdrawal of domestic term deposits**, including the penalty or reduction in interest that may apply when a term deposit is broken before maturity.

For **rupee deposits of non-residents**, including **NRE deposits**, the directions regulate the interest rate treatment and impose specific restrictions, including a **prohibition on marking lien** on such deposits. They also set the rules for **premature withdrawal penalties** on NRE deposits and the interest payable when the **NRE term deposit account holder has died**, ensuring that banks follow RBI’s specified settlement method rather than their own ad hoc policies.

For **foreign currency deposits**, the directions govern **FCNR(B)** accounts and related foreign-currency resident accounts. They specify how interest must be **calculated on FCNR(B) deposits**, how interest is to be handled **upon renewal**, what interest is payable when the **FCNR(B) depositor dies**, and how interest is treated when an **NRI returns to India** and the FCNR(B) account is converted to a **Resident Foreign Currency (RFC) account** or resident rupee account. The directions also regulate **premature withdrawal** of foreign currency deposits and impose a penalty framework for such withdrawals, while separately addressing the **Resident Foreign Currency Accounts Scheme**.

Finally, the directions include **prohibitions and exemptions** and end with **repeal and saving provisions**, meaning earlier inconsistent instructions are superseded to the extent covered while preserving valid actions taken under the prior framework. For a compliance team, the key point is that these are operative RBI rules for local area banks’ deposit products: the bank must ensure its product terms, customer disclosures, account-opening and renewal processes, death/claim settlement procedures, non-resident account handling, and premature-withdrawal treatment are aligned with the exact RBI requirements in the directions and any applicable schedule.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025** apply specifically to **Local Area Banks (LABs)** and are **effective immediately upon issuance**. The Directions are issued under **section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and replace the prior LAB capital adequacy framework through a **repeal-and-saving mechanism** in Chapter IV, while preserving actions already taken under the earlier framework to the extent saved by the new Directions.

Substantively, the document sets out the full **prudential capital adequacy regime** for LABs, covering the definition of **regulatory capital**, the composition of **Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital**, deductions from capital funds, limits on Tier 2 elements, cross-holding restrictions, and capital treatment for subsidiaries. It also prescribes how LABs must calculate **risk-weighted assets (RWAs)** for **credit risk, market risk, and interest rate derivatives**, and then compute the overall capital ratio. The table of contents shows dedicated chapters for **minimum regulatory capital**, **definition of capital funds**, **Tier 1 capital**, **Tier 2 capital**, **deductions**, **limits for Tier 2 elements**, **norms on cross holdings**, and **capital for subsidiaries**, indicating that compliance teams must review both the eligibility of instruments counted as capital and the calculation methodology for exposures.

The definition section establishes key technical terms that drive the capital calculations, including **banking book**, **basis risk**, **credit risk**, **DTA/DTL** (using the meanings from the applicable accounting standards), **derivative** (as defined in **section 45U(a) of the RBI Act, 1934**), and **duration (Macaulay duration)** as a measure of price volatility and interest rate risk for fixed-income securities. Although the excerpt provided cuts off partway through the definitions, it is clear the Directions are designed to standardize the prudential treatment of balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet items for capital adequacy purposes. The document also includes an **Annex I** requiring a **reporting format for details of investments by FIIs and NRIs in Perpetual Non-Cumulative Preference Shares qualifying as Tier 1 Capital**, which indicates a specific ongoing reporting obligation where such instruments are issued or held.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that LABs must ensure their capital instruments, deductions, and risk-weighted asset calculations conform to the new RBI framework immediately, with particular attention to any **eligibility conditions for Tier 1/Tier 2 instruments, deduction requirements, exposure treatment, and subsidiary capital rules**. Because the Directions explicitly cover **market risk** and **interest rate derivative** capital charges in addition to credit risk, banks with trading activity or derivative positions must verify that those positions are captured correctly in capital computations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on January 22, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction applies specifically to **Local Area Banks (LABs)** and takes effect **immediately** upon issuance. It sets out the framework for how LABs must meet and report **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** and **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** requirements, and it requires CRR maintenance to be reported through **statutory return Form A** and SLR maintenance through **statutory return Form VIII**. The directions are issued under the RBI’s authority under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, along with **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.

The document defines the key measurement concepts that compliance teams will need to apply. **Aggregate deposits** means the total of **demand deposits and time deposits**. For savings bank accounts, banks must split balances into demand and time liabilities using the specified half-yearly methodology: as of the close of business on **March 31** and **September 30**, the bank must calculate the proportion of savings balances treated as demand vs. time liability under Regulation 7 of the RBI Scheduled Banks’ Regulations, 1951; the **average of the minimum balances maintained in each account during the half-year** is treated as the **time liability** portion, and the remainder of the average actual balances during that half-year is the **demand liability** portion. That ratio then applies to all reporting fortnights in the **next half-year**.

The directions also specify what counts as **approved securities / SLR securities**. These include **Government of India dated securities** issued under the market borrowing programme and Market Stabilization Scheme, **Government of India Treasury Bills**, **State Development Loans (SDLs)** issued by state governments under the market borrowing programme, and any other instrument later notified by RBI. For **Form A reporting**, banks must report the **total investment in approved securities as per the investment book, including encumbered securities**. However, for **SLR compliance**, only the **unencumbered portion** of investments in approved securities qualifies as the specified SLR asset.

The excerpt also begins to clarify an important exception: certain securities that are **lodged with another institution** are treated as **not encumbered for SLR purposes** and therefore continue to qualify as SLR assets, though the text provided cuts off before listing all such cases. A compliance team should therefore note that this instrument is not merely definitional—it establishes the reporting basis, the apportionment methodology for savings deposits, and the distinction between investment-book reporting and eligible SLR assets, all of which affect regulatory returns and liquidity compliance for LABs.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Governance) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Governance) Directions, 2025** were issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and take **immediate effect**. They apply to **all Local Area Banks** and establish the governance framework banks must follow for board composition, director appointments, leadership roles, board functioning, board committees, remuneration governance, and RBI approvals/reporting.

The directions define key governance terms used throughout the framework, including **Chairperson** (the bank’s part-time chairman), **Clawback** (a contractual right requiring return of previously paid or vested remuneration in specified circumstances), **Malus** (the ability to prevent vesting of deferred remuneration before vesting occurs), **Retention period** (the post-vesting period during which awarded variable-pay instruments cannot be sold or accessed), **Independent Director** (as per **Section 149(6) of the Companies Act, 2013**), and **Substantial interest** (as per **Section 5(ne) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**). Where the Directions do not define a term, the meaning from the **RBI Act, 1934**, **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, **Companies Act, 2013**, and related rules applies.

Although the excerpt provided stops before the substantive chapters, the table of contents shows that the Directions impose binding rules on: the **constitution of the board and appointment of directors**; the appointment and roles of the **MD&CEO, part-time Chairman, and whole-time directors**; the **role and responsibilities of the board and individual directors**; a **calendar of reviews and board meeting procedures**; mandatory board committees, specifically a **Nomination and Remuneration Committee** and an **Audit Committee of the Board**; and detailed rules on **remuneration** for **non-executive directors, whole-time directors, MD&CEO, material risk takers, and control function staff**. The Directions also include a chapter on **regulatory approvals and reporting**, indicating that certain governance actions will require RBI approval or notification and associated reporting obligations.

For compliance purposes, the immediate operational implication is that every Local Area Bank must review its existing board structure, committee composition, leadership appointments, meeting procedures, and remuneration policies against the new RBI framework as soon as possible. The document also indicates that **Annexes I–VI** contain supporting requirements or formats, which likely include the detailed standards and reporting templates that banks will need to implement to remain compliant.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025** apply only to **Local Area Banks** and become **effective on January 1, 2026**. The directions define and regulate three digital channel types: **internet banking** (web-browser based, excluding mobile apps), **mobile banking** (mobile apps, USSD, and SMS), and broader **digital banking channels** accessed through customer electronic devices for automated financial/banking transactions. They also distinguish between **“view only” banking**, which permits only non-liability-changing functions such as balance enquiry, balance viewing, and statement downloads, and **“transactional” banking**, which includes fund movement and other transactions that affect the customer’s assets or liabilities.

For **view only banking**, a Local Area Bank is eligible only if it has **implemented Core Banking Solution (CBS)** and its public-facing IT infrastructure is **enabled for IPv6 traffic**.
