Merchant acquiring is separately authorized and regulated, meaning RRBs may participate in payment acceptance/acquiring services, but only within the RBI-prescribed structure.

Finally, the document includes standard legal provisions on **repeal and saving**, application of other laws, and interpretation, meaning the RBI’s directions are intended to operate alongside other applicable statutes rather than override them unless explicitly stated. For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that an RRB must map all existing and proposed non-core financial-service activities against these directions, confirm board oversight and approvals are in place, and pay particular attention to interactions with AIFs, mutual funds, insurance distribution, and merchant acquiring because these are the expressly permitted service lines.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025** are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and apply specifically to **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)**. They take effect on **January 1, 2026**. The directions require RRBs to put in place comprehensive policies for all digital banking channels, with explicit coverage of statutory and regulatory compliance, as well as management of **liquidity risk** and **operational risk** in digital banking. The document defines digital banking channels to include internet banking, mobile banking, and other digital channels used through customers’ electronic devices for banking transactions, and it distinguishes between **view only banking** (balance enquiry, balance viewing, statement download, etc., with no transactions that alter customer assets/liabilities) and **transactional banking** (full fund-moving and other banking transactions).

For **view only banking facilities**, only RRBs that have implemented **Core Banking Solution (CBS)** and have enabled their public-facing IT infrastructure to handle **IPv6 traffic** are eligible. Any bank that begins offering a view-only digital banking channel on or after the effective date must **inform the RBI’s Department of Regulation through the PRAVAAH portal within 30 days of the board-approved decision to launch**, and must submit a copy of the **“Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy” (GAICA)** report referred to in the directions; a copy of that submission must also be sent to **NABARD**. The process is expressly subject to compliance with the required assessment and internal-control requirements, meaning banks cannot simply launch the service without first completing the prescribed governance and control review.

The directions also make clear that a bank offering only view-only access **cannot provide loans, funds transfers, or other services that create liability for the customer or move funds**, although it may provide downloadable forms for those services. Overall, the document is an authorization and control framework for RRB digital channels rather than a general technology note: it conditions participation on specific infrastructure readiness, board-approved launch decisions, formal regulator intimation, and evidence of adequate internal controls before a bank can commence view-only digital banking services.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks (Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025** apply to all **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. They take effect **from the date of issue** of the directions, and they were issued under RBI’s powers in **Sections 35A and 23 read with Section 51** of the Act. The document replaces the earlier branch-authorisation framework for RRBs and sets out the requirements for opening and operating banking outlets, using off-site/mobile ATMs and cash-handling machines, engaging Business Facilitators/Business Correspondents, and reporting these locations to RBI.

A central compliance requirement is that each RRB’s **Board of Directors must approve a formal policy** governing branch authorisation and related outlet placement/expansion, and the Board retains key oversight responsibility for ensuring the bank’s network expansion and outsourcing arrangements are aligned with the directions. The directions define several operational categories carefully: an **Administrative/Controlling Office** may supervise units and do internal administration only, but it **cannot directly interface with customers** or carry out banking/business transactions; **Back Offices** are limited to processing and verification-type functions. These definitions matter because the directions distinguish between locations that count as banking outlets or customer-facing points and those that do not.

For **branch authorisation**, the directions prescribe how RRBs may open **banking outlets, branches, offices, and customer service points**, and they also address **off-site/mobile ATMs, cash deposit machines (CDMs), and bunch note acceptor machines (BNAMs)**. The document indicates that these devices and outlets are subject to specific authorisation and reporting rules, so compliance teams should treat each new outlet or machine deployment as a regulated event rather than a routine operational decision. The directions also establish a structured framework for the **Business Facilitator (BF) / Business Correspondent (BC) model**, including who is eligible to be engaged and the conditions under which BFs and BCs may be used, which means RRBs need due diligence, engagement controls, and monitoring over third-party customer-interface arrangements.

The directions also create an **information reporting obligation** for banks to submit details of their **banking outlets, branches, offices, customer service points, and similar locations** to the RBI in the manner required in the relevant chapter. Finally, the document contains **repeal and saving provisions**, clarifies that other applicable laws are **not barred**, and provides an interpretation clause; this means compliance should read these directions together with other banking, outsourcing, KYC/AML, and local regulatory requirements rather than assuming they are exhaustive.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025** is a comprehensive consolidation of requirements for urban co-operative banks (“UCBs”) covering governance, depositor fund obligations, compliance procedures, prohibited activities, restructuring, and conditions for opting out of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. It is issued by the RBI on **28 November 2025** and applies to UCBs subject to the scope set out in the preliminary chapter; the document also expressly **repeals prior directions** on the covered subjects to the extent stated in the repeal chapter, so compliance teams should treat this as the controlling framework for the matters it addresses.

A major portion of the directions deals with the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF)**. The bank must follow RBI-prescribed procedures for transferring unclaimed amounts/eligible balances to the Fund, handling refund and interest claims, and maintaining required records, returns, disclosures, audit support, and contact information. The directions require UCBs to have compliant procedures for identifying balances due for transfer, processing depositor claims against amounts transferred to DEAF, furnishing returns and information to RBI, and making appropriate **disclosures in notes to accounts**; they also impose **preservation of records** and audit-related obligations. In practical terms, this means the bank must be able to trace affected customer balances, document transfers to the Fund, respond to claims, and demonstrate compliance through periodic reporting and audit-ready records.

The document also addresses **market operations and customer outreach**, including the ability of UCBs to participate in **currency futures** where permitted, and to conduct **camps and campaigns for periodic KYC updation**, which implies that banks should structure customer due-diligence refresh drives in a controlled, documented way. On the regulatory/legal side, the directions cover **changes in the bank’s name**, **display requirements for the bank’s name**, and handling of **court directives**, so any rebranding, signage, or litigation-related compliance must align with RBI requirements rather than being treated as a purely internal or state-level matter.

The conduct rules section imposes a number of direct prohibitions and permissions affecting management and business activities. UCBs may face restrictions regarding **membership in Mahila Urban Co-operative Banks**, **holding shares in other co-operative societies**, and making **donations/contributions for public or charitable purposes**, and they must comply with restrictions on **payment of bonus**. The bank is prohibited from **accepting deposits at the instance of private financiers or unincorporated bodies** and from **associating with prize chit schemes or selling lottery tickets**, which means distribution relationships, referral arrangements, and any affiliated fundraising/marketing activity must be screened to ensure the bank is not indirectly participating in prohibited products or collection channels.

The operational chapter requires compliance with **mandatory leave** requirements, so banks must maintain leave policies and records that meet the RBI’s minimum expectations and cannot allow key personnel to bypass required absences. The restructuring chapter addresses **financial restructuring**, indicating that where a UCB undergoes restructuring the bank must follow the RBI’s prescribed framework rather than relying only on general corporate approvals. Finally, the opt-out chapter sets out the circumstances and procedure under which certain UCBs—specifically **salary earners’/employees’ co-operative banks** and **other UCBs**—may opt out of the **purview of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, so affected institutions need to assess eligibility carefully and follow the stated process if considering such a change in regulatory status.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Managing Risks in Outsourcing Directions, 2025** establishes a comprehensive outsourcing risk-management regime for **urban co-operative banks**, covering both **financial services outsourcing** and **IT services outsourcing**. It is issued as **DOR/2025-26/293 / DOR.ORG.REC.No.212/21-04-158/2025-26 dated November 28, 2025**; however, the excerpt provided includes the title, table of contents, and chapter structure, but **does not include the operative text for the substantive requirements**, so the specific obligations, thresholds, prohibitions, dates of implementation, and compliance procedures cannot be reliably extracted from the excerpt alone.

From the table of contents, the directions are organized to require a **board-approved outsourcing policy**, defined **board responsibilities**, and a governance structure for oversight by **senior management** and, for IT outsourcing, the **IT function**. The document clearly indicates that it addresses both the **outsourcing of financial services** and the **outsourcing of information technology services**, and that it contains separate sections for **authorisation, accountability, risk evaluation, confidentiality and security of information, outsourcing agreements, monitoring and control, business continuity/disaster recovery, termination, offshore outsourcing, and grievance redressal**. That means UCBs are expected to have formal controls over vendor selection, contractual safeguards, ongoing supervision, and customer complaint handling where outsourced services affect bank operations or customers.

A material feature apparent from the structure is that the RBI is likely imposing **distinct compliance frameworks for financial outsourcing and IT outsourcing**, rather than a single generic policy. The chapter outline suggests the financial-services chapter addresses activities that **may not be outsourced**, with specific governance over what can and cannot be delegated, while the IT chapter includes tailored controls for **service provider evaluation** and **IT-risk management**, reflecting heightened expectations around confidentiality, cybersecurity, resilience, and dependency on third parties. The presence of dedicated sections on **business continuity and disaster recovery** and **termination** indicates that banks must ensure service continuity, exit planning, and orderly transition away from vendors if needed.

For a compliance team, the practical takeaway from the excerpt is that this is a **new RBI outsourcing compliance framework for UCBs issued on November 28, 2025**, and institutions in scope should expect formal obligations to: adopt or update board-approved outsourcing policies; define management accountability; assess and monitor outsourced arrangements; protect confidential and sensitive information; execute detailed outsourcing agreements; ensure continuity and grievance redress mechanisms; and address offshore/vendor-specific risks. Because the operative provisions are not included in the text provided, a compliance officer would need the full circular to determine the **effective date, any transition period, exact prohibited activities, approval thresholds, reporting requirements, and any numerical limits or special conditions**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
This document is the Reserve Bank of India’s comprehensive conduct and customer-protection framework for all Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs), issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. It is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025** and, by its own terms, becomes effective **from the date of issue unless a specific provision says otherwise**; the document shown is dated **November 28, 2025** and is marked **updated as on July 1, 2026**. It applies to **all UCBs**, meaning **Primary Co-operative Banks** as defined under **section 5(ccv) read with section 56** of the Banking Regulation Act.

The part provided begins the definitions section and sets up the terminology that will control later compliance obligations across the Directions. It defines, among other things, **“accounts with survivorship clause”** as joint deposit accounts styled **“either or survivor,” “anyone or survivor,” “former or survivor,” “latter or survivor,”** or similar wording; **“apostille”** as the Hague Convention authentication for public documents used across member countries; and **“APR”** as the **Annual Percentage Rate**, meaning the **annual cost of credit including interest and all other charges associated with the credit facility**. It also begins defining **“bank induced transaction”** as a transaction in a customer account initiated by the UCB under its policy, such as charges and similar debits, indicating the directions will regulate not only customer-initiated activity but also bank-originated account actions.

The table of contents shows the scope of the regulatory regime that UCBs will have to implement. The Directions cover **institutional framework**, **customer service**, **customer guidance and protection**, **financial inclusion and accessibility**, **payment and remittance services**, **deposit and other liabilities**, **responsible lending conduct**, and **miscellaneous instructions**, followed by **repeal and other provisions**. The annexures indicate that RBI is also prescribing or retaining specific operational forms and standardized documents, including a **comprehensive notice board format**, a **quick-reference rate table**, multiple **claim, indemnity, disclaimer, affidavit, locker inventory, safe custody inventory, and bond forms**, and a **Key Facts Statement (KFS)** format. For compliance purposes, this means UCBs should expect detailed process requirements not just on lending and deposits, but also on branch disclosures, customer claims, nominee/survivorship handling, safe deposit locker procedures, and standardized disclosure of loan terms.

Because only the opening pages are provided, the substantive operational rules beyond these definitions are not visible here, so no later deadlines, thresholds, pricing caps, or procedural mandates can be confirmed from the excerpt alone. What can be said with certainty is that the RBI is issuing a bank-wide conduct framework for UCBs that will require institution-wide alignment of customer-facing disclosures, account and claim handling, lending documentation, and accessibility practices, with the annexed forms and tables serving as mandatory compliance tools where referenced in the later chapters.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
This RBI Master Direction replaces and consolidates KYC/AML/CFT obligations for **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, effective **November 28, 2025**, and updated through **December 29, 2025**. Its purpose is to prevent UCBs from being used for **money laundering or terrorist financing**, and it must be read together with the **Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002** and the **Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**, as amended. The document applies to UCBs and imposes governance, customer onboarding, risk-based due diligence, recordkeeping, and reporting obligations, with multiple cross-references to RBI policy instructions and financial intelligence reporting requirements.

At a governance level, the bank’s **Board of Directors** must approve and oversee a written KYC/AML policy framework covering customer acceptance, customer identification, ongoing due diligence, record retention, transaction monitoring, reporting, and risk categorisation. UCBs must maintain a **risk-based approach**: customers are to be classified by money-laundering/terrorist-financing risk, and the intensity of due diligence must match the risk profile. The directions require institutions to have controls to ensure they do not open or maintain anonymous or fictitious accounts, and to apply enhanced checks where higher risk is identified.

For **customer identification and due diligence**, the directions require obtaining and verifying specified identity and address information before opening accounts or establishing relationships, with separate procedures for **individuals, sole proprietorships, legal entities, and beneficial owners**. The bank must identify and verify the **beneficial owner** of legal entities and understand the ownership/control structure, and it must conduct **ongoing due diligence** by monitoring transactions against the expected profile of the customer, source of funds, and risk category. The document also provides for both **enhanced due diligence** in higher-risk situations and **simplified due diligence** where the customer or product qualifies for lower-risk treatment under the RBI framework.

The directions include obligations for **record management** and **reporting to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND)**, meaning UCBs must preserve relevant customer and transaction records for the statutory period under the PML framework and file required reports such as suspicious transaction reports and other mandated regulatory submissions. They also contain requirements tied to **international sanctions/communications from international agencies**, which means UCBs must screen and act on such communications where applicable. The final chapters address repeal/savings and interpretation, indicating that these directions supersede prior RBI KYC instructions for UCBs while preserving actions already taken under the old framework.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025** apply **immediately upon issuance** and are effective from **November 28, 2025**. They apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, defined here as **Primary Co-operative Banks** under **section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. These Directions were issued under the RBI’s powers in **section 35A read with section 56 of the BR Act, 1949**.

A UCB may declare dividends only if it satisfies all of the following conditions: it must be in compliance with the **applicable regulatory capital requirement**; its **Net Non-Performing Asset (NNPA) ratio must be below 5%** after making all necessary provisions, including any provisions required based on the RBI’s last inspection report; there must have been **no default in maintaining CRR/SLR during the financial year for which the dividend is proposed**; and all required provisions must have been made for **NPAs, investments, and other assets** under prudential and accounting norms. In addition, the dividend must be paid **out of the net profit of the same financial year for which the dividend is being paid**, after making **all statutory and other provisions** and after fully adjusting **accumulated losses**.

If a UCB meets all the above conditions **except the NNPA threshold**, it may still seek RBI approval: where the NNPA ratio is **less than 10%**, the bank must **approach the relevant RBI Regional Office for permission** before declaring dividends. This creates a specific exception process for otherwise-compliant banks with higher asset stress, and compliance officers should ensure no dividend is declared under this route without prior regional office permission.

The Directions also state that issues relating to **reversal of excess provision**, **dividend payment on reversal of such provisions**, and **unrealized profits arising from transfer of loans and Government of India–guaranteed Security Receipts** are governed by the RBI’s separate **Urban Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025**. Finally, when the Board considers declaring dividends on equity shares, it must explicitly assess the bank’s **current and projected capital position relative to applicable capital requirements**, the **adequacy of provisions**, and the **economic environment and profitability outlook**, so the decision is not purely backward-looking but must incorporate forward-looking prudential judgment.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures Directions, 2025** apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, defined here as **Primary Co-operative Banks under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The directions were issued under **section 35A read with section 56 of the BR Act, 1949** and are stated to take effect **on the day they are placed on the RBI’s official website**; the title indicates an updated version **as of April 1, 2026**. For compliance purposes, this means UCBs must align financial statement preparation and disclosures with these RBI directions immediately upon their website publication, subject to the updated status shown in the document.

At a foundational level, the directions require UCBs to prepare their **Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account** for all business transacted, **as on the last working day of the year or period**, using the **Forms in the Third Schedule of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** as substituted by **clause (zl) of section 56**. The document also states that banks must follow **ICAI pronouncements on Accounting Standards**, but only **to the extent they are not overridden by RBI directions or guidelines**. So, where ICAI guidance and RBI requirements differ, the RBI directions prevail.

The document’s structure shows that it goes beyond form formatting and also prescribes **notes, instructions, specific accounting treatments, disclosure requirements, and other compliance instructions** for UCB financial statements. It includes sections on **general presentation and detailed disclosure requirements in the notes to accounts**, plus separate operational/accounting instructions for items such as **inter-branch accounts and provisioning for net debit balances, reconciliation and treatment of Nostro account outstanding entries, transfers to or appropriations from reserve funds, provisioning for fraud, handling unreconciled balances, deferred tax liability on the special reserve created under section 36(1)(viii) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, payment of fees and allowances to directors, and restrictions on window dressing**.

The document also includes a **repeal and saving** framework, meaning prior directions on this subject are superseded except to the extent specifically preserved, and it clarifies that application of other laws is **not barred**. In practical compliance terms, a UCB should treat this as the governing RBI framework for **financial statement presentation, accounting policy application, and required disclosures**, and ensure its year-end financial reporting processes, reserve/provision calculations, inter-branch/Nostro reconciliations, fraud provisioning, director remuneration, and anti-window-dressing controls are all aligned with the specific RBI-prescribed treatments in the full directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters” Directions, 2025** take effect **immediately** and are aimed at creating a **non-discriminatory, transparent, natural-justice-based process** for identifying wilful defaulters and sharing that information so lenders can prevent further institutional finance from being extended to them. The directions apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, meaning **Primary Co-operative Banks** under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949; however, the **wilful defaulter** provisions apply only to **Scheduled UCBs** and **non-scheduled UCBs in Tier 3 and Tier 4**, while the **restrictions on further financial accommodation to wilful defaulters** and the **large defaulter provisions** apply more broadly to **all entities regulated by the RBI**, including **Tier 1 and Tier 2 UCBs**, even if they would not otherwise fall within the document’s definition of “lender.”

The directions define key terms that matter for compliance: a **borrower** is anyone who has availed a credit facility from a UCB; a **credit facility** includes both **fund-based and non-fund-based** facilities, expressly covering **off-balance-sheet items such as derivatives, guarantees, and letters of credit**; and **default** has the same meaning as in the RBI’s **UCBs – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025**. The term **director** is defined specifically for these rules as a director of a company that was classified as a **large defaulter or wilful defaulter**, who was associated with the company when the acts or omissions by the company or its directors led to the default. The document also defines **director identification number (DIN)** by reference to the Companies Act, 2013 and **credit information company (CIC)** by reference to the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005.

A major substantive compliance concept in the excerpt is **“diversion of funds,”** which is defined to capture several behaviors that may support wilful-defaulter treatment. These include: using **short-term working capital** for **long-term purposes** contrary to the sanction terms; using borrowed funds to create **assets other than those for which credit was sanctioned**; transferring borrowed funds to **subsidiaries, group companies, or other entities** without approval of the UCB or all consortium lenders; and **routing funds through another lender or consortium member without the UCB’s prior written permission**. Because the directions are designed to support classification of wilful default and dissemination of credit information, these definitions are operationally important for lenders’ review, classification, and reporting processes.

The document’s structure also shows that it imposes governance and control obligations on the **board**, reporting obligations for **wilful defaulters and large defaulters**, and additional requirements around **preventive measures and the role of auditors**. It includes specific **reporting formats** in Annex I for the **list of large defaulters** and Annex II for **data on cases of wilful default**, indicating that UCBs will need to maintain records and submit standardized information in the prescribed manner. Finally, the directions sit under the RBI’s statutory powers in the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and the **Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005**, and they explicitly indicate a coordinated framework for classification, reporting, and lender cautioning rather than a narrow internal-bank policy.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025** and shown as **updated through July 1, 2026**) create a consolidated regulatory framework for how urban co-operative banks must identify, classify, restructure, settle, write off, and report stressed assets. The stated purpose is to harmonize earlier instructions on stressed-asset resolution, including **compromise settlements** and **technical write-offs**, and to provide a consolidated treatment for changes in the **Date of Commencement of Commercial Operations (DCCO)** for infrastructure and non-infrastructure projects. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that these Directions are not merely advisory: they are a bank-wide framework governing board-approved policy, early stress detection, prudential treatment after restructuring, and special handling for certain borrower categories and special situations.

At the general governance level, the Directions require each covered urban co-operative bank to have **board-approved policies** for resolution of stressed assets and to put in place processes for **early identification and reporting of stress**, along with required disclosures. The document’s structure makes clear that the bank must have formal internal procedures, not ad hoc decisions, for recognizing stress, escalating it, and tracking treatment over time. This means compliance functions should expect formal policy documentation, management information systems, and reporting lines tied to the board-approved framework.

For **restructuring of accounts**, the Directions set out the prudential rules applicable when an account is restructured, including how the account must be classified after restructuring, when any **special regulatory treatment** may apply, how **additional finance** should be handled, when an account may be **upgraded after satisfactory performance**, and the **provisioning** and **income recognition** consequences after restructuring. The framework also covers special treatment for borrowers who have committed **frauds, malfeasance, or wilful default**, as well as **compromise settlements and technical write-offs**, indicating that these cases are governed by separate, specific prudential rules rather than ordinary restructuring treatment. Compliance officers should treat these as distinct resolution pathways with separate eligibility and accounting consequences.

The Directions also specifically address **projects under implementation**, which is important for infrastructure and other project finance exposures where the **DCCO changes**. The document indicates that it provides a consolidated regulatory treatment for such changes, meaning banks must follow the RBI’s prescribed approach when project timelines slip, rather than relying on legacy practices. There is also a dedicated section on **advances granted under rehabilitation packages approved by term lending institutions**, showing that such sanctioned rehabilitation cases receive tailored regulatory treatment and should be tracked separately from ordinary borrower restructurings.

A separate chapter deals with **accounts impacted by calamities**, requiring the bank to formulate a **resolution plan**, take any **ancillary measures** needed, and comply with associated **reporting requirements**. This means calamity-affected borrowers are not left to general restructuring policy alone; banks need a specific operational response, likely including relief measures, documentation, and regulatory reporting. The Directions also contain a chapter on **Government Debt Relief Schemes (DRS)**, setting out the **prudential treatment** applicable when government-backed debt relief programs are involved, so any such accounts must be identified and classified under those specific rules.

The final chapters cover **trade relief measures** and the **repeal/saving** provisions, plus interpretive provisions and the relationship with other laws not barred by the Directions. From a compliance standpoint, the important point is that this is a **consolidated replacement-style framework** intended to supersede or harmonize prior instructions in these areas, so banks must review existing internal policies, manuals, and accounting/reporting practices to ensure they align with the 2025 Directions as updated through **July 1, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions, 2025** (as updated through **July 1, 2026**) set out the prudential rules UCBs must follow for classifying advances, recognizing income, and making provisions. They are issued under the RBI’s statutory powers and are intended to bring greater consistency and transparency to bank accounts; the document replaces prior instructions through a repeal-and-saving framework, so compliance teams should treat these directions as the governing reference for UCB asset quality and income/provisioning treatment from the effective period stated in the final text. The instructions apply to **urban co-operative banks** and govern their lending portfolio, including treatment of advances, investments in shares and bonds, and recovery accounting in stressed asset situations.

The directions require the **board** of each UCB to oversee lending prudence and consumer education, and they impose disclosure obligations so that banks publish the required asset-quality and provisioning information. The core of the document is the asset-classification framework: accounts must be identified as **non-performing assets (NPAs)** based on the RBI’s specified overdue/default criteria, with special rules for accounts regularised close to the balance-sheet date, for particular asset types and restructuring situations, and for valuation of security supporting the exposure. Once a loan is classified as an NPA, the bank must follow the mandated **upgradation** rules before moving it back to performing status, and it must apply the prescribed treatment to recoveries from NPAs, including how such recoveries are appropriated and how any previously recognized income is reversed.

On provisioning, the directions prescribe minimum provisioning for **standard assets, substandard assets, doubtful assets, and loss assets**, and they also allow/require additional specific provisioning in some cases, including where a resolution plan has been implemented under the RBI’s separate **Urban Cooperative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025**. The document also addresses special circumstances where provisions may need to be **higher than the prescribed rates**, meaning banks cannot assume the stated percentages are always the ceiling if risk is greater or other supervisory requirements apply. Income-recognition rules are aligned with asset classification: banks may not continue to recognize income on assets that have become non-performing, and they must reverse income already booked when an account is classified as an NPA; there are also specific rules for recognizing income on **investments in shares and bonds** and for other special cases.

For compliance purposes, the key operational takeaway is that these directions create a full end-to-end framework for **when to stop booking interest**, **when to classify an exposure as NPA**, **how to value collateral/security**, **what provisions must be held at each asset stage**, and **how to handle restructuring/resolution and recoveries**. The document’s structure shows that it also includes general principles, definitions, and interpretive/repeal provisions, so banks should ensure internal policy, loan-system triggers, accounting entries, board reporting, and disclosures are all aligned with the RBI’s specific classification and provisioning mechanics as updated in the July 1, 2026 version.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Asset Liability Management Directions, 2025** set a revised, more detailed framework for how UCBs must govern, measure, monitor, and report liquidity, currency, and interest rate risk. These directions are issued under the Banking Regulation Act framework and are meant to replace prior ALM instructions through a formal **repeal-and-savings** structure, while preserving actions already taken under the old regime. The document applies to **urban co-operative banks**, with certain provisions applying differently depending on whether a bank is **Scheduled UCB**, **Non-Scheduled UCB**, or **Level I UCB**; some requirements are expressly **not applicable to Level I UCBs**, while others apply to Level I as well.

At a governance level, the directions place primary responsibility on the **Board of Directors** to approve the bank’s ALM policy, set risk limits, and review them periodically, and to ensure that the bank has a robust ALM information system, organization, and process. The Board must ensure the institution has systems to measure and manage liquidity risk, interest rate risk, and currency risk where relevant, and that management information is timely enough to support active decision-making. The ALM framework is not just a reporting exercise: banks must maintain internal controls, escalation procedures, and ongoing board/management review of exposure positions, assumptions, and exception handling.

For **liquidity risk management**, all applicable UCBs must prepare and review liquidity statements, including a **Structural Liquidity Statement (SLS)** and a **short-term dynamic liquidity statement**, with separate annexed formats for scheduled and non-scheduled banks. The directions also require banks to base liquidity analysis on **behavioural patterns** rather than only contractual maturities, meaning they must model customer withdrawal patterns, prepayments, drawdowns, and other non-contractual behaviours when assessing liquidity gaps. For **Scheduled UCBs**, the framework additionally recognizes access to the **Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF)** and **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)**, implying that those banks must manage liquidity with these RBI facilities in mind; the document distinguishes this from non-scheduled institutions.

The directions also introduce a dedicated framework for **currency risk** and **interest rate risk (IRR) management**. Currency risk management is required for applicable UCBs and is **not applicable to Level I UCBs**, while IRR management must include **traditional gap analysis**, an **Interest Rate Sensitivity (IRS) statement**, and behavioural modeling. In other words, banks must not rely solely on balance-sheet maturity buckets; they must also assess how repricing, deposits, loans, and other items actually behave under changing rates and how those behaviours affect earnings and capital. This is especially important for compliance because it requires documented assumptions, periodic validation, and management approval of the models and thresholds used.

The monitoring and reporting chapter requires banks to prepare the prescribed statements and submit regulatory returns at the periodicity specified for each category of UCB. The document separately addresses **Scheduled UCBs**, **Non-Scheduled UCBs (excluding Level I)**, and **Level I UCBs**, indicating that the reporting obligations and frequency are not uniform across all institutions. The annexes provide the official statement formats, including the **Structural Liquidity Statement for Scheduled UCBs**, **Structural Liquidity Statement for Non-Scheduled UCBs**, **Short-term Dynamic Liquidity Statement for UCBs**, and **Interest Rate Sensitivity Statement for Scheduled UCBs**, so compliance teams must align internal ALM systems to those formats rather than using bespoke templates.

The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and identified as **DOR/2025-26/285** and **DOR.LRG.No.204/13-10-006/2025-26**. A compliance team should treat this as a mandatory ALM overhaul for UCBs, with immediate focus on whether the bank is scheduled, non-scheduled, or Level I, because that classification determines which statements, risk categories, and RBI facilities apply.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on September 2, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Directions, 2025** on urban co-operative banks’ investment portfolios set out the full framework these banks must follow for **investment policy, classification, valuation, market-value determination, and permitted dealing practices** in securities. The directions apply to **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** and cover both **government securities and non-SLR instruments**; they are intended to govern how a UCB’s board approves investment policy, how investments are categorized between **Held to Maturity (HTM), Held for Trading (HFT), and Available for Sale (AFS)**, and how those instruments are subsequently valued and reclassified. The document is a comprehensive operational compliance framework rather than a narrow rule change, so compliance teams should treat it as the governing manual for investment accounting, treasury controls, and securities-market activity for UCBs.

At the governance level, the directions require the **board** to be actively responsible for the bank’s investment policy and associated controls, rather than leaving investment management purely to treasury staff. The policy must address the bank’s approach to classification, valuation, permissible instruments, and transaction handling, and the document also establishes **general instructions** that constrain how investments are made and managed. Compliance teams should expect formal board-approved policies, documented procedures, and internal limits to align with the RBI’s requirements, because the directions are drafted as mandatory operational rules rather than recommendations.

The document then sets out the classification regime for investment portfolios, including the rules for placing securities into **HTM, HFT, and AFS** and the circumstances in which securities may be shifted between categories. It specifically distinguishes **shifts to and from HTM** from **shifts between AFS and HFT**, which indicates that reclassification is permitted but regulated and likely subject to recordkeeping and valuation consequences. The valuation chapter separately prescribes how HTM holdings are valued versus HFT/AFS holdings, with the latter categories subject to market-based valuation, and the market value chapter explains how to determine market value for **quoted securities, unquoted SLR securities, and unquoted non-SLR securities**. For compliance purposes, this means the bank must have reliable pricing methodology, documentation for unquoted instruments, and processes to ensure valuation treatment matches the applicable category.

A substantial portion of the directions governs **government securities operations**. UCBs are given instructions on access to the **Negotiated Dealing System – Order Matching (NDS-OM)**, the use and maintenance of **Subsidiary General Ledger (SGL) accounts** and **gilt accounts**, settlement of government-security transactions, participation in **primary auctions**, **short sale**, **when-issued transactions**, **value-free transfers**, exchange-based transactions, and **repo/reverse repo** activity in government securities. The document also addresses **retail participation in government securities** and the handling of **STRIPS** (Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal Securities). Compliance teams should read this as requiring operational readiness for settlement, custody, and market access controls, along with procedures to ensure transactions occur only through approved channels and in line with RBI-prescribed settlement and transfer mechanisms.

The directions also cover **non-SLR investments**, including the universe of permissible non-SLR instruments, the **prudential limit** framework applicable to such investments, and dealings in **repo in corporate bonds**, **commercial papers (CPs)**, and **certificates of deposit (CDs)**. It further addresses **trading and settlement in corporate bonds**, meaning banks must ensure that treasury activity in these instruments is performed within RBI constraints and in line with the bank’s internal exposure limits and settlement controls. Even though the excerpt provided does not display the specific numerical prudential caps, the presence of a dedicated prudential-limit section means compliance officers should verify the bank’s exposure monitoring, approved counterparty/instrument limits, and transaction approval workflow against the full text before undertaking or booking any non-SLR activity.

Because the document is titled as **updated on September 2, 2026**, compliance teams should treat that date as the effective latest revision of the directions and ensure that any internal policy, treasury procedure, accounting practice, or trading control reflects the updated version rather than the original 2025 issuance date. The header shows the instrument was originally issued on **November 28, 2025** under **DOR/2025-26/284** and then updated later, so implementation and audit review should be based on the consolidated, updated text. In practical terms, the bank should confirm that board-approved investment policy, valuation systems, treasury dealing procedures, settlement controls, and limits monitoring are all aligned to this updated RBI framework.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025** apply **immediately upon issuance** and are binding on **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, meaning **Primary Co-operative Banks** as defined under **Section 5(ccv) read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The RBI has issued them under its powers in the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** (including **Sections 21 and 35A read with Section 56**) and related enabling laws. The core purpose is to standardize and tighten how UCBs set and disclose lending rates, while still leaving them flexibility to determine rates based on business judgment with Board approval.

On pricing, each bank may set lending rates by considering **cost of funds, transaction costs, and similar factors**, but only with **Board-approved policies**. The bank must ensure interest rates are **transparent and known to customers**, and must **publish the minimum and maximum interest rates** it charges and **display that information in every branch**. Although interest rates are deregulated, the Directions specifically caution that rates above a certain level may be viewed as **usurious** and inconsistent with normal banking practice; accordingly, the Board must lay down **internal principles and procedures** to prevent excessive pricing.

For **all advances**, interest must be charged at **monthly rests**. There is an express carve-out for **agricultural advances**, where the existing practice tied to **crop seasons** continues: for **long-duration crops**, interest should be charged at **annual rests**. For other agricultural loans, including those for **short-duration crops** and allied activities such as **dairy, fishery, piggery, poultry, and bee-keeping**, the bank may align due dates with the borrower’s cash-flow cycles and the **harvesting/marketing season**, and may compound overdue interest accordingly if instalments are not paid on time.

The Directions also impose more detailed governance expectations for **small-value loans, especially personal loans and similar products**. Banks should have a suitable **prior-approval process** that considers the borrower’s **cash flows** before sanction. Pricing must reflect a **reasonable and justified risk premium** based on the borrower’s **internal rating**, and should also account for whether security exists and its value. The **total cost to the borrower**—including interest and all charges—must be justifiable relative to the bank’s cost of extending the loan and the expected return, and banks may set and publicize an **appropriate ceiling** on interest, processing fees, and other charges for such loans.

The excerpt ends mid-provision, but it clearly states one additional limit: the **total interest debited to an account must not exceed the principal amount**. For compliance purposes, the key immediate action is to confirm that the bank’s lending-rate policy, branch disclosures, Board approvals, agricultural-loan treatment, and small-loan pricing/approval controls all align with these Directions as of the issuance date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025** create a consolidated framework for credit-risk transfer and loan-distribution activities for UCBs, issued under sections **21, 35A and 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The Directions **take effect on the day they are placed on the RBI’s official website** and apply specifically to **Urban Co-operative Banks / Primary Co-operative Banks** as defined under the Banking Regulation Act. The document is designed to govern transfer of loan exposures, stressed-loan transfers, and certain lending/risk-sharing arrangements, replacing the need to rely on fragmented prior guidance.

A key restriction is that **UCBs are not permitted to act as transferor or transferee in any loan transfer other than the transfer of stressed loans under Part A, Chapter III**. In other words, for ordinary loan-transfer markets, UCBs cannot buy or sell loans unless the transaction falls within the stressed-loan framework specifically allowed for them. The Directions also state that banks may acquire loans only from a transferor identified as a lender under the relevant paragraph, and that **no bank may undertake loan transfers or acquisitions except as expressly permitted under these Directions and in the prescribed manner**. The framework applies to loan transfers done through **novation or assignment**, and where loans are transferred, **legal ownership must be transferred to the transferee to the extent of the economic interest transferred**.

The Directions also make clear that the new framework is meant to coexist with certain other RBI-permitted arrangements, because the restriction on loan transfers is stated to be **without prejudice to External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits, Structured Obligations (Master Direction dated March 26, 2019), guarantees, and other products explicitly permitted under RBI guidelines**. That means institutions should not treat the Directions as a blanket prohibition on all credit risk transfer mechanisms, but rather as the controlling framework for loan exposure transfers unless another RBI rule expressly governs the product.

For compliance purposes, the most important immediate takeaway is that **UCBs’ permissible role is narrow and must be checked transaction-by-transaction**: if the transaction is not a stressed-loan transfer permitted under Part A, Chapter III, the UCB should assume it is outside scope and therefore not allowed. Because the Directions are stated as a **comprehensive and self-contained framework**, banks should expect operational, legal, and documentation controls to align precisely with the prescribed transfer mechanics, ownership transfer requirement, and the limited set of permissible counterparties and transaction types.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025** consolidate the prudential rules that limit concentration risk for **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, including limits on exposures to single borrowers, connected borrower groups, unsecured advances, inter-bank exposures, and large/small value lending. The directions were issued under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** (Sections **21, 35A, and 56**) and **take effect immediately upon issuance** on **November 28, 2025**. They apply to all **Urban Co-operative Banks**, defined as **Primary Co-operative Banks** under **Section 5(ccv) read with Section 56** of the Banking Regulation Act.

For exposure measurement, the document defines **“credit exposure”** broadly to include **funded and non-funded credit limits**, underwriting and similar commitments, equipment leasing and hire purchase financing, and ad hoc contingency limits. For limit calculation, the **sanctioned amount or outstanding amount, whichever is higher, must be counted**; however, for **fully drawn term loans with no scope for re-drawal**, a UCB may use the **outstanding** amount instead. For **non-funded credit limits**, **100% of the limit or outstanding, whichever is higher**, must be included. The directions also state that a UCB’s share in **consortium / multiple banking / syndication** arrangements is governed by the **single borrower / group exposure** rules, and loans secured against the UCB’s **own term deposits** are excluded from credit exposure. “Exposure” is defined to include both **credit exposure** and **investment exposure in non-SLR securities** under the separate RBI investment portfolio directions, and **Tier-I capital as of March 31 of the preceding financial year** is the capital base used to fix exposure limits.

The document also sets the approach for identifying **“groups”** of connected borrowers: the UCB itself determines group membership based on its knowledge of the customer base, with the guiding principle being **commonality of management and effective control**. It specifically provides that **different firms with one or more common partners engaged in the same line of business** (such as manufacturing, processing, or trading) are to be treated as a **connected group**, and entities under **common ownership** are treated as a **single party**. In compliance terms, UCBs will need to ensure their credit and investment systems, borrower-group mapping, and exposure monitoring are aligned to these definitions so that all relevant funded, non-funded, and investment positions are captured consistently against the applicable prudential exposure limits.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction set, issued on November 28, 2025 and effective immediately upon issuance, establishes the credit-risk management framework that applies to all Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs), meaning primary co-operative banks as defined under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The circular is expressly grounded in the RBI’s powers under sections 20, 21, and 35A read with section 56, and it is designed to strengthen prudential control over UCB credit exposures because credit risk can affect other risk categories and has systemic implications across sectors, borrower types, and products.

At a high level, the directions consolidate and reinforce RBI’s requirements on credit-risk governance, statutory and regulatory restrictions, credit administration, borrower identification, property valuation, CERSAI filing, account conduct, and loan structuring. The document includes multiple chapters covering board-approved policies, credit risk evaluation, statutory restrictions, regulatory restrictions, credit administration, Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) requirements for borrowers, empanelment of valuers, filing of security interests in CERSAI for immovable, movable, and intangible assets, maintenance of cash credit/current account/overdraft accounts, and the loan system for delivery of bank credit. The directions also state that they update and replace prior RBI guidance for these matters through a repeal-and-savings framework in the final chapter.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that UCBs must align their lending and credit-control processes to the RBI’s specified prudential tools and prohibitions, not merely internal policy preferences. The directions emphasize that certain activities may be statutorily restricted or prohibited, and that credit-risk management must be governed by board-approved policies and formal administration controls. UCBs should therefore expect mandatory internal policy revision, board approval, operational procedures for borrower screening and monitoring, and documentation controls across the full credit lifecycle.

The document’s defined terms show that it governs standard lending instruments such as bank guarantees, bills purchased and discounted, and cash credit facilities. In the cash credit context, the text begins to define the facility as a running account with drawing power periodically determined against security such as hypothecation or pledge of goods, book debts, and standing crops, indicating that account conduct and limit monitoring are part of the regulated credit-risk framework. Because the contents list also specifically calls out LEI compliance, property valuation controls, and CERSAI filing, compliance teams should assume the directions require tighter borrower/entity identification, independent valuation discipline for secured lending, and timely registration of security interests for covered assets.

From a governance and implementation standpoint, the directions take effect immediately and therefore require UCBs to have already moved toward compliance as of issuance, with the updated-as-on July 1, 2026 version reflecting any subsequent amendments or clarifications. A compliance officer should treat the document as a mandatory operating framework for UCB lending, requiring review of all credit policies, lending templates, account-monitoring procedures, and secured-transaction filings to ensure they conform to the RBI’s direction-by-direction standards.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025** (updated as of **July 1, 2026**) create a standardized, mandatory framework for how Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) report, correct, disseminate, and protect credit information. The stated policy objectives are to ensure credit data is reported and shared in a uniform way, to protect the confidentiality and security of sensitive credit information, and to give consumers a process to access their credit information and pursue grievances related to credit reporting. The Directions are issued under **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulations) Act, 2005 (CICRA)** and, unless a provision specifies otherwise, **take immediate effect**. They apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks** (the document begins defining them as the regulated entities covered), and the obligations are framed around their role as credit information reporters and users.

At a high level, the Directions require UCBs to become and remain members of credit information companies (CICs), and to report credit information in the formats and timelines prescribed by RBI. The reporting framework covers the **data formats** to be used, **reporting timelines and updation obligations**, detailed **reporting guidelines**, and procedures for handling **rejected data**, including **rectification of rejected data and review of the Data Quality Index (DQI)**. The Directions also require a process for **correction of Credit Information Reports (CIRs)** where errors are identified, and they set out how UCBs may use credit information reports in **credit appraisal**. There are also rules on the **display of information** and on how these Directions interact with other RBI Department of Regulation instructions.

The document additionally imposes governance and technical coordination obligations. It establishes a **Technical Working Group** chapter, indicating formal mechanisms for ongoing technical coordination and implementation support around credit reporting requirements. For customer-facing compliance, the Directions create explicit requirements on **customer service and grievance redressal**, including a strengthened customer service framework, a **compensation framework for customers**, and reference to the **Reserve Bank-Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021** for complaint escalation and resolution. The overall compliance expectation is that UCBs must not only report accurate credit data on time, but also maintain reliable internal processes for data quality, error correction, customer access, and complaint handling.

Finally, the Directions include a chapter on **best practices** and a chapter on **repeal and other provisions**, including **repeal and saving**, confirmation that application of other laws is not barred, and interpretive provisions. While the excerpt does not show specific numeric thresholds, fee amounts, or time limits, it makes clear that compliance officers must treat this as a comprehensive regulatory framework covering membership in CICs, data reporting and update cycles, error remediation, consumer transparency, and compensation/grievance processes. Since the text notes an updated version as of **July 1, 2026**, compliance teams should verify any amendments reflected in the updated text when implementing procedures and controls.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025” apply to Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs), meaning Primary Co-operative Banks as defined under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The Directions take effect immediately as of November 28, 2025, and they govern the general and conduct requirements for credit cards, debit cards, and co-branded debit cards; they expressly exclude co-branding credit cards from this document’s scope, while still requiring banks to read these Directions together with any applicable prudential, payment, technology, and cyber-security instructions issued by RBI. RBI states that these Directions are issued under section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 read with section 56, and all other enabling provisions, as a public-interest measure.

The document sets out key card-related definitions that matter for product design and compliance. It defines, among other things, add-on credit cards as supplementary cards issued to persons with a predefined relationship to the primary cardholder and within the primary cardholder’s credit limit and liability; annual percentage rate as the total annual cost of credit including interest and all other charges; charge cards as cards requiring full payment of the billed amount on the due date with no revolving credit; co-branded cards as jointly issued cards bearing both entities’ names; convenience fees as fixed or pro-rata charges for card use where cards are not ordinarily accepted as a payment method; corporate credit cards as cards issued to employees of a corporate employer with liability potentially resting with the corporate, the employee, or both depending on product design; and credit cards as physical or virtual instruments with a pre-approved revolving credit limit that may be used for purchases and cash advances, subject to prescribed terms. The definitions also introduce reward/loyalty programmes as card-linked schemes offering coupons, points, discounts, cashbacks, or other monetary-value benefits that can be redeemed on current or future transactions.

From a compliance perspective, the document is not merely descriptive; it is the framework for how UCBs must issue and conduct card business going forward. UCBs offering credit or debit cards must align their card issuance, conduct, and associated customer treatment with these Directions, including any product rules, billing practices, liability allocation, and fee structures that are addressed in the later chapters of the instrument. Because the Directions are immediately effective, affected banks should treat them as an operational requirement now, and ensure that card products, customer disclosures, back-office processes, and third-party/co-brand arrangements are reviewed for conformity. The excerpt provided ends partway through the definitions section, so additional substantive obligations likely appear in later chapters, but based on the text shown, the immediate compliance impact is that UCBs must treat these Directions as binding now and map all card products and arrangements to the RBI-defined terms and scope.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** and updated through **July 15, 2026**) set a comprehensive prudential and conduct framework for **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** across multiple lending products and credit-related activities. The document applies to UCBs and covers board-approved lending policies, digital lending through lending service providers, gold and silver-backed loans, microfinance, project finance, non-fund-based credit facilities such as guarantees and co-acceptances, and housing finance. A compliance team should treat this as a consolidated source of operational, disclosure, underwriting, technology, monitoring, and customer-protection requirements, with the specific obligations varying by product line.

A major part of the directions is the **digital lending** framework. UCBs entering into arrangements with **lending service providers (LSPs)** must meet general requirements on governance and customer protection, including technology and data controls, credit-information reporting, and rules on default-loss sharing arrangements. The directions also impose requirements on digital lending applications (DLAs), and compliance teams should ensure that any outsourced or platform-based lending activity is subject to board-approved oversight, transparent customer treatment, appropriate data handling, and reporting discipline. Where loss-sharing structures are used in case of borrower default, they must comply with the specified RBI conditions rather than being left to private contract alone.

For **lending against gold and silver collateral**, the document introduces or consolidates restrictions, ceilings, valuation/assaying standards, and **loan-to-value (LTV)** limits, together with other operational safeguards. UCBs must follow RBI-prescribed procedures for the valuation and assaying of pledged precious metal, and lending must stay within the applicable LTV ratio and any product-specific ceilings. Compliance officers should pay close attention to whether their bank is lending to retail borrowers, traders, or other eligible categories, because the chapter contains separate restrictions and operational rules depending on the collateral and purpose.

The **microfinance** chapter sets out the RBI’s definition of microfinance and requires banks to assess **household income** before extending such loans. It also caps the **aggregate repayment obligations of a household** as a share of household income, so lending decisions must test the borrower’s total debt service burden across all lenders, not just the UCB’s own exposure. This means underwriting processes need to capture reliable household-income information and existing repayment obligations, with lending systems and staff training aligned to the household-level affordability test. The chapter also contains other operational requirements that must be built into product design and monitoring.

For **project finance**, the directions distinguish phases of a project and impose prudential conditions both at **sanction** and at **disbursement/monitoring** stages. This is intended to ensure that funding is tied to project readiness, implementation progress, and ongoing oversight, rather than being disbursed loosely against incomplete documentation or weak milestones. Compliance teams should expect detailed requirements around credit appraisal, stage-wise disbursement, and monitoring of project execution, including documentation and control expectations for construction or other long-duration financing. The chapter also includes additional prudential provisions that will affect credit administration and risk management.

The chapter on **non-fund-based (NFB) credit facilities** governs guarantees, electronic guarantees (**e-guarantees**), co-acceptances, and guarantees involving overseas current or capital account transactions. UCBs must comply with the general conditions for issuing such exposures, and the document specifically addresses how guarantees may be issued, the use of e-guarantee systems, guarantees in favor of another regulated entity, and the regulatory treatment of co-acceptances. Compliance must ensure that contingent liabilities are tracked and approved under the prescribed framework, and that any cross-border or overseas-linked guarantee activity follows the RBI’s foreign-exchange and credit rules. This chapter is especially important because NFB exposures can create credit risk without immediate fund outflow and therefore require careful limit, documentation, and monitoring controls.

The **housing finance** chapter sets eligibility rules for borrowers, eligibility criteria for housing finance itself, and limits on loan amount and margin requirements. It also includes rules on **interest rates**, **foreclosure charges/prepayment penalties**, and the **reset of floating interest rates on EMI-based housing loans**, along with **penal charges** and a required **Key Facts Statement** regime. For compliance purposes, this means UCBs must ensure retail home-loan pricing and disclosures are transparent and consistent with RBI standards, and that borrowers receive the mandated pre-contract and ongoing disclosures. Because the document is a consolidated directions instrument, the effective obligations are not limited to one-off underwriting rules; they also govern how housing loans are priced, how prepayment is treated, and how changes to floating rates are communicated and implemented.

Overall, the document is a broad RBI credit-compliance framework for UCBs that requires banks to align board policies, lending workflows, outsourcing arrangements, collateral valuation, income assessment, project monitoring, contingent-credit issuance, and retail housing-loan disclosures with the specific prudential and customer-protection standards set out in the directions. A compliance officer should review each product line against the relevant chapter, confirm that internal policy, system controls, and customer disclosures match the RBI text, and verify that any activities involving digital platforms, precious-metal collateral, microfinance households, project disbursements, guarantees, or housing-loan repricing are operating within the prescribed limits and procedures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Urban Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits” Directions, 2025, as updated on August 25, 2026, set the RBI’s binding framework for how urban co-operative banks may offer, calculate, pay, and disclose interest on deposit products, with separate rules for domestic rupee deposits, non-resident rupee deposits, and foreign-currency deposits. The directions are issued under the RBI’s regulatory authority and apply to urban co-operative banks covered by the framework; the document is organized as a comprehensive operational rulebook, so compliance teams should treat it as controlling both product design and day-to-day deposit operations from the commencement date stated in the instrument (not shown in the excerpt). It replaces or consolidates prior instructions through repeal-and-savings provisions, while preserving actions already taken under earlier directions where applicable.

For domestic rupee deposits, the directions govern current accounts, savings deposits, term deposits, additional interest, overdue deposits, floating-rate term deposits, the periodicity of savings-interest crediting, payment on death of the depositor, and penalties for premature withdrawal. The bank must ensure interest is paid only in the manner and at the rates permitted by the RBI framework, with specific operational rules for when interest can be added to balances, when overdue deposits continue to earn interest, and how floating-rate term deposits are repriced and settled. The directions also require banks to follow RBI-prescribed treatment for deceased depositors’ accounts and to apply any premature-withdrawal penalty only as permitted under the applicable product terms and RBI rules.

For deposits held by non-residents, the document separately regulates rupee deposits and FCNR(B)-type foreign-currency deposits. It prohibits marking liens on certain non-resident deposit accounts, prescribes the interest treatment for NRE deposits and FCNR(B) deposits, and sets out the treatment when the depositor dies, when an NRI returns to India, or when funds are converted from FCNR(B) into Resident Foreign Currency (RFC) or resident rupee accounts. The directions also address premature withdrawal of non-resident and foreign-currency deposits and allow penalties only within the limits and conditions set by the RBI. Compliance teams must therefore verify that account opening, renewal, conversion, and closure workflows distinguish clearly between resident, NRI, returning Indian, and deceased-depositor scenarios.

The foreign-currency chapter covers FCNR(B) deposits in detail, including how interest is calculated, how interest applies on renewal, and what happens to deposits after the depositor’s death or return to India. It also includes the Resident Foreign Currency Accounts Scheme, so banks must ensure products and systems support the permissible conversion and payment rules across FCNR(B), RFC, and resident rupee accounts. The “Prohibitions and Exemptions” chapter indicates that some activities are expressly barred while certain entities or transactions may be exempted, and the final chapter clarifies repeal, savings, application of other laws, and interpretative rules. Because the excerpt does not reproduce the operative rate tables or specific numeric thresholds, a compliance officer should review the full body of the directions and any schedules for exact interest ceilings, permitted exceptions, and product-specific implementation details.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on June 16, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025** were issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance**. They apply to all **Urban Co-operative Banks**, defined here as **Primary Co-operative Banks under section 5(ccv) read with Section 56 of the BR Act, 1949**. The directions establish the full capital adequacy framework for UCBs, including how capital is defined, what counts toward regulatory capital, how risk-weighted assets (RWAs) are computed, and how banks must report capital ratios.

At a high level, the document sets out the prudential capital rules that banks must use to determine **net worth, statutory requirements, minimum regulatory capital, and the composition of capital**. It splits capital into **Tier 1 capital** and **Tier 2 capital**, and then sets out the methodology for calculating RWAs for **credit risk** and **market risk**. It also introduces specific requirements on **share linking to borrowings**, **refund of share capital**, **protection of investors in regulatory capital instruments**, and **reporting**, including prescribed reporting formats in **Annex I** and **Annex II** for capital ratio monitoring.

The definitions section is relevant for compliance because it establishes the regulatory meaning of key terms used throughout the directions. For example, **credit risk** is the risk that a borrower or counterparty fails to meet agreed obligations or that their credit quality deteriorates; **market risk** is the risk of loss from movements in market prices affecting on- and off-balance-sheet positions; **derivatives** take the meaning given in **Section 45U(a) of the RBI Act, 1934**; and **DTA/DTL** are to be understood under applicable accounting standards. Compliance teams should treat these definitions as controlling for capital classification and RWA calculations under the directions.
