In addition, the directions include **best practices**, repeal-and-saving provisions, and rules clarifying how they interact with other laws and existing RBI instructions. The document is intended to replace or supersede inconsistent prior arrangements to the extent specified, while preserving lawful actions already taken and clarifying that other applicable legal requirements are not barred by these directions. For compliance purposes, the key point is that rural co-operative banks must treat credit information reporting as a regulated, ongoing operational obligation with requirements for **timely, accurate reporting; error rectification; data-quality controls; customer access and complaint handling; and compensation/ombudsman escalation where applicable**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Rural Co-operative Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025”** take **immediate effect** and apply to **all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The directions govern the **general and conduct rules for debit cards**, including **co-branded debit cards**, and must be read together with any other RBI requirements on **prudential, payment, technology, and cyber-security matters** that apply to debit and co-branded debit cards.  

Each bank must put in place **Board-approved comprehensive policies and procedures** covering debit card issuance, co-branding arrangements where relevant, a **standard operating procedure for discretionary blocking, deactivation, or suspension of debit cards**, the **time period for completing formalities after a lost card is blocked**, and a **grievance redressal and compensation framework**. The document makes clear that these policy requirements are not standalone; they are to be implemented in line with the more detailed requirements set out in the later chapters of the Directions.  

On issuance, the bank must adopt a **Board-approved comprehensive debit card issuance policy** and issue cards only in accordance with it. The document also defines the key instruments and relationships: a **debit card** may be **physical or virtual**, must be linked to a **savings or current account**, and may be used for cash withdrawal, online payments, PoS/QR transactions, fund transfers, and similar transactions subject to prescribed terms; a **form factor** is any physical or virtual substitute used to carry out a payment or banking transaction; a **co-branded card** is issued jointly with a co-branding entity and bears both entities’ names; and a **card loyalty/reward programme** includes incentives such as digital coupons, points, discounts, cashbacks, or other monetary benefits that can be redeemed on the same or later transactions after accumulation.  

The Directions also specify that “convenience fee” means a **fixed or pro-rata charge** for using a debit card as an alternative payment method where that payment method is **not ordinarily accepted** compared with other forms of payment. Finally, any terms not specifically defined in the Directions are to take their meaning from the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **RBI Act, 1934**, or, where appropriate, their ordinary commercial meaning.  

Because the excerpt provided cuts off mid-provision in Chapter III, there may be additional operational or product-specific requirements later in the document that are not visible here. However, from the text provided, the compliance-critical immediate obligations are: **implement Board-approved debit card and co-branding policies, establish procedures for card blocking and lost-card follow-up, and ensure grievance/compensation handling is formally documented and aligned with RBI’s broader card-related requirements**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This Reserve Bank of India directive, effective as updated through **April 1, 2026**, consolidates the RBI’s requirements for **rural co-operative banks** on credit facilities, with detailed rules spanning board-approved lending policies, digital lending, gold/silver-backed lending, microfinance, housing loans, and non-fund-based credit facilities. It applies to the banks covered by the “rural co-operative banks” framework and requires those institutions to align their lending practices, customer protections, underwriting, valuation, reporting, and technology controls to the specific standards set out in the directions.

A major compliance theme is **digital lending**: rural co-operative banks that lend through **lending service provider (LSP)** arrangements must meet RBI-prescribed governance, conduct, data, and technology requirements, including customer-protection controls, reporting of credit information and digital lending applications (DLAs), and rules for **loss-sharing arrangements in case of default**. The document also imposes general provisions for how these arrangements must be structured and supervised, meaning banks need documented policies, board oversight, and operational controls rather than ad hoc outsourcing. Compliance teams should treat this as a substantive regulatory regime for third-party digital loan sourcing, servicing, and customer interaction.

The directions also set out strict rules for **loans against gold and silver collateral**, including restrictions and ceilings, valuation and assaying standards, **loan-to-value (LTV)** requirements, and other operational conditions. This means banks must ensure collateral is properly tested and valued before disbursement, loans remain within permitted exposure limits, and procedures exist to manage pledge, safekeeping, and release of precious-metal collateral in line with RBI expectations. Any credit product secured by gold or silver will need controls around purity assessment, valuation documentation, and exposure monitoring.

For **microfinance lending**, the directions define the product and require banks to assess **household income**, then use that assessment to cap the **total loan repayment obligations of a household**. The compliance implication is that the bank cannot rely only on borrower self-declaration or single-loan underwriting; it must have a household-level affordability assessment process and ensure aggregate repayments stay within the RBI’s permitted threshold. The chapter also includes additional provisions that banks must follow when originating and servicing these loans.

The **housing loan** chapter sets out which housing schemes are eligible, who the permissible borrower categories are, the security requirements, loan tenor, and rules for **graduated instalments** and **additional/supplementary finance**. It also addresses lending to housing boards, defines borrower categories, sets **individual housing loan limits**, and permits certain **innovative housing loan products** including **upfront disbursal of housing loans** under specified conditions. Separate rules cover finance for housing and for **construction of buildings/ready-built houses**, so banks need product-specific underwriting and disbursal controls rather than a single generic housing policy.

Finally, the directions regulate **non-fund based (NFB) credit facilities**, including **guarantees** and **co-acceptances**, plus requirements for certain other specific guarantees and exclusions. Rural co-operative banks therefore need to verify that their contingent exposure practices comply with RBI’s conditions for issuing guarantees, handling co-acceptances, and identifying transactions that are not permitted or require special treatment. In practice, this document requires banks to maintain board-approved policies, product-level controls, customer-protection procedures, and reporting/technology systems across all of these lending activities, with the updated rules effective as of **April 1, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025** set the operative framework for how rural co-operative banks may pay interest on deposits, and the document was later **updated as of August 25, 2026**. It applies to **rural co-operative banks** and governs both **domestic rupee deposits** and **non-resident / foreign currency deposit products**, including current, savings, term, NRE, FCNR(B), and RFC-related accounts where relevant. The directions establish the RBI’s general interest-rate framework and then prescribe specific rules for each deposit category, so compliance teams must review both the general chapter and the product-specific chapters to ensure their deposit offerings, interest calculations, and account-handling processes conform to the RBI’s requirements.

For **domestic rupee deposits**, the directions cover the interest-rate treatment of **current accounts, savings deposits, term deposits, additional interest, overdue deposits, floating-rate term deposits, interest-payment periodicity, deceased depositor accounts, and premature withdrawal penalties**. The document requires banks to follow RBI-prescribed rules on how interest is calculated and credited, including any special treatment for term deposits that are renewed, withdrawn early, or remain unpaid past maturity. It also addresses the payment of interest in the event of a depositor’s death, which means banks must have procedures to determine the correct continuation or settlement of interest on such accounts. While the table of contents does not show the detailed rates here, the directions clearly indicate that specific formulae, periods, and penalty rules are prescribed and must be operationalized by the bank.

For **rupee deposits of non-residents**, the directions specifically regulate **interest rates on non-resident rupee accounts**, prohibit **marking lien** on such deposits, and set rules for **premature withdrawal penalties on NRE deposits** and for **interest on NRE term deposits when the depositor dies**. This means compliance must ensure that non-resident rupee accounts are handled under the RBI’s permitted interest structure, that no lien is placed in violation of the prohibition, and that premature-closure and death-settlement systems apply the correct penalty and interest logic. The document therefore affects not only deposit pricing but also account documentation, lien controls, and customer-service workflows for non-resident accounts.

For **foreign currency deposits**, the directions cover **FCNR(B) accounts**, how interest is calculated on those deposits, how interest is treated on **renewal**, how interest is paid on the account of a **deceased FCNR(B) depositor**, how interest is handled when an **NRI returns to India**, and how FCNR(B) balances are converted into **Resident Foreign Currency (RFC)** or resident rupee accounts with corresponding interest treatment. The document also regulates **premature withdrawal of foreign currency deposits** and the associated **penalties**, and it includes provisions for **Resident Foreign Currency Accounts Scheme** accounts. In practical terms, banks must have controls for currency-conversion events, residency-status changes, rollover handling, and closure/withdrawal penalties, because the RBI directions impose different interest consequences depending on whether the deposit is maintained, renewed, converted, or prematurely withdrawn.

The document also contains a chapter on **prohibitions and exemptions**, a **Schedule I**, and a chapter on **repeal and other provisions** that confirms prior instructions are superseded or saved as applicable, clarifies that other laws are not barred, and provides interpretation rules. Although the excerpt provided does not list the detailed operational clauses, the structure makes clear that the directions are intended to be a comprehensive, binding deposit-interest framework for rural co-operative banks, replacing or consolidating earlier guidance. For compliance purposes, the key action is to map every deposit product and lifecycle event—opening, renewal, overdue status, premature closure, death claims, residency changes, and foreign-currency conversion—against the RBI-prescribed rules in the full text, and to ensure customer disclosures, core-banking interest engines, and exception-handling procedures are updated to match the directions as effective through the **August 25, 2026** update.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI Directions document establishes the prudential capital adequacy framework for Rural Co-operative Banks, and it applies specifically to State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks as defined in the NABARD Act, 1981. It is issued under Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and it came into effect immediately upon issuance on November 28, 2025; the version provided is updated as of May 15, 2026. For compliance purposes, the key point from the excerpt is that RBI is formally setting out the capital adequacy regime for these banks, including definitions that will govern how capital, risk, and regulatory instruments are interpreted in later chapters.

The document defines several terms that matter for implementation and reporting, including “credit risk” (borrower/counterparty non-payment risk and losses from deterioration in credit quality), “deferred tax assets/liabilities” as per applicable accounting standards, “derivative” as per Section 45U(a) of the RBI Act, “other approved securities” as defined under RBI’s CRR/SLR Directions for rural co-operative banks, “subordinated” debt as debt repaid only after depositors and other debt in insolvency/liquidation, and “public financial institution” as defined in the Companies Act, 2013. Any term not defined in this circular takes its meaning from the BR Act, 1949, the RBI Act, 1934, the relevant State Co-operative Societies Act and rules/regulations, or commercial parlance, as applicable.

The table of contents shows that the Directions are structured to cover: minimum regulatory capital requirements; the composition and rules for Tier 1 capital and Tier 2 capital; the computation of risk-weighted assets (RWA); and operational matters such as refund of share capital, investor protection for regulatory capital instruments, and reporting. It also includes repeal-and-savings provisions, clarification that other laws are not barred, and interpretive provisions. An Annex is provided for the “Statement of Capital, RWAs and CRAR,” indicating that banks will need to calculate and report capital adequacy in a specified format.

Because the excerpt cuts off just as Chapter II begins (“Statutory Re…”), the specific numerical capital ratios, buffers, deductions, or detailed eligibility criteria for capital instruments are not visible here; however, the document clearly signals that those substantive prudential requirements are contained in the subsequent chapters and are binding on all covered rural co-operative banks from the effective date. From a compliance standpoint, the bank should treat this as a mandatory capital adequacy framework applicable immediately, review its capital instruments and RWA methodology against the forthcoming Tier 1/Tier 2 and reporting provisions, and ensure its internal policies, regulatory returns, and capital monitoring systems align with the RBI-prescribed definitions and Annex format.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the RBI Act, 1934, establishes the cash reserve ratio (CRR) and statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) framework for **Rural Co-operative Banks**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs)** and **District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs)**. It took **immediate effect** on **November 28, 2025**, and the update shown is **as of August 25, 2026**. The directions replace/operate as the governing compliance framework for these banks’ reserve maintenance and reporting obligations, and they also include a repeal/other-provisions chapter plus annexures (indicating additional detailed schedules/forms/requirements).

For **CRR**, the banks must maintain the required cash reserve with RBI and report compliance through the applicable statutory return: **Form B Return for Scheduled Co-operative Banks** or **Form I Return for non-scheduled Co-operative Banks under Section 18 read with Section 56** of the Banking Regulation Act. The document defines key computation concepts such as **“aggregate deposits”** as the sum of demand and time deposits. It also prescribes how to split **savings bank deposits** between demand and time liabilities: the bank must compute the proportion as at the close of business on **March 31 and September 30** each year, use the **average of the minimum balances maintained in each account during the half-year** as the “time liability” portion, and treat the difference between that and the average actual balances as the “demand liability” portion. Those calculated proportions apply to **all reporting fortnights during the next half-year**, so compliance teams must ensure the ratio used in periodic CRR reporting is updated semi-annually on this basis.

For **SLR**, all co-operative banks covered by the directions must report maintenance through **Form I Return (for SLR)** under **Section 24 read with Section 56** of the Banking Regulation Act. The directions define **approved securities/SLR securities** to include, at minimum, **Government of India dated securities issued under the market borrowing programme and the Market Stabilization Scheme, Government of India Treasury Bills, and State Development Loans (SDLs)**. The document therefore requires compliance staff to distinguish qualifying SLR assets from non-qualifying holdings and to ensure the bank’s reported SLR position is supported by the prescribed securities classification and computation procedure.

The document also creates a broader compliance structure covering **reporting, penalties, and procedural requirements**, which means banks are not only required to maintain the ratios but also to file the relevant returns accurately and on the RBI’s prescribed basis. Even though the excerpt provided does not show the numerical CRR/SLR percentages or penalty amounts, it is clear that the directions are binding operational requirements for the affected rural co-operative banks, and compliance teams should use the annexures and subsequent chapters for any detailed computation rules, filing formats, or sanctions attached to non-compliance.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Governance) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Governance) Directions, 2025** apply to all **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning both **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs)** and **Central Co-operative Banks (CCBs)** as defined under the **NABARD Act, 1981**. The directions are issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they **take effect immediately**. For compliance purposes, this is a governance framework for RCB boards, directors, board meetings, and board committees, replacing/overriding prior RBI governance directions to the extent addressed in these Directions.

At the board constitution level, RBI states that RCB directors must be **knowledgeable and of high integrity** and must work cohesively to ensure efficient management of the bank. The document also sets out **disqualifications for directors**; the visible portion expressly says that persons who are **not eligible for admission even as members** are ineligible to become directors, **except co-opted and nominated directors**, and it begins listing other barred categories (the excerpt cuts off while starting with persons engaged in money lending/financing). Compliance teams should therefore treat director eligibility as a formal pre-appointment screen, not merely an internal fit-and-proper review.

The directions also govern the role of the **Board of Directors (or equivalent governing body)** and individual directors, including a **code of conduct** for board behavior and responsibilities. The board is expected to exercise direction and control over management affairs, and the RBI has signaled that governance duties are not optional or symbolic: they are part of the statutory framework applicable to RCBs. This means banks must ensure their board charters, conduct standards, and director onboarding materials are aligned with the RBI’s prescribed governance expectations.

On operational governance, the Directions require specific **board meeting procedures**, including a **model agenda** for meetings and a **calendar of reviews**. In practice, this means the bank should structure its board agenda and periodic review cycle around RBI’s prescribed governance review topics rather than ad hoc scheduling. Compliance teams should confirm that board secretarial processes, annual calendars, and management reporting packs are built to support these required recurring reviews.

The Directions further establish board committees, specifically an **Audit Committee of the Board** and a **Risk Management Committee**, with dedicated provisions for each. These committees are not merely advisory; they are part of the regulatory governance structure and must be constituted and operated in accordance with the RBI’s direction. The excerpted text shows the framework continues into detailed committee requirements, and the document also includes a **repeal and saving** section, a statement that other applicable laws are not barred, and RBI interpretive authority. For a compliance officer, the key takeaway is that RCB governance must be checked against these Directions immediately, with attention to board composition, director eligibility, formalized meeting/review cycles, and functioning audit and risk oversight committees.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 27, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025** apply to **all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The directions were issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and **came into force immediately** on issuance; the title page also notes the document is **updated as on April 27, 2026**, and one provision is marked as **modified w.e.f. January 1, 2026**. A key definitional point for compliance is that an **“RCB”** is the regulated entity, while a **“debtor company”** is any company to which the RCB has or previously had **loan or investment exposure (excluding equity instruments) at any time during the preceding 12 months**; **equity instruments** are defined to include **equity shares, compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS), and compulsorily convertible debentures (CCD)**.

The directions set the framework for RCBs undertaking selected financial services and investing in/connecting with financial services entities. A **“Financial Services Company”** is defined broadly to cover companies engaged in the business of financial services, including the forms of business listed in the Banking Regulation Act and RBI Act, **credit information businesses**, **payment system operations**, **stock/commodity/derivatives/other exchanges**, **depositories**, and **asset reconstruction companies** (the excerpt continues beyond that point). This matters because the later restrictions and permissions in the document are tied to whether an activity or counterparty falls within these defined categories.

On governance, the directions assign responsibility to the **Board of the RCB** for overseeing and approving the bank’s engagement in permitted financial services activities, implying that these activities cannot be handled as routine branch-level or ad hoc arrangements without board-level oversight. The document also contains a dedicated chapter on **investments in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)**, indicating RBI has imposed specific controls on how RCBs may invest in or interact with AIFs; compliance teams should treat this as an explicit investment-governance subject rather than a discretionary treasury choice.

The core operational permissions and restrictions are set out for four activities: **insurance business as a corporate agent without risk participation**, **insurance business on a referral basis without risk participation (including arrangements involving sharing of physical space)**, **merchant acquisition business**, and **issue of prepaid payment instruments (PPIs)**. In each case, the substance is that RCBs may undertake these activities only within the RBI-prescribed framework, and the recurring compliance theme is **no risk participation** by the RCB unless specifically allowed. Because the document is a banking-direction instrument issued under statutory powers, compliance officers should also note that it contains **repeal/saving provisions**, confirms that **other applicable laws are not barred**, and includes **interpretation clauses**—meaning the directions operate alongside, not in place of, other licensing, insurance, payments, AML/KYC, and operational law requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Rural Co-operative Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025” apply to State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks operating in India, and they take effect on January 1, 2026. The directions are issued under Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and they set the framework for rural co-operative banks to offer digital banking channels such as internet banking, mobile banking, and other device-based digital channels.

A key prudential requirement is that every bank covered by the directions must put in place comprehensive policies for all digital banking channels, explicitly covering compliance with all statutory and regulatory requirements as well as management of liquidity and operational risks in a digital banking environment. For eligibility to offer a **view only banking facility**—which is limited to functions that do not alter a customer’s asset or liability position, such as balance enquiry, balance viewing, and account statement downloads—the bank must already have implemented a Core Banking Solution (CBS) and have enabled its public-facing IT infrastructure to handle IPv6 traffic. The document is clear that view-only access cannot be used to provide loans, funds transfers, or any other service that creates customer liability or moves funds; however, banks may provide downloadable forms for those services.

For banks that begin offering view-only digital banking channels on or after the effective date, the directions require an intimation to the Reserve Bank of India’s Department of Regulation through the PRAVAAH portal, together with a copy of the “Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy” (GAICA) report referenced in the directions. This means compliance teams need to ensure not only technical readiness (CBS and IPv6 capability) but also formal internal control assessment documentation and timely regulatory intimation before launching the service. The excerpt provided ends mid-reference to para 7.1, so additional procedural and technological requirements may appear later in the full text, but the material obligations shown here are the effective date, applicability, eligibility thresholds, and the filing requirement through PRAVAAH for new view-only channel rollouts.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025**, under **Sections 44A and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** (as amended by the **Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020**) read with **Section 56**, and the directions take **immediate effect** from **November 28, 2025**. They apply to all **Rural Co-operative Banks**, meaning specifically **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs)** and **Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs)** as defined under the **NABARD Act, 1981**.

The directions cover only two voluntary amalgamation structures: **(i) one or more DCCBs in a State amalgamating with the StCB**, or **(ii) one DCCB amalgamating with another DCCB**. The document defines the “amalgamated entity” as the entity transferring its business and the “amalgamating entity” as the entity acquiring that business under the scheme of amalgamation, and it states that other undefined terms will take their meaning from the RBI Act, the Banking Regulation Act, the NABARD Act, RBI glossary usage, or ordinary commercial usage, as applicable.

For shareholder approval, the **draft scheme of amalgamation must be approved by a two-thirds majority of the shareholders, both by number and by value, present and voting at a General Body Meeting of each bank involved**, in line with **Section 44A read with Section 56 of the BR Act, 1949**. The notice for each shareholder meeting must be **published in newspapers at least once a week for three consecutive weeks**, in **not less than two newspapers** circulating in the locality where the registered offices of the banks are situated, and **at least one newspaper must be in a language commonly understood in that locality**.

Although the excerpt cuts off before the RBI-approval chapter details, the document clearly establishes that RBI approval is a separate required step after shareholder approval, and the directions also govern the **implementation of the scheme of amalgamation** and include **repeal/savings and interpretation provisions**. For compliance teams at affected StCBs and DCCBs, the key operational requirements visible in this excerpt are: confirm the transaction falls within the permitted amalgamation categories, obtain the prescribed **two-thirds shareholder approval by number and value**, and ensure the **three-week newspaper publication requirement** is met exactly as specified before proceeding to RBI approval and implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
This RBI circular, titled the **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025**, was issued on **28 November 2025** and takes **immediate effect**. It applies to the five **All-India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**: **EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID**, but only to the extent the directions are not inconsistent with their governing statutes or other instructions. The directions introduce or restate governance, compliance, and operational requirements for these institutions, with several obligations requiring **Board-approved policies** and documented procedures.

At the governance level, each AIFI must have a **Board-approved policy for courses/certifications** required for specialized operational areas, as referenced in the directions. The Board may permit **deferment of option premium** only after carrying out **due diligence of users** in line with a Board-approved policy; this means the facility cannot be offered as a blanket product feature and must be gated by an internal approval and suitability process. The document also permits an AIFI to constitute an **apex Audit Committee of the Board (ACB)** of about **five directors**; one or more members may be Chartered Accountants or have experience in management, finance, accountancy, and audit systems, but **staff प्रतिनिधing directors, if any, cannot be included**. If constituted, the ACB must meet **at least once per quarter and not less than six times in a year**.

On market operations, the directions include a specific requirement on **reporting of corporate bond transactions** and a separate rule on **deferment of option premium**, indicating that AIFIs must maintain compliant reporting and controls around these activities. The circular also adds a **regulatory compliance requirement** relating to the **Inter-Governmental Agreement (IGA) with the United States under FATCA**, with **registration requirements** to be followed by the affected institutions. In addition, the document contains a human resource/capacity-building element requiring AIFIs to maintain appropriate internal arrangements for **certifications** and **staff rotation and audit** in sensitive areas, tied to the Board-approved policy framework mentioned above.

Finally, the circular includes standard legal provisions on **repeal and saving**, application of other laws not barred, and interpretation, meaning the new directions are meant to operate alongside existing legal and regulatory requirements unless there is a direct inconsistency. For a compliance team, the key immediate action items are to confirm that the institution has updated **Board-approved policies** for specialized certifications and deferment of option premium, verify whether an **ACB** exists and whether its composition and meeting frequency meet the specified standards, ensure FATCA/IGA registration processes are complete where relevant, and confirm that corporate bond transaction reporting and any option premium deferment practices are aligned with the new directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025**, under its powers in **Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934** and related enabling provisions. The Directions are **effective immediately** as of **November 28, 2025**, and they replace the RBI’s earlier outsourcing framework for these institutions through the repeal/saving provisions in Chapter IV.

For a compliance team, the key point is that these Directions establish a formal, RBI-mandated framework for how **All India Financial Institutions** manage outsourcing risk, with a particular focus on **outsourcing of IT services** and related arrangements. The document’s structure shows that the obligations are not limited to contracting alone: they require board-level governance, a documented outsourcing policy, senior management oversight, IT-function involvement, risk-management controls, confidentiality and security protections, vendor evaluation and contracting standards, ongoing monitoring, maintenance of an inventory of outsourced services, business continuity and disaster recovery planning, exit planning, termination controls, and grievance-redress mechanisms for outsourced services.

The document also signals that the Directions cover several specific outsourcing scenarios that compliance teams must review in practice: **outsourcing within a group or conglomerate**, **offshore or cross-border outsourcing**, **outsourcing of Security Operations Centre (SOC) services**, and the **use of cloud computing services**. That means institutions must assess not only third-party vendors but also affiliate arrangements and technology-service models that may involve data transfer, cross-border dependencies, or shared-service structures. Even though the excerpt provided does not include the detailed substantive clauses, the table of contents makes clear that the RBI expects a formal governance and control framework around each of these categories, rather than ad hoc management.

Because the Directions took effect immediately, institutions subject to them should treat compliance as current and ongoing, not as something that can be phased in later. A compliance officer would need to confirm that the institution’s board has approved an outsourcing policy, management responsibilities are assigned, service-provider due diligence and contractual safeguards are in place, outsourced services are being monitored against an inventory, contingency arrangements and exit strategies are documented, and customer grievance handling covers complaints arising from outsourced activities. The document also indicates that Chapter IV addresses how these Directions interact with other laws and how they are to be interpreted, so institutions should ensure their outsourcing controls are aligned not only with RBI requirements but also with any other applicable legal/regulatory obligations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued under Section 45L of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, sets mandatory “Responsible Business Conduct” requirements for all All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs), namely EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID. It took effect on the date of issuance unless a specific provision states otherwise, and it is intended to govern customer-facing conduct, lending practices, complaint handling, recovery, and certain special situations such as calamities. For a compliance team, the main impact is that the board of each AIFI must put in place board-approved policies and periodic review mechanisms to ensure better customer service, with specific policies covering the Fair Practices Code, grievance redressal, and penal charges; the grievance mechanism must ensure disputes arising from decisions of the institution’s functionaries are heard and disposed of at least at the next higher level. The board must also periodically review compliance with the Fair Practices Code and the functioning of the grievance system at controlling offices, and may receive consolidated review reports at intervals it prescribes.

On responsible lending, AIFIs must clearly disclose in loan application forms all processing-related charges/fees and transparently communicate to borrowers, before sanction/disbursal, the processing fees, the amount refundable if the loan is not sanctioned or disbursed, any prepayment options and charges, delayed repayment penalties if any, conversion charges for switching between fixed and floating rates, any interest reset clause, and any other matter affecting the borrower’s interests. The directions also contain a dedicated framework on penal charges in loan accounts, meaning AIFIs must follow RBI’s requirements on how such charges are levied and disclosed, rather than using hidden or ambiguous charges. Pre-payment charges on loans are separately regulated, so any such charges must be applied only in the manner permitted by these directions and with the required disclosure. If an AIFI uses recovery agents, it must follow specific responsibility and governance requirements for their conduct and oversight.

The directions further incorporate a requirement to comply with the Supreme Court’s order dated April 30, 2025 in the matters of Pragya Prasun and Ors. vs Union of India and Ors. (W.P.(C) 289 of 2024) and Amar Jain vs Union of India and Ors. (W.P.(C) 49 of 2025), meaning affected AIFIs must align their procedures with that court order wherever applicable. They also include a special section for “measures in case of declaration of calamity,” requiring AIFIs to take prescribed relief-oriented actions when a calamity is declared. Finally, the directions repeal prior instructions to the extent stated in the document, include a saving clause for other laws, and clarify interpretations for implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“All India Financial Institutions – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025”** are a consolidated AML/CFT compliance framework for **all India financial institutions (AIFIs)**, issued under the RBI’s statutory powers and intended to prevent these institutions from being used for **money laundering or terrorist financing**. The directions sit within India’s broader AML regime under the **Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002** and the **Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**, and require regulated entities to apply customer identification, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting controls both when opening account-based relationships and when undertaking transactions otherwise. The document is structured as a full KYC framework covering governance, customer acceptance, risk management, customer identification and due diligence, record management, FIU-India reporting, handling of requests under international agreements, and other operational instructions, with repeal/transitional provisions at the end.

For compliance teams, the most important point is that these directions require AIFIs to maintain a **board-approved KYC/AML policy**, align it to the institution’s risk profile, and operationalize risk-based customer due diligence rather than apply a one-size-fits-all process. The framework covers **individuals, sole proprietorships, legal entities, beneficial ownership identification, ongoing due diligence, and enhanced/simplified due diligence** depending on the customer’s risk category and nature of relationship. It also requires institutions to retain prescribed records, report relevant information to the **Financial Intelligence Unit–India (FIU-IND)**, and comply with communications received under applicable **international agreements**. The document’s compliance significance is that it is not limited to onboarding: it also imposes continuing monitoring and periodic review obligations, so firms must ensure their KYC systems, escalation rules, and recordkeeping are designed for the full lifecycle of the relationship.

The directions are issued as **DOR/2025-26/335 / DOR.AML.REC.No.254/14.01.011/2025-26** dated **November 28, 2025**, and the title notes that the text is **updated as of December 29, 2025**. The table of contents shows the operative chapters cover: preliminary matters; board/policy governance; customer acceptance policy; risk management; customer identification procedure (CIP); customer due diligence (CDD) procedure; record management; FIU-India reporting; obligations under international agreements; other instructions; and repeal/other provisions. Because the document is an RBI direction under multiple enabling statutes, it functions as a binding compliance requirement for the covered financial institutions rather than as guidance only.

Based on the portions provided, the document is specifically relevant to institutions that fall within the RBI’s definition of **AIFIs / regulated entities** under the cited legal powers. Compliance officers should treat it as requiring: formal customer onboarding controls; beneficial owner identification; monitoring of transactions for suspicious or unusual activity; periodic updating of customer information; retention of KYC and transaction records for the prescribed period; and filing of mandated reports with FIU-IND. If your institution onboards corporate, partnership, sole proprietor, or individual customers, the later chapters on CDD will be the core operational requirements, because they determine what documents and verification steps are needed, when enhanced due diligence must be applied, and how risk should drive the depth of checks.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025** apply to all **All-India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**, specifically **EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID**. The Directions take **immediate effect** and are issued under **Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934**. They require each AIFI to comply strictly with the **Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021**, as amended, but always subject to any RBI directions or guidelines that override or supplement those standards.

At the financial statement level, each AIFI must prepare a **balance sheet and profit and loss account for all business transacted**, as of the **last working day of the year or relevant period**, using the **form and manner prescribed under the governing statute for that institution**. In addition to standalone/solo financial statements, every AIFI must also prepare and disclose **Consolidated Financial Statements (CFS)**. The CFS must follow **AS 21 (Consolidated Financial Statements)**, **AS 23 (Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements)**, and **AS 27 (Financial Reporting of Interests in Joint Ventures)**, and the ordinary accounting-standard meanings of **parent, subsidiary, associate, joint venture, control, and group** apply for these purposes.

From the content provided, the document is primarily establishing the **mandatory reporting framework** for AIFIs rather than imposing numerical capital or prudential thresholds. The key compliance obligation is that AIFIs must ensure their financial statements are prepared in the required statutory format and that consolidation is not optional: group-level financial reporting is expressly required in addition to solo accounts. The document is marked **“Updated as on April 1, 2026,”** but the excerpt provided does not show any later effective-date deferral or separate transition rule beyond the stated **immediate commencement**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“All India Financial Institutions – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025”** were issued on **November 28, 2025** and apply **with immediate effect**. They are directed at all **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**—specifically **EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI, and NaBFID**—and also state that the **restrictions on further financial accommodation to wilful defaulters and the provisions on large defaulters apply to all RBI-regulated entities**, even if a given entity does not fit the document’s definition of “lender.” The stated purpose is to create a **non-discriminatory, transparent process consistent with natural justice** for classifying borrowers as wilful defaulters and to ensure that information on such defaulters is shared so lenders can avoid extending further institutional finance to them.

The Directions define key terms broadly enough to capture both funded and non-funded exposures: a **“credit facility”** includes **fund-based and non-fund-based facilities**, including **off-balance-sheet items such as derivatives, guarantees, and letters of credit** extended by an AIFI. A **“borrower”** is anyone who has availed credit from an AIFI. The document also carries forward the same meaning of **“default”** as in the RBI’s **All India Financial Institutions – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025**. Importantly, it defines **“director”** for this framework as a director of a company that was classified as a **large defaulter or wilful defaulter**, but only if that person was associated with the company at the time the acts or omissions leading to default occurred. The definition of **“diversion of funds”** is detailed and includes, among other things, using short-term working capital for long-term purposes contrary to sanction terms, using borrowed funds to create assets not covered by the credit sanction, moving funds to subsidiaries/group entities without approval, routing funds through other lenders without prior written permission, and investing credit proceeds in other companies via equity or debt instruments without approval.

From a compliance perspective, the document establishes the formal regime for **classifying, treating, and reporting wilful defaulters and large defaulters**. Although the excerpt provided does not yet show the later procedural chapters in full, the table of contents makes clear that the Directions require AIFIs to follow board-level governance, implement treatment rules for wilful defaulters, report wilful defaulters and large defaulters, maintain preventive controls, and ensure auditors play a role in detection/oversight. The document also includes **Annex I** and **Annex II**, which specify required **formats for submitting the list of large defaulters** and **data on cases of wilful default**, indicating mandatory reporting obligations rather than discretionary disclosure. The key operational takeaway is that affected institutions must immediately align borrower classification, lender restrictions, reporting workflows, and internal controls to the RBI’s new framework for wilful and large defaulters.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** and updated **as of July 1, 2026**) set out the mandatory framework AIFIs must follow for identifying stress early, attempting resolution, restructuring exposures, applying provisioning, and reporting to RBI. The directions apply to the specified All India Financial Institutions covered by the instrument, and they replace/organize the prudential treatment for stressed asset resolution across general cases, special cases, calamity-affected accounts, government debt relief schemes, and instruments received in restructuring. Compliance teams should treat the document as a binding operational and prudential rulebook: it requires board-approved policies, defined internal review timelines, formal inter-creditor coordination where multiple lenders are involved, and specific accounting/provisioning consequences if resolution is delayed or fails.

At the front end, AIFIs must have **board-approved policies** for stress identification, resolution strategy, delegation of authority, and monitoring. The directions require **early identification and reporting of stress** before a borrower becomes irretrievably impaired, along with prescribed disclosures and readiness for **supervisory review** by RBI. The resolution framework is built around a **review period** and an **Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA)** when more than one lender is involved; institutions must actively participate in negotiating and implementing a viable **resolution plan** within the allowed period, rather than simply waiting for default to deepen. If a resolution plan is **delayed or not implemented on time**, the institution must make **additional specific provisioning** as mandated in Chapter IV, creating a direct capital impact for non-compliance or inertia.

For **restructuring**, the directions specify how an account must be classified after restructuring, when **additional finance** can be provided, when a post-restructuring **upgrade in asset classification** is permitted, what happens if the borrower defaults again during the **monitoring period**, and how **provisioning** and **income recognition** must be handled after restructuring. The rules also address **change in ownership**, indicating that restructuring outcomes can depend on whether there has been a genuine ownership transfer and whether the transaction meets regulatory conditions. Special rules apply to **sale-and-leaseback transactions**, **foreign currency borrowings**, borrowers involved in **fraud, malfeasance, or wilful default**, **compromise settlements and technical write-offs**, and **projects under implementation**, reflecting RBI’s intent to prevent misuse of restructuring while still allowing resolution where recovery is feasible. A separate chapter covers accounts **impacted by calamities**, assigning roles to the **SLBC/UTLBC/DCC** mechanism, permitting the AIFI to implement a resolution plan with ancillary relief measures, and imposing **reporting requirements** for such cases.

The directions also provide prudential treatment for **Government Debt Relief Schemes (DRS)**, meaning exposures covered by any government-led relief program must be accounted for under specific RBI norms rather than general restructuring rules. Finally, Chapter VIII governs **instruments acquired as part of restructuring**—their **asset classification**, **provisioning**, and **valuation**—so compliance teams must not only manage the original stressed exposure but also the accounting treatment of any securities, instruments, or claims received in settlement or restructuring. Overall, the document creates a tightly controlled resolution process with concrete obligations on governance, timing, borrower monitoring, inter-creditor action, provisioning, classification, and reporting, and the compliance risk is not limited to borrower distress itself but extends to any failure to execute the prescribed process exactly.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025**, effective as a prudential framework for **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**, replacing and consolidating prior RBI instructions on income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning for advances. The document is **dated November 28, 2025** and is marked **“updated as on July 01, 2026,”** so compliance teams should treat the July 1, 2026 version as the operative text for current requirements. It is intended to align AIFI prudential treatment with RBI’s broader credit-system oversight and international prudential practice, and it covers how these institutions must recognize income, classify assets, and create provisions across their loan/advances portfolios.

At a governance level, the directions place responsibility on the **Board of the AIFI** to ensure that the institution has sound policies, systems, and controls for lending prudence, asset classification, provisioning, and disclosure, and they require customer-facing communication/education where relevant. The framework also introduces or continues **disclosure obligations** so that prudential classification and provisioning impacts are appropriately reflected in financial statements and other required disclosures, with the institution expected to maintain transparency about stressed assets and provisioning coverage.

The core compliance burden is in the **asset classification** rules: AIFIs must classify exposures based on performance and collectability, move accounts to **non-performing asset (NPA)** status when the specified default/non-payment conditions are met, and apply special treatment to particular situations such as regularisation near the balance-sheet date, multiple credit facilities, restructuring/resolution, and other specified cases. Once an account becomes an NPA, **income recognition stops on accrual for that exposure**, previously recognized income related to the NPA must be **reversed**, and any subsequent recoveries must be appropriated according to the prescribed sequence. The document also sets out the categories of NPAs and the conditions under which an NPA can be **upgraded back to standard** after the underlying default is cured, rather than merely through temporary payment arrangements.

On provisioning, the Directions require AIFIs to maintain **minimum provisions for standard assets, substandard assets, doubtful assets, and loss assets**, with detailed rates and rules applicable to each category, and they permit/require **additional specific provisioning** in certain stressed-asset resolution cases under Chapter VI-A of the RBI’s **Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025**. The framework also includes provisions for **special circumstances**, which can require higher-than-prescribed provisioning, and it establishes a **Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR)** concept, meaning institutions must track and maintain overall coverage of credit losses at the level required by the Directions and their internal policy. For compliance teams, this means provisioning is not only category-based but also affected by resolution status, special asset characteristics, and any RBI-prescribed higher provisioning triggers.

Finally, the Directions contain explicit rules on **tax treatment of provisions**, and they repeal/replace prior inconsistent instructions while preserving actions already taken under earlier rules where the saving clause applies. In practical terms, AIFIs should review and, if needed, update their **credit policies, NPA recognition triggers, recovery appropriation procedures, provisioning matrices, resolution-account accounting, board reporting, financial statement disclosures, and tax/provision tracking** to ensure alignment with the 2025 Directions as updated through **July 1, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, under **Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934** and other enabling provisions. These Directions apply to **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)** and establish a unified framework for **asset-liability management (ALM)**, **liquidity risk management**, **currency risk management**, and **interest rate risk (IRR) management**, replacing prior RBI instructions on these topics. From a compliance perspective, the document is not just advisory: it imposes governance, measurement, reporting, and periodic review obligations, and it also provides for **repeal and saving** of earlier directions while preserving actions taken under them.

At the governance level, the **Board of Directors** is made explicitly responsible for overseeing the institution’s ALM framework, including approving the overall policy, approving risk limits, and reviewing them periodically. The Board must ensure the institution has a suitable ALM information system, an ALM organization, and an Asset-Liability Committee (**ALCO**) with a defined composition and operating process. The Directions require AIFIs to maintain an ALM process that is integrated into decision-making, so compliance officers should expect board-level documentation, formal policy approvals, and evidence of periodic review rather than informal treasury monitoring.

For **liquidity risk**, the Directions require AIFIs to manage liquidity on an ongoing basis through statements and maturity-profile analysis, with separate treatment for **Indian rupee** and **foreign currency** positions. The document includes prescribed formats in **Annex-I** for the rupee liquidity statement, **Annex-I-A** for foreign currency liquidity, and **Annex III** for the maturity profile used in that statement. The institution must prepare and review these statements regularly, using behavioral assumptions where applicable, and must monitor cash inflows and outflows across defined time buckets so that mismatches can be identified and controlled before they become funding stress.

For **currency risk**, AIFIs must monitor exposures in foreign currencies and manage mismatches between foreign currency assets and liabilities through the ALM framework rather than treating them as incidental treasury positions. The document includes a dedicated **foreign currency interest rate sensitivity / risk statement** in **Annex II-A**, indicating that foreign-currency exposures are to be tracked in a structured manner. This means compliance teams should ensure systems capture currency-wise positions, conversions, and sensitivity impacts consistently and in a manner suitable for supervisory review.

For **interest rate risk**, the Directions require institutions to measure the sensitivity of their portfolio to changes in interest rates using a **traditional gap analysis** and an **Interest Rate Sensitivity Statement**. Separate prescribed statements are given for **rupee assets and liabilities** in **Annex II** and for **foreign currency assets and liabilities** in **Annex II-A**, with an additional **Interest Rate Sensitivity Profile** in **Annex IV**. The framework requires analysis of how changes in rates affect earnings and economic value, so compliance should confirm that repricing gaps, behavioral assumptions, and embedded optionality are captured in internal models and reported in the approved statement formats.

The Directions also address **behavioral patterns and embedded options**, requiring institutions to account for customer prepayments, early withdrawals, premature renewals, and similar optionality when mapping assets and liabilities into maturity buckets. In addition, **internal transfer pricing** must be structured so that funding costs and liquidity risks are appropriately reflected in product pricing and business line performance measurement. This is important for compliance because it means treasury and business-line P&Ls must not distort risk-taking incentives by ignoring liquidity and rate-risk costs.

Finally, the Directions impose **monitoring, reporting, and periodic review** obligations: the prescribed statements must be prepared, reviewed, and retained as part of the institution’s risk-management records, and regulatory returns must be filed at the periodicity specified by RBI. The document’s final chapter repeals earlier RBI ALM instructions for AIFIs but preserves actions taken under the old regime, and it also clarifies that other applicable laws are not barred by these Directions. For implementation, a compliance officer should treat this as a full ALM framework update requiring policy revision, board approval, system and process validation, and ongoing periodic reporting in the RBI-prescribed formats.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
This Reserve Bank of India (RBI) directions document, issued on November 28, 2025 as DOR/2025-26/329 / DOR.MRG.REC.No.248/00-00-017/2025-26, sets the framework for how All India Financial Institutions must classify, value, account for, and operationally manage their investment portfolios. It applies specifically to All India Financial Institutions covered by RBI regulation, and it replaces earlier instructions on investment classification/valuation/operations through the repeal provisions referenced in the final chapter, meaning compliance teams should treat this as the controlling consolidated rulebook once it takes effect. The document is organized around board oversight, portfolio classification, valuation, market value determination, government and non-government security transactions, internal controls, audits/reporting, and accounting/provisioning, so it is not just a valuation circular but a full operating and governance standard for investment activity.

At a governance level, the Board is expected to approve and oversee a formal investment policy framework, with internal controls and operating limits embedded in that policy. The directions separate investments into Held to Maturity (HTM), Available for Sale (AFS), and Held for Trading (HFT), and set rules for how securities may be shifted among those buckets; compliance teams should therefore expect binding restrictions on portfolio designation, reclassification, and the documentation/approval process for movements between categories. Valuation requirements differ by category: HTM holdings are treated on an amortized-cost style basis, while AFS and HFT holdings require mark-to-market discipline with recognition of valuation changes according to the category-specific rules laid down in the valuation chapter. The document also prescribes how to determine market value for quoted and unquoted securities, so institutions must ensure they have approved pricing sources and valuation methodologies for instruments that do not trade on an exchange or otherwise have a readily observable price.

A substantial portion of the directions governs government securities operations, including transactions through SGL accounts, dealing in “when issued” government securities, value-free transfers (VFT), STRIPS, repos in government securities, and settlement procedures. Compliance teams should note that these are not merely optional market practices; the directions create process requirements for how government securities may be held, transferred, traded, and settled. Separate operational rules are also laid out for non-government securities, including investments in unlisted securities, repos in corporate bonds, over-the-counter transactions in CDs/CPs/NCDs with original maturity up to one year, and trading/settlement in corporate bonds and securitised debt instruments. The document further addresses “other requirements” and board responsibilities in this area, indicating that oversight is expected not only at the transaction level but also through institution-wide investment controls.

The prudential/control chapter requires a strong internal control system and also regulates the engagement of brokers, which implies documented broker-selection criteria, transaction oversight, and likely limitations on how brokers are used for investment execution. Audit, review, and reporting obligations are also expressly included, so institutions should expect ongoing monitoring, periodic internal review, and reporting to management/board and, where applicable, to the RBI in the form prescribed by the directions. In accounting and provisioning, the document covers income recognition, broken period interest, the Investment Reserve Account (IRA), and treatment of Non-Performing Investments (NPI), meaning institutions must align their books, accrual practices, reserve transfers, and impairment/provisioning processes to the RBI’s specified rules for investment assets. Because the provided excerpt does not include the detailed operative paragraphs, no specific numerical thresholds, percentages, or deadlines beyond the issuance date can be confirmed from the text shown; however, the document clearly establishes a comprehensive compliance regime that affects portfolio classification, valuation, settlement mechanics, internal governance, and financial reporting for all covered All India Financial Institutions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Securitisation Transactions) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions – Securitisation Transactions Directions, 2025** (issued **28 November 2025**, reference **DOR/2025-26/328 / DOR.STR.REC.247/21.04.177/2025-26**) set a comprehensive framework for securitisation activities undertaken by **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**, including rules for originating securitisations, investing in them, and providing structural support such as credit enhancement and liquidity facilities. The directions are organized into requirements for eligibility of assets, minimum retention by the originator, origination standards, payment priorities and observability, limits on retained exposure, issuance/listing, special purpose entity conditions, warranties, accounting, STC treatment, support facilities, investor due diligence/stress testing, capital treatment, disclosure, and repeal/saving provisions.

For **originators**, only qualifying assets may be securitised, and the originator must comply with a **Minimum Retention Requirement (MRR)** and a cap on **total retained exposures**. The rules also impose standards on how assets are originated, how cash flows and payment priorities are structured and observed, and what representations, warranties, and accounting treatment must be applied. Securitisation structures must satisfy conditions applicable to the **special purpose entity (SPE)**, and there are specific requirements on issuance and listing of securitisation instruments.

The directions create a separate regime for **Simple, Transparent and Comparable (STC) securitisations**, including criteria that must be satisfied for regulatory capital purposes and accompanying disclosure/prudential oversight obligations. In addition, the document regulates any **facilities supporting securitisation structures**—including **credit enhancement, reset of credit enhancement, liquidity facilities, underwriting facilities, and servicing facilities**—by imposing general conditions and facility-specific safeguards. These provisions are intended to control the extent to which AIFIs may support securitisation vehicles and to ensure such support does not undermine risk transfer or create hidden exposures.

For **AIFI investors** in securitisation exposures, the directions require **due diligence, stress testing, credit monitoring, and valuation** of securitisation positions. The later chapters establish **capital requirements for securitisation exposures** and corresponding **disclosure norms**, which means AIFIs must determine regulatory capital charges for any securitisation holdings and provide the disclosures required by the RBI framework. The final chapter contains **repeal and saving** provisions, clarifies that other applicable laws are not barred, and preserves the RBI’s interpretive authority.

The document excerpt provided does **not include the detailed numeric thresholds, percentages, dates, or formulae** from the body chapters and annexes, so a compliance team would need to review the operative text in the full directions for the exact MRR levels, exposure caps, capital calculations, STC criteria, and any implementation timelines. From the title and structure alone, however, it is clear that the new directions are intended to replace and consolidate the RBI’s securitisation framework for AIFIs and impose a more explicit compliance regime across origination, structuring, investment, support facilities, capital, and disclosure.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025** issue a single, consolidated framework for how **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)** may transfer and distribute credit risk, replacing the fragmented approach that previously applied to loan transfers, co-lending, consortium/multiple banking, and related arrangements. The directions apply to **EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID**, and are issued under **section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934**. The document becomes effective **when placed on the RBI website**, except that **Part B (Co-Lending Arrangements)** has a later implementation date: it applies from **January 1, 2026**, or earlier if an individual AIFI elects that date through its internal policy.  

For **Part A (Transfer of Loan Exposures)**, AIFIs are permitted to acquire loans only from a transferor that is recognized as a lender under the specified rules, and the framework is intended to support a functioning credit risk transfer market while ensuring risk is distributed to investors with appropriate capacity and appetite. The Part A rules are divided between **loans that are not in default** and **stressed loans**, with separate chapters for general conditions, performing-loan transfers, and stressed-asset transfers. The direction indicates that loan transfers can be used for liquidity management, balance-sheet rebalancing, and strategic sales, but only within the RBI’s structured conditions.  

For **Part B (Co-Lending Arrangements)**, the key compliance point is the transition rule: **existing co-lending arrangements executed before August 6, 2025**, and **new CLAs entered into before the applicable effective date**, continue to be governed by the **existing regulations**; only CLAs entered into on or after the effective date must follow the new Part B framework. This means compliance teams need to identify the execution date of each CLA and determine whether it is grandfathered or newly subject to the 2025 directions.  

The document also contains **Part C (Other Types of Lending and Risk Transfer Arrangements)**, which specifically addresses **lending under consortium and multiple-banking arrangements**, indicating that the RBI intends the directions to cover other forms of shared lending/risk distribution as well, not just outright loan sales and co-lending. Finally, **Part D** deals with **repeal and other provisions**, and the document includes annexures that likely contain operational and reporting details supporting the main rules.  

For compliance purposes, the critical operational implications are: AIFIs must map all loan transfer, co-lending, consortium, and multiple-banking transactions to the relevant part of the new framework; determine whether each arrangement is new or grandfathered; ensure any post-effective-date CLA is brought into conformity with Part B; and align internal policies, product documentation, approval workflows, and risk-transfer controls with the new consolidated RBI requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“All India Financial Institutions (Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025”** apply immediately upon issuance, and they bind all AIFIs specifically named in the document: **EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID**. The Directions are issued under the RBI Act, 1934 and are intended to govern concentration-risk controls through exposure limits and related prudential requirements.

At the core of the new framework is a **large exposures regime**: a **“Large Exposure”** is defined as any exposure to a counterparty or a group of connected counterparties that is **10% or more of the AIFI’s eligible capital base**. “Eligible capital base” is tied to the institution’s **effective Tier 1 capital** as determined under the RBI’s separate **All India Financial Institutions (Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025**, using the **last audited balance sheet**, but the document also permits use of **capital infused after the balance-sheet date** and **profits accrued during the year** as part of Tier 1 capital, subject to the prescribed adjustments. However, before counting post-balance-sheet capital additions, the AIFI must obtain an **external auditor’s certificate confirming completion of the capital infusion** and submit that certificate to the **RBI (Department of Supervision / DOS)**.

The document also defines key terms that drive scope and attribution, including **“counterparty,” “group of connected counterparties,” “central counterparty (CCP),” “clearing member,” “control,” “derivative,” “net worth,”** and **“infrastructure projects / infrastructure lending.”** The CCP provisions are notable because a CCP linked to another CCP is treated as a **clearing member** of the first CCP, and the treatment of collateral transferred between CCPs depends on the **legal arrangement**; where needed, the RBI is to be consulted to determine whether such collateral is treated as **initial margin or default fund contribution**. Infrastructure lending is defined by reference to the **latest updated Harmonized Master List of Infrastructure Sub-sectors** published by the Government of India, so the scope of infrastructure exposures will track that external list.

The excerpt provided establishes the legal framework and definitions, and it signals that the operational exposure rules are set out later in the Directions, including the **Large Exposures Framework** and **Other Permitted Exposures and Prudential Limits** chapters. From a compliance perspective, the immediate action items are to confirm whether the institution is one of the five covered AIFIs, map all counterparties and connected-counterparty groups against the **10% of eligible capital base** threshold, ensure capital calculations are aligned with the RBI’s capital adequacy directions, and put in place controls for **auditor certification and RBI submission** whenever post-balance-sheet capital is counted toward exposure limits.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This direction applies to all All India Financial Institutions, specifically EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID, and it took effect immediately upon issuance on November 28, 2025. It replaces and consolidates RBI’s credit risk management expectations for AIFIs, reflecting the RBI’s intent to strengthen prudential controls over lending, borrower assessment, exposure monitoring, and related compliance processes because credit risk can create wider financial and systemic risk.

The document’s structure shows that it sets out board-approved policy requirements, credit risk evaluation rules, regulatory restrictions, LEI requirements for borrowers, mandatory filing of security interests in CERSAI, and rules for working capital finance and revolving facilities. It also explicitly notes a deleted Chapter III, meaning there is no operative content there, and a later Chapter VII for repeal/other provisions. For compliance teams, the key point is that these are not merely guidance notes: they are directions issued under section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934, so the named AIFIs must align internal policies, credit processes, and control frameworks accordingly.

In the definitions section, the document defines “bank guarantee” broadly to include financial, performance, and deferred payment guarantees, which matters for credit exposure treatment and related internal controls. It also defines “bills purchased and discounted,” covering negotiable instruments where funding is provided either by purchase of sight bills or by discounting usance bills, and clarifies that inland bills are bills of exchange drawn and paid in India to a person in India. These definitions indicate that trade finance and bill-related exposures fall within the document’s scope for credit risk management purposes.
