A new or clarified governance requirement appears in the inserted definition of “committee on lending to related parties,” which is a board-established committee specifically tasked with handling lending to related parties; the Board may designate an existing committee other than the Audit Committee for this role. This definition was inserted with effect from April 01, 2026, and it ties the institution’s related-party lending oversight to a formal board-level process. The text also imports the Companies Act, 2013 meanings of “contract or arrangement” under section 188(1)(a) to (g) and “control” under section 2(27), which means compliance teams must interpret related-party lending and control concepts consistently with company-law standards when applying the RBI directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025**, updated as of **July 1, 2026**, create a unified framework for how **All India Financial Institutions** must report, correct, disseminate, and safeguard credit information under the **Credit Information Companies (Regulations) Act, 2005 (CICRA)**. The directions take effect **immediately upon issuance** unless a provision states otherwise, and they apply to these institutions as **“Credit Institutions (CIs)”**. The stated purpose is to standardize credit information reporting, protect the confidentiality and security of sensitive credit data, and ensure consumers can access their credit information and obtain grievance redressal.

A major operational requirement is that covered institutions must participate in the credit information ecosystem and comply with the RBI’s prescribed reporting, data quality, and customer-service standards. The directions require reporting in the RBI/CIC framework using specified **data formats**, with defined **reporting timelines and periodic updation** obligations, and they set out procedures for handling **rejected data**, monitoring and improving the **Data Quality Index (DQI)**, and correcting **Credit Information Reports (CIRs)** when errors are identified. The document also governs how credit information may be used in **credit appraisal**, and it imposes rules on **displaying information** and applying other RBI Department of Regulation instructions where relevant.

On the consumer-facing side, the directions strengthen **customer service and grievance redressal** by requiring institutions to provide a framework for complaint handling and to implement a **compensation mechanism** for customers in specified circumstances. The document also includes a chapter on **best practices**, indicating that entities are expected to follow operational standards beyond the minimum compliance rules, and it contains **repeal and saving provisions** so that prior instructions are superseded to the extent covered, while preserving actions already taken under earlier rules where applicable. The annexures referenced in the table of contents indicate that the directions are supported by detailed technical and procedural requirements, likely including formats, workflows, and operational guidance that compliance teams would need to map into internal reporting and grievance-handling processes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** and updated through **July 15, 2026**) consolidate and govern how **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)** may extend, structure, monitor, and report credit facilities. The document is framed as a prudential and customer-protection regime for the credit system, and it applies to the AIFI sector under RBI supervision rather than to all financial institutions generally. It replaces/updates prior directions, with Chapter VII expressly addressing repeal and saving, so compliance teams should treat this as the operative framework for AIFI credit activity unless a specific grandfathering or savings clause preserves an earlier treatment.

A major portion of the directions concerns **digital lending**, where AIFIs must ensure that any arrangement with a **Lending Service Provider (LSP)** is supported by board-approved governance, clear customer-facing disclosures, and robust technology/data controls. The directions require AIFIs to retain responsibility for the end-to-end conduct of the loan, including compliance with customer protection standards, and to implement procedures for reporting credit information, using Digital Lending Apps (DLAs), and managing any **loss-sharing arrangement in case of default**. Compliance officers should assume that digital loan origination, servicing, grievance handling, data use, and default-sharing arrangements are now regulated as formal compliance processes rather than delegated vendor functions.

The directions also introduce detailed rules for **project finance**, covering the life cycle of projects from sanction through disbursement and monitoring. These provisions require AIFIs to evaluate project phases, apply prudential conditions at the sanction stage, and continue monitoring after disbursement so that funding aligns with project progress and risk containment. The document separately regulates **non-fund-based (NFB) credit facilities** such as guarantees, co-acceptances, and other contingent exposures, including specific requirements for **partial credit enhancement** structures and exclusions for certain arrangements. In practice, AIFIs will need board-approved policies and transaction-level controls for guarantees and similar off-balance-sheet commitments, rather than treating them as routine treasury or trade-finance activities.

Chapter VI imposes **additional restrictions and special conditions**, including limitations on **finance to NBFCs**, restrictions on **infrastructure financing**, rules for other permissible exposures, and requirements relating to **interest rates on export credit**. The directions also contain other operational instructions and special measures, indicating that the RBI expects AIFIs to review legacy lending practices, product terms, and sectoral exposure limits against the new framework. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the document is not just descriptive: it creates a consolidated control regime covering board oversight, digital lending conduct, project-loan discipline, contingent liabilities, sector-specific exposure restrictions, and reporting/monitoring obligations, all effective from the updated directions’ operative date and subject to any transition or saving provisions in Chapter VII.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions– Resource Raising Norms) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Resource Raising Norms) Directions, 2025** apply to the five RBI-regulated All India Financial Institutions: **EXIM Bank, NABARD, NaBFID, NHB, and SIDBI**. The directions take effect **on the day they are placed on the RBI’s official website**. They replace the older resource-raising framework in part by reflecting the fact that, since the **Leverage Ratio under Basel III became effective on April 1, 2024**, the earlier **Overall Borrowing Limit (OBL)** has been dispensed with, but the institutions must still comply with the new/continuing **Umbrella Limit (UL)**.

The core requirement is that an AIFI’s **aggregate borrowings under the UL may never exceed 100% of its Net Owned Funds (NOF)**, based on the **latest audited balance sheet**, unless the RBI specifically approves otherwise. The UL covers only four permitted funding instruments: **term deposits, term money borrowings, certificates of deposit, and commercial papers**. Compliance teams should treat this as a hard cap on resource raising through these instruments and verify that all related liabilities are tracked against NOF continuously, not just at reporting dates.

For **term deposits (TDs)**, an AIFI may accept deposits only with a maturity of **at least 1 year and not more than 5 years**, and the **minimum denomination is ₹10,000**. Brokerage paid on accepted deposits **cannot exceed 1%**. Premature withdrawal is generally **prohibited before completion of one year**, except in limited cases specifically allowed: **death of the depositor, medical exigencies, educational expenditure, and other reasons approved by the AIFI’s Board**. The institution may set its own **penal interest rate** for premature withdrawal, but any such policy must be consistently applied and aligned with the permitted exceptions.

The excerpt provided ends while beginning the detailed rules on penalties for premature withdrawal, so a compliance review should also verify the remaining provisions in the full text for any additional interest, notice, or operational requirements. More broadly, because the directions govern all resource raising through the four specified instruments, an AIFI must ensure its treasury and liability-management policies, board approvals, and internal controls are updated to reflect the **100% of NOF UL cap**, the **instrument-specific maturity/denomination restrictions**, and the **limited exception framework** for early withdrawal.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions - Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on June 16, 2026)
rows.summary:
This document sets out the Reserve Bank of India’s prudential capital adequacy framework for All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) under DOR/2025-26/321 dated November 28, 2025, and it is updated through June 16, 2026. It replaces and organizes the rules governing capital adequacy, regulatory capital composition, risk-weighted assets, ICAAP/SREP, leverage ratio, disclosures, and transitional treatment, so compliance teams should treat it as the controlling capital framework for AIFIs from the commencement date stated in Chapter I. It applies to AIFIs and addresses both solo and consolidated treatment where relevant, including the scope of application of capital requirements to subsidiaries, minority interests, and capital issued through consolidated entities.

The core substantive requirements are the prudential capital rules: the directions define how Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1), Additional Tier 1 (AT1), and Tier 2 capital are recognized, what instruments qualify, and what regulatory deductions/adjustments must be made from capital. The document also prescribes minimum loss-absorption features for AT1 instruments at their trigger points and for all non-equity regulatory capital instruments at the point of non-viability, meaning firms issuing such instruments must ensure the contractual terms satisfy RBI’s specified write-down/conversion or other absorbency requirements. It further explains how to recognize minority interest and other capital issued by consolidated subsidiaries but held by third parties, and it provides transitional arrangements for AIFIs, which means some capital elements may be phased or grandfathered according to the timetable set out in Chapter III(H).

For risk-weighted assets, the directions cover capital charges for credit risk, external credit assessments, credit risk mitigation, market risk, and operational risk, so compliance officers must ensure internal models, risk classifications, credit rating usage, collateral recognition, and operational risk capital calculations align with the prescribed methodology. The document’s supervisory review and evaluation process (SREP) section requires an AIFI to maintain an Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) and to support it with board-approved policies, documented capital planning, stress testing, and governance processes; the board must review specified policies and documents, and the ICAAP must be prepared in the prescribed format. In other words, capital adequacy is not only a numerical requirement but also a governance and documentation obligation, with ongoing supervisory scrutiny and market-discipline disclosures.

The leverage ratio framework imposes a separate minimum capital-to-exposure requirement, with rules on the capital measure, exposure measure, consolidation scope, and disclosure/reporting templates. AIFIs must therefore calculate and disclose leverage exposure in addition to risk-based capital ratios, which creates a second capital constraint that can bind even if risk-weighted capital ratios are met. Finally, Chapter VII contains repeal and other provisions, and Annex I includes a reporting format for investments by FIIs and NRIs in PNCPS qualifying as AT1 capital, indicating that the framework also affects capital instrument investor reporting and classification.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 27, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025** apply **immediately** to the five All-India Financial Institutions: **EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID**. The directions are issued under **Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934** and replace the prior framework through a separate repeal-and-savings structure; the document also states that any other laws continue to apply unless specifically barred. Compliance teams should note that the document is specifically about when and how these AIFIs may **undertake financial services** directly or through subsidiaries/branches, and it is not a general governance circular.

The definitions section is material because it determines the scope of restrictions and approvals. A **“debtor company”** means any company to which the regulated entity currently has, or had within the **preceding 12 months**, a **loan or investment exposure other than equity instruments**. **“Equity instrument”** is limited to **equity shares, compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS), and compulsorily convertible debentures (CCD)**. **“Capital funds”** means the AIFI’s total regulatory capital under the RBI’s **Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025**, based on the **last audited balance sheet**. The document also defines **control** by reference to Section 2(27) of the Companies Act, 2013, and broadly defines **“financial services company”** to cover entities engaged in financial services businesses listed in the AIFI’s statutory acts and in specified business categories under the Banking Regulation Act, RBI Act, Credit Information Companies Act, Payment and Settlement Systems Act, and exchange/depository activities.

For investments, the AIFI may invest in a financial services company only if the activity is permitted for the AIFI under its governing statute and the RBI directions. The document sets a clear concentration limit: the AIFI’s exposure in a financial services company, **including all forms of loans, investments, guarantees, commitments, and underwriting exposures**, cannot exceed **15% of the AIFI’s capital funds**, unless the RBI grants prior approval for a higher amount. The AIFI must also ensure that the financial services company itself does not undertake activities outside the permitted financial services business, and the AIFI must not use a financial services company as a vehicle for regulatory circumvention. Any investment or exposure that results in control, or the acquisition of a subsidiary structure, must be reviewed for compliance with the separate rules on subsidiaries and foreign/IFSC operations.

The directions also impose a formal **application/approval procedure** before undertaking financial services where approval is required. The AIFI must submit a proposal to the RBI with details of the proposed financial services activity, the rationale, the expected business plan, governance arrangements, and the impact on capital, risk, and compliance. The RBI may approve, reject, or impose conditions, and the AIFI must not commence the activity until the approval or applicable permission is received. Where the activity is to be carried out through a subsidiary or branch, the AIFI must ensure the entity is properly organized and that its scope stays within the approved financial services perimeter.

For **subsidiaries and branch operations**, the directions allow AIFIs to undertake financial services through subsidiaries and branches, including in **foreign jurisdictions and International Financial Services Centers (IFSCs)**, but only subject to RBI conditions. The AIFI remains responsible for the subsidiary’s or branch’s compliance, oversight, and risk management, and must ensure there is no misuse of the structure to bypass Indian regulatory limits. If a subsidiary or branch operates abroad or in an IFSC, the AIFI must comply with the host jurisdiction’s legal and regulatory requirements in addition to the RBI framework. The document is updated as of **April 27, 2026**, so compliance teams should verify whether any subsequent modifications in the updated version affect existing approvals, structures, or exposure calculations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on February 26, 2026)
rows.summary:
This document is the Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Miscellaneous Directions, 2025**, issued under the RBI Act, 1934, the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011, and the National Housing Bank Act, 1987 to regulate NBFC conduct in the public interest and to prevent practices detrimental to investors, depositors, or the NBFC itself. The Directions **take effect on the date they are placed on the RBI website**; the version provided is marked **updated as of February 26, 2026**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that the document creates a **layer-based applicability framework**: **Base Layer NBFCs (NBFC-BL)** must comply with **Chapter II**, while **Middle Layer and above** NBFCs must comply with **Chapters II and III**, unless a provision says otherwise.

The Directions expressly apply, subject to the relevant chapter and paragraph references, to a broad set of regulated entities: **NBFC-D, NBFC-ICC, NBFC-Factor, NBFC-MFI, NBFC-IFC, IDF-NBFC**, and also certain other RBI-regulated entities such as **HFCs**, **Mortgage Guarantee Companies (MGCs)**, **Systemically Significant Depository Participants (SPD)**, **NBFC-P2P**, **NBFC-AA**, and **Core Investment Companies (CICs)**. The document is very specific about which provisions apply to which entity type—for example, HFCs are subject to **paragraphs 6 to 22 and 24 to 27**, MGCs to **paragraphs 6, 7, 14, 15, 25 and 26**, and CICs to **paragraphs 6, 7, 9 to 20, and 25 to 27**. It also states that **Chapter IV** applies to **NBFC-Factors and NBFC-ICCs registered under the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011**, and **Chapter V** applies to **IDF-NBFCs**.

The Directions also identify entities to which they **do not apply**, specifically **NOFHCs registered with RBI as NBFCs** under the RBI Act, 1934. The overall compliance implication is that firms must first determine their **regulatory category and layer** to know which chapters and paragraphs bind them, because the document is not universally applicable across all NBFC-related entities. This means a compliance team must map every regulated entity in the group to the exact applicability clauses, rather than assuming one set of miscellaneous rules applies uniformly.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Operative Financial Holding Companies) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 05, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Operative Financial Holding Company (NOFHC) Directions, 2025** take **immediate effect** and apply to **every NOFHC** as defined in the document. The core definition is important for compliance: an NOFHC is a **non-deposit-taking NBFC** that holds the shares of a **banking company** and the shares of all other **financial services companies in its group**, whether those entities are regulated by the RBI or another regulator, **only to the extent permitted by the applicable regulatory rules**. The directions also define “promoter” broadly to include the person in effective control of the bank/NOFHC, their relatives under the Companies Act, 2013, and, where relevant, all entities in the promoter group; “consolidated capital funds” means capital, reserves, and surplus on a consolidated basis, including subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures per applicable accounting standards.

From the structure of the document, the compliance obligations are organized into five main areas: **registration and regulatory structure**, **shareholding**, **corporate governance**, **prudential norms**, and **restricted activities**, followed by **consolidated supervision** and transition/repeal provisions. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed operative clauses of those chapters, it makes clear that the RBI is imposing a full regulatory framework on NOFHCs covering how they must be registered, how ownership must be structured, how they must govern themselves, what prudential limits apply on both a standalone and consolidated basis, and what activities are prohibited. The prudential chapter specifically indicates that exposure norms are addressed separately for the **standalone NOFHC**, the **consolidated NOFHC**, the **bank held by the NOFHC**, and **other financial entities held by the NOFHC**, which signals that compliance teams must expect distinct limits and monitoring requirements at each level of the structure.

The document also states that the RBI issues these directions under **Section 45JA of the RBI Act, 1934** and related enabling powers, indicating they are binding regulatory directions rather than guidance. The title shows the document is **updated as on December 05, 2025**, while the issuing date is **November 28, 2025**. Because the excerpt does not yet contain the later chapter text, no specific numerical capital, leverage, exposure, or ownership thresholds appear in the portion provided; however, the headings indicate that such thresholds and restrictions are contained in the full directions and are intended to govern the NOFHC structure comprehensively.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Microfinance Institution) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Microfinance Institution Directions, 2025** are a new binding framework issued under sections **45JA, 45L and 45M of the RBI Act, 1934** for **all NBFC-MFIs registered with the RBI**. The directions take effect **on the date they are placed on the RBI website**. They are intended to regulate NBFC-MFIs in the public interest and to prevent their affairs from being conducted in a manner detrimental to investors or otherwise prejudicial to the institutions themselves.

A key feature of the document is that it does **not operate in isolation**: NBFC-MFIs must also comply, to the extent not inconsistent with these Directions, with a long list of other RBI NBFC frameworks depending on the NBFC-MFI’s scale-based regulatory layer. These referenced regimes cover registration/exemptions and scale-based regulation, branch authorization, undertaking of financial services, acquisition of shareholding or control, governance, capital adequacy, credit risk, credit facilities, concentration risk, securitisation, transfer/distribution of credit risk, income recognition/asset classification/provisioning, resolution of stressed assets, wilful and large defaulters, investment portfolio valuation/operation, asset-liability management, outsourcing risk, and additional provisions referenced in the continuation of the list.

From the excerpt provided, the Directions are organized into chapters covering: **preliminary matters; board responsibilities and registration requirements; qualifying assets and permissible activities; prudential regulations; shareholding and corporate governance; risk management; miscellaneous instructions; and repeal/other provisions**. Because the document text supplied stops partway through the applicability cross-references and does not include the detailed operative chapters, the specific numerical asset thresholds, exposure caps, provisioning rules, governance limits, or procedural filings are not visible in the excerpt and therefore cannot be summarized from the text shown. For compliance purposes, the immediate action item from this excerpt is to confirm whether the institution is an **RBI-registered NBFC-MFI**, identify its **scale-based layer**, and map all internal policies and controls against these new Directions and the incorporated RBI directions that apply unless overridden.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Peer to Peer Lending Platform) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on NBFC Peer-to-Peer Lending Platforms replace and update the framework for all Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) carrying on peer-to-peer lending platform business in India. The Directions are titled the “Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Peer to Peer Lending Platform) Directions, 2025” and take effect on the day they are placed on the RBI website; they are issued under the RBI Act, 1934 powers referenced in the preamble and apply to every NBFC-P2P as a framework for registration and operation. They also make clear that NBFC-P2Ps remain in the Base Layer under the RBI’s Scale Based Regulation framework.

The document explicitly states that the following RBI directions continue to apply to NBFC-P2Ps unless inconsistent with these new Directions: the 2025 directions on Registration/Exemptions/Scale Based Regulation, Dividend Declaration, Credit Information Reporting, Financial Statements (except paragraphs 13–15 and 20), Governance (paragraphs 8–13, with paragraphs 12 and 13 expressly applying to NBFC-P2Ps despite their Base Layer status), Acquisition of Shareholding or Control (except paragraphs 6(3) and 6(4)), Outsourcing, Responsible Business Conduct (paragraphs 98–100), Miscellaneous (paragraphs 6, 7, 14, 15, 25 and 26), Voluntary Amalgamation, and KYC. The Directions also emphasize that their own provisions apply in addition to, not instead of, those other applicable rules.

For a compliance team, the practical significance is that any NBFC engaged in P2P lending must assess its existing registration, governance, outsourcing, KYC, credit reporting, financial statement, and related compliance programs against this updated standalone framework as well as the cross-referenced RBI directions. The introduction confirms the RBI is exercising its powers because it is satisfied the framework is necessary for NBFCs that run peer-to-peer lending platforms, so the document is not merely guidance but binding regulatory direction. The excerpt provided cuts off in the definitions section, so any entity-specific thresholds, operational caps, prudential ratios, board obligations, or procedural requirements likely appear later in the document and would need review of the full text for a complete operational checklist.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Mortgage Guarantee Companies) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on March 10, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Mortgage Guarantee Companies (MGCs) Directions, 2025** apply only to entities that have been granted a **Certificate of Registration under the RBI’s mortgage guarantee company registration scheme**. The directions take effect **on the date they are placed on the RBI website** (the document is dated November 28, 2025 and marked updated as of March 10, 2026), and they are intended to regulate MGCs to prevent conduct prejudicial to investors or the MGC itself and to support the orderly financial system.

A key feature of the framework is that MGCs are subject not only to these directions, but also to a set of other RBI non-banking financial company directions, **to the extent those provisions are not inconsistent with the MGC directions**. The document expressly lists the incorporated frameworks, including the RBI’s scale-based regulation framework for NBFCs, capital adequacy norms, stressed asset resolution rules, financial statement presentation/disclosure rules, miscellaneous instructions, income recognition/asset classification/provisioning rules, concentration risk rules, governance rules, outsourcing rules (including IT-specific provisions), dividend declaration rules, KYC directions, and voluntary amalgamation directions. Where there is any conflict, **the MGC Directions prevail**.

The directions also state that an MGC may fall into any layer of the RBI’s **Scale Based Regulatory (SBR)** structure depending on the applicable SBR parameters, meaning the level of regulatory requirements depends on the company’s classification under that framework. The document further provides that an MGC may use the RBI’s **“Guidance Note on Operational Risk Management and Operational Resilience,” as amended from time to time**, which signals an expected operational risk governance reference point, though not a separate hard mandate in the excerpt shown. Finally, the directions are **in addition to, not a substitute for,** other relevant RBI instructions referenced in the document, so compliance teams should treat this as a cumulative regime rather than a standalone code.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Account Aggregator) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Account Aggregator Directions, 2025** establish the regulatory framework for any **NBFC undertaking the business of an Account Aggregator (NBFC-AA)** in India. The directions are issued under **section 45JA of the RBI Act, 1934** and **take effect on the day they are placed on the RBI website**. They apply specifically to **NBFC-AAs**, and the document makes clear that these entities will **always remain in the Base Layer** under RBI’s scale-based regulation framework, even though they are treated as NBFCs-BL for that framework.

The directions also incorporate, by reference, several other RBI frameworks that continue to apply to NBFC-AAs **so long as they are not inconsistent** with the new AA directions. These include the RBI’s 2025 directions on **registration/exemptions/scale-based regulation**, selected governance paragraphs, **financial statements and disclosures** (with specified paragraphs excluded), **acquisition of shareholding or control** (with certain paragraphs excluded), **dividend declaration norms**, **outsourcing risk management**, **voluntary amalgamation**, and selected provisions of the **Miscellaneous Directions, 2025**. Importantly, the AA directions are stated to operate **in addition to, and not in substitution for,** those other applicable RBI instructions, so compliance teams must read the AA framework together with the incorporated NBFC directions rather than treating it as a standalone rulebook.

The document defines the **“business of an account aggregator”** as the activity of an NBFC that, **for a fee or otherwise**, undertakes account aggregation as defined in the directions. It also sets out core definitional terms such as “bank,” including banking companies, SBI, corresponding new banks, subsidiary banks, RBI-notified other banks, and **co-operative banks** as defined under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. From a compliance perspective, this means firms operating as account aggregators must verify not only their own status as NBFC-AAs but also whether their activities, governance structure, disclosures, outsourcing, capital/shareholding changes, and any amalgamation plans comply with the RBI frameworks that are expressly made applicable here.

More broadly, the directions frame the **registration and operation** of NBFC-AAs in India and signal that the RBI expects these entities to follow the full set of AA-specific requirements together with the cross-referenced NBFC governance, prudential, and disclosure obligations. Because the directions became effective immediately upon publication on the RBI website, compliance teams should treat them as **already operative** from the date of posting and ensure internal policies, board oversight, and regulatory checklists are aligned without delay.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Core Investment Companies) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on March 10, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Core Investment Companies (CIC) Directions, 2025** were issued under the RBI Act and apply to **every CIC**, meaning an NBFC whose business is acquisition of shares and securities and that, as of its **last audited balance sheet**, meets all of the CIC tests in the directions. The directions took effect **when placed on the RBI website** (the document does not give a separate future commencement date), and the updated version is marked **as on March 10, 2026**.

To qualify as a CIC, the company must hold **at least 90% of its net assets** in specified investments in **group companies**—equity shares, preference shares, bonds, debentures, debt, or loans—and **at least 60% of net assets** must be in **equity shares (including instruments compulsorily convertible into equity within 10 years)** of group companies and **units of InvITs only as sponsor**. The InvIT exposure is tightly limited: CICs may hold InvIT units only in their capacity as sponsors, and at no time may they exceed the **minimum holding of units and tenor required under SEBI’s Infrastructure Investment Trusts Regulations, 2014, as amended**. A CIC also must **not trade** in its investments in group-company shares, bonds, debentures, debt, or loans **except through a block sale for dilution or disinvestment**. The only other financial activities permitted are limited investments in **bank deposits, money market instruments (including money market mutual funds that invest in debt/money-market instruments with maturity up to 1 year), government securities, and bonds/debentures issued by group companies**, plus **granting loans to group companies** and **issuing guarantees on behalf of group companies**.

The directions also clarify how the asset thresholds are measured. The **90% of net assets** test may include up to **10% of net assets** in **real estate or other fixed assets needed for effective functioning**, but **not** other financial investments or loans in non-group companies. For the calculation, only **direct investments in group companies appearing on the CIC’s balance sheet** count; investments held through subsidiaries in step-down subsidiaries or other entities **do not count** toward the 90% test. The document also signals that “block sale” is to be understood as a **long-term or strategic sale** rather than ordinary trading, so compliance teams should ensure any sale of group-company holdings fits that limited exception.

Because the text provided is only the opening part of the directions, the document clearly establishes the **scope, core asset-composition tests, permitted activities, and restricted trading rules** that determine CIC status and ongoing compliance. A compliance officer should therefore focus on whether the entity’s balance sheet composition, group-investment exposure, InvIT sponsorship holdings, and any sale activity remain within these thresholds and exceptions, because failure would mean the company may no longer qualify as a CIC under RBI’s framework.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Standalone Primary Dealers) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on March 10, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Standalone Primary Dealers (SPDs) Directions, 2025** are an immediately effective, consolidated regulatory framework issued under the RBI Act, 1934. They apply to **all SPDs registered with RBI as NBFCs**, and they do not stand alone: SPDs must also comply with other RBI directions issued by other RBI departments that apply to them. The document specifically states that several other NBFC directions continue to apply to SPDs **to the extent they are not inconsistent** with these Directions, including RBI’s directions on **NBFC registration/exemptions and scale-based regulation, governance, financial services, outsourcing, KYC, capital adequacy, financial statement presentation/disclosures (except specified paragraphs 13–15 and 20), concentration risk management, dividend declaration, miscellaneous provisions, and voluntary amalgamation**.

The Directions came into force **with immediate effect** and were issued on **November 28, 2025**; the version provided is **updated as on March 10, 2026**. The text makes clear that these Directions are meant to **consolidate** the RBI Department of Regulation’s requirements for SPDs, but they do **not override other applicable laws, rules, regulations, or RBI directions**. In practice, this means a compliance team must treat the SPD framework as a layered regime: the SPD-specific Directions are primary, but other NBFC and RBI requirements remain enforceable where they do not conflict.

From the excerpt provided, the document also signals that SPDs may use a **“Guida…”** resource referenced at the end of the visible text, but the full instruction is cut off in the excerpt. No numerical prudential thresholds, capital ratios, filing deadlines, or reporting frequencies are visible in the supplied portion, so those items cannot be summarized from this excerpt alone. For compliance purposes, the key requirement visible here is the **broad applicability of the new SPD Directions immediately upon issuance**, together with the continued obligation to comply with the listed RBI frameworks in parallel.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Housing Finance Companies) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) Directions, 2025** are a consolidated regulatory framework issued under the RBI Act, 1934 and the NHB Act, 1987 to govern HFCs and prevent conduct that could harm depositors, investors, or the financial system. The directions **take effect when placed on the RBI website** and apply generally to **all HFCs registered under section 29A of the NHB Act, 1987**; however, **Chapter IX (Auditor’s Report)** applies specifically to **auditors of HFCs** rather than to the HFCs themselves. The document also states that a number of other RBI/NHB directions continue to apply to HFCs—so long as they are not inconsistent with these directions—based on the HFC’s scale-based regulatory layer, including directions on registration and exemptions, branch authorisation, financial services, acquisition of shareholding or control, governance, prudential capital adequacy, and other prudential/operational areas.

A compliance team should note that this document is not just a standalone rulebook: it is the controlling HFC framework that sits alongside other specified RBI directions and incorporates them by reference where applicable. That means compliance obligations will depend in part on the HFC’s regulatory layer and on the interaction between these Directions and the cited underlying frameworks, rather than on this document alone. The introductory provisions make clear that the RBI is exercising its statutory powers to regulate HFCs in the public interest, with explicit concern for investor and depositor protection and for preventing prejudicial conduct by HFCs.

The excerpt provided is primarily the **introductory/structural part** of the Directions and does not yet include the substantive capital, provisioning, governance, deposit-acceptance, or reporting rules that appear in later chapters. In the portion shown, the only concrete operative requirement is the scope statement: HFCs must comply with these Directions from the effective date, auditors must follow Chapter IX, and HFCs must also continue to observe the listed incorporated RBI directions to the extent they are applicable and not inconsistent. The document is titled as **“updated as on April 15, 2026,”** which indicates a later consolidation/update date, but no separate delayed compliance deadline is stated in the excerpt beyond the immediate website-publication effective date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Climate Finance and Management of Climate Change Risks) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Climate Finance and Management of Climate Change Risks) Directions, 2025** take effect **immediately** and are intended to require NBFCs to build climate-risk assessment into their governance and risk-management systems while also creating a framework for **green deposits** and deployment of funds into approved **green finance**. The directions apply specifically to **deposit-taking NBFCs (NBFC-Ds) registered with the RBI** and **deposit-taking Housing Finance Companies registered with the RBI under the NHB Act, 1987**; the document explicitly ties applicability to the existing scale-based regulatory structure for NBFCs. The stated regulatory objective is to help NBFCs assess climate-change risks comprehensively, integrate those risks into existing frameworks, and channel credit to green activities/projects while reducing greenwashing and protecting depositors and customers pursuing sustainability goals.

The document defines key terms that determine compliance scope. A **“green deposit”** is an **interest-bearing deposit** accepted for a **fixed period** whose proceeds are **earmarked for green finance**. **“Green finance”** means lending to and/or investing in **green activities/projects** that meet the criteria in paragraph 13, and the definition expressly includes financing aimed at **climate mitigation, climate adaptation and resilience, and other climate/environmental objectives such as biodiversity management and nature-based solutions**. The meaning of **green activities/projects** is also tied to paragraph 13, so compliance teams will need to map any intended use of proceeds against that rule set before offering products or booking assets as green.

Although the excerpt does not include the later operative paragraphs, it shows the structure of the new regime and the areas where compliance obligations will appear: a **Board role** chapter, then a detailed **framework for acceptance of green deposits** with requirements for **policy**, **denomination, interest rates and tenor**, a **financing framework**, **use of proceeds**, **third-party verification/assurance**, **impact assessment**, and **reporting/disclosures**. For compliance purposes, that signals that an NBFC cannot simply label a deposit “green”; it must have board-approved policies, define product terms, ensure proceeds are used only for eligible green finance, obtain independent verification or assurance, evaluate impact, and make ongoing disclosures. The introduction also emphasizes anti-greenwashing and depositor protection, so any internal controls, product approvals, marketing materials, and portfolio monitoring should be designed to support substantiation of green claims.

The document also contains a **repeal and saving** chapter and a section stating that **other applicable laws are not barred**, meaning these directions operate alongside, not instead of, other legal and regulatory requirements. Because the directions commenced immediately on issuance (**November 28, 2025**), affected institutions should treat them as in force now and prepare to align governance, product design, risk management, and disclosure processes without delay.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Managing Risks in Outsourcing Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** (DOR/2025-26/363, DOR.ORG.REC.No.282/21-04-158/2025-26). These Directions establish a new, comprehensive outsourcing-risk framework for **NBFCs** covering both **financial services outsourcing** and **IT outsourcing**, with separate chapters and more detailed governance, risk-management, contract, monitoring, continuity, termination, grievance-redressal, and offshore/group outsourcing requirements. From the table of contents, the document is structured to require board-approved policies, senior-management accountability, formal risk assessments, vendor evaluation, contractual controls, business continuity/disaster recovery planning, and ongoing oversight of outsourced arrangements.

For **outsourcing of financial services**, the Directions set out what can and cannot be outsourced, while keeping the NBFC fully responsible for the underlying activity; they also require clear authorization and oversight, a documented outsourcing policy, defined senior-management roles, assessment of risks, protection of confidentiality and security of information, and formal outsourcing processes. Those processes include evaluating the service provider before engagement, entering into a written outsourcing agreement, monitoring and controlling outsourced activities, ensuring business continuity and disaster recovery, and having a termination framework. The document also addresses **specific arrangements** such as outsourcing **within a group/conglomerate** and **offshore outsourcing**, and it separately requires a grievance-redressal mechanism for complaints tied to outsourced services.

For **outsourcing of IT services**, the Directions create a parallel regime with IT-specific definitions and obligations, again emphasizing that the NBFC remains accountable even when functions are outsourced. The IT chapter requires board/senior-management oversight, an IT outsourcing policy, a role for the IT function in governance, a risk-management framework, protections for confidentiality and information security, and a structured service-provider evaluation process before outsourcing is undertaken. While the excerpt provided does not show the detailed operative clauses, the table of contents makes clear that the final document covers the full lifecycle of IT outsourcing, including governance, risk controls, contractual requirements, monitoring, continuity, and exit/termination expectations.

Because the text provided stops at the table of contents, it does **not** include the substantive clause-by-clause standards, any specific thresholds, exceptions, deadlines, reporting timelines, or transition dates beyond the document’s issue date of **November 28, 2025**. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the RBI has formalized a more detailed and likely more stringent outsourcing-control regime for NBFCs, and affected entities should review existing financial-service and IT outsourcing arrangements, board policies, vendor contracts, oversight processes, and grievance/BCP/DR arrangements for alignment with the final Directions once the full operative text is reviewed.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025** are binding conduct rules for **all layers** of the specified NBFC categories, unless a provision says otherwise: **NBFC-D, NBFC-ICC, NBFC-Factor, NBFC-MFI, NBFC-IFC, and NBFC-P2P** (the excerpt begins listing the applicable entities and indicates the directions apply broadly to those registered with the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934 or the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011, as relevant). The directions were issued on **November 28, 2025** and, by default, are **effective from the date of issuance** unless a particular requirement has a later start date. They are grounded in the RBI’s powers under **sections 45JA, 45L, and 45M** of the RBI Act, 1934 and other enabling laws.

For a compliance team, the document is a consolidated conduct framework covering: the **board’s institutional oversight responsibilities**, a **Fair Practices Code**, **Key Facts Statement** requirements for loans and advances, rules on **penal charges** in loan accounts, **reset of floating-rate EMI-based personal loans**, **pre-payment charges**, return of **movable and immovable property documents on repayment or settlement of personal loans**, conduct expectations for **lending against gold and silver collateral**, special protections for **microfinance borrowers**, and responsibilities of **DSAs, DMAs, and recovery agents** acting for NBFCs. It also contains operational requirements on **public notice before branch/office closure**, **rounding transactions to the nearest rupee**, provision of **safe deposit locker facilities** by NBFCs, compliance with a specified **Supreme Court order dated April 30, 2025** in the matters of *Pragya Prasun and Ors. v. Union of India and Ors.* and *Amar Jain v. Union of India and Ors.*, and measures to be taken in the event of a **declared calamity**.

The table of contents shows that the document is not just principles-based; it imposes specific procedures and customer-facing obligations in lending and recovery operations, with dedicated annexures including a **Key Facts Statement format** and detailed rules for **lending against gold jewellery**. Chapter V also addresses **repeal and saving**, confirms that the directions do **not bar application of other laws**, and provides interpretation provisions, meaning firms must align these directions with all other applicable statutes, RBI instructions, and internal policies rather than treat them as a standalone code. The provided excerpt does not include the detailed operative thresholds, rates, or timelines for each chapter, but the document clearly establishes a comprehensive compliance regime for NBFC governance, loan documentation and disclosures, fee/charge practices, secured lending conduct, borrower treatment, agent oversight, and contingency handling.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction updates and consolidates KYC/AML obligations for all categories of Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), across all regulatory layers, except NBFCs that have no customer interface. It took effect immediately on the date it was placed on the RBI’s official website, and it also applies to overseas branches and majority-owned subsidiaries of NBFCs so long as local host-country law does not conflict; where foreign law does conflict, the NBFC must still apply RBI requirements to the extent possible and, if compliance is legally impossible, report the issue and the steps taken to the RBI. The document is issued under the RBI Act, FEMA, the NHB Act, and the PMLA/PML Rules framework, and its purpose is to prevent NBFCs from being used for money laundering or terrorist financing while aligning customer identification and transaction monitoring with FATF and Indian AML/CFT law.

The core compliance requirement is that NBFCs must implement a formal customer acceptance policy, risk management framework, customer identification procedure (CIP), customer due diligence (CDD), record retention, and FIU-India reporting controls. The Directions require customer identification not only when opening account-based relationships, but also for non-account transactions and ongoing monitoring, with the NBFC expected to identify and verify customers and beneficial owners using reliable, independent sources and to apply enhanced scrutiny where risk is higher. The rules also require NBFCs to maintain records of identity and transactions, and to report prescribed information to the Financial Intelligence Unit–India in line with the PML Rules.

The document also places specific obligations on NBFCs to ensure governance and operational controls: policies must be proportionate to the nature, scale, and complexity of the business, and must be risk-based. Where customers, transactions, geographies, or products present higher money-laundering or terrorist-financing risk, the NBFC must apply stronger due diligence and monitoring; where risk is lower, simplified measures may be permitted only to the extent allowed by the Directions and by law. The compliance framework is intended to be implemented through internal systems, staff procedures, and documented controls, rather than as a one-time onboarding exercise.

Finally, the Directions replace and/or consolidate prior KYC instructions for NBFCs through the repealing chapter and related saving provisions, so compliance teams should treat this as the operative KYC/AML framework for NBFC activity from its commencement date. Because the document is structured into chapters covering customer acceptance, risk management, CIP, CDD, recordkeeping, FIU reporting, international-agency communications, and other instructions, a compliance officer should review the detailed chapters and annexes for any sector-specific thresholds, exception handling, verification standards, or reporting timelines that apply to the NBFC’s products, customers, and cross-border operations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025** apply **immediately upon issuance** and govern dividend declarations by a broad set of regulated entities: **NBFC-Ds, NBFC-ICCs, NBFC-Factors, NBFC-MFIs, NBFC-IFCs, NBFC-IDFs, HFCs, MGCs, Standalone Primary Dealers (SPDs), CICs, NBFC-P2Ps, and NBFC-AAs**, with applicability stated for **all layers unless otherwise specified**. The Directions expressly **do not apply to Non-Operative Financial Holding Companies (NOFHCs)**. They are issued under the RBI Act, 1934, the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011, and the NHB Act, 1987, and they also define key terms used throughout the framework, including **Adjusted Net Worth (ANW)**, **Capital to Risk Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR)**, **dividends (including interim dividends)**, and **Dividend Payout Ratio**.

In substance, the document is a **prudential dividend framework**: before paying dividends, covered NBFCs must comply with RBI-prescribed **board oversight**, **eligibility criteria**, **quantum limits**, and **reporting requirements**. The rules are designed to ensure that dividends are declared only when the institution is sufficiently capitalized and otherwise compliant with prudential norms, rather than as a routine corporate action. The Directions also create a formal **reporting system**, with **Annex I** providing the reporting format for an **NBFC declaring dividend** and **Annex II** providing the reporting format for an **SPD declaring dividend**, meaning the declaration is not just an internal board decision but must be accompanied by prescribed reporting to the RBI.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that these Directions replace a discretionary approach with a **mandatory regulatory process** for dividend declarations by the listed regulated entities. The document’s structure shows that the operative obligations are concentrated in Chapter II: companies must satisfy eligibility thresholds, determine the permissible dividend amount using the RBI’s formula/limits, and submit the required report in the prescribed format. Because the document expressly covers **interim dividends** as well as ordinary dividends, compliance teams should treat any proposed shareholder distribution as within scope and ensure the institution’s capital metrics, prudential compliance status, and regulatory reporting are checked before board approval or payment.

The updated version is dated **July 01, 2026**, but the text provided does not show any later substantive amendment language in the excerpt beyond the title update; the effective date stated in the body remains **“immediately upon issuance.”** No specific numeric dividend cap, threshold, or ratio is visible in the excerpt you provided, so a compliance officer would need the remainder of Chapter II—especially the eligibility and quantum provisions—to determine the exact capital tests and payout restrictions before authorizing any dividend.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures Directions, 2025** take effect **immediately** and apply, unless specifically exempted, to **all layers** of the main NBFC categories registered with the RBI: **NBFC-D, NBFC-ICC, NBFC-Factor, NBFC-MFI, NBFC-IFC, IDF-NBFC, HFCs, and CICs**. The Directions also apply, subject to carve-outs, to **Standalone Primary Dealers (SPDs), Mortgage Guarantee Companies (MGCs), NBFC-P2P platforms, and NBFC-Account Aggregators**, with the document expressly stating that certain paragraphs do **not** apply to SPDs, NBFC-P2Ps, NBFC-AAs, and, in the case of MGCs, all provisions except paragraph 20 apply according to layer-wise applicability. The legal basis cited includes the RBI Act, 1934, the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011, and the NHB Act, 1987, indicating these are mandatory regulatory reporting directions rather than guidance.

Substantively, the document sets the RBI’s requirements for how NBFC financial statements must be **prepared, presented, and disclosed**, including the **balance sheet, profit and loss account, notes to accounts, and consolidated financial statements**. The table of contents shows that the Directions cover: preparation of financial statements, the accounting standards to be followed, specific guidance for applying certain accounting standards, other instructions, and detailed disclosure requirements in the notes. It also contains a separate chapter on **consolidated financial statements**, meaning regulated entities with subsidiaries or other group structures must consider group-level presentation/disclosure obligations, not just standalone accounts.

For compliance purposes, the most important operational point from the excerpt is that the Directions are **binding from the date of issue** and establish a structured reporting framework that NBFCs must align with for all relevant financial statements. The document anticipates detailed rules on **presentation formats, note disclosures, and standards-based treatment of specific accounting issues**, which would affect year-end close, drafting of financial statements, audit coordination, and internal review controls. Because the applicability is explicitly **layer-based** and the exemptions differ by entity type, compliance teams should first confirm which group entities fall within each carve-out before finalizing reporting templates and disclosure checklists.

The version provided is marked **“Updated as on July 01, 2026,”** so the compliance team should treat this as the operative consolidated text as of that date, even though the underlying Directions were originally issued on **November 28, 2025**. Since the excerpt does not include the actual body text of the chapter-level requirements, it is clear that the document imposes detailed disclosure and presentation obligations, but the specific line-item disclosures, formatting rules, thresholds, or accounting treatments would need to be checked in the full chapters and annexes before implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
These Directions, issued by the Reserve Bank of India on November 28, 2025, came into force immediately and are titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025**. Their stated purpose is to create a **non-discriminatory, transparent process consistent with natural justice** for classifying borrowers as wilful defaulters and to ensure that information about such defaulters is disseminated so that further institutional finance is not extended to them.

The Directions apply, as a rule, to **NBFCs in the Middle Layer and above**: **NBFC-D, NBFC-ICC, NBFC-Factor, NBFC-MFI, NBFC-IFC, IDF-NBFC, HFC, and CIC**. They do **not** apply to **Mortgage Guarantee Companies, NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA, SPD, NOFHC, or Type I NBFCs**; however, the document expressly states that the **restrictions on further financial accommodation to wilful defaulters and the provisions relating to large defaulters apply to all entities regulated by the RBI**, even if a particular entity does not fall within the document’s own definition of “lender.” The document also notes that the applicability aligns with the RBI’s **Scale Based Regulation framework**, and the updated version referenced is **as on July 01, 2026**.

For compliance purposes, the key procedural requirement is that NBFCs covered by the Directions must follow a formal framework for identifying, classifying, and reporting **wilful defaulters** and **large defaulters**. The document defines a “borrower” broadly as any person who has availed a credit facility from an NBFC, and a “credit facility” includes both **fund-based and non-fund-based exposures**, including off-balance-sheet items such as **derivatives, guarantees, and letters of credit**. The table of contents shows that the Directions also contain specific chapters on the **Board’s role**, the **treatment of wilful defaulters**, **reporting obligations**, **preventive measures**, and the **role of auditors**, which indicates that compliance is not limited to classification alone but extends to governance, internal controls, and external reporting.

The Directions are issued under the RBI’s statutory powers under **Section 45JA and Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934**, and **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005**. The compliance takeaway is that affected NBFCs must maintain a structured and fair process for default classification, and they must be prepared to share information on wilful defaulters and large defaulters in the formats prescribed in **Annex I** and **Annex II**. Since the document expressly emphasizes preventing further finance to wilful defaulters, the practical effect is that covered entities need controls to ensure that credit decisions, reporting, and any restriction on additional facilities are aligned with the RBI’s direction and apply across the regulated entity’s exposures where required.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) set out a consolidated framework for identifying, resolving, restructuring, provisioning for, and disclosing stressed assets, with the updated text noted as of July 1, 2026. The rules apply primarily to a non-deposit-taking NBFC with asset size of ₹500 crore or more and to all deposit-taking NBFCs, and they establish Board-approved policies for early stress detection, reporting, resolution governance, and disclosures, along with supervisory review expectations. Compliance teams should treat these Directions as a lifecycle framework: they begin with mandatory early identification of borrower stress, proceed through a defined review period and resolution process, and then prescribe how assets, income, and provisions must be treated if restructuring is used.

A major requirement is the creation and use of a formal resolution process, including the execution of an Inter-Creditor Agreement where multiple lenders are involved and the preparation and implementation of a resolution plan within the applicable review period. If implementation is delayed, the Directions impose additional specific provisioning requirements, meaning the NBFC must make extra provisioning charges when a resolution plan is not implemented on time. The document also specifies prudential norms for restructuring, including how assets must be classified after restructuring, when additional finance may be extended, how an upgraded classification may be permitted only after satisfactory performance over the required monitoring period, and how a borrower’s subsequent default after that monitoring period affects classification and provisioning.

The Directions also address special situations that compliance teams must monitor carefully. They include restructuring involving sale-and-leaseback transactions, borrowers involved in fraud, malfeasance, or wilful default, compromise settlements and technical write-offs, projects under implementation, and accounts impacted by calamities, each with its own prudential treatment, reporting, and implementation rules. In these special cases, the NBFC must follow the specific restrictions or procedural safeguards applicable to the category; for example, accounts affected by calamities have a separate chapter covering implementation of resolution plans, ancillary measures, and reporting requirements.

Finally, the Directions extend to government debt relief schemes and to instruments acquired as part of restructuring, for which separate prudential treatment is prescribed. NBFCs must follow rules on asset classification, provisioning, valuation, and income recognition for such instruments, so compliance should ensure the accounting and risk teams are aligned on when such assets can be recognized, how they are to be valued, and what provision levels apply. Overall, the document is a detailed prudential framework that requires affected NBFCs to maintain formal stress-identification systems, Board-approved restructuring policies, timely resolution governance, strict provisioning discipline, and granular reporting across all restructuring and relief scenarios.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025** were issued on **November 28, 2025** and take effect **immediately**; the version provided is **updated as of July 1, 2026**. These Directions are intended to standardize prudential accounting and provisioning for NBFC loan/advances portfolios to improve consistency and transparency in published financial statements, and they are issued under the RBI Act, 1934 and, for factoring companies, the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011. They apply to the specified RBI-regulated NBFC categories named in the document, including **NBFC-D, NBFC-ICC, NBFC-Factor, NBFC-IFC, and other NBFCs within scope of the Directions**, with additional layer-based rules for **NBFC–Base Layer (NBFC–BL), NBFC–Middle Layer (NBFC–ML), and NBFC–Upper Layer (NBFC–UL)** where applicable.

At a high level, the Directions impose prudential norms covering **lending prudence and consumer education, asset classification, provisioning, income recognition, and disclosure requirements**, and they also include a separate provision set for cases where a **resolution plan is implemented under Chapter VI-A of the RBI’s 2025 Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions**. The document signals that non-performing and doubtful-asset treatment, provisioning calculations, and recognition of income must follow RBI-prescribed criteria rather than management discretion, and that NBFCs must maintain disclosures aligned with these classifications and provisions. Compliance teams should treat these Directions as the governing framework for how advances are classified, when interest/income can be recognized, and what reserve/provision levels must be maintained in financial reporting.

The document is organized so that **all NBFCs** are subject to the core rules in Chapter II, while Chapters III–V add stricter layer-specific requirements for NBFCs classified as **BL, ML, or UL**. It also contains a **repeal and saving** chapter, meaning earlier inconsistent provisions are superseded to the extent covered, while preserving certain actions taken under the prior framework. Chapter VI further clarifies that these Directions do **not bar the application of other laws**, and it provides interpretation provisions for how the Directions should be read and applied in practice.

For a compliance officer, the key takeaway is that this is a comprehensive RBI prudential regime for NBFC lending/advances accounting that is already in force, applies by entity type and regulatory layer, and requires firms to ensure their internal policies, credit monitoring, classification engines, provisioning models, financial reporting, and disclosures are aligned to the RBI’s detailed asset-classification and income-recognition rules. If your organization is any of the covered NBFC types—or holds exposures managed by a covered NBFC entity—this document will directly affect credit loss provisioning, NPA recognition timing, and public financial statement disclosures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued on November 28, 2025 and updated as of July 1, 2026, establishes the asset-liability management and liquidity risk framework for non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) and related regulated entities under RBI’s jurisdiction. It applies from the date of issue and is grounded in RBI’s statutory powers under Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934, the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011, the National Housing Bank Act, 1987, and other enabling laws. For a compliance team, the key point is that this is not just a disclosure document: it imposes ongoing governance, measurement, reporting, and liquidity-buffer requirements, with separate treatment for liquidity risk management, maturity profiling, interest rate risk, and liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) obligations.

The directions require the board to approve and oversee the institution’s ALM and liquidity-risk framework, including policies, internal limits, review cycles, and the organization responsible for ALM. Entities covered must maintain ALM information systems capable of measuring and monitoring liquidity mismatches and related risks, and must implement formal governance for liquidity risk management rather than leaving it to ad hoc treasury practice. The document specifically addresses maturity profiling of assets and liabilities, mismatch management, stock-based liquidity risk measurement, currency risk management, and interest rate risk management, with prescribed formats and reporting periodicity in the annexures. It also requires public disclosure on liquidity risk in the specified format, meaning compliance is not only internal but also external through prescribed disclosures.

A major substantive component is the Liquidity Coverage Ratio chapter, which requires covered entities to hold sufficient High Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) against total net cash outflows calculated over the relevant stress horizon. The direction prescribes how assets must be classified for HQLA computation, how outflows and inflows are determined, and how net cash outflows are computed, with disclosure requirements for LCR as well. Compliance teams should treat this as a rulebook for both the numerator and denominator of the LCR, rather than a general principle, because the document includes specific computational rules and return formats in annexures. Any entity subject to the direction must therefore ensure its liquidity buffer, cash-flow mapping, and reporting systems are aligned to RBI’s classification and calculation methodology.

The document also contains repeal-and-savings provisions, meaning prior inconsistent directions are superseded to the extent specified while other laws continue to apply unless expressly barred. In practice, firms should review whether any existing ALM, liquidity risk, or LCR policies, board approvals, MIS, and regulatory returns need to be amended immediately to match these directions and the annexed formats. Because the title indicates an “Updated as on July 01, 2026” version, compliance staff should verify the update history and any amendments or transitional provisions reflected in the 2026 update before concluding that earlier implementation assumptions still hold.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio Directions, 2025** took effect **from the date of issue, November 28, 2025**, and the version provided is **updated as of July 1, 2026**. The directions are issued under the RBI Act, the NHB Act, and the Factoring Regulation Act, and they apply to **NBFC-D, NBFC-ICC, NBFC-Factor, NBFC-MFI, NBFC-IFC, IDF-NBFC, HFCs, and CICs**. The compliance impact depends on layer classification: **NBFCs in the Base Layer must comply with Chapter II; NBFCs in the Middle Layer and Upper Layer must comply with both Chapters II and III**. The document also states that certain entities are **not covered**, beginning with **MGC registered with RBI under the scheme** (the excerpt cuts off before listing the rest), so firms should confirm whether any exclusion applies before implementing the directions.

For **NBFC-BL**, Chapter II imposes requirements on **accounting, investment policy, government securities transactions, corporate bond reporting, accounting for investments by non-Ind AS NBFCs, income from investments, AIF investments, currency futures, and interest rate futures**. This means covered NBFCs must have policies and accounting treatment aligned to the new RBI framework for their investment portfolios, including operational controls around government securities and reporting of corporate bond transactions on the specified platform. Non-Indian Accounting Standards NBFCs have explicit investment accounting rules under the directions, and income recognition from investments is separately regulated.

The directions also specifically regulate **investments in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)** by NBFCs, which signals a compliance review requirement for any NBFC exposure to AIF units or fund structures. In addition, **currency futures and interest rate futures** are addressed at the NBFC-BL level, indicating that even base-layer entities need to check whether such derivative activity is permitted and, if so, ensure it is conducted only in the manner authorized by RBI.  

For **NBFC-ML and NBFC-UL**, Chapter III adds stricter derivatives and trading controls: it covers **ready forward contracts in corporate debt securities, participation in currency options, and participation in interest rate futures**. A compliance team should treat these as distinct permissions/restrictions beyond the base-layer rules and ensure that any such activity is supported by policy, approvals, limits, and operational procedures consistent with the RBI directions.

Chapter IV provides for **repeal and saving**, says that **other laws are not barred unless expressly inconsistent**, and includes an **interpretation** provision, which means firms should read these directions as the controlling RBI framework for investment portfolio classification, valuation, and operations while still checking other applicable laws. Overall, the document is a comprehensive RBI rulebook for how covered NBFCs must classify, value, account for, report, and conduct investment-related transactions, with the strictest operational permissions applying to Middle and Upper Layer NBFCs.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Securitisation Transactions) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) – Securitisation Transactions) Directions, 2025** are the RBI’s updated framework for how NBFCs may originate, structure, support, invest in, and account for securitisation transactions, with the version provided updated through **July 1, 2026**. The directions replace the earlier framework by setting detailed rules on **which assets may be securitised**, the **minimum retention requirement (MRR)** for originators, **origination standards**, **payment waterfalls and observability**, limits on **total retained exposures**, conditions for **issuance and listing**, requirements for the **special purpose entity (SPE)**, rules on **representations and warranties**, and **accounting treatment**. They also create a separate framework for **simple, transparent and comparable (STC)** securitisations for regulatory capital purposes, plus disclosure and prudential oversight expectations for such transactions.

For transactions involving NBFC-originated securitisation, the document requires compliance with RBI standards on **asset eligibility** and **originator skin-in-the-game** through MRR, meaning the originator must retain a prescribed portion of the securitised exposure rather than transferring all risk away. It also requires adherence to **origination standards** so that the securitised assets meet defined underwriting and performance criteria, and it restricts the extent to which the originator may continue to hold other exposures to the same transaction or pool through the **limit on total retained exposures**. Where the transaction uses an SPE, the SPE must satisfy specific conditions to ensure the structure is bankruptcy-remote and operationally sound, and the document prescribes how payment priorities must be set out so cash flows are allocated in an observable and rule-based manner. Any issuance and listing requirements must also be met where applicable, and the originator must make and honor defined representations and warranties, with associated accounting treatment governed by the directions rather than left solely to general accounting practice.

The directions also govern **support facilities** provided to securitisation structures, including **credit enhancement**, **liquidity**, **underwriting**, and **servicing** facilities. These support arrangements are permitted only under specified conditions, and the framework expressly limits how and when they may be provided, reset, or used so they do not create hidden recourse or undermine true risk transfer. In addition, an NBFC that **invests in securitisation exposures** must follow its own due diligence obligations before investing, conduct **stress testing**, and maintain ongoing **credit monitoring and valuation** of those exposures.

Finally, the directions establish **capital requirements for securitisation exposures** and related **disclosure norms**, which means NBFCs must calculate regulatory capital for these positions in the manner prescribed and provide the required disclosures.
