rows.summary:
This RBI circular, titled **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026**, was issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, and it **takes effect immediately upon issuance**. It applies to **commercial banks only**—specifically banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and Local Area Banks, as well as corresponding new banks and the State Bank of India. The scope is broad: it covers **digital payment products and services** offered by the bank for both financial and non-financial functions, including balance enquiry, setting/changing PIN, mobile banking registration, OTP generation, mini-statements, transaction status checks, and dispute/grievance initiation, whether delivered directly by the bank or through RBI-operated systems or RBI-authorised Payment System Operators; the associated IT assets (applications, systems, infrastructure) are also within scope.

The document’s core requirement is that covered banks must implement RBI-prescribed **digital payment security controls** across governance, security management, application security, authentication, fraud management, reconciliation, customer protection, internet banking, mobile app security, and card payment security. At the governance level, the Board is expected to approve policies and oversee security-risk management, which means compliance is not just technical but also a board-level governance obligation. The directions indicate that the RBI is setting minimum control expectations for how banks design, operate, secure, monitor, and support their digital payment channels and related systems.

From the portions provided, the document does not yet list the detailed control clauses, but it clearly signals that banks will need to align their internal policies, procedures, and technical controls to the RBI’s prescribed framework across the full digital payments lifecycle. Compliance teams should therefore treat this as a mandatory enterprise-wide control regime for retail and other customer-facing digital payment activity, with responsibilities likely spanning IT/security, operations, fraud/risk, customer service, and board oversight. Since the directions are effective immediately, banks subject to the instrument should assume they must begin gap assessment and implementation without waiting for a later commencement date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework” Directions, 2026** set out a comprehensive, board-level and operational cybersecurity/IT governance regime for commercial banks. They are issued by the RBI Department of Supervision on **31 July 2026** and are designed to require banks to move from ad hoc technology controls to a formal, risk-based framework covering governance, security, resilience, assurance, and third-party oversight. The document applies to **commercial banks** and organizes obligations across board responsibilities, senior management oversight, IT risk management, baseline cybersecurity controls, and ongoing surveillance/assurance.

At the governance level, the directions require each bank’s **Board** to approve the institution’s key IT and cybersecurity policies and to oversee implementation through appropriate **board-level committees** and formal reporting. Banks must establish an IT governance framework, maintain separate or clearly defined **Information Security Policy** and **Cybersecurity Policy**, and create structured oversight through an **IT Strategy Committee of the Board**, **IT Steering Committee**, **Information Security Committee**, and designated senior management roles. The framework also requires the appointment/clear definition of a **Head of IT Function** and a **Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)**, with responsibilities for governance, operational control, security monitoring, and reporting embedded into the management structure. This means banks cannot treat cyber risk as a purely technical matter; it must be governed at the board and senior management levels with documented accountability.

The directions also require banks to maintain a formal **IT and information security risk management framework** with periodic review of IT-related risks, including structured **risk identification, assessment, and documentation**. In practice, this means banks must inventory and assess technology, application, data, infrastructure, access, and third-party risks on an ongoing basis, and keep evidence of how those risks are tracked and treated. The document’s framework is clearly intended to create auditable governance, so compliance teams should expect documentation requirements, board-approved policies, meeting records, risk registers, and management reporting to become essential evidence of compliance.

A major part of the directions is the set of **baseline cybersecurity and resilience requirements**. Banks are required to manage an **inventory of information assets**, implement a **data leak prevention strategy**, put in place **controls for data migration**, prevent the execution of **unauthorised software**, and maintain **physical/environmental security controls** for IT assets and facilities. They must also have controls for **capacity management**, **secure configuration**, **network management and security**, and an **application security life cycle** that covers development, testing, deployment, and maintenance. In addition, banks must maintain **audit logs** with appropriate maintenance, monitoring, and analysis; operate **patch, vulnerability, and change management** processes; enforce **user access control/management**; and apply specific controls for **teleworking**, **secure mail and messaging systems**, and **removable media**. The directions also cover **cryptographic controls**, **straight-through processing**, and **continuous surveillance**, indicating that banks are expected to implement ongoing monitoring and technical safeguards rather than rely only on periodic reviews.

The framework further addresses customer-facing and outsourced-risk issues. Banks must implement an **authentication framework for customers**, meaning customer access and transaction authentication must be built on defined security controls rather than legacy or weak methods. For **third-party arrangements**, the directions impose compliance obligations over vendors and outsourced service providers, signaling that banks remain responsible for risk arising from external technology dependencies. This includes due diligence, contractual controls, security requirements, monitoring, and assurance over outsourced activities. The document also signals an assurance-oriented regime, so banks should expect to be able to demonstrate not just that controls exist, but that they are tested, monitored, and periodically validated.

No specific monetary thresholds or numerical capital-style ratios are stated in the excerpt provided, but the document clearly imposes **mandatory operational and governance requirements** for commercial banks and is intended to be implemented as a formal supervisory framework. The title and structure suggest the directions are meant to be effective from the **2026 issuance date**, with banks needing to align board policies, management structures, and technical controls accordingly. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these directions require a bank-wide, documented cybersecurity and technology risk framework with board oversight, designated accountability, continuous monitoring, and controls across systems, users, data, vendors, and customer authentication.

The Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Concurrent Audit) Directions, 2026 apply to all commercial banks, meaning banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and Local Area Banks, as well as corresponding new banks and the State Bank of India. They take effect immediately upon issuance, and are issued under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The document’s purpose is to formalize concurrent audit as an early-warning and control mechanism intended to shorten the time between a transaction and its independent review, helping detect errors, irregularities, fraud, and other preventive-vigilance issues.

At the governance level, the detailed scope of concurrent audit must be approved by the Audit Committee of the Board (ACB), or by Local Management (LM) in the case of foreign banks. The ACB/LM must also determine the maximum tenure of external concurrent auditors and the remuneration to be paid to them. The document defines an “Audit Firm” broadly to include proprietorship firms, partnership firms, and limited liability partnerships (LLPs).

Because the supplied text cuts off in Chapter II, only these explicit requirements can be confirmed from the excerpt. The available content does not yet disclose the later procedural requirements on audit coverage, auditor appointment, accountability, tenure limits, reporting, or any transition/repeal provisions that may appear further in the full directions. For compliance purposes, however, the clearly stated immediate obligation is that each affected bank must ensure its ACB or LM has formally approved the concurrent audit scope and set the auditor tenure and fee framework under the new RBI directions.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Compliance Function) Directions, 2026** on **July 31, 2026**, and they take effect **immediately upon issuance**. The Directions apply to **commercial banks**; for these purposes RBI also frames the compliance function as part of broader corporate governance and notes that the framework extends to **bank-led financial conglomerates** for **group-wide compliance risk** management. The document states that banks must organize the compliance function and prioritize compliance risk management in a way that is **commensurate with the bank’s size, complexity, risk profile, and organizational structure**, while still meeting the minimum standards set by RBI.

At a governance level, the **Board** is expected to oversee the compliance framework and ensure the bank has an effective compliance policy and sufficient independence, stature, staffing, and resources for the compliance function. **Senior management** is responsible for implementing the board-approved compliance policy and ensuring day-to-day compliance risk management is embedded into operations. The **compliance policy** must be formally established and maintained, and the compliance function is treated as a distinct assurance line alongside **internal audit** and **risk management**. The Directions are explicitly aligned with the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision** framework, adapted for the Indian environment.

The Directions set out requirements on the **scope, structure, staffing, roles and responsibilities, compliance culture, and quality assurance/internal audit** aspects of the compliance function. Banks must define the scope of compliance across the institution and, where relevant, across the group. They must also create a structure and staffing model that is appropriate for the bank’s complexity and risks, and ensure responsibilities are clearly assigned so that compliance monitoring and escalation are effective. The document also requires banks to support a strong compliance culture and to have **quality assurance and internal audit** coverage over the compliance framework.

A dedicated chapter governs the **Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)**, including **appointment**, **authority/stature/independence**, **reporting requirements**, and **responsibilities**. While the excerpt provided does not list the detailed qualification thresholds or reporting line in full, the structure makes clear that the CCO is intended to be a senior, independent compliance leader with defined authority and direct reporting obligations. The Directions also include a chapter on the **use of technology for monitoring**, indicating that banks are expected to use technological tools to support compliance surveillance and controls, and a chapter on **repeal and other provisions** covering repeal/saving, the continued application of other laws, and interpretive rules.

From a legal basis perspective, the RBI states it is issuing these Directions under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and any other enabling provisions/laws, because it considers the Directions necessary and expedient in the public interest. A compliance team should treat this as a mandatory, immediately effective governance framework for commercial banks’ compliance functions, requiring review of the bank’s compliance policy, compliance reporting lines, independence of the function, group-wide compliance arrangements if applicable, and the extent to which monitoring is supported by technology.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Miscellaneous Supervisory Directions, 2026** are a consolidated supervisory framework issued on **31 July 2026** and addressed to **small finance banks (SFBs)**. The document is structured as mandatory directions covering operational, governance, fraud-control, complaint-handling, vigilance, and disclosure obligations; compliance teams should treat it as binding supervisory guidance applicable to SFBs and their relevant officers, systems, and processes.

A major operational requirement is the direction on **access to IT systems**, which requires SFBs to maintain appropriate controls over access to information technology systems used for banking operations, including safeguards around user access, monitoring, and accountability so that access is restricted to authorized persons and auditable. The directions also cover **monitoring of end use of funds**, requiring banks to put in place procedures to verify that funds are used for the purpose for which they were sanctioned, especially where loan conditions or specific utilization requirements apply. Under the **Fair Practices Code – Charging of Interest**, SFBs must ensure that interest charges are transparent and in accordance with disclosed policy, so that customers can understand how interest is applied and there are no arbitrary or undisclosed charges.

The directions contain customer-account compliance obligations for **inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits**, requiring banks to follow RBI-prescribed processes for identifying such accounts, handling them appropriately, and ensuring they are managed in line with applicable reporting and transfer requirements. On **nomination facility**, SFBs must provide and operationalize nomination in the manner required by RBI so that customers can designate nominees and the bank can process death claims or succession-related issues efficiently. These provisions matter for deposit operations, customer-service workflows, and account maintenance controls.

A substantial part of the document is devoted to **fraud prevention measures**, which impose detailed controls across multiple risk areas. These include preventive steps for **frauds involving collusion of bank officials**, controls for **large value frauds**, restrictions and verification requirements for **bulk sanction of retail loans**, safeguards against **frauds involving fake title deeds of property**, and specific precautions for **non-resident accounts**. The directions also require banks to maintain safe custody of critical documents, regulate **accounts opened by employees**, and implement **legal compliance certificates** and **legal compliance audits**. In addition, banks must conduct **forensic scrutiny** where needed, exercise **discretionary powers** prudently, and follow a **best practices code**; these requirements are intended to strengthen internal controls, ensure escalation and review of suspicious activity, and reduce supervisory exposure from weak documentation or inadequate verification.

The document also establishes and details the **Protected Disclosure Scheme**, which covers the **scope and coverage** of protected disclosures, the **procedure for lodging complaints**, and the required **protected disclosure policy** within the bank. Compliance teams should ensure that the internal policy allows employees and other covered persons to make disclosures through the prescribed channels, that confidentiality and non-retaliation protections are built in, and that complaints are tracked and handled in accordance with the scheme. Finally, the **Vigilance** chapter imposes governance and investigative expectations, including the identification of a **Chief of Internal Vigilance**, rules for **appointment**, **tenure**, and **association with sensitive matters**, and the submission of reports and returns for review. It further requires **preventive vigilance** measures, **staff rotation and mandatory leave** in sensitive functions, processes for handling **complaints**, designation of the **investigation agency** for conducting inquiries, review of cases entrusted to external or internal investigators, and action against persons making **false complaints**.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Small Finance Banks - Supervisory Returns” Directions, 2026** apply **only to Small Finance Banks** and take effect **immediately upon issuance** on **July 31, 2026**. The directions are issued under the RBI’s statutory powers and replace/operate alongside the RBI’s supervisory reporting framework for this bank category. For compliance purposes, “supervisory returns” is defined broadly to mean **all periodic or ad hoc data submitted to RBI in any prescribed format, regardless of platform, frequency, or submission mode**, and the directions also define **CIMS** as RBI’s online platform for return submission and related data dissemination.

At the governance level, the document requires the **Board and Senior Management** to treat **data quality risk** as part of the institution’s overall risk management framework. That framework must explicitly cover **both in-house and outsourced data-related risks**, and must include policies and standards addressing **data confidentiality, integrity, availability, and risk management**. The bank must also ensure that its **risk data aggregation capabilities and risk reporting practices are fully documented** and subject to **high standards of validation** aligned with RBI expectations, meaning compliance teams should expect formal documentation, controls, and governance over the data used for regulatory and supervisory reporting.

Although the excerpt provided cuts off before the full list of filing requirements, the structure of the Directions shows that they also contain binding rules on **which supervisory returns apply, the filing timelines, exceptions, penalties, and other instructions**. The key compliance implication from the text available is that Small Finance Banks must maintain a controlled, auditable reporting environment with clear governance over data quality and reporting processes, because the RBI is explicitly tying supervisory reporting compliance to the bank’s broader risk management and data governance obligations.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Statutory Audit Directions, 2026** take effect **immediately upon issuance** and apply to **all Small Finance Banks** for the **appointment and reappointment of Statutory Central Auditors (SCAs) / Statutory Auditors (SAs)**. The document distinguishes between banks that appoint **separate Statutory Branch Auditors (SBAs)**—for which the term **SCA** is used—and all other cases, where the term **SA** applies. These Directions were issued under **Section 30(1A) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and are intended to replace earlier RBI audit guidance for this segment.

From a compliance and governance perspective, the Directions place explicit responsibility on the **Board and senior management** to oversee the statutory audit function, including the auditor appointment process and related governance controls. The Directions are not merely advisory; they create binding requirements for how a bank must select, appoint, and manage its external statutory auditors, and they also govern the audit reporting structure through the **Long Form Audit Report (LFAR)** framework. Because the document is structured around appointment, eligibility, independence, tenure, fees, procedure, and reporting, a compliance team should treat it as the controlling framework for all statutory audit decisions for Small Finance Banks going forward.

The Directions also set out detailed rules in Chapter III for **how many auditors may be appointed, branch coverage expectations, eligibility standards, auditor independence requirements, professional standards, tenure and rotation limits, fee and expense arrangements, and the appointment procedure**. Although the excerpt provided here does not show the numeric thresholds or all specific eligibility criteria, the document clearly signals that these are not discretionary choices: banks must comply with the RBI’s prescribed limits and procedural requirements when filling statutory audit roles. Any future appointment or reappointment must therefore be checked against the RBI’s rules on auditor composition, conflict safeguards, rotation, and the formal approval and selection process.

Chapter IV introduces requirements for the **Long Form Audit Report**, including **procedure and timelines** and distinct responsibilities for both **SCAs** and **SBAs**. The LFAR section indicates that auditors must provide reporting not just on financial statement audit matters, but also on the **objectives, strategy, scope, and coverage** of the audit and the **indicative coverage** expected from the audit teams. In practical terms, this means the bank must ensure its audit engagement letters, internal coordination, and reporting calendar are aligned with RBI expectations, because the Directions contemplate structured audit documentation and deadlines rather than ad hoc reporting.

Finally, Chapter V provides for **repeal and saving**, confirms that the Directions do not override other applicable laws unless expressly stated, and includes interpretation provisions. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that these Directions establish the governing RBI framework for statutory audit of Small Finance Banks from the effective date onward, and any existing audit policies, board procedures, appointment calendars, or auditor contracts should be reviewed and updated immediately to ensure they conform to the new RBI requirements.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026** under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, stating that Small Finance Banks must move away from a primarily transaction-checking audit model and adopt a **Risk Based Internal Audit (RBIA)** approach. The directions are **effective immediately upon issuance** and apply to **all Small Finance Banks**. RBI’s stated purpose is to align internal audit with stronger governance standards and international best practices by requiring assessment of **risk management systems and internal controls**, in addition to selective transaction testing.

For compliance purposes, the key structural change is that each Small Finance Bank must maintain an internal audit function that is designed around **risk assessment, governance oversight, and independence**, rather than only periodic transactional verification. The directions indicate that the bank’s **Board** and **senior management** each have specific roles in overseeing and supporting the internal audit framework, implying that internal audit is not just an operational function but a governance responsibility requiring board-level attention. The document also introduces formal requirements around the **internal audit policy**, **functional independence**, **risk assessment methodology**, **scope of audits**, **communication/reporting**, **performance evaluation**, and the **use of outsourcing** for internal audit activities.

The directions further require a designated **Head of Internal Audit** with defined **authority, stature, independence, tenure, and reporting lines**, signaling that the internal audit head must have sufficient organizational standing and direct reporting access to preserve objectivity. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed chapter text, the table of contents makes clear that banks must implement procedures covering how audit risks are identified and prioritized, how audit findings are communicated, and how the effectiveness of the internal audit function is monitored. The document also includes a chapter on **repeal and saving**, **application of other laws not barred**, and **interpretations**, indicating these directions are intended to operate as the governing RBI framework for SFB internal audit unless inconsistent with other applicable laws or RBI instructions.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026** on **31 July 2026** to create a formal framework for **fraud prevention, early detection, timely reporting to law enforcement agencies (LEAs) and the RBI, and RBI-led dissemination of fraud information** for **small finance banks (SFBs)**. The directions are issued under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and apply specifically to **Small Finance Banks**; they are intended to govern fraud risk management across the bank’s operations, with particular emphasis on credit facilities/loan accounts, reporting processes, and governance.

A key requirement is the establishment of a **governance structure for fraud risk management** within each SFB, with responsibility for oversight of fraud controls, early warning systems, red-flagging of accounts, and reporting obligations. The directions also require SFBs to implement a framework for **Early Warning Signals (EWS)** and **red-flagging of accounts** for both **credit facilities/loan accounts** and other **banking/non-credit transactions**, so that potentially fraudulent activity can be identified early and escalated through formal internal procedures. The document makes clear that fraud management is not limited to post-fact reporting; the bank must maintain systems and governance to detect suspicious patterns and act promptly.

Once a credit facility or loan account is classified as a **red-flagged account**, the directions require a structured process for **further reporting and fraud classification**, including the treatment of such accounts under the general instructions chapter. The framework also requires **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, where relevant, so that the bank does not rely solely on internal assertions when assessing transactions or documents. The directions additionally cover **staff accountability**, specifying that employees involved in fraud or lapses leading to fraud are subject to accountability review, and they provide for **penal measures** and the **treatment of accounts under resolution**, meaning fraud processes continue to apply even where the borrower/account is undergoing restructuring or other resolution measures.

The directions require SFBs to **report frauds to law enforcement agencies** and to **report incidents of fraud to the RBI** in the prescribed manner. RBI will maintain and use a **Central Fraud Registry**, and the directions set out the **modalities for reporting incidents of fraud** as well as the **closure of fraud cases once reported**, so banks must ensure completeness, timeliness, and accurate status updates. A separate chapter addresses **cheque-related frauds**, which must also be reported to both **LEAs and the RBI** under the specified process. The document further includes other compliance obligations such as **legal audit of title documents for large-value loan accounts**, treatment of accounts already classified as fraud and later **sold to other lenders or Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs)**, and the **role of auditors** in fraud-risk oversight. It also requires reporting of incidents involving **theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery**. Finally, the directions contain **repeal and saving provisions**, state that other applicable laws are not barred, and reserve interpretive authority, so SFBs should treat these directions as the controlling RBI fraud-risk framework for their operations from the effective date of the circular.

rows.summary:
This RBI direction, titled **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026**, was issued on **July 31, 2026** by the Department of Supervision and **takes effect immediately upon issuance**. It is legally grounded in the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and **Chapter IV of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, and it applies specifically to **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)**. The scope is broad: it covers **all digital payment products and services offered by an SFB to customers** for both **financial and non-financial transactions**, including **balance enquiry, PIN set/change, mobile banking registration, OTP generation, mini-statements, transaction status checks, and dispute/grievance raising**, whether these services are provided directly by the bank or through a system operated by the **RBI** or by an **RBI-authorised Payment System Operator (PSO)**. The associated **IT assets**—including the applications, systems, and infrastructure supporting those services—are also within scope.

The Directions are organized around security governance and operational controls, starting with a requirement for **board-approved policies** and general security governance. Although the excerpt provided only begins the definitions section, the table of contents shows that the document imposes requirements across **general controls**, **internet banking security**, **mobile payments application security**, and **card payment security**, as well as **fraud risk management, reconciliation, customer protection, awareness, and grievance redressal**. For compliance purposes, this means SFBs should assume RBI expects formal oversight by the board and management over the security of all digital payment channels, not just a technology team-level control environment.

The document also makes clear that its terminology is intended to align, unless otherwise stated, with the **Financial Stability Board (FSB) Cyber Lexicon**, and it begins defining core security concepts such as **availability** and **confidentiality**. Even though the excerpt cuts off before the full list of definitions and substantive control requirements, the structure indicates that the full Directions will set mandatory control expectations for the security lifecycle of digital payment services, including authentication, fraud prevention, reconciliation, and user protection obligations. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these are **mandatory RBI Directions for all SFB digital payment activity** and they are **already in force as of July 31, 2026**, so the bank must assess all covered digital payment products, channels, and supporting IT systems against the complete text of the Directions and implement any required controls immediately.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks (Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026** establish a comprehensive, mandatory governance and control framework for **small finance banks (SFBs)** covering board oversight, IT governance, cybersecurity, resilience, third-party controls, and operational assurance. The document is structured as binding directions issued by the RBI’s Department of Supervision and is dated **July 31, 2026**; the table of contents shows the directions are organized into chapters on applicability, board responsibilities, IT governance, IT/security risk management, and baseline cybersecurity/resilience controls. Although the excerpt provided does not reproduce the operative clauses in full, it clearly indicates the directions require SFBs to put in place formal policies, committees, management structures, and controls across the full technology lifecycle.

At the governance level, the framework requires **board-approved policies** and **board-level committees** to oversee cybersecurity and technology risk. It specifically contemplates an **IT Strategy Committee of the Board**, senior management oversight through an **IT Steering Committee**, an **Information Security Committee**, a designated **Head of IT Function**, and a **Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)**. The bank must maintain an **IT governance framework**, an **information security policy**, and a **cybersecurity policy**, and these functions are expected to cover IT project management, IT architecture, and IT services management. In other words, compliance is not just about having technical safeguards; the bank must establish a documented governance model with clear accountability at both board and executive levels.

The directions also require an ongoing **IT and information security risk management framework**. The table of contents shows obligations to **periodically review IT-related risks** and to perform **risk identification, assessment, and documentation**, which means banks must have a repeatable process for identifying technology exposures and recording how they are managed. The framework is intended to address resilience and assurance, so the bank must be able to demonstrate that technology risks are systematically tracked rather than handled ad hoc. This would be relevant for internal audit, compliance testing, and supervisory inspections.

A major portion of the document sets out **baseline cybersecurity and resilience requirements** that appear to apply across core operational areas. The listed control areas include **inventory management of information assets**, **data leak prevention**, **controls over data migration**, **prevention of unauthorized software execution**, **physical and environmental controls**, **capacity management**, **secure configuration**, **network management and security**, **application security life cycle controls**, **audit log maintenance/monitoring/analysis**, **patch/vulnerability/change management**, **user access control/management**, **teleworking controls**, **customer authentication framework**, **secure mail and messaging systems**, **removable media controls**, **third-party arrangements**, **cryptographic controls**, **straight-through processing**, and **continuous surveillance**. For a compliance team, this signals that the RBI expects end-to-end preventive, detective, and corrective controls across infrastructure, applications, users, and vendors, not just perimeter cybersecurity.

From a practical compliance perspective, the excerpt indicates that SFBs will need to ensure they have formal procedures and evidence for: maintaining accurate inventories of assets and software; restricting or monitoring data transfers and migrations; enforcing secure builds and configuration baselines; monitoring logs and vulnerabilities; controlling privileged and user access; governing remote work; and setting security requirements for third parties and outsourced services. The mention of **customer authentication**, **straight-through processing**, and **continuous surveillance** suggests the framework also extends into transaction security and real-time monitoring of suspicious or abnormal activity. Because the table of contents includes dedicated sections for each of these topics, the final directions likely impose detailed, auditable controls rather than general principles.

The excerpt does **not** include the detailed operative text, so the specific implementation deadlines, numerical thresholds, exemption criteria, or phased compliance dates are not visible here. However, the title, structure, and chapter headings make clear that this is a **mandatory supervisory framework** for SFBs that will require board-level approval, designated owners, documented policies, periodic risk review, and concrete technical and operational safeguards. A compliance officer should treat this as a full-spectrum technology risk regime affecting the bank’s governance, security operations, vendor management, and customer-facing transaction controls.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Concurrent Audit) Directions, 2026 apply to all Small Finance Banks and take effect immediately upon issuance, replacing the prior framework on this subject. The purpose of the directions is to require a concurrent audit system that shortens the time between a transaction and its independent review, with the stated goal of strengthening internal accounting controls, acting as an early warning mechanism for serious errors and irregularities, and helping prevent fraud and other misconduct.

At the governance level, the Audit Committee of the Board (ACB) must approve the detailed scope of the concurrent audit, and it is also responsible for setting both the maximum tenure and the remuneration of external concurrent auditors. The ACB must review the effectiveness of the concurrent audit system and the performance of the concurrent auditors every year, and it must take whatever steps are needed to strengthen the system based on that review. This means banks need a documented board-level governance process for both defining the audit scope and monitoring whether the program is working as intended.

The document defines “Audit Firm” broadly to include a proprietorship firm, partnership firm, or LLP. Other terms not specifically defined in the directions are to be interpreted according to the relevant RBI, banking, or company law frameworks, or as used in commercial parlance where applicable. Compliance teams should therefore expect the directions to operate alongside existing statutory and RBI definitions rather than creating a wholly separate terminology set.

Although the excerpt provided cuts off before the full coverage and procedural rules in Chapter III, the directions clearly establish that the concurrent audit function is mandatory for SFBs, must be overseen by the ACB, and must be periodically assessed for effectiveness. Because the directions are stated to come into force immediately, banks should treat them as effective from July 31, 2026 and ensure their current concurrent audit policies, committee approvals, auditor tenure arrangements, and remuneration approvals are aligned without delay.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Compliance Function) Directions, 2026**, effective **immediately upon issuance on July 31, 2026**, and they apply to **all Small Finance Banks (SFBs)**. The Directions set minimum standards for the compliance function as part of a bank’s corporate governance and overall assurance framework, alongside internal audit and risk management, and they are intended to align with Basel Committee principles while being adapted to the Indian environment; the RBI also states that the framework extends to **bank-led Financial Conglomerates** for group-wide compliance risk management. Although the Directions are prescriptive minimum standards, each bank is expected to organize and prioritize its compliance function in a manner proportionate to its **size, complexity, risk profile, and organizational structure**.

A central requirement is that each SFB must maintain a **formal compliance framework** covering the bank’s own operations and, where relevant, **group-wide compliance** across the financial conglomerate. The document makes clear that compliance is not merely a control activity but a board-level governance matter: the **Board** and **senior management** are expected to oversee, approve, and support the compliance function, including the bank’s compliance policy and the resourcing and authority needed to make it effective. The compliance function must have a defined **scope, structure, staffing model, roles and responsibilities, compliance culture, and quality assurance/internal audit support**, with the organization tailored to the bank’s risk and complexity rather than being purely symbolic or nominal.

The Directions require appointment of a **Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)** with sufficient authority, stature, and independence to operate effectively. The CCO’s role includes reporting on compliance matters, supporting adherence to regulatory requirements, and ensuring the compliance framework functions as intended; the Directions also specify reporting requirements and set expectations around the CCO’s direct access and independence from line management pressures. This means banks must ensure the compliance function is not subordinated in a way that could undermine objective oversight or timely escalation of issues.

The Directions also address the **use of technology for monitoring**, indicating that banks should use appropriate technological tools to support compliance monitoring and oversight rather than relying solely on manual controls. Finally, the document includes a chapter on **repeal and other provisions**, indicating that prior inconsistent directions are repealed/superseded while preserving valid actions already taken, and clarifying that the new Directions do not bar application of other laws. For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that the bank should review its current compliance governance, board policies, CCO appointment/authority, staffing, group-wide oversight, and technology-enabled monitoring arrangements to confirm they meet the new RBI baseline from the date of issuance.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026** on **July 31, 2026** under RBI/DoS/2026-27/434, addressed to payments banks and covering a set of supervisory obligations across IT access controls, dormant/unclaimed accounts, nomination facilities, fraud controls, protected disclosures, vigilance, and related compliance processes. The document is organized into chapters on **access to IT systems**, **inoperative accounts/unclaimed deposits**, **nomination**, **fraud prevention measures**, **protected disclosure scheme**, **vigilance**, and **repeal/saving and interpretation**, indicating that these are not merely guidance notes but supervisory directions intended to be operationally implemented by covered institutions.

For **IT system access**, the directions require payments banks to control access to their IT systems in a manner consistent with supervisory expectations, meaning access governance, authorization, and control over who can use core banking and related systems is a compliance obligation. The chapter on **inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits** imposes duties on banks to identify, monitor, and handle accounts and balances that have remained inactive or unclaimed, which is relevant for customer communication, account status monitoring, and transfer/escheat handling where applicable. The **nomination facility** chapter requires compliance with RBI expectations that customers be offered and processed through the nomination framework, so banks need to maintain procedures for capturing, updating, and evidencing nominations and related customer instructions.

A substantial portion of the document addresses **fraud prevention measures**, including frauds arising from **collusion of bank officials**, **large-value frauds**, **safe custody of critical documents**, **accounts opened by employees**, **legal compliance certificates**, **legal compliance audits**, **forensic scrutiny**, **exercise of discretionary power**, and a **best practices code in banks**, followed by “other instructions.” For compliance teams, this means banks must have internal controls to prevent staff-facilitated fraud, protections around sensitive documents and employee-linked accounts, formal compliance sign-offs and audits, procedures for forensic review when fraud is suspected, and controls around management discretion to prevent misuse. The reference to large-value frauds signals additional scrutiny and escalation expectations for material incidents, though the excerpt does not state a numeric threshold in the visible text.

The **Protected Disclosure Scheme** chapter establishes a whistleblowing framework covering scope, complaint-filing procedure, and the bank’s protected disclosure policy. Compliance teams should treat this as requiring a secure, non-retaliatory mechanism for employees or other eligible persons to report wrongdoing, along with defined intake and handling steps so complaints can be reviewed while preserving protection for the complainant. This is paired with the **vigilance** chapter, which sets out a vigilance structure for the bank, including the concept of a **Chief of Internal Vigilance**, how that role is appointed and for what tenure, restrictions on association with sensitive matters, and the need to submit reports/returns for review.

The vigilance provisions also require **preventive vigilance**, **staff rotation**, and **mandatory leave** in certain cases to reduce fraud and conflict risks, plus formal treatment of complaints and a defined **investigation agency** arrangement for conducting inquiries. The directions further address **review of cases entrusted to investigating agencies**, **action against persons making false complaints**, and **liaison with agencies**, meaning the bank must be prepared to coordinate with internal and external investigators, manage allegations responsibly, and deter malicious reporting. Finally, the last chapter provides for **repeal and saving**, states that other applicable laws are not barred, and includes interpretation provisions, so the compliance team should assume these directions operate alongside—not in place of—other statutory and regulatory obligations.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks - Supervisory Returns Directions, 2026** apply specifically to **Payments Banks** and take effect **immediately upon issuance**. The Directions are issued under **Section 27 and Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and related RBI powers, and they replace the prior supervisory-return framework for this category through the repeal-and-saving provisions in Chapter IV. RBI defines “**Supervisory Returns**” broadly to cover **all periodic and ad-hoc data submitted to RBI in formats prescribed from time to time**, regardless of the technology platform, frequency, or submission mode, and identifies **CIMS (Centralised Information Management System)** as RBI’s online platform for return submission and data dissemination.

From a governance perspective, the Directions impose explicit board- and senior-management-level responsibility for **identifying, assessing, and managing data quality risk** within the bank’s overall risk management framework. The framework must cover both **in-house and outsourced** risks tied to data-related processes and must include policies addressing **data confidentiality, integrity, availability, and risk management**. The bank must also ensure that its **risk data aggregation capabilities and risk reporting practices are fully documented** and subject to **high standards of validation** aligned with the bank’s other independent risk-management reviews.

The document then sets out mandatory rules for filing supervisory returns. Payments Banks must follow RBI-prescribed operational guidelines, comply with the list of applicable returns and submission timelines, and observe any exceptions and other instructions specified by RBI. Although the excerpt provided does not reproduce the full schedule of returns or due dates, it makes clear that compliance is driven by the RBI-prescribed formats and timelines in force from time to time, and that the obligation applies to both **routine periodic filings and ad-hoc submissions**.

The Directions also include enforcement and procedural provisions. Chapter III expressly contemplates **penalties** for non-compliance and provides for additional instructions, while Chapter IV addresses **repeal and saving**, confirms that the Directions do not bar the application of other laws, and reserves RBI’s interpretive authority. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that a Payments Bank must have a controlled, well-documented, and validated data-governance and reporting process, with clear board oversight, because RBI is placing supervisory-return accuracy, integrity, and timely submission at the center of ongoing supervisory compliance.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026, issued under Section 30(1A) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, take effect immediately upon issuance and apply to all Payments Banks for the appointment or reappointment of their statutory auditors. The Directions distinguish between “Statutory Central Auditors” (SCAs) for banks that also appoint separate Statutory Branch Auditors (SBAs) and “Statutory Auditors” (SAs) in all other cases. From a compliance standpoint, this means Payments Banks must align their audit appointment framework, governance, and audit reporting processes with these RBI Directions as soon as they are issued.

The document begins with preliminary provisions and definitions, indicating that the detailed requirements will govern how auditors are selected, rotated, paid, and supervised, as well as how audit reports are structured and submitted. Although the excerpt provided cuts off before the full definitions section, the table of contents shows that the Directions also cover governance and oversight responsibilities of the Board and senior management, so compliance teams should expect explicit accountability on audit oversight at the bank’s top governance level. The inclusion of a dedicated governance chapter indicates the RBI expects audit appointment and audit-quality oversight to be managed formally, not merely as a procurement or finance function.

The Directions also contain a full chapter on “Guidelines for Appointment,” which will set the binding rules on the number of SCAs/SAs a Payments Bank may appoint, the eligibility criteria those auditors must satisfy, independence requirements, applicable professional standards, auditor tenure and rotation, audit fees and expense treatment, and the appointment procedure. For compliance purposes, this is significant because it suggests the RBI is prescribing not only who may be appointed but also how long they may serve and the process by which appointments must be made or renewed. The document therefore affects audit committee actions, board approvals, vendor onboarding, and any conflict-of-interest screening or independence certification process used for auditors.

A separate chapter on the Long Form Audit Report (LFAR) requires procedures and timelines for both SCAs and SBAs, with specific objectives, strategy, scope, and indicative coverage laid out for each. This means Payments Banks will need to ensure their auditors deliver more than a standard financial statement audit opinion; they must also produce a detailed LFAR covering prescribed areas within the RBI-mandated schedule. The presence of separate LFAR provisions for SCAs and SBAs indicates that banks using branch auditors will need additional coordination and documentation controls to ensure branch-level findings are captured and escalated appropriately.

The Directions also include repeal/saving language and an “application of other laws not barred” provision, which means the new framework is intended to coexist with, and not automatically override, other applicable legal and regulatory requirements unless expressly inconsistent. In practical terms, compliance teams should treat this as a specialized RBI audit regime that supplements general banking, accounting, and corporate law obligations. Since the excerpt ends before the operational details and annexures, the main immediate compliance takeaway is that Payments Banks must prepare for RBI-controlled auditor appointment, rotation, independence, and reporting requirements effective immediately, with more detailed procedural obligations likely contained in the later chapters and annexes.

rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued on 31 July 2026 under section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, applies specifically to all Payments Banks and takes effect immediately upon issuance. It replaces the prior transaction-centric internal audit approach with a mandatory Risk Based Internal Audit (RBIA) framework, meaning the audit function must focus not only on sample transaction testing but also on assessing the bank’s risk management systems and internal controls in line with current governance standards and international best practices.  

From a governance standpoint, the Board is required to establish, approve, and oversee the internal audit framework, while senior management must implement it and ensure that the internal audit function is adequately resourced and independent. The document’s structure shows that the Board and management have explicit responsibilities for policy approval, oversight, risk assessment, scope setting, communication of findings, performance evaluation, and outsourcing controls, so compliance teams should expect a formalized governance chain rather than an informal audit setup.  

The Directions require each Payments Bank to maintain an internal audit policy built around RBIA, with functional independence of the audit function, a documented risk assessment process, a defined audit scope, formal reporting/communication of audit results, and performance evaluation of the internal audit function. The document also addresses outsourcing of internal audit-related activities, indicating that any outsourcing must be governed within the RBIA framework rather than allowing unrestricted delegation of core audit responsibilities.  

A separate chapter is devoted to the Head of Internal Audit, indicating that the position must have sufficient authority, stature, and independence, with a specified tenure and a defined reporting line. For compliance purposes, this signals that the bank must designate a senior, independent internal audit leader who can report appropriately and operate without management interference, ensuring the audit function has direct access and credibility within the organization.  

The Directions also include repeal/saving and interpretation provisions, meaning any earlier internal-audit-related instructions inconsistent with these Directions are intended to be displaced to the extent applicable, while other laws and RBI requirements continue to apply unless expressly barred. Because the document excerpt provided does not include the detailed numbered requirements in Chapters II–V, a compliance officer should treat the immediately effective date and the mandatory shift to RBIA for Payments Banks as the central obligations, and then map the final operational controls once the full text is reviewed.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks (Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026** establish a mandatory framework for **preventing fraud, detecting it early, and reporting fraud incidents promptly** to both law enforcement agencies and RBI, with RBI also using the information for dissemination and supervisory purposes. These Directions are issued under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and related enabling powers, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance**; they apply specifically to **all Payments Banks (PBs)**.

For compliance purposes, the core change is that PBs must maintain a formal **fraud risk management governance structure** and a **system for early warning signals and red-flagging of accounts**, so suspicious activity can be identified before losses deepen. The framework is intended not just for post-fraud reporting but for **prevention and early detection**, and it extends to the handling of fraud-related information sharing with RBI’s **Central Fraud Registry (CFR)**, which is described as a **web-based searchable database maintained by RBI**. The directions also require PBs to have procedures for reporting incidents of fraud to RBI, closing reported fraud cases properly, and separately reporting **cheque-related frauds** and incidents involving **theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery**.

The Directions further impose **general instructions** covering the use of **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, plus rules on **staff accountability** and **penal measures** where fraud control failures or misconduct are involved. They also set out responsibilities for **auditors**, indicating that fraud-risk oversight is not limited to internal control functions and must be reflected in external assurance and supervisory review as well. In substance, compliance teams at payments banks should expect obligations to cover the entire fraud lifecycle: governance, monitoring, detection, escalation, external reporting, record closure, and audit oversight.

The document’s stated purpose is to ensure **timely reporting to law enforcement agencies and RBI** and to enable **dissemination of fraud information by RBI**, so any PB subject to these Directions should verify that its incident-response, fraud-monitoring, reporting, and board/management oversight processes are aligned to this RBI framework from the date of issuance.

The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls Directions, 2026** apply specifically to **all Payments Banks** and cover the banks’ **digital payment products and services**, whether provided directly by the bank or through an RBI-operated system or a system operated by an RBI-authorised Payment System Operator (PSO). The Directions are issued under RBI’s powers under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and **Chapter IV of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**.

The Directions are titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Supervisory Directions, 2026** and **take effect immediately upon issuance**. The document is structured around board governance, general security controls, internet banking controls, mobile payments application controls, card payment controls, and repeal/saving provisions, indicating that compliance is not limited to one channel but extends across the full digital payments ecosystem of a payments bank. Although the excerpt provided does not yet detail the substantive control requirements chapter-by-chapter, it makes clear that the Directions establish a supervisory framework for **security risk governance, authentication, fraud risk management, reconciliation, customer protection, awareness, and grievance redressal** in relation to covered digital payment activities.

A compliance team should note that the document expressly treats the covered services and the associated technical environment as part of the regulated scope, so obligations will likely attach not only to customer-facing features but also to the supporting infrastructure and control environment. The definitions section begins by adopting terms from the **Financial Stability Board (FSB) Cyber Lexicon** unless otherwise stated, including key cyber-risk concepts such as **availability** and **confidentiality**, signaling that the directions are intended to be interpreted using a cyber-security and operational-risk lens. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Payments Banks - Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026”** sets a comprehensive, mandatory technology-risk and cybersecurity regime for **payments banks**. It is issued by the RBI Department of Supervision and is dated **July 31, 2026**; the document is intended to replace or formalize the minimum governance, security, resilience, and assurance expectations that payments banks must implement across their technology stack and third-party arrangements. The directions cover board oversight, senior-management responsibilities, IT governance, risk management, baseline cybersecurity controls, logging/monitoring, patch and vulnerability management, customer authentication, secure communications, crypto controls, straight-through processing, and continuous surveillance.

A major focus is **board-level accountability**. Payments banks must have **board-approved policies** for IT, information security, cybersecurity, risk management, and resilience, and the board is expected to oversee these through dedicated committees and formal reporting. The framework requires clear assignment of roles across the **Board, IT Strategy Committee, senior management, IT Steering Committee, Information Security Committee, Head of IT, and Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)**, with the CISO having a defined assurance and security leadership role rather than a purely operational one. The document also requires structured IT governance, IT project management, architecture control, and IT services management, meaning technology decisions are not left to ad hoc operational teams.

The directions impose a **formal IT and information-security risk management process**. Payments banks must periodically review IT-related risks, maintain an IT/security risk management framework, and document risk identification and assessment in a way that supports ongoing oversight and auditability. The document goes beyond general risk statements and requires specific baseline cybersecurity and resilience controls, including **inventory management of information assets, data leak prevention, controls over data migration, prevention of unauthorized software execution, physical/environmental safeguards, capacity management, secure configuration, network security, application security life-cycle controls, audit-log monitoring, patch/vulnerability/change management, user-access controls, teleworking controls, customer authentication, secure mail/messaging, removable-media controls, third-party controls, cryptographic controls, straight-through processing controls, and continuous surveillance**.

The third-party provisions are especially important for compliance teams: any outsourcing or external technology arrangement must be governed through formal controls, not treated as a substitute for the bank’s own accountability. The framework makes clear that security obligations continue even when services are delivered by vendors, cloud providers, or other outsourced parties, so contracts, oversight, monitoring, and assurance mechanisms must be in place. The presence of requirements on **secure configuration, logging, patching, access management, and continuous surveillance** indicates an expectation of active, ongoing defense and detection rather than a one-time implementation exercise.

Because the text provided is only the table of contents and introductory header, **no specific effective date, grace period, numerical threshold, or deadline is visible in the excerpt** beyond the document date itself (**July 31, 2026**). For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these directions are a broad and detailed supervisory framework for payments banks’ technology and cybersecurity programs, and they likely require a gap assessment against existing policies, board governance, security tooling, monitoring practices, and vendor-management controls to determine what must be updated to meet RBI expectations.

The ACB is also responsible for deciding the **maximum tenure** for external concurrent auditors and the **remuneration** paid to them. In addition, the ACB must conduct an **annual review** of both the effectiveness of the Concurrent Audit System and the performance of the concurrent auditors, and must take corrective action where needed to strengthen the system.

The document defines **“Audit Firm”** broadly to include a **proprietorship firm, partnership firm, or LLP**. It also states that any terms not specifically defined will have the meanings given in the RBI Act, the Banking Regulation Act, the Companies Act, RBI regulations, the RBI Glossary of Terms, or commercial usage as applicable. No specific numerical thresholds or dates other than the immediate commencement date are provided in the introductory sections shown.

Because the excerpt cuts off before the detailed “Coverage” and later chapters, a compliance team should expect further operational requirements on audit scope, auditor appointment, accountability, tenure, remuneration, reporting, and any repeal/saving provisions in the remaining text. From what is visible, the key compliance obligations already imposed are board-level approval of audit scope, governance over auditor tenure and pay, and annual effectiveness review of the entire concurrent audit function.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks - Compliance Function Directions, 2026** establish mandatory minimum standards for the **compliance function of all Payments Banks** in India, effective **immediately upon issuance on July 31, 2026**. The RBI frames compliance as a core part of corporate governance and assurance, alongside internal audit and risk management, and states that although the directions set minimum standards, each bank must organize its compliance framework in a way that is proportionate to its **size, complexity, risk profile, and organizational structure**. The directions are issued under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and apply specifically to **Payments Banks**, referred to collectively as “banks” and individually as “bank.”

For governance, the document requires the **Board** to approve and oversee the compliance policy and ensure the bank has an effective compliance function, while **senior management** must implement the policy and maintain an effective compliance culture. The bank must adopt a formal **compliance policy** that covers the structure, roles, responsibilities, escalation procedures, staffing, reporting lines, monitoring, and governance of the compliance function. The directions also extend the compliance expectation to **bank-led Financial Conglomerates**, requiring group-wide compliance risk management where relevant.

The document sets out requirements on the **scope, structure, staffing, and responsibilities** of the compliance function, including clear segregation of duties and defined accountability across the organization. It also requires the bank to maintain a **compliance culture**, meaning compliance obligations should be embedded in business processes and staff conduct, not treated as a standalone checklist. In addition, the bank must have **quality assurance** over the compliance function and integrate compliance oversight with **internal audit** arrangements to ensure ongoing effectiveness.

A significant governance requirement is the appointment of a **Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)**. The CCO must have appropriate **authority, stature, independence, and access to the Board/senior management**, and the directions prescribe reporting requirements and specific responsibilities for that role. The bank must ensure the CCO’s position is sufficiently senior and independent to supervise compliance risk and raise issues without undue interference, and the CCO is expected to be a central point for compliance reporting and oversight.

The directions also require the use of **technology for monitoring compliance**, indicating that banks should employ technological tools to help identify, track, and manage compliance risk and obligations more effectively. Finally, the document includes **repeal and saving provisions**, states that other applicable laws are **not barred** by these directions, and provides interpretation provisions to clarify how the directions should be read and applied.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Local Area Banks (Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026** under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** (and other enabling powers), addressed to **local area banks (LABs)**. The document is a supervisory directions compendium that brings together requirements on fair-practice interest charging, treatment of inoperative/unclaimed accounts, fraud prevention, protected disclosures, vigilance, network management, and cyber-security controls for third-party ATM switch application service providers. It appears to be a binding supervisory framework for LABs, with the stated date of issuance being **31 July 2026**.

For compliance purposes, the most immediate takeaway from the excerpt is that LABs must follow RBI requirements on **charging interest fairly**, and on **identifying, handling, and reporting inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits** in accordance with the specific chapter-level directions referenced in the table of contents. The directions also impose a detailed **fraud-prevention framework**, including controls for frauds involving **collusion of bank officials**, **large-value frauds**, **fake title deeds of property**, **safe custody of critical documents**, and **accounts opened by employees**; these topics indicate that LABs must maintain formal preventive controls, document custody safeguards, and employee-account monitoring processes. In addition, the RBI has included a **Protected Disclosure Scheme**, which means banks must have a mechanism for receiving and processing complaints/whistleblower disclosures under a protected reporting framework, along with a protected disclosure policy and a defined complaint procedure.

The document also contains extensive **vigilance requirements**, including rules on the **Chief of Internal Vigilance** (appointment, tenure, involvement in sensitive matters, and reporting/review of returns), as well as **preventive vigilance**, **staff rotation**, and **mandatory leave**. LABs will need to maintain complaint-handling and investigation arrangements, including the use of an **investigation agency** where applicable, periodic **review of cases entrusted to investigating agencies**, procedures for action against persons making **false complaints**, and liaison with external agencies. These obligations suggest a formal internal-control and disciplinary architecture that compliance, HR, audit, and vigilance teams would need to coordinate and evidence through policies, records, and periodic reporting.

The directions further address **network management** and, importantly, **cyber-security controls for third-party ATM switch application service providers**, indicating that LABs that outsource ATM switching functions must ensure appropriate cyber controls, oversight, and governance over those vendors. The final chapter also includes **repeal and saving** provisions, an **application-of-other-laws-not-barred** clause, and an **interpretation** section, which means the new directions are intended to sit alongside other applicable legal/regulatory requirements rather than replace them entirely. Because the excerpt provided is largely the table of contents and introductory citation, it does not show the chapter-by-chapter operational thresholds or specific technical parameters, but it clearly establishes that LABs are subject to a comprehensive RBI compliance regime across deposits, fraud, vigilance, and outsourced technology oversight, effective from the date of the 2026 directions.

The table of contents also shows separate chapters on **filing of supervisory returns**, **timelines**, **exceptions**, **penalties**, and **other instructions**, indicating that the final document includes operational submission requirements and consequences for non-compliance, though those specific provisions are not contained in the excerpt provided.

Compliance teams should therefore treat the issuance date as the operative effective date for any new appointment or reappointment decisions, and ensure the bank’s audit governance, auditor due diligence, and LFAR reporting processes are aligned to the new RBI framework.  

Only the opening portion of the document is visible in the provided text, so the specific numerical limits, eligibility thresholds, rotation periods, fee rules, or detailed LFAR content are not available here; however, the structure shows those substantive requirements are covered in the later chapters and annexes and would need to be reviewed in full before finalizing any audit appointment or compliance implementation plan.

The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026** on **July 31, 2026**, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance**. They apply specifically to **Local Area Banks (LABs)**, which are referred to collectively as “banks” in the directions. The core policy change is that LABs are required to move away from a purely transaction-checking internal audit model and instead adopt a **Risk Based Internal Audit (RBIA)** framework that evaluates risk management systems and internal controls, while still performing selective transaction testing.

From a compliance and governance standpoint, the document establishes that internal audit is a key part of the bank’s internal control and risk management architecture, and it is being mandated under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and other enabling RBI powers. The directions are structured to require board-level oversight, senior management execution, a formal RBIA policy, functional independence of the audit function, periodic risk assessment, defined audit scope and communication standards, performance evaluation of the internal audit function, and rules for outsourcing. Although the excerpt shown stops before the detailed chapter provisions, the table of contents and introduction make clear that the full directions also require appointment, authority, tenure, and reporting-line arrangements for the **Head of Internal Audit**, plus repeal/saving and interpretive provisions.

The board is expected to have oversight responsibility, while senior management must operationalize the framework, including controls around independence, scope setting, reporting, and evaluation. Because the directions are effective immediately, banks should treat implementation as an immediate compliance obligation rather than a future-dated transition requirement.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (LABs) – Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026**, issued on **July 31, 2026** and cited as **RBI/DoS/2026-27/446** / **DoS.CO.FMG.40/23.04.001/2026-27**, establish a mandatory fraud-risk framework for LABs covering **prevention, early detection, and timely reporting** of fraud to both **law enforcement agencies (LEAs)** and the **RBI**, along with RBI-led dissemination of fraud information. The Directions are issued under the RBI’s powers under **Sections 21 and 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and apply specifically to **Local Area Banks**. They replace or consolidate prior RBI instructions on this subject through a **repeal-and-saving** framework, while preserving actions already taken under earlier directions.

At a governance level, LABs must maintain a formal **fraud risk management governance structure** and an **early warning signals (EWS)/red-flagging framework** to detect potential fraud in time. The document distinguishes between (i) **credit facilities/loan accounts** and (ii) **other banking / non-credit related transactions**, and requires LABs to build processes that identify suspicious patterns and escalate them promptly. Once a credit facility or loan account is classified as a **red-flagged account**, the bank must follow the prescribed fraud-reporting and escalation process, and the Directions also address how accounts under resolution are to be treated to avoid inappropriate delay or dilution of fraud action.

The Directions require LABs to **report fraud incidents to law enforcement agencies** and separately **report frauds to the Reserve Bank of India**, including via the **Central Fraud Registry**. They also set out the **modalities for reporting incidents of fraud** and the **closure process for fraud cases already reported**, meaning banks must ensure their internal case-management and regulatory-reporting workflows are aligned so that reports are accurate, timely, and capable of being updated or closed in accordance with RBI procedure. A separate chapter specifically covers **cheque-related frauds**, requiring reporting to both LEAs and RBI under the dedicated framework, rather than treating them as ordinary operational incidents.

The Directions also impose several related compliance obligations beyond core reporting: LABs must carry out a **legal audit of title documents** in respect of **large value loan accounts**, and they must apply the prescribed treatment when accounts classified as **fraud** are **sold to other lenders or asset reconstruction companies (ARCs)** so that fraud tagging and regulatory consequences are not lost in transfer. The document also sets out the **role of auditors**, indicating that audit functions are part of the fraud-control architecture and not merely a retrospective review. Additionally, there are specific provisions for reporting **theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery**, reflecting that not all loss events are handled identically and that these incidents have their own reporting expectations.

Finally, the Directions include **staff accountability and penal measures**, meaning individual employee involvement, negligence, or lapses in fraud handling may trigger internal accountability actions, and the bank must have procedures to enforce consequences where required. The document also states that its provisions coexist with **other applicable laws**, so compliance with these Directions does not displace criminal, civil, or other regulatory obligations arising under separate statutes. For a compliance team, the key operational takeaway is that LABs need a documented, end-to-end fraud framework spanning detection, internal escalation, regulatory and police reporting, account tagging/classification controls, audit verification, and closure tracking, all implemented under the 2026 RBI Directions.
