rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Concurrent Audit Directions, 2026** apply to **all Local Area Banks** and take effect **immediately upon issuance**. RBI issues them under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and related enabling powers, with the stated objective of ensuring that concurrent audit serves as an early-warning control mechanism to detect serious errors, irregularities, fraudulent transactions, and other control failures quickly.

For governance, the **Audit Committee of the Board (ACB)** must **approve the detailed scope** of the concurrent audit. The ACB is also required to set both **the maximum tenure for external concurrent auditors** and **their remuneration**, and it must **review the effectiveness of the concurrent audit system and the auditors’ performance annually**, taking whatever corrective or strengthening measures are needed. This makes the ACB directly responsible for the design, oversight, and periodic reassessment of the audit function.

The document defines an **“Audit Firm”** broadly to include a **proprietorship firm, partnership firm, or LLP**. It also states that unless otherwise defined, terms carry the meanings given under the **RBI Act, 1934**, **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, **Companies Act, 2013**, any statutory modification or re-enactment, other RBI regulations, RBI’s Glossary of Terms, or ordinary commercial usage as applicable.

Although the excerpt provided cuts off at the start of Chapter III’s “Coverage” section, the operative requirements visible already establish that Local Area Banks must have a board-approved concurrent audit framework, that external concurrent auditors are subject to ACB-determined tenure and pay, and that the ACB must conduct an annual effectiveness review. A compliance team should therefore treat these directions as immediately binding on LABs and ensure the bank’s governance documents, audit charter, and ACB processes reflect these responsibilities.

These Directions apply specifically to **Local Area Banks (LABs)** and are effective **immediately upon issuance**. RBI states that the compliance function is a core part of corporate governance and an assurance function alongside internal audit and risk management, and that the framework is aligned with the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision** but adapted for the Indian environment, including **bank-led financial conglomerates** for group-wide compliance risk management.

The core requirement is that each LAB must maintain a **formal compliance function** with governance, staffing, independence, monitoring, and reporting arrangements that are **commensurate with the bank’s size, complexity, risk profile, and organisational structure**. The Board is responsible for oversight of the compliance framework, senior management must implement it, and the bank must have a **compliance policy** and defined compliance structure with clear responsibilities. The document indicates dedicated chapters on the **scope, structure, staffing, roles and responsibilities, compliance culture, quality assurance, and internal audit interface**, meaning compliance cannot be treated as an informal or purely control-room activity; it must be embedded in governance and operational processes.

A key named requirement is the appointment of a **Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)**, with specific provisions on **appointment, authority, stature, independence, reporting lines, and responsibilities**. The Directions also include a chapter on the **use of technology for monitoring**, indicating that banks are expected to employ technology-enabled compliance monitoring rather than relying solely on manual review. Although the excerpt does not reproduce the detailed definitions or chapter rules, the table of contents shows that the Directions also address **group-wide compliance**, implying obligations may extend beyond the standalone bank to entities within a bank-led group where applicable.

The document also contains a **repeal and saving** section, a statement that other laws are **not barred**, and an **interpretations** section, which means these Directions are intended to operate alongside existing legal/regulatory requirements rather than replace them entirely. In compliance terms, LABs should treat this as a new minimum supervisory framework requiring immediate gap assessment of current governance, policy documentation, CCO status, reporting lines, staffing adequacy, monitoring tools, and board/senior management oversight to ensure alignment with RBI’s prescribed compliance-function standards.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks - Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) – Miscellaneous Supervisory Directions, 2026** were issued on **31 July 2026** and **take effect immediately upon issuance**. They apply to **all Regional Rural Banks** as defined under **section 5(ja) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The directions are issued under **section 35A read with section 51 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and related enabling powers.

The main substantive requirement is that every RRB must **review and, where needed, correct its lending and interest-charging practices** to ensure fairness and transparency. RBI specifically flags as unfair: charging interest **from the date of sanction or loan agreement instead of actual disbursement**; for cheque disbursements, charging interest **from the date the cheque is issued even if handed over later**; charging EMIs on the **sanctioned amount rather than the actual amount disbursed without borrower knowledge or consent**; failing to communicate any **changes to the amortisation schedule in the Key Facts Statement (KFS)** when a loan is disbursed in parts; charging **full-month interest when disbursement or repayment occurs partway through a month** instead of only for the period outstanding; and taking **advance instalments while still charging interest on the full loan amount**. RBI states these and similar non-standard interest practices are inconsistent with fair treatment of customers, so RRBs must make whatever **corrective action and system-level changes** are necessary to stop them.

The directions also indicate that RRBs **may use online account transfers instead of cheques for loan disbursal**, which is presented as an acceptable operational alternative to reduce the risk of the cheque-based interest issue. In the fraud-related provision, where there is a **prima facie case against loan-dealing officials**, the RRB must initiate action under **Central Vigilance Commission guidelines** for placing those officers in the **list of officers with doubtful integrity**, and this must be done **in consultation with the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)**. The final chapter also repeals prior directions to the extent specified while preserving actions already taken under them, and clarifies that these directions do not bar application of other laws or RBI powers, with interpretive issues to be resolved in accordance with the stated RBI/legal framework.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) – Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026** establish a mandatory framework for **prevention, early detection, red-flagging, investigation support, and timely reporting of fraud incidents** by RRBs to **law enforcement agencies (LEAs)** and **NABARD**, with NABARD also expected to disseminate relevant fraud information. The directions are issued under RBI’s powers under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance** (dated **July 31, 2026**). They apply to **Regional Rural Banks**, and the document is structured to cover governance, early warning signals, red-flagged accounts, fraud reporting, treatment of resolved accounts, interactions with third parties/professionals, staff accountability, auditor roles, and reporting of theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery.  

A key compliance requirement is that RRBs must maintain a **board-level or equivalent governance structure** for fraud risk management, with defined internal responsibilities for monitoring, escalation, and reporting. The framework specifically requires banks to implement **Early Warning Signal (EWS)** mechanisms and a **Red Flagging of Accounts (RFA)** process for both **credit facilities/loan accounts** and **other banking/non-credit transactions**, so institutions must be able to detect suspicious conduct early, classify accounts appropriately, and trigger investigative and reporting actions without delay. The directions also require **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, where those parties are used in connection with fraud-risk related work, which means banks cannot rely solely on internal assertions when validating facts relevant to fraud detection or reporting.  

For accounts identified as suspicious or fraudulent, the directions require a formal process to **classify a credit facility or loan account as a red-flagged account** and to **report fraud** in accordance with the prescribed framework. They also address **staff accountability and penal measures**, meaning employee involvement, negligence, or complicity in fraud-related events must be examined and may lead to disciplinary or other punitive action under the bank’s internal and regulatory processes. Where an account is under **resolution**, the directions provide specific treatment rules so that fraud-risk handling does not stop simply because recovery or restructuring is underway; compliance teams should assume fraud monitoring and reporting obligations continue notwithstanding resolution status.  

The directions also impose obligations on **reporting frauds to LEAs** and on **reporting incidents of fraud** more generally, including a separate chapter on **cheque-related frauds** that must be reported both to **law enforcement agencies** and to **NABARD**. Additional instructions cover the **legal audit of title documents for large-value loan accounts**, reflecting heightened due diligence expectations for collateral-backed exposures. If an account already classified as fraud is **sold to another lender or to an asset reconstruction company**, the document specifies how that account must continue to be treated, so sale/assignment does not eliminate fraud classification consequences. Finally, the directions recognize the role of **auditors** in fraud oversight and require reporting of **theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery** incidents as distinct events, indicating the bank’s incident-reporting obligations extend beyond classic fraud to other criminal losses as well.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Miscellaneous Supervisory Directions, 2026** take effect **immediately upon issuance** and apply to **all Urban Co-operative Banks**, defined as Primary Co-operative Banks under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 as applicable to co-operative societies. A key applicability carve-out is for **Chapter III (Prompt Corrective Action Framework)**: it applies only to **Tier 2, Tier 3, and Tier 4 UCBs**, **excluding banks currently under All Inclusive Directions (AID)**; **Tier 1 UCBs are not covered by Chapter III**, though they remain under enhanced supervisory monitoring, and **UCBs under AID continue under their existing AID conditions** until they exit AID, after which RBI will provide a suitable transition period before Chapter III applies.

The directions are issued under **Section 35-A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and supersede prior directions to the extent covered by the new framework (with repeal/saving provisions in Chapter VIII). The document consolidates several supervisory topics into one set of directions, including **core banking solution implementation**, the **prompt corrective action framework**, **fair practices in charging interest**, **nomination facility requirements**, **fraud prevention measures**, and **vigilance-related requirements**. For compliance teams, the practical significance is that the bank must map its obligations against these chapters based on its **tier classification** and whether it is under **AID**, because obligations differ materially by category.

Chapter III is the only part whose applicability is explicitly limited by tier, so compliance officers should verify whether the institution is in **Tier 2/3/4** and not under AID to determine whether the new PCA triggers, escalation, and supervisory response requirements apply. The direction also signals that **Tier 1 UCBs are not exempt from supervision**, but will be managed through the existing supervisory framework rather than the new Chapter III PCA provisions. Since the document states that the directions are effective on issuance, institutions should treat the requirements as immediately operative unless a specific chapter or provision elsewhere provides a transition arrangement.

If you want, I can also turn the full text into a **chapter-by-chapter compliance checklist** for UCB operations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
These Directions, issued by the Reserve Bank of India under Section 27 and Section 35-A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and related enabling provisions, are titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026** and **take effect immediately upon issuance** on **31 July 2026**. They apply to **all Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, meaning Primary Co-operative Banks as defined under Section 5(ccv) read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The Directions define **“Supervisory Returns”** broadly to include **all periodic and ad-hoc data** submitted to RBI in the prescribed formats, regardless of the technology platform, submission frequency, or mode of submission, and define **CIMS** as RBI’s online platform for return submission and related data dissemination.

From a governance perspective, the document requires the **Board and Senior Management** of each UCB to explicitly include **identification, assessment, and management of data quality risks** as part of the bank’s overall risk management framework. It also places responsibility on the bank to maintain appropriate **data architecture and IT infrastructure** to support accurate supervisory reporting, and to ensure **accuracy and integrity in reporting**. In practical compliance terms, this means supervisory return submission is not treated as a purely operational task; it is a governance and control obligation requiring board-level oversight, management accountability, and robust reporting controls.

The Directions establish that UCBs must follow RBI-prescribed **operational guidelines** for filing supervisory returns, and they must comply with the **list of applicable returns** and associated **timelines** set out in the Directions and any related RBI instructions. The document indicates that there are specific provisions for **exceptions**, **penalties**, and **other instructions**, which means compliance teams must monitor whether a particular return is required, whether any exemption or special treatment applies, and whether delays, omissions, or inaccuracies could trigger consequences. Because “supervisory returns” includes both periodic and ad-hoc submissions, the obligation is ongoing and extends beyond routine scheduled reporting to any RBI-requested data submission.

The Directions also contain a **repeal and saving** framework, meaning prior inconsistent provisions are superseded to the extent covered by the new Directions, while certain prior actions or instructions may remain effective where preserved. They further state that the Directions do **not bar application of other laws**, so UCBs must continue to comply with other applicable legal and regulatory requirements in parallel. For compliance officers, the key operational takeaway is that the bank should ensure its reporting governance, systems, and escalation processes are aligned immediately with the new RBI framework, with particular attention to data quality controls, board oversight, and adherence to RBI-prescribed submission requirements through CIMS or other applicable channels.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued on 31 July 2026 and effective immediately upon issuance, applies to Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) as defined under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and governs the appointment and reappointment of their statutory auditors. It distinguishes between UCBs that appoint separate Statutory Branch Auditors, where the lead auditor is referred to as a Statutory Central Auditor (SCA), and all other UCBs, where the term Statutory Auditor (SA) applies. The document is issued under section 30(1A) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, read with section 56 of the Act as applicable to co-operative societies, and states that it supersedes prior RBI directions on this subject subject to saving provisions, while leaving other laws and interpretations not barred by the directions applicable.

The document’s scope is broader than just appointment mechanics: it establishes governance and oversight expectations for the board and senior management, and sets out eligibility, independence, professional standards, tenure/rotation, audit fees and expenses, and the appointment procedure for auditors. The compliance team should note that the directions are intended to govern both initial appointment and reappointment of auditors, so annual or periodic auditor renewal decisions must be aligned with these requirements. The text also defines relevant institution categories such as All India Financial Institutions, including NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, EXIM Bank, and NaBFID, as well as other banking and co-operative banking terms used throughout the directions.

Although the excerpt provided cuts off before the substantive clauses and Annexures, the table of contents shows that the operative requirements are organized around: board/senior management responsibilities; the permissible number of SCAs/SAs and branch coverage; auditor eligibility criteria; independence requirements; professional standards; tenure and rotation rules; fee and expense rules; and the formal appointment process. For compliance purposes, this means the bank should expect explicit restrictions and procedural steps around how many audit firms may be engaged, which firms are eligible, how independence is assessed, how long auditors may serve before rotation is required, and what governance approvals/documentation are needed for appointment or reappointment. Because the Directions took effect immediately on issuance, UCBs should treat the rules as currently binding from 31 July 2026 onward and ensure audit-planning, board approvals, and audit committee processes are aligned without delay.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026** on **31 July 2026** under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, to establish a harmonized, risk-based internal audit framework for **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**. The stated purpose is to strengthen internal audit as the **third line of defence** and ensure the Board and senior management receive assurance on the adequacy and effectiveness of internal controls, risk management, and governance. These Directions replace fragmented practices with a uniform set of requirements covering governance, audit design, independence, staffing, reporting, outsourcing, and audit coverage.

The Directions apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks**, with the internal audit function required to be structured around a **Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA)** framework. UCBs must have a formal internal audit policy approved by the Board, and the policy must define the objectives, scope, authority, independence safeguards, risk assessment process, annual audit planning, compliance monitoring, and any outsourcing arrangements. The Board remains responsible for overseeing the internal audit function, while senior management must ensure implementation, adequate staffing, and timely remediation of audit observations.

A key requirement is that internal audit must be **independent, sufficiently empowered, and not be assigned operational responsibilities that could compromise objectivity**. The Head of Internal Audit must have appropriate stature, direct reporting access, and independence from the activities being audited, with a defined reporting line to the Board/Audit Committee as specified in the Directions. The audit plan must be risk-based, derived from periodic risk assessments, and should focus audit resources on higher-risk areas rather than relying solely on fixed-cycle reviews.

The Directions also require UCBs to establish a clear system for **monitoring compliance with audit findings**, including tracking of exceptions, overdue rectifications, and reporting of unresolved issues to governance bodies. Where internal audit work is outsourced, the bank remains fully responsible for the quality, independence, confidentiality, and oversight of the outsourced function, and outsourcing cannot dilute management or Board accountability. The document further prescribes periodicity and minimum coverage expectations for inspection/internal audit activities, permits **special audits** where needed, and includes repeal/saving provisions along with interpretative rules for applying the Directions alongside other laws and RBI instructions.

In practical compliance terms, UCBs should expect to review and, if necessary, redesign their internal audit governance, risk assessment methodology, annual audit planning, reporting structure, and follow-up mechanisms to ensure alignment with these Directions by their effective date and any implementation timeline specified in the operative chapters.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026** establish a mandatory fraud-risk framework for UCBs aimed at **prevention, early detection, prompt reporting to law enforcement agencies (LEAs), and reporting/dissemination to the RBI**. The directions are issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and related enabling powers, and they apply specifically to **urban co-operative banks**; the document is organized around governance, early warning signals, fraud reporting, cheque frauds, audit requirements, and treatment of fraud cases.

For compliance purposes, the most important operational requirement is that UCBs must maintain a **formal fraud risk management governance structure** and an **early warning signal (EWS) framework** to detect suspicious activity in both **credit facilities/loan accounts** and **other banking or non-credit transactions**. The bank must have procedures to identify and investigate indications of fraudulent activity, and it must obtain **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, where relevant. The directions also address **staff accountability** and **penal measures** where employee conduct is implicated, and they provide specific treatment rules for **accounts under resolution** that are relevant to fraud classification and reporting.

The directions require UCBs to report fraud incidents to both **LEAs and the RBI** using prescribed modalities, and they also create a separate reporting framework for **cheque-related frauds** to LEAs and RBI. They additionally require banks to report **cases of theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery**, indicating that the framework is broader than classic credit fraud and covers physical loss/criminal incidents that may affect banking operations. The document also includes instructions on **closure of fraud cases reported to RBI**, meaning banks must follow a defined process before a reported case can be treated as closed in regulatory reporting.

Several other compliance points are expressly addressed: UCBs must carry out a **legal audit of title documents for large-value loan accounts**, and there are specific instructions for the **treatment of accounts classified as fraud and then sold to other lenders or asset reconstruction companies (ARCs)** so that the fraud classification and related obligations are not lost in transfer. The directions also describe the **role of auditors**, indicating that audit functions are expected to support fraud detection and compliance verification rather than being purely retrospective. A repeal-and-saving section is included, along with a statement that the directions do not bar the application of other laws, so UCBs must comply with these directions **in addition to** any applicable criminal, banking, or regulatory obligations.

The excerpt provided does **not include the detailed effective date, transition deadlines, numeric thresholds, or reporting timelines**, but the document title and issuance date indicate it is the **2026 RBI framework** and is intended to be immediately relevant to UCB fraud governance once in force. A compliance team should therefore review the full text for any exact timelines, thresholds, and form requirements embedded in the chapter provisions, especially those governing EWS triggers, fraud classification, LEA/RBI reporting, cheque fraud reporting, and closure procedures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026** were issued on **31 July 2026** and take effect **immediately upon issuance**. They apply to **all Urban Co-operative Banks / Primary Co-operative Banks** as defined under **Section 5(ccv) read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and cover **digital payment products and services** offered by the UCB whether delivered directly by the bank or through RBI-operated systems or systems operated by RBI-authorised **Payment System Operators (PSOs)**. The scope explicitly includes both **financial and non-financial transactions**, such as **balance enquiry, PIN set/change, mobile banking registration, OTP generation, mini-statements, transaction status checks, and customer dispute/grievance raising**, along with the related IT assets supporting those services, including applications, systems, and infrastructure.

At a high level, the directions create a mandatory security framework for UCB digital payment activity and are organized around board oversight, governance and risk controls, application security, authentication, fraud management, reconciliation, customer protection, and channel-specific controls for internet banking, mobile apps, and card payments. The document states that the RBI is issuing these requirements under its authority in **Section 35-A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, and other enabling laws, indicating they are binding supervisory directions rather than advisory guidance.

The opening provisions also make clear that the directions incorporate technical definitions, largely drawn from the **Financial Stability Board (FSB) Cyber Lexicon**, unless otherwise specified. Although the excerpt provided does not yet include the detailed control prescriptions in later chapters, the table of contents shows that the regulations will require UCBs to implement formal **board-approved policies**, **general security controls**, an **application security lifecycle**, an **authentication framework**, **fraud risk management**, **reconciliation mechanisms**, and **customer protection/awareness/grievance redressal procedures**, plus distinct controls for **internet banking**, **mobile payment applications**, and **card payment security**.

From a compliance perspective, the key immediate takeaway is that this is a **bank-wide mandatory security control regime for UCB digital payment offerings**, effective immediately, with applicability tied to whether the bank offers any of the covered digital payment services or related transaction-support functions. UCBs should treat the issuance date as the start of the compliance clock and assess all impacted products, channels, outsourced or platform-dependent payment flows, and supporting IT assets against the eventual chapter-by-chapter requirements of the Directions.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular is a consolidation for all Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) of the RBI’s instructions on exposure norms and statutory/other restrictions, updated to capture all guidance issued up to **March 31, 2025**. The RBI expressly states that it **does not introduce any new instructions or guidelines**; it only compiles existing requirements, replacing the earlier consolidated circular dated **January 16, 2024**. Compliance teams should therefore treat this as the operative consolidated reference for exposure limits, prohibited/regulated lending, and related restrictions, but not as a source of new policy changes.

On the exposure framework, UCBs must continue to set limits for exposure to **individual borrowers, group borrowers, specific sectors, and unsecured advances** as a prudential risk-management measure. “Exposure” is defined broadly to include both **credit exposure** and **investment exposure in Non-SLR securities**. Credit exposure includes **funded and non-funded limits**, underwriting and similar commitments, **equipment leasing and hire purchase financing**, and **ad hoc limits** granted for contingencies; it excludes loans and advances secured by the bank’s **own term deposits**. For exposure computation, the **sanctioned amount or outstanding amount, whichever is higher**, is to be counted, except in the case of **fully drawn term loans with no redrawal possibility**, where outstanding may be used; for **non-funded limits**, **100% of the limit or outstanding, whichever is higher**, must be included. In consortium, multiple banking, or syndication arrangements, each bank’s share remains subject to the relevant **single-borrower/group exposure** limits.

For determining exposure ceilings, Tier-I capital is to be taken **as on March 31 of the preceding financial year**, using the same Tier-I capital definition applicable under the RBI’s **Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy** for UCBs. The circular also notes that investment exposure in **Non-SLR securities** must follow **Chapter VII of the Master Direction on Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio of UCBs dated April 1, 2023**, as amended from time to time. The circular’s structure also confirms that UCBs remain subject to longstanding chapters on **real estate exposure**, **inter-bank exposure**, **placement/acceptance of deposits**, **ceiling on unsecured advances**, and multiple **statutory/regulatory restrictions**.

The statutory and regulatory restriction topics specifically carried forward for UCB compliance include: loans and advances to **directors and their relatives**; the **maximum ceiling on advances to nominal members**; advances against **fixed deposit receipts issued by other banks**; salary earners’ primary urban co-operative banks making advances against **term deposits of non-members**; **bridge loans/interim finance**; loans and advances against **shares, debentures, and bonds**; bank finance against **preference shares and long-term subordinated deposits**; finance to **NBFCs**; financing of **equipment leasing and hire purchase**; financing for **agricultural activities**; loans to **Self Help Groups (SHGs) / Joint Liability Groups (JLGs)**; and restrictions on advances to **defaulters of statutory dues**. Since the circular is explicitly only a consolidation, compliance action is to verify that existing internal policies, credit approval controls, and exposure monitoring systems already reflect these instructions as updated through **March 31, 2025**.

Attached is the revised Master Circular, updated to reflect all instructions issued upto March 31, 2025 on the above matter, as listed in the Appendix. It may be noted that this Master Circular only consolidates all instructions on the above matter issued up to March 31, 2025 and does not contain any new instructions/guidelines. Yours faithfully (Vaibhav Chaturvedi) Chief General Manager Encl.: as above Withdrawn 2 Master Circular on Management of Advances – UCBs Contents Sl No. Particulars 1 Introduction 2 Working Capital Requirements 3 Loan System for delivery of bank credit 4 Credit Administration 5 Reporting / Exchange of credit information 6 Prudential Guidelines on Restructuring of Advances 7 Specific Lending Activities 8 Discounting/Rediscounting of Bills by UCBs 9 Loans to Self Help Groups (SHGs) / Joint Liability Groups (JLGs) 10 Relief measures to be extended in areas affected by natural calamities Annex - 1 Key Facts Statement Annex - 2 Guidelines on Valuation of Properties – Empanelment of Valuers Annex - 3 Safeguards-Advances against pledge of Gold/Silver ornaments Annex - 4 Guidelines for Relief Measures by UCBs in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities Appendix - List of circulars consolidated in the Master Circular Withdrawn 3 1. Introduction Primary (Urban) Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are expected to lay down, with the approval of their boards, transparent policies and guidelines for credit dispensation, in respect of each broad category of economic activity, keeping in view the credit exposure norms and various other guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India from time to time. In order to ensure that the loan policy of the UCB reflects approved internal risk appetite and remains in alignment with the extant regulations, it shall be reviewed by the Board at least once in a financial year. 2. Working Capital Requirements 2.1 The assessment of working capital requirement of borrowers, other than micro and small enterprises, requiring fund based working capital limits up to ₹1 crore and micro and small enterprises requiring fund based working capital limits up to ₹5 crore from the banking system may be made on the basis of their projected annual turnover. 2.2 In accordance with these guidelines, the working capital requirement is to be assessed at 25% of the projected turnover to be shared between the borrower and the UCB, viz. borrower contributing 5% of the turnover as Net Working Capital (NWC) and UCB providing finance at a minimum of 20% of the turnover. rows.summary:
This Master Circular is a **consolidation-only update** for **all Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, issued on **April 1, 2025**, replacing the earlier consolidated circular dated **July 25, 2023**. The RBI expressly states that it **does not introduce any new instructions or guidelines**; it only brings together all instructions on management of advances issued up to **March 31, 2025** (with the consolidated list of source circulars provided in the Appendix). For compliance purposes, the operative obligation is that UCBs should continue to follow the underlying RBI instructions now compiled in this Master Circular.

On credit policy governance, UCBs are expected to have **board-approved, transparent policies and guidelines for credit dispensation** for each broad economic activity, aligned with RBI exposure norms and other RBI directions. The bank’s loan policy must reflect the board-approved internal risk appetite and be **reviewed by the Board at least once every financial year**.

For **working capital assessment**, the circular restates that for borrowers **other than micro and small enterprises (MSEs)** seeking **fund-based working capital up to ₹1 crore**, and for **MSEs seeking fund-based working capital up to ₹5 crore**, the requirement may be assessed on the basis of **projected annual turnover**. The prescribed working capital need is **25% of projected turnover**, with the borrower contributing **5% as Net Working Capital (NWC)** and the UCB financing at least **20% of turnover**; “projected turnover” is to be interpreted as **gross sales including excise duty**. UCBs may choose either the turnover method or the traditional method, but if the traditional production/processing-cycle method yields a higher credit need, that higher amount may be sanctioned; however, the borrower must still be financed to at least the **minimum 20% of projected annual turnover**. For borrowers whose working capital limits exceed those thresholds, UCBs may assess needs using their own credit judgment through the turnover method, cash-budgeting method, or another suitable method, but **book-debt finance for inland credit sales must not exceed 75% of the sanctioned limit**, with the remaining **25%** intended to be financed through bills to encourage bill financing.

The circular also reiterates that drawals against sanctioned limits must be subject to normal safeguards, including **drawing power controls**, and UCBs must ensure funds are used for the intended purpose. Banks must obtain **regular and timely monthly statements of stocks, receivables, etc.**, and carry out **periodic verification against physical stocks** by bank officials. The content visible in the document is truncated before the rest of the loan-system and subsequent sections, but the stated purpose of the document is to compile the RBI’s current instructions on management of advances for UCBs as of **March 31, 2025**.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular consolidates RBI instructions on housing finance for Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) as of March 31, 2025, and replaces the prior master circular dated April 2, 2024; it explicitly states that it does **not introduce any new instructions or guidelines**. It is addressed to all UCBs and continues the framework under which UCBs may extend housing finance from their own resources, with the stated policy intent of supporting housing access, especially for weaker sections and priority-sector needs.

The circular confirms the categories of borrowers UCBs may finance: individuals, co-operative/group housing societies, housing boards undertaking schemes for EWS/LIG/MIG, and owners of houses/flats seeking extension, upgradation, or major repairs. The permissible purposes include construction or purchase of houses/flats, repairs/alterations/additions, housing and hostel schemes for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, slum clearance financing either directly to slum dwellers against Government guarantee or through statutory boards, and financing of ancillary institutions/centres and shopping/market facilities that are part of and necessary for a housing project or township.

For individual borrowers, the circular sets tier-wise maximum loan amounts per dwelling unit, subject to existing single-borrower exposure limits: Tier 1 UCBs may lend up to ₹60 lakh, Tier 2 up to ₹1.40 crore, Tier 3 up to ₹2 crore, and Tier 4 up to ₹3 crore. UCBs retain discretion, subject to Board-approved commercial judgment and prudential considerations, to decide borrower eligibility, margins, and loan sanctioning based on repayment capacity; the circular also references prudential exposure limits for single borrowers/connected groups as part of the governing framework.

The document also indicates that the instructions cover the full set of housing-loan terms and controls relevant to compliance, including interest rate provisions, foreclosure/prepayment policy, floating-rate reset rules for EMI-based loans, penal charges, Key Facts Statements, security requirements, loan tenure, graduated instalments, aggregate housing-finance limits, supplementary finance, lending to housing boards and builders/contractors, priority-sector treatment, precautions, and National Building Code considerations. For a compliance team, the key operational point is that this 2025 circular is a consolidation document effective April 1, 2025 for the updated compilation, not a policy change instrument; therefore, institutions should align internal policies to the consolidated instructions and verify they are applying the current tier-wise ceiling, exposure limits, and permitted end-uses exactly as stated.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular for Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs), issued by RBI on April 1, 2025 as RBI/2025-26/14 (DOR.STR.REC.10/21.04.048/2025-26), is an updated consolidation of all prudential instructions on income recognition, asset classification, provisioning, and related matters for advances, replacing/refreshing the prior consolidated circular dated April 2, 2024. RBI explicitly states that this circular does **not introduce any new instructions or guidelines**; it only compiles instructions issued up to March 31, 2025, with the list of consolidated circulars in Annex 9.  

For compliance purposes, the document restates the core prudential framework: income recognition must be objective and based on actual record of recovery, not judgment; asset classification must be based on objective criteria applied consistently; and provisioning must follow the asset classification. It also notes that where State Co-operative Societies Acts, related rules, or other statutory enactments impose stricter requirements, those stricter requirements continue to apply. The circular therefore functions as the controlling compliance reference for UCBs on these topics as of March 31, 2025.  

The NPA rules are reaffirmed in substance. A loan/advance becomes a non-performing asset when interest and/or principal remains overdue for more than 90 days for term loans; when an overdraft/cash credit account (including OD/CC-type facilities, even if not for business purposes, and accounts where only interest credits are received) is “out of order”; when bills purchased/discounted remain overdue for more than 90 days; and when direct agricultural advances are governed by the separate overdue norms in Annex 1. The circular also continues the borrower-wise NPA treatment principle rather than facility-wise treatment, meaning classification must be applied at the borrower level in the cases covered by the RBI rules.  

The document’s other substantive compliance themes, as consolidated in the table of contents and annexes, include: treatment of accounts becoming NPAs and reversal of accrued income; recognition of income on investments, shares, and bonds when such instruments are treated as NPAs; partial recovery of NPAs; interest application rules; provisioning norms for loans and advances; special provisioning for retirement benefits and fraud accounts; transfer of loan exposures; and multiple special cases such as agricultural advances affected by natural calamities, housing loans to staff, government-guaranteed credit facilities, project financing, restructuring of advances, and loans under rehabilitation packages. It also includes operational support materials such as the proforma, illustrative accounting entries, FAQs, restructuring concepts/report formats/illustrations, and project-implementation asset classification guidance, all of which compliance teams should treat as the consolidated RBI reference set for internal policy, accounting, classification, reporting, and provisioning controls.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular for Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs), issued on 1 April 2025, is a consolidation of all instructions on guarantees, co-acceptances, and letters of credit (LCs) updated through 31 March 2025; RBI explicitly states that it does **not** introduce any new instructions or guidelines, but republishes the existing requirements in one place. For guarantees, UCBs are generally expected to provide **financial guarantees rather than performance guarantees**, although scheduled banks may issue performance guarantees with due caution; guarantees should ordinarily be short-term and **must not exceed 10 years** in maturity. The total outstanding guarantee exposure at any time is capped at **10% of the bank’s total owned resources** (paid-up capital, reserves, and deposits), and within that overall limit, **unsecured guarantees** are further constrained to the **lower of 25% of owned funds (paid-up capital + reserves) or 25% of total guarantees outstanding**. Banks are instructed to prefer **secured guarantees**, meaning guarantees backed by assets (including cash margin) whose market value is never less than the contingent liability, or fully covered by counter-guarantees from the Central/State Government, public sector financial institutions, or insurance companies.

The circular also requires banks to avoid concentration of unsecured guarantee commitments to particular customers or trades, and the Board of Directors must set reasonable limits on unsecured guarantees for any single constituent so that exposure does not become excessive relative to the bank’s overall unsecured-guarantee book or the constituent’s shareholding in the bank. Deferred payment guarantees should normally be backed by adequate tangible security or acceptable counter-guarantees from government/public sector/insurance entities and other banks; where such guarantees are issued for a borrower’s capital asset acquisition, the bank must ensure that **total credit facilities plus the proposed deferred payment guarantees remain within the applicable exposure ceilings**. The document further indicates that proposals for deferred payment guarantees must be properly examined before issuance, reflecting a need for internal scrutiny and exposure-limit compliance.

Although the excerpt shown cuts off before the later sections, the table of contents makes clear that the circular also covers rules and safeguards for **guarantees on commodities under selective credit controls, immediate settlement of invoked bank guarantees, delayed production of certified court judgments, correspondence with government departments, co-acceptance of bills, and opening/payment of LCs**, plus common rules on **credit exposure norms and statutory/other restrictions on non-fund-based limits**. From a compliance perspective, the key operational takeaway is that UCBs must verify that all guarantee and LC activity stays within the RBI’s exposure ceilings, security/counter-guarantee requirements, maturity limits, and board-approved internal concentration controls, and should treat this circular as the current consolidated reference for all such requirements through 31 March 2025.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular, dated April 1, 2025, consolidates and updates all instructions on prudential norms for capital adequacy for Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) through March 31, 2025, replacing the prior circular dated April 1, 2024. It applies to all UCBs and restates the statutory minimum capital requirement under Section 11 of the Banking Regulation Act (AACS): a co-operative bank may not commence or carry on banking business unless paid-up capital plus reserves is at least ₹1 lakh, and RBI continues to prescribe entry-point capital norms for new Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks under Section 22(3)(d).

The circular tightens and standardizes net worth requirements by bank tier. UCBs operating in a single district (Tier 1) must maintain minimum net worth of ₹2 crore, while all other UCBs (all other tiers) must maintain minimum net worth of ₹5 crore. Banks that do not currently meet the applicable minimum must do so in phases: at least 50% of the required amount by March 31, 2026, and the full minimum by March 31, 2028. “Net worth” is to be calculated in accordance with Annex 1.

Capital adequacy requirements are also restated by tier. Tier 1 UCBs must maintain a minimum Capital to Risk Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 9% on an ongoing basis, while Tier 2 to Tier 4 UCBs must maintain 12% CRAR on an ongoing basis. For Tier 2 to Tier 4 banks that are not yet at 12%, RBI requires a phased build-up: at least 10% by March 31, 2024, 11% by March 31, 2025, and 12% by March 31, 2026. Eligible capital for CRAR consists of Tier I and Tier II capital, with Tier II capital capped at 100% of Tier I capital for compliance purposes, and risk weights are to be applied as set out in Annex 2.

The circular also begins the detailed definition of Tier I capital, which includes paid-up share capital from regular voting members, contributions from associate/nominal members where permitted by bye-laws and subject to withdrawal restrictions, non-refundable admission fees from nominal and associate members held separately as reserves, Perpetual Non-Cumulative Preference Shares (PNCPS) that meet Annex 3 requirements, and free reserves from audited accounts. The document’s structure shows additional operative provisions on market risk capital, share-linking to borrowings, refund of share capital, investor protection for regulatory capital instruments, and periodic returns, with forms and detailed issuance rules contained in the annexes.

rows.title: Master Circular on Board of Directors - UCBs
rows.desc: RBI/2025-26/07 DoR.HGG.GOV.No.1/18.10.010/2025-26 April 1, 2025 The Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer All Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks Dear Sir/Madam, Master Circular on Board of Directors - UCBs Please refer to our Master Circular DoR.HGG.GOV.No.1/18.10.010/2024-25 dated April 1, 2024 on the captioned subject (available at RBI website www.rbi.org.in). The enclosed Master Circular consolidates and updates all the instructions / guidelines on the subject issued till date. Yours faithfully (Manoranjan Padhy) Chief General Manager Withdrawn - 2 - Master Circular - Board of Directors - UCBs S.No. Content Page no. 1 Constitution of Board of Directors 3-4 2 Role of Directors 4-6 3 Committees of the Board 7-8 4 Calendar of Reviews – Matters to be placed before the Board of Directors 8 5 Donations to trusts and institutions where directors or their relatives hold position or are interested 8-9 6 Payment of fees and allowances to Directors 9 7 Annex 1 - Recommendation made by the Madhava Das Committee on Urban Co-operative Banks with regard to Board of Directors 10-12 8 Annex 2 - Reviews to be submitted to the Board of Directors of primary (urban) co-operative banks 13-15 9 Appendix – List of Circulars consolidated in the Master Circular 16-17 Withdrawn - 3 - Master Circular - Board of Directors – UCBs 1. Constitution of Board of Directors 1.1 Primary (urban) co-operative banks (UCBs or banks) have been functioning under the regulation and supervision of Reserve Bank of India (Reserve Bank or RBI) in terms of the powers vested in it inter alia under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (BR Act) and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (RBI Act). 1.2 The directors on the boards of UCBs must be knowledgeable and persons of high integrity. To ensure professionalism in the Board, banks should, at all times, have at least two professional directors, i.e., persons with suitable banking experience (at middle/senior management level) or with relevant professional qualification in the fields of law, accountancy or finance. Banks should also have a suitable provision in their byelaws to ensure this. However, these instructions would not be insisted upon in case of Salary Earners' Banks in view of the nature of their membership. 1.3 UCBs (other than those having deposit size less than Rs.100 crore and salary earners’ banks) are also required to constitute a Board of Management (BoM) to facilitate professional management and focused attention to their banking-related activities, by making suitable amendments to their bye-laws, in accordance with the guidelines contained in RBI circular DoR(PCB).BPD.Cir.No.8/12.05.002/2019-20 dated December 31, 2019. 1.4 Since the directors are elected from amongst the members (except co-opted and nominated directors), the persons who are not eligible for admission even as members cannot become directors of UCBs. In particular, persons engaged in money lending, financing and investment activities, either in individual capacity or as proprietor/partner/employee/director of any concern as also those convicted of any criminal offences including moral turpitude are ineligible in terms of clause b (ii) of the model by-law no.9 and/or the provisions contained in the co-operative societies law concerned. Besides, certain eligibility/qualification/disqualification criteria for becoming director in a UCB are also prescribed in the BR Act and the co-operative laws concerned. Withdrawn - 4 - 1.5 The recommendations made by the “Committee on Urban Co-operative Banks”, headed by Shri Madhava Das, regarding the Board of Directors of UCBs and recommended by the Reserve Bank for adoption by the banks are given in Annex 1. 1.6 It was observed during the course of supervisory reviews that some of the UCBs have adopted the practice of creating honorary designations (remunerated or otherwise) / conferring titles at Board level, such as Chairman Emeritus, Group Chairman, etc., which are not recognised in applicable statutes or regulations. While such positions/titles may be indicative of certain privileges/rights for the incumbent to access all board materials and participate in board/committee meetings, enforcing liability or obligations on such person may be difficult. Such positions may be seen as creating conflicts of interest as well as creation of a parallel or shadow authority impeding effective and independent functioning of the legally constituted board in the best interest of all its stakeholders. As such, UCBs are directed not to create any honorary positions/titles at Board level or confer such titles that are non-statutory in nature 1 . 2. Role of directors 2.1 The Board of Directors (BOD or Board) is primarily concerned with formulation of policies keeping in view the applicable statutory provisions and the guidelines issued by the RBI. The Board should also exercise overall supervision and control over the functioning of the bank, leaving the day-to-day administration to the Managing Director
rows.summary:
The RBI’s April 1, 2025 Master Circular on Board of Directors for Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) consolidates and updates all prior instructions on board governance, replacing the April 1, 2024 circular. It requires UCB boards to comprise knowledgeable, high-integrity directors and mandates that banks maintain at least two “professional directors” with either suitable banking experience at middle/senior management level or relevant qualifications in law, accountancy, or finance; banks must also have bye-law provisions to support this requirement. This professional-director requirement is expressly not insisted upon for Salary Earners’ Banks because of their membership structure.

The circular also reiterates that UCBs other than those with deposit size below ₹100 crore and Salary Earners’ Banks must constitute a Board of Management (BoM), and they must amend their bye-laws accordingly in line with RBI’s December 31, 2019 circular on BoMs. In addition, only persons eligible for membership can be directors (other than co-opted or nominated directors), so persons engaged in money-lending, financing, or investment activities—whether personally or as proprietor/partner/employee/director of another concern—or persons convicted of criminal offences including moral turpitude are ineligible, subject to the model bye-law and applicable co-operative society law, BR Act, and related disqualification rules.

A notable new governance prohibition is that UCBs are directed not to create any honorary or non-statutory Board-level positions or titles such as Chairman Emeritus or Group Chairman. RBI notes that such titles can create conflicts of interest, a shadow authority parallel to the legally constituted board, and difficulty in enforcing duties or liabilities, so banks must not confer or maintain them. Beyond these points, the circular says the Board remains responsible for policy formulation under the relevant statutes and RBI guidelines, with overall supervision and control of the bank while day-to-day administration stays with the Managing Director.

INTRODUCTION Banks, with their vast branch network throughout the length and breadth of the country, occupy a very strategic position in the financial system and have an important role to play in providing credit to the housing sector. 2. VARIOUS REGULATIONS While formulating their policies, banks have to take into account the following RBI guidelines and ensure that bank credit is used for production, construction activities and not for activities connected with speculation in real estate. (A ) ACQUISITION OF LAND Bank finance can be granted only for purchase of a plot, provided a declaration is obtained from the borrower that he intends to construct a house on the said plot, with the help of bank finance or otherwise, within such period as may be laid down by the banks themselves. (B ) CONSTRUCTION OF BUILDING / READY-BUILT HOUSE (i) Banks may grant loans to individuals for purchase/construction of dwelling unit per family and loans for repairs to the damaged dwelling units of families. (ii) Banks may extend finance to a person who already owns a house in town/village where he resides, for buying/ constructing a second house in the same or other town/ village for the purpose of self-occupation. (iii) Banks may extend finance for purchase of a house by a borrower who proposes to let it out on rental basis on account of his posting outside the headquarters or because he has been provided accommodation by his employer. (iv) Banks may extend finance to a person who proposes to buy an old house where he is presently residing as a tenant. (v) Banks may finance for construction meant for improving the conditions in slum areas for which credit may be extended directly to the slum-dwellers on the guarantee of the Government, or indirectly to them through the State Governments. (vi) Banks may provide credit for slum improvement schemes to be implemented by Slum Clearance Boards and other public agencies. Withdrawn 5 (vii) Banks are advised to also adhere to the following conditions, in the light of the observations of Delhi High Court on unauthorized construction: (a) In cases where the applicant owns a plot/land and approaches the banks/FIs for a credit facility to construct a house, a copy of the sanctioned plan by competent authority in the name of a person applying for such credit facility must be obtained by the Banks/FIs before sanctioning the home loan. (b) An affidavit-cum-undertaking must be obtained from the person applying for such credit facility that he shall not violate the sanctioned plan, construction shall be strictly as per the sanctioned plan and it shall be the sole responsibility of the executants to obtain completion certificate within 3 months of completion of construction, failing which the bank shall have the power and the authority to recall the entire loan with interest, costs and other usual bank charges. (c) An Architect appointed by the bank must also certify at various stage
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Master Circular – Housing Finance** is a **consolidation-only update** for all **Scheduled Commercial Banks (excluding Regional Rural Banks)**. It replaces and updates the earlier master circular dated **April 2, 2024** by incorporating all RBI housing finance instructions issued **up to March 31, 2025**, but it explicitly states that **no new instructions or guidelines are being introduced** in this circular itself. For compliance purposes, this means banks should treat it as a restatement of the existing housing finance framework under RBI’s statutory powers, not as a fresh policy change.

The circular requires banks, when designing housing finance policies, to ensure that credit is used for **production and construction activities** and **not for speculation in real estate**. Housing finance may be granted for the **purchase of a plot only if the borrower gives a declaration** that a house will be constructed on that plot, either with bank finance or otherwise, within a period set by the bank. Banks may finance individuals for **purchase or construction of a dwelling unit per family**, repairs to damaged dwelling units, and in specified cases such as financing a borrower who already owns a house but wants a **second house for self-occupation**, a borrower buying a house to **let it out because of employer posting/accommodation**, or a borrower purchasing an **old house they currently occupy as a tenant**. Banks may also finance **slum improvement and slum clearance projects**, either directly to slum-dwellers on **Government guarantee** or indirectly through State Governments and public agencies such as Slum Clearance Boards.

A specific compliance-sensitive requirement is added for cases where the borrower **owns the plot/land and seeks a loan to construct a house**: banks/FIs must obtain a **copy of the sanctioned building plan issued by the competent authority in the borrower’s name before sanctioning the home loan**. They must also obtain an **affidavit-cum-undertaking** from the borrower confirming that construction will strictly follow the sanctioned plan, that the borrower will obtain the **completion certificate within 3 months of completion of construction**, and that if this is not done, the bank will have the right to **recall the entire loan along with interest, costs, and other usual bank charges**. In addition, the bank-appointed **architect must certify the construction at various stages**.

The remainder of the circular, as shown in the excerpt, signals that the consolidated framework also covers the broader housing finance rules on **loan quantum, innovative housing loan products and upfront disbursal, interest rate practices, approval requirements from statutory/regulatory authorities, disclosure obligations, exposure to real estate, priority sector housing loans, long-term bonds for affordable housing, fair lending practices, and additional guidelines**. Because the circular is a consolidation of prior instructions, compliance teams should review the annexed list of circulars and ensure their current housing finance policies, underwriting conditions, documentation standards, monitoring processes, and borrower undertakings reflect the full set of instructions in force through **March 31, 2025**.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular, issued on April 1, 2025 to all Scheduled Commercial Banks other than Regional Rural Banks, is a consolidation of RBI instructions on bank finance to NBFCs and explicitly states that it contains no new instructions or guidelines; it updates the prior April 24, 2024 circular to reflect all instructions issued through March 31, 2025. It is a statutory guideline issued under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and it governs how banks may lend to NBFCs, including Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) registered under Section 29A of the National Housing Bank Act, 1987. The circular notes that NBFCs, including HFCs, are mandatorily required to be registered with RBI/NHB as applicable, and that while bank financing of NBFCs has largely been deregulated, restrictions still apply for sensitive activities.

For NBFCs that are registered with RBI and engaged in principal business of asset financing, loan, factoring, investment, infrastructure financing, equipment leasing, and hire-purchase, the earlier ceiling on bank credit linked to Net Owned Funds has been withdrawn. Banks may therefore provide need-based working capital facilities and term loans to these NBFCs, subject to the prudential requirements in paragraph 8 and the condition that banks do not finance the prohibited activities described later in the circular. Banks may also finance NBFCs against second-hand assets financed by the NBFC, reflecting an explicit permission added/recognized in the circular. Banks are required to frame suitable loan policies approved by their Boards of Directors, consistent with RBI prudential guidelines and exposure norms, for extending credit to NBFCs.

The circular also defines key terms for compliance purposes: “current investments” are investments shown as current assets and intended to be held for less than one year; “long term investments” are all investments other than current assets; “NBFCs” includes RBI-registered NBFCs and RBI-registered HFCs; and “unsecured loans” are loans not secured by any tangible asset. It further states that financing of certain NBFC activities remains restricted despite the general deregulation, and that banks must observe the specific prohibitions and prudential ceilings contained in the later sections, including restrictions on activities that are not eligible for bank credit, bridge loans/interim finance, advances against shares collateral to NBFCs, guarantees for placement of funds with NBFCs, investments by banks in securities/instruments issued by NBFCs, and the applicable risk weights on bank credit to NBFCs.

Because this is a consolidated master circular rather than a fresh policy change, the key compliance action for banks is to ensure their internal lending policies, credit approvals, exposure calculations, and product restrictions align with the updated compilation of rules effective as of March 31, 2025. Any bank business line lending to or investing in NBFCs should verify the NBFC’s registration status, the activity being financed, and whether the intended exposure falls within the permitted categories and prudential constraints.

rows.title: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances
rows.summary:
This RBI master circular is a **consolidation only**: it updates the earlier circular dated **April 2, 2024** and incorporates all instructions on prudential norms for income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning for advances issued **through March 31, 2025**. RBI states explicitly that the revised circular **does not introduce any new instructions or guidelines**; it is intended to replace/withdraw the prior consolidated version and serve as the up-to-date reference for **all commercial banks except RRBs**.

For compliance purposes, the practical requirement is to use this document as the governing consolidated source for how banks must recognize income on advances, identify and classify NPAs, and make provisions. It covers the full framework for **non-performing asset definitions**, including “out of order” and “overdue” concepts, **income recognition policy**, reversal of income, appropriation of recoveries in NPAs, interest application, and computation of NPA levels. It also consolidates the rules for **asset classification** into categories of NPAs and the detailed guidelines for classification of assets, as well as the complete **provisioning regime** for loss, doubtful, standard, and substandard assets.

The circular also consolidates special prudential rules relating to **floating provisions**, including when banks may create and use them, and permits **additional provisions at higher-than-prescribed rates** in specified cases. It includes provisions for **leased assets** and other detailed prudential treatment under the bank’s advance portfolio. Because the circular is a consolidation rather than a substantive change notice, the key compliance obligation is to ensure internal policies, monitoring systems, classification triggers, provisioning calculations, and income recognition processes are aligned to the amended master text and its referenced annexures, particularly the instructions listed in **Annex 5**.

The operative date is important for version control: this revised master circular reflects the RBI’s complete instruction set as of **March 31, 2025**, and should be treated as the applicable consolidated guidance from **April 1, 2025** onward for the covered banks. Compliance teams should therefore verify that any local policy documents, accounting treatment manuals, and NPA/provisioning workflows map to this consolidated circular and that any prior references to the April 2, 2024 version are updated accordingly.

rows.summary:
This revised Master Circular for Guarantees and Co-acceptances is a consolidation of RBI instructions applicable to all Scheduled Commercial Banks **except Payment Banks and Regional Rural Banks**; it is issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 as a **statutory directive**. It **does not introduce new requirements**: the RBI states it only updates and consolidates all existing instructions on guarantees and co-acceptances issued up to **31 March 2025**, replacing the prior master circular dated **1 April 2024** and incorporating the circulars listed in Annex 2. For compliance purposes, the operative point is that banks must use this consolidated circular as the current reference set for guarantee/co-acceptance business, but the document itself does not alter policy beyond compiling prior directions.

Substantively, the circular reiterates that banks should generally prefer **financial guarantees** over performance guarantees and exercise greater caution with performance guarantees, and should normally confine guarantees to **shorter maturities**. As a rule, no bank guarantee should normally exceed **10 years**, although banks may issue guarantees beyond 10 years where they have extended **long-term loans for periods longer than 10 years** for projects; in that case they must consider the impact on **Asset-Liability Management (ALM)** and may adopt a Board-approved policy for such long-duration guarantees. Banks are also reminded to avoid issuing non-fund-based facilities to, or on behalf of, constituents who do not meet the bank’s normal lending standards, and to ensure guarantees are consistent with prudential credit judgment rather than being used to bypass lending discipline.

The circular consolidates detailed operational controls on guarantee issuance, including precautions against fraud, internal control expectations, and specific restrictions around guarantees issued for various categories of counterparties and transactions. It includes guidance on guarantees on behalf of **banks’ directors**, guarantees under the **Government of India Bank Guarantee Scheme**, guarantees for **share and stock brokers / commodity brokers**, and rules governing **personal guarantees of promoters, directors, other managerial personnel, and shareholders of borrowing companies**. It also covers guarantees of **State Governments**, issuance of **bid bonds and performance guarantees for exports**, unconditional guarantees in favour of **overseas employers/importers** on behalf of Indian exporters, precautions for **project exports** and **export advances**, and conditions for guarantees connected to **overseas investments** involving a foreign entity or its step-down subsidiary.

In addition, the circular reiterates restrictions on guarantees used for **placement of funds with NBFCs or other non-bank entities**, the requirements for **payment when guarantees are invoked**, and safeguards for **co-acceptance of bills**. It also reminds banks to take precautions when issuing or dealing with **letters of credit**, and to ensure compliance with both the **Foreign Exchange Management Act, 2000** and applicable **prudential norms**. Annex 1 provides a **model form of bank guarantee bond**, and Annex 2 lists the circulars that have been consolidated; compliance teams should treat this master circular as the reference compilation of all pre-31 March 2025 RBI instructions on these topics.

This document is the Reserve Bank of India’s updated Master Circular on Basel III Capital Regulations, issued on 1 April 2025 as RBI/2025-26/08 (DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26). It applies to all Scheduled Commercial Banks **other than Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and Regional Rural Banks**; the RBI specifically notes that Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks must instead follow their own licensing and operating guidelines for capital adequacy. The circular consolidates and updates the prudential Basel III capital adequacy instructions previously issued up to the date of the 1 April 2024 master circular, and states that the 2025 version incorporates all relevant guidelines issued as of the current date; Annex 26 contains the list of circulars consolidated into this Master Circular.

Substantively, this is a comprehensive Basel III capital regulation compendium rather than a single new rule, but it is the operative consolidated reference for compliance. It covers the full capital framework for affected banks, including minimum capital requirements under Pillar 1, the scope of application of the capital adequacy framework, the composition of regulatory capital, minority interest recognition, deductions and regulatory adjustments, and transitional arrangements. It then sets out the detailed risk-weighted capital treatment for credit risk, including exposures to sovereigns, central banks, PSEs, MDBs/BIS/IMF, banks, primary dealers, corporates/NBFCs, retail portfolios, residential property, commercial real estate, NPAs, specified categories, other assets, off-balance-sheet items, securitisation exposures, and banking book CDS positions, including recognition of third-party CDS hedges and internal hedges.

The circular also restates the approved external credit assessment and credit risk mitigation framework, covering eligible rating agencies, how external ratings are mapped and used for long-term and short-term claims, treatment of unsolicited and multiple ratings, and whether issue ratings can be extended to issuer/other claims. For credit risk mitigation, it addresses collateralised transactions, repo/reverse repo-style transactions, OTC derivatives collateral, on-balance sheet netting, guarantees and counter-guarantees, sovereign and ECGC guarantees, proportional cover, currency mismatches, maturity mismatches, and pooling of CRM techniques, with legal certainty and operational requirements emphasized as conditions for recognition. In the market risk section, it prescribes capital charges for interest rate risk, equity risk, foreign exchange risk, and CDS trading-book exposures, including general market risk, specific risk to the reference entity, counterparty credit risk, treatment below materiality thresholds, aggregation of market risk capital, and illiquid positions.

Finally, the circular sets out the operational risk capital framework, defining operational risk and specifying the measurement methodologies, including the Basic Indicator Approach. Under Pillar 2, it explains the RBI’s Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) and the banks’ Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP), including governance expectations, management integration, proportionality, independent review and validation, forward-looking and risk-based assessment, and the use of stress testing/scenario analysis and capital models. The document’s table of contents also shows that Part C addresses market discipline under Pillar 3, indicating that disclosure requirements are part of the consolidated Basel III compliance package, even though the excerpt provided cuts off before the full disclosure section.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular, issued on June 16, 2025 and addressed to all Scheduled Commercial Banks, including Small Finance Banks, consolidates all RBI instructions issued to date on credit facilities for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. It does not introduce a single new standalone scheme, but it requires banks to continue and operationalize a set of lending, planning, servicing, and procedural measures intended to increase and improve credit flow to SC/ST borrowers, with special attention at the district and block levels.

Banks are expected to use the District Level Consultative Committees under the Lead Bank Scheme as the main coordination forum, and district credit plans should explicitly link credit to employment and development programmes. Lead banks must also work closely with District Industries Centres, give weightage to SC/STs in block-level credit planning, and prepare special bankable schemes suited to SC/ST self-employment needs; the circular specifically says loan proposals from SC/ST applicants should be considered with “utmost sympathy and understanding.” In formulating Block/District Credit Plans, banks should give special focus to villages with sizeable SC/ST populations and to bastis/localities in towns or villages where these communities are concentrated.

On the operational side, bank staff are instructed to help SC/ST borrowers complete application forms and other formalities so that credit is provided within a stipulated period from receipt of the application. Banks must build awareness of available schemes through brochures, field staff visits, and branch meetings held more frequently and exclusively for SC/ST beneficiaries, so that borrowers understand the features and benefits of the schemes and can have their credit needs reflected in the credit plan. RBI and NABARD circulars relevant to this subject must be circulated internally to staff for compliance.

The circular also sets important lending safeguards for government-sponsored poverty alleviation and self-employment programmes: banks must not insist on deposits from SC/ST borrowers when processing such loan applications, and they must ensure that any applicable subsidy is released upfront rather than being withheld until full repayment of bank dues. RBI explicitly states that withholding subsidy causes under-financing and impairs asset creation and income generation. Banks are also required to provide all necessary institutional support to the National Scheduled Tribes Finance & Development Corporation and the National Scheduled Castes Finance & Development Corporation, which operate under the Ministry of Tribal Affairs and the Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment, respectively.

Finally, the circular states that loans sanctioned to State Sponsored Organisations for SC/ST beneficiaries are eligible for priority sector classification when the purpose is purchase and supply of inputs and/or marketing of the beneficiaries’ outputs. If a loan application under a government programme from an SC/ST borrower is rejected, the rejection must be taken up at the next higher level rather than decided at branch level, and the reasons for rejection must be clearly recorded. The circular is framed as a consolidation of existing RBI instructions rather than a fresh policy with a new compliance deadline, so banks should treat it as an updated master reference for ongoing compliance and implementation.
