the Lead Bank Scheme (LBS) can be traced to the Study Group headed by Prof. D. R. Gadgil (Gadgil Study Group) on the Organizational Framework for Implementation of the Social Objectives, which submitted its report in October 1969. The Study Group drew attention to the fact that commercial banks did not have adequate presence in rural areas and also lacked the required rural orientation. The Study Group, therefore, recommended the adoption of an 'Area Approach' to evolve plans and programmes for the development of an adequate banking and credit structure in the rural areas. (ii) A Committee of Bankers on Branch Expansion Programme of Public Sector Banks (PSBs) appointed by the Reserve Bank of India under the Chairmanship of Shri F. K. F. Nariman (Nariman Committee) endorsed the idea of an ‘Area Approach’ in its report (November 1969), recommending that in order to enable the PSBs to discharge their social responsibilities, each bank should concentrate on certain districts where it should act as a 'Lead Bank'. (iii) Pursuant to the above recommendations, the LBS was introduced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in December 1969. The Scheme aims at coordinating the activities of banks and other developmental agencies through various fora to achieve the objective of enhancing the flow of bank finance to the priority sector and other sectors and to promote banks' role in the overall development of the rural sector. For coordinating the activities in a district, a particular bank is assigned ‘Lead Bank’ responsibility of the district. The Lead Bank is expected to assume a leadership role for coordinating the efforts of the credit institutions and the Government. (iv) In view of the several changes that had taken place in the financial sector, the LBS was last reviewed by the High Level Committee headed by Smt. Usha Thorat, former Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank of India in 2009. (v) The Committee held wide ranging discussions with various stakeholders, viz., State Governments, banks, development institutions, academicians, NGOs, MFIs, etc. and noted that the scheme has been useful in achieving its original objectives of improvement in branch expansion, deposit mobilisation and lending to the priority sector, especially in rural/semi urban areas. There was overwhelming consensus that LBS needs to continue. Based on the recommendations of the Committee, guidelines 4 were issued to State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC) Convenor banks and Lead Banks for implementation. (vi) Envi
rows.summary:
This Master Circular, issued by RBI on 1 April 2025 as RBI/2025-26/04 (FIDD.CO.LBS.BC.No.03/02.01.001/2025-26), consolidates all Lead Bank Scheme (LBS) guidelines and instructions issued up to 31 March 2025 and supersedes the need to track the earlier scattered instructions listed in Appendix I. It is addressed to SLBC/UTLBC convenor banks and lead banks, and is the current consolidated reference for compliance with LBS expectations, meeting processes, data flows, and related banking inclusion initiatives. The circular itself does not introduce a single new policy change in the excerpted text; rather, it restates and organizes the operative framework for the scheme and signals that the RBI-hosted version is the authoritative compiled source.

The document explains that the Lead Bank Scheme was created in December 1969 in response to the Gadgil Study Group and Nariman Committee recommendations to address weak rural banking presence through an “area approach.” Under the scheme, RBI assigns one bank as the lead bank for each district to coordinate with credit institutions and government agencies to expand bank finance, especially to the priority sector and the rural economy. The last major review was by the Usha Thorat Committee in 2009, which found the scheme useful for branch expansion, deposit mobilization, and priority-sector lending, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas, and recommended continuation of the scheme.

For compliance teams, the structure of obligations in the circular is important: it covers the governance fora under LBS (Block Level Bankers’ Committees, District Consultative Committees, District Level Review Committees, and State Level Bankers’ Committees), plus requirements for meeting conduct, agenda setting, annual calendars of meetings, role of Lead District Managers, quarterly public meetings and grievance redressal, SLBC website standardization, liaison with State Governments, and capacity-building/sensitization programs. It also covers implementation requirements around preparation and monitoring of credit plans, Potential Linked Credit Plans (PLPs), revised data-flow mechanisms for LBS forum meetings, assignment of lead bank responsibility, and banking penetration initiatives such as the roadmap for unbanked villages, brick-and-mortar branches in villages with population above 5,000 that do not have a scheduled commercial bank branch, alignment with branch authorization policy, and the NSFI 2019–2024 goal of universal access to financial services.

The circular further includes operational policy areas that banks must continue to address through the LBS framework: maintaining and improving Credit Deposit Ratio performance in rural and semi-urban areas, implementing recommendations of the Expert Group on CD Ratio, supporting Direct Benefit Transfer, applying the Service Area Approach including dispensing with the “No Due Certificate,” improving farmers’ income, and expanding and deepening the digital payments ecosystem. In practical compliance terms, this means lead banks and convenor banks must ensure their district/state coordination machinery, reporting, meeting cadence, public grievance processes, website disclosures, and inclusion/planning activities remain aligned with the consolidated RBI instructions as of 31 March 2025.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular dated **April 1, 2025** consolidates and updates all prior instructions on **Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM)** and **replaces the earlier Master Circular dated April 16, 2024**. It is addressed to **Public Sector Banks and Private Sector Banks, including Small Finance Banks**, and it restates the framework for bank participation in the Government of India’s flagship rural poverty-reduction program, which was originally launched as NRLM on **April 1, 2013** and renamed **DAY-NRLM on March 29, 2016**. The scheme is designed to build strong institutions of the poor, especially women, and help them access financial services and livelihoods through a demand-driven, state-specific approach.

The circular confirms that DAY-NRLM primarily promotes **affinity-based women Self Help Groups (SHGs)**, with an exception allowing **men and women together only for SHGs formed for persons with disabilities and other special categories such as elders and transgenders**. Standard women SHGs must have **10 to 20 members**; however, in difficult areas, groups with disabled persons, and remote tribal areas, the minimum may be **5 members**. Federations of SHGs formed at village, gram panchayat, cluster, or higher levels may be **registered under the relevant state law**. For financial support, the Ministry of Rural Development will provide a **Revolving Fund (RF) of ₹20,000 to ₹30,000 per SHG** to strengthen institutional and financial management capacity and help build internal credit history, but only SHGs that have existed for at least **3/6 months**, follow the “**Panchasutras**” (regular meetings, regular savings, regular internal lending, regular recoveries, and proper books of account), and have **not previously received RF** are eligible. The circular expressly states that **no capital subsidy** will be sanctioned to any SHG under DAY-NRLM. It also notes that **Community Investment Support Fund (CIF)** will be provided to SHGs in all blocks, routed through village- or cluster-level federations and **kept in perpetuity** by those federations; CIF may be used by the federations to make loans to SHGs and/or finance common collective socio-economic activities. In addition, the scheme includes **interest subvention for women SHGs**, with the detailed features set out in **Annex II**.

For banks, the circular makes clear that their role begins with **opening savings/current accounts for all SHGs and SHG federations**, including groups with members who have disabilities. SHGs are eligible to open savings accounts when they are engaged in promoting savings among members. For **KYC of SHG members**, banks must follow the **Master Direction on KYC dated February 25, 2016, as updated from time to time**; for **PAN/Form 60**, banks must follow **Section 33A(b) of the Master Direction on KYC**. The circular also permits **Business Correspondents (BCs)** to open SHG savings accounts, but only if this is done in accordance with existing BC guidelines and the bank’s **Board-approved BC policy**. The excerpt provided ends mid-sentence after beginning a further instruction on opening savings accounts for all members, so any additional account-opening requirement appears to continue beyond the visible text and should be checked in the full circular and annexes before implementation.

rows.desc: RBI/2025-26/01 FIDD.CO.FID.BC.No.4/12.01.033/2025-26 April 01, 2025 The Chairman/ Managing Director/ Chief Executive Officer All Scheduled Commercial Banks Madam/ Dear Sir Master Circular on SHG-Bank Linkage Programme The Reserve Bank of India has, from time to time, issued a number of guidelines/instructions to banks on SHG-Bank Linkage Programme. The enclosed Master Circular c onsolidates the circulars issued by Reserve Bank on the subject up to March 31, 2025, as indicated in the Appendix. Yours faithfully (Nisha Nambiar) Chief General Manager-in-Charge Encl: As above 2 Master Circular on SHG-Bank Linkage Programme Self Help Groups (SHGs) have the potential to bring together the formal banking structure and the rural poor for mutual benefit. Studies conducted by NABARD in a few states to assess the impact of the linkage project have brought out encouraging and positive features like increase in loan volume of the SHGs, definite shift in the loaning pattern of the members from non-income generating activities to production activities, nearly 100 per cent recovery performance, significant reduction in the transaction costs for both the banks and the borrowers etc., besides leading to a gradual increase in the income level of the SHG members. Another significant feature observed in the linkage project is that about 85 per cent of the groups linked with banks were formed exclusively by women. 2. Recognizing the importance of SHG Bank linkage, banks have been advised to meet the entire credit requirements of SHG members, as envisaged in Paragraph 93 of the Union Budget announcement for the year 2008-09, made by the Honorable Finance Minister, wherein it was stated as under: "Banks will be encouraged to embrace the concept of Total Financial Inclusion. Government will request all scheduled commercial banks to follow the example set by some public sector banks and meet the entire credit requirements of SHG members, namely, (a) income generation activities, (b) social needs like housing, education, marriage, etc. and (c) debt swapping". Linking of SHGs with banks has thus been emphasized in the Monetary Policy Statements of Reserve Bank of India and Union Budget announcements from time to time and various guidelines have been issued to banks in this regard. 3. Banks should provide adequate incentives to their branches in financing the SHGs and establish linkages with them, making the procedures simple and easy. The group dynamics of working of the SHGs need neither be regulated nor formal structures imposed or insisted upon. The approach to financing of SHGs should be totally hassle-free and may also include consumption expenditures. Accordingly, the following guidelines should be adhered to enable effective linkage of SHGs with the banking sector. 3 4. Opening of Savings Bank A/C The SHGs, registered or unregistered, which are engaged in promoting savings habit among their members are eligible to open savings bank accounts with banks. These SHGs need not necessarily have already availed of credit facilities from banks before opening savings bank accounts. The instructions on simplified Customer Due Diligence (CDD) applicable to SHGs as prescribed in Chapter VI of the Master Direction - Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction, 2016 ( as updated from time to time) shall be adhered to. 5. Lending to SHGs a) Bank lending to SHGs should be included in branch credit plan, block credit plan, district credit plan and state credit plan of each bank. Utmost priority should be accorded to the sector in preparation of these plans. It should also form an integral part of the bank’s corporate credit plan. b) As per operational guidelines issued by NABARD, SHGs may be sanctioned savings linked loans by banks (varying from a saving to loan ratio of 1:1 to 1:4). However, in case of matured SHGs, loans may be given beyond the limit of four times the savings as per the discretion of the bank. c) A simple system requiring minimum procedures and documentation is a precondition for augmenting flow of credit to SHGs. Banks should strive to remove all operational irritants and make arrangements to expeditiously sanction and disburse credit by delegating adequate sanctioning powers to branch managers. The loan application forms, procedures and documents should be made simple. It would help in providing prompt and hassle-free credit. 6. Interest rates The banks would have the discretion to decide on the interest rates applicable to loans given to SHGs/member beneficiaries, subject to regulatory guidelines on interest rate on advances contained in Master Direction - Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rate on Advances) Directions, 2016 issued vide DBR.Dir.No.85/13.03.00/2015-16 dated March 3, 2016, as updated from time to time. 4 7. Service/ Processing charges The instructions on service charges applicable to priority sector loans to SHGs as prescribed in the Master Directions - Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classif
rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular, dated April 1, 2025, consolidates all prior RBI instructions on the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme up to March 31, 2025 and is addressed to all Scheduled Commercial Banks. It does not announce a wholly new regime, but it restates and consolidates the compliance expectations that banks must follow when opening accounts for, and lending to, Self Help Groups (SHGs), with the goal of supporting “total financial inclusion” and ensuring banks meet the full credit needs of SHG members, including income-generating activity, social needs such as housing/education/marriage, and debt swapping.

Banks must allow both registered and unregistered SHGs that promote savings among members to open savings bank accounts, even if the group has not previously borrowed from a bank. While doing so, banks must apply the simplified customer due diligence (CDD) requirements applicable to SHGs under Chapter VI of the Master Direction on KYC (2016, as updated). The circular also emphasizes that banks should not impose rigid formal structures on SHGs and should keep the process hassle-free, including permitting consumption expenditure as part of the financing approach.

For lending, SHG credit must be built into the bank’s branch, block, district, state, and corporate credit plans, with “utmost priority” in those plans. NABARD operational guidance permits SHG loans generally within a savings-to-loan ratio of 1:1 to 1:4; however, for mature SHGs, banks may lend beyond four times the savings at their discretion. Banks are required to simplify loan applications, procedures, and documentation, eliminate operational bottlenecks, and delegate sufficient sanctioning authority to branch managers so that credit can be sanctioned and disbursed quickly.

On pricing and charges, banks may decide the interest rate on SHG and SHG member loans, but only within the limits of the RBI’s Master Direction on Interest Rate on Advances (March 3, 2016, as updated). The circular also points to the separate RBI priority sector lending instructions for service/processing charges on SHG loans, meaning any applicable charge waivers or restrictions must be followed under those directions. The document’s stated “effective” status is as a consolidation of the extant instructions as of March 31, 2025, so compliance teams should treat it as the current master reference for SHG-bank linkage requirements unless and until superseded.

rows.summary:
On August 12, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India issued for public comment a draft of the **“Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026”**, pursuant to its August 5, 2026 Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies. The draft is intended to **harmonize and consolidate interest-rate rules across all regulated entities (REs)**, rather than applying only to commercial banks as the current framework largely does, and it is meant to establish a **broad, principles-based framework** for setting interest rates on **both fixed-rate and floating-rate loans** in a way that is proportionate to the **nature, complexity, and scale** of each RE’s operations.

The RBI explains that its existing framework already covers **Commercial Banks, including Small Finance Banks and Local Area Banks**, with requirements around **internal and external benchmark-based lending** for floating-rate loans and the **determination of spreads over those benchmarks**. For other REs—specifically **Non-Banking Financial Companies, All India Financial Institutions, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, and Rural Cooperative Banks**—the existing instructions are described as being mostly limited to **conduct-related aspects**. The RBI also notes that it has observed **divergent practices** among commercial banks in certain areas, including how the **MCLR (Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate)** and its components are determined, and that the current guidelines contain **very limited instructions for fixed-rate loans**, which is one reason it is proposing the new harmonized directions.

For compliance purposes, the key immediate obligation is not a substantive rule change yet, but a **public consultation deadline**: comments and feedback on the draft must be submitted **on or before September 11, 2026**. Submissions may be made either through the RBI website’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section or by **email**, with the subject line exactly identified as **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Amendment Directions)”**. The RBI states that after reviewing the feedback, it will issue **final Directions separately for each category of RE**, so firms should assume that the current draft may be refined and then republished in category-specific form before becoming binding.

rows.title: RBI invites public comments on the draft Directions on ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’
rows.desc: August 7, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Directions on ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’ Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) reflects the adjustment to the default risk-free prices of derivatives to account for potential counterparty default. CVA risk refers to losses resulting from changes in CVA values, driven by shifts in counterparty credit spreads and market risk factors. The CVA capital charge ensures banks hold sufficient capital to cover these risks. 2. The extant CVA framework was issued by the Reserve Bank in 2011, which was based on the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) standards issued in 2010. The BCBS has, since, issued revised CVA guidelines under the final Basel III framework. Accordingly, it has been decided to issue revised instructions on CVA framework permitting banks in India to adopt the basic approach (BA-CVA). Banks may choose to implement either the full or reduced version of BA-CVA. Alternatively, in line with BCBS guidelines, banks with an insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives may calculate their CVA capital charge as 100 per cent of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge. 3. The revised instructions: (a) allow eligible banks to choose a simpler approach; (b) clarify the eligibility and recognition of CVA hedges; (c) increase the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties by sector and credit quality; and (d) separate systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full BA-CVA calculation, addressing imperfect alignment of indirect CVA hedges. These revisions enhance risk sensitivity and improve consistency in the CVA framework. 4. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank has released today the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026. 5. The comments on the draft Directions are invited from Regulated Entities, market participants, and other interested parties till August 28, 2026. The comments / feedback may be submitted through the link under the ‘Connect 2 Regulate’ Section available on the Reserve Bank’s website or may alternatively be forwarded to The Chief General Manager Market Risk Group Department of Regulation, Central Office Reserve Bank of India, 12 th Floor Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg Fort, Mumbai – 400 001 Or by email With the subject line ‘Feedback on Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’ (Brij Raj) Press Release: 2026-2027/836 Chief General Manager � � PRESS RELEASE � � RESERVE BANK OF INDIA : www.rbi.org.in/hindi , �� , � , , - 400 001 Website : www.rbi.org.in Department of Communication, Central Office, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, - /email : helpdoc@rbi.org.in Mumbai - 400 001 /Phone: 022 - 2266 0502
rows.summary:
On August 7, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released draft updated directions on the **Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework** and invited public comments before finalizing them. The revision updates the older RBI CVA framework issued in 2011 to align with the **Basel Committee’s revised CVA standards under the final Basel III framework**. For banks in India, the draft directions would permit adoption of the **basic approach (BA-CVA)**, with banks able to choose either the **full** or **reduced** version of BA-CVA; alternatively, banks with an **insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives** would be allowed to compute their CVA capital charge as **100% of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge**, consistent with BCBS guidance.

The draft also makes several substantive changes intended to improve risk sensitivity and consistency. It **clarifies which CVA hedges are eligible and how they are recognized**, **increases the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights** by counterparties’ sector and credit quality, and in the **full BA-CVA calculation** it requires the **separation of systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components**, specifically to address imperfect alignment of indirect CVA hedges. RBI states these revisions are meant to enhance the accuracy of CVA capital requirements and make the framework more consistent with current international standards.

The draft directions themselves were issued as the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026**. RBI is seeking comments from **regulated entities, market participants, and other interested parties**. The deadline for submissions is **August 28, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through the RBI website’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section, or sent by email with the subject line **“Feedback on Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework”**; written submissions may also be mailed to the **Chief General Manager, Market Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, RBI, 12th Floor, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**.

rows.title: Review of Guidelines on Concentration Risk Management - Rural Co-operative Banks
rows.desc: August 06, 2026 Review of Guidelines on Concentration Risk Management - Rural Co- operative Banks In pursuance of the announcement made with regard to the captioned subject in the Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies dated August 5, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India has today issued the following draft Directions for public comments: (i) Draft Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) – Directions, 2026 to replace Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) – Directions, 2025 (ii) Draft Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) – Amendment Directions, 2026 to amend certain provisions of Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 2. The above draft Directions prescribe, inter alia, prudential exposure limits for single/group counterparty, enhanced housing loan limits, and prudential exposure limits on unsecured advances. Additionally, it is proposed to allow flexibility to larger Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) with deposits above ₹1,000 crore in deciding the tenor and moratorium requirements for housing loans, while increasing the ceilings for these parameters in cases of other RCBs. Further, the prescribed prudential sectoral exposure limits, except for real estate sector, are proposed to be withdrawn. 3. The comments / feedback on the draft Directions may be submitted by the regulated entities and other stakeholders / members of public on or before August 28, 2026 through the following channels: (i) The ‘Connect 2 Regulate’ section on the website by following the corresponding hyperlink provided against each document in the page where they are hosted; or (ii) by email with the subject line ‘Feedback on (full name of the draft Directions)’. rows.summary:
On August 6, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India issued draft directions for public comment to revise the framework for **rural co-operative banks (RCBs)** on concentration risk and related credit facility rules. The RBI proposes two instruments: **(1) Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2026**, which would **replace** the existing **2025 concentration risk management directions**, and **(2) Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) – Amendment Directions, 2026**, which would amend selected provisions of the **2025 Credit Facilities Directions**.

The draft package would set/clarify **prudential exposure limits for single and group counterparties**, introduce **enhanced housing loan limits**, and establish **prudential exposure limits for unsecured advances**. It also proposes to give **larger RCBs with deposits above ₹1,000 crore** flexibility to determine the **tenor and moratorium** conditions for housing loans, while at the same time **raising the ceilings for those parameters for other RCBs**. In addition, the RBI proposes to **withdraw the currently prescribed prudential sectoral exposure limits for all sectors except real estate**, meaning RCBs would no longer need to comply with the prior sector-specific caps other than the real-estate restriction.

The public consultation deadline is **August 28, 2026**. Comments may be submitted either through the RBI’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** portal on the website page hosting the draft documents, or by **email** with the subject line **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Directions)”**. This consultation is addressed to **regulated entities and other stakeholders/members of the public**, so compliance teams at affected RCBs should review the draft directions for any exposure-limit, housing-loan, unsecured-advance, tenor, or moratorium changes that may require policy updates, lending-process revisions, or system changes if the drafts are finalized.

rows.title: Rationalisation of Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 – Draft Rules for Comments
rows.desc: July 21, 2026 Rationalisation of Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 – Draft Rules for Comments Foreign investment into India is presently governed by the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 ('NDI Rules'). The Union Budget 2026- 27 announced a comprehensive review of the NDI Rules to create a more contemporary, user-friendly framework for foreign investments, consistent with India's evolving economic priorities. Pursuant thereto, a committee was constituted by the Central Government to undertake a comprehensive review of the extant regulatory framework. Based on the recommendations of the Committee, and in consultation with the Central Government and other stakeholders, the Reserve Bank of India has prepared a draft of the rationalized Rules. The salient features of the proposed draft Rules, inter alia, are as under: a) Simplified and principle-based framework: Rationalization of provisions, harmonization of definitions and a simplified regulatory architecture to enhance clarity and reduce regulatory complexity. b) Alignment with the FDI Policy: Clear demarcation of procedural FEMA provisions from policy and sector-specific requirements, improving regulatory coherence and facilitating timely policy changes. c) Enhanced ease of doing business: Streamlined procedures, reduced compliance burden and greater operational flexibility through a transparent and investor-friendly regulatory framework. d) Future-ready regulatory framework: Adoption of principle-based, investee-neutral and investor-neutral provisions aligned with evolving business practices, while preserving necessary regulatory safeguards. � � PRESS RELEASE � � RESERVE BANK OF INDIA : www.rbi.org.in/hindi , �� , � , , - 400 001 Website : www.rbi.org.in Department of Communication, Central Office, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, - /email : helpdoc@rbi.org.in Mumbai - 400 001 /Phone: 022 - 2266 0502 The Rules will be finalized after wider public consultations. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank of India has today placed on its website draft Foreign Exchange Management (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2026 for comments / feedback from all stakeholders. Comments/feedback on the draft Rules may be submitted through the respective link under the 'Connect 2 Regulate' section available on the RBI's website or may be forwarded via email by August 31, 2026, with the subject line "Feedback on Draft Foreign Investment Rules". (Brij Raj) Press Release: 2026-2027/726 Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued draft Foreign Exchange Management (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2026 for public comment as part of a broader rationalization of the current Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019. This initiative follows the Union Budget 2026–27 announcement of a comprehensive review of the existing foreign investment framework and a Central Government committee’s recommendations, with the stated goal of creating a more contemporary, user-friendly regime aligned with India’s changing economic priorities.

Substantively, the draft rules are described as a move toward a simplified, principle-based framework that rationalizes provisions, harmonizes definitions, and reduces regulatory complexity. The RBI says the draft is intended to better align FEMA procedural rules with the FDI Policy and sector-specific requirements, so that policy changes can be made more efficiently while improving regulatory coherence. The press release also says the draft will streamline procedures, reduce compliance burden, and give investors greater operational flexibility, while shifting to investee-neutral and investor-neutral provisions that preserve necessary safeguards.

No specific rule text, thresholds, caps, or rates are provided in this press release, and it does not identify particular sectors or classes of investors affected; instead, it indicates a general overhaul of the foreign investment rules framework. The only concrete compliance obligation announced here is participation in the consultation process: stakeholders may submit comments or feedback through the RBI website under the “Connect 2 Regulate” section or by email, and the deadline is August 31, 2026. If emailing feedback, the subject line must be “Feedback on Draft Foreign Investment Rules.”

The document also makes clear that these are draft rules only and are not yet final; the rules will be finalized after wider public consultations. For compliance teams, the immediate action item is to review the draft once accessed on the RBI website and assess whether any proposed simplification or reclassification of FEMA/FDI procedural requirements could affect internal investment, onboarding, reporting, or sectoral compliance processes once finalized.

rows.summary:
On July 15, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance”** for public comment. The draft is intended to strengthen data governance across regulated entities by setting broad regulatory expectations for how data should be managed throughout its lifecycle, with an emphasis on ensuring data is **accurate, consistent, secure, and fit for purpose** across functions and systems. RBI says the guidance is being issued because the increasing digitization of the financial sector and technology-driven business models have made data a critical asset, and weaknesses in data governance can create **financial, operational, compliance, and reputational risks**.

The draft applies to a wide set of RBI-regulated entities: **commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), asset reconstruction companies, and credit information companies**. The draft guidance specifically covers RBI’s expectations on **data governance roles, architecture, metadata and lineage, data quality, and third-party arrangements involving data sharing**. Compliance teams at affected entities should treat this as a proposed supervisory framework that may require formal governance, controls, accountability mapping, and oversight over external data-sharing relationships once finalized.

RBI has invited comments from regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders by **August 17, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on RBI’s website, or sent by mail to **The Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance.”** No final effective date is stated in the release, since this is only a draft consultation at this stage.

rows.summary:
On June 24, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management”** for public comment. The draft is aimed at establishing **holistic regulatory expectations for model risk management across the full model lifecycle** and is intended to address the fact that regulated entities are increasingly using models — including **AI/ML-based models** — across business and decision-making processes, where weak governance, oversight, controls, or risk management can create **financial, operational, compliance, and reputational risk**.

The draft applies to a broad set of RBI-regulated entities: **commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies, asset reconstruction companies, and credit information companies**. It also makes clear that the guidance applies to **all models used by these entities**, including **third-party models** and models employing **artificial intelligence / machine learning (AI/ML)**, not just credit models or internally developed tools.

This draft follows RBI’s earlier **August 5, 2024** draft on **“Regulatory Principles for Management of Model Risks in Credit”** and the **August 13, 2025** report of the Committee on Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence (FREE-AI). The current draft expands the focus from credit-related model risk to a broader model-risk framework across use cases and lifecycle stages.

RBI has invited **comments from regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders by July 24, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through RBI’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** portal on its website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management.”** For compliance teams, the immediate action item is to review whether the entity uses any models — especially outsourced or AI/ML-enabled models — that would be covered by the draft and to assess whether internal model governance, validation, monitoring, and control processes would need to be upgraded once the guidance is finalized.

rows.title: RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’
rows.desc: June 10, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’ The extant guidelines require the use of the Current Exposure Method (CEM) for the computation of Counterparty Credit Risk (CCR) exposure. In 2016, RBI issued final ‘Guidelines for Computing Exposure for Counterparty Credit Risk arising from Derivative Transactions’ and ‘Guidelines on Capital Requirements for Bank Exposures to Central Counterparties’, both based on the Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR), with an intended implementation date of April 1, 2018. However, the implementation of these guidelines was subsequently deferred. 2. Since then, the Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020, has been enacted, while the margining framework has been implemented under the Reserve Bank of India (Margining for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives) Directions, 2024. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) has also, over time, issued various FAQs providing further clarity on the SA-CCR guidelines. 3. Considering the time elapsed and the recent legal and regulatory developments, the guidelines have been comprehensively reviewed. The key changes between the 2016 guidelines (currently part of the Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions, Directions, 2025) and the proposed draft Directions include, inter alia, (i) clarification on the scope of CCR across both banking and trading book exposures, (ii) treatment of multiple margin agreements and multiple netting sets elaborated in view of the legal / regulatory developments in netting and margining guidelines, (iii) guidance on the treatment of transactions where a bank acts as a clearing member of SEBI- recognised stock exchanges in the equity derivatives and commodity derivatives segments, (iv) treatment for deferment of option premium, (v) guidance on computation of effective notional for options, and (vi) inclusion of disclosure templates for SA-CCR. 4. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank has today released the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Amendment Directions, 2026. 5. The comments on the draft Amendment Directions are invited from the Regulated Entities, market participants, and other interested parties till July 1, 2026. The comments / feedback may be submitted through the link under the ‘Connect 2 Regulate’ Section available on the Reserve Bank’s website or may alternatively be forwarded to The Chief General Manager Market Risk Group Department of Regulation, Central Office PRESS RELEASE � RESERVE BANK OF INDIA : www.rbi.org.in/hindi � , � , � � , , - 400 001 Website : www.rbi.org.in Department of Communication, Central Office, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, - /email : helpdoc@rbi.org.in Mumbai - 400 001 /Phone: 022 - 2266 0502 Reserve Bank of India, 12 th Floor Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg Fort, Mumbai – 400 001 Or by email With the subject line ‘Feedback on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’ (Brij Raj) Press Release: 2026-2027/430 Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
On June 10, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released draft Amendment Directions on the **Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)** and invited public comments. The draft reflects a comprehensive review of the earlier 2016 SA-CCR-based guidelines, which had originally been intended to take effect on **April 1, 2018** but were later deferred; under the extant framework, banks still compute counterparty credit risk exposure using the **Current Exposure Method (CEM)**. The review was prompted by subsequent legal and regulatory changes, including the enactment of the **Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020**, the implementation of the margining framework under the **Reserve Bank of India (Margining for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives) Directions, 2024**, and additional clarification issued by the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)** through FAQs.

The draft directions make several substantive changes relevant to compliance and risk systems: they clarify the scope of counterparty credit risk across **both banking book and trading book exposures**; expand guidance on **multiple margin agreements** and **multiple netting sets** in light of the new netting and margining regime; address transactions where a bank acts as a **clearing member of SEBI-recognised stock exchanges** in the **equity derivatives and commodity derivatives segments**; provide treatment for **deferment of option premium**; explain how to compute the **effective notional for options**; and add **disclosure templates** for SA-CCR. RBI states that it has now issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Amendment Directions, 2026**, which implies affected institutions should review whether their CCR calculation methodologies, margin/netting documentation handling, and disclosure processes need to be updated once these amendments are implemented.

Comments on the draft are due by **July 1, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Market Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Mumbai 400 001**, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’”**. The consultation is open to **regulated entities, market participants, and other interested parties**.

rows.summary:
On June 5, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released draft **Amendment Directions, 2026** for six categories of regulated entities: **commercial banks, small finance banks, regional rural banks, payment banks, local area banks, and urban co-operative banks**. The stated purpose is to give banks **greater flexibility in pricing Rupee bulk deposits** while also maintaining **uniform disclosure of deposit interest rates** across the regulated sector. This is a consultation-stage document, so it does not yet impose the final amended requirements, but it signals upcoming changes to the existing RBI directions on interest rates on deposits for those six entity types.

RBI is specifically inviting comments and feedback from **regulated entities and members of the public/other stakeholders** on or before **June 20, 2026**. Submissions may be made either through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on RBI’s website by using the hyperlink provided for each draft document, or by email. If sent by email, the subject line must be **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Amendment Directions (including the type of Regulated Entity))”**.

For compliance teams, the key immediate action item is to review the draft amendments applicable to the entity’s own license category and assess any operational, product-pricing, or disclosure impacts relating to **Rupee bulk deposits** and interest-rate publication/disclosure practices. Although the press release does not set out the detailed amended rule text itself, it confirms that RBI intends to revise the deposit-interest-rate framework across the six named regulated entity classes and is seeking feedback before finalization.

rows.title: RBI Issues Revised Draft Amendment Directions on ‘Conduct of Regulated Entities in Recovery of Loans and Engagement of Recovery Agents’
rows.desc: May 20, 2026 RBI Issues Revised Draft Amendment Directions on ‘Conduct of Regulated Entities in Recovery of Loans and Engagement of Recovery Agents’ In pursuance of the announcement made in the Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies dated February 6, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India had issued the draft Amendment Directions on ‘Conduct of Regulated Entities in Recovery of Loans and Engagement of Recovery Agents’ for public comments on February 12, 2026. Substantial feedback has been received from stakeholders on the draft Amendment Directions, which has resulted in changes in many key draft provisions. Feedback has also been submitted by stakeholders regarding regulatory enablement to the lenders to deploy technology-based mechanisms, which restrict or disables some of the functionalities of a financed mobile device such as mobile phone, tablet, etc., to recover loan dues from the borrower in cases of default. The published draft Amendment Directions have been suitably amended to incorporate the accepted feedback. It has now been decided to issue revised draft Amendment Directions for another round of public consultation. 2. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank of India has today issued the following revised draft Amendment Directions for public comments. (i) Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Amendment Directions, 2026 (ii) Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Amendment Directions, 2026 (iii) Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Amendment Directions, 2026 (iv) Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Amendment Directions, 2026 (v) Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Amendment Directions, 2026 (vi) Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Amendment Directions, 2026 (vii) Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions - Responsible Business Conduct) Amendment Directions, 2026 (viii) Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Responsible Business Conduct) Amendment Directions, 2026 (ix) Reserve Bank of India (Housing Finance Companies) Amendment Directions, 2026 � � PRESS RELEASE � � RESERVE BANK OF INDIA : www.rbi.org.in/hindi , �� , � , , - 400 001 Website : www.rbi.org.in Department of Communication, Central Office, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, - /email : helpdoc@rbi.org.in Mumbai - 400 001 /Phone: 022 - 2266 0502 2 3. The comments / feedback on the revised draft Amendment Directions may be submitted by the regulated entities and members of public / other stakeholders on or before May 31, 2026 through the following channels: i. the ‘Connect 2 Regulate’ section on the website by following the corresponding hyperlink provided against each document in the page where they are hosted; or ii. by email with the subject line ‘Feedback on (full name of the draft Amendment Directions (including the type of Regulated Entity))’. (Brij Raj) Press Release: 2026-2027/298 Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued **revised draft Amendment Directions** on **“Conduct of Regulated Entities in Recovery of Loans and Engagement of Recovery Agents”** after receiving substantial stakeholder feedback on the version released for public comment on **February 12, 2026**. The RBI says the earlier draft has been **materially revised** in several key areas based on that feedback, including changes to provisions related to lenders’ proposed use of **technology-based mechanisms to restrict or disable certain functions of financed mobile devices** (such as **mobile phones and tablets**) in order to recover dues from borrowers in default.  

The revised draft is now being issued for **another round of public consultation** and applies across a broad set of RBI-regulated institutions through entity-specific amendment directions, namely: **commercial banks, small finance banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies, and housing finance companies**. The press release does not set out the substantive final rules yet; rather, it announces that these revised drafts have been published and remain open for comment.  

**Comments/feedback must be submitted on or before May 31, 2026.** Regulated entities and other stakeholders may file comments either through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website using the hyperlink for each document, or by **email** with the subject line formatted as **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Amendment Directions (including the type of Regulated Entity))”**.  

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that RBI is signaling a potential change in how recovery practices and recovery-agent engagement will be regulated, and that the revised drafts may affect debt-recovery procedures, borrower-device restrictions, and related conduct controls once finalized. Organizations in any of the covered entity categories should review the revised drafts promptly and determine whether their current loan-recovery, collections, outsourcing, and technology-enabled recovery practices would need policy, process, legal, customer-notice, or governance updates.

Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Seventh Amendment Directions, 2026 ii. rows.summary:
On May 19, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released draft amendment directions intended to align Indian capital adequacy disclosure rules more closely with the Basel Pillar 3 disclosure framework. The drafts cover two sets of regulated entities: commercial banks, through the proposed “Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Seventh Amendment Directions, 2026,” and small finance banks, through the proposed “Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Fifth Amendment Directions, 2026.” The notice does not set out the substantive text of the changes, thresholds, or reporting items in the press release itself; it only states the purpose is greater consistency with Basel Pillar 3 disclosure requirements.

RBI has invited public comments on the draft directions by June 2, 2026. Feedback may be submitted through the “Connect2Regulate” section on the RBI website, or sent by post to the Chief General Manager, Balance Sheet Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, 12th Floor, Central Office Building, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400001. Comments may also be emailed, provided the subject line is exactly: “Feedback on (full name of the draft Amendment Directions).”

From a compliance perspective, the immediate action item is to review the draft amendment directions themselves and determine whether current Pillar 3 disclosure processes, governance, internal controls, and reporting templates for commercial banks or small finance banks need to be updated if the drafts are adopted. The press release is a consultation notice rather than a final rule, so no implementation date or binding compliance deadline is stated here beyond the comment deadline of June 2, 2026.

Accordingly, RBI today released the draft Master Direction on Prepaid Payment Instruments. The comments / feedback on the draft Direction may be submitted by the regulated entities and members of public / other stakeholders on or before May 22, 2026 through the ‘Connect 2 Regulate’ section on the website by following the corresponding hyperlink provided against each document in the page where they are hosted. rows.summary:
On April 22, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released a **draft Master Direction on Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs), 2026** as part of a broader review of the PPI framework aimed at supporting long-term growth in PPI usage while strengthening transaction security. This is a **draft** rather than a final rule, so the immediate action for compliance teams is not implementation of new requirements yet, but close review of the proposed direction and assessment of operational impact on any business issuing, distributing, or otherwise dealing in PPIs.

The RBI is inviting **comments/feedback from regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders**. The submission deadline is **May 22, 2026**, and feedback must be filed through the RBI’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, using the hyperlink provided against the relevant document on the hosted page. Compliance teams should treat this as a formal consultation process and ensure any internal review of the draft is completed in time to submit institution-specific concerns or suggested changes by that date.

The press release does not itself specify the detailed substantive changes to the PPI rules or any numeric thresholds, limits, or effective dates for the final requirements; it only states that RBI has undertaken a **comprehensive review of the PPI guidelines** and has issued the draft Master Direction for consultation. Accordingly, the key compliance obligation at this stage is monitoring the draft closely, identifying whether the organization is a **regulated entity affected by the PPI framework**, and preparing feedback before the consultation closes on **May 22, 2026**.

rows.title: RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on review of methodology for identification of NBFC-UL and inclusion of Government owned NBFCs in NBFC-UL
rows.desc: April 10, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on review of methodology for identification of NBFC-UL and inclusion of Government owned NBFCs in NBFC-UL The Reserve Bank has issued today the following draft Amendment Directions relating to review of methodology for identification of NBFCs in Upper Layer (NBFC- UL), inclusion of Government owned NBFCs as NBFC-UL and other related aspects. (i) The draft ‘Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Second Amendment Directions, 2026’; and (ii) The draft ‘Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Concentration Risk Management) Third Amendment Directions, 2026’ 2. The feedback / comments on the draft Amendment Directions are invited from the NBFCs, members of public and all other relevant stakeholders till May 04, 2026. The feedback / comments may be submitted through the link under the ‘Connect 2 Regulate’ Section available on RBI’s website or may alternatively be forwarded to: Chief General Manager - in - Charge Department of Regulation (SIG-NBFCs) Reserve Bank of India 12 th Floor, Central Office Building Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001 Or by email With the subject line ‘Feedback on the draft Amendment Directions on review of methodology for identification of NBFC-UL and inclusion of Government NBFCs in NBFC-UL’. Background and Objective The Scale Based Regulatory (SBR) Framework for NBFCs prescribes a two- pronged methodology for identification of NBFC-UL viz., top ten eligible NBFCs by asset size and parametric scoring methodology. With a view to adopt a transparent, simple and absolute criteria for identification of NBFC-UL, it is proposed to replace the existing methodology with asset size criteria, which is currently proposed as ₹1,00,000 � � PRESS RELEASE � � RESERVE BANK OF INDIA : www.rbi.org.in/hindi , �� , � , , - 400 001 Website : www.rbi.org.in Department of Communication, Central Office, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, - /email : helpdoc@rbi.org.in Mumbai - 400 001 /Phone: 022 - 2266 0502 crore and above. Further, the SBR Framework currently places Government owned NBFCs in the Base Layer or Middle Layer and not in the Upper Layer. In pursuance of the principle of ownership neutral regulatory regime for NBFCs, it is now proposed to consider eligible Government owned NBFCs also for inclusion in the list of NBFC- UL based on the revised criteria. Additionally, it is proposed to allow all NBFC-UL to use State Government guarantees as credit risk transfer instrument without any limit subject to the specified conditions. (Brij Raj) Press Release: 2026-2027/65 Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The RBI has released two draft amendment directions for public comment on changes to the framework for identifying NBFCs in the Upper Layer (NBFC-UL) and for related concentration-risk rules: the draft **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Second Amendment Directions, 2026** and the draft **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Concentration Risk Management) Third Amendment Directions, 2026**. Comments are invited from **NBFCs, members of the public, and all other relevant stakeholders** by **May 04, 2026**; submissions can be made through the RBI website’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** facility, or sent to the RBI’s **Department of Regulation (SIG-NBFCs)** in Mumbai, or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on the draft Amendment Directions on review of methodology for identification of NBFC-UL and inclusion of Government NBFCs in NBFC-UL.”**

Substantively, the RBI proposes to **replace the current two-pronged NBFC-UL identification method** under the Scale Based Regulatory (SBR) framework—currently based on **the top ten eligible NBFCs by asset size plus a parametric scoring methodology**—with a **single asset-size threshold**. The draft says that threshold is **₹1,00,000 crore and above** (i.e., NBFCs with assets at or above that level would be identified for NBFC-UL consideration under the revised approach), making the framework more “transparent, simple and absolute.”

The RBI also proposes to change how **Government-owned NBFCs** are treated. Under the current SBR framework, such entities are placed in the **Base Layer or Middle Layer**, not the Upper Layer; the draft would instead allow **eligible Government-owned NBFCs** to be considered for inclusion in **NBFC-UL** on the revised criteria, reflecting an **ownership-neutral regulatory regime**. In addition, the RBI proposes to permit **all NBFC-ULs** to use **State Government guarantees as a credit risk transfer instrument without any limit**, but only **subject to specified conditions** in the amended concentration-risk framework.

rows.summary:
The notice is an informational compliance circular from Listing Operations dated **24 Aug 2026** for **all listed entities**. It does **not introduce a new standalone rule or threshold** in the text provided; instead, it formally issues an attached set of **Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on the intimation of Record Date for Corporate Actions** and directs listed entities to use that guidance for compliance purposes.

For a corporate compliance team, the key point is that the exchange/regulator is reminding listed companies that they must **properly intimate the record date for corporate actions** in accordance with the guidance contained in the attached FAQ document. The notice itself does not spell out the detailed procedural requirements, deadlines, or corporate-action types, but it expressly states that the FAQs are provided “for your reference and guidance” and that listed entities are **requested to take note of the same and comply accordingly**.

In practical terms, this means compliance teams at listed entities should review the annexed FAQ document and align their internal process for announcing, recording, and communicating record dates for corporate actions with the guidance there. Because the notice is addressed broadly to **all listed entities** and concerns **corporate actions**, it is relevant to any issuer that declares events where entitlement depends on holding securities as of a specified record date.

rows.title: Adherence to Compliance Requirements for Handling Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
rows.desc: NOTICE NoticeNo. 20260807-20 NoticeDate 07Aug2026 Category CircularsListedCompanies Segment General Department ListingCompliance-Monitoring Subject AdherencetoComplianceRequirementsforHandlingUnpublished PriceSensitiveInformation(UPSI)undertheSEBI(Prohibitionof InsiderTrading)Regulations,2015 Attachments NoAttachment To, All Listed Entities Dear Sir/Madam, SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 “(PIT Regulations)”, as amended from time to time, and the relevant circulars issued by SEBI and the Stock Exchanges detail, inter-alia, the manner in which the listed companies are required to deal with Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI). The provisions of the PIT Regulations are further supplemented and clarified through the Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) issued by SEBI. In light of the observations made in certain cases, it is considered imperative that listed companies diligently adhere to best practices to ensure full compliance with the PIT Regulations as amended from time to time including the following: 1. Listed companies shall maintain a structured digital database containing the nature of UPSI, the names and PANs (or any other identifier authorized by law) of persons who have shared the information, and the names and PANs of persons with whom such information has been shared. In case where UPSI is shared with a listed company, intermediaries, or fiduciaries, the names and identifier of the individuals handling such information shall be recorded. 2. Listed companies shall diligently implement and periodically review internal policies designed to prevent the leakage of UPSI. Such measures must be in alignment with the statutory and regulatory provisions prescribed under the PIT Regulations. 3. To ensure a culture of compliance, companies shall conduct periodic training and awareness programs for all employees and fiduciaries regarding the prescribed manner of handling UPSI. 4. Listed companies shall ensure compliance with the Code of Conduct formulated by the company with respect to the PIT Regulations, ensuring that the same is effectively operationalized. 5. Listed entities are advised to implement any other such measures as may be necessary to ensure that the objectives of the PIT Regulations are achieved. Netra Sahani Hasti Vora Deputy Vice President – Listing Compliance Deputy Manager – Listing Compliance
rows.summary:
This notice reminds all listed entities that they must strictly comply with the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 (PIT Regulations), as amended from time to time, together with the related SEBI and stock exchange circulars and SEBI FAQs governing handling of unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI). It does not introduce a new rule date or numerical threshold, but it is a compliance-focused direction issued on 07 Aug 2026 emphasizing that, based on observations in certain cases, listed companies must follow best practices to avoid UPSI leakage and ensure the regulatory framework is being fully implemented in practice.

The first specific requirement is maintenance of a structured digital database for every instance of UPSI sharing. The database must record the nature of the UPSI, the names and PANs (or any other legally authorized identifier) of the person who shared the information, and the names and PANs of the persons with whom it was shared. Where UPSI is shared with a listed company, intermediary, or fiduciary, the identities of the individuals handling that UPSI must also be recorded, using the relevant name and identifier.

The notice also requires listed companies to diligently implement and periodically review internal policies intended to prevent UPSI leakage, ensuring those policies are aligned with the PIT Regulations and related statutory/regulatory requirements. In addition, companies must conduct periodic training and awareness programs for all employees and fiduciaries on the correct manner of handling UPSI, so that compliance is embedded across the organization rather than left only to legal or compliance teams.

Further, listed entities must ensure that their internal Code of Conduct under the PIT Regulations is complied with and is actually operationalized in day-to-day conduct. The notice closes by advising companies to implement any other measures necessary to achieve the objectives of the PIT Regulations, which means compliance teams should treat this as an expectation to proactively strengthen controls beyond the minimum listed items where needed.

rows.summary:
SEBI has issued Notification No. **SEBI/LAD-NRO/GN/2026/312 dated July 10, 2026**, making a further amendment to the **SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015**. The amendment is titled the **SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2026**.

For compliance purposes, the key point in this notice is that the amended regulations **take effect immediately upon publication in the Official Gazette**; no separate implementation date, grace period, or transitional timeline is provided in the notice itself. The notice is addressed to **all listed companies**, so every entity whose securities are listed on a recognized stock exchange should treat this as applicable unless the underlying Gazette notification specifies a narrower scope.

The circular does **not** describe the substantive regulatory changes, thresholds, reporting obligations, or filing deadlines introduced by the amendment; it only states that the notification is attached for reference and instructs listed companies to “take note and comply accordingly.” Accordingly, a compliance team should review the attached Gazette notification and update internal LODR compliance checklists, disclosure controls, and board/management processes as needed once the precise amended provisions are identified.

rows.summary:
This notice updates the Exchange’s “single filing system” through API-based integration between stock exchanges, building on Exchange notice no. 20240930-60 dated September 30, 2024. The key change is that, effective June 20, 2026, the single filing system is extended to cover XBRL filings for the listed disclosure events set out in the notice, and the Exchange will treat the initial PDF filing as compliance under Regulation 30 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015. However, listed entities must then file the same disclosure in XBRL mode within 24 hours of submitting the PDF filing, so the PDF is no longer the end of the process for these covered events.

The notice also states that the XBRL utility for the single event under Para B of Part A of Schedule III of SEBI LODR 2015 relating to awarding, bagging/receiving, amendment, or termination of awarded/bagged orders/contracts not in the ordinary course of business will be discontinued effective June 20, 2026, because it will be merged into the single utility for Para B events. The Exchange says the new XBRL utilities will be available in the Listing Center path “Listing Compliance >> XBRL >> XBRL utility,” and the resulting XBRL filings will also be published in iXBRL (readable) format on the Exchange website at https://www.bseindia.com/corporates/ann.

The disclosures brought into the API-based single filing/XBRL framework include the following Regulation 30 and related events: commencement or postponement of commercial production/operations; strategic, technical, manufacturing, or marketing tie-ups; adoption of new line(s) of business; closure of operations of any unit/division/subsidiary; capacity addition or product launch; the award/bagging/receipt/amendment/termination of orders or contracts not in the normal course of business; binding agreements and changes/termination of those agreements; disruption of operations due to natural calamity, force majeure, strikes, or lockouts; effects of changes in the regulatory framework; material litigation/dispute developments; frauds or defaults by employees affecting the listed entity; options to purchase securities including ESOP/ESPS; guarantees/indemnities/surety provided for third parties; grant, withdrawal, surrender, cancellation, or suspension of key licenses or regulatory approvals; and delay or default in payment of fines, penalties, dues, etc. to any regulatory, statutory, enforcement, or judicial authority.

The notice also extends the system to certain other disclosure categories with their own effective dates: schedule of analysts’ or institutional investors’ meetings, investor presentation, transcripts, and audio/video recording under Regulation 30 read with sub-para 15 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III becomes covered from May 29, 2026; actions initiated or orders passed by any regulatory, statutory, enforcement authority or judicial body under Regulation 30 read with sub-para 19 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III becomes covered from May 29, 2026; actions taken or orders passed by any regulatory, statutory, enforcement authority or judicial body under sub-para 20 becomes covered from May 29, 2026; initiation of forensic audit under Regulation 30 read with sub-para 17 becomes covered from May 05, 2026; and prohibition of insider trading under Regulation 7(2) of the SEBI PIT Regulations becomes covered from May 05, 2026. For the categories visible in the notice, the applicability is indicated for listed entities that are equity-only, equity-plus-debt, and, for some events, exclusively debt and REIT/InvIT categories, so compliance teams should check the entity type against the applicability matrix before assuming the filing route applies.

The operational compliance obligation introduced by the notice is therefore two-step: make the required disclosure in PDF form first, then file the corresponding XBRL version within 24 hours for the events covered by the new system, while also noting that some event-specific XBRL utilities are being discontinued and consolidated. Entities subject to SEBI LODR and, where applicable, SEBI PIT should update internal disclosure calendars, escalation workflows, and filing controls to ensure the PDF-to-XBRL timing requirement is met from the relevant effective dates, especially the June 20, 2026 go-live for the expanded Para B/XBRL single filing coverage.

rows.summary:
This notice does not create a new substantive rule; it issues an FAQ annex for listed entities to use when submitting the “Quarterly Integrated Filing – Governance,” which is the renamed form of the former Corporate Governance Report. The notice is addressed to all listed entities and was issued on 12 Jun 2026 as Notice No. 20260612-13 under the Listing Compliance-Monitoring department. The only express compliance instruction in the notice itself is that listed entities should take note of the attached FAQs and comply accordingly when preparing and submitting the governance filing.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that the governance filing terminology has changed from “Corporate Governance Report” to “Integrated Filing – Governance,” and the exchange is providing guidance through the annexed FAQs on how to submit it. No separate effective date, deadline, threshold, rate, or financial amount is stated in the notice text provided. The operational obligation is therefore to review the attached FAQ document and ensure internal filing procedures, templates, and responsibility assignments reflect the updated filing name and any clarification contained in the annexure.

rows.title: Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 54L of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
rows.desc: NOTICE NoticeNo. 20260601-34 NoticeDate 01Jun2026 Category CircularsListedCompanies Segment Equity Department ListingOperations Subject Pre-PackagedInsolvencyResolutionProcessunderSection54Lof theInsolvencyandBankruptcyCode,2016 Attachments NoAttachment To All Listed Entities, Sub: Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 54L of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 Attention is invited to the provisions relating to Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (“PPIRP”) under Chapter III-A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (“IBC”). In this regard, as advised by SEBI, it is clarified that, the exemptions available under various SEBI Regulations in respect of a Resolution Plan approved under Section 31 of the IBC are not available in case of a Resolution Plan approved under Section 54L of the IBC under the PPIRP framework. Accordingly, listed entities undergoing PPIRP shall be required to comply with all applicable procedural and regulatory requirements prescribed under the relevant SEBI Regulations. The listed entities are advised to take note of the above and ensure compliance of the same. For and on behalf of BSE Limited Vishal Jhaveri Janardhan Wagle Deputy Chief Regulatory Officer - Issuer Oversight Deputy Vice President Listing Compliance Listing Compliance June 01, 2026
rows.summary:
This circular applies to **all listed entities** and concerns the **Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP)** under **Chapter III-A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016**, specifically a resolution plan approved under **Section 54L** of the IBC. BSE states, based on advice from **SEBI**, that the **regulatory exemptions that are available under various SEBI Regulations for a resolution plan approved under Section 31 of the IBC do not apply** when the resolution plan is approved under **Section 54L** in the PPIRP framework.

As a result, any listed company undergoing **PPIRP** must **comply fully with all applicable procedural and regulatory requirements** prescribed under the relevant SEBI regulations; there is no carve-out or exemption simply because the resolution plan is approved under PPIRP. The notice does not introduce any new numeric thresholds, filing deadlines, or rate changes, but it does impose a clear compliance expectation: listed entities in PPIRP should review all applicable SEBI listing and procedural obligations and ensure they are met in the same way as required outside the exempted Section 31 insolvency context. The notice is dated **01 June 2026** and instructs listed entities to take note and ensure compliance immediately.

rows.summary:
The exchange is extending its **single filing system through API-based integration between stock exchanges** to cover additional **XBRL filings** for listed entities, effective **29 May 2026**, building on the earlier framework referenced in **Exchange notice no. 20240930-60 dated 30 September 2024**. From that date, certain disclosures submitted through one exchange can be shared through the integrated system so that listed entities do not need to file separately across participating exchanges for the covered events, subject to the applicability indicated in the notice.

The update applies primarily to **listed entities with equity, equity+debt, and in some cases exclusively debt securities and REITs/InvITs**, depending on the disclosure type. The notice specifically states that the system is now available for filings such as: analyst/institutional investor meeting schedules, investor presentations, transcripts, and audio/video recordings; actions initiated or orders passed by regulatory, statutory, enforcement, or judicial bodies; actions taken or orders passed by such authorities; initiation of forensic audit; prohibition of insider trading disclosures under **Regulation 7(2) of the SEBI PIT Regulations**; board meeting outcomes for dividend, buyback, bonus, and voluntary delisting; agreements/contracts/arrangements/MOUs under **Regulation 30** and Schedule III; notice of shareholders’ meetings; CIRP events; issuance/allotment/alteration/restriction on transferability of securities; awards/bagging/receiving/amendment/termination of orders not in the normal course of business; loss of share certificate/duplicate share certificate matters under **Regulation 39**; annual report XBRL filing under **Regulation 34**; acquisitions/amalgamations/mergers/demergers/sale/disposal/restructuring; and changes in directors, KMPs, senior management, auditors, compliance officer, and registrar/transfer agent, including resignation-related filings and supporting resignation letters. It also covers filings for **Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report** under **Regulation 34(2)(f)**, prior intimation of board meetings under **Regulation 29**, closure of trading window under the SEBI PIT Regulations, fraud/default/arrest disclosures, corporate debt restructuring, resolution plans/restructuring relating to bank/financial institution borrowings and inter-creditor arrangements, and one-time settlement (OTS) matters; the notice additionally mentions an **Issue Summary Document (ISD) for buyback via open and tender route** in the list, but the text provided cuts off before the full details of that item.

The notice includes several **specific effective dates** for certain filings becoming available under the integrated single-filing utility: **21 February 2026** for fraud/default/arrest; **7 March 2026** for prior intimation for board meetings; **31 March 2026** for the BRSR; **20 April 2026** for the annual report XBRL; **25 April 2026** for board meeting outcomes relating to dividend/buyback/bonus/voluntary delisting; **5 May 2026** for forensic audit and prohibition of insider trading; and **29 May 2026** for the investor meeting-related disclosures, regulatory/judicial action disclosures, and action/orders passed disclosures. The notice uses applicability markers indicating that many of these filings are available for **equity** and **equity+debt** listed entities, while some are also available for **exclusively debt** and **REITs/InvITs**; compliance teams should check their security class against the table because not every disclosure is enabled for every category.

For compliance purposes, the practical requirement is that covered listed entities should use the **API-based single filing route** for the specified XBRL disclosures once the relevant effective date has arrived, rather than treating the filing as exchange-specific manual submissions. The notice also highlights a procedural enhancement for resignation-related disclosures: the utility allows submission of both the resignation details and the **resignation letter(s)** required under **sub-paras 7A, 7B, and 7C of Para A, Part A of Schedule III** of SEBI LODR.
