rows.title: Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)on application filed under Regulation 37 of SEBI (Listing Obligation and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 w.r.t. Scheme of Arrangements
rows.summary:
This NSE circular, dated **November 2, 2021** (Download Ref. No. **NSE/CML/2021/43**), sets out a **standard operating procedure for listed companies filing a draft Scheme of Arrangement under Regulation 37 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015** for stock exchange **NOC/observation** before approaching NCLT. It applies to **all listed companies** submitting such schemes and is issued with reference to the earlier **SEBI circular dated March 10, 2017**, its amendments, and the **SEBI Master Circular dated December 22, 2020**.

A listed entity must **submit the scheme to the stock exchange within 15 working days of the board meeting approving the draft scheme**, together with **all documents required under the exchange checklist**. If the filing is not made within that 15-working-day window, the company must obtain **fresh board approval** based on updated inputs such as **fresh financials and valuation report**, rather than relying on the earlier approval. At the time of filing, the company must also provide the **audited financials of the last 3 years** for any **unlisted company(ies) involved in the scheme**, and those financial statements must **not be older than 6 months** at the time of submission; these financials are specifically to be used for the valuer’s **Income Approach**. In addition, the exchange will require an **undertaking** from the listed entity that the unlisted company financials will still be **no more than 6 months old when the scheme papers are filed with NCLT**.

For valuation materials other than the Income Approach, the **period under consideration cannot be older than 3 months**. The **board must consider the scheme within 7 working days of issuance of the valuation report**, so the company needs to align its internal approval process with that deadline. The circular also makes clear that the filing submitted under Regulation 37 must be **complete in all respects** with all documents listed in **para I(A)(2) of the March 10, 2017 SEBI circular** as amended and the relevant exchange checklist; incomplete submissions or material non-compliances can trigger rejection and return of the application.

The SOP then defines a strict query-and-rectification process. If the exchange finds the documents incomplete, needs clarification, or identifies any **material inadequacy/non-compliance**, it will raise an **“Exchange 1st Query”** and return the scheme to the company for rectification, allowing only **5 working days** to cure the defects. If the company cannot respond within that period, **any fee paid for processing the application will be forfeited** by the exchange/regulator and the scheme documents will be returned. If further clarification is needed after the company’s response, the exchange may issue an **“Exchange 2nd Query”** and provide a similar response period; if the exchange does not receive adequate responses within the applicable timelines, the company may have to **re-file the scheme as a fresh application**, again with **forfeiture of the earlier fee**.

Where a filing is re-submitted because the earlier filing was unsatisfactory, the company must file a **fresh set of valuation report, fairness opinion, recommendation of the audit committee, and related materials**, and it must also pay **fresh fees** to the exchange/regulator. In practical terms, this SOP imposes tighter timing and completeness requirements on Regulation 37 scheme filings, increases the risk of forfeited fees for delay or inadequate responses, and requires listed entities to ensure that their internal board, valuation, and documentation processes are coordinated so the filing remains within the prescribed age limits and response deadlines.

rows.title: Transmission of Securities to joint Holder(s)
rows.summary:
This circular is a forwarder from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited, dated October 19, 2021, addressed to the Company Secretary of all listed companies through the stock exchanges. It notifies listed companies that SEBI issued Notification/Circular No. SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD_RTAMB/P/CIR/2021/644 on October 18, 2021, titled “Transmission of Securities to joint Holder(s),” and states that the SEBI circular is enclosed and should be acted on as necessary. The NSE circular itself does not set out the substantive transmission procedure, thresholds, or deadlines; rather, it serves as an information and compliance alert directing listed companies to review the underlying SEBI notification.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that there is a new SEBI requirement concerning transmission of securities in the case of joint holders, and listed companies must align their processes with that SEBI direction. The NSE specifically says the circular is for information and for “necessary action at your end,” indicating that affected entities are listed companies and their registrar/share transfer or investor servicing functions, to the extent they handle transmission requests involving joint holdings. Because the NSE note does not reproduce the substantive rules, the exact operational obligations, effective mechanics, and any documentary or procedural requirements must be obtained from the referenced SEBI notification itself.

rows.title: XBRL based filing of Related Party Transactions for Listed Companies at NSE
rows.summary:
NSE Circular NSE/CML/2021/42 dated October 19, 2021 clarifies the earlier requirement in NSE circular NSE/CML/2021/34 dated September 6, 2021, which had mandated that all listed companies file Related Party Transactions disclosures under Regulation 23(9) in XBRL mode only. The October 19 circular carves out an exception for listed banking companies: for the half year ended September 30, 2021, they are not required to use XBRL for this filing and should continue submitting Related Party Transactions in PDF format instead.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the XBRL-only filing obligation still applies to listed companies generally, but listed banking companies received a one-time relief for the September 30, 2021 half-year reporting period. The document does not specify any other change to the content of the disclosure, any new threshold, or any new deadline beyond the existing half-yearly Regulation 23(9) reporting cycle; it only changes the format requirement for this particular class of companies and this specific reporting period.

rows.title: Contact details of NSE’s Listing department officials
rows.summary: NSE has published the contact details of its Listing department officials, together with the specific profiles they handle, on the NEAPS portal under **Help > Contact Us**. This is aimed at improving operational convenience and giving listed companies a direct reference for resolving listing-related queries. Listed companies are advised that they may contact the relevant NSE officers for query resolution **between 9:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m. on all working days**. The notice also states that **NSE Circular No. NSE/CML/2018/34 dated November 27, 2018 has been repealed**, so any prior guidance or reference contained in that circular should no longer be relied upon.

rows.title: Amendments to manner and mechanism of providing exit option to dissenting unit holders pursuant to Regulation 22(6A) and Regulation 22(8) of SEBI (Real Estate Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014 (“SEBI (REIT) Regulations”)
rows.summary: This circular is a transmission notice from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited to all REITs, informing them of a SEBI notification dated October 5, 2021 that amends the “manner and mechanism” for providing an exit option to dissenting unit holders under Regulation 22(6A) and Regulation 22(8) of the SEBI (REIT) Regulations, 2014. The NSE letter itself does not spell out the substantive rule changes; it advises REITs that SEBI has issued the amendment and that the enclosed SEBI circular/notification should be reviewed and acted upon as necessary. The affected entities are all Real Estate Investment Trusts and, by implication, their managers/operating teams responsible for handling unitholder approvals and dissenting-holder exit processes. The only explicit date in the notice is the SEBI notification date and the NSE circular date, both October 5, 2021, and no separate implementation deadline, threshold, rate, or procedural detail is provided in the NSE covering circular itself. For compliance purposes, the key action is to obtain and review the attached SEBI circular/notification because that is the operative document containing the actual amended requirements.

rows.title: Amendments to manner and mechanism of providing exit option to dissenting unit holders pursuant to Regulation 22(5C) and Regulation 22(7) of SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014 (“SEBI (InvIT) Regulations”)
rows.summary:
This circular is an intimation from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited to all Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) that SEBI has amended the rules governing the exit option to dissenting unit holders under Regulation 22(5C) and Regulation 22(7) of the SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014. The NSE circular itself does not restate the substance of the amendment; it only identifies the SEBI notification, No. SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS_Div3/P/CIR/2021/639, dated October 5, 2021, and directs InvITs to refer to the enclosed SEBI circular for necessary action. The compliance impact is therefore on all InvITs that may need to provide an exit option in connection with the specified regulatory provisions, but this document does not specify the revised procedure, thresholds, pricing, timelines, or implementation mechanics in the text provided.

For a compliance team, the key points from this document are: the amendment exists, it is effective as of October 5, 2021, and InvITs are expected to align their processes with the SEBI notification. However, because the NSE notice is only a forwarding communication, it does not itself impose additional operational details beyond alerting recipients that the SEBI circular is available and should be followed. To determine the exact compliance obligations—such as the manner of offering the exit option, who qualifies as a dissenting unit holder, any deadlines for action, and any valuation or payment mechanics—the enclosed SEBI circular would need to be reviewed directly.

rows.title: Relaxations relating to procedural matters - Issues and Listing
rows.summary: The notice is a transmission from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited to all listed companies informing them of SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/DIL2/CIR/P/2021/633 dated October 1, 2021, titled “Relaxations relating to procedural matters – Issues and Listing.” On its face, the document does not itself create new substantive requirements, thresholds, or deadlines; it simply forwards the SEBI circular for the recipient’s information and “necessary action,” and states that the circular is enclosed for reference. The affected entities are all listed companies, particularly those involved in issues and listing processes that are governed by SEBI’s procedural framework. For compliance purposes, the key point is that any company undertaking an issue/listing activity should review the enclosed SEBI circular and determine whether any procedural relaxations or updated filing/listing steps apply to its current or planned transaction. No specific numeric thresholds, rates, or deadline dates are stated in this NSE cover note itself.

rows.title: Guidance note on Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulation 23(9) regarding disclosure of related party transactions
rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) issued this clarification on September 29, 2021, to supplement its earlier guidance note dated April 1, 2021 and its September 6, 2021 circular on XBRL-based filing of related party transactions. The clarification concerns disclosure obligations under Regulation 23(9) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, and it is directed to all listed companies/“listed entities.”

The substantive change is a filing-format clarification for related party transaction disclosures: if a listed entity files only standalone financial results under Regulation 33, it must also disclose related party transactions on a standalone basis under Regulation 23(9). If a listed entity files both standalone and consolidated financial results under Regulation 33, it must disclose related party transactions only on a consolidated basis under Regulation 23(9), not separately on a standalone basis. The circular does not introduce a new monetary threshold, rate, or quantitative limit; instead, it clarifies the basis of reporting that compliance teams must use to ensure the RPT disclosure aligns with the type of financial results being filed.

For compliance purposes, the key obligation is to match the related party transaction submission to the financial reporting scope already used under Regulation 33. Listed entities should review their existing filing workflow and confirm whether their quarterly/periodic financial results are standalone-only or both standalone and consolidated, because that determines whether the Regulation 23(9) disclosure must be standalone or consolidated. The circular is effective immediately from its date of issuance, September 29, 2021, and is intended to be read together with the earlier NSE guidance and the XBRL filing requirements for listed companies at NSE.

rows.title: Bank accounts for payment of fees to SEBI under the SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014, SEBI (Real Estate Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014, SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003, SEBI (Issue and Listing of Non-convertible Securities) Regulations, 2021 and SEBI (Issue and Listing of Securitized Debt Instruments and Security Receipts) Regulations, 2008
rows.summary:
This circular informs InvITs, REITs, issuers of public issues of non-convertible securities, securitised debt instruments, and security receipts that SEBI has changed the way regulatory and filing fees must be paid. Effective **October 1, 2021**, fees are to be remitted **only to designated SEBI virtual accounts** maintained with **ICICI Bank Ltd.** (IFSC **ICIC0000106**) in the name of **Securities and Exchange Board of India**; the circular also specifies separate virtual account codes for each fee type, including filing fees for InvITs and REITs, regulatory fees for public issues of debt securities and non-convertible redeemable preference shares, filing fees for public issues of securitised debt instruments, registration fees for trustee/SPDE applications, registration and annual fees, exemption fees under LODR/NCS, and Informal Guidance fees. The circular specifically requires that **application fee and registration fee payments for REIT and InvIT registration be made only through the SEBI Intermediary Portal**, not by any other channel.

The document warns issuers not to use any alternate payment mode because doing so may create reconciliation problems and delay processing. It also imposes a notification requirement: immediately after remitting fees, the remitter must email SEBI at **od-ddhs@sebi.gov.in** with the remittance particulars in a prescribed format, including the **name of remitter, date of remittance, amount remitted, name of origin bank, UTR/transaction reference number, and purpose of remittance**. For compliance purposes, the key operational change is that from the effective date onward, all covered entities must use the specified virtual accounts/portal and provide the remittance details promptly to SEBI to avoid processing delays or reconciliation issues.

rows.title: XBRL based filing of Related Party Transactions for Listed Companies at NSE
rows.summary:
This NSE circular, dated **September 6, 2021** (Ref. **NSE/CML/2021/34**), applies to **all listed companies** and implements a new filing method for **Related Party Transactions disclosures under Regulation 23(9) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015**. Under Regulation 23(9), listed entities must submit, **within 30 days from the date of publication of their standalone and consolidated financial results for the half-year**, related party transaction disclosures on a **consolidated basis**; this circular does not change that underlying deadline, but it changes the filing format.

The key change is that NSE, in consultation with SEBI, has made **XBRL filing mandatory for Related Party Transactions submissions** under Regulation 23(9), **with immediate effect**. The circular expressly states that such filings **should be filed by all listed companies in XBRL mode only**, so paper, email, or non-XBRL submissions are no longer the compliant route for this requirement. NSE has attached an **Excel utility** (Annexure 1) that companies must use to prepare the report in the prescribed XBRL format.

For submission, companies must use the **NEAPS portal** and upload the generated **XML/XBRL file** through **Compliance > Common XBRL upload > Related Party Transactions** in the Modules dropdown, selecting the appropriate **financial year** and **period type** before uploading. The circular allows two ways to generate the XML: either by using an XBRL utility provided by another stock exchange and uploading the resulting XML, or by using the **NSE-provided Related Party Transactions Excel utility** to generate the XML and then uploading it. After successful upload, the system displays **“File Uploaded successfully”** and an **acknowledgement email** is sent to the registered email address.

If a company has difficulty with the process or needs clarification, NSE directs it to contact **nsexbrl@nse.co.in**. From a compliance perspective, the main operational obligation is to ensure that every Regulation 23(9) related party transaction disclosure is now prepared and filed **only in XBRL/XML format through NEAPS**, within the existing **30-day post-financial-results deadline**.

rows.title: Guidelines on issuance of non-convertible debt instruments along with warrants (''NCDs with Warrants’) in terms of Chapter VI – Qualified Institutions Placement of SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
rows.summary:
This notice is a forwarding circular addressed to **all listed companies** by the National Stock Exchange of India Limited, drawing attention to **SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/DIL/CIR/P/2021/614 dated August 13, 2021**. The referenced SEBI circular introduces **guidelines for issuing non-convertible debt instruments together with warrants (“NCDs with Warrants”)** under **Chapter VI on Qualified Institutions Placement (QIP)** of the **SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018**.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that SEBI has issued a formal framework governing this specific fundraising structure, so any listed company considering a QIP-style issuance that combines **debt instruments and warrants** must review and follow the SEBI circular’s requirements before proceeding. The text provided here does **not itself set out the substantive conditions, thresholds, pricing rules, allotment mechanics, or timelines**; instead, it serves as an information/forwarding communication and states that the SEBI circular is enclosed “for your reference and for necessary action.”  

No separate deadline is stated in this notice beyond the fact that the underlying SEBI circular is dated **August 13, 2021**, and no additional procedures are prescribed in the covering letter itself. The only affected entities identified in the notice are **listed companies**, and the relevant activity is the **issuance of NCDs along with warrants under the QIP framework**.

rows.title: Disclosure of shareholding pattern of promoter(s) and promoter group entities
rows.summary:

rows.title: Automation of Continual Disclosures under Regulation 7(2) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 - System driven disclosures - Ease of doing business
rows.summary:

For compliance purposes, the key point is that this relates to **continual disclosures under Regulation 7(2) of the SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015**, which are the disclosures connected with insider trading reporting obligations, and the change is specifically described as **automation/system-driven disclosures**. The circular is addressed to the **Company Secretary of all listed companies**, so the affected population is all entities whose securities are listed on NSE and, by extension, companies subject to SEBI PIT reporting obligations.  

The NSE circular is dated **August 16, 2021** and points readers to the NSE website for access to the circular, but it does **not itself provide a separate compliance deadline, numerical threshold, or implementation date beyond the reference to SEBI’s August 13, 2021 notification**. A compliance officer should therefore treat this as a notice to review the underlying SEBI circular immediately and assess any operational changes needed to support the shift to system-generated disclosure reporting under Regulation 7(2).

rows.title: Holding of Annual General Meeting (AGM) by top 100 listed entities by market capitalization
rows.summary: The National Stock Exchange of India issued this 23 July 2021 communication to all listed entities in the top 100 by market capitalization, forwarding SEBI Notification No. SEBI/HO/CFD/CMD1/P/CIR/2021/602 dated 23 July 2021 on “Holding of Annual General Meeting (AGM) by top 100 listed entities by market capitalization.” The NSE letter itself does not create new obligations; it simply informs companies that SEBI has issued the attached circular and that they should take necessary action in line with it. rows.title: Continuous disclosures in compliances by InvITs -Amendments
rows.summary: This NSE communication does not itself create new compliance requirements; it forwards SEBI Notification No. SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS_Div3/P/CIR/2021/600 dated 22 July 2021, titled “Continuous disclosures in compliances by InvITs - Amendments,” to all Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) for information and necessary action. rows.title: Continuous disclosures in compliances by REITs - Amendments

rows.title: Guidance note for companies undergoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process
rows.summary:
This NSE guidance note, dated July 9, 2021, is addressed to all listed companies and is specifically relevant to companies undergoing a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). It is issued as a reference to earlier IBBI Circular No. IP/002/2018 dated January 3, 2018, and reiterates that an insolvency professional acting as Interim Resolution Professional, Resolution Professional, or Liquidator must exercise reasonable care and diligence to ensure the corporate person complies with applicable laws; if non-compliance occurs because of the insolvency professional’s conduct, that professional may be responsible for it, and any loss or penalty arising from non-compliance is not to be treated as CIRP cost or liquidation cost.

The document emphasizes that CIRP companies must comply with applicable securities and listing laws, including the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018, as reflected in the LODR framework. It notes that LODR was amended in 2018 to insert point 16 in Para A of Part A of Schedule III, effective May 31, 2018, requiring disclosures at various stages of CIRP, and that SEBI further amended the disclosure framework in 2021, effective January 8, 2021, to enhance the disclosure requirements. The Exchange states that the LODR framework already contains the list of CIRP-related events that must be disclosed, and companies/insolvency professionals must follow those requirements in addition to ordinary listing compliance.

Beyond the existing LODR disclosure obligations, the note adds three specific Exchange submission requirements, in consultation with SEBI. First, the company must provide at least two working days’ prior intimation of the date of the NCLT hearing at which the resolution plan will be considered. Second, the approval of the resolution plan must be disclosed to the Exchange immediately upon oral pronouncement or otherwise of the order, and in any event no later than 30 minutes after such pronouncement. Third, the Resolution Professional must use the Exchange platform to inform investors of any effect of the resolution plan on existing holders of listed securities, including impacts on the status of listing, the value of holdings, and any write-off, cancellation, or extinguishment of existing equity shares, preference shares, debentures, or similar securities without payment to holders, where applicable.

The note also directs companies and Resolution Professionals to maintain confidentiality of the resolution plan until the relevant details are submitted on the Exchange platform. It concludes by reminding recipients that this guidance is only an aid and does not replace the obligation to comply with the Listing Regulations and any other applicable regulations as amended from time to time.

rows.title: Standard Operating Procedure for listed subsidiary company desirous of getting delisted through a Scheme of Arrangement wherein the listed parent holding company and the listed subsidiary are in the same line of business

For compliance purposes, the operative subject matter is a standard operating procedure governing a listed subsidiary that wants to be delisted through a scheme of arrangement where both the listed parent holding company and the listed subsidiary operate in the same line of business. The notice does not provide the procedure’s substantive steps, thresholds, or conditions; it only alerts regulated entities that such a SEBI framework now exists and may require action by affected companies considering this transaction structure.

The affected entities are listed companies with equity and convertibles on NSE, especially those in a parent-subsidiary structure in the same business line contemplating a delisting via scheme of arrangement. No compliance deadline, numerical threshold, or filing date is stated in the notice itself beyond the circular’s issue date of 6 July 2021. rows.title: Guidance Note on Analyst/Institutional Investors meet
rows.summary:
This guidance note from the National Stock Exchange of India (NSE), dated June 29, 2021, explains clarifications arising from SEBI’s May 5, 2021 amendments to the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, specifically the enhanced disclosure requirement under point 15 of para A of Part A of Schedule III. For analyst/institutional investor interactions, NSE clarifies that disclosure of **group meetings** is mandatory, including both the **schedule** of the meeting and the **post-meeting disclosures**, but disclosure for **one-on-one meetings** is **not mandatory** under this particular clarification. It also states that **audio or video recordings and transcripts of post-earnings/quarterly calls**—whether held physically or through digital means and regardless of whether conducted by the listed entity itself or by any other entity—must be disclosed to the recognized stock exchange.

The note then adds a further compliance expectation under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, but only **if Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) is actually shared during the meet**. SEBI/NSE’s concern is that analyst/research/investor meetings involving representatives of the listed company, even if not organized by the company, may result in selective disclosure and information asymmetry if price-sensitive information is communicated. To avoid this, all listed companies are required to disclose the **audio recordings or transcripts of all such meetings where UPSI is shared**, regardless of whether the meeting was arranged by the listed company or by another party.

The compliance basis cited for this requirement is **Regulation 8(1) of Chapter IV** of the SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015, read with **Schedule A** (the code of fair disclosure and conduct). No specific implementation date is stated in the note beyond the underlying regulatory change already effective from the SEBI amendment date referenced above, so compliance teams should treat this as an immediate disclosure obligation for covered meetings and calls. The practical takeaway is that listed companies should ensure they can identify whether UPSI was discussed in analyst/investor interactions, and if so, preserve and disclose the relevant recordings or transcripts to the exchange, while also continuing to comply with any future amendments to the applicable regulations.

rows.title: FAQ’s - LODR amendments dated May 05, 2021
rows.summary:
SEBI amended the LODR Regulations, 2015 by notification dated May 5, 2021, and NSE issued these FAQs on June 28, 2021 to explain how listed companies should apply the changes. The note is advisory in form, but the underlying message is that listed entities must comply with the amended LODR provisions and any other applicable regulations, and the FAQs are only for assistance.

For applicability under regulation 3(2), the market-capitalization cutoff date to determine whether the amended provisions apply is **March 31, 2021**. For the revised risk management committee rules in regulation 21(2) and 21(5) and the related Schedule III, Part D requirement to frame a detailed risk management policy, the companies already subject to RMC requirements (the then-top 500 companies) must comply with the amended regulation 21(2) within **3 months from the date of notification or by the next board meeting, whichever is later**; companies newly brought in through the expansion from top 500 to top 1000 must comply within **6 months from the date of notification or by the next board meeting, whichever is later**. Regulation 21(2) now requires the Risk Management Committee to have **at least 3 members**, with a majority being board members, including **at least 1 independent director**; if the listed entity has outstanding **SR equity shares**, then **two-thirds of the RMC must be independent directors**.

The frequency of RMC meetings under regulation 21(3A) changes from “once” to **twice**, and this amended requirement applies only to companies whose financial year ends **after September 30, 2021**; it does **not** apply to companies with a financial year ended **June 30, 2021**. NSE’s examples clarify that companies with financial year ends on or before **September 30, 2021** are required to hold **1** RMC meeting, while companies with financial year ends after that date, such as **December 31, 2021** or **March 31, 2022**, must hold **2** meetings.

The FAQs also state that corporate governance provisions apply to **public sector banks** starting **September 1, 2021**. For regulation 31A reclassification matters, if notice to shareholders was sent **before May 5, 2021**, the **old** version of regulation 31A applies; if the application is being made under the proviso to sub-regulation 3(a)(iii), it must be filed with the exchange within **30 days of the board meeting**. Finally, under regulation 30(6) and Schedule III, when a board meeting continues across more than one day without interruption, the disclosure of the board meeting outcome/financial results must be filed within **30 minutes from the actual end of the meeting**, not 30 minutes after the end of the day on which the item was considered.

rows.title: Action(s) to be initiated against listed companies for non-payment of outstanding Annual Listing Fees (“ALF”)
rows.summary:
This circular directs listed entities that have not paid outstanding Annual Listing Fees (“ALF”) to comply with SEBI’s SOP for non-payment, and it applies specifically to all listed entities with unpaid ALF. The exchange will first send reminder letters for up to six months from the date the ALF invoice is issued; if the fee remains unpaid after that six-month period, the exchange will issue a notice giving the company 15 days to pay. If payment is still not made within that 15-day notice period, the exchange will stop granting approval for further listing of securities.

If the default continues, the exchange will then issue notice(s) to the promoter(s) of the defaulting entity based on information available with the exchange, requiring compliance and payment of the ALF within 30 days. Promoters may submit representations only by email to **listingsop@nse.in** within the stipulated time; representations sent by any other mode, to any other email address, or after the deadline will not be treated as valid and the exchange will proceed with action. If the ALF still is not paid within 30 days of the promoter notice, the exchange will inform depositories to freeze the demat accounts of the promoter(s), using the latest shareholding pattern and promoter/promoter-group disclosures filed by the company.

If the fee remains unpaid even after **three months from the freezing action**, the exchange will issue another notice to the entity requiring payment within **30 days**; failing that, the securities will be suspended from trading. The exchange will also give the market a **30-day notice** of the proposed suspension. After suspension is initiated, the shares will be allowed to trade only on a **“trade to trade” basis on the first trading day of every week** until the ALF is paid; once payment is made, weekly trading will stop and all punitive actions taken under this process will be reversed, with a public notice issued by the exchange.

The circular also states that if the entity’s securities are already suspended for other reasons, including but not limited to non-payment of ALF, those other suspension actions will continue to apply, and ALF-related actions may operate alongside any other actions imposed by the exchanges. Where a company is listed on more than one stock exchange, the actions relating to denial of listing approvals, freezing of promoter demat accounts, trading suspension, and reversal of such actions must be coordinated among the exchanges. Finally, the stated measures do **not** apply to **Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)**, though the PSU exemption also extends to freezing of PSU promoter demat accounts, and the document begins to exclude companies with only debt/infrastructure-related listings, but that sentence is cut off in the provided text.

rows.title: Relaxation from the requirement of minimum vesting period in case of death of employee(s) under SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefit) Regulations, 2014
rows.summary:
This notice from NSE informs all listed entities that SEBI issued Circular No. **SEBI/HO/CFD/DCR2/CIR/P/2021/576 dated June 15, 2021**, titled **“Relaxation from the requirement of minimum vesting period in case of death of employee(s) under SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefit) Regulations, 2014.”** The practical effect is that, under the **SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefit) Regulations, 2014**, the usual **minimum vesting period requirement is relaxed when an employee dies**, so listed companies operating employee stock option/share-based benefit plans should not apply the standard vesting minimum in that death scenario.

The NSE communication itself is dated **June 16, 2021** and is addressed to the **Company Secretary of all listed entities**, indicating the change is relevant to any listed company that has or administers share-based employee benefit plans. No numerical thresholds, rates, or monetary limits are stated in this NSE notice; the key compliance point is that companies should review their plan rules, vesting schedules, and administration procedures to ensure that vesting treatment on an employee’s death aligns with the SEBI relaxation and does not continue to impose the normal minimum vesting period.

The circular is provided “for information and necessary action,” and NSE notes that the SEBI circular is also available on the NSE website. For compliance teams, the immediate action is to verify whether any existing scheme documents, trust arrangements, internal SOPs, or award letters need updating to reflect the death-related vesting relaxation and to ensure future grants or outstanding awards are administered consistently with the SEBI directive.

rows.title: Guidance note on communications by Listed Entities
rows.summary:
This guidance note, issued by the National Stock Exchange of India Limited on June 11, 2021, applies to all listed companies and is aimed at how they communicate with stakeholders through the Exchange platform/website and other public channels. NSE’s core direction is that listed entities must not disclose any price-sensitive information unless it has first been disclosed to the stock exchanges, and any public communication should be made with stakeholder protection in mind. The note specifically cautions that company updates, performance highlights, awards/recognition claims, leadership positioning statements, and interview comments by key managerial personnel or other representatives can all create compliance risk if they are inaccurate, incomplete, or misleading.

For public communications, the listed entity must ensure statements are truthful, fair, evidence-based, and not manipulative, deceptive, distorted, untrue, or misleading. Communications should use clear, concise, understandable, simple language, avoiding excessive technical or legal terminology, and should contain only adequate and appropriate detail so investors are not distracted by unnecessary information. The note also says companies should avoid making non-factual or unsubstantiated statements, and should not provide forward-looking statements; any information shared should be limited to publicly reported financial information.

If a listed entity includes financial data in a communication, it must also include comparable data for the past three years, along with particulars relating to sales, gross profit, net profit, share capital, reserves, earnings per share, dividends, debts, and book values. The company should also provide a link to the website where the relevant details are available and can be verified. This means financial performance claims need to be supported by a broader, transparent data set rather than selective figures.

The note is particularly strict on “leader,” “pioneer,” “expert,” or similar superiority claims: such positioning can only be made if based on factual data that is widely available, not on a single source unless that source is a recognized source with third-party certification. The company must identify the source of the claim, and that source information must be public and verifiable. Likewise, if the company publicizes awards or recognition, it must disclose whether it has any relationship with the awarding agency, the number of participants evaluated, whether the awarding agency is recognized in that field, and other publicly available information about the awarding body. The note is expressly “indicative,” but listed entities are expected to follow its substance to protect stakeholder interests.

rows.title: Comprehensive FAQs and Compilation of informal guidance- SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 (Period October 2015 - March 2021)
rows.summary:
This notice from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited, dated 4 May 2021, is an informational circular to all listed companies (sent through the stock exchanges) advising them of two SEBI reference documents relating to the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. The circular itself does **not** introduce new substantive requirements, deadlines, thresholds, or procedural changes; instead, it points compliance teams to SEBI’s published clarifications for use in interpreting and implementing the insider trading regime.

The two documents referenced are: (1) “Comprehensive FAQs on SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015,” dated 29 April 2021, and (2) “Compilation of Informal Guidance Relating to SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015 for the period Oct 2015–Mar 2021,” issued by SEBI on 3 May 2021. NSE provides direct URLs to both documents and states that copies are enclosed and also available on the NSE website. For compliance purposes, the practical significance is that listed companies should review these SEBI clarifications to ensure their insider trading policies, controls, disclosures, trading window procedures, designated person monitoring, and related compliance practices align with SEBI’s interpreted positions under the PIT Regulations.

Because the circular is only a forwarding notice, it does not itself specify which PIT provisions changed or what exact compliance actions are newly mandated. The only operative point is that SEBI has issued updated FAQs and an informal guidance compilation covering the period October 2015 through March 2021, and companies are expected to use those materials as authoritative interpretive guidance when assessing their existing insider trading compliance framework.

rows.summary:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has amended its earlier “Obligatory Cession for the financial year 2026–27” notification dated 9 April 2026. Using its powers under Section 101A(2) and (4) of the Insurance Act, 1938, and with approval of the Central Government after consultation with the Advisory Committee under Section 101B, IRDAI has replaced para 2 of that earlier notification.

The revised rule sets the obligatory cession at **4% of the sum insured on each General Insurance Policy** for insurance attaching during the financial year **1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027**. This means general insurers must reinsure that 4% portion with Indian reinsurer(s), but there is an explicit exception: the premium ceded to the **Terrorism Pool, Nuclear Pool, and Bharat Maritime Insurance Pool** will be **NIL**. In other words, those pool-related amounts are not subject to obligatory cession under this amendment.

A key compliance point is that the **entire obligatory cession must be placed only with General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re)**. For compliance teams, this means general insurers writing policies attaching in FY 2026–27 need to ensure their reinsurance placement processes, bordereaux, and reporting align with the 4% cession requirement and that the obligatory portion is routed exclusively to GIC Re, while excluding the specified pool premiums from cession.

The delegation concerns IRDAI’s powers under section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938, and it specifically reallocates who may issue directions under that provision.

Under the new arrangement, where the matter involves an enforcement proceeding for identified violations, the power to issue directions to a particular insurer or insurance intermediary has been delegated to a panel of two Whole Time Members constituted by the Chairperson. For any other matter under section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938, the power to issue directions remains with the Chairperson. The notification does not create a new substantive obligation for insurers or intermediaries, but it changes the internal IRDAI decision-making authority for section 34 directions, which matters for identifying the valid approving/signing authority in enforcement and other regulatory actions.

The notification is dated 15 April 2026 and was published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary on 16 April 2026. No separate compliance deadline, filing requirement, threshold, or monetary amount is set out in the text.

That means customers must continue to be able to purchase those products if available before the de-notification, even though the tariffs themselves are no longer legally in force.

From 1 April 2024 onward, any coverage falling within the scope of these de-notified tariffs must comply with the IRDAI (Insurance Products) Regulations, 2024 and the Authority’s Master Circular (Guidelines) on products and procedures in general insurance business. The **Insurance Ombudsman (Amendment) Rules, 2023** were issued by the Ministry of Finance under section 24 of the IRDA Act, 1999 and **came into force on the date of publication in the Official Gazette, 9 November 2023**. The amendments apply to the **Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017** and primarily update governance terminology, resignation procedures, compensation treatment, complaint-handling language, and award formalities.

In **rule 7(2)**, the references to **“Bank Board Bureau”** in clauses (b) and (c) are replaced with **“Financial Services Institutions Bureau.”** The explanation is also replaced to define that term specifically as the body constituted by the Ministry of Finance, Department of Financial Services through **Resolution F. No. 14/1/2022-BO-I dated 1 July 2022**. This is a nomenclature and reference update, but compliance teams should ensure any internal policies, templates, or delegation references to the appointing/recommending body use the new name.

In **rule 8**, a new resignation mechanism is inserted for an Insurance Ombudsman: the Ombudsman may resign by giving **written notice of not less than 90 days** to the **Council for Insurance Ombudsmen** in lieu of **three months’ salary**. If the final day of the notice period falls on a **Saturday, Sunday, or holiday**, the Ombudsman is to be relieved on the **next working day**. The Council also has explicit discretion to **waive the notice period in part or in full**. This affects how resignation letters, settlement of pay-in-lieu, and relieving dates are processed.

In **rule 10(1)**, the requirement that **any Central or State Government pension payable to the Ombudsman be deducted from salary** has been **deleted**. This changes the compensation calculation for any Ombudsman who receives a pension from government service, because that pension is no longer mandated to be offset against salary under the rule.

In **rule 16**, the marginal heading is revised to **“Complaint settled through mediation by Insurance Ombudsman,”** clarifying that the provision concerns mediation-based settlement. In **rule 17(2)**, awards issued by the Insurance Ombudsman must now be **in writing, duly signed personally or digitally**, and must include **reasons** for the award. Finally, in **rule 17(3) proviso clause (ii)**, the monetary figure **“thirty”** is replaced with **“fifty,”** increasing the relevant threshold under that proviso from **30 to 50** (the document does not restate the underlying unit in the excerpt, so the compliance team should read this as a direct increase in the amount referenced in rule 17(3)(ii)).

This IRDAI notification titled **“Obligatory Cession for the financial year 2023–24”** applies to **Indian Re-insurers and other insurers covered under Section 101A of the Insurance Act, 1938**. For all **general insurance policies attaching during 1 April 2023 through 31 March 2024**, insurers must cede **4% of the sum insured** as obligatory cession to Indian re-insurer(s), but **terrorism premium and premium ceded to the Nuclear pool are excluded and must be treated as NIL cession**. The notification also states that the **entire obligatory cession must be placed only with General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re)**, not spread across other reinsurers.

The document removes any **sum insured ceiling** for cessions made during this period, but it gives the Indian re-insurer the right to require **immediate underwriting information** for any cession above a limit specified by that reinsurer; ceding insurers must provide such information whenever those specified thresholds are exceeded. For commission on obligatory cession, the minimum rates are fixed by class: **5% for Motor TP and Oil & Energy insurance**, **10% for Group Health**, **7.5% for Crop Insurance**, **Averaging Terms for Aviation**, and **15% minimum for all other classes**, with any higher commission to be agreed separately between the parties.

The notification also sets the **profit commission framework** for the obligatory portfolio: the Indian re-insurer must share profit commission **50:50 with the ceding insurer**, based on the performance and surplus of the total obligatory portfolio, after factoring in **2% management expenses**, **5% profit**, **15% commission**, and a **loss ratio range of 50% to 78%**. Profit commission is **not payable if the loss ratio exceeds 78%**, and the profit commission itself is capped at **14%**. In practical compliance terms, insurers writing general insurance business for the 2023–24 financial year need to ensure that their obligatory cession processes, documentation, cession placement, information-sharing triggers, and commission accounting are aligned with these mandatory IRDAI requirements.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI amendment, notified on 5 December 2022 and effective from publication in the Official Gazette, updates the **IRDAI (Insurance Intermediaries) Regulations, 2022** by amending two existing 2015 frameworks: the **Registration of Corporate Agents Regulations, 2015** and the **Registration of Insurance Marketing Firm Regulations, 2015**. Its stated policy objective is to give prospects and policyholders broader choice in how they buy insurance through multiple distribution channels and to expand insurance reach and penetration across India. It applies to entities operating as **Corporate Agents** and **Insurance Marketing Firms (IMFs)**, and it changes the scope and applicability rules for both.

For **Corporate Agents**, the amendment replaces Regulation 3 so that a corporate agent can only have arrangements with a capped number of insurers during the validity of its registration certificate. A **Corporate Agent (Life)** may tie up with a maximum of **nine life insurers**; a **Corporate Agent (General)** may tie up with a maximum of **nine general insurers**; and a **Corporate Agent (Health)** may tie up with a maximum of **nine health insurers**, each for soliciting, procuring, and servicing those insurers’ products. The amendment adds a specific activity restriction for general business: a **Corporate Agent (General)** may solicit, procure, and service **retail lines** of general insurance and only those **commercial lines** where the **total sum insured does not exceed ₹5 crores per risk, for all insurances combined**. For a **Corporate Agent (Composite)**, the same per-segment limits apply, but the composite agent may exceed the separate nine-insurer caps only so long as the **total number of arrangements across life, general, and health insurers does not exceed 27 at any point in time**.

For **Insurance Marketing Firms**, the amendment replaces Regulation 3(a)(i) on insurer tie-ups. An IMF may engage Insurance Sales Persons to solicit and procure insurance products from a maximum of **six life insurers, six general insurers, and six health insurers at any point in time**, and it must do so **under intimation to the Authority**. If an insurer relationship changes because of cancellation, termination, or discontinuity, the arrangement must follow the terms of the IMF-insurer agreement, and there must be **suitable arrangements for servicing existing policyholders by the concerned insurer**. The IMF must also **inform IRDAI of any such change in the format specified by the Authority**, so compliance teams should ensure internal controls track insurer tie-ups, manage policyholder servicing continuity, and maintain the prescribed notification process.  

The amendment also changes the **area of operation** rule for IMFs under Regulation 19(3) and Schedule IV: the “Area” is defined as **the State for which the IMF’s registration is valid**. Compliance teams should treat this as a state-specific operating restriction tied to the registration, rather than a broader geographic permission.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI (Other Forms of Capital) Regulations, 2022 establish a new regulatory framework for insurers to issue “Other Forms of Capital” (OFC), and they replace the 2015 OFC regulations. They came into force on the date they were published in the Official Gazette and are stated to remain in force for three years from publication unless reviewed or amended sooner. The stated purpose is to govern issuance of OFC by insurers other than a foreign re-insurer’s branch and to set minimum reporting and disclosure requirements.

Under the regulations, OFC consists only of two instrument types: preference share capital and subordinated debt. Preference shares must satisfy the Companies Act definition and the specific criteria in these regulations, and subordinated debt includes debentures under the Companies Act plus any other debt instrument later permitted by IRDAI. General legal terms not defined in the regulations continue to have the meanings given in the Insurance Act, 1938, the IRDAI Act, 1999, the Companies Act, 2013, and the relevant rules/regulations under those laws.

To qualify as OFC, the instruments must be issued and fully paid up in cash, and their claims must rank behind policyholders and all creditors. Preference shareholders must rank ahead of equity shareholders but behind policyholders and creditors. For subordinated debt, the claims must be subordinated to those of policyholders and all creditors, and also to other specified obligations depending on the instrument structure, consistent with the regulations’ ranking rules. The document also contains additional qualification conditions for OFC instruments, including requirements on voting rights, redemption, conversion, and maturity/profile restrictions, though the excerpt provided is partial.

The regulations impose a minimum regulatory capital framework: insurers may issue OFC only within the limits and conditions set by IRDAI, and the treatment of these instruments for regulatory purposes depends on the instrument type and compliance with the qualifying conditions. A specific quantitative provision appears in the definition of subordinated debt, indicating that any permitted amount/threshold calculations are to be determined within the regulatory framework rather than purely by company choice. The text also references detailed compliance rules for reporting and disclosures, meaning insurers issuing OFC must follow prescribed filing and transparency requirements with IRDAI.

Affected entities are insurers issuing capital instruments in India, excluding foreign re-insurer branches. Compliance teams should note that any existing OFC issuance must be checked against the 2022 rules because the 2015 regulations are superseded. The key operational obligation is to ensure any preference shares or subordinated debt intended to count as OFC are fully cash-paid, correctly ranked in insolvency/claim priority, and otherwise satisfy the regulatory criteria before issuance and on an ongoing basis.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI (Indian Insurance Companies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2021 were issued by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India on 7 July 2021 and took effect immediately on publication in the Official Gazette. Their stated purpose is to harmonize IRDAI insurance-company regulations with the Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2021 and the Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2015, by amending several existing regulations that apply to Indian insurance companies.

The most significant change is the insertion of a new regulation 5A in the Registration of Indian Insurance Companies Regulations, 2000 for Indian insurance companies with foreign investment. It requires that a majority of the board directors be Resident Indian Citizens, a majority of Key Management Persons also be Resident Indian Citizens, and at least one of the chairperson, managing director, or chief executive officer must be a Resident Indian Citizen. “Resident Indian Citizen” is defined by reference to rule 2(1)(o) of the Foreign Investment Rules, 2015.

A new regulation 5B is also inserted for Indian insurance companies with foreign investment exceeding 49%. If such a company pays dividend on equity shares in a financial year and, at any time in that year, its solvency margin is below 1.2 times the control level of solvency, then at least 50% of that year’s net profit must be retained in general reserve. In addition, unless the chairperson of the board is an independent director, at least 50% of the directors must be independent directors; if the chairperson is independent, then at least one-third of the board must be independent directors.

The amendment also changes the application/registration filing requirements in regulation 10. The foreign investment threshold in regulation 10(2)(e) is increased from 49% to 74%, clauses (f) and (g) of regulation 10(2) are omitted, and new affidavit requirements are introduced: where the applicant has foreign investment, the managing director, chief executive officer, or whole-time director together with the promoters must file an affidavit certifying compliance with regulation 5A; where the applicant has foreign investment exceeding 49%, a separate affidavit is required confirming compliance with the more stringent requirements applicable to that level of foreign ownership. The document also makes corresponding textual amendments to Regulations 29, 30, and 31, and to other linked provisions, to align those regulations with the new foreign-investment framework and Resident Indian Citizen requirements.

rows.summary:
The Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Amendment Rules, 2021, issued by the Ministry of Finance on 19 May 2021, take effect immediately on publication in the Official Gazette. They amend the Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2015 and were made under section 114(2)(aaa) of the Insurance Act, 1938, read with section 2(7A)(b); the government had earlier published draft rules on 15 April 2021 and considered public comments before finalizing them.

The most significant change is that the foreign investment ceiling in an Indian insurance company is raised from 49% to 74%. The definition provisions are also revised: several definitions in rule 2 are deleted, the definition of “Resident Indian Citizen” is replaced so that it now means what is provided in the Central Government’s current FDI policy, and “Total Foreign Investment” is redefined to mean the sum of direct and indirect foreign investment by foreign investors, calculated in the manner specified by the Authority’s registration regulations. A new interpretive clause is added so that undefined terms take their meanings from the Insurance Act or rules/regulations made under it.

Governance requirements are tightened for insurers with foreign investment. In any Indian insurance company with foreign investment, a majority of directors must be Resident Indian Citizens, a majority of Key Management Persons must be Resident Indian Citizens, and at least one of the chairperson of the board, the managing director, or the chief executive officer must be a Resident Indian Citizen. The rule expressly applies the existing corporate-governance meaning of “Key Management Person.” Companies that already had foreign investment on or before the commencement date must comply with these governance requirements within one year of commencement.

The amendment also adds a new dividend restriction for companies with foreign investment exceeding 49%. For any financial year in which equity-share dividends are paid and at any time during that year the solvency margin is below 1.2 times the control level of solvency, at least 50% of net profit for that financial year must be retained; the text provided cuts off after “not less than fifty per cent. of the net profit for the finan…,” so any remaining sub-clauses are not visible in the excerpt. Compliance teams should therefore treat the visible portion as clearly imposing a profit-retention condition tied to dividend distribution and solvency status, effective from the amendment’s commencement date.

This IRDAI notification titled **“Obligatory Cession for the financial year 2021-22”** was issued on **28 December 2020** and applies to **Indian re-insurers and other insurers covered under Section 101A of the Insurance Act, 1938**. It sets the compulsory reinsurance cession for policies attaching during the financial year **1 April 2021 through 31 March 2022** at **5% of the sum insured on each General Insurance Policy**, and specifies that this cession is to be placed **only with General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re)**. The notification expressly excludes **terrorism premium** and premium ceded to the **Nuclear Pool**, for which the obligatory cession is **nil**.

For the cessions made during this period, the notification states that there is **no limit on sum insured** applicable to obligatory cessions, but the **Indian re-insurer may require immediate underwriting information notice** for any cession exceeding a limit it specifies, and the ceding insurer must provide such information whenever those thresholds are exceeded. This means insurers must be prepared to comply with any information-request threshold set by the Indian re-insurer, even though the regulation itself does not impose a universal monetary cap.

The notification also prescribes **minimum commission rates** on obligatory cession by class of business: **5% minimum for Motor TP and Oil & Energy insurance**, **10% minimum for Group Health insurance**, **7.50% minimum for Crop Insurance**, **average terms for Aviation insurance**, and **15% minimum for all other classes of insurance business**. It further allows any commission above these minimums only by **mutual agreement between the Indian re-insurer(s) and the ceding insurer**.  

On **profit commission**, the Indian re-insurer must share profit commission with the ceding insurer on a **50:50 basis**, based on the performance and surplus of the ceding insurer’s total obligatory portfolio, after taking into account: **incurred loss percentage measured at the end of 3 financial years**, **management expenses at 2%**, **profit at 5%**, **commission at 15%**, and a **loss ratio range of 50% to 78%**. No profit commission is payable if the **loss ratio exceeds 78%**, and the **profit commission is capped at 14%**.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has upgraded its Business Analytics Platform (BAP) and migrated several reinsurance-related regulatory and approval processes onto the new integrated portal. The circular is addressed to all insurers, reinsurers, and foreign reinsurer branches (FRBs), including Lloyd’s India and its constituents, and it makes the BAP the required submission channel for the affected reinsurance functions.

The migration covers Reinsurance Regulatory Returns, Reinsurance Summary Formats (both Advance and Final), and applications for issuance of File Reference Numbers (FRNs) to Cross Border Reinsurers (CBRs). It also brings onto BAP the applications relating to appointment and remuneration of the Chairperson/CEO of reinsurers and FRBs, and requests for approvals for CEOs/KMPs more generally. IRDAI states that these functions are now available through the BAP portal and that operational guidelines and user instructions for each reinsurance function will be provided on the portal itself.

The circular specifies the reporting periods from which submissions must be made on the integrated Reinsurance BAP portal: Reinsurance Regulatory Returns from FY 2024–25; Corporate Governance Returns from FY 2025–26; Pool Administrator Returns from FY 2024–25; and Reinsurance Programme Summary Returns / Final Reinsurance Programme Summary Returns from FY 2026–27. In practical terms, entities covered by the circular must shift their relevant filings and approval requests to the BAP as soon as each specified reporting stream becomes applicable for the relevant financial year.

The document does not set a separate filing deadline date beyond these fiscal-year applicability dates, nor does it prescribe new numerical thresholds or rates. It is issued with the approval of the Competent Authority and is signed by the Head of Department (Reinsurance).

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular dated **27 August 2026** allowing **all insurers** to invest in **New Development Bank (NDB) Maharajah INR Bonds / Onshore Rupee Bonds** as part of their **approved investments**. The circular notes that NDB intends to raise **INR 25,000 crore over a five-year period**, and that the proceeds are expected to be used for **general corporate purposes and onward lending/financing of sustainable development, sustainable infrastructure, and green/social projects in India**.

For compliance purposes, these bonds are treated as **“securities” under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956**, and insurers may invest in them only if several conditions are met. The bonds must comply with any **Government of India norms**, the **public issue must be approved by SEBI**, and insurers must comply with **Section 27E of the Insurance Act, 1938** when making the investment. In addition, the bonds must satisfy the **rating criteria for “Approved Investments” under Schedule III of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, as amended from time to time; where SEBI waives the requirement for ratings from SEBI-registered agencies based on ratings from international rating agencies, the equivalent international rating may be used.

The circular also creates a potential **“infrastructure investment”** classification if the bond proceeds are invested in **infrastructure sub-sectors listed in the Ministry of Finance’s Harmonized Master List** from time to time. IRDAI has assigned category codes for reporting/classification purposes: **EORB** for “Onshore Rupee Bonds issued by NDB” under **Approved Investments**, **IORB** for “Onshore Rupee Bonds issued by NDB (Infrastructure-approved)” under **Approved Investments**, **OORB** for “Onshore Rupee Bonds issued by NDB” under **Other Investments**, and **IOOB** for “Onshore Rupee Bonds issued by NDB (Infrastructure-others)” under **Other Investments**. This circular is issued under **clause 12(6) of Schedule III of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024** and effectively expands insurers’ permissible investment universe, but only within the stated regulatory, approval, and rating conditions.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued Circular No. IRDAI/NL/GDL/98(01)/07/2026 dated 31 July 2026 to all CEOs/CMDs of all insurance companies, including life and stand-alone health insurers, in response to floods beginning 19 July 2026 that were declared a natural disaster and affected the Assam districts of Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, and Golaghat. The circular requires insurers to take immediate steps to reduce hardship for affected policyholders by speeding up claim registration and settlement, rather than treating this as ordinary claims handling.

Insurers must immediately mobilize all available resources, including surveyors and investigators, and appoint senior Nodal Officers to supervise claims in the affected areas; the appointment of the Nodal Officer must be communicated immediately to the Chief Secretary. Insurers may also designate a District Claims Service Head for district-level oversight. They are required to activate and publicize 24x7 customer support helplines, and to run an awareness campaign using the press and digital media; the contact details of district heads must be posted on the insurer’s website and otherwise widely publicized.

For claims processing, insurers are instructed to use special empowered district desks to conduct prompt surveys, speed up processing, and make early claim payments, including on-account/interim payments where needed to help restore property or business operations. Claims should be surveyed immediately and payments made at the earliest possible time. Policyholders should be encouraged to communicate electronically and submit documents digitally wherever possible, and insurers are expected to streamline document requirements so that only materials necessary to substantiate the claim amount are insisted upon.

The circular also relaxes documentation for death claims: where a death certificate cannot be obtained because the body is not recovered, the claim may still be processed without insisting on a death certificate if the insured’s details match those of the deceased as published by the State/Central Government or other appropriate government authorities. Finally, all insurers—life, general, and health—must submit weekly claims data to IRDAI in the prescribed reporting format enclosed with the circular.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular to **all insurers except reinsurers** directing them to speed up and complete their responses to the Offices of the Insurance Ombudsmen. The regulator says it observed significant delays in insurers submitting **Self Contained Notes (SCNs)**, supporting documents, and follow-up information requested by Insurance Ombudsman offices, often in piecemeal form, which is delaying disposal of policyholder/beneficiary complaints.

The circular ties this requirement to the **Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017**, specifically **Rule 15(2)** (which allows the Ombudsman to seek additional information/documents) and **Rule 17(4)** (which contemplates decision of a complaint within **90 days of receipt of all required material from the complainant**). To support timely complaint handling, insurers are now advised to provide the required **SCN and supporting documents within 7 days** of receiving notice from the concerned Ombudsman office, and to provide any **additional information or documents within 3 days** of the request under Rule 15(2).

The circular also requires that insurers submit all information and documents **in one submission rather than piecemeal**. In addition, insurers must **clear all pending SCN and document demands within 30 days from the date of the circular**. If an insurer does not comply, the relevant Ombudsman office is instructed to **proceed ex parte without further delay**, using the material already on record, so that the Rule 17(4) timeline can be met. The circular is dated **July 23, 2026** and is issued with the approval of the competent authority.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI’s circular dated 14 July 2026 provides additional clarifications for insurers on implementing Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS), building on the earlier circular of 1 April 2026, and is intended to ensure consistent application across the industry. It applies to all insurers and specifically addresses three areas: the role of the Appointed Actuary in preparing Ind AS financial statements, the requirement for independent validation in the first year of Ind AS implementation, and the nature of Ind AS-compliant financial statements for consolidation purposes.

For financial statement preparation, the circular states that under Clauses 6 and 7 of Part II of Schedule I of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024, the Appointed Actuary must provide actuarial expertise, advice, and other actuarial inputs relevant to the preparation of financial statements under the applicable Ind AS. This responsibility explicitly includes actuarial valuation and measurement of policy liabilities, covering insurance contract liabilities under Ind AS 117, liabilities arising from investment contracts under Ind AS 109, and service contracts under Ind AS 115; review and determination of the actuarial methodologies and assumptions used; actuarial inputs for disclosures relating to insurance contracts and reinsurance contracts held; and any other actuarial matters necessary to comply with Ind AS, IRDAI regulations/circulars/directions, and IAI professional standards or guidance notes.

The circular also imposes a formal reporting obligation on the Appointed Actuary: a technical report must be submitted to the Board of Directors on the actuarial valuation of policy liabilities for Ind AS financial statements. That report must cover the material actuarial methodologies, assumptions, judgments, reliance placed on information from management or other functions, compliance with applicable IAI professional standards/guidance notes, and any other matters the Appointed Actuary considers material. On first-time adoption of Ind AS, the report must additionally include a reconciliation between policy liabilities under the previous accounting framework under Schedule II of the 2024 regulations and those under Ind AS, together with an explanation of material differences. The report must be placed before the Board for consideration, and a copy approved by the Board must be submitted to IRDAI along with the annual financial statements.

On independent validation, the circular requires every insurer to obtain an independent validation of the process adopted for implementing the applicable Ind AS during the first year of implementation. This requirement applies in FY 2026–27 for insurers implementing Ind AS from FY 2026–27, and in FY 2027–28 for insurers that have been granted forbearance. The circular also notes that paragraph 8 of the earlier 1 April 2026 circular is being clarified, indicating that insurers should follow the updated guidance together with the 2024 regulations when determining how Ind AS-compliant financial statements are prepared for consolidation purposes.

rows.summary:
The circular, dated **8 July 2026**, is issued by **IRDAI** to **all insurers and reinsurers** to update the **formats for publishing financial results** that listed insurance entities must use for disclosures under **SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015**. It explains that SEBI’s master circular on financial results for listed companies requires listed insurers to follow IRDAI-prescribed formats, and that because insurers have adopted **Ind AS**, the existing stock-exchange filing formats needed to be revised for those insurers preparing financial statements under Ind AS. Accordingly, IRDAI has issued updated formats for **unaudited/audited quarterly financial results** for **all listed life insurers, general insurers, health insurers, and reinsurers** that are required to prepare financial statements under **Ind AS**.

For those affected entities, the circular requires the following disclosures and reports to be filed in the updated annexure formats: **quarterly financial results in Annexure I**, **segment-wise revenue, results, and capital employed in Annexure II**, **limited review reports in Annexure III**, **audit reports for audited financial statements in Annexure IV**, and **newspaper-published financial results under Regulation 47(1)(b) of LODR in Annexure V**. This is the substantive compliance change: listed insurers/reinsurers that are on Ind AS must move to these revised IRDAI formats when publishing quarterly results and related audit/review disclosures to stock exchanges and newspapers.

There is an explicit exception for listed insurers that were **granted forbearance for FY 2026-27 for Ind AS implementation** and that must still prepare financial statements under **Schedule II of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**. Those entities do **not** shift to the new Ind AS-based formats; instead, they must **continue using the existing formats** under **IRDA/F&I/REG/CIR/208/10/2016 dated 25 October 2016** and **IRDA/F&A/CIR/LFTD/027/01/2017 dated 30 January 2017**.

IRDAI also clarifies that the circular is issued **only to enable compliance with SEBI’s disclosure requirements under LODR**, and it does **not** change the financial-statement preparation or disclosure requirements under the **Insurance Act, 1938**, the **IRDA Act, 1999**, or regulations made under those laws. In other words, it is a **disclosure-format update for listed insurer/reinsurer filings**, not a change to the underlying statutory accounting framework.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated 25.05.2026 and issued under Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938, Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999, and Regulation 12 of the Corporate Governance for Insurers, 2024, amends the Master Circular on Corporate Governance for Insurers with immediate effect. It specifically revises the remuneration framework for key management persons (KMPs) and also adds new disclosure obligations and website transparency requirements for insurers.

First, Clause 8.1 is amended so that the Board-level corporate governance disclosures must now include the parameters forming the basis of remuneration packages, including incentives, for the MD & CEO, all other directors, and all KMPs, as well as payments made to group entities and related parties. A new Clause 8.3 is inserted requiring insurers to disclose on their website the insurer’s performance against the parameters used to determine remuneration for all KMPs, together with the corresponding information for the preceding three years, in an “easy to access” and “easy to understand” format; the insurer must not ask for personal details such as a visitor’s telephone number in order to access this information, because the intent is to support informed decision-making by the public and policyholders.

The new Clause 8.3 also sets specific reporting frequency for year-to-date (YTD) disclosures: financial soundness metrics must be updated quarterly, while product performance, claim responsiveness, grievance redressal, and improvements in those areas must be updated monthly. In practice, this means insurers must maintain and publish these performance indicators on an ongoing basis, rather than only in annual reports or internal remuneration papers.

Clause 9.2(b) is tightened to require the Nomination and Remuneration Committee, working in consultation with the Risk Management Committee, to take a coordinated and integrated approach to the remuneration policy. The policy must ensure remuneration is aligned to policyholder outcomes, adjusted for all types of risk, produces pay outcomes that are symmetric with risk outcomes, pays out in a way that reflects the time horizon of the underlying risk, and uses a cash/equity mix that is consistent with risk alignment.

Most importantly for FY 2026-27, new minimum performance parameters must mandatorily be considered when assessing all KMPs for variable pay, incentives, and the new disclosure under Clause 8.3. These minimum parameters include overall financial soundness and improvements in that soundness, with separate indicators for life insurers and non-life/general insurers. For life insurers, the listed indicators begin with the “assets under management” to “total premium” ratio, the “renewal premium” to “new business premium” ratio, and additional financial performance measures that are set out in the circular’s detailed list. The circular also states that performance assessment must cover not just financial soundness but also products’ performance, claim responsiveness, grievance redressal, and related improvements, and these metrics are tied to the new monthly or quarterly disclosure cadence.

Overall, the compliance impact is immediate: insurers must update their remuneration policies, committee processes, and public disclosure controls now; ensure the NRC and RMC jointly document a risk-aligned remuneration framework; and implement website publication of KMP performance metrics with three years of history and the required frequency for YTD updates.
