This circular clarifies the transitional fee and registration regime for **Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors (SLAs)** following the **Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025 (SBSR Act)**, and it is issued as a continuation of IRDAI Circular **IRDAI/INT/CIR/MISC/41/3/2026 dated 16 March 2026**. It applies to **all SLAs** and explains that, with effect from **5 February 2026**, the earlier **licensing model** for SLAs (which had a **three-year validity period** and renewal requirements) has been replaced by a **registration-based framework** under amended **Section 42D of the Insurance Act, 1938**. Under this new framework, SLAs will receive a **Certificate of Registration (CoR)**, and the registration will remain in force subject to payment of an **annual fee** as prescribed by the amended law and upcoming regulations; the CoR will be available for download through the **BAP portal**.

For the transitional period, if an application for **new registration or renewal** is approved between **5 February 2026 and 30 June 2026**, the applicant must pay an **interim annual fee before the CoR is issued**. The fee is **₹400 plus 18% GST (₹72) = ₹472 total** for an **individual SLA**, and **₹2,000 plus 18% GST (₹360) = ₹2,360 total** for a **corporate SLA**. For applications approved on or after **5 February 2026** where some fee has already been paid, that amount must be **adjusted against the interim annual fee** to the extent applicable, and any remaining balance will be handled under the regulations yet to be notified.

The circular also distinguishes between **lapsed license revival** cases filed before and after the cut-off date. Applications to revive lapsed licenses submitted **on or before 4 February 2026** will continue to be processed under the **IRDAI (Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors) Regulations, 2015**, whereas revival applications submitted **on or after 5 February 2026** will be treated as **applications for new registration**, which means the applicant may have to meet **examination and training requirements** again. Operationally, IRDAI says the requirement to submit **all categories of applications**—including **new, renewal, modification, and related requests**—through the **BAP portal** will continue until further notice. The circular emphasizes that these arrangements are **interim and transitional only**, pending the final regulations to be issued under the amended legal framework.

rows.summary:
This circular, issued by IRDAI on 1 April 2026 under Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938 and Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999 read with Regulations 7 and 8 of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024, provides implementation clarifications for Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) for insurers. The underlying regulatory amendments that enable Ind AS for insurers take effect from 1 April 2026, and the purpose of the circular is to standardize how insurers should apply the new framework and meet related reporting and governance expectations.

For financial reporting, insurers must prepare financial statements under Ind AS in accordance with Schedule IIA of the Regulations, and those statements become the basis of financial reporting. At the same time, insurers must continue parallel reporting of both Financial Statements and Financial Information for two years from the implementation date, unless the Competent Authority specifies a different period. Financial Information must be prepared under Schedule II, and both Financial Statements and Financial Information must be prepared and filed quarterly, with both sets of disclosures also posted on the insurer’s website.

The circular also specifies assurance requirements: the Financial Statements for the first three quarters are subject to limited review under the applicable ICAI Standards on Review Engagements, while annual Financial Statements must be audited under the Insurance Act, 1938 and Companies Act, 2013. Financial Information for all four quarters is also subject to limited review under the ICAI review standards. In addition, insurers must include an appropriate reconciliation between the Financial Statements and the Financial Information as required by Ind AS 101, so compliance teams should expect and plan for a formal bridging/reconciliation process in the reported packs.

For the transition year 2026–27, the first-three-quarter Financial Statements and Financial Information must be submitted within three months from the end of each respective quarter. A specific carve-out is provided for listed insurers: the timing for disclosure of Financial Statements continues to follow SEBI norms instead of the three-month submission timeline. This means listed insurers need to align Ind AS reporting calendars with applicable securities law disclosure deadlines as well as IRDAI requirements.

The circular also creates a forbearance process for insurers seeking a one-year deferral in preparing Ind AS financial statements. Any insurer seeking this forbearance must apply to IRDAI on or before 30 April 2026 and must attach a Board-approved action plan. The application must include a detailed implementation roadmap with monthly milestones, timelines for system and data readiness, and the preparedness status of the actuarial and finance functions, indicating that IRDAI expects a documented, board-backed transition plan rather than a generic request. The excerpt provided cuts off mid-sentence after this roadmap requirement, so there may be additional details later in the document, but the material obligations visible here are the transition to Ind AS from 1 April 2026, parallel reporting for two years, quarterly filing and website disclosure, limited review/audit requirements, reconciliation under Ind AS 101, the special 2026–27 submission timeline, and the 30 April 2026 deadline for forbearance applications.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued Circular No. IRDAI/PP&GR/CIR/MISC/02/01/2026 dated 6 January 2026 to all insurers and insurance intermediaries, directing immediate preparation for compliance with TRAI’s mandatory 1600-series adoption requirement for customer-facing voice communications. The circular explains that TRAI’s Direction dated 16 December 2025, issued under section 13 read with section 11(1)(b)(i) and (v) of the TRAI Act, 1997, requires all IRDAI-regulated entities to use the 1600-series for all service and transactional voice calls made to consumers, with the stated objectives of reducing unsolicited commercial communication (UCC), preventing impersonation-based fraud, and improving consumer trust.

The key compliance deadline is 15 February 2026, by which insurers and insurance intermediaries must complete adoption of the 1600-series for all service and transactional voice calls. After that date, no service or transactional voice calls may be initiated from any number other than numbers allocated under the 1600-series, even where the customer has given explicit or implied consent. This means consent does not provide an exception to the numbering requirement once the deadline passes.

The circular also warns that any UCC complaint against an entity that does not comply may trigger action under the TRAI regulatory framework applicable to unregistered telemarketers, in addition to whatever further action the Authority may deem appropriate. In other words, non-compliance may create both TRAI-related exposure and separate supervisory consequences from IRDAI.

Operationally, insurers and intermediaries are instructed to coordinate with their Telecom Service Providers for timely allocation, activation, and operationalization of 1600-series numbers. They must also submit the status reports required by TRAI on a timely basis and send a copy of those reports to IRDAI. The circular references an Annexure containing contact details of the nodal officers of the access providers to support implementation, and the overall instruction is to ensure strict compliance.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated **19 December 2025** and addressed to **all insurers and reinsurers**, expands the set of permissible fixed-income investments for insurers by allowing investment in securities issued by **RBI-regulated All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**. Specifically, insurers are now permitted to invest in **(i) AT1 bonds** and **(ii) debt capital instruments and preference share capital instruments forming Tier 2 capital**, with the explicit exception of **Perpetual Cumulative Preference Shares**. The circular states that this change is intended to broaden insurers’ investment options and support portfolio diversification.

The permission applies to instruments issued by AIFIs that are regulated by the RBI, which began issuing **Additional Tier 1 Bonds and Tier 2 capital instruments from 1 April 2024** under the Basel III prudential framework. IRDAI is not creating a new investment regime from scratch; instead, it requires insurers to follow the **same investment provisions that already apply to insurer investments in banks**, specifically the rules in **paragraphs 1.6(b) and 1.6(d) of Chapter 3 of the Master Circular on Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers dated 17 May 2024**. In other words, the existing bank-investment compliance framework is to be used as the operational benchmark for these AIFI investments.

For compliance and reporting purposes, insurers must also use the **existing category codes used for investments in the corresponding instruments of PSU banks** when booking these AIFI holdings. The circular is issued under **clause 12(6) of Schedule III of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, so compliance teams should treat it as a formal regulatory instruction rather than guidance. No separate implementation deadline is specified beyond the circular date, so the effective position is that insurers may apply this permission immediately, subject to the existing bank-investment limits and requirements referenced above.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has announced that it is ending the long-standing practice of permitting an individual Surveyor/Loss Assessor (SLA) to add an additional line of business (LOB) to a surveyor licence merely on the basis of the categorization letter issued in 2001–02. The circular explains that, under the earlier categorization exercise, individual SLAs who held valid licences before the 2000 Licensing/Professional Requirements/Code of Conduct Regulations were categorized across multiple departments/LOBs, and they were originally allowed only 3 LOBs on their licence from that categorized list. Then, by Circular Ref. IRDA/SUR/CIR/MISC/042/02/2020 dated 4 February 2020, IRDAI had allowed additions to an individual SLA’s licence based on that old categorization letter if the person had the relevant educational qualification and had continuously renewed the licence without break, and it also removed the earlier cap on the number of LOBs.

IRDAI says it is now receiving modification applications from SLAs seeking to add LOBs even though they have not done any survey work in that LOB since 2002, and it considers pre-2001/02 experience and knowledge in those areas to be obsolete because of technological change over the last 23 years. To ensure fair assessment of insured losses, IRDAI has decided to stop this practice entirely. As a result, Circular Ref. IRDA/SUR/CIR/MISC/042/02/2020 dated 4 February 2020 is repealed with immediate effect, meaning applications relying on the 2001–02 categorization letter as the basis for adding LOBs should no longer be entertained under that route.

Going forward, an individual surveyor may still be eligible for any LOB on the surveyor licence, but only if the person meets the eligibility criteria under Regulation 3 of the IRDAI (Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors) Regulations, 2015, as amended. In addition, to add an LOB, the individual SLA must now comply with the Proviso under Regulation 27 of the same 2015 Regulations, as amended from time to time. The notice is effective immediately and was issued with the approval of the Competent Authority.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated 14 August 2025, launches **Quantitative Impact Study-2 (QIS 2)** for the proposed **Risk Based Capital (RBC)** framework for the Indian insurance sector. It follows the first quantitative impact study conducted in 2023 and is intended to refine the RBC framework based on the results and insurer feedback from that earlier exercise.

The circular applies broadly to **all life insurers, general insurers, standalone health insurers, reinsurers, branches of foreign reinsurers, and Lloyd’s India**. Insurers are required to perform QIS 2 using the **Technical Guidance document**, with the **data used for actuarial valuation as of 31 March 2025**. IRDAI states that the technical guidance, data submission template, result submission requirements, submission mode, and any supplementary information will be communicated separately.

The key compliance deadline is that **QIS 2 results must be submitted on or before 15 October 2025**. IRDAI emphasizes that this exercise is **only for QIS 2** and should **not** be treated as a final or binding indication of IRDAI’s ultimate RBC framework; it is an additional study to support the transition toward an RBC regime. Insurers must also continue to meet all existing regulatory filing obligations under the current regulatory regime, with no suspension or replacement of ordinary returns by virtue of this exercise.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular on Rural, Social Sector and Motor Third Party Obligations, 2025 is issued by IRDAI under Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938, Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999, and Regulation 9 of the 2024 Rural, Social Sector and Motor Third Party Obligations Regulations. It applies to all life insurers, general insurers, and stand-alone health insurers, and it governs obligations for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27; the earlier 2024 Master Circular applies only to FY 2024-25. The circular also defines the relevant insurer categories: “General Insurer–1” excludes stand-alone health insurers, AIC, and ECGC, while “General Insurer–2” includes general insurers and stand-alone health insurers other than AIC and ECGC; “base data” is the number of lives in the relevant Gram Panchayat for life and General Insurer–2 obligations, and the number of dwellings, shops, and motor vehicles in the Gram Panchayat for General Insurer–1 obligations.

For rural sector obligations, life insurers must cover the minimum specified percentage of lives under individual and/or group policies in allocated Gram Panchayats, while the circular separately prescribes obligations for general insurers based on dwelling/shops and motor vehicles, and on lives for General Insurer–2. The detailed compliance targets increase materially from FY 2025-26 to FY 2026-27: where the document specifies 25,000/50,000 and percentage bands, the applicable obligation levels rise from 15% in FY 2025-26 to 25% in FY 2026-27 for one component and to 10% for another component, with separate treatment for the insurer categories referenced in the circular. For social sector obligations, the circular requires coverage of specified beneficiary groups and sets higher numeric targets for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 than in the prior year, including thresholds of 10% and 12% in the relevant provision.

The motor third-party liability section requires compliance with the obligations prescribed in Regulation 4(1) and Regulation 5, with the circular reiterating the rates and procedural requirements for underwriting motor third-party business. In the life insurance “base data” allocation rules, insurers must use the base data figures communicated for the relevant Gram Panchayats and comply with the allocation process laid down by the respective councils. The circular also requires insurers to submit the specified statements and returns in the prescribed formats and timelines, including annual/periodic reporting tied to the FY 2025-26 compliance cycle, with at least one submission deadline expressly stated as 30 June 2025 for the 2024-25 reporting reference data.

Where an insurer cannot comply with an allocated rural-sector requirement, the circular requires the insurer to document the reasons and follow the prescribed allocation/transfer process through the councils, rather than simply ignoring the obligation. It also sets out compliance mechanics for reassignment and reconciliation of obligations between insurers, including the use of the prescribed annexures/forms, and provides that the Authority may require additional information or reporting to monitor compliance. Overall, the document is a binding operational compliance framework for insurers’ rural, social sector, and motor third-party obligations, with specific year-by-year thresholds, insurer classification rules, allocated-area compliance, and mandatory reporting/recordkeeping requirements.

IRDAI has issued the **Information and Cyber Security Guidelines, 2026** by circular dated **6 April 2026**, replacing/refreshing the earlier IRDAI information and cyber security guidelines issued on **24 April 2023**. The stated purpose is to respond to the evolving cyber threat landscape, industry feedback, and committee recommendations, with the goal of strengthening insurers’ cyber defenses and related governance arrangements. IRDAI says the revised guidelines establish the **minimum standards and governance mechanisms** that regulated entities must adopt.

The compliance scope is broad and expressly includes **all insurers, including foreign reinsurers/FRBs**, as well as **insurance intermediaries** such as **brokers, corporate agents, web aggregators, TPAs, IMFs, insurance repositories, ISNPs, corporate surveyors, MISPs, CSCs**, and the **Insurance Information Bureau of India (IIB)**. These entities are directed to **strictly adhere** to the guidelines and ensure implementation **from the current financial year**. No separate staggered compliance date is stated in the circular itself, so the operational expectation is immediate readiness and implementation within the ongoing financial year.

The document also states that a **brief summary of major changes** is provided in **Annexure A**, and the full text of the new requirements is in **Annexure B**. A compliance team should therefore treat the circular as a mandatory update to the prior framework and review both annexures to identify any revised controls, governance changes, reporting expectations, or technical/security requirements that may affect internal policies, vendor management, incident response, or board/management oversight.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued revised “Guidelines on Establishment and Closure of Liaison Office in India by an Insurance Company registered outside India,” replacing the earlier version issued on 17 October 2022. The new guidelines take effect from the date of issue, 11 February 2026, and apply to overseas insurers seeking to establish or close a liaison office (LO) in India. A liaison office is defined narrowly as an office used only as a communication channel between the overseas insurer’s head office and entities in India; it may not carry on any commercial, trading, solicitation, or industrial activity, directly or indirectly, and it must be funded only through foreign remittances received through normal banking channels.

For eligibility to open an LO, the overseas insurer must have a financially sound track record, specifically a profit-making record during the immediately preceding three financial years in its home country and a minimum net worth of USD 65 million. The document defines net worth as paid-up capital plus free reserves, less intangible assets, based on the latest audited balance sheet or equivalent account statement certified by a qualified accountant/practitioner in the home country. IRDAI may relax the minimum net worth requirement in exceptional cases, particularly for a foreign state-owned enterprise/reinsurer, or a specialized insurer with strong credit ratings or demonstrated expertise, where bilateral trade significance and market development potential justify the exception.

To obtain approval, the overseas insurer must apply to IRDAI in Form IRDAI-FIC-1 (Annexure I) and submit supporting documents. The application requires a non-refundable processing fee of USD 6,000, payable by demand draft, pay order, or online transfer in favor of the regulator’s designated account. The guidelines also set out reporting and notification obligations: once approved, the LO must operate strictly within the permitted scope and comply with ongoing filing/closure procedures in the annexed forms and timelines. The document further states that the amended guidelines supersede all prior instructions on this subject, so compliance teams should treat the 11 February 2026 version as the controlling framework for both opening and closing liaison offices in India.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI (Insurance Fraud Monitoring Framework) Guidelines, 2025, issued under Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938 and Section 14(1) of the IRDAI Act, 1999, create a sector-wide fraud governance framework for insurers and distribution channels. They apply to all insurers and distribution channels unless a specific provision says otherwise, and they come into force on 1 April 2026.

The core requirement is that every insurer must implement systems and processes across its functions to deter, prevent, detect, report, and remedy fraud, with a stated “zero tolerance” stance and a fraud risk management framework tailored to the insurer’s business profile. Insurers are expected to treat fraud as an enterprise risk, and the Risk Management Committee (RMC) is specifically made responsible for effective oversight of the fraud risk management framework. The guidelines define “insurance fraud” broadly as any act or omission intended to gain advantage through dishonest or unlawful means, including misappropriation of funds, deliberate misrepresentation, concealment, or nondisclosure of material facts, and abuse of a position of trust or fiduciary relationship.

The framework also requires insurers to classify and monitor fraud across five categories: internal fraud involving employees or senior management; distribution channel fraud; policyholder and/or claims fraud occurring in connection with purchase, servicing, or claims; external fraud involving parties such as service providers or vendors; and affinity/complex fraud involving collusion among perpetrators across those categories. It separately defines “red flag indicators” as warning signs that may require further investigation, and “cyber or new age fraud” as insurance fraud using digital or new-age technologies. These definitions matter because insurers must build monitoring, escalation, and investigation procedures around them.

The document also makes clear that “distribution channels” are to be understood as defined in the IRDAI (Protection of Policyholders’ Interests and Allied Matters of Insurers) Regulations, 2024. Insurers will need to ensure their fraud controls cover not only internal operations and claims handling, but also intermediaries, channel partners, external vendors, and technology-enabled fraud risks. The summary text provided cuts off in the middle of Section 5, so any additional operational obligations, reporting timelines, board/RMC duties, or procedural details contained later in the 19-page document are not visible here and should be checked in the full text before compliance implementation.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has amended Clause 15(a) of the “Revised Guidelines on Insurance Repositories and Electronic Issuance of Insurance Policies” dated 29 May 2015. The earlier requirement was that the insurance repository’s controls, systems, procedures, and safeguards be reviewed annually by an external system audit firm approved by IRDAI. Under the revised wording, that review must still be conducted at least once every year, but it must now be done **at the repository’s own cost** by an **external auditor** who qualifies as either a **Certified Information System Auditor (CISA)**, a **Chartered Accountant with DISA (ICAI) qualification**, or a **CERT-In certified expert**.

This change affects **insurance repositories** and their annual compliance/audit arrangements for the controls and safeguards described in **Clause 14** of the guidelines. The practical effect is that repositories can no longer rely only on a generic “external system audit firm approved by the Authority” under this clause; instead, they must ensure the reviewer meets one of the specified professional qualifications. The amendment is **effective immediately** from the date of the circular, **29 July 2025**, and no grace period or delayed implementation date is stated. Compliance teams should therefore confirm that future annual reviews are assigned to a properly qualified auditor and that the cost of the review is borne by the repository itself.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued new **Guidelines on Hedging Through Equity Derivatives** dated **28 February 2025**, addressed to **all life, general and health insurers**. The circular states that, after previously allowing insurers to use fixed-income derivatives (FRA, IRS, IRFs) and, later, CDS as protection buyers, the Authority is now permitting insurers to hedge equity-market exposure using equity derivatives because insurers have increased equity investments and face higher volatility in equity prices. The guidelines are issued under the applicable insurance regulatory framework and materially expand the set of derivative tools insurers may use, but only for hedging purposes and subject to the limits/procedures in the document.

The document sets out the framework for **what equity derivative activity is allowed, what is prohibited, and how it must be controlled internally**. It requires insurers to have formal governance, board-approved policies, and internal processes covering authorization, risk limits, accounting, reporting, and monitoring of equity-derivative hedges. The guidelines also specify that insurers must use derivatives only in connection with permitted hedging activity and not for speculative purposes, and they must ensure that any hedging instrument and exposure stay within the defined scope and controls. The document includes detailed formulas and methodology for measuring exposure and hedge effectiveness, which indicates that insurers must track and calculate hedge position values using prescribed parameters rather than ad hoc internal methods.

On the **quantitative restrictions**, the document provides specific limits and thresholds for equity-derivative hedging. It refers to a **15% limit** in one context, a **20% limit** in another, and a **9% threshold** for a stated ratio/measure tied to the permitted hedge framework, along with an **80–125 range** referenced for hedge effectiveness or an acceptable band. It also defines a **“safe harbour” range** and includes formulas for calculating exposures and outcomes, implying that insurers must test positions against these prescribed bands to qualify as compliant hedges. These numbers are material because they function as the practical constraints on the size and quality of derivative hedges that insurers can maintain.

The guidelines also impose **new compliance, valuation, and reporting obligations**. They require insurers to establish valuation and reporting procedures for equity derivatives, including treatment of gains/losses and position measurement under the specified formulas. The document references detailed procedural requirements for recording, monitoring, and reviewing derivative positions, including internal controls over execution and ongoing oversight. Because the circular is addressed to all life, general, and health insurers, any insurer with equity investment activity should review its treasury/investment policies immediately to align them with the new hedging permissions, restrictions, and documentation requirements.

The document itself is dated **28 February 2025**, so that is the operative issuance date for the new framework. No separate effective date is visible in the provided text, so compliance teams should treat the circular date as the starting point unless the full PDF contains a later effective-date provision.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued the **Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Bima Vahak) Guidelines, 2023** on **9 October 2023** under **Section 14(2)(e) of the IRDAI Act, 1999**. The guidelines take effect **from the date of launch of “Bima Vistaar”** (described in the document as a forthcoming comprehensive insurance product). Their core purpose is to create a **women-centric dedicated distribution channel** to improve insurance awareness, inclusion, and access at the **village/Gram Panchayat** level, while also developing local resources who are trusted by their communities.

For compliance purposes, the guidelines allow insurers to **engage Corporate Bima Vahaks and/or directly appoint Individual Bima Vahaks** for solicitation of insurance business and for policy/claims servicing. The insurer remains **fully responsible for all actions and conduct** of the Bima Vahaks it engages. A Corporate Bima Vahak may appoint individuals as Bima Vahaks only under the terms of its agreement with the insurer and is responsible for their conduct; it may solicit insurance products and facilitate policy/claims servicing **only through its appointed Bima Vahaks**. Bima Vahaks themselves may **sell and service Bima Vistaar and any other products specifically notified by IRDAI**, and they may do so **only through handheld electronic communication devices directly integrated with the insurer’s electronic platform**.

The guidelines also impose strict payment and conduct restrictions: Bima Vahaks are **not permitted to collect any fees or charges from a policyholder or prospective policyholder other than the insurance premium**. The **Life Insurance Council and General Insurance Council** must jointly establish common operational and conduct standards for Bima Vahaks, including **minimum educational qualifications, commission scales, training requirements** (explicitly covering **customer due diligence/KYC, personal data protection, policy handling, and claims support**), standard appointment terms, due diligence, ID cards, and database/confidentiality requirements for all policies sourced through Bima Vahaks; these standards are to be reviewed periodically. Each insurer must also maintain a **Board-approved Bima Vahak policy** aligned to those council-issued standards.

The guidelines further create a rollout obligation: insurers must work toward deploying Bima Vahaks in **every Gram Panchayat by 31 December 2024**. Lead insurers designated for each State/Union Territory must coordinate deployment to maximize coverage, with the stated structure allocating coverage targets of **40% to Lead Life Insurer(s), 40% to Lead Non-Life Insurer(s), 5% to Lead Health Insurer(s), and a minimum of 15% to all other insurers together**. After those initial deployment expectations, insurers may engage as many additional Bima Vahaks as needed based on demand. Finally, the scope of Bima Vahak activities may include at least **filling proposal forms, completing KYC through handheld devices, and issuing insurance policies**; the excerpt cuts off as it begins to list additional servicing functions.

The IRDAI issued the **Information and Cyber Security Guidelines, 2023** on **24 April 2023** to replace and consolidate earlier cyber/information-security directions for the insurance sector, in response to broader adoption of digital technologies and the rising incidence of cyberattacks. These guidelines are attached as **Annexure A** and are intended to strengthen both technical defenses and governance arrangements for handling cyber risk across the industry.

The requirements apply broadly to **all insurers, including foreign reinsurance branches (FRBs)**, and to a wide set of **insurance intermediaries and related entities**, specifically **brokers, corporate agents, web aggregators, TPAs, IMFs, insurance repositories, ISNPs, corporate surveyors, MISPs, CSCs, and the Insurance Information Bureau of India (IIB)**. IRDAI explicitly states that **those entities that have already completed their security audit for FY 2022–23 must begin complying with the new guidelines from the next financial year**, rather than immediately retrofitting the completed-year audit cycle.

From a compliance perspective, the document is a **replacement regime**: it **supersedes** the earlier IRDAI circulars/guidelines issued on **7 April 2017**, **29 December 2020**, **2 September 2022**, and **11 October 2022**. That means compliance teams should treat the 2023 guidelines as the controlling framework going forward and should verify that internal policies, audit plans, cyber governance, and security controls are aligned to the updated annexed requirements by the applicable next financial-year deadline for their organization.

rows.summary:
IRDAI issued these **Guidelines on Operational Issues pertaining to the Regulatory Sandbox** on **31 March 2023** under **sub-regulation (3) of Regulation 13 of the IRDAI (Regulatory Sandbox) Regulations, 2019**. The guidelines set the operating procedure for submitting and handling sandbox proposals intended to promote or implement innovation in insurance in India, and they apply to applicants seeking relief under the sandbox framework.

An applicant must file its proposal in **Form RG-1** and only in one or more of the categories permitted under **Regulation 4** of the 2019 Sandbox Regulations. IRDAI requires the applicant to show that the innovation will **increase insurance penetration or provide enhanced services to policyholders**; a proposal made only to obtain regulatory relaxation is not acceptable, and the **Chairperson’s decision on whether something qualifies as an innovation is final**. Every applicant must appoint an **experienced and responsible Single Point of Contact (SPOC)**, and IRDAI will also appoint its own SPOC; **all communications must be routed through these designated contacts**.

The guidelines permit **limited regulatory relaxation** only where the proposal genuinely promotes innovation in insurance in India, but they expressly state that **no application should be made if no regulatory relaxation is required**. At the same time, IRDAI says it will **not relax compliance with the Insurance Act, 1938, the IRDA Act, 1999, or any other applicable statutory provisions**. For customer-facing proposals, the applicant must clearly tell participants that the outcomes are uncertain, obtain **prior written consent**, ensure participation is **voluntary and conscious**, and provide a **detailed exit strategy** to prospects before participation.

The sandbox proposal must remain within the size limits prescribed: it will end if, within the stipulated time, it reaches **up to 1 lakh customers** or **premium collected up to ₹5 crore**, or any other parameter the Authority sets. For applications in defined categories, the applicant must file **in association with an insurer**, clearly identify the specific regulatory provisions for which relaxation is sought, and explain the **inherent risks** of the proposal along with the **measures to eliminate or mitigate those risks**. IRDAI also reserves the right to **limit relaxations** where needed to protect policyholder interests and grievance redressal processes, and any relaxation must **not prejudice existing policyholders** and should support insurance penetration or policy servicing.

If the applicant itself is an insurer, it must **apprise its Board**, put in place measures for **close monitoring of implementation**, and keep the Board updated on developments. Finally, IRDAI states that an application in **Form RG-1** that is not complete in all respects or does not comply with **Regulation 6** of the 2019 Regulations and these guidelines is **liable to be rejected**; the excerpt cuts off while describing the pre-rejection process, so any further procedural safeguard is not fully visible in the provided text.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI’s January 3, 2023 guidelines replace the earlier January 22, 2021 guidance on issuing File Reference Numbers (FRNs) to cross-border reinsurers (CBRs) and are intended to streamline the approval process and enable insurer-led auto-renewal where eligibility conditions are met. The rules apply to any insurer that wants to place reinsurance business with a CBR: before placing business, the insurer must ensure the CBR meets the rating and regulatory eligibility requirements under the IRDAI (Reinsurance) Regulations, 2018 and must have an FRN issued through the IRDAI CBR portal at https://cbr.irdai.gov.in/login.aspx. For new FRNs, insurers must submit an online application in the prescribed Annexure 1 format for the CBR to be classified either as an “Eligible CBR” or “Non-Eligible CBR”; the Authority can seek additional information if needed, and the insurer’s application should be aligned with its reinsurance programme.

A key change is that FRNs may now be auto-renewed by the insurer itself for CBRs that qualify, rather than requiring the Authority to renew annually in every case. To qualify for auto-renewal, the CBR must have a latest credit rating of at least S&P A- or equivalent, and that rating must be no older than 12 months from the date of the auto-renewal application; the CBR must also have been allotted FRN status as an “Eligible CBR” in the immediately preceding financial year; the latest required information must be filed; and the CBR must continue to satisfy the other conditions in Regulation 4(1) of the IRDAI (Reinsurance) Regulations, 2018. If the insurer finds that the CBR does not meet any of these auto-renewal conditions, it must instead follow the normal annual renewal process described in the guidelines. The portal will be open for auto-renewal for the current financial year and also three months in advance of the next financial year, so compliance teams should plan renewals accordingly and verify the CBR’s rating, filing status, and eligible status before using the auto-renewal route.

rows.summary:
IRDAI issued **Master Guidelines on Anti-Money Laundering/Counter Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT), 2022** under reference **IRDAI/IID/GDL/MISC/160/8/2022** dated **1 August 2022**. The circular explains that IRDAI had previously issued separate AML/CFT master guidelines for **general insurers (2013)** and **life insurers (2015)**, along with multiple later circulars, and that this new instrument **consolidates and updates** those requirements into a **single master set of guidelines** covering the **PML Act, the PML Rules, and other applicable norms as amended from time to time**. It is addressed to **all insurers** and explicitly applies to **all classes of Life, General, and Health insurance business**.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is the **effective date: 1 November 2022**. From that date, insurers in scope are required to comply with the consolidated AML/CFT framework instead of relying on the earlier fragmented insurer-specific guidelines and circulars. The document itself does not set out detailed customer due diligence thresholds, reporting limits, or penalty amounts in the excerpt provided; rather, it signals that the controlling AML/CFT obligations are now to be read from this **single updated master document** together with the underlying statutory regime.

rows.desc: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India Survey No.115/1, Financial District, Nanakramguda, HYDERABAD 500 032. IRDAI/NL/GDL/SIC/01/01/2022 3 rd January, 2022 To The Chairman-cum- Managing Directors/Chief Executive Officers of General Insurance Companies (except ECGC Ltd and AIC Ltd) Madam/Sir, IRDAI (Surety Insurance Contracts) Guidelines, 2022 The Authority, considering the specific nature of Surety Insurance owing to the unique risk and features of the products, hereby issues the following guidelines to regulate and develop Surety Insurance business. The guidelines shall come into force with effect from 1 st April, 2022. The guidelines have been placed on the IRDAI website (https://www.irdai.gov.in). Yours faithfully, Chief General Manager (Non-Life) IRDAI (Surety Insurance Contracts) Guidelines,2022 Page 1 of 6 IRDAI (Surety Insurance Contracts) Guidelines, 2022 1. Introduction The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (‘‘the Authority’’), having considered it necessary to promote and regulate sustainable and healthy development of Surety Insurance Business, in exercise of the powers conferred under section 14 (2) (i) of IRDA Act, 1999, hereby issues the following guidelines. 2. Short title, commencement 2.1 These guidelines shall be called the “IRDAI (Surety Insurance Contracts) Guidelines, 2022.” 2.2 These guidelines shall come into force with effect from 1st April, 2022. 3. Applicability 3.1 All Insurers registered under the Insurance Act, 1938, to transact the business of general insurance may transact the business of Surety Insurance, subject to compliance with eligibility criteria as set out in these guidelines. 3.2 No person shall, after the commencement of these guidelines, transact the business of Surety Insurance in India unless the person is an Indian Insurance Company as defined in Section 2 (7A) of the Insurance Act, 1938. 4. Essential Features of Surety Insurance contract The essential features of a Surety Insurance contract shall be as follows. 4.1 It shall be a contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. It is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default. The person who gives the guarantee is called the “Surety”; the person in respect of whose default the guarantee is given is called the “principal debtor”, and the person to whom the guarantee is given is called the “creditor”. 4.2 A contract of Surety shall be deemed to be an insurance contract only if made by a Surety who or which, is an insurer registered under the Insurance Act, 1938 to transact the business of general insurance. IRDAI (Surety Insurance Contracts) Guidelines,2022 Page 2 of 6 5. Types and Definitions of Surety Contracts (a) In these guidelines, unless the context otherwise requires, the terms herein shall bear the meanings assigned to them below. (i) Advance Payment Bond: It is a promise by the Surety provider to pay the outstanding balance of the advance payment in case the contractor fails to complete the contract as per specifications or fails to adhere to the scope of the contract. (ii) Bid Bond : It is an obligation undertaken by a bidder promising that the bidder will, if awarded the contract, furnish the prescribed performance guarantee and enter into contract agreement within a specified period of time. It provides financial protection to an obligee if a bidder is awarded a contract pursuant to the bid documents, but fails to sign the contract and provide any required performance and payment bonds. (iii) Contract Bond: It provides assurance to the public entity, developers, subcontractors and suppliers that the contractor will fulfil its contractual obligation when undertaking the project. Contract bonds may include: Bid Bonds, Performance Bonds, Advance Payment Bonds and Retention Money. (iv) Customs and Court Bond: This is a type of guarantee where the obligee is a public office such as tax office, customs administration or the court, and it guarantees the payment of a public receivable incurred from opening a court case,clearing goods from customs or losses due to incorrect customs procedures. (v) Performance Bond: It provides assurance that the obligee will be protected if the principal or contractor fails to perform the bonded contract. If the obligee declares the principal or contractor as being in default and terminates the contract, it can call on the Surety to meet the Surety’s obligations under the bond. (vi) Retention Money: It is a part of the amount payable to the contractor, which is retained and payable at the end after successful completion of the contract. (b) All words and expressions used herein and not defined but defined in the Insurance Act, 1938 or the IRDA Act, 1999, or in any Rules or Regulations made thereunder shall have the meanings assigned to them in those Acts, Rules, or Regulations. IRDAI (Surety Insurance Contracts) Guidelines,2022 Page 3 of 6 6. Requirements
rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued the **“IRDAI (Surety Insurance Contracts) Guidelines, 2022”** on **3 January 2022**, and they **take effect on 1 April 2022**. They are addressed to the **Chairman-cum-Managing Directors/Chief Executive Officers of general insurance companies**, but specifically **exclude ECGC Ltd. and AIC Ltd.** The purpose is to regulate and support the development of **Surety Insurance business** in India, which IRDAI treats as distinct because of the product’s unique risk characteristics.

For applicability, **all insurers registered under the Insurance Act, 1938 that are authorized to transact general insurance business may transact Surety Insurance, but only if they satisfy the eligibility criteria in the guidelines**. The document also imposes a market-entry restriction: **after commencement, no person may transact Surety Insurance in India unless that person is an “Indian Insurance Company” as defined in Section 2(7A) of the Insurance Act, 1938**. Compliance teams should therefore confirm both registration status and whether the entity meets the Indian Insurance Company definition before offering these products.

The guidelines define the legal nature of a surety insurance product as a **contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872**, involving a **surety**, **principal debtor**, and **creditor**. However, IRDAI makes clear that such a contract is treated as an **insurance contract only when issued by a surety that is an insurer registered under the Insurance Act, 1938 to transact general insurance**. In other words, the same guarantee structure is not insurance unless it is written by a qualifying general insurer.

IRDAI also provides specific product definitions that compliance teams should use when classifying business: **Advance Payment Bond** covers the surety’s promise to pay the outstanding balance of an advance payment if the contractor fails to complete the contract as specified or fails to meet the contract scope; **Bid Bond** covers a bidder’s obligation to furnish the required performance guarantee and sign the contract within the prescribed period if awarded; **Contract Bond** is a broader umbrella covering assurance to public entities, developers, subcontractors, and suppliers that the contractor will meet contractual obligations, and it may include bid bonds, performance bonds, advance payment bonds, and retention money; **Customs and Court Bond** covers guarantees to public offices such as tax offices, customs administrations, or courts for public receivables arising from court cases, customs clearance, or incorrect customs procedures; **Performance Bond** protects the obligee if the principal/contractor defaults and the contract is terminated; and **Retention Money** is the portion of contract payment withheld until successful completion. The document also states that any undefined terms will take their meanings from the **Insurance Act, 1938**, the **IRDA Act, 1999**, and regulations/rules made under them.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued revised **Trade Credit Insurance Guidelines, 2021** for **general insurance companies in India**, specifically addressed to **all general insurers except ECGC Ltd. and AIC Ltd.** The new framework is issued under **Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999**, was **published on 8 September 2021**, and **takes effect from 1 November 2021**, replacing the earlier IRDAI trade credit insurance guidelines dated **10 March 2016**. The guidelines are also expressly stated to be **in addition to any other applicable laws, rules, regulations, or guidelines**.

Substantively, the document clarifies that **trade credit insurance can only cover credit risk directly linked to an underlying trade transaction**, meaning the **delivery of goods or services**; if there is no such direct link, the outstanding amount is **not insurable** under this product. It permits coverage for a range of **commercial risks**, including **insolvency or protracted default** by the buyer, by the bank responsible for payment in **letter of credit** transactions, or by the **stock-holding agent** in consignment transactions; **rejection of goods** after delivery when permitted by contract, or before shipment when goods are being specially manufactured for the buyer and cannot be sold elsewhere; and **non-receipt of payment due to failure of the collecting bank**. It also allows **political risk cover**, but only for **buyers outside India** and only for **countries specifically agreed upon**; political risks include legal or regulatory actions blocking transfer of payment from the buyer’s country to India, war or civil unrest in the buyer’s country or between that country and India, restrictions or cancellations preventing import into the buyer’s country, and certain additional handling/transport/insurance costs arising from interruption or diversion of shipment outside India that cannot practicably be recovered from the buyer.

The stated regulatory objective is to promote the **sustainable and healthy development** of trade credit insurance and to enable insurers to offer covers not only to suppliers but also to **licensed banks and other financial institutions** that finance trade. The guidelines specifically emphasize improving access to customized trade credit insurance for **SMEs and MSMEs**, recognizing changing risk needs and market conditions. For compliance teams, the key operational takeaway is that any trade credit product design, underwriting, and policy wording issued on or after **1 November 2021** must fit within this narrower “directly linked to a trade transaction” requirement and must stay within the enumerated commercial and political risk parameters, with political risk cover limited to the defined cross-border and country-specific circumstances.

The IRDAI issued these Guidelines on 5 May 2021 to all general insurers and stand-alone health insurers, directing them to make a **Standard Domestic Travel Insurance Product (SDTIP)** available and to structure it on a uniform basis across the market. The product is intended to cover domestic travel only, and insurers must comply not only with these guidelines but also with the IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016, the Consolidated Guidelines on Product Filing in Health Insurance Business dated 22 July 2020, the Master Circular on Standardization of Health Insurance Products dated 22 July 2020, and any later amendments. The guidelines say insurers “shall endeavour” to offer this product, and it may also be offered as a **group product**.

The standard product must include only the mandatory benefits set out in the guidelines, and any optional cover may be offered only if it appears in the prescribed list. Insurers may set the premium, but only in line with the covers offered and subject to the health insurance regulatory framework. The document also states that the product should be designed to meet the “basic mandatory covers” common to domestic travelers, with standardized features across the market rather than insurer-specific variants.

The permitted plan structure distinguishes coverage by mode of travel, distance, and journey type. Plan A covers taxi/bus travel **within 100 km from the place of origin**; Plan B covers taxi/bus travel **more than 100 km from the place of origin**; Plans C, D, and E have **no distance restriction**. All plans are for a **single journey from place of origin to place of destination**, except Plan E, which covers the trip from the place of origin **until return to the place of origin/place of residence**. The maximum trip duration is stated as **up to 30 days** for domestic trips under Plan E, while the other plans cover the duration of the journey.

The mandatory benefits include: **hospitalization expenses due to accident** with a sum insured of **minimum Rs. 1 lakh and maximum Rs. 10 lakh**, paid on an indemnity basis with a **Rs. 500 deductible**; **accidental death** with a minimum of **Rs. 1 lakh for adults** and a maximum of **Rs. 1 crore per person**, with minors to be offered a **benefit-based cover subject to underwriting**; **permanent total disability** and **permanent partial disability**, both linked to the accidental death cover and on a benefit basis; and **repatriation of mortal remains** with a minimum of **Rs. 20,000 and maximum of Rs. 1 lakh**, benefit-based. The table also indicates **automatic trip extension** as a mandatory benefit for **Plan E only**.

The optional benefits the insurer may offer are **compassionate allowance** (minimum **Rs. 10,000**, maximum **Rs. 1 lakh**, indemnity basis), **missed flight connection** (minimum **Rs. 2,500**, maximum **Rs. 50,000**, indemnity basis), and **loss of checked-in baggage** applicable only to air travel (minimum **Rs. 2,000**, maximum **Rs. 20,000**, benefit-based). The compliance implication is that insurers launching or revising domestic travel products must ensure the policy wording, plan design, benefit structure, sum insured limits, and eligibility by mode of travel exactly match the standardized framework in the annexed terms and filing format.

rows.summary:
This circular, issued by IRDAI on 31 March 2021 under Ref. IRDA/SUR/GDL/MISC/068/03/2021, sets out the practical training requirements for licensed surveyors and loss assessors seeking fresh or renewal licences under the Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors Regulations, 2015, in continuation of the earlier circular dated 01/12/2020. It applies to all licensed surveyors and loss assessors and is framed under Section 14 of the IRDAI Act, 1999 and Regulation 3(2)(b) and (c) of the 2015 Regulations.

The circular requires **institutional practical training for two months** with either the **National Insurance Academy (NIA)** or the **Insurance Institute of India (III)**. This two-month programme must cover: introduction to different types of policies, endorsements, insurance terminology, and the nature of claims; industrial and field visits in coordination with insurers and other stakeholders to examine practical cases; use of technology and advanced tools for risk and loss assessment; report-writing standards, including accurate presentation of facts, policy terms and conditions, claim admissibility, and timely submission of reports in line with regulatory requirements; and the code of conduct for treating policyholders fairly throughout the loss-assessment process. A person may enroll for **up to three departments** during this institutional programme, subject to eligibility, and for each additional department the applicant must pass the relevant examination and then undergo **2 weeks of practical training**. The fee payable to the institution is whatever is specified by III or NIA, as applicable.

The circular also provides an alternative route of **six months’ practical training with an individual experienced surveyor** who has **at least 8 years of experience in the concerned department**. The curriculum for this route remains the same as the institutional training described above, and the applicant may also enroll for **up to three departments** at the time of enrolment, subject to eligibility criteria. For each additional department, after passing the relevant examination, the applicant must complete **8 weeks of training** with an experienced surveyor who holds a licence and has at least eight years of experience in that line of business. The document emphasizes that such training is part of the surveyor’s professional code of conduct and is to be imparted **without charging any fee** by the experienced surveyor.

rows.summary:
The Corporate Mitra course registration window was extended for candidates from the North Eastern States, with enrollment running from **15 Jul 2026 through 14 Aug 2026**, and the notice says the enrollment period has now **closed** because it ended on **14 Aug 2026**. The course is an initiative under the **Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA)** and is aimed at building **para-professionals** who can support India’s **MSMEs** and other corporate entities with **compliance, accounting, and financial expertise**. It is specifically designed to develop practical, compliance-oriented capability in **Accounting, Banking & Financial Management, Cost & Management Accounting, Legal & Secretarial, and Taxation**, with the stated objective of enabling learners to support accurate record-keeping, regulatory compliance, and financial decision-making.

The listing identifies the course as **credit eligible** under **NCrF 5.5** and shows a duration of **150 hours**. The eligibility criterion shown in the course description is **up to 30 years of age**. The course is delivered in **English** and is offered by **IITM Pravartak**, with partner/related references to **ICAI, ICSI, and ICoAI** in the listing. The fee is shown as **₹3,000** in the course metadata, and the enrollment page adds that payment is subject to **18% GST**, indicating a total payable amount above the base fee at checkout.

For compliance purposes, the practical obligation in the notice is simply to ensure any eligible North Eastern States candidates who intended to enroll did so before **14 Aug 2026**; no ongoing reporting, filing, or other regulatory submission requirement is described in the document itself. The content is informational/course-registration related rather than a substantive regulatory change, but it does set a hard closing date for enrollment and ties participation to the stated age limit, fee, language, and course format.

rows.title: NFRA Circular on Effective Communication Between Statutory Auditors and Those Charged with Governance, Including Audit Committees
rows.desc: NF-25013/3/2025--NFRA National Financial Reporting Authority ***** 7 th Floor, Hindustan Times House, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi Dated: 07.01.2026 CIRCULAR To 1. All listed companies 2. Companies and bodies corporate as specified in Rule 3 of NFRA Rules, 2018 3. Auditors of the above companies Subject: Effective Communication Between Statutory Auditors and Those Charged with Governance, Including Audit Committees In the course of discharging of NFRA’s statutory functions, it has been noticed that there is a need to strengthen the communications between Statutory Auditors (Auditors), Those Charged with Governance (TCWG), including Audit Committees (ACs), in line with the requirements of the Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013), the Standards on Auditing (SAs) prescribed under CA 2013, and other relevant Rules and Regulations. 2. Provisions of CA 2013 and other Relevant Rules: The CA 2013 has placed certain important obligations on the Board of Directors (BOD or the ‘Board’), Independent Directors (IDs), Audit Committees and Statutory Auditors of Companies in respect of Accounts and Audit of Companies. 2.1 Board of Directors: Section 134 of CA 2013 and related Rules require that the financial statements, including the consolidated financial statements, if any, be approved by the Board of Directors. A report by the Board shall be attached to the financial statements, which shall include, inter alia, an important statement called Directors’ Responsibility Statement. According to sub-section 5 of Section 134, this statement shall disclose the Board’s assertions regarding certain critical aspects, such as adherence to applicable accounting standards; selection and application of accounting policies and making of judgements/estimates on reasonable and prudent basis; maintenance of adequate records for safeguarding the assets of the company and preventing and detecting fraud and other irregularities; preparation of accounts on a going concern basis; implementation of adequate internal financial controls and ensuring their operating effectiveness; and implementation of proper systems to ensure compliance with all applicable laws. 2.2 Independent Directors: Schedule IV to the CA 2013 lays down a Code for Independent Directors. Sub-clause 4 of Clause II casts an obligation on them to satisfy themselves of the integrity of financial information and that financial controls and the systems of risk management are robust and defensible. Further, Clause III casts several duties on the independent directors, such as appropriate induction and regular updation of their skills, knowledge and familiarity with the company; clarification or amplification of information; remaining well informed about the company and the external environment it operates; paying sufficient attention and ensuring that adequate deliberations are held before approving related party transactions. Reporting concerns about unethical behaviour, actual or suspected fraud or violation of the company’s Code of Conduct or Ethics Policy; and where there are concerns about the running of the company or proposed action, the independent directors are to ensure that these are addressed by the Board and, to the extent that they are not resolved, insist that their concerns are recorded in the minutes of the Board meeting. 2.3 Audit Committees: Section 177 of CA 2013, the related Rules stipulate several important roles and responsibilities of the Audit Committee. One of the critical responsibilities is to review and monitor the Auditor’s independence and performance, and the effectiveness of the audit process. Other areas of critical significance relate to related party transactions, inter-corporate loans and investments, the valuation of assets of the company, the evaluation of internal financial controls and risk management systems, the review of major accounting entries involving estimates based on the exercise of judgment by management and discussions with Auditors before the audit commences, about the nature and scope of audit as well as post-audit discussions to ascertain any area of concern and so on. 2.4 Auditors: Section 143 of CA 2013 is titled ‘Powers and duties of auditors and auditing standards’. Sub-section 2 of section 143 requires the Auditor to make a report to members of the company on the accounts examined and the financial statements, inter alia, after taking into account the provisions of CA 2013, the accounting and auditing standards, and whether the financial statements give a true and fair view. Further, subsection 9 of section 143 of CA 2013 casts a statutory obligation on the Auditor to comply with the auditing standards. 3. Provisions of the SAs prescribed under CA 2013: There are two SAs, viz. SA 260 (Revised) 1 and SA 265 2 that deal with the communication between the Auditors and Those Charged with Governance (TCWG), Audit Committee and Management. Also, there are many other SAs, including SQC 1, that have specific communication requirements
rows.summary: NFRA says listed companies and auditors must improve communication with boards and audit committees to strengthen audit oversight and compliance.

rows.title: NFRA Circular on Responsibilities of Principal Auditor and Other Auditors in Group Audits
rows.desc: / Government of India /National Financial Reporting Authority ***** 7 th Floor, Hindustan Times House, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi NF- 25013/2/2023-O/o Secy-NFRA Dated 3.10.2024 Circular under Section 132(2) (b), (c), and (d) read with Rule 4(1), 4(2)(e) and Rule 9 of NFRA Rules 2018 To 1. Auditors of the entities under the purview of Rule 3 of NFRA Rules 2018 Subject: Responsibilities of Principal Auditor and Other Auditors in Group Audits The Statutory Audit of financial statements, both standalone financial statements (SFS) and consolidated financial statements (CFS) under Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013 or Act), require the auditors to mandatorily comply with the Standards on Auditing (SAs), and related Standards and Codes, prescribed under section 143 of CA 2013. As of now, the auditors are required to ensure adherence to the following sets of Standards and Codes to remain compliant with the extant laws in India: a) Standard on Quality Control (SQC); b) 35 SAs addressing various aspects during the entire life cycle of an audit; and c) Code of Ethics including Independence standards. 2. Audit of SFS, where the company has branches, and the audit of CFS of companies with subsidiaries, associates etc, called as audit of Group Financial Statements (GFS), requires special considerations by the auditor (called Principal Auditor), who is ultimately responsible for issue of group audit opinion, and also by the auditors (called Other Auditor) engaged to undertake audit of components such as branches and subsidiaries etc. ‘SA 600 - Using the Work of Another Auditor’ deals with the requirements in the audit of GFS. 3. In the contemporary business and economic environment, there are audit areas of material and/or significant risk in almost all the audits of GFS due to the following features (this list is not exhaustive). a. Complex group structures including special purpose vehicles, auto pilot structures, cross holdings of interests across group entities and shared service centres in different geographies b. Shell or dummy companies as a conduit to siphon off funds from Public Interest Entities (PIEs) c. Regular/frequent formation or acquisition of new businesses and/or entities including schemes of merger and demerger d. Significant transactions with related parties e. Significant transactions outside the normal course of business f. Unusual or abnormal variances in financial data g. Rapid technological developments 4. However, in the course of performing its functions such as exercising oversight and monitoring and enforcing compliance, the National Financial Reporting Authority (‘NFRA’) has observed gross negligence and audit failure in audits of GFS (cases of Group Audits involving various companies). Instances include Reliance Capital Limited, Reliance Home Finance Limited, Reliance Commercial Finance Limited (together accounting for alleged fraud of ₹ 29000 Crores), Coffee Day Enterprises Limited (alleged fraud of ₹ 3500 Crores), Dewan Housing and Finance Limited (alleged fraud of ₹ 34000 Crores), and audit quality review of IL&FS (which collapsed with a debt of ₹ 90000 Crores). In these cases, moneys were diverted through subsidiaries and associates. The Principal Auditors did not raise red flags at the right time despite indicators of fraud, going concern issues and diversion of funds, as they relied on fallacious interpretations of SA 600 to not go into these issues and instead completely relied upon the clean audit reports of the Component Auditors. 5. The combined effect of these have resulted in a loss of tens of thousands of crores in the financial and capital market, adversely impacting investors, including retail investors, and creditors, involving huge public interest. Therefore, in exercise of NFRA’s powers under Section 132 (2) (b), (c), (d) read with Rule 4 (1), 4 (2) (e) and Rules 3, 4 and 9 of NFRA Rules 2018, the auditors’ obligations, under CA 2013 and existing requirements in SA 600 and related standards, are hereby reiterated in the following paragraphs, so that interpretations of the provisions of SA 600 by the auditors remain consistent with their obligations under CA 2013, Standard on Quality Control (SQC) and other applicable Standards of Auditing. Observations by NFRA across various enforcement cases (illustrative) 6. Significant gaps have been noted by NFRA in audits, across various enforcement cases, relevant to audit of GFS. These include: a. Inadequate coordination/discussion with Component Auditors at most stages of audit b. Discrepancies in the number of components as per CFS and mandatory filings in MCA 21 which were not assessed by the auditors, c. Non-assessment of inclusion by Management of unaudited financial statements of some components in the CFS. In respect of the latter, the Principal Auditor stated that “........ preparation of consolidated financial statements (CFS) is the responsibility of management and accordingly, use of component’s unaudited financial statemen
rows.summary: NFRA says principal and component auditors in group audits must follow audit standards and quality rules, with the principal auditor ultimately responsible for the group opinion.

rows.title: NFRA circular on Statutory Auditors’ responsibilities in relation to Fraud in a Company
rows.desc: / Government of India / National Financial Reporting Authority ***** 7th Floor, Hindustan Times House, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi NF-25013/2/2023 Dated 26.06.2023 Circular To 1. Auditors of the Entities Regulated by the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) Subject: Statutory Auditors’ Responsibilities in relation to Fraud in a Company In course of discharge of its statutory functions, NFRA has noticed that auditors are not fulfilling their statutory responsibilities relating to reporting of fraud as mandated under the Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013) read with the relevant Rules and the applicable Standards on Auditing (SAs). 2 The CA 2013, the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order (CARO) and the Standards on Auditing (SAs) place mandatory reporting obligations on auditors to report fraud and/or suspected fraud to the Central Government and the Board/Audit Committee. 2.1 Section 143 (12) of CA 2013 and related Rules places certain reporting obligations on the auditor, in relation to frauds: “Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, if an auditor of a company in the course of the performance of his duties as auditor, has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving such amount or amounts as may be prescribed, is being or has been committed in the company by its officers or employees, the auditor shall report the matter to the Central Government within such time and in such manner as may be prescribed: ....” Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014, prescribes detailed steps that need to be followed by the auditor if he has reason to believe that an offence of fraud, which involves or is expected to involve individually an amount of rupees one crore or above, is being or has been committed against the company by its officers or employees. The auditor is required to report the matter to the Board or Audit Committee and to the Central Government in the form of a statement as specified in Form ADT-4. 2.2 Clause (xi) of Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order, 2020 1 also requires auditors to make statements relating to reporting of fraud in his/her report. 2.3 Section 140 (5) of the CA 2013, contains consequences for auditors if they have acted, directly or indirectly, in a fraudulent manner or abetted or colluded in any fraud by, or in relation to, the company or its directors or officers. Under the section, the auditor shall also be liable for action under section 447 of CA 2013 apart from removal and debarment for a period of five years. In this regard, it is pertinent to note that the definition of fraud under section 447 of CA 2013 is wide and states that, “fraud” in relation to affairs of a company or anybody corporate, includes any act, omission, 1 Additional matters to be reported in the Auditor’s Report in terms of Order issued by the Central Government in exercise of powers u/s 143 (11) of the CA 2013. concealment of any fact or abuse of position committed by any person or any other person with the connivance in any manner, with intent to deceive, to gain undue advantage from, or to injure the interests of, the company or its shareholders or its creditors or any other person, whether or not there is any wrongful gain or wrongful loss” (emphasis supplied). 2.4 SA 240 2 -The Auditor’s Responsibilities Relating to Fraud in an Audit of Financial Statements- elaborately deals with the auditor’s responsibilities relating to fraud in an audit of financial statements. The SA requires the auditor to maintain professional skepticism throughout the audit and states: “12. In accordance with SA 200, the auditor shall maintain professional skepticism throughout the audit, recognizing the possibility that a material misstatement due to fraud could exist, notwithstanding the auditor’s past experience of the honesty and integrity of the entity’s management and those charged with governance.” 2.5 The guidance provided in paras A59-A66 of SA 240, details the Communications to Management, Those Charged with Governance (TCWG) and Regulatory and Enforcement Authorities regarding reporting of the fraud/suspected fraud. 3 There is a misconception amongst some Auditors that resigning from an audit engagement absolves them of their reporting obligations relating to fraud and the consequences under CA 2013 for nonreporting of fraud. In this regard, the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in a recent judgment dated 03.05.2023 (Union of India and Another versus Deloitte Haskins and Sells LLP & Anr CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.2305-2307 OF 2022), has held that the consequences of section 140 (5) of CA 2013 will be applicable also on those auditors who resign from the their audit engagements without reporting fraud/suspected fraud. The Hon’ble Apex Court observed: “7.... Therefore, on true interpretation, even on resignation by an auditor of a company even during the enquiry/proceedings under section 140(5) or even prior to that, there shall not be any termination of the proceedings under section 140(5) as ob
rows.summary: NFRA says company auditors must promptly report suspected fraud to management and the government under law and auditing standards.

rows.title: NFRA Circular Non Compliance with Ind AS policies on Revenue
rows.desc: mw � I Government of India � � R4 "" 1fl�1 � /National Financial Reporting Authority ***** 7 th Floor, Hindustan Times House, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi NF-25011/1/2023-O/o Secy-NFRA Dated 29.03.2023 Circular To 1. All listed companies 2. Unlisted companies specified in Rule 3 of NFRA Rules, 2018 3. Auditors of the above companies Subject: Instances of non-compliance with Indian Accounting Standards (Ind ASs) on Accounting Policies for measurement of Revenue from Contracts with Customers and Trade Receivables As per sub-section 2(b) of section 132 of the Companies Act 2013 (the Act) read with rule 4(2)( c) of the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules 2018 (NFRA Rules 2018), the National Financial Reporting Authority is mandated to monitor and enforce compliance with accounting standards and auditing standards. Further, NFRA is required by sub-section 2( d) of section 132 of the Act read with rule 4(2) (g) of NFRA Rules, to perform such other functions and duties as may be necessary or incidental to the aforesaid functions and duties. 2. NFRA monitors compliance with accounting standards by Companies as part of its review of published financial statements of companies. During its recent review, instances of apparent non­ compliance with the prescriptions of the Ind ASs in the critical areas of Revenue Recognition and Measurement, and Initial Measurement of corresponding Trade Receivables have come to light. In order to ensure adherence to high-quality Ind AS Reporting Framework, which is substantially aligned with globally accepted IFRS Standards, the instances of non-compliance are highlighted below for the urgent attention of the Company Management/Audit Committees and the Statutory Auditors. Revenue from Contracts with Customers - Recognition and Measurement 3. Para 46 of Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, requires that the entity shall recognise as revenue the amount of the transaction price, excluding the estimates of variable consideration that is allocated to that performance obligation. However, it has been noticed that the significant accounting policies disclosed by many companies wrongly state t h at revenue is recognised and measured at fair value of the consideration received or receivable. One example of such erroneous accounting policy of a large listed company 1 , as observed by NFRA, states as follows: " ... Revenue is measured at the fair value of consideration received or receivable taking into account the amount of discounts, incentives, volume rebates, and outgoing taxes on Sales ....... " However, there are several listed companies which correctly state their accounting policies in this regard. An example of correct accounting policy stated by a company is as follows: " .. Revenue towards satisfaction of a performance obligation is measured at the amount of transaction price (net of variable consideration) allocated to that performance obligation. The transaction price of goods sold and services rendered is net of variable consideration on account of 1 Name of Companies withheld. Page 1 of3 various discounts and schemes offered by the Company as part of the contract ... " 4.Appendix A to Ind AS 115 defines the 'transaction price' as the amount of consideration to which an entity expects to be entitled in exchange for transferring promised goods or services to a customer, excluding amounts collected on behalf of third parties. It is important to note that the transaction price defined in appendix A to Ind AS 115 is different from 'fair value' de f ined in Ind AS 113 and Ind AS 32, Financial Instruments: Presentation. Under Ind AS 115, the application of fair value is relevant only in a limited set of situations; for example, under para 66 oflnd AS 115, where the customer promises consideration in a form other than cash, an entity shall measure the non-cash consideration at fair value. Trade Rcceiva bles -Initial Measurement 5.Trade receivables are financial assets within the scope of measurement requirements of Ind AS I 09, Financial Instruments. All financial assets are required to be initially measured at fair value plus or minus the transaction costs. However, those financial assets classified as 'fair value through pro f it or loss' are required to be measured at fair value (para 5.1.1 of Ind AS 109). Further, as an exception to these principles, according to para 5.1.3 read with para 5.1.1 of Ind AS 109, financial assets in the form of trade receivables, shall be initially measured (initial recognition amount) at their transaction price (as defined in Ind AS 115) unless those contain a significant financing component determined in accordance with Ind AS 115 (or when the entity applies the practical expedient in accordance with para 63 of Ind AS 115). 6.It has, however, been noticed that many companies in their accounting policy, either stated separately for trade receivables or stated as part of the accounting policy for financial assets which include tra
rows.summary: NFRA flagged possible Ind AS non-compliance in how companies recognize revenue and measure related trade receivables, and expects corrective adherence.
