rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s December 18, 2025 Order (Release No. 105-2025-038) censures CPA Jennifer A. Crofoot, bars her from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and requires her to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education (CPE) in PCAOB auditing standards before she can seek Board consent to associate with a registered firm again. She may not petition for Board consent until three years after the date of the Order, and the settlement does **not** impose a civil money penalty because the Board took her financial resources into account; however, the Board states it would otherwise have imposed a $50,000 penalty. The sanctions arise from PCAOB findings that Crofoot violated PCAOB rules and standards in connection with audits of four issuer clients.

For compliance purposes, the key issue is that Crofoot was the engagement partner and an audit partner at Fruci & Associates II, PLLC during the relevant period, and the Board found her conduct met the statutory standard for sanctions under Section 105(c)(5) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act because it involved intentional, knowing, or reckless conduct, or repeated negligent conduct, resulting in violations of applicable standards. The Order covers audits of issuers including Clean Vision Corp., Hammer Fiber Optics Holdings Corp., and at least one additional issuer whose name begins later in the document excerpt but is not fully included here. The PCAOB specifically tied the sanctions to violations related to audit evidence and quality control issues at Crofoot’s former firm, meaning the matter is not just an individual disciplinary action but also signals firm-level control deficiencies affecting audit execution.

The proceeding was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and Crofoot accepted a settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205 without admitting or denying the findings, except as to the Board’s jurisdiction. The Order’s findings are based on the version of PCAOB rules and standards in effect at the time of the audits, so firms should evaluate historical audit files against the standards then applicable, not just current requirements. For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that registered firms must ensure engagement partners properly obtain and document sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and that firm quality-control systems are strong enough to prevent repeated audit standard violations that can lead to individual bars, mandated remedial education, and public sanctions.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB sanctioned Beckles & Co. Inc., a registered public accounting firm in West Palm Beach, Florida, for repeatedly failing to timely file required Form APs identifying audit participants, in violation of PCAOB Rule 3211. The Order, issued December 4, 2025 (PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-036), censures the firm, imposes a civil money penalty of $35,000, and requires the firm to comply with its policies and procedures designed to ensure future compliance with PCAOB reporting requirements for audit participants.

Rule 3211 requires every registered public accounting firm to file a Form AP for each issuer audit report, disclosing information about the engagement partner and other accounting firms that participated in the audit, and the filing deadline is the 35th day after the audit report is first included in an SEC-filed document. PCAOB found that Beckles repeatedly missed this deadline across multiple issuer audits, including OpGen, Inc. (2023 fiscal-year audit report dated June 3, 2024 and included the same day in the Form 10-K); Token Communities, Ltd. (2023 audit report dated August 2, 2024, included in a Form 10-K/A filed August 5, 2024, and 2024 audit report dated December 31, 2024, included the same day in the Form 10-K); UbuyHoldings, Inc. (2023 audit report dated March 7, 2024 and 2024 audit report dated June 6, 2025, each included the same day in the respective Form 10-K filings); and Vestiage, Inc. (2023 audit report dated April 16, 2024 and 2024 audit report dated April 15, 2025, each included the same day in the respective Form 10-K filings).

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB is treating Form AP timing failures as an enforceable audit-reporting violation, not a technicality. Any registered firm performing issuer audits must have controls to track the SEC filing date of each audit report and ensure the Form AP is submitted within 35 days, especially where the audit report is first included in an original 10-K or in an amended filing such as a 10-K/A. The Order also states that the sanctions are imposed under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and that Beckles accepted the settlement without admitting or denying the findings, except for PCAOB jurisdiction.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered an order on December 4, 2025 censuring TPS Thayer LLC, imposing a $100,000 civil money penalty, and requiring contingent remedial actions described later in the order. The sanctions arose from TPS Thayer’s use of audit work performed in a substantial-role capacity by Firm A, a Beijing-based public accounting firm that was not registered with the PCAOB, in five issuer audits. The Board found that TPS Thayer failed to properly plan those audits and failed to reasonably supervise Firm A’s work, and also failed to accurately disclose Firm A’s participation in both Form AP filings and communications to the issuers’ audit committees.

The affected issuers were Huadi International Group Co., Ltd. and Ostin Technology Group Co., Ltd., both Cayman Islands holding companies with principal operations in China and both “issuers” under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act/PCAOB rules. Huadi’s subsidiaries manufacture and sell steel products, while Ostin’s subsidiaries supply display modules and polarizers for consumer electronics, commercial LCDs, and automotive displays. TPS Thayer is a Texas-based PCAOB-registered firm, but Firm A was not PCAOB-registered at any relevant time.

The order was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1) and (2), and TPS Thayer submitted an Offer of Settlement under Rule 5205 that the Board accepted. TPS Thayer did not admit or deny the findings, except it admitted the PCAOB’s jurisdiction over it and the subject matter. The order notes that TPS Thayer filed a Form 1-WD on April 7, 2025 seeking withdrawal from PCAOB registration, and that request will be addressed under PCAOB Rule 2107.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that a PCAOB-registered firm may not allow an unregistered foreign accounting firm to perform a substantial role in an issuer audit without proper planning, supervision, and disclosure. The order also underscores that related disclosures to the PCAOB on Form AP and to audit committees must accurately reflect the participation of such firms. The document states that the Board’s findings are based on TPS Thayer’s settlement offer and are not binding on any other person or entity.

The PCAOB issued an October 7, 2025 disciplinary order against former EY Peru audit partner Daniel Carpio Diaz for violations of PCAOB rules and standards in connection with the audit of issuer Gilat Satellite Networks Ltd.’s 2020 financial statements and 2020 internal control over financial reporting. Carpio submitted an Offer of Settlement without admitting or denying the findings, and the PCAOB accepted it and made findings for purposes of the proceeding only. The PCAOB cited the action as necessary to protect investors and the public interest in accurate, informative, and independent audit reports, and noted that Carpio had already been removed from PCAOB audit work by EY Peru in March 2021 and transferred to a non-PCAOB-registered affiliate.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s September 23, 2025 Order censures Marcum Asia CPAs LLP (formerly Marcum Bernstein & Pinchuk LLP), imposes a $100,000 civil money penalty, and requires the firm to conduct training on communications between predecessor and successor auditors. The sanctions arise from the Board’s finding that MarcumBP violated PCAOB rules and auditing standards governing predecessor/successor auditor communications in connection with its transition off the Gridsum Holding Inc. audit.

The underlying matter began when the PCAOB instituted disciplinary proceedings on October 23, 2024 under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1). The Board determined the hearing could be public for good cause under Section 105(c)(2) and Rule 5203; the Division of Enforcement and Investigations agreed, but MarcumBP did not consent. MarcumBP then submitted an Offer of Settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205, which the Board accepted; the firm neither admitted nor denied the findings, except that it admitted the Board’s jurisdiction over it and the subject matter.

MarcumBP is a New York-headquartered registered public accounting firm, licensed in New York, Texas, and California. It served as Gridsum Holding Inc.’s external auditor from June 28, 2018 until Gridsum dismissed it on January 6, 2019, but it did not issue any audit reports on Gridsum’s financial statements. Gridsum was an SEC issuer listed on Nasdaq and headquartered in Beijing, China, while its successor auditor, Shandong Haoxin Certified Public Accountants Co., Ltd. (Haoxin), a PCAOB-registered firm licensed by China’s Ministry of Finance, took over on January 6, 2019 and remained auditor until Gridsum terminated its SEC registration in April 2021.

The conduct at issue was MarcumBP’s transfer of draft work papers to Haoxin, and the Board concluded that this transfer, and the surrounding predecessor/successor communications, breached PCAOB requirements. The Order notes that Haoxin had previously been sanctioned by the PCAOB on November 30, 2023 for conduct related to its audits of Gridsum’s 2015–2017 financial statements, placing this matter in the context of broader audit-related enforcement involving the same issuer. The compliance takeaway is that predecessor auditors must handle communications and transfer of work papers in a manner consistent with PCAOB rules and auditing standards when a successor auditor is taking over an issuer engagement, because failures in that process can lead to public censure, monetary penalties, and mandated remedial training.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s July 22, 2025 disciplinary order against Hong Kong registered firm Centurion ZD CPA & Co. and its managing/sole equity partner, CHAN Kam Fuk (Dominic), imposes three principal sanctions: a censure, permanent revocation of Centurion’s PCAOB registration, and a permanent bar preventing Chan from being associated with any PCAOB-registered public accounting firm. In addition, the PCAOB imposed a **$75,000 civil money penalty**, jointly and severally against the Firm and Chan. The action was brought under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and it was resolved through Offers of Settlement submitted under PCAOB Rule 5205; the respondents did **not** admit or deny the findings, except they admitted the PCAOB’s jurisdiction.

The PCAOB found that the respondents violated PCAOB rules and auditing standards in connection with audits of the **2021 financial statements of two issuer clients** and in audit procedures for subsidiaries of a **third issuer**, and that the Firm also violated PCAOB audit-reporting rules in connection with the two issuer audits. The order further states that Centurion filed **inaccurate and/or untimely Form APs** (the PCAOB’s required auditor reporting forms), and that the Firm violated PCAOB **quality control standards**. Chan was found to have **directly and substantially contributed** to the Firm’s audit reporting violations.

The order identifies Centurion as a Hong Kong public accounting firm that had been PCAOB-registered since **September 6, 2006**, through predecessor firms, and notes that it cancelled its Hong Kong accounting license in **December 2024** and its business registration in **March 2025**. Chan was identified as the Firm’s managing partner and sole equity partner, a Hong Kong CPA, and the engagement partner for two issuer audits as well as the partner responsible for certain subsidiary audit work. The order states that these sanctions were imposed because the PCAOB found the conduct met the statutory standard for sanctions based on intentional/knowing or reckless conduct, or repeated negligent conduct, and the stated policy purpose was protection of investors and the public interest in informative, accurate, and independent audit reports.

For compliance teams, the practical effect is that **Centurion can no longer act as a PCAOB-registered audit firm**, and **Chan cannot serve in any associated-person capacity at a PCAOB-registered firm**. The order is a significant enforcement action tied to audit execution, audit reporting, Form AP filing accuracy/timeliness, and quality control failures, and it underscores the PCAOB’s willingness to impose permanent bars and registration revocations where it believes the standards have been repeatedly or seriously violated.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB sanctioned Goldman & Company, CPA’s, P.C., a registered public accounting firm headquartered in Marietta, Georgia, for violating audit documentation rules in connection with its audit of Broker-Dealer A, a Georgia broker-dealer registered with the SEC. In the Order dated July 8, 2025, the PCAOB censured the firm, imposed a $25,000 civil money penalty, and required remedial actions described later in the Order; the firm accepted the settlement without admitting or denying the findings, other than PCAOB jurisdiction.

The violation centered on AS 1215’s audit documentation completion requirement. Goldman issued its audit report on Broker-Dealer A’s 2022 financial statements on March 30, 2023, which made the documentation completion deadline May 14, 2023—no later than 45 days after report release. After the PCAOB’s Division of Registration and Inspections notified the firm on May 31, 2023 that the audit would be inspected, firm personnel then changed 28 work papers and added 4 new work papers between June 6 and June 22, 2023, weeks after the documentation completion date.

The added and altered work papers related to multiple core audit areas, including risk assessment, cash, notes payable, prepaids and other assets, income statements, income taxes, equity, investments, and review of the system and organization controls report. Based on those post-deadline changes, the PCAOB found the firm did not assemble a complete and final set of audit documentation by the required deadline, which is a breach of PCAOB audit documentation standards. This matter is important for compliance teams because it shows that audit files must be complete and final within 45 days of report release, and any substantive additions or alterations after that deadline can trigger enforcement action, especially once an inspection has been announced.

The Order states that the sanctions were imposed under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and that the proceeding was instituted to protect investors and promote informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The document also notes that the findings apply only to the firm in this proceeding and are not binding on others.

rows.summary:
PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-026, issued July 8, 2025, sanctions Michael Coglianese, CPA P.C., an Illinois-licensed public accounting firm registered with the PCAOB and also licensed in Connecticut, New Jersey, Georgia, and North Carolina. The PCAOB censured the firm, imposed a $50,000 civil money penalty, and required remedial actions because the firm repeatedly violated PCAOB standards on 17 broker and/or dealer engagements by failing to obtain a required engagement quality review from a qualified engagement quality reviewer before issuance of the engagement reports.  

The violation concerned PCAOB AS 1220, Engagement Quality Review, which requires an engagement quality review for all audits and for broker-dealer attestation engagements under Attestation Standard No. 1 (examinations of compliance reports of brokers and dealers) and No. 2 (reviews of exemption reports of brokers and dealers). The Order also cites failure to comply with QC Section 20.01 because the firm did not maintain a system of quality control that provided reasonable assurance that engagement quality reviews would be performed on all audits in accordance with PCAOB standards. The Board found that the firm was not ensuring the required “concurring approval of issuance” by a qualified engagement quality reviewer before allowing clients to use the engagement reports, and that the reviewer had to be a partner or equivalent at the issuing firm.  

The proceeding was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the firm settled under PCAOB Rule 5205 without admitting or denying the findings, except as to PCAOB jurisdiction. The practical compliance takeaway is that registered firms performing broker-dealer audit or attestation work must have controls in place to ensure every covered engagement receives a properly qualified engagement quality review and formal approval of issuance before the report is released; failure to do so can result in PCAOB censure, monetary penalties, and mandated remedial measures.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 24, 2025 Order against Deloitte Accountants B.V. (“Deloitte Netherlands”) censures the firm, imposes a $3.0 million civil money penalty, and requires remedial actions under Section IV of the Order. The Board found that, from at least 2018 through 2022, Deloitte Netherlands failed to establish and maintain adequate policies and procedures to administer and oversee its internal training exams, violating PCAOB rules and quality control standards tied to integrity and personnel management. Those failures allowed the firm to miss widespread misconduct involving hundreds of personnel who improperly shared answers or access to test questions and answers, or received such access without reporting it, in mandatory online training courses covering subjects such as U.S. auditing standards, U.S. GAAP, and professional ethics.

The misconduct occurred through unauthorized methods including electronic communications and joint test-taking, and most of the involved personnel worked in the firm’s Audit & Assurance practice. Deloitte Netherlands is a Rotterdam-headquartered affiliate within the Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited network, registered with the Dutch Authority for the Financial Markets and, at the relevant times, registered with the PCAOB. The settlement was entered under PCAOB Rule 5205; the firm consented without admitting or denying the findings, except as to the Board’s jurisdiction.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the PCAOB treated weak controls over mandatory internal training assessments as a quality control failure serious enough to support sanctions under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. The Order indicates that firms must have effective systems to govern training exam administration, monitoring, and escalation/reporting of improper answer sharing, not merely policies on paper. The Board found the conduct satisfied the statutory sanction standard because it involved intentional/knowing or reckless conduct, or repeated negligent conduct, over multiple years.

Studer CPA P.C.; the order also censures both Studer and the firm and imposes a joint-and-several civil money penalty of $20,000. The proceedings were instituted on June 20, 2024 under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1); the Board determined there was good cause to make the hearing public under Section 105(c)(2) and PCAOB Rule 5203, although the respondents did not consent to a public hearing. The respondents submitted settlement offers under PCAOB Rule 5205, which the Board accepted; they neither admitted nor denied the findings, except they admitted the Board’s jurisdiction over them and the subject matter.

The firm was registered with the PCAOB on November 5, 2003 and is located in Freeport, New York. The misconduct related to three audits on which the firm issued unqualified opinions with going-concern explanatory paragraphs: JMU Limited’s fiscal year ended December 31, 2018 audit report issued June 28, 2019; UBI Blockchain Internet Ltd.’s fiscal year ended August 31, 2018 audit report issued December 5, 2018; and The Greater Cannabis Company, Inc.’s fiscal year ended December 31, 2018 audit report issued April 15, 2019. Studer, a New York-licensed CPA (license no. 033662), is the firm’s founder, sole stockholder, and president, and served as the engagement partner on each of the three audits.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB treated the failures as sufficiently serious to warrant the most severe firm/person sanctions available in this proceeding: permanent firm registration revocation, a permanent bar on Studer as an associated person of any registered firm, and a monetary penalty. The order also confirms that intentional, knowing, reckless, or repeated negligent conduct can support these sanctions under Section 105(c)(5) of the Act.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered a settlement order on June 12, 2025 against Heaton & Company, PLLC (doing business as Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah) and its partner Kristofer Heaton, CPA, for audit documentation and quality-control failures tied to five issuer audits. The Board found that the firm did not timely assemble a complete and final set of audit documentation for retention on those five audits, and that Heaton did not adequately perform the required engagement quality reviews (“EQRs”) for those same five issuer audits; the Board also found that the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards and that Heaton directly and substantially contributed to those quality-control violations. The sanctions are severe: the firm is censured, its PCAOB registration is revoked, Heaton is barred from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, and both respondents must pay civil penalties—$35,000 for the firm and $25,000 for Heaton.

The order also imposes forward-looking compliance conditions. If the firm seeks to reapply for PCAOB registration in the future, it must first complete remedial measures required by the order before submitting any new application. Heaton must complete 40 hours of continuing professional education, in addition to any CPE required for his state or other professional licenses, before he may file any petition seeking PCAOB consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm. The order states that both the firm and Heaton may reapply/petition only after two years from the date of the order, meaning no earlier than June 12, 2027.

For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that the PCAOB treated the failures as serious enough to warrant registration revocation and a bar, not merely a reprimand, because the conduct involved repeated audit-documentation breakdowns and deficient EQR performance across multiple issuer engagements. The order was entered pursuant to Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the respondents settled without admitting or denying the findings except as to PCAOB jurisdiction.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s April 22, 2025 Order (Release No. 105-2025-020) censures Adeptus Partners LLC, a registered public accounting firm, and Howard S. Krant, CPA, for audit-related failures tied to supervision, review, and quality control. Krant is suspended for one year from acting as an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and he must pay a $50,000 civil money penalty; Adeptus must pay a $75,000 civil money penalty. In addition, the firm is required to engage an independent consultant to review Adeptus’s system of quality control and make recommendations, with the consultant work to be performed under the conditions specified in Section IV of the Order.

The sanctions were imposed because the PCAOB found that Krant violated PCAOB rules and standards in connection with the audits of two issuers—Blockchain of Things, Inc. and Applied UV, Inc.—and that Adeptus violated PCAOB rules and quality control standards. Krant was the engagement partner for both audits, so the misconduct directly implicates engagement-level supervision and review responsibilities. Adeptus is headquartered in New York, New York, and is registered with the PCAOB; it is also licensed in New Jersey and Maryland, which may matter for broader state practice oversight, though the PCAOB action itself is under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB rules.

The proceeding was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the respondents resolved it through settlement offers under PCAOB Rule 5205 without admitting or denying the findings, except as to the PCAOB’s jurisdiction. The Board stated that the conduct met the statutory standard for sanctions because it involved intentional or knowing conduct, including reckless conduct, or repeated negligent conduct resulting in violations of applicable standards. The order is aimed at protecting investors and promoting informative, accurate, and independent audit reports, so the key compliance takeaway for audit firms is that deficient engagement supervision, review, and quality control can lead not only to firm censure and monetary penalties, but also to individual suspension and mandated third-party quality-control remediation.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s March 25, 2025 order against James Pai CPA PLLC and its sole partner, Yu-Ching James Pai, resolves disciplinary proceedings over audit failures in two issuer audits and imposes both firm-level and individual sanctions. The Board censured both respondents, revoked the firm’s PCAOB registration, barred Pai from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and imposed a $40,000 civil money penalty jointly and severally on the firm and Pai. The order states that the firm may reapply for PCAOB registration only after three years from the date of the order, and Pai may seek PCAOB consent to associate with a registered firm only after three years from the date of the order.

The sanctions are based on findings that the respondents violated PCAOB rules and standards in connection with two audits of one issuer client’s financial statements; that the firm failed to obtain the required engagement quality review (EQR) for those audits; that the firm filed inaccurate PCAOB Form APs in connection with one of the audits; and that the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards. The PCAOB also found that Pai directly and substantially contributed to the EQR, Form AP, and quality control violations, and that the conduct met the statutory standard for sanctions under Section 105(c)(5) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act because it involved intentional or knowing, reckless, or repeated negligent conduct. These findings were made pursuant to settlement offers, which the respondents submitted without admitting or denying the findings, except for the Board’s jurisdiction.

Beyond the monetary penalty and prohibitions, the order requires the firm to undertake specific remedial actions to its system of quality control before it can submit any future PCAOB registration application, and to provide evidence of those remedial measures with any future application. Pai is also required to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education, in addition to any CPE required for licensure, before filing any petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm. For compliance teams, the key operational takeaway is that PCAOB registration status, public-company audit eligibility, and future association rights are restricted for at least three years, and any re-entry effort must be supported by documented quality-control remediation and Pai’s additional education completion.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s March 11, 2025 order censures Jaslyn Sellers, CPA, bars her from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and imposes a $15,000 civil money penalty. The Board found that Sellers, acting as engagement partner on BF Borgers CPA PC’s audits of NetSol Technologies, Inc. The matter involved an issuer audit, a registered public accounting firm, and an associated person under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), so firms should view this as a reminder that engagement partners must ensure adequate evidence for significant-risk areas and strict adherence to independence rules before audit reports are issued, including where critical audit matters are described in the report.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB, in Release No. 105-2025-018 dated March 11, 2025, sanctioned PwC Singapore (PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, a PCAOB-registered public accounting firm in Singapore) for violations of PCAOB rules and quality control standards connected to the firm’s Personal Independence Compliance Testing (PICT) process. The Board found that, from 2022 through mid-2024, the firm failed to establish and implement adequate policies and procedures governing PICT and failed to foster an ethical culture within its Independence Office, which undermined the integrity of its quality control system. While those weaknesses existed, personnel in the Independence Office created and used methods to influence the PICT results reported to the PCAOB’s Division of Registration and Inspections and to understate the rate at which firm personnel failed to timely report financial interests and relationships.

As sanctions, the PCAOB censured PwC Singapore, imposed a civil money penalty of $1,500,000, and required the firm to undertake remedial actions described later in the Order. The proceeding was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the Board accepted PwC Singapore’s settlement offer under Rule 5205; the firm did not admit the findings except for the PCAOB’s jurisdiction. The document makes clear that the Board viewed the conduct as intentional/knowing or at least reckless, or alternatively as repeated negligent conduct, meeting the statutory conditions for sanctions.

For compliance purposes, the key substantive requirement is that PCAOB-registered firms must maintain and properly operate a system of quality control with documented policies and procedures that provide reasonable assurance that personnel perform professional responsibilities with integrity, and that responsibility assignments and documentation are adequate to make the system effective. This order signals that misleading internal compliance-testing results, especially where they affect reported independence-deficiency rates, can itself be treated as a serious PCAOB violation even if the underlying issue is within an internal independence or quality-control function rather than an audit engagement. The remedial actions referenced in Section IV are part of the enforcement outcome and should be reviewed as compliance obligations imposed on the firm, though the excerpt provided does not specify those steps.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered a settled disciplinary order on March 11, 2025, against KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda. (KPMG Brazil), a PCAOB-registered public accounting firm headquartered in São Paulo and a member of the KPMG International network. The Board censured the firm, imposed a $700,000 civil money penalty, and required remedial actions, all under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1); KPMG Brazil accepted the settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205 without admitting or denying the findings, except as to jurisdiction.

The Order says the violations occurred between 2020 and 2023 and involved repeated compliance failures tied to issuer audits. First, KPMG Brazil failed to make required communications to the relevant audit committee or audit committee equivalent in connection with 38 issuer audits for fiscal years between 2019 and 2022, violating AS 1301.10d, which governs communications with audit committees. Second, it failed to report on PCAOB Form 2 the audit reports or consents it issued in connection with six issuer audits, violating PCAOB Rule 2200 (Annual Report). Third, it filed two inaccurate Form APs, violating PCAOB Rule 3211(a), which requires accurate disclosure of audit participants.

The PCAOB also found that KPMG Brazil violated PCAOB quality control standards, specifically in the areas of engagement performance and monitoring. The Order notes that KPMG Brazil served as principal auditor for between 10 and 14 issuer clients annually during the relevant period, and that KPMG Assurance Services Ltda., an unregistered São Paulo-based affiliate, performed audit procedures in connection with numerous issuer audits conducted by KPMG Brazil. The Order’s summary indicates that the remedial requirements are set out in Section V, so compliance teams should review that section for any mandated enhancements to controls, communications, reporting, or quality-control remediation.

From a compliance perspective, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB treated the failures as repeated and systemic rather than isolated: audit committee communications, Form 2 reporting, and Form AP accuracy are all directly implicated, along with broader quality control obligations. Firms in a network structure, or those using affiliated non-registered entities in audit work, should treat this as a reminder that PCAOB obligations apply at the engagement and firm level, and that failures in reporting or communications can lead to censure, monetary penalties, and mandated remedial actions.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s February 25, 2025 Order (Release No. 105-2025-006) resolves disciplinary proceedings against Natalie Murphy, CPA, a former partner and engagement partner at Heaton & Company, PLLC (d/b/a Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah), a PCAOB-registered firm. The Board found that, in connection with the firm’s 2022 inspection, Murphy failed to cooperate by giving PCAOB inspectors misleading information about two issuer audits; failed to adequately document work paper additions and modifications made after the documentation completion date for those two audits; and failed to timely assemble and retain a complete, final audit file for a total of five issuer audits. The conduct was treated as meeting the Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 105(c)(5)(A) standard for sanctions based on intentional/knowing or repeated negligent violations.

As a result, PCAOB censured Murphy, barred her from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, imposed a $50,000 civil money penalty, and required her to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education before she can file any petition asking the Board to consent to her re-association with a registered firm. The bar is not permanent: she may petition for Board consent to associate again only after five years from the date of the Order, subject to Board approval. The 40 CPE hours are in addition to any continuing education already required for any professional license she holds.

The proceeding was brought under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and Murphy consented to the Order through a settlement offer under PCAOB Rule 5205 while neither admitting nor denying the findings, except as to PCAOB jurisdiction. The Order identifies Murphy as a Utah-licensed CPA (license no. 7388678-2601) and confirms that at all relevant times she was an “associated person of a registered public accounting firm.” The firm involved, Heaton & Co., was PCAOB-registered at the time and located in Farmington, Utah. The Order also references one of the affected issuers, Issuer A, a Wyoming-incorporated mobile application company with a principal executive office in New York, whose 2021 Form 10-K included an audit report dated March 31, 2022, issued by Heaton & Co.

rows.summary:
This PCAOB inspection report for Ernst & Young LLP, dated July 22, 2026, summarizes the Board’s 2025 inspection of the firm’s issuer-audit practice and its compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and other applicable regulatory/professional requirements. The PCAOB reviewed 64 issuer audits, generally involving fiscal years ended in 2024, and also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. The report is a public version; portions of the complete report are omitted to comply with Sections 104(g)(2) and 105(b)(5)(A) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002.

The most serious findings are in Part I.A: three of the 64 audits reviewed were included because the deficiencies were significant enough for the PCAOB to conclude that, at the time the audit reports were issued, EY had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinions on the issuer’s financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting. The identified Part I.A issues centered on EY’s testing of controls and/or substantive testing over revenue and related accounts, income taxes, and insurance-related assets and liabilities, including insurance reserves. The most common Part I.A problems were failures in testing the design or operating effectiveness of controls selected for testing.

Part I.B describes other PCAOB-standard or rule violations that did not rise to the level of unsupported audit opinions. These involved retention of audit documentation, audit committee communications, audit planning, management communications, and Form AP reporting. Part I.C addresses apparent independence-rule noncompliance, with the most common issues relating to financial relationships, employment relationships, non-audit services, and tax services provided to persons in financial reporting oversight roles. The report states that inclusion of a deficiency in Part I.A, I.B, or I.C does not automatically mean the financial statements were materially misstated, that a material weakness existed, that the Board concluded the firm lacked objectivity and impartiality throughout the engagement period, or that the firm has not already addressed the deficiency. The report is organized into sections covering inspection observations and quality-control observations, and includes EY’s response to the draft report in an appendix.

This PCAOB inspection report covers PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP’s 2025 inspection, issued June 12, 2026, and evaluates the firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and other applicable regulatory/professional requirements for issuer audits. The PCAOB reviewed 64 issuer audits, generally for fiscal years ending in 2024, and also assessed elements of PwC’s system of quality control. The report is organized into three types of findings: Part I.A deficiencies, which were serious enough that the PCAOB believes PwC had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its audit opinion(s) on certain financial statements and/or ICFR; Part I.B deficiencies, which are other PCAOB non-compliance issues not tied to sufficient audit evidence; and Part I.C deficiencies, which are apparent independence-rule violations.

The report states that 6 of the 64 audits reviewed were included in Part I.A. Those deficiencies were concentrated in testing controls and/or substantive testing of revenue and related accounts and long-lived assets. The most common Part I.A issues were failures in evaluating the appropriateness of the issuer’s accounting method or disclosure, testing the design or operating effectiveness of controls selected for testing, and testing estimates. The report also notes that inclusion of a Part I.A deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements were materially misstated or that an undisclosed material weakness in ICFR existed, but it does mean the PCAOB found the audit evidence insufficient for the opinion issued in those engagements.

For Part I.B, the report identifies deficiencies involving audit committee communications, management communications, critical audit matters, the firm’s audit report, and Form AP. These are compliance problems with PCAOB requirements other than the “unsupported opinion” issues discussed above. For Part I.C, the report identifies apparent independence-related noncompliance, with the most common issues involving audit committee pre-approval, unpaid fees, financial relationships, and non-audit services. The report emphasizes that a Part I.C finding does not necessarily mean the Board concluded the firm was not objective and impartial throughout the audit and engagement period.

No specific remediation deadline or effective-date change is announced in the excerpted text, but the report is a public inspection report and serves as a compliance signal for issuers, audit committees, and the firm that these categories of deficiencies were found in the 2025 cycle. The document also indicates there is a Part II section on quality control observations and an appendix containing the firm’s response to the draft report, which may contain further firm-level remediation or explanations beyond the executive summary.

Our inspection was conducted in cooperation with the South African Independent Regulatory Board for Auditors. We selected for review two audits of issuers. For each issuer audit selected, we reviewed a portion of the audit. We also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. 2025 Inspection Approach In selecting issuer audits for review, we use a risk-based method of selection. We make selections based on (1) our internal evaluation of audits we believe have a heightened risk of material misstatement, including those with challenging audit areas, and (2) other risk-based characteristics, including issuer and firm considerations. In certain situations, we may select all of the firm’s issuer audits for review. When we review an audit, we do not review every aspect of the audit. Rather, we generally focus our attention on audit areas we believe to be of greater complexity, areas of greater significance or with a heightened risk of material misstatement to the issuer’s financial statements, and areas of recurring deficiencies. We may also select some audit areas for review in a manner designed to incorporate unpredictability. Our selection of audits for review does not necessarily constitute a representative sample of the firm’s total population of issuer audits. Additionally, our inspection findings are specific to the particular portions of the issuer audits reviewed. They are not an assessment of all of the firm’s audit work or of all of the audit procedures performed for the audits reviewed. View the details on thescope of our inspections and our inspections procedures. rows.summary:
This is a public PCAOB inspection report for Ernst & Young Limited Corp. (headquartered in Panama City, Panama) covering the 2025 inspection, issued June 11, 2026, and it addresses the firm’s compliance with PCAOB rules, laws, and professional standards applicable to issuer audits. The PCAOB selected three issuer audits with fiscal years ending in 2024 for review, and the report emphasizes that the inspection was risk-based and only covered portions of those audits, so the findings are limited to the specific areas reviewed and are not a full evaluation of all of the firm’s audit work or all issuer audits. The report also notes that the PCAOB reviewed elements of the firm’s system of quality control, meaning the inspection was not limited to individual engagement workpapers but also considered firm-level controls.

From the summary table, the firm had one issuer audit client where it acted as lead/principal auditor and six additional issuer audits where it was not the lead/principal auditor; it reported one engagement partner on issuer audit work in 2025, compared with seven in 2022. The PCAOB reviewed a total of two audits in 2025, the same number as in 2022, and both were integrated audits of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). Unlike the prior inspection year, when one of three reviewed audits had Part I.A deficiencies, the 2025 inspection found no Part I.A deficiencies in any of the reviewed audits, resulting in a 0% deficiency rate versus 33% in 2022.

For compliance purposes, the important point is that the report does not announce a new rule, rate, or filing deadline; rather, it documents the outcome of an oversight inspection and signals whether the firm’s issuer audit work and quality-control environment met PCAOB expectations in the reviewed areas. Because the PCAOB inspected only selected portions of three 2024 fiscal-year issuer audits, the absence of Part I.A deficiencies should not be read as a blanket clean bill of health for all engagements or all firm processes. The report also includes sections on other potential non-compliance, independence, and quality control observations, but the excerpt provided does not contain the substance of any specific deficiencies or remedial requirements beyond the inspection methodology and the comparative data shown.

This PCAOB inspection report covers KPMG AG, headquartered in Zurich, Switzerland, for the 2024 inspection cycle, with the public report issued on September 25, 2025. The PCAOB, working with the Swiss Federal Audit Oversight Authority, reviewed portions of three issuer audits for fiscal years ending in 2023 and also evaluated selected elements of the firm’s quality control system. The report notes that KPMG AG had 4 issuer audit clients where it was the principal auditor, 11 issuer audits where it was not the principal auditor, and 12 engagement partners on issuer audit work; of the 3 audits reviewed, 2 were principal-auditor engagements and 1 was an integrated audit of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). All 3 reviewed audits had Part I.A deficiencies, so 100% of the inspected audits contained deficiencies in the reviewed areas, although the PCAOB emphasizes that these findings relate only to the portions reviewed and do not necessarily mean the firm failed to remediate the issues after identification.

The inspection methodology is important for compliance purposes because the PCAOB states it uses a risk-based selection process and does not review every aspect of each audit. It focuses on higher-risk, more complex, more significant, or recurring deficiency areas, and may also include some unpredictably selected areas; therefore, the findings are not a representative sample of all KPMG AG issuer audits. The report also cautions that inspection results are not necessarily comparable across years or firms because the mix of audits, audit areas, standards, and other factors may change over time.

The key compliance takeaway is that the PCAOB identified audit deficiencies and also reviewed the firm’s compliance with PCAOB rules, standards, and independence requirements, as well as quality control elements. The public excerpt shown here does not include the specific factual deficiency narratives, independence findings, or quality-control criticisms, but the table of contents shows that the full report contains separate sections for “Audits with Unsupported Opinions,” “Other Instances of Non-Compliance with PCAOB Standards or Rules,” “Independence,” and “Observations Related to Quality Control.” For a compliance team, this means the report is not just an audit-quality review; it is also an examination of whether the firm’s practices met PCAOB standards and independence obligations in the inspected engagements and whether any systemic quality-control weaknesses were observed.

The report also notes that the public version omits portions of the complete report under Sections 104(g)(2) and 105(b)(5)(A) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002. Because the excerpt does not disclose any remediation deadlines, monetary penalties, or explicit new regulatory deadlines, the immediate actionable requirement is to review the full PCAOB report sections for the specific deficiencies, any independence issues, and any quality-control recommendations or criticisms that may require corrective action by the firm.

rows.title: Mercurius & Associates LLP (India)
rows.summary:

The Board reviewed three issuer audits for fiscal years ended 2023 and also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control; the inspection used a risk-based selection process, focused only on selected audit areas rather than every aspect of each engagement, and the PCAOB expressly cautions that the findings are not a representative sample of the firm’s entire issuer-audit population. The report also notes that inspection findings relate only to the specific audit portions reviewed and do not necessarily indicate that the firm failed to take remedial action after an issue was identified.

The quantitative data in the report show that Mercurius had 8 issuer audit clients in 2025 where it was the lead auditor, up from 5 in 2022, and 1 total engagement partner on issuer audit work in both years. The PCAOB reviewed 3 audits in 2025, all of which were lead-auditor engagements, compared with 2 in 2022; none were integrated audits of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting. One of the three 2025 audits — 33% of the audits reviewed — contained a Part I.A deficiency, whereas there were none in 2022.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the PCAOB identified at least one audit with an unsupported opinion in the portion reviewed, meaning the firm’s procedures in that engagement were insufficient under PCAOB standards for the area reviewed. The report also contains separate sections for other non-compliance with PCAOB standards or rules, independence matters, and quality-control observations, indicating that the inspection was not limited solely to one audit finding and that the firm’s overall control environment was also under review. Because this is a PCAOB inspection report under PCAOB Release No. 104-2025-151 dated September 25, 2025, the relevant compliance takeaway is that the firm should assess whether the identified deficiency was remediated through additional audit procedures or other corrective actions, and whether any broader audit methodology, supervision, documentation, independence, or quality-control changes are needed to prevent recurrence in future issuer engagements.

The inspection also covered elements of the firm’s system of quality control, although the excerpt provided does not include the specific quality control observations themselves. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that Haskell & White was subject to a targeted PCAOB review of issuer audit work with material deficiencies identified in all reviewed audits, and the report should be read as signaling heightened inspection risk in the areas the PCAOB chose to test rather than as a complete evaluation of all the firm’s audit engagements.

rows.title: Wei, Wei & Co., LLP
rows.summary:

The PCAOB reviewed two issuer audits—one for a fiscal year ending in 2024 and one for a fiscal year ending in 2023—and evaluated selected portions of those audits as well as elements of the firm’s system of quality control. The most material compliance point is that both audited engagements reviewed had Part I.A deficiencies, meaning the PCAOB identified audits with unsupported opinions in the inspected areas. In the overview table, the report states that the firm had two issuer audits reviewed, both of which were principal-auditor engagements, and both had Part I.A deficiencies, for a deficiency rate of 100%. The report also notes that a deficiency finding does not necessarily mean the firm failed to remediate it, because firms may have already taken corrective actions after the deficiency was identified, such as performing additional audit procedures, notifying management that the financial statements or ICFR report may need changes, or taking steps to prevent reliance on prior audit reports.

The historical data show that the firm’s inspection profile changed significantly from the prior inspection year: the number of issuer audit clients for which the firm served as principal auditor increased from 12 in 2022 to 21 in 2024, while the number of engagement partners on issuer audit work decreased from 6 to 3. The report also cautions that inspection results are not necessarily comparable across years or firms because the PCAOB’s selection of audits and focus areas changes over time and may vary based on risk, firm characteristics, and evolving standards. Compliance teams should therefore treat this report as evidence of recurring inspection risk in the firm’s issuer audit practice, especially given that every inspected audit had a Part I.A deficiency.

The document is not itself a rulemaking or a new deadline-driven regulatory requirement, but it is a public enforcement-and-oversight signal that the firm’s inspected audit work did not fully satisfy PCAOB standards in the reviewed areas. For compliance purposes, the key operational takeaway is that any issuer relying on this auditor should understand that the PCAOB identified unsupported audit opinions in the sampled engagements and that the firm may need enhanced quality-control remediation to address the issues.

rows.title: KPMG Cardenas Dosal, S.C. (Mexico)
rows.summary:
PCAOB’s 2024 inspection of **KPMG Cardenas Dosal, S.C. (Mexico City, Mexico)**, released publicly on **September 25, 2025** as PCAOB Release No. **104-2025-149**, assessed the firm’s compliance with applicable PCAOB laws, rules, and professional standards for public company audits and reviewed elements of its quality control system. The inspection was **risk-based** and did **not** review all of the firm’s work; it focused on selected audit areas judged to present higher risk, greater complexity, significant judgment, or recurring deficiencies, so the findings apply only to the specific audit portions reviewed and are not a blanket assessment of all engagements. For 2024, PCAOB selected **three issuer audits** for review, all for issuers with **fiscal years ending in 2023**, and all three were **integrated audits of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR)**; the firm had **7** issuer audit clients where it was principal auditor and **27** issuer audits where it was not principal auditor, compared with **4** and **37**, respectively, in the prior inspection year.  

The inspection found that **2 of the 3 audits reviewed (67%)** had **Part I.A deficiencies**, and the report states these deficiencies involved audits with **unsupported opinions**—meaning the PCAOB identified cases where the audit evidence or procedures reviewed were insufficient to support the firm’s issued opinion for the audited portions. The table of historical data shows this **67% deficiency rate** was the same in the prior inspection year, indicating a recurring level of concern rather than an isolated result. The report’s structure indicates additional sections covering **other non-compliance with PCAOB standards or rules**, **independence**, and **quality control observations**, so compliance teams should review those sections for any firm-wide or control-system issues beyond the specific deficient engagements.  

A practical compliance takeaway is that PCAOB’s findings do **not** impose a new standalone deadline or remediation date in the excerpt provided, but they do signal that the firm’s audit execution and/or quality control in selected high-risk areas was not sufficient to support all opinions issued in the reviewed work. Because the PCAOB explicitly notes that its selections are not representative of all issuer audits and that inspections can vary by year, the right way to use this report is as a targeted indicator of areas where the firm may need to strengthen audit documentation, supervision, and evidence-gathering processes, especially for **integrated audits involving ICFR** and other higher-risk engagements.

The report shows that M&K CPAS had **70 total issuer audit clients** in 2024, compared with **68** in 2022, and the firm had **1 engagement partner** on issuer audit work in 2024 versus **3** in 2022. The PCAOB notes that a deficiency listed in Part I.A does **not automatically mean the firm failed to remediate** it; in many cases firms take post-identified remedial actions such as performing additional procedures, informing management that financial statements or ICFR reporting need changes, or taking steps to prevent reliance on a prior audit report.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB found audit quality issues serious enough to support **Part I.A unsupported-opinion findings** in most of the inspected engagements, which signals heightened regulatory risk around the firm’s audit execution, documentation, and conclusion support on selected high-risk areas. The report also includes sections on **other non-compliance with PCAOB standards or rules**, **independence**, and **quality control observations**, which are relevant because they may indicate broader process or governance weaknesses beyond the individual engagement deficiencies. However, the document excerpt provided does not include the specific details of those observations, so the actionable compliance point from the visible text is that the firm remained under PCAOB scrutiny for audit quality and quality-control effectiveness as of the 2024 inspection cycle.
